<margin>6.</margin>
Moreover, from this point, just like the Iliac vein which is joined to it, it tends toward the foramen of the pubic bone. Before it passes through this, it receives a branch originating from the outer Iliac ramus, and thus it exits the foramen. Once it has departed from there, it is expended into the muscles, partly those by which the foramen is occluded, and partly those which arise from the pubic bone, just as the internal Iliac Vein is expended. Finally, where it terminates at about the middle of the length of the femur, its end joins and unites with the extreme branches of the internal crural muscle, concerning which I shall speak in the following chapter.

<margin>
1. Iliac.
2. Epigastrica.
3. Pudenda.
</margin>
The larger, or outer, [artery] similarly produces two branches, of which the first is called the External Epigastric, and it arises from the outer part a little before it perforates the peritoneum. It is reflected upward and ascends along the inner side of the rectus muscle until, around the navel, it is joined by anastomosis with the descending mammary artery. The other, the Pudenda, which is the interior, small branch, is not divided into as many branches as the vein. Immediately after it departs from the peritoneum, it arises and is carried transversely along the junction of the pubic bones to the pudendal parts, where it is exhausted into the skin of the penis. The remainder of this trunk passes into the thigh, of which we shall now speak.

<- CHAPTER V ->

<- The branches of the outer Iliac ramus propagated through the thigh. ->

<margin>
Truncus cruralis, & eius antequã diuidatur propagines.
1.
2.
3.
4.
</margin>
After the outer trunk has led out the branches already described, it departs from the peritoneum and is carried to the groin into the thigh, through the same path as the crural vein, to which it is positioned underneath and is joined as a companion everywhere, and thus it constitutes the Crural trunk (as we always call it). Immediately as soon as it has passed the peritoneum, it leads out a branch from the outer part, which they call the outer crural muscle, which, carried downward, is propagated into the muscles embracing the bone of the thigh on the anterior side. In the region opposite this, sometimes, and more often a little below, but in the internal position nevertheless, another is led out, called the internal crural muscle, which is distributed through the third muscle that flexes the femur, or the <term>Tricipitem</term> <gloss>three-headed muscle/triceps</gloss>, and through those that occupy the inner region of the thigh, as far as the knee in several branches, the ends of which are joined with the ends of the internal Iliac [artery], which we said descends to the thigh through the foramen of the pubic bones. Having led out these branches, the Crural trunk descends from the groin with the crural vein and is reflected next to the femur so that, when it arrives at the popliteal fossa, it rests between the two posterior heads of the femur. For clever Nature always observes this: that she leads vessels around that part of a joint where there is flexion, so that if they went through the part where the joint is extended, they would be compressed. In the middle of this path, as it descends through the thigh, it leads out a branch which, divided into several twigs, runs out through the muscles situated in the posterior region of the thigh together with the popliteal vein, and finally, descending through the popliteal fossa (whence it is called the Popliteal), it is divided into a frequent branch in the calf. While resting in the popliteal fossa, on both sides it leads out a branch to the sides of the knee joint, which is immediately buried deeper, which are exhausted partly in the joint itself, and partly in the two <term>Gasterocnemos</term> <gloss>calf muscles/gastrocnemius</gloss> muscles that constitute the calf, whence they are also called the Sural arteries.

<keywords>Iliac artery, Epigastric artery, Pudenda artery, Crural trunk, Femur, Popliteal artery, Anatomy, Spigelius</keywords>
</translation>

<header>OF THE HUMAN FABRIC BY ADRIAAN VAN DE SPIEGEL</header>

After the Crural trunk rests in the popliteal fossa, it brings forth a branch from the outer side, which descends next to the fibula and is concealed between the muscle that abducts the foot and the muscles that flex the second part of the tarsus, and it is distributed into the rest of those occupying the anterior part of the tibia, until they become fleshy and begin to be twisted around the outer ankle. A little below this mentioned one, another is led out from the posterior seat of the trunk, which descends as far as the junction of the tendons of the gastrocnemii. Then another proceeds from the same posterior seat of the trunk, but below the second, which, descending and passing the transverse ligament, runs out through the dorsum of the foot, diffused into the muscles that abduct the toes. The remainder of the trunk is carried downward through the posterior parts of the tibia, and around the inner ankle it offers a fork to the foot, which approaches the big toe and crawls over the dorsum of the foot. The trunk itself, hiding between the tendons of the muscles of the toes of the foot, is divided into two branches, of which the inner one provides two to the big toe, two to the index, and one to the middle toe; the outer one, however, bestows two to the little toe and two to the toes next to it, on the lower side. But although the progress of the arteries happens for the most part such as we have described, nevertheless what we said above regarding the veins—that their distribution varies greatly not only according to the diversity of individuals, but also of the sides in the same human being—that must also be held for the arteries, which behave in one way in some humans and in another way in others.

<- CHAPTER VI ->

<- It contains the history of the arterial vein and the venal artery. ->

<margin>
Vena arterialis.
Arteria venalis.
Ortus.
Infertio.
Distribuitio.
</margin>
So that this discussion of the veins and arteries may be perfect and absolute in all its parts, we have chosen to append, in place of a conclusion, the history of the third vein and the second artery. The vein is called <term>arterial</term> <gloss>arterial vein</gloss>, and indeed a vein by function, because the Ancients believed it carried blood from the right ventricle of the heart; but arterial from its tunic, which is similar to the membrane of arteries, since it is not simple, like that of the veins, but double. The artery, on the contrary, is called <term>venal</term> <gloss>venal artery</gloss>, and indeed an artery, because the Ancients established that it carried air attracted through the lungs; but venal because its substance corresponds to the body of the veins, since its tunic is simple and not very thick. We have deferred the discussion of both to this place specifically, so that we might treat both together, since they are both born from the same organ and are inserted into the same, and furthermore they enjoy the same distribution. For they arise from the Heart, the vein indeed from the higher seat of the right ventricle, but the artery from the left. Both are implanted into and expended in the substance of the Lungs, and the vein is extended through the right side of the <term>aspera arteria</term> <gloss>trachea/windpipe</gloss>, but the artery through the left. Soon each is cut into two branches, of which one goes to the right and the other to the left part of the lungs, each being cut again in two, and these into other branches, until they are dispersed into the most minute twigs. <translation page="21">
In the *Manuscript on Theological Ecclesiastical History* 8, he himself cites Theophilus Raynaud on good and bad books, page 119; Possevin in the *Apparatus*, Volume II, page 389; and from our own, Varenius in *Rationarium of the First Century*, page 150. Whatever objection Jacobus Faber Stapulensis raises, who in his *Commentary on the Epistles of Paul* asserts that Seneca lowered himself to such a simplicity of style so that he would not be recognized by his own people and incur their hatred, see the Schediasma of the most famous M. Goetzius on the spurious and lost writings of Paul. Other things are more certain, which are rightly attributed to the philosopher Lucius Annaeus Seneca, and which we know were recently ascribed to the same man by the most famous Johannes Albertus Fabricius in his *Bibliotheca Latina*; specifically: *Three Books on Anger*, *Book of Consolation to his mother Helvia*, *Book of Consolation to Polybius*, *Book of Consolation to Marcia*, *On the Tranquility of the Mind*, *On the Constancy of the Wise*, *On Clemency*, *On the Shortness of Life*, *On the Happy Life*, *On the Leisure or Retirement of the Wise*, *Seven Books on Benefits*, *124 Letters to Lucilius*, *Seven Books of Natural Questions*, and the most witty satire on Claudius, the <term>apocolocyntosis</term> <gloss>pumpkinification</gloss>, regarding which I would have you compare what is found, beyond the observations of Fabricius, in the *Introduction to Ecclesiastical History* of B. Sagittarius, a historian of Jena, on page 602. However, the *Book on the Cardinal Virtues*, *On Morals*, *On Poverty*, *Eight Letters to Paul*, and others are held to be supposititious. I cannot restrain myself from suggesting a few things regarding a most vexing question: do the Tragedies also acknowledge the philosopher Seneca as their author? For it is known how commonly three men are reckoned as illustrious under the name of Seneca: M. Annaeus the Rhetorician, L. Annaeus Seneca the Philosopher, and finally Seneca the Tragedian. One may read about this in Baillet’s *Judgments of the Learned Concerning the Principal Works of Authors*, Volume IV, Part II, page 363, and the authors cited at the end. Indeed, learned men hold diverse opinions regarding the Tragedies. They bring forth the judgments already mentioned that they are not by a single author; the most famous Fabricius also asserts in the cited place, while claiming *Hercules Furens* for M. Annaeus Seneca the father, *Hippolytus* for Seneca the philosopher, and thus vindicating the rest for various authors. Olaus Borrichius, a noble name among the Danes, says the following in his dissertation on poets: *Although it is still contested under a judge whether that illustrious work of the Tragedies, which bears his name, should be attributed to him (Seneca the Philosopher), yet most of the learned, if not all, incline to the view that at least most of these same Tragedies are justly attributed to him.* Borrichius writes that it cannot be denied that L. Annaeus Seneca the Philosopher was skilled in the poetic art, intending to prove his opinion from the epitaph which Seneca the Philosopher is said to have written for himself, and which is annotated by Lilius in Book VII of his *Poetic History*, Volume II of his works, folio 317.

> ->*Yet, greedy one, receive the body for customary stones,*<-

unless perhaps <unclear>inire</unclear> Mr. Cellarius, Professor at Halle, has some validity when he adds these words in the continuation of the Faber-Buchner Lexicon: *I, for my part, can never be brought to believe that Seneca wrote these verses. Let those, therefore, judge who have made a deeper investigation.* For our business at present is not with the writer of the Tragedies—if there was one, whether he was the philosopher's son, or brother, or nephew by a brother—but with the philosopher himself, whose name, lineage, and books we have enumerated; nor shall we be lazy in noting what seems to the learned to be his style of speaking.

How Aulus Gellius—who in Book 12, number 2, does not merely cite judgments about Seneca, but also attacks his style, claiming his common and proper erudition seemed to be whipped by Muretus and others—is well known. He judges him with the reason of a more elegant man in these words:

> A more sublime diction
> which descends more deeply into the breast; speech so concise
> and most pugnacious in the weight of arguments, with great force
> everything conforms to the brow of all, and so diverse
> it cannot seem a wonder.

When Quintilian in Book 10 <note>Quintilian's *Institutio Oratoria* discusses Seneca's style</note> says he breaks himself by weight, these things without doubt are from the invidious, as Rabner conjectures, because the rhetorician preferred a Laconian brevity of words. Maresius, in Book I, Epistle 1, is less than friendly, because he wrote letters to a friend about philosophy. <note>Regarding Seneca's style</note> in the *Historian* <note>referring to a contemporary scholar's work</note>, Book I, Chapter 23, [it says] quite well:

> Nothing is more [of his writing]
> and sententious, which I advise to be turned and returned
> ...than a farrago of various sentiments in unity.

**Erasmus** criticizes base words in Seneca, but he is defended by <unclear>Budaeus</unclear>. Everyone admits that Seneca gave excellent precepts. He breathes nothing else, nor does he differ more regarding virtue than he asserts and inculcates. <note>The text mentions Wilkins's introduction to Cicero's *De Officiis*.</note> Concerning L. Annaeus Seneca, Doctor Kirchmayer treated this at Wittenberg in 1690; yet [he did not] foster the opinions of the <unclear>philosophy</unclear> which some reject. For the 70th Epistle is very insane: *Let him go out, from where he took the impetus, whether [by] iron or some potion occupying the veins, let him proceed, and [break] the bonds of slavery.* He praises the young man who, because of a troublesome illness, [practiced] starvation. The lack of space on the paper forbids discussing these individual things more prolixly, or recounting the instruction by which he taught Nero, and more; especially where [they spend the holidays] in the book of <note>Lord Ziegler</note> cited. Also excellent are the Seven Books *On Benefits*, from which one may extract the most beautiful sentiments and examine them according to logical rules. [A passage] taken from the same is to be read in Book II, Chapter 9: *Some benefits are to be given openly, some secretly, etc.*, which four students of the Gymnasium have taken upon themselves to treat, so that the speech [may be] a matter [of study]. For we thought that in this way both the solemn custom could be satisfied and the benefits [of our] <term>TRITIORUM</term> <gloss>presumably referring to the patrons or contributors</gloss> could be rightly acknowledged with a grateful mind. We ask most honorably, if it is convenient for you and your affairs, [that you attend] for the honor of GOD and the Patrons of the School, <term>panegyrikos</term> <gloss>in a laudatory manner</gloss>, at Schleusingen... respectfully, dutifully, and friendly. From the Gymnasium of Schleusingen... Lucius Annaeus Seneca the Philosopher, in the year of the Christian era 1660...

->List of Those Attending<-

**Friedericus Abraham Müller** will discourse on benefits, in a Greek oration.

**Joh. Christoph. Steltzner** [on] benefits to be given openly.

**Joh. Nicol. Jungglaß** will demonstrate a grateful mind for benefits given, and the same toward the MOST SERENE LORDS, in the Hebrew idiom.

**Joh. Fridericus Kern** [on] the prologue and epilogue.

->From the GOEBELIAN Press<-

it will be permitted for everyone to assert: There is no doubt today about the <term>glandulae conglomeratae</term> <gloss>conglomerate glands</gloss>, since their lymph, or secreted juice, is presented to the eyes, just as it is sufficiently manifest concerning the salivary glands, the pancreas, and others. §. 58. Concerning certain others, the matter still seems obscure, but from the explanation of each one it will become clear that we have spoken most truly, and that they all secrete a certain liquid; whether you call it lymph or simply a liquid, it is the same to me, for different glands secrete different humors.

§. 59. For while we see the glands under the armpits and groins secrete a foul-smelling humor, the prostate an oily one, the tunic of the palate a viscous one, those in the ears a bilious one, and the tonsils a phlegmatic one, it will be permitted to argue the same for all others.

§. 60. For it seems that more trust should be placed in experiments and autopsy than in arguments, although reasons are not lacking to confirm this opinion.

§. 61. Indeed, while we observe lymphatic vessels emerging from all glands, we firmly conclude that lymph and other humors are secreted from the blood within them. For nothing is secreted from another substance to which it is intimately admixed, except by some agency and secretory principle. It is also convenient to argue from the conglomerate glands to the rest, since they consist of <term>conglobatae</term> <gloss>conglobate/simple glands</gloss>. Therefore, what they do when they are united and many are connected to one another, the solitary ones will also perform, by the example of the testicles and the kidneys.

§. 62. The only doubt concerns the gland of the mesentery, called the pancreas by <term>Wharton</term>, into which the lacteal and lymphatic vessels are inserted, as is commonly believed, and whether it primarily secretes anything
</translation>

<translation page="22">
<header>❁ (20) ❁</header>

is rightly questioned; but in truth it also secretes something, and I judge perhaps not ineptly that a peculiar ferment to be mixed with the chyle is secreted in it. This is certain, that neither lacteal nor lymphatic vessels are inserted into the very substance of this gland; rather, they deposit chyle and lymph into a certain cistern or larger duct behind the gland, whence an entirely different use will have to be assigned to this gland, namely the same as in others, which is to secrete something.

§. 63. And while I thus establish that the proper action of the glands is to secrete humors from the blood, I also assert at the same time that they consequently purify the blood mass. For some glands secrete useful humors, others even useless ones; indeed, while even the useful ones are being secreted, the blood mass is purified. <translation page="22">is God's representative, and the assistance he provides is piously believed to be brought about by God Himself, mediately through him. He who wills that all things be done in order and decently, and to whom we exhibit the honor due to the magistrate he has given us, from him in turn we expect the duties and protections appropriate to a magistrate, following the example of Paul. Regarding cruelty, the Roman Emperor was a lion to him, 2 Timothy 4:17, and yet in danger of his life and in a political case, he correctly appealed to him as an ordinary magistrate, Acts 25:10 and 11.

I also add this: where a divine calling—which is the permission of the supreme magistrate—has joined us with people of a different religion in the same province or city, there we can remain with a clear conscience, provided it is permitted to us to practice our religion rightly and safely. For then the pious are comforted by that promise of God, by which he pledges that he will be present with everyone in their calling and their paths, Psalm 91:11, 15. This can be seen in Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob descending into Egypt at his command, and in Daniel and his companions living as captives in Babylon. And to this I draw what certain legal scholars and politicians urge so strongly: that different religions can be tolerated. I concede this, but only by us who are subjects, when the superior magistrate has granted it. But whether a less Orthodox religion should be admitted anew in a free Republic, I have seen no one who could prove it from Scripture.

Finally (to omit other minor objections which can easily be dissolved from what has already been said), the examples of Abraham (Genesis 14 and 21) and Isaac (Genesis 26) making treaties differ immensely from the present question. First, there are not lacking some (among whom is also our Luther) who deny that they formed treaties with the ungodly, the profane, or those alien to the religion of the Patriarchs, which they attempt to prove by several arguments taken from the text. I assert that this can be proven quite clearly from the cited passages: these were not ecclesiastical or mixed treaties, but only political ones, concerning civil matters—and this, not so much by defending as by not offending. Moreover, both were contracted by the Patriarchs when they themselves were not in great need of their help; indeed, when Abimelech requested this from them. What, therefore, is this consequence? The Patriarchs could contract with their pious neighbors (as Luther establishes in his Commentaries on Genesis) concerning civil matters and non-offense, invited and so forth</translation>

<translation page="23">treaties. Therefore, we can also enter into a treaty of defense with people who are either entirely ungodly or blasphemous toward God and His word, even granting them free exercise of their own religion, inviting them, and enticing them in every way. For who does not see from what preceded that the most diverse types of treaties are being confused? That there are different principles, objects, ends, and circumstances here, and therefore the action cannot be the same?

But as far as the Calvinists are concerned (for I believe that is the only thing remaining in this Question), whether they dissent from us in certain principal articles of Faith—and those fundamental ones, namely, most especially in the article concerning the person of CHRIST, Predestination, Baptism, and the Lord’s Supper, etc.—I would not believe anyone to be such a stranger to Theology who would either ignore this or at least doubt it, since it is sufficiently explained in all Catechetical and Symbolic books, as well as in Compendiums of Theology in antithesis, and is otherwise established by many polemical works published by both sides for about eighty years. For this reason, I forgo a longer commentary on a clear matter.

And I proceed to purely political treaties, which I affirm to be lawful even with the profane and <term>heterodoxis</term> <gloss>those of another opinion</gloss>, for the following reasons: I. Because they are just and good when viewed from their principle, object, end, and circumstances. II. Because they are not only permitted by God but also commanded. Psalm 34:13; Romans 12:18; Hebrews 12:14. In this way, all the pious are commanded to intercede with God for kings and all those set in authority, so that they may lead a tranquil and quiet life with all piety and reverence (1 Timothy 2:1-2), and Jeremiah urges the captives in Babylon by letter in this way (chapter 29:7): "Seek the prosperity of that city to which I have carried you away, says Jehovah, and pray for it to Jehovah; for in its prosperity, there will be prosperity for you." III. Because there are proven examples of the pious: Jacob with Laban (Genesis 31:44), David (2 Samuel 5:11), and Solomon (1 Kings 5:12) contracting a political treaty with Hiram, king of Tyre. IV. Because God severely punished those who violated them: Saul and his descendants (2 Samuel 21:1-2, etc.; compare Joshua 9 and 1 Samuel 28:3, 9). Ladislaus, King of Hungary, breaking a political treaty entered into with Amurath at the instigation of the Roman Pontiff, see Book 3 of Carion’s Chronicle. And it is worthy of note what the annals of the Silesians report: that Amurath, already almost thrown into flight with his men, after he had looked upon the image of the crucified Christ raised up by the Christians</translation>

Since all had equally and by common consent condemned that booklet of Johannes Reuchlin—as being more injurious to the Church of God than is credible, irreverent toward holy doctors, suitable for his own goods, apt for the wicked, appropriate for the worst, scandalous to Christians, and finally, too indulgent toward Jewish perfidy and savoring too much of depraved heresy—and since they had judged by their open letters, with their seals attached, that it should be heartily condemned and immediately removed from the use of Christians like deadly poison and a dangerous, proliferating pestilence, only then did the Inquisitor, fortified by the determination, sentence, and authority of such great and learned men, proceed with the matter itself in the diocese and city of Mainz, with the consent and exhortation of the Archbishop, inasmuch as those nefarious booklets had first been exposed and publicly sold there to everyone. Therefore, the Inquisitor himself, a venerable doctor, received from the most reverend lord Archbishop of Mainz, in the city of Mainz, four judges as his colleagues. To these, the most reverend lord Archbishop of Cologne—a man worthy of all praise and honor—had, with the consent of the prince of Mainz, added a most distinguished and in all respects admirable official of his own court: men who were truly most learned, most upright, and excellent, and who by no merit of any mortal, even the most wicked, should be held as suspect in the least. One of these was the suffragan bishop of Mainz; the second was the magnificent rector of that illustrious university; three were doctors of sacred theology; and two others were doctors of canon law. With these excellent and venerable men, the Inquisitor instituted a process of equity and justice there. And later, after citations—not indeed to any effect regarding the person of anyone, but generally and specifically against all who thought it their interest to defend the heretical obscenities of the said booklet—had been legally executed and judicially (as we say in the vernacular) reproduced, the process, happily and holily begun, continued for the sake of his office of faith. But truly, when at the time of the citation, that doctor—more concerned for his own honor than for the integrity of the Catholic faith and for himself avoiding an intolerable scandal—recused the Inquisitor himself (who in no way rejoiced in this) as suspect through his procurator, using certain frivolous and (if I may say so) ineffective motives, the Inquisitor, being sufficiently animated by the cause of justice and distrusting none of the judges, and in order to avoid the unpleasant plurality of recusations, arbitrations, and appeals—which they call frivolous and clearly weak exceptions—wisely exonerated himself from the office of hearing, judging, and defining, and rejected the entire examination of the cause to his colleagues, acting only in the office of accuser. Although the matter stood thus, the procurator of the opposing party nonetheless, in that very process, without a hearing, interposed a certain childish and clearly inept appeal to the holy Apostolic See from the Inquisitor, as a judge already recused. And since now—to say much in few words—all terms of law had been duly and legally observed, with the counsel and assistance (as it is said) of those learned in the law, and with mature deliberation preceding the pronouncement of the sentence in this cause, it was suspended for an interval of fifteen days at the request of the lords of the major church.</translation>

<translation page="9">of Mainz, the aforementioned judges, with the consent of the Inquisitor, were graciously suspended. And furthermore, second, when these fifteen days had now elapsed and the above-mentioned judges, being fully resolved and constant in the cause of the faith, were sitting to pronounce judgment before the tribunal, with the parties legally cited and called, certain letters of the most reverend lord of Mainz supervened, obtained in such a manner—alas—by a less than good man in favor of heretical depravity, by which he had commanded his commissaries or mandatories that, unless the Inquisitor suspended the cause for one entire month beyond the aforementioned fifteen days graciously granted, the Archbishop himself would entirely revoke the commission given to the judges. And thereafter, if anything were attempted by them within the aforementioned time, he wished it to be entirely void. Thus, everything was overturned and clearly (as you have heard) changed before the expectation. Although the lord of Mainz himself, now deceased and subject to the just Judge, had often at various times given faithful obedience to the Inquisitor in this, and even so that the lord Inquisitor, seeking the salvation of the Church (which, in the strict judgment of God, will be clear to everyone), was not a little encouraged by his help and counsel, and trusting in his most pious words, was expecting a most happy end, desired by all good men. But otherwise, as we have heard, because these things were performed sinisterly by some, good men could easily understand that for the reverend Inquisitor, in the most pious cause of our Lord Jesus Christ and the most holy faith, justice itself was not only manifestly denied, but violently snatched from his hands. Especially since the aforementioned Archbishop of Mainz neither advocated the cause to himself, nor made it ratified or certain in what manner or at what time it was finally to be absolved, nor, after the month had now elapsed, did he propose to the reverend Inquisitor any hope of the expedition of this cause—either short or of any kind—which is what ought to have been done. Wherefore, in the judgment of prudent and learned men, no hope of a good outcome seemed to be left there for the Inquisitor at the hands of the archbishop, but rather (a thing unworthy to be heard) the contempt, mockery, and vilification of the Inquisitor. For he did not take care to terminate the cause of Christ as he ought to have done by law, nor to transmit it duly instructed to the Apostolic See. It is not doubted that this was contrived or (as they say) practiced by the adversary, who was poorly conscious of his own case, lest by chance, if the Apostolic See were sought, it might recognize the depraved teachings of the <term>Ocularis speculi</term> <gloss>Ocular Mirror</gloss> and some intolerable errors (which, undoubtedly, would happen) and condemn them as soon as possible with a more severe censure. He knew truly that the above-written judges would undoubtedly pronounce sentence against his said scandalous and most pernicious booklets through our Inquisitor, especially if they had not been revoked by the Archbishop himself and from the office of equity. Hence it is truly clearer than light that the cause, as we have now heard, has been finished. However, two of those judges, in the name of and through the sacred commission of the entire theological faculty of Mainz, handed over the pre-noted booklets, legally requested, with a legitimate condemnation fortified by the seal of their faculty, stating with a sincere heart that they were most saddened and clearly groaning that in the causes of the Christian faith, things had been acted upon so lightly and captiously. These things having been so done, the adversary himself, for the rescission of the principal matter—that is, to impede the sentence itself in any way possible...</translation>

<summary>This text details the legal proceedings conducted by the Inquisitor against Johannes Reuchlin's "Ocular Mirror," describing how initial consensus among university scholars for the book's condemnation was thwarted by political interference from the Archbishop of Mainz.</summary>
<keywords>Johannes Reuchlin, Ocular Mirror, Inquisitor, Mainz, heresy, Catholic faith, legal process, ecclesiastical politics</keywords>

Otherwise, the story of Philander of Sittwaldt is known, which he mentions in his *Satirical Visions*.

*Leeches* are conveniently applied to those accustomed to the flow of hemorrhoids, if the malady has received its fuel from that source.

*Fontanels* <gloss>artificial ulcers used for drainage</gloss>, when properly induced, contribute to preservation.

*Frictions* are used for revulsion and discussion; *vesicants* <gloss>blistering agents</gloss> are sometimes admitted for the purpose of a series of evacuations; but *cauterization* and the excision of veins find almost no place in the modern age.

### II.

From the PHARMACEUTICAL store, a collection of various evacuant and altering medicines, both simple and compound, of the ancients and the moderns, is drawn. Since this is treated quite extensively by practitioners, and their almost countless volumes are filled with prescriptions and formulas, and one must not insist absolutely on such things in treatment, but must look above all to the circumstances and accidents that the present state of the arthritic patient demands: it has pleased me to relate only very few from that category of medicines pertaining to this matter.

Regarding *purgatives*, they cannot be safely used either in the beginning or in the augmentation of pains (unless they are very mild); since the paroxysm is exacerbated more by a strong agitation of the humors. They must therefore be taken before or after the invasion, with *lenients and preparations* <note>preparatory medicines</note> having been administered first.

Let such a lenient be prescribed:

| | | |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Take. | Leaves of Alexandrian senna, in sufficient quantity | 1 ounce |
| | Root of Indian rhubarb | 1/2 ounce |
| | Polypody <gloss>a type of fern</gloss> | 1/2 ounce |
| | Seeds of anise and fennel, of each | 2 drams |
| | Lesser raisins | 2 ounces |

Let them be boiled in a closed vessel with 2 pounds of spring water until a third part is consumed. Let them be taken in the morning hours</translation>

<translation page="21">3 drams; let the dose be repeated until the bowels are gently moved. More [preparations] can be composed, if necessity requires, from crystals of <note>The symbol for Tartar is used here.</note> *Mechoacan root, cassia, laxative syrups*, and many others.

*Aloetic* <gloss>preparations containing aloe</gloss> can be used in every case of gout <term>podagra</term> <gloss>gout of the foot</gloss> as a preservative, and if the bowels are constipated. Examples are the *aloëphanginae* <gloss>aloe-based</gloss> and *Frankfurt* pills.

*Lenient clysters* <gloss>enemas</gloss> are also conveniently admitted, the supply of which is well known.

For the *preparation* and incision of humors, it is customary to take *salts of germander, ground pine, volatile salt of amber, of juniper* or *resta bovis* <gloss>restharrow</gloss>, mixed with sugar, in a dose of 16 or 18 grains.

*Stronger purgatives* taken from the chests of chemists are *Antimony-based* preparations and *royal* <note>The symbol for 'regal' or 'royal' (often related to antimony or gold preparations) is used here.</note> ones, provided they are rightly prepared. The ancients, following the dogmatists, used *scammony, hedge hyssop, hellebore, turpeth*, etc. The *hermodactyl pills* <gloss>pills made from Colchicum tuber</gloss> are praised, which *Paracelsus* also approves. Yet milder ones are generally recommended. For example:

> Take <note>Recipe symbol (℞)</note> *magistery of jalap,*
> *crystals of* <note>The symbol for Tartar is used here.</note> *of each 9 grains.*
> *oil of anise & fennel, of each 2 drops.*
> *Mix, let it be a powder.*

*Sudorifics* <gloss>sweat-inducing agents</gloss> are considered very useful in this affliction, provided they are not too hot. Used here are *philosophical calcinated magistery of hartshorn, Bezoar tincture, diaphoretic mercury <term>hydrargyrum</term> <gloss>mercury/quicksilver</gloss>, extract of sarsaparilla root.* At one time, a decoction of china root and sarsaparilla was in great use among the Spanish. They should not, however, be given while the body is impure.

*Diuretics* are likewise beneficial. In this case, it is better to use spirit of juniper and rose hip <gloss>fruit of the wild rose</gloss> tempered with parsley water. Medicines prepared from turpentine promise the same. *Spirit of* <note>The symbols for Salt, Vitriol, and Tartar are used here, along with an alchemical sign for a preparation.</note> *impregnated with volatile salt of urine. Tincture of Tartar, etc.*

Regarding the salivary treatment <gloss>treatment by salivation</gloss> by *mercury*, it is left to each one to choose his own way.</translation>

<translation page="15">After a few days, the state of the body eluded the inexperienced, as it seemed to have changed for the better, having been freed in some part from the burden of the humors by mild, gentle medicines, and the fever—which had been accompanying the disease—had already diminished in its slow pace. But as a tree does not depart from its own roots, so the disease could not abandon the source that was rooted deeper. The rot, the fever, the sleeplessness, and other symptoms took on strength and grew more and more, and they began to threaten the danger of death more clearly, when Lord Dr. Nicolaus Hannekenius was also called in for consultation. Nature had by then already begun to expel the hostile humor through the bowels, as well as the putrid masses of blood, the unhappy offspring of a liver already rotting and consumed. Everything that such a great disease and such great symptoms required was attempted. But Nature did not cease from this work of excretion until the strength was completely cast down, the frame of the body was dissolved along with the parenchyma <note>the functional tissue</note> of the liver, and was liquefied; and thus a better, eternal origin of life received the morbid, fleeting life. So far, the words of the physician.

Thus, we have perceived the origin, progress, vigor, and deeds of this most distinguished man, delineated with a simple mind <note>a classical idiom, *rudi minerva*, meaning created without excessive artistic polish</note>, without the splendor of flowery words. I must now finally approach the sad epilogue of his life, alas! Concerning this, I must speak in very few words, since I have found no one who could teach me more about the manner of his blessed passing, about his final words, or what else usually happens at this turning point and boundary of life. Yet, since this most praised man never lived otherwise than piously and religiously before God, justly toward his neighbor, and temperately toward himself, we neither should nor can doubt that he died well and blessed. This blessedness</translation>

<translation page="16">eternal, we congratulate with our whole heart, wishing for ourselves a similar passing, with a prayer and a desirable sigh: If only he were still living, safe and happy, and could perform this sad duty for many others, and especially for me, who is far more mature for death, a duty which I, by a perverse order of nature, perform for him. But as it pleased the Lord, so it is done. May His holy name be blessed both in favorable and in adverse times.

Since it has been decided to commit the remains of his blessed soul to their resting place <note>original: *Conditorio*</note> tomorrow, the 12th of September, the Magnificent Lords Consuls, the Most Noble and Most Consulted Lord Syndic, the Most Noble, Most Consulted, and also Most Experienced Lords Doctors, as well as the Reverend and Most Distinguished Lords Pastors and Churchmen, and also the Most Ample and Most Prudent Lords Senators and Secretaries, and the rest of the no less honest citizens of this city, the supporters of the School, are requested and invited, with the observance, reverence, and diligence that is proper, to be present in large numbers at the funeral procession and obsequies.

<note>A square woodcut depicts an hourglass resting on a flat base. The hourglass is flanked by a stalk of grain on the left and a leafy branch on the right, serving as a memento mori symbol for the passage of time and the cycle of life and death.</note>
</translation>

For who is not aware of the impious voice of Machiavelli in chapter XV of *The Prince*, claiming that it is *necessary for the safety of a Prince that he not be good*? And by this very thing, he does not merely recommend evil arts to one who governs regions, but even persuades them that such arts are most necessary for establishing a Principality and preserving power. We omit other Doctors who even today attempt to defend the same most pestilential error to the immense damage of cities. But this foul opinion has long since been refuted and condemned by ancient writers of great name, whose authority is not to be despised, by means of suitable arguments. For it could not have been obscure to those most serious men that the honest is by no means to be separated from the useful in a state, nor should anything be thought honest that is not useful, nor useful that is not honest and consistent with virtue; since these two are connected by a natural and most tight bond. However, it easily appears what utility was understood by them; that surely, which applies right reason <term>ratio recta</term> <gloss>sound judgment/rectitude</gloss> to counsel, from which neither the principles and causes of things are neglected, and what is to follow is accurately weighed and compared with present things. And they judged that this alone is worthy of the name of utility. For utility ceases to be, or is even the greatest ruin, in which a person <unclear>calculates</unclear></translation>

follows the corrupt judgment of his own passions, chooses a present good which indeed seems joyful and salutary, but, if weighed on a fair scale, is deceitful, slippery, and inconstant, and is the source and origin of many inconveniences. Many think that great fruits are gathered when faith is not kept, when injury is brought upon the weak, when no treaties are observed, when power and wealth are sought by iniquitous arts, and other things are done which laws and justice intend to be diligently avoided by all kinds of men. But when those who do these things expect the same from others, who seek their own advantages from any source whatsoever, it must follow that from such actions, separated from the honest, there can be no fruit or pleasure for a wise person; rather, they bring much detriment and the gravest calamity to men by confusing the order of things. Therefore, that which is most beneficial must be looked to in the republic in such a way that it is joined with honest and praiseworthy things, and that nothing be done or thought which seems to be absent from virtue and the probity of morals. In order that this may be more easily obtained, it will be necessary to diligently observe those things by which the honesty of morals and the pursuit of virtue are helped and promoted. Since not a few of these have been brought forth by those who, concerned for the most salutary precepts, have well weighed such a great matter in their own minds, we judge, saving the opinions of others, that these three are the most important: religion, discipline, and good laws. It is superfluous to speak about these at greater length now; since it will be that they are explained more broadly and abundantly by some young men who are to declaim publicly tomorrow. We add only a little concerning religion and briefly note what the Fathers and Doctors of the church have thought about it in relation to virtues and honest morals.

# LATER DECLAMATION.

A few days ago, listeners and others, someone appeared in this very chair to denounce, in a speech, the infamous pursuit of foreign travel. You sustained the speaker with benevolence and liberal attention, I believe, because in your judgment he had occupied a topic that was not unworthy of the present place; and because it was not tiresome for either your renowned assembly or the rest of the gathered audience to listen. In that favor of spirits and tongues, after others, as was fitting, I had also prepared myself so that I might be free in mind and ears for the speaker. Regarding the others, I can guess what he achieved; of myself, I can clearly affirm that my mind was so brought to bear that I began to abhor these customs and detest this insanity of studies. Therefore, it seemed to me that I had not at all wasted my effort, especially on a topic in which one might rightly test his wit, and also because it did not at all suffer from sterile lack. For when the orator had decided, according to the rationale of his plan, to reveal the baseness of this pursuit, it was understood that the topic was represented with such abundance that, in explaining it, one’s wit would be better restrained than fatigued by anxious</translation>

<translation page="6">
378
# LATER DECLAMATION.

contemplation. If anyone wished to append other things of that kind that were omitted, he would undoubtedly fill a new speech. Indeed, I will not hide that the desire then entered my mind to test what I myself could bring forth in the same genre. But the prize is set in the middle for all; let anyone make the attempt who wishes. I, after having debated the matter more carefully with myself, from the moment I chose to be a reserve in this arena, decided it was better, rather than arming myself from the same arsenal, to take up new weapons with which to contend against this most empty pursuit. I decided to show that just as that pursuit was judged base and infamous, it should also be considered harmful to both public and private interests. I am persuaded that in this, the rationale of my plan did not elude me much. For, in order to add something of wit to the previous speech, I saw that the main points had already been exhausted; I understood that if this latter type of argument were omitted, the critique would be imperfect. Add to this that the minds of men are so constituted that they are little moved by the mere baseness of a thing; if you demonstrate that something is joined with ruin, you will drag them, terrified, wherever you wish, even against their will. Therefore, let this pursuit of foreign travel be base because it is the mark of the ungrateful, the servile, the insane, and finally, the inept. I will strive to demonstrate that it is rightly called a plague to private wealth, and from that, a subversion to the public.</translation>

However, because these scribes were frequently compelled to go into the provinces with their patrons (for in the retinue of the governors going into the provinces, all those were assistants, ministers, and companions whom the use and reason of the province, as well as the very dignity of the magistrates and of the Republic demanded, for example, legates, military tribunes, centurions, prefects, decurions, and other assistants and ministers of military works and accounts; furthermore, truly, scribes, <term>accensi</term> <gloss>attendants to a magistrate</gloss>, heralds, lictors, interpreters, couriers, augurs, chamberlains, doctors, and messmates, and the rest), those <term>decuriae</term> <gloss>divisions of offices</gloss> were often sold by the scribes, and conversely bought by others. I shall have those scribes with you as arbitrators of this crime, who are annoyed that those [others] are scribes. Livy has things related to this. In Book Forty, Quintus Petillius, the Urban Praetor, took those books from Lucius Petillius, a scribe. And there was a familiar usage, because the Quaestor Quintus Petillius had selected him as a scribe into the <term>decuria</term> <gloss>division of office</gloss>.

### §. XI.

The duties of the public scribes were primarily these: (1) To attend the magistrates, which, besides those things that we have already brought forward, is also confirmed by a passage of Plutarch in [his life of] Cato, which, translated into the Latin language, sounds thus: "Cato, when he had entered upon the quaestorship, restrained the ministers and scribes who, handling public records and laws, when they had found young men as magistrates to whom they were to attend, because those men were in need of masters due to their inexperience, did not yield their power, but were themselves the magistrates. Cato treated them, however, as what they were, in the place of servants; when he accused some of fraud, others of inexperience." (2) To read aloud publicly to the people all those things which a magistrate wished to be published from a written text, and to submit them to a herald to be proclaimed. Regarding this, Philip Beroaldus [writes] in the Ninth Book of Apuleius. # OF THE APOSTLE PAUL'S
### §. II.

Festus provided the opportunity for this Apostle to appeal to Caesar while he stood before Caesar’s tribunal in Caesarea, as has already been stated in *Section I, §. VI, page 7*. For he, desiring to curry favor with the Jewish accusers, had asked in *verse 9, Chapter XXV*, whether Paul wished to be judged in Jerusalem. But the Apostle, when he perceived the intent of this question, quite opportunely and prudently *appealed to Caesar*: for, just as a wise man, to speak with Gregory Nazianzen, *avoids all burdensome and dangerous things, just as a shipmaster avoids storms*, so too did Paul, taught by experience that he would never and nowhere be safe in Judea, cautiously and diligently avoid these snares of Jewish deception. Above all, he did so because he dreaded (1.) **THE JEWS**, whose number, as is abundantly clear from the *Evangelical and Apostolic History*, were most bitter enemies of the Christian doctrine which he, inflamed by pious emulation and divine zeal, was propagating; and (2.) **THE CITY OF JERUSALEM**, where prophets were slaughtered and apostles were stoned (*Matthew XXIII, v. 37, compared with Acts VII, v. 52*), indeed, where he had already been received by the Jews who were seeking to kill him with dire beatings (*Acts XXI, v. 31, 32*); and (3.) **THE JOURNEY**, on account of the traps for slaughter to be set for him by assassins on the road (*Acts XXV, v. 3, compared with Acts XXIII, v. 12--15*).

### §. III.

Regarding the *offenses* for which the Jews were laboring to accuse Paul gravely before Festus, they are called in general terms in *Acts XXV, v. 7* <term>πολλά καὶ βαρέα αἰτιάματα</term> <gloss>many and grave accusations</gloss>. What kind of accusations, and how great those <term>αἰτιάματα</term> <gloss>accusations</gloss> were in particular, the *Pauline Apology, in the following verse, 8*, indicates not obscurely, since</translation>

<translation page="15">
# ON THE APPEAL TO CAESAR.

from it, it is gathered that there were three main heads of the accusation: *namely, that Paul had sinned against the law and the temple of the Jews, and against Caesar. ### §. II.

Festus provided the opportunity for this Apostle to appeal to Caesar while he stood before Caesar’s tribunal in Caesarea, as has already been stated in *Section I, §. VI, page 7*. For he, desiring to curry favor with the Jewish accusers, had asked in *verse 9, Chapter XXV*, whether Paul wished to be judged in Jerusalem. But the Apostle, when he perceived the intent of this question, quite opportunely and prudently *appealed to Caesar*: for, just as a wise man, to speak with Gregory Nazianzen, *avoids all burdensome and dangerous things, just as a shipmaster avoids storms*, so too did Paul, taught by experience that he would never and nowhere be safe in Judea, cautiously and diligently avoid these snares of Jewish deception. Suetonius in *Caesar*: *The funeral being proclaimed, the pyre was built in the Campus Martius.* Cicero in *Oratio pro domo sua ad pontifices* and *De Provinciis Consularibus*. The illustrious Scaliger long ago noted the formal words of this proclamation from Terence (*Phormio*, Act 5, last scene) and Varro (Book 4, *On the Latin Language*). Indictive Funerals were the most elaborate and, beyond other sumptuous displays, were also celebrated with games. Cicero, Book 2, *On the Latin Language*; Becman, *On Origin*, p. 706; Rosinus and Kirchmann in the aforementioned locations; Scaliger, Book 1, *Ausonian Lectures*, Chapter 28; with tumblers also employed. Festus Pompeius, Book 17; Dempster on Rosinus, *Antiquities*, Book 5, Chapter 24. The Public funeral can be referred to here, which was sometimes the same as the Indictive, as in Apuleius (Book 11, *Metamorphoses*), sometimes only a part of it, when, for instance, a cessation of business was proclaimed, or public mourning, or expenses were made from the public treasury (Kirchmann, ibid.). This honor was granted to Syphax, King of Numidia (Valerius Maximus, Book 5, Chapter 1; Suetonius in *Vitellius*, Chapter 3); to Sphaerus, Augustus’s freedman and tutor (Dio, Book 48); to Piso, Urban Prefect (the same, Dio, Book 64). Illustrious women were not without a share of this (Idem, Book 47; Xiphilinus in *Tiberius*). There were furthermore various kinds of Public Funerals according to the diversity of honors managed by the deceased, such as Praetorian, Consular, Censorial, and Triumphal, as Polybius indicates (Book 6, *Histories*), where, however, Lipsius noted that the triumphal was confused with the censorial under the emperors. The most worthy was the Censorial, by which princes were carried out, such as Claudius (Tacitus, Book 12). Whence Spartianus in *Aelius Verus* calls it an Imperial funeral; in *Opilius Macrinus*, a Royal one. For the Censorship was the most honored among the magistracies (Plutarch in *Cato the Elder*).

## Other Silent or Simpludearian Funerals. Thesis VII.

This is the second type, called by another name the Vulgar funeral in Capitolinus (*Marcus Antoninus the Philosopher*). Also the Common funeral, Ausonius (*Parentalia*). These funerals were performed without pomp, without a master of ceremonies, herald, or proclamation.</translation>

### Thesis VIII.

## **Those which either precede the funeral, or concern the dying themselves.**

When every hope of life seemed to have failed in the sick person, friends and those nearest by blood were accustomed to kiss the dying person and embrace their body. Seneca, *On the Shortness of Life*: *He perished in the embrace and kisses of his own.* Ausonius, in his 23rd poem of the *Parentalia*:

> That hand died among the kisses of the mother and father, and so forth.

Thus Suetonius, in his *Life of Augustus* (Chapter 90), records that Augustus Caesar passed away in the kisses of Livia. Kirchmann has the causes of this custom in Book 1, Chapter 5 of *On Roman Funerals*. Furthermore, if the sick person died at home, when they began to exhale their breath, those who were closest would catch their spirit with their mouths and wished to transfer it into themselves: which the ancients womanishly believed could be done. Cicero in the fifth *Verrine Oration*; Virgil, Book 4 of the *Aeneid*:

> If any last breath yet wanders above,
> I will catch it with my mouth.

For the ancients believed that the soul, about to depart from the body, exited through the mouth as if through some door. Seneca, *Epistle* 30, and in *Hercules Furens*, line 1310. Furthermore, rings were also accustomed to be drawn off from the dying.</translation>

<summary>This text details the various categories of Roman funerals, distinguishing between public, indictive, and silent (simpludearian) rites, and begins a discussion on the rituals performed at the moment of death, including the final kiss and the belief in catching the soul as it leaves the body.</summary>

<margin>How did Pippin break through those [obstacles]?</margin>
The oath of faith, by which Pippin and the others owed obedience to Childeric. He chose to spin the web in the way that Pierre Matthieu explains in his <term>Genealogia Regum Francorum</term> <gloss>Genealogy of the Kings of the Franks</gloss>, fol. 50, as well as Buffier and others. After he had bound many through benefits, more through promises, and all through his companionship; and after he had excited old friends with the hope of new things and inflamed new friends with a rivalry of the old, conversation began to spread everywhere through his arts, starting with the courtiers and soon reaching the common people: that the sloth of the Franks, already displayed by so many kings, was a disgrace to their glory; that those who were fit to rule neither themselves nor others should be cast aside; and that another should be chosen, by whose virtue the kingdom might stand. Nor did one need to look far, for Pippin the Prince was at hand—a dwarf in body, indeed, but a giant in spirit.

Following this, the task was delegated by Zachary to Boniface, Archbishop of Mainz, who was the first to introduce the Roman rites of sacred worship and the vanity of dogmas into Germany, which was already steeped in better things in some places, to anoint Pippin as King, whom the Franks themselves had already chosen by their own votes. Therefore, as the legates returned to France, the anointing of Pippin was performed at Soissons by Boniface, and soon Pippin was called King by all, and according to the custom of the people, he was carried around on a shield and placed upon the throne. Finally, the last act to close the scene was the deposition of Childeric, who was led from the rustic villa in which he resided to a monastery in Regensburg (they also destined his wife Gisela to a nunnery), his hair was shorn, his robes were laid aside, and he donned the monk's habit, with no heavier loss than that of his hair, since he was not stripped of a kingdom he had not possessed, and losing his wife might perhaps be considered a gain. For he, since he feared the Greek Emperors—from whom the Pope had defected, having formed a new empire for themselves—as avengers of Roman perfidy, and at the same time wished to win over Pippin as a firm protection against the Greeks and Aistulph, King of the Lombards, who was threatening Roman territory as if it were the empire of the Greeks, decided to please Pippin with this new example of perfidy. Following this, the task was delegated by Zachary to Boniface, Archbishop of Mainz, who was the first to introduce the Roman rites of sacred worship and the vanity of dogmas into Germany, which was already steeped in better things in some places, to anoint Pippin as King, whom the Franks themselves had already chosen by their own votes. Therefore, as the legates returned to France, the anointing of Pippin was performed at Soissons by Boniface, and soon Pippin was called King by all, and according to the custom of the people, he was carried around on a shield and placed upon the throne. Finally, the last act to close the scene was the deposition of Childeric, who was led from the rustic villa in which he resided to a monastery in Regensburg (they also destined his wife Gisela to a nunnery), his hair was shorn, his robes were laid aside, and he donned the monk's habit, with no heavier loss than that of his hair, since he was not stripped of a kingdom he had not possessed, and losing his wife might perhaps be considered a gain. This happens more elegantly for them than for the Romans or the *Athenians*, because those ancients were compelled by their laws to decorate with praises those who died fighting for the Fatherland; you, whatever you do, attribute it freely and spontaneously to their virtue, and you fulfill the duty of the most grateful citizens. from the highest watchtower of heaven, I seem now to see, and I see your grateful hearts, and thus I rejoice that they understand that, through the embellishment of words, everlasting praise is accustomed to reach those who have performed illustrious deeds among their listeners. XXIII. There is no doubt that even excommunicated persons and heretics have this right to send Legates. For excommunication pertains to ecclesiastical discipline, whereas an embassy pertains to civil and secular affairs. Furthermore, the act of sending, which exists by the law of nations, views and considers men according to the law of nations, as they are with us solely as men, and not according to the law and custom of any region or religion. And the rights of peace are not abolished by diversity of religion; much less are the mutual dealings of an embassy abolished by a contradiction of faith: says Kirchner in book 1, chapter 3, whose words it pleased me to insert here.

XXIV. Although there are some who ascribe the right of embassies to the free nobles and Hanseatic cities dwelling in France, Swabia, and along the Rhine, we deny that they possess this right, because they are not states of the Empire, are not found in the register of the Empire, and are not summoned to the diets, following Kirchner in book 1, chapter 3, number 56, and Heiden on Embassies. For the free cities contained within the Hanseatic league cannot communicate and affix their own right to others and to certain foreign cities as well.

XXV. We also deny the right of sending Legates to Queens, if they are married and the authority rests with the husband: for then they send messengers only, not Legates, since according to the law "Woman" 2 of the Pandects on Rules of Law, they are barred from all administration of public offices: Yet with the exception of those who hold supreme power and exercise supreme rule, whether they be unmarried, as was Elizabeth of England, and still is today Christina, Queen of Sweden, or if they are involved in marriage but have retained the rights of Majesty and Empire for themselves, and have not communicated them to the husband, examples of which we have in Isabella of Castile, Mary, Queen of Hungary, and Mary of England. Kirchner, book 1, chapter 3; Bodin, book 6 of The Republic, chapter 5.

XXVI. Pontiffs, Bishops, Clerics, and Superintendents in churches professing Apostolic doctrine, and the Bishops of Denmark, Sweden, and England, in so far as they are occupied with ecclesiastical affairs and do not possess secular rule,

do not have the rights of sending Legates: But because they are secular princes and Dukes, and exercise political rule, we cannot deny that the same right belongs to them as to other Princes. Meanwhile, this right cannot be ascribed to Academics under any title, since they are in the position of subjects. Kirchner.

XXVII. We exclude, furthermore, from this right of sending Legates those rebels who, without any preexisting just cause, tear themselves by force from the jurisdiction of their Lords, over whom the right and authority of the Prince always remains safe, and who, having disregarded divine and human laws, dissolve civil society and tear apart every bond of humanity. To these we add those who are proscribed. For when they lose all privileges, rights of dignities, and royal prerogatives, they cannot possess that right within the empire from which they are proscribed. been fatigued. However, although I do not have this matter fully settled, I will gladly offer my opinion, so that I might at least provide more learned men with a starting point for debating such things more thoroughly and subtly. Pliny embraces both the <term>gale</term> <gloss>weasel</gloss> and the <term>ictis</term> <gloss>marten</gloss> under the name of "weasel." For what Aristotle writes, "when the <term>gale</term> fights a snake, it eats rue," Pliny translated almost word for word when he says, "The weasel, about to do battle with snakes, carries rue in its mouth" (Book 29, Chapter 4). Those animals which Aristotle called <term>ictides</term> <gloss>martens</gloss>, he himself also calls weasels. For he writes as follows: "There are two kinds of weasels. The other is wild; they differ in size; the Greeks call them <term>ictides</term>." From these passages already cited, it is clear enough that "weasel" is a general name for Pliny, and that in Latin, the animal is called a "weasel" which the Greeks call <term>gale</term> and <term>ictis</term>. 

EUCHARIUS. The language of the Latins is therefore poorer than the Greek language. 

ANONYMOUS. The Latins are surpassed by the Greeks not only in the abundance of things, but also of words. And just as nothing is lacking for the Greeks, so many things are desired by the Latins. And in my own judgment, Cicero exclaims somewhat too intemperately: "O the impoverished Greek language at times." 

EUCHARIUS. But in such great poverty among the Latins, what shall we say or do? 

ANONYMOUS. We shall borrow names from the common people. For common names are not to be despised if Latin ones are lacking.

Regarding why the ox that was buried was stoned, which is mentioned in Exodus 21, the *Weimar interpreters* give this reason in verse 32: *so that the homicide might not remain unavenged.* But *Jacob Bonfrère*, in his commentary on this passage (Antwerp, fol. 465), does not admit this reason, writing: *Furthermore, all these things are decreed against the ox, not because of any guilt, which cannot exist in a brute, but for the greater detestation and horror of homicide.* Similar things are read in *Cornelius à Lapide*, in his commentary on this passage (Antwerp edition, Vol. 1, p. 489), where he comments as follows: *If an ox has struck a man or a woman with its horn, and they have died, it shall be overwhelmed with stones, not because of the ox's guilt (for this cannot exist in a brute), but for the terror and example of men, so that men may thereby be more deterred from homicide, whence even today pigs and other beasts are killed if they kill children or men.* Other matters pertaining to this stoned ox may be seen in the *Mishna Bava Kama, ch. 4, §. 5.*

### §. XIX.

But another question is still raised concerning the stoned and buried ox: if the heirs wished, could the owner of the ox, who was guilty of death, redeem its life with silver? *Grotius* affirms this question in Exodus 22, verse 29. But *Varenius* opposes Grotius, because he followed *Rashi* and *Ibn Ezra*, and thinks that the owner of the brute could redeem its life only if it could not be solidly convicted of gross negligence.

<translation page="12">other things described by Suetonius and Dio, namely falling thunderbolts, running torches, new stars, and the appearance of the Sun surrounded by a triple circle, the most prominent of which shadowed a fiery crown of ears of corn. It has been confirmed with greater authority and more certain tradition that the Oracles of the Gentiles, themselves filled with the fascinations of Demons, indicated their conqueror and, upon his presence, retreated sadly into the underworld. Indeed, the Prince of Darkness yielded to the Phosphorus of the rising Sun; the mists of deceptions were dispersed and the frauds detected as the serene Light approached.

<margin>
Pythian Oracle
A Hebrew boy, ruling over the blessed gods, commands me to leave this house and return to the underworld; therefore, depart in silence from our altars.
</margin>

For indeed, Augustus, intending to inquire from the Pythian Demon who would administer the Roman Empire once he was removed from human affairs, received only such an indignant response after repeated sacrifice:

> What end or period will there ever be to my wearying troubles, since that Firstborn of the Gods, ruling not only the heavens but also the underworld, has now placed a limit? He has driven the Hebrew Boy, recently shadowed by a prodigious flux and indicated by so many parhelia <note>original: "PARELIIS" - sun-dogs or mock suns</note>, from the seats he occupied until now, and has relegated the Demons to the Caucasus, nay, to the most wretched jaws of the underworld. That celestial Oil, derived not from a common tavern but from the very springs of Palestine, has filled the prophetic caverns with splendor, fragrance, and an intolerable whiteness.

He continues to address Caesar himself:

> You will by no means be able to serve the opposing Princes of Light and Darkness; while you recently surrendered yourself to the homage of the One, you have voluntarily renounced the service of the other by Altar, by veneration. The fasces have been submitted to a more eminent, more powerful, and greater One. Leave this house which I must abandon immediately; flee our sanctuaries, for you must be girded not with Laurel, but with Cypress.

<summary>This page recounts the decline of pagan oracles and the arrival of the "Firstborn of God," noting that supernatural portents and the voice of the Pythian Demon signaled the end of demonic power upon the birth of the Hebrew Boy.</summary>
<keywords>Augustus, Pythian Oracle, Hebrew Boy, Demons, Oracles, Light, Darkness, Palestine</keywords></translation>

<translation page="13">from now on. Neglect the Altars of Apollo, you who have recently built Christian ones. You invoke my help in vain, since I must seek another dwelling, not in the mundane machine—which is now entirely tributary to the New Monarch—but in the mournful chasm of Tartarus, the squalid prison of Avernus, the horrific Empire of Rhadamanthus, the smoky abode of Pluto, and the monstrous chasm of Acheron. He spoke, and the formidable Tyrant of the underworld sought the caves of the Stygian Dragon with such a horrific murmur. Be stupefied, O Demons, groan together, and tremble, O Tripods! Realize your ruin! The flaming and celestial Light has dispelled our darkness; the clarity of the Oracles is failing, and I know that the authority of my own, which has remained unshaken until now, will fail. The tabernacle of the Pythia is sealed, and the trapping of souls has withered. Indeed, even that most wicked apostate Porphyry, who is worse than the Avernal Spirit, explains with blasphemous mouth the discovered causes of this silence: it is no wonder that cities are vexed by plague, as Aesculapius and the other gods are absent, and since that Jesus is honored, adored, and invoked, the Demons no longer promise any utility to mortals. Thus, the testimonies of this divine childbirth, resounding with so many heralds, proven by so many documents, and indicated by so many portents, have illuminated the intricate prophecies of the Sibyls, revealed the depraved poems of others, and explained the common monuments of human wisdom. Now at last, Tully <note>referring to Cicero</note> himself observes from their leaves that some King must be called for, a steward of every kind of salvation, whom he judges would appear as soon as the Romans had brought back the King of Egypt. Nor did his conjecture deceive him: to Ptolemy

<margin>
Apollo:
Alas, alas, tripods, you shall grow silent; Apollo is gone, etc. Alas, alas, my tongue is left without oracles.
</margin>
<margin>
Cicero, Book II, On Divination.
</margin>

<note>continues from previous page: by the argument of Law 10, § 1, and Law 12, at the end of the Digest on Managed Affairs; Law 1, § 10 of the Digest on Extraordinary Cognizances.</note> Furthermore, if anything is promised in place of an annual honorarium, it must be paid by the client. However, clients are not bound to pay tax levies which are imposed by reason of superiority and jurisdiction <note>Caspar Glocken, *On Empire Contributions, Thesis 6, letter a and b*</note>, since the simple right of protection does not confer that, <note>Wehner and Besold on the words "Protection and Shield." Gail, Book 2, Observation 54</note> but if the people are free, nothing should prejudice their liberty <note>Law: "I do not doubt," 7, Digest on Captives and Postliminy</note>. Likewise, neither the right of patronage properly so called, since this is annexed to spirituality <note>Chapter "When," 3, on Judgments; Chapter "On the Right," 16, on the Right of Patronage</note>, can be claimed for oneself, nor can the Protector change anything regarding religion, since protection is a merely temporal right <note>Synz, Thesis 22</note>.

### XXVI.

The Right of Clientage is dissolved by the destruction and desolation of the thing, such as the destruction of a city which one has undertaken to defend <note>by the argument of Law 5, § 2; Law: "If usufruct," 21, Digest on In what ways usufruct is lost</note>. And the payment of the honorarium established for the sake of defense expires. A great diminution of status <note>Law: "Of cognitions," 5, Digest on extraordinary cognitions</note> or proscription, or the Imperial Ban, extinguishes the clientage in the person of either the Patron or the Client; for those who are proscribed are stripped of all clientage, loyalty, and protection, and thus of all liberty and privileges <note>Ordinance of the Chamber, Part 2, Law 9, § 2; Gail, *On Public Peace*, Book 2, Chapter 1, number 20; Mynsinger, Century 1, Observation 50, and Century 3, Observation 52; They fall out of compacts, titles, oaths, treaties, and all rights, Bechl, *On Security*, Thesis 118 and following</note>. However, it is truer that no one is deprived of that right on account of a change in Catholic or Augustan <note>referring to Lutheran/Protestant</note> religion <note>Constitution of the Religious Pacification of the year 55, § "Es sol auch" (It shall also); Syrinus, *On Religious Peace*, Conclusion 37; Besold, *On the Right of Treaties*, Chapter 5, number 15</note>, nor by major excommunication, as if it were lost by the Ban; for the latter is mortal, as Magerus speaks <note>Chapter 16, number 199</note>, whereas the former is medicinal <note>Hopingk, *On the Right of Protection*, Thesis 6, letter d</note>.

When the powers of the Patron are worn out and rendered useless for defense

rendered, it is truer that the right of defense does not perish <note>argument: chapter "Briefly," Extr. on Oaths; chapter "The fact," legitimately, on the Rule of Law in the Sext; Law "In ambiguous," § "It is not new," Digest on the same</note>, for a completed contract is not immediately vitiated, even if it arrives at a contingency from which it could not have begun <note>Law: "The penultimate," § "Even if," Digest on Verbal Obligations</note>. And it is easier for a right to be preserved by civil law than to be granted anew <note>argument: Law 3, Digest on New Works</note>. Yet, in extreme necessity, if the Patron is suffering from such poverty that there is no hope of better fortune or restitution, it could be conceded that the right of clientage also dies.

### XXVIII.

Clientage contracted for a specific day is dissolved when that day arrives. Because contracts and any agreements concluded for a certain duration are dissolved and cease when that time has elapsed <note>argument: Law: "If one," § 1, Digest on Pacts; Law: "Of obligations," 44, § "It pleases," Digest on Obligations and Actions</note>. It is also dissolved by the mutual consent and will of the parties <note>Law: "Nothing so natural," 35, Digest and there Gothofred on the Rule of Law</note>. However, the dissent of one party does not remove it when the matter is no longer entire and the interest of the other has already begun <note>Law 5, Code on Obligations and Actions</note>. Unless the law of the convention has been fulfilled by one party: for then the one who has fulfilled it can withdraw from the contract against the will of the other, and before fulfilling it, can repent with impunity <note>Law: "If monies," in the beginning, Digest on Conditions, where Gothofred notes that this holds even if the convention was sworn; chapter "It comes," on Oaths; chapter "In vain," on the Rule of Law in the Sext, where Peckius and others comment</note>.

### XXIX.

A civil obligation arises from this contract <note>Law 5, § 1, Digest on Prescribed Words</note>. A useful action is also given <note>Law 3, § 4, Digest on Conditions for a given cause</note> to the Client, so that the faith of the promised patronage may be fulfilled, or that which was given for the sake of protection may be restored <note>Law: "The last," Code on Condemnation for a given cause</note>, or that the value of the Client's interest, had the contract been fulfilled, may be provided <note>Law 7, Digest on Prescribed Words</note>.

</translation>

# On the Human Mind.

we contemplate only the concept and the idea, and set them before ourselves. Judgment, however, is called that by which, from the intuition of those things we have perceived, we affirm or deny something about the things themselves. There is a triple affirmation and negation, of existence, essence, and accidents, just as when I have affirmed that the mind exists, I have explained what its essence is and what kind it is. I call it an affirmation when judgment attributes the predicate to the subject in an intentional, unitive manner of tending. I call it a negation when it intentionally severs and tears away the same predicate from its subject in a divisive manner of tending. Reasoning, or discourse, is a connection and a certain comparison of several thoughts and judgments, or if you prefer, a passage from one thought to another, since discourse necessarily encloses two cognitions within itself and does not require more. <margin>Death of his wife.</margin>
To a body already pressed by such a weight of labors, there was added a lethal wound, a pain penetrating to the very vitals, from the premature passing of his most sweet wife. By how much more gentle the marriage bed had been for so many years without any discord, by how much more fruitful it had been with noble offspring, emulators of their father’s virtues, by so much more did he lament that his joys were snatched away, that all pleasures had perished with his wife, and that he himself was carried out in the same funeral procession as she. Forgive, *Auditors*, forgive that I include in these arguments the inevitable necessity of fate, or rather of God, the arbiter of life and death, whose dictates are not to be moved, by which fixed limits are set for us and an immovable goal is fixed by the years, which our mind often perceives falsely, being blind to the rest. These were the decrees of the Fates, to reclaim this deposit of heaven and to insert an immortal head among the stars, one which had illuminated *Cimbria* with such great rays. The spheres of the earth seemed too narrow for such a vast mind, therefore it was to be summoned to the ampler spaces of the heavens. Although he was always desirous of these, he was not so disdainful of the present that, had the fates and God allowed, he would not have indulged us with the use of himself further, especially so that he might set his hand to the divine work he had begun. The sons of the physicians were consulted; everything was sought from every quarter that might strengthen the powers of his body, which was failing day by day, and restore what had collapsed. But human counsels are in vain where Divine ones are contrary! The earth retains in vain while heaven summons. Among the

wonders of nature are the acidulae <gloss>mineral/carbonated springs</gloss>, the fountains of *Spada*, gushing through mountain conduits by secret channels, which, as if in support of failing art and human aid, nurturing mother Nature, or rather God, the great father of nature, seems to have produced. By these medicinal fountains, the languor of torpid bodies was often shaken off, fevers were extinguished, pains were repelled, the pristine vigor of the year was returned, and the strength that had been in the limbs was restored.
