Moreover, the task of Theology is not only that which we have just explained, namely, to defend its principles against those who deny or attack them, and to gather from the force of reason conclusions—this one and that one—which serve to protect and illustrate the Christian matter; but also, by employing internal and external safeguards and aids of this science, to confirm both sides effectively.

### LXIIII.

We call the internal and proper safeguards of Theology those arguments which are sought from the Canonical Scripture: from the faithful tradition of Christ and the Apostles: from the authority of the Catholic and Apostolic Church, from the Canons of General Councils and Roman Pontiffs: and finally, from the monuments of ancient and recent Fathers and Theologians.

### LXV.

<margin>+</margin> External safeguards, and those which might be called borrowed from a foreign fund, are those which are taken from the tenets of natural Philosophers, from the responses of Jurists—for they too wish to be counted among the professors of true Philosophy—from the chronicles of history, and finally, from the very resources of human reason.

### LXVI.

For since there is a twofold type of argumentation: the one resting on authority, which is proper to the Theologian; the other instructed by reason, which is peculiar to the Philosopher; if it is not permitted to use the former and proper one, the Theologian, seizing upon what is closest to the former, defends himself by reason instead of authority; yet he often joins both types of proof together.

### LXVII.

But in divine things, the mode and the substance do not differ really, nor is any distinction of essence to be admitted in the divine persons, except only of reason, lest any composition of essence and person be established in God. They differ infinitely, therefore, as much as finite and infinite essence and person: a finite essence is individual because of unity, and incommunicable to multiple persons because of finiteness; the infinite, although it is supremely individual because of supreme unity, is nevertheless truly communicable to multiple persons because of infinity. In finite things, one person is distinguished from another no less by the singularity of being than by the incommunicability of subsisting. But in the mystery of the <term>Trinitas</term> <gloss>Trinity</gloss>, the persons are distinguished from one another by the incommunicability of subsisting at the very least, but not by the singularity of essence; one is not the other, yet it is of the same numerical essence as the other. There, any person is entirely distinct from another person and separated, and they have no intrinsic connection. Here, although the persons are really distinguished, they cannot nevertheless be separated in being, but by the reason of it, one is in the other, nor can it exist outside the other because of the identity of essence. ### §. XV.

Such was the condition of the old man <note>referring to Herod the Great</note>, whom we recall flourished elsewhere due to his inveterate favor with Caesar, above other friends. Why, therefore, should it be a wonder if the sons were in a much worse position? Certainly, Archelaus had to fear the Prince, whose will initially diminished his dignity, and later clearly laid it low with anger, having chosen Vienna <note>Vienne, in Gaul, the place of Archelaus's exile</note> to endure the bitterness of exile. *Nold. p. 229.* Josephus did not pass over the imperious voice of the Prince, *Ant. l. 17. c. 15.* so that we may easily agree with Spanheim, a defender of the Evangelist, who does not circumscribe the term <term>βασιλεύειν</term> <gloss>to reign as king</gloss> with such narrow boundaries, but that he occasionally includes in its meaning power inferior to royal authority. *vol. 2. Dub. 86. conf. l. c.*

### §. XVI.

Will the Tetrarchs, therefore, be angry with us, those restricted to the region of Palestine, if we indicate that they obtained their power only on precarious terms? They certainly lay struck down, without doubt, whenever they appeared to have plotted anything against the Prince. As happened to Antipas, incited by Herodias; not to Philip, a composed man who consulted his own interests more wisely; although both otherwise testified to their obedience to the Prince with many services. *Ant. 18. c. 9.* I omit the fates of Lysanias, and of Zenodorus, and of others, who necessarily had to feel a grave calamity, if they occasionally caused their Master to become angry through scandals or party zeal. *Ant. 15. c. 13.*

### §. XVII.

Thus we have examined the Tetrarchs in general, expressing with suitable brevity that they were rulers of fourth parts <note>referring to the etymology of tetrarch</note>; now nothing hinders or forbids us from seeing them individually. ### §. XV.

Such was the condition of the old man <note>referring to Herod the Great</note>, whom we recall flourished elsewhere due to his inveterate favor with Caesar, above other friends. Why, therefore, should it be a wonder if the sons were in a much worse position? Dub. 86. conf. l. c.*

### §. XVI.

Will the Tetrarchs, therefore, be angry with us, those restricted to the region of Palestine, if we indicate that they obtained their power only on precarious terms? **XX V.** To the second genus of mental acts belongs the mental enunciation, which, in order for the moderns to distinguish it from a proposition—which pertains to the third operation of the mind and includes virtual discourse—they rightly define as an immediate judgment about some thing: that is, such a one that affirms a predicate of a subject because of the connection between the subject itself and the predicate. Whereas, on the contrary, every discourse is a mediate judgment, because it mediates in approving the connection of the predicate with the subject. The most powerful property of these acts is formal truth, which is nothing other than the conformity of the judgment with the object, just as, conversely, falsity is the disconformity of the judgment with the object; so that, therefore, a true judgment is that which enunciates the object as being in such a way as it is on the part of the thing itself, and a false one is that [which enunciates it] if the object is not as it enunciates it to be.

**XX VI.** An enunciation once true can never pass into a false one, nor conversely can a false one pass into a true one; for the same cognition always represents the same thing. Therefore, the cognition that with truth represented Adam as writing, for this instant which the verbal copula designated, represented for eternity Adam as writing at this instant. For just as it is impossible for Adam to have written at this instant A and not to have written at this instant A, so it is impossible that the cognition which truly represents him as having written at this instant A should ever represent him as not having written; since the proposition speaks for eternity only of this instant, and of no other. Falsity is to be argued in a similar way, because if the proposition were to represent a different time from that which it had first represented, by this very fact it would not be the same, but a different and new representation, and consequently a new cognition.

**XX VII.** To the third and primary genus of the operations of the human intellect pertains formal discourse, or the syllogism; which is an expression in which, certain things being posited, something else necessarily follows from those which have been posited, for the reason that these things are so. And essentially it involves not only the conclusion, but also the premises themselves, nor is anyone considered to have constructed a formal syllogism who either infers something without any premises, or, having made premises, infers nothing. But in order for the assent of the conclusion to be distinguished from another immediately judgmental assent, it must intrinsically reach the object of the premises as a motive and the formal reason for assenting. This is proved from the fact that every act tending toward some material object because of another formal one must reach that formal object: but the formal motive of the conclusion as such is the object of the premises, or the identity of the extremes with a third middle term, therefore the act of the conclusion, as such, must reach that object. This is confirmed because, unless the act of the conclusion reaches the formal motive again, in some syllogisms it will not be possible to provide a reason why this proposition is a conclusion rather than another from the three, for any of them can be inferred by way of a conclusion from the others.

**XX VIII.** Besides the object of the conclusion and the object of the premises, there must also be reached by the act of the conclusion the goodness of the inference, which is the identity between the object of the premises and the object of the conclusion: for this goodness is also a partial motive, which, together with the object of the premises, moves the intellect to infer the conclusion; for with this single connection between the object of the premises and the object of the conclusion removed</translation>

<translation page="12">, no matter how much the object of the premises remains, the intellect would not be moved to the conclusion. Therefore, just as when we love medicine because of health, we also love the connection that medicine has with the restoration of health, because with this connection excluded we would not love the medicine, so too the intellect, in order to be moved to conclude, must not only reach the object of the premises, but also the goodness of the inference.

**XXIX.** Some doubt whether the judgment concerning the goodness of the inference must be a distinct and intermediate act between the assent of the premises and the assent of the conclusion, through which the intellect reflexively knows that this conclusion is rightly inferred from these premises, because those things are identified with each other which are identified with a third. We think it more probable that *a judgment concerning the goodness of the inference distinct from the act of the conclusion is not necessarily always required*, especially in practiced men, to whom that principle is most clearly known: *whatever things are the same as one third, etc.* For such people, after they have seen in the premises that the extremes of the conclusion are identified with a third, immediately infer the act of the conclusion, which at once and together reaches the object of the premises, the goodness of the inference, and the object of the conclusion. However, in those men who are not practiced in making syllogisms, and who even, after having seen that two things are identified with a third, can still doubt whether those two are identified with each other, we think that *a judgment concerning the goodness of the inference, distinct and preceding the conclusion itself, is entirely necessary*: for the intellect of such people is not so imperfect as to be sufficiently determined by the object of the premises to infer the conclusion without any hesitation.

# *Operations of the Human Will.*

**XXX.** That the will is a spiritual, free virtue, appetitive of an object, is certain among all; that it is not distinguished from the intellect nor from the soul, we suggested above in the third thesis. The *material object* about which it is concerned is everything that the intellect can know under the aspect of good or evil. The *formal object*, or that which immediately moves the will, is good and evil; the former moves it toward acts of pursuit, the latter toward acts of avoidance. The good that moves the will is threefold: *honest, delightful, and useful*. None of these can allure the will unless it is first known: yet the cognition itself is not the motive of the will, but a mere condition applying the motive. The will cannot love *evil as evil*, or proposed only under the aspect of evil; it is otherwise if it is presented under the aspect of at least an apparent good.

**XXXI.** Speaking ordinarily, in order for us to love and desire some good for ourselves, it suffices to know that the good is suitable to us; nor is it necessary that we recognize in ourselves any goodness on account of which we might be worthy that we should love such a good for ourselves. But if we love or desire some good for another person, it is required that we apprehend in that person some goodness on account of which we esteem them worthy of such a good. For (speaking ordinarily) in order for me to be able to join myself through affection with the good of my neighbor, insofar as it is a good for him, I must first join myself through affection</translation>

So far, O distinguished Auditors, you have traversed with me the spacious field of the vices by which the Learned are accustomed to be afflicted; but many things still remain to be said in that genre, which, excluded by the narrowness of time, we willingly pass over. But since I feel that the nature of these vices is such that many other men, not a few, are also agitated by the same goads, and these stains do not emanate from the abuse of learning itself, we refrain from examining them more fully. ### ERROR XIV.
## That the Rational Soul resides in only one part of the body.

I. Philo the Jew established the Rational Soul in the heart; Parmenides and Epicurus in the entire chest; Strato the Physicist in the middle of the eyebrows; Erasistratus in the small membranes; Herophilus in the cavity or base of the brain; Hippocrates in the brain; Xenocrates in the crown of the head; others in the whole head as if in a fortress; and finally others elsewhere. Indeed, some placed it in a certain hidden and obscure place, from which, like a spider, it would run throughout the whole body to catch flies, according to the convenience of circumstances.

II. So too, the author of the *Compendium of the Entirety of Theological Truth* <note>book 2, Venetian edition, year 1565, chapter 54, page 192</note> says that the soul, placed in the center of the heart without its own distension, gives sensation, vivifies, and moves the whole body united to it, just as a spider, sitting in the middle of its web, feels any movement made in the web, whether externally or internally. A truly remarkable opinion of the man.

I. The Rational Soul is not in only one part of the body, for otherwise it would not substantially inform the others; rather, it is whole in the whole continuous body, and whole in any part of it, as all sane philosophers and theologians believe, along with the interpreters of Aristotle. *On the Soul, book 1, text 93*, where the Philosopher says that one cannot even imagine which part (that is, a specific and solitary one) the intellect, that is, the Spiritual Soul, has in the body.

And although Aristotle, *On Respiration, chapter 1*, says explicitly that the soul exists in some particle of the body, he is not to be considered as agreeing with the aforementioned ancients, because he immediately adds that it has its virtue in particles, that is, in certain operations, and it also depends on certain and determined organs; and it has its virtues or material powers residing in and subjected to those particles or organs.

I. First of all, the Epicureans denied that the Rational Soul is immortal, as witnessed by Ruvius in *On the Separated Soul*, whom Pliny followed in *Natural History, book 7, chapter 55*, and many others, especially the Sadducees, who thought that even the Rational Soul perishes with the body through diseases. ex-philosophers, especially the Stoics, thought that the soul did not always endure, but that when released from the body, it would weaken after a long time and eventually perish, although the souls of the wise would persevere until the end of the world.

# CORRECTION.

I. The greater and better part of philosophers, even the ancients, admitted the immortality of the Rational Soul, as can be seen in Eugubinus in book 9 of *On Perennial Philosophy* and others. Dandinus also, in book 1 of *On the Soul*, commentary 39, says that Pythagoras also acknowledged the immortality of the Rational Soul; for he said that if you leave the body and, purified, come to the heavens, you will be an immortal God, incorruptible, and no longer mortal. Saint Thomas also explains Aristotle in favor of this opinion in *Against the Gentiles, book 2, chapter 79*, as does the more common opinion of the moderns, especially since he said the Rational Soul comes from outside.

II. But whatever may be said of Aristotle, immortality certainly pertains to and is owed to the Rational Soul by its own nature, as it is to the Angels, as witnessed by Ruvius in *On the Separated Soul, question 4, number 52*. Since it is truly created, it does not have a natural cause of its corruption; for Christ says in Matthew 10 that they cannot kill the soul. Nor is it an objection that in the letter of Sophronius, recited in the 6th Council of Constantinople, session 11, intellectual beings are said to be immortal only by grace and not by nature, and that this is approved by the Council. For Sophronius only denied such immortality to the Angels and the Rational Soul as God alone possesses, who therefore in 1 Timothy 6 is said to possess immortality alone, since he has it from himself and by his own utterly immutable essence.

III. Therefore, since it is certain from the 5th Lateran Council under Leo X, session 8, that immortality pertains to the Rational Soul by itself and by its own nature, some deduce that it is also certain that it can be clearly demonstrated from physical principles, and that it is known, so to speak, from its own terms, at least in itself, even if perhaps not yet known to us. For the primary Truth cannot lie, nor can the light of nature, which was given to us by that same Truth for the sake of knowing the truth, be repugnant to it, just as Aristotle in the *Categories of Quality* teaches that the quadrature of the circle is explicitly demonstrable, even if the demonstration by which it might be proven has not yet been discovered.

IV. And indeed, it is at least morally evident that it pertains to divine Providence that the wicked be punished, while the good are rewarded with a reward worthy of their merit. Since this does not happen in this life—as experience bears witness—one must either concede the immortality of souls, or else conclude that divine Providence fails in many things and God is unjust, not treating everyone according to their merit, which is blasphemous. Saint Chrysostom, in homily 4 *On Providence*, said that this reasoning is more evident than the noon-day light for the immortality of the Rational Soul.

### Sixth Question.

### §. 11. Whether, if Christ were on earth after the Ascension, he would not be our Priest?

In the Epistle to the Hebrews, chapter 8, verse 4, these words are to be read: "For if he were on earth, he would not be a Priest." From these, the adversaries <unclear>furtively</unclear> gather that Christ dwells with his body in the heavens and is not on earth. It is therefore our task to wrest the club from Hercules <note>A proverbial expression for defeating a formidable opponent.</note> and to respond soundly. First: If Christ could not be a Priest (if he were on earth), it would follow that when he lived on earth, offered himself to his Father on the altar of the cross, and showed himself to his disciples with many proofs for 40 days, he was not a priest. The consequent is absurd. Therefore, the antecedent is as well. The logic of the connection is manifest, because he was on earth at that time. Second: If Christ, because he is a Priest, could not be on earth, he would not be a Priest as God (because he is always as much on earth as he is in heaven). The latter is absurd, by the confession of the opposing party. Therefore, the former is as well. Third: If Christ, because he is a Priest, were not on earth, he would not be a Priest according to his human nature, because according to that nature, by their own admission, he is in Heaven. The latter is absurd, because the Priesthood belongs to his office, and thus to both Natures. Therefore, the former is as well. Finally, this: If he were not on earth, he would not be an eternal Priest, because he is to return from Heaven on the last day. This is false, therefore that [position] is as well. It is a wonder, then, that the adversaries prop up the building of their opinion on this passage, as if it were some support or beam. But indeed, they act through tunnels <note>A metaphor for conducting an argument by underhanded or secretive means.</note>. For, 1, they inject the words "according to human nature" into the text; 2, they interpret the words as applying to only one of Christ's natures, when the Epistle speaks of the whole Christ. Now, turn the syllogistic wheel; what will emerge? Is it not this?</translation>

He urged the priests with his own voice not to condemn all works without discrimination, but to teach the doctrine of the Law and the Gospel, of faith and works—which is necessary for true piety—distinctly and moderately. He urged them not to abolish feast days at their own whim, nor, by untimely and overly vehement invectives against the Pope, Cardinals, and Roman Bishops, to drive the simple people, not yet illuminated by the true light of the Gospel, toward apostasy and sedition rather than toward piety, tranquility, and obedience, and finally, not to cause tumults after the manner of the fanatical Anabaptists. ### §. XVI.

Yet these wretched men did not escape a deadly end. For we have learned that <term>Rinckius</term> <note>Melchior Rinck, an Anabaptist leader</note>, because he would not cease from his errors, was consigned to perpetual imprisonment by the Landgrave of Hesse and thus miserably ended his life. See Seckendorff, *Luther*, Book III, §. XXV, p. 71. The other, however, sustained an even harsher punishment, having acted as an actor in the <term>Münster</term> <note>refers to the Münster Rebellion</note> tragedy. For he was led before the princes, along with others of the same dregs of humanity, for the sake of spectacle and mockery. Then, brought to a raised place, he was tied to a stake: two executioners were present, with heated pincers. He was torn by many bites, and finally, with a blade thrust through his chest, he expired. Once dead, he was bound in an iron cage and hung exposed upon the highest tower of the city, along with the others, the King indeed in the middle, and as high as a man’s stature, even higher. See Sleidanus, *On the State of Religion*, Book X, p. 283. It is a wonder to say that this man was hung upon the highest tower of the city to be exposed to the eyes of all. Concerning whom Chytræus says: *On a stage, built in the middle of the forum, torn apart by glowing pincers, and in iron*</translation>

cages enclosed, and hung at the tower of Saint Lambert, he paid the penalties for his impiety and rashness. *Saxony*, Book XVI, p. 413.

However, after the schemes of the Anabaptists in Sweden were suppressed, that most flourishing kingdom remained sufficiently immune from disturbances of this kind. This is to be attributed to divine mercy, but it also pertains to the immortal glory of so many Kings and Northern Heroes, who, inflamed by a certain heavenly zeal for religion, struggled strenuously for the preservation of the integrity of the purer faith, as if for hearths and homes. ...he calmed the disturbances stirred up by unskilled pastors, by the untimely changing of rites, and by absurd clamors concerning doctrine. He urged the priests with his own voice not to condemn all works without discrimination, but to teach the doctrine of the Law and the Gospel, of faith and works—which is necessary for true piety—distinctly and moderately. He urged them not to abolish feast days at their own whim, nor, by untimely and overly vehement invectives against the Pope, Cardinals, and Roman Bishops, to drive the simple people, not yet illuminated by the true light of the Gospel, toward apostasy and sedition rather than toward piety, tranquility, and obedience, and finally, not to cause tumults after the manner of the fanatical Anabaptists. Yet these wretched men did not escape a deadly end. We shall say they exist. Many affirm they have seen ships capable of carrying eighty rowers. There is no use of iron found among them; therefore, our men were filled with great wonder as to how they built either their houses, which they saw were crafted with marvelous skill, or any other things pertaining to their use. But from certain river <margin>Incredible savagery of some men</margin>
they learned by rumor that they exist, and they later reported the reason why they fled so fearfully to our men for help: they thought they were <term>Canibales</term> <gloss>Cannibals</gloss>, for so they call those truculent ones, or <term>Caribes</term> <gloss>Caribs</gloss>. They left the islands of these obscene people behind, almost in the middle of their journey, toward the south. The gentle islanders complain that their own islands are perpetually vexed by the frequent incursions of the <term>Canibales</term> for the sake of plunder, just as hunters in the woods pursue wild beasts by force and ambush. The boys they capture, they castrate to rear them until they are fatter and more tender, just as we do chickens or pigs that we intend for food; when they reach a mature age and fall into their hands, they slaughter and divide them: they feast on the extremities of their limbs while fresh, and they preserve the limbs salted, just as we do with ham, for later times. It is considered an abomination and obscene among them to eat women; if, however, they capture young women, they care for and guard them for the purpose of procreating offspring, just as we do with hens, sheep, and other animals; they keep old women as slaves to perform chores. Both men and women of the islands, which we can now call ours, find no safety other than flight when they perceive the <term>Canibales</term> approaching; although they use sharp reed arrows, they have found them to be of little use in repressing the violence and fury of the <term>Canibales</term>, for all the natives admit that ten <term>Canibales</term> would easily overcome a hundred of the others if they should clash. What either people worship, besides the sky and its luminaries, they did not sufficiently explore. Due to the shortness of time and the lack of interpreters, they were not permitted to learn more about the other customs of the islands. For food, the gentle islanders use the roots of our <margin>Island foods</margin>
turnips, similar in size and shape but sweet in taste, like tender chestnuts. They call these <term>ages</term>, and they also have another kind of root which they call <term>iucca</term> <gloss>yucca/cassava</gloss>; they make bread from this as well. They use the <term>ages</term> more roasted or boiled than for the purpose of making bread. They grind the <term>iucca</term> after it is cut and pressed, for it is juicy, and bake it into cakes. But this is a marvel: they say the juice of the <term>iucca</term> is more lethal than monkshood and kills immediately if drunk; yet everyone has experienced that bread made from its mass is tasty and healthy. They also make bread from a certain panic grain, which is found in great abundance among the <term>Infrubes</term> and the <term>Granatenses</term> <gloss>people of Granada</gloss> Spaniards, without much difference. The ear of this is longer than a span, tapering to a point, and almost the thickness of an arm. The grains are fixed by nature in a wonderful order, and in shape and body, they emulate the pea legume: they are white when unripe, but they become very black when they have matured; when broken, they surpass snow in whiteness; they call this kind of grain <term>maizium</term> <gloss>maize</gloss>. Gold is of some estimation among them, for they wear it inserted into their earlobes and pierced nostrils, drawn out into very thin plates. However, when our men learned that neither did merchants travel to them, nor did the islanders know any other shores besides their own, they began to ask them through signs where they obtained that gold. As far as could be gathered from signs, they obtained it, not without great labor, from the sands of rivers flowing down from high mountains; they would bind it into pellets before it was drawn into plates. However, it was not in that part of the island which that king held: this became evident later by experience, for when they had already departed from there, they chanced upon a river, and when they disembarked to get water and fish, they perceived that its sand was mixed with much gold. They say they saw no four-footed animal, except for three types of rabbits. The islands harbor snakes, but they are very harmless. They found wild geese, turtle doves, and ducks, larger than ours and white as swans, with purple heads. Of the parrots, some were green,</translation>

<translation page="34">
<header>OCEANIC DECADE</header>

<margin>Parrots distinguished by wonderful colors</margin>
some yellow over their whole body, and others similar to those of India with collars of minium <gloss>red lead/vermilion</gloss>, as Pliny says; they brought back forty, but they are especially vivid and cheerful in their colors. They have variegated wings, for they have certain blue and purple feathers mixed with green and yellow, which variety produces delight. I have wished to relate these things about the parrots, most illustrious Prince, although the opinion of this Christopher Columbus concerning the magnitude of the sphere and the opinion of the ancients about the non-navigable world seems to be contradicted, yet the parrots brought back from there, and many other things, indicate that these islands savor of the Indian soil, either by proximity or by nature; especially since Aristotle toward the end of his book <italic>On the Heavens and the World</italic>, Seneca, and other not ignorant geographers attest that the Indian shores are not far distant from Spain toward the west. The earth there produces by its own nature an abundance of mastic, aloes, cotton, and other things of this kind. From the trees, as among the <term>Seres</term> <gloss>the Chinese/people of the Silk Road</gloss>, wool is collected. They brought back certain wrinkled grains of different colors, sharper than Caucasian pepper; they also brought back branches from trees like coconuts, in the form of cinnamon, but in taste and smell imitating sharp ginger, both in their pith and in the upper bark. Content, therefore, with these signs of the newly discovered land and of another unheard-of world, and with a prosperous return, with the west winds now blowing, he decided to return because our spring was near, and he left thirty-eight men with the king we mentioned above, who were to investigate the nature of the places and seasons until he himself returned. That king was said by the inhabitants to be <term>Guaccanarillus</term>; having struck a pact of singular friendship with him, he did what he could to ensure the life, safety, and protection of those he left behind. The king, touched by compassion for our men because they were being abandoned in foreign lands, seemed to shed tears and promised all aid. Thus, having embraced one another, Columbus, about to return to Spain, ordered the sails to be set, taking with him ten men from those [islands], from whom it was discovered that the language of all those islands could be written with our Latin letters <margin>D</margin>
without any difficulty. For they call heaven <term>turei</term>, house <term>boa</term>, gold <term>cauni</term>, a good man <term>tayno</term>, and nothing <term>mayani</term>. They pronounce all other words no less clearly than we do our Latin. This is what I deemed worthy of memory regarding his first voyage. The King and Queen, all of whose thoughts, even when sleeping, are set upon the increase of our religion, hoping that so many nations and simple people could easily be drawn to the law of Christ, were moved by these accounts. They treated the arriving Columbus honorably, as he deserved for such undertakings. They made him sit before them in public (which is the greatest sign of love, gratitude, and supreme respect among Spanish kings). They ordered that Columbus be called Admiral from then on. He is called Admiral Columbus among the Spaniards. They also honored his brother, Bartholomew Columbus, himself skilled in maritime affairs, with the title of Prefect of the island of Hispaniola. This office they commonly call <term>Adelantatus</term> <gloss>Governor/Lieutenant-General</gloss>. I will therefore occasionally call the Admiral and the <term>Adelantatus</term>, and the presence of ships, and other things of this kind, by their common names on purpose, so that I may be more clearly understood. Now let us return to our subject. It was believed that the greatest commodities, which all mortals pursue with all their might, would result from the islands, as Columbus himself, now Admiral, promised at the beginning. Moved by these two reasons, these two most holy partners ordered seventeen ships to be prepared for the second expedition: three large cargo ships with cages, and twelve of the type of ships we wrote are called <term>Carauelas</term> <gloss>caravels</gloss> among the Spaniards, without cages. Two of the same kind, somewhat larger, and suitable for supporting cages due to the size of the masts. They handed over the care of preparing this fleet to John Fonseca, a man of noble birth, Dean of Seville, and possessed of great talent and spirit. They ordered over twelve hundred armed infantrymen to be hired for him, among whom they ordered countless craftsmen and workers of all mechanical arts to be taken on salary; they would mix certain cavalrymen with the other armed men. For the purpose of breeding, they took mares, sheep, heifers, and many others of their kind.</translation>

<summary>This passage describes the customs of the Caribbean peoples, the encounter with the cannibals, the resources of the islands including gold and maize, and the royal reception of Columbus upon his return to Spain.</summary>
<keywords>Cannibals, Caribs, gold, maize, parrots, Christopher Columbus, Guacanagari, Bartholomew Columbus, John Fonseca, exploration, colonization</keywords>

### XXIX.

<margin>Properly.</margin>
But in this place, it is taken properly, since the word <term>peri</term> <gloss>fruit</gloss> is general, pertaining to the fruit-bearing of anything. Hence, it is joined with various words, as can be seen in many passages of Scripture.

### XXX.

<margin>Fruit of the womb of David. Proof. From the testimony of the Psalm.</margin>
Here it suffices that we have proven the only and natural son of God is called, and is, the fruit of the womb of David. We read in Psalm 132:11: Jehovah swore the truth to David himself, he will not turn from it, nor will he deflect or depart from it:

> Of the fruit of your womb I will place upon your throne or seat.

### XXXI.

Although many understand this promise only as a political kingdom, we, following the divine Luther, believe that God confirmed by an oath that a king should be set up from the fruit of the womb of David, whose kingdom shall be eternal.

### XXXII.

And truly, this is a remarkable promise: because it defines a certain person, and does not allow the succession to wander toward an uncertain person.

### XXXIII.

Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob also had a promise concerning Christ, but under an uncertain person if you look to their multiplied posterity.

### XXXIV.

In this promise, however, there is a certain description, because a certain person is named: so that although the whole people were to be led into captivity, yet as long as the posterity of David survived, they retained hope of the kingdom.

### XXXV.

For this family was like a certain star among

<summary>This page explores the theological interpretation of Christ as the fruit of David's womb, specifically focusing on the Messianic promise in Psalm 132 and its significance for the hope of Israel.</summary>

</translation>

<translation page="13">
this people, whose posterity, as long as it was visible, left behind a certain hope of future liberation through Christ, even in the Babylonian captivity and all other dangers, and so forth.

### XXXVI.

<margin>From the concordances.</margin>
In the Latin Bibles, concordances are added to this verse, which themselves show that the Psalmist is speaking here of Christ.

### XXXVII.

Such is that statement in 2 Samuel 7:12: When your days are fulfilled and you shall sleep with your fathers, I will raise up your seed after you, which shall come forth from your womb, and I will establish his kingdom. Luke 1:55: As he spoke to our fathers, to Abraham, and to his seed forever.

### XXXVIII.

In the margin of the German version, Psalms 89 and 110 are cited, which openly speak of Christ, as can easily be demonstrated.

### XXXIX.

<margin>From the authority of the orthodox.</margin>
In a similar way, Urbanus Regius in his Dialogue, Pomeranus, and other faithful and orthodox interpreters explain this passage.

### XL.

<margin>Fruit of the loins of David.</margin>
Peter, without any doubt, refers to this in Acts 2:30, where he calls Christ the fruit of the loins of David, saying that David, since he was a Prophet, knew that God had sworn to him with an oath that the fruit of his loins would sit upon his throne.

### XLI.

<margin>Fruit of the earth</margin>
Isaiah in chapter 4:2 names him—to bring forward his true humanity—the fruit of the earth, since in Genesis 3:19, man is earth, as the Seventy <note>the Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> interpret:

<summary>This page reinforces the identity of Christ as the promised heir of David through various biblical cross-references and the testimony of Protestant theologians, concluding with a reference to Christ's humanity as the fruit of the earth.</summary>
<keywords>Christ, David, 2 Samuel, Luke, Urbanus Regius, Pomeranus, fruit of the loins, humanity, Septuagint</keywords>
</translation>

In the Latin Bibles, concordances are added to this verse, which themselves show that the Psalmist is speaking here of Christ.

### XXXVII.

Such is that statement in 2 Samuel 7:12: When your days are fulfilled and you shall sleep with your fathers, I will raise up your seed after you, which shall come forth from your womb, and I will establish his kingdom. Luke 1:55: As he spoke to our fathers, to Abraham, and to his seed forever.

### XXXVIII.

In the margin of the German version, Psalms 89 and 110 are cited, which openly speak of Christ, as can easily be demonstrated.

### XXXIX.

<margin>From the authority of the orthodox.</margin>
In a similar way, Urbanus Regius in his Dialogue, Pomeranus, and other faithful and orthodox interpreters explain this passage.

### XL.

<margin>Fruit of the loins of David.</margin>
Peter, without any doubt, refers to this in Acts 2:30, where he calls Christ the fruit of the loins of David, saying that David, since he was a Prophet, knew that God had sworn to him with an oath that the fruit of his loins would sit upon his throne.

### XLI.

<margin>Fruit of the earth</margin>
Isaiah in chapter 4:2 names him—to bring forward his true humanity—the fruit of the earth, since in Genesis 3:19, man is earth, as the Seventy <note>the Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> interpret:

<keywords>Christ, David, 2 Samuel, Luke, Urbanus Regius, Pomeranus, fruit of the loins, humanity, Septuagint</keywords>

Behold, since Severus felt very well that the duties of rendering justice and of warfare should be kept separate (see Aelius Lampridius in <term>Alexander Severus</term> <gloss>biography of the Emperor</gloss>), he established salaries for the <term>Assessors</term> <gloss>legal advisors</gloss> of such magistrates. It is reported that he was accustomed to grieve that men were promoted who could not manage the state on their own in the specific matter over which they were placed; he believed that military men should have their own administrations, which they ought to conduct by themselves, and that the learned should have theirs as well, so that each person ought to do what they know. Hence, the excellent Princeps himself, if matters of law were being discussed, employed only the learned in his council; but if the matter concerned military affairs, he used veteran soldiers who were elderly, well-deserving, and experienced in those territories, inquiring what history recorded that the ancient Emperors had done in similar cases, and so on for each matter. To say nothing of the fact that it once moved the Persians to laughter that, among the Romans, unlearned men held the office of judge, while the learned stood behind them, as witnessed by Marcellinus in book 23, almost near the end.

But indeed, we do not entirely condemn the institutions of the ancient Emperors, in that they chose military men, distinguished for their bravery, to govern provinces in their place. For if the men sent to the provinces were eminent in practical experience and civic prudence, who does not see that they could aptly govern their political state, preserve them, and defend them from the assault of enemies? Therefore, although they may not have been instructed in the exact science of the laws, they were nevertheless able to render justice well through the aid of their <term>Assessors</term>. By this same logic, just as in our current time some provinces are governed by <term>ProReges</term> <gloss>viceroys</gloss> appointed by Princes, in whom civic prudence is eminent, who is it that requires the highest science of laws? It is sufficient, and necessary, for them to preside with their authority so that the <term>Assessors</term>, who truly pronounce the law, are deterred from judging wrongly out of corruption; indeed, it makes the authority of the judgment more august and its splendor greater. However, a different standard prevailed, and ought to have prevailed, for other judges, whose duty was solely the resolution of forensic</translation>

<translation page="10">controversies. It was necessary for these men, during the time of the Emperors, to be highly learned in the laws and customs of the Roman people. For then, because judges were required to render justice based on their own knowledge of the laws, it is sufficiently clear that the unskilled should not have been placed in charge of the duty of judging. Indeed, Alexander decreed to the captains that a sentence pronounced against the <term>jus civile</term> <gloss>civil law</gloss> and the constitutions of the Princes is of no moment (*Code 2.13: When an appeal is not necessary*), to such an extent that—as Gajus responded in the time of Hadrian and Justinian approved (*Digest 47.10: Concerning extraordinary trials, and Institutes 4.5: On obligations arising from quasi-delicts*)—a judge makes the lawsuit his own and begins to be held liable as if for a wrong (*quasi ex maleficio*) if he judges poorly through carelessness and lack of skill. Not to mention that it is the duty of a judge not only to hear what the litigants bring forward of their own accord, but also to inquire from them whether they wish to bring forward and answer anything specific on their own behalf (*Code 7.43: Concerning judges*). From this, those skilled in the law argue that the door to the courts is closed to the unskilled, because one unlearned in law and statutes cannot perform those interrogations. But Emperor Justinian confirms our opinion most clearly, as he cuts off all access for the unskilled judge in *Novel 82, preface*:

> "For we did not think it proper," says the most lauded Emperor, "to have the names of certain judges, especially those unlearned in the laws, and furthermore those who have no experience in cases. For our administrators are accompanied in all ways by <term>Assessors</term>, both explaining what pertains to the laws and fulfilling their duties; because they are detained by many cares which they have in our service, they rightly fulfill the part of the judicial process through the presence of their <term>Assessors</term>. But those who hold neither the <term>cingulum</term> <gloss>official belt of office</gloss> nor serve us, unless they can know what is just by themselves, but instead have to beg for the honesty of judgment from elsewhere; how will it not be a very great vice for the <term>reipublicae</term> <gloss>republic/state</gloss> not to entrust lawsuits to those who know from themselves what ought to be done, but to allow them to seek others from whom it is permitted to learn what it is proper to follow in judging. Thus Justinian."</translation>

<summary>This text examines the historical evolution of Roman judicial qualifications, contrasting the role of experienced "Assessors" with the ideal requirement that judges themselves possess legal knowledge, supported by citations from Emperor Justinian and historical precedents.</summary>
<keywords>Roman law, Assessors, Justinian, Alexander Severus, judicial competence, Roman administration, legal history</keywords>

A greater doubt exists regarding whether this privilege also exerts its effect outside the place of the markets; specifically, whether while they are ongoing, no arrest whatsoever can be obtained in any part of that province, whereby at least the goods of a debtor existing in the market, but situated outside their location, might be seized? This question seemed so difficult to Ziegler <note>original: "Zieglero"</note> at the cited location, §. 6 and following, that after presenting arguments on both sides, he finally suspended his judgment and desired a legislative decision from the supreme Prince. But we think this knot is not entirely a Gordian one, which cannot be untied by any art. For as far as the inhabitants of the market place are concerned, the clearly remembered words of the Constitution seem to imply that they cannot obtain such arrests by which they might seize the goods of their debtors situated elsewhere; for they explicitly prohibit the inhabitants from inflicting any annoyance upon the market-goers under the pretext of a private debt, and they would undoubtedly inflict a grave annoyance upon them if they sought and obtained arrests on their assets elsewhere. We do not hesitate to assert the same regarding foreigners as well. For the security of the market-goers is no less harmed by such arrests obtained by foreigners than by inhabitants, and trade itself in the markets is hindered. To which is added the fact that solemn markets are not of one city but of the entire province, and therefore their privilege ought deservedly to be observed in all places of the province or empire. Confer what we have said above in §. 20.

### §. XXV.

Against this opinion it is primarily objected that the market privilege appears to be local, that is, restricted solely to the place of the markets. For just as, for example, the Leipzig markets cannot be held outside Leipzig, so too its privilege, they say, must be restricted to Leipzig alone, as if it were affixed to it. But that market privileges can sometimes be extended outside the place of the markets as well is evident from the fact that Princes very often grant to a certain place the right of prohibition, so that within a few miles 

<summary>This page discusses whether market privileges protect a debtor's assets located outside the specific market town from arrest, arguing that such protections must extend to the entire province to ensure the security of commerce.</summary>
<keywords>market privilege, arrest of assets, debt, legal jurisdiction, commerce</keywords>
</translation>

<translation page="18">
similar markets may not be held. We also saw above in §. 23 that this very privilege of which we are speaking is very rightly extended to the places through which market-goers approach and return; what, therefore, will prevent the same from being done in the present case for the most just reasons?

## §. XXVI.

The effects of this noble privilege are also not ignoble, among which, in the very first place, comes the <term>plenissima & omnimoda ad nundinas commeantium securitas</term> <gloss>fullest and all-encompassing security for those traveling to the markets</gloss>; for they are completely immune from any molestation, harassment, and disturbance by their creditors, such that all judicial acts undertaken against them are null <term>ipso jure</term> <gloss>by the law itself</gloss> and are devoid of any value and effect. For what is done against a prohibitive law cannot but be null <term>ipso jure</term> <gloss>by the law itself</gloss>, as stated in <term>l. 5. §. 1. C. de LL.</term> <gloss>Code, Title: Concerning Laws</gloss>. And since this nullity is notorious, a judge proceeding *de facto* <gloss>in practice/fact</gloss> is not obeyed with impunity, as argued in <term>l. fin. ff. de Jurisd.</term> <gloss>Digest, Law: Final, Title: Concerning Jurisdiction</gloss>, nor does the debtor need to fear the penalty of contempt or appeal from the sentence.

## §. XXVII.

This security is closely followed by the <term>preclara egregiaque lucrandi occasio</term> <gloss>distinguished and excellent opportunity for profit</gloss>. For he who enjoys ready money also enjoys the opportunity of making a profit, and debtors would certainly emerge from their distresses very often if they were not stripped down to their sack and wallet by inhuman and harsh creditors, and if all the sinews for seeking wealth were cut from them. Especially since an ample opportunity to increase one's patrimony offers itself in the markets, the Emperors have most wisely fortified debtors with the present privilege, by virtue of which they can not only frequently struggle out of foreign debt but also restore themselves and their own to a more prosperous state. For who does not know that one happy hour can often repay a merchant as much as a hundred unfortunate days have taken away?

## §. XXVIII.

And this opportunity for seeking and increasing wealth in the markets is the magnet that attracts and

<summary>This page elaborates on the legal effects of market privileges, specifically the immunity from judicial harassment and the resulting economic opportunity for debtors to improve their financial status.</summary>
<keywords>debtor protection, judicial immunity, economic opportunity, merchant, commerce</keywords>
</translation>

<translation page="21">tiani breast, the Petrobrusians the feet, the Albigensians the arms; let the Nestorians, Eutychians, Pelagians, and finally all the rest of the wanderers obtain from Luther and Calvin the portion that either chance may grant or the judges' urn may decree. By this method, the contentions of the factions will be removed, and just punishment will come to the accused. This is my decision, Aeacus, unless you, in your wisdom, feel otherwise. AEAC. Certainly, equity and manifest reason command me to think otherwise than either of you. For the crimes of these two are greater than to be justly punished by such light evils as those you have proposed. No pigsty of Orcus, no stable of Augeas, no dung-heap of Cerberus is sufficient to atone for the filth of Luther and the curses of Calvin. And although you might cut each into small strips and fragments and scatter them throughout the crossroads of Hell, it will still be nothing in proportion to their merit. For they would be removed by only one kind of death, whereas it would be just to die a thousand deaths, and that distribution of their members could stir up a riot among the shades, with some claiming one part and others contentiously demanding another. It is also to be feared that these men, whom you struggle to slaughter for their disgrace and ignominy, might think themselves honored and affected by you with a kind of triumph when they learn that their limbs and bones will be distributed man by man, like the relics of great saints and demigods and venerated remains. Therefore, another method must be entered upon by us, so that while the laws of Hell are kept safe, the crimes of Luther and Calvin may be weighed with punishments as just as can be. First, judges, you must establish that from the time the world was founded, no heresy has ever been devised by anyone as equally harmful and pestilential to the human race as that which Luther and Calvin introduced under unlucky auspices. No Manichaeism, no Arianism, no Macedonianism, Nestorianism, Eutychianism, or Pelagianism (and yet these were the capital sects among all) produced such a slaughter of souls, nor plunged so many peoples into Orcus, as Luthero-Calvinism. Look, if you please, at the vast spaces of the underworld; run through the ranks of the damned with your eyes; review the orders of the shades dwelling among us; count the Manichaeans, Arians, and Macedonians; examine the Nestorians, Eutychians, and Monothelites; weigh the Pelagians, Donatists, and Albigenses; then recite the Lutherans and Calvinists. When you have called each group to the tally, compare these last ones to all the rest—number to number, sum to sum—and by the immortal God, see if they do not far surpass them all. RHAD. You speak most truly, Aeacus. But what could be the cause of this most brilliant ruin? For indeed, if we weigh the ancient errors, some of them are indeed much fouler than those which Luther and Calvin brought forth. AEAC. Even if there are some errors among the ancients that departed further from the truth of faith, they were either</translation>

<translation page="22">of short duration or confined to small areas of the earth, and did not spread their poison very widely. MIN. But there were others whose contagion flowed most extensively and infected almost the entire world. Arianism embraced the rising and the setting sun so that it left almost nothing at all sound. Nestorianism and Eutychianism occupied all of Asia, Africa, Egypt, Abyssinia, and the entire coasts of the Orient, and, propagated through so many centuries, it endures even to the present light. AEAC. You are right in those points, Minos. Those heresies spread themselves most widely, yet they never brought, nor could they bring, such destruction to the salvation of the people as the one currently under discussion, Luthero-Calvinism. MIN. I am eager to understand from you how that happened. For that it has happened, both the situation speaks for itself and Hell, filled with the multitude of shades arriving here from it, abundantly testifies; but how it has happened is not equally clear to me. AEAC. Yet this matter is not of very deep investigation. Come, tell me, does the eternal salvation of the faithful not depend in large part on the use of the sacraments? MIN. Indeed it does. They are instruments and certain vessels of grace, prepared by God for the use of mortals. They are certain perennial fountains, established in the garden of the Church, from which a copious wave of divine gifts flows forth. They are wholesome boxes <note>referring to the sacred vessels or pyxes used to hold the Eucharist</note> from which the miserable seek a cure for their wounds and remedies for souls damaged by sin, day by day. AEAC. But these instruments of grace and antidotes to harm, which the older heretics had left to the Christian populace, Luther and Calvin, with the worst cunning of the devil, have practically abolished entirely. MIN. How so? AEAC. For the Macedonians, Arians, Nestorians, Eutychians, Monothelites, and even the Greeks—whether schismatic or heretical—preserved the matter and form of baptism intact. Furthermore, they retained Confirmation, they retained the true orders, the legitimate priesthood, the valid Episcopate; they retained Penance, confession, and the absolution of sins; they retained the true sacrament and sacrifice of the Eucharist. In a word, they retained the most certain and immediate safeguards for attaining salvation. RHAD. But what does it matter to have the Sacraments at hand if you carry a mind infected by heresy? Where there is even one mortal sin for which you do not grieve, even if not seven but a thousand sacraments are present, you have perished nonetheless. And yet the Arian, Nestorian, and Eutychian heresy is a mortal sin. How then could those peoples scattered throughout Asia and Africa be helped by the aid of the sacraments? AEAC. Heresy is indeed a lethal evil of the soul if it is accepted voluntarily and with guilt. However, if someone is led into error without guilt and invincibly, then it is no sin at all, nor does it prevent the mysteries of the holy faith from being received with fruit. Now, as for the common mass of people scattered widely to the East and South, even if they were Arian, or Nestorian, or Eutychian <margin>mysteries...</margin> <margin>... [unclear] ...</margin></translation>

<summary>Aeacus and Minos debate the unprecedented destructiveness of Luthero-Calvinism in the underworld, concluding that its primary evil lies in the removal of the sacraments, which were preserved even by earlier, more foul heresies.</summary>
<keywords>Luther, Calvin, Aeacus, Minos, Rhadamanthus, heresy, sacraments, Luthero-Calvinism, Arianism, Nestorianism, Eutychianism, salvation, damnation</keywords>

They are instruments and certain vessels of grace, prepared by God for the use of mortals. They are certain perennial fountains, established in the garden of the Church, from which a copious wave of divine gifts flows forth. They are wholesome boxes <note>referring to the sacred vessels or pyxes used to hold the Eucharist</note> from which the miserable seek a cure for their wounds and remedies for souls damaged by sin, day by day. AEAC. But these instruments of grace and antidotes to harm, which the older heretics had left to the Christian populace, Luther and Calvin, with the worst cunning of the devil, have practically abolished entirely. MIN. How so? AEAC. For the Macedonians, Arians, Nestorians, Eutychians, Monothelites, and even the Greeks—whether schismatic or heretical—preserved the matter and form of baptism intact. Furthermore, they retained Confirmation, they retained the true orders, the legitimate priesthood, the valid Episcopate; they retained Penance, confession, and the absolution of sins; they retained the true sacrament and sacrifice of the Eucharist. However, if someone is led into error without guilt and invincibly, then it is no sin at all, nor does it prevent the mysteries of the holy faith from being received with fruit. <translation page="21">
<header>ON THE IMAGE OF GOD 19</header>

with the image of God, an entrance into the eternal kingdom of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ is abundantly provided; but he who thinks he possesses it, through a reckless abuse of the Gospel, finds that everything is taken away from him. 2 Peter 1:11, Luke 8:18.

### OBSERV. V.
#### When we speak of the image of God restored, it is not always necessary to add that it is understood as begun, and not perfect.

1. The foundation lies in this: although the image of God is not restored totally in this life, or in such a way that it attains the perfection of that state which existed before the fall, nevertheless, it is restored in man truly and really, so that the conformity with God is no less true than that which existed at the beginning. Now, whatever things possess absolute truth (that is, things which are not such only by a certain respect or condition, although they may be found subject to different degrees of perfection), they can also be rightly and deservedly named without an added qualifier, so that, if the inferior condition is not expressed, no one is deceived by the absolute appellation. Just as in natural things, not only those advanced in age and stature, but even infants and the most tender are called human beings with the utmost correctness.

2. Indeed, nothing can be brought forward to the contrary, unless even a first consideration shows it to be frivolous. For it is most false that the image of God, without any qualifier, can be understood as nothing but perfect on account of the mention of God; because common reason itself dictates that predicates are not to be taken otherwise than as the nature of the subjects or the underlying argument allows.
</translation>

<translation page="22">
<header>ON THE IMAGE OF GOD</header>

<note>Handwritten page number 510 in upper left corner</note>

or as the nature of the underlying argument allows. The error lies in this, that perfection is wrongly assumed regarding the constitution of any image of God whatsoever, seeing as such perfection belongs to the essence of God; in this there is a significant confusion. But truly, if the image of God is understood as nothing but perfect when set forth absolutely, because God is perfect, then certainly it could not have been said even of Adam before he fell, since you might perhaps conceive of it as infinite, likewise on account of the mention of God, who is infinite. What is clearer than this instance? Nor does it have any inconvenience if there is attributed to the reborn the same image of God which was co-created with man and lost by Adam. For if an equal one were proclaimed, it would not be without error: but to be the same designates nothing except one and the same truth of the image of God. For he who hears that the reborn have received the image of God which Adam lost does not thereby think about perfection, because it was perfect, but about what is to be understood by the image of God; and so far is such a mode of speech from insinuating perfection that, rather, a new question would be needed on the part of the hearer: whether those who recover it possess it as perfect? Full of aberration, and therefore this consequence is null: It is said that the same image of God was received which was lost through Adam; therefore it must necessarily be understood as perfect.

3. And so that light may shine most clearly in this matter, let the dangers be considered which threaten from both extremes. For if it is always urged, wherever the discourse falls upon the image of God restored in the reborn, that it must be spoken of as <term>inchoata</term> <gloss>begun/incomplete</gloss>, and that nothing more should be attributed to the regenerate, the hearers seize an opportunity for sloth, and think that the image of God itself is merely begun, and, when they are taught about the zeal for increasing it
</translation>

<summary>Breithaupt argues that referring to the "image of God" in the reborn does not inherently imply perfection, nor is it always necessary to label it as merely "begun," as this can foster sloth in believers.</summary>
<keywords>Image of God, Imago Dei, perfection, regeneration, Adam, restoration, theological discourse</keywords>

<translation page="51">§ XXIX. It is disputed whether both parents, or only the father, must bring this rebellious son to the <term>synedrium</term> <gloss>high court/Sanhedrin</gloss>. Theodoret, Volume 1 of his works, Paris edition, page 168, believes that both Father and Mother had to agree in the accusation of the son before he could be killed. This opinion is approved with a clean slate <note>a reference to a unanimous vote</note> in the *Mishnah of the Sanhedrin, chapter 8, cited § 4*, where it is said: "If his father wishes (to accuse him) but the mother does not, or if the father does not wish but the mother does, the son does not become a rebellious and contumacious son until both have willed it." Next it is added: "If one of them (the parents) is maimed, or lame, or mute, or blind, or deaf, the son does not become a rebellious and contumacious son, because it is said: 'His father and mother shall seize him'; therefore they must not be maimed. 'And they shall bring him out'; therefore they must not be lame. 'And they shall say'; therefore they must not be mute. 'This is our son'; therefore they must not be blind. 'He does not listen to our voice'; therefore they must not be deaf."

§ XXX. But a new question arises: should Deuteronomy 21, verses 22 and 23, "And if a man has committed a sin worthy of death, and he is executed, and you hang him on a tree, his body shall not remain overnight on the tree, but you shall bury him that day, for he who is hanged is accursed of God, and you shall not defile your land, which the Lord your God is giving you as an inheritance"—should those verses, I ask, be referred to the rebellious and contumacious son? Certainly the ancient Hebrews are of that opinion, and they say that if parents spare their son and do not wish to accuse him, that he is then killed by the <term>synedrium</term> <gloss>high court/Sanhedrin</gloss>, or overwhelmed with stones, and suspended, because if he is a notorious sinner, he is investigated by the senate. See <term>Jarchii</term> <gloss>Rashi</gloss> on this passage, and Elias Misrachi, the most diligent interpreter of Jarchii, in this passage, Cracow edition, folio 304, column 4.

§ XXXI. It remains for us to add something concerning the staying overnight on the tree. This is certain: that the accused were punished by suspension after death among the ancient Hebrews, as Obadiah of Sforno testifies among others in *Biur al Hattora*, Venice edition, folio 73, column 1, where he calls suspension</translation>

<translation page="52">an insult inflicted after death. Abarbanel acts in agreement with him, who in *Perusch al Hattora*, p. 379, col. 2, vigorously defends this opinion. Compare also *Aruch*, Venice edition, fol. 93, col. 1, end. For it is evident that suspension was a penalty, as Calovius teaches in *Deut. 21*. Why, however, the bodies should not have been left on the tree must be investigated.

§. XXXII. Jacobus Bolducius, Volume 2, in the Book of Job, Paris edition, p. 132, reports from Andreas Masius the reason why the law wished for those affected by the punishment of the cross to be buried: that because, from a long spectacle on the cross, one might easily seem to be led to the opinion of the extinction of the soul, and think less rightly about the future resurrection of bodies.

§. XXXIII. But a more potent reason seems to have been so that people would not be defiled by the touch of a corpse, especially since the defilement contracted from a dead person was the greatest among all defilements in the Hebrew nation. To this tends the exposition of Lucas Osiander in *Deut. 21*, at the end.

§. XXXIV. And thus suspension has been examined, as it was among the Jews. Although the wood on which the condemned were suspended can be called a gallows, as Jeckutbiel calls it in his German translation of the Bible in *Deut. 21*, Amsterdam edition, and wood is also taken for a gallows, as Flacius teaches in *Clavis, title "Wood," Jena edition, p. 587*, nevertheless the punishment of crucifixion was not practiced among the Hebrews, because crucifixion is not recounted among the punishments as a peculiar punishment, but only mention is made of suspension as another consequential punishment. Nor does the word <term>תלה</term> <gloss>talah</gloss> precisely signify to suspend a living man, or to put on a cross, since it is also used for those things onto which crucifixion does not fall; for example, meats or fish or breads are said to be suspended on a wooden nail, which are not said to be crucified. See Nathan ben Jehiel in *Sefer HeAruch*, Venice edition, fol. 162, col. 4.

->GLORY TO GOD ALONE.<-

<summary>This page concludes the analysis of legal procedures regarding the "rebellious son," specifically the necessity of parental unity and the nature of post-mortem suspension under Jewish law.</summary>
<keywords>rebellious son, Sanhedrin, Jewish law, Deuteronomy 21, suspension, burial, crucifixion, biblical commentary</keywords>

<translation page="11">overcomes. Law the last, Code on curators for the mad and the prodigal. Parents are more easily frightened through their children. Law 8, section the last, Digest on that which is done because of fear. Nor is this surprising, as they are part of one's body and affections, and we often worry for them no less than for ourselves, indeed often more, as Vwesenbecius says in his paratitla <note>commentary/summary of titles</note> on the Digest, on that which is done because of fear, number 8. To this point, the notable deed of Charlemagne seems relevant; when he understood that a father and son, accused of a crime, refused to confess even when questioned under torture, and having proved that one of them had truly committed the homicide, he ordered both to be hanged. Thus the father, when he was already being led to execution and saw no hope of redemption, terrified more by the death of his own son than his own, confessed the crime to free the son from the punishment. From this appears to follow that which is read in the 3rd Book of Kings, chapter 3, concerning Solomon judging between two women contending over a son.

### XXXI.
Or because of craftiness or deceit <term>dolus</term> <gloss>deceit/fraud</gloss>; which we use here not as an epithet of malice, but for the sake of distinction and difference; for the ancients spoke of "good deceit" and used this term to mean skill, such as when one schemes against an enemy or a bandit, Law 1, section 3, Digest on bad deceit, which is permitted if good faith is maintained. Law 26, on captives and those returned by postliminy. Canon 2, "Lord," 23, question 2. For "deceit" is a middle word, which can be taken in a good or a bad sense, just like "poison." Law 3, section 2, Digest on the Cornelian Law regarding assassins. Law "who [uses] poison," 236, Digest on the Meaning of Words. Nevertheless, when used simply and without addition, it denotes evil deceit.

### XXXII.
Or because of age; yet not any age, but that which begins in the 14th year for males and the 12th for females, and lasts until the twenty-fifth year, without distinction of sex; for although females mature earlier in body, they do not mature earlier in judgment and counsel. The Praetor assists those under 25 years of age, following natural equity, since it is agreed by all that the judgment of such an age is fragile and infirm, and prone to many deceits and exposed to the traps of many. Law 1, in the beginning, Digest on minors. The Praetor assists these individuals whether they are children under parental power or heads of households. Law 3, section 4, Digest on minors, but not those who are older, per the said Law 3, section 4. Exception: if something was done with an adult, the inconvenience of which pertains to the minor, see the last Law of the Code on if one acts against a judgment, because from that the action of a judgment is given against the minor, Law 4, in the beginning with the following section, Digest on judgments.

### XXXIII.
Infants, who...</translation>

<translation page="12">since they do not understand what they are doing, are bound by no contract; and where there is no obligation, the Praetor certainly should not intervene. <note>Digest, Book 4, Title 4, Law 16, section 3</note>. This assistance is also denied to wards contracting without the authority of their tutor, whether they have become richer or not: for in this case they are protected by the law itself, and therefore do not need this extraordinary aid. <note>Digest, Book 4, Title 4, Law 16, in the beginning and the following sections</note>. But as for the former, since they are not bound unless they have become richer (in which case they are civilly obligated and an action is given against them, <note>see Digest, Book 12, Title 1, Law 1, section 15; Digest, Book 26, Title 8, Law 5, section 1; Digest, Book 13, Title 6, Law 3, in the beginning; Digest, Book 3, Title 5, Law 3, section 4</note>), no prejudice is generated against them by denying this aid, since indeed one should not become richer through the loss of another. <note>Digest, Book 12, Title 6, Law 14</note>. It is otherwise, however, if they have done something with the authority of their tutor that could harm them, as in the case of <note>Code, Book 2, Title 24, Laws 2 and 3</note>, concerning which we have already treated above.

### XXXIV.

Or because of the loss of status <term>capitis diminutio</term> <gloss>diminution of legal status</gloss> of the person with whom the act or contract was previously made. <note>Digest, Book 4, Title 5, Law 2, section 1</note>. Now, <term>capitis diminutio</term> is a change of status. <note>Digest, Book 4, Title 5, Law 1; Institutes, Book 1, Title 16, in the beginning</note>. Just as status is threefold—of liberty, of citizenship, and of family—(for these are the three things we possess, not indeed by our own act and contract, but by public benefit, as the principles of the remaining rights that can belong to us <note>Digest, Book 4, Title 5, the last law; Locamerus on the beginning of the Institutes of the same title</note>), so also there is a threefold change of it: maximal, by which liberty is changed; intermediate, by which citizenship is changed; and minimal, by which family is changed. <note>The said last law, in which the whole title of the Institutes of the same name is contained</note>. What each is, when, and in what ways they happen, is explained. Ulpian teaches that this aid or restitution pertains to the minimal <term>capitis diminutio</term> in <note>Digest, Book 4, Title 5, Law 2, in the beginning</note>.

### XXXV.

Or because of absence; not any absence, but a just one, if the absent person, or one who was absent, acts against one who is present. Absence is called "just" when it occurs due to just fear <note>Digest, Book 4, Title 6, Law 1</note>, such as the fear of death or bodily torture, not merely any fear. <note>Digest, Book 4, Title 6, Law 3</note>. And indeed, it must be without bad deceit <term>dolus malus</term> <gloss>malicious fraud</gloss>. We accept that bad deceit pertains to this: if someone, for example, is absent not because they were compelled, but to seek some advantage <note>Digest, Book 4, Title 6, Laws 4 and 36</note>, or if one left too early, or did not return when they could have, the privilege is revoked from such a person <note>the said Law 4 and Law 5 of the cited title</note>. It is otherwise if the person present...</translation>

<summary>These pages discuss the legal grounds for restitution <term>restitutio in integrum</term>, covering circumstances such as duress (fear), fraud, minority, age-related incompetence, changes in legal status, and absence from legal proceedings.</summary>
<keywords>restitution, duress, fraud, <term>capitis diminutio</term>, legal minority, Roman Law, Praetorian law</keywords>
