<translation page="9">Pererius also urges this, saying: 
> Since that translation of Enoch occurred more than six hundred years before the flood, it could be that Enoch was then led into the earthly Paradise, which we do not deny endured until the flood: however, one may not argue from this that said Paradise remained intact after the flood, and still exists, and that Enoch and Elijah dwell in it. And so forth.

What the adversaries have therefore obtained from this passage of Ecclesiasticus, I leave to be discussed by the benevolent readers. I for one cannot grasp what support they seek here, much less what they find. That the words **INTO PARADISE** were added seems to be gatherable from another passage of Siracides, (z) where Enoch is said to be **FROM THE EARTH** <term>ἀπὸ τῆς γῆς ἀναληφθείς</term> <gloss>taken up from the earth</gloss>, that is, taken up or received from the earth or out of the earth. For <term>ἀναλαμβάνεσθαι</term> <gloss>to be taken up</gloss> frequently means to be lifted upward. (α) If therefore Enoch was lifted up from the earth, he was not lifted into an earthly Paradise, unless you wish to maintain with some, or rather to speak foolishly, that Paradise is closest to the Lunar Sphere, as if suspended on high, and by no means to be sought on earth. And consequently, if Siracides had written that Enoch had been lifted into an earthly Paradise, and had nonetheless asserted that he had been carried up from the earth into the heights, he would have contradicted himself, or else would have placed that earthly Paradise in the air. But even if he had said that he was lifted into Paradise, he would have understood, by the force of another passage, the heavenly Paradise into which we truly believe he was received, and which some from the very camp of the Papists assert, as we have insisted in the preceding dissertation; not to mention the Fathers who, with Ambrose, assert that Enoch was snatched into **HEAVEN**, or the heavenly Paradise, to whose statements Cornelius à Lapide indeed attempts to respond; (γ) but he satisfies neither the reader nor himself, as is clear from his own words.

Finally, a third time, from the sacred Scriptures, and indeed from the canonical book of Genesis, Bellarmine, and with him the Jesuit Jacob Tirinus, (δ) argue that Paradise still remains on earth; because, if the waters of the flood had even devastated Paradise, the dove sent out from Noah’s ark or ship could not have brought back a branch of a green olive. But truly, I would almost call this argument ridiculous. I do not wish to repeat what Pererius himself has argued against this: (ε) I urge at least this, that Moses most evidently testifies that the waters of the flood had already been alleviated or diminished by that time, and that the ark had rested on the mountains of Ararat for some days. Why then could an olive tree not have emerged simultaneously on some high mountain, which, on account of its strength and firmness, especially with God so arranging it, might have endured under the waters? Pererius reports from natural philosophy that its leaves also never fall, and Pliny testifies (ζ) that it lives more than two hundred years, and that this is agreed upon among authors. And thus we have also cleared away this third false argument <term>ψευδύλλιον πῆμα</term> <gloss>a lying little misery</gloss>. The order now requires that, as we promised above, we show with the most solid arguments that an earthly Paradise does not exist even now. But because the thread must be broken here, and we must arrive at the **ONE WHO IS ABOUT TO BID FAREWELL**, we shall defer this part to the following dissertation. That one about to bid farewell</translation>

<translation page="10">is JOHANNES HEINRICUS AMELONGUS, our fellow citizen or from Gera, son of the most honorable and learned man, Lord FRIEDRICH AMELONG, <term>τοῦ νῦν μακαρίτου</term> <gloss>the now blessed one</gloss>, who, while he lived, was secretary of the Archive and Consistory of Rutheno-Plavia, a man certainly most worthy, by human judgment, to have lived longer, but who, alas, was extinguished by most bitter fate, and not without the grief of the pious, which is known to no one. With what care he raised this his younger son, as long as he lived, the nature of this paper does not permit us to explain at greater length or to praise more diffusely. He spared no vigils and no expenses. For beyond the fact that he ensured his son was polished by public instruction, he always kept tutors at home who would repeat, within the study, what had been inculcated publicly, and who ensured that not even the smallest amount of time was wasted. And he obtained those in whom, as far as I remember, he lacked almost nothing. Nor did his excellent mother, who must also be mentioned with singular praise on account of the outstanding gifts of the gentler sex, neglect anything since the blessed departure of her husband (for I would not easily call it an "obituary") that could seem capable of contributing to the cultivation of his talent. The son himself did not rashly withdraw himself from either public or private lectures; but he attended rather assiduously, unless prevented by health, or unless matters arose at home which, lest he seem to be lacking to his mother, he could not brush aside. He so ordered his way of life that his instructors, whom he always held and revered as parents of his soul, had no need for reprimand, especially of a harsher kind. He has published not just one specimen of the progress he made in his studies, and he will prove how far he has progressed according to the nature of his talent in his Farewell Oration, in which he is to speak about the reasons for which God, the most just arbiter of all things, has permitted such victories to the most powerful Tyrant of the Turks, who has afflicted the Church with so many disasters, against the Christians; and he will also prove this through various <term>εὐχαριστικοῖς</term> <gloss>thanksgiving</gloss> poems. He will come forward tomorrow, God willing, around two o'clock in the afternoon, and will recite from the podium what he labored upon at home. Therefore, we request the most venerable and honorable Lords INSPECTORS, and OTHER MOST EXCELLENT MEN, as well as the esteemed students who now reside within our walls, that they may deign to listen most benevolently to this son, who does not degenerate from his excellent parent. Just as we shall always recognize and celebrate this with a most grateful mind, so we wish for him, as he departs, all things most prosperous, especially the fatherly grace of God, and the most abundant growth in his studies. WOLFGANG WACHTER / Ebersd. Var. P. P. will deliver the <term>Λόγον προσφωνητικὸν</term> <gloss>welcoming address</gloss> from memory. June 16, 1664.</translation>

<summary>This page concludes a theological argument against the contemporary belief in an earthly Paradise by critiquing interpretations of the Book of Sirach and the story of Noah's Ark, followed by a public announcement for a farewell oration by Johannes Heinricus Amelongus.</summary>
<keywords>Paradise, Enoch, Sirach, theological debate, earthly Paradise, Noah's Ark, farewell oration, Amelongus, 1664</keywords>

§. VIII. Therefore, although the doctrine of the Waldensians was simple and sincere for the state of those times, the inquisitor monks nonetheless traduced it with monstrous calumnies and accused them of the most execrable heresies that have ever existed, calling them <term>Gnostics</term>, <term>Cathars</term>, <term>Nicolaitans</term>, as well as <term>Manichaeans</term> and <term>Arians</term>, and imputing to them many errors against the due obedience to Magistrates, against legitimate swearing of oaths, against infant baptism, the resurrection of the bodies, and so forth. (q) In particular, the monks affixed the most wicked heresy of the <term>Adamites</term>, concerning the promiscuous licit use of women and incestuous pollutions, upon innocent men, (r) just as the pagans once did to the Christians, (s) unjustly ascribing to them the most base shameful acts and enormous crimes of incestuous mixing, and even falsely attributing to them execrable blasphemies against Christ and the saints out of hatred and envy, only so that they might render them hateful to Christian Princes and expose them to the fury of the ignorant populace under this specious pretext.

(q) On this matter, let *Reinerius* be read, who is contradictory here to himself, attributing not a few errors to the *Waldensians*, *in Flacius, pages 752, 755, 756, and so forth*. Compare also *Trithemius, Hirsau Chronicle, folio 145*, and *Binius* in the cited place, *folio 563*, enumerating the dogmas and heresies, as he calls them, of the *Waldensians* from *Guido the Carmelite*, *Bernard of Luxemburg*, *Antoninus*, and *Sanderus*. I pass over the rest now, who present their doctrine with equal—that is, unreliable—faith, and in the harshest words, attributing abominable heresies to them out of hatred.

(r) The writings of the monks are full of such calumnies and fabrications. See *Paris, in the cited place, folio 231; Trithemius, Hirsau Chronicle, folio 179*, and many others. But that it may be known to some extent with what faith and authority these writers have for the most part used in describing the *Waldensian* dogmas, it is pleasing to submit the words of *Nauclerus*</translation>

<translation page="16">which exist in his *General Chronography* 41, folio 211a, in the edition of Tübingen, the year 1516. In those days, he says, in the province of Narbonne, very many despisers of Christian purity appeared from the Albigensian region and so forth, of whom, however, no writer known to this day has left a dogma. And although they call them heretics and the authors relate that they were exterminated for that fault, they nevertheless pass over the type of heresy. I think, as far as I can reach by conjecture, that they followed a hidden plague, and indulged in foul loves and masculine copulations, and therefore condemned legitimate marriages and the eating of meat. Thus far Nauclerus. A truly notable specimen of the monastic desire to invent anything at will! He relies here on mere conjectures, and yet he does not fear to brand innocent people with such a mark of ignominy, and to affix abominable crimes to them, without further scrutiny of the truth and without trustworthy and suitable witnesses. But the very name of heretic once had so much power that, upon hearing it, men imagined the worst possible things for themselves, miserably bound by the strongest chain of blind obedience to the Pope, as if he were incapable of deception. Abraham Bzovius, a monk, is to be consulted on this matter regarding the *Impieties and Sacrileges of the Albigensians*, which he is said by Spanheim (in the cited place, page 574) to have collected from such monastic fabrications everywhere.

(s) Let the already-cited Joannes Forbesius of Corse, a Scottish-British Theologian and Public Professor in the Academy of Aberdeen, be consulted: book 1, *Historical-Theological Instructions*, chapter 37, § 7, folio 72, and book 4, chapter 8, § 2, folio 191. He exhibits the most unjust calumnies of the pagans against the Christians regarding Thyestean feasts, promiscuous and incestuous lust, and so forth, from Justin Martyr, Athenagoras, Minucius Felix, Tertullian, and Eusebius; where he teaches, however, that the occasion had been wrongly seized by the Gentiles from the wicked customs of certain heretics, especially the <term>Gnostics</term> (whose heresy and filth, as well as that of the <term>Carpocratians</term> and the remaining <term>Adamites</term> in the primitive Church, he described at greater length in book 1, chapter 37, folio 71). I have brought these things forward to suggest that the tricks of the pagans, once devised to traduce the Christians, were renewed by the Romanists and expressed in their entirety by imitation. But it is not a vain conjecture of Heidegger (in the cited place, page 112) and Spanheim (pages 525, 573) that the calumnies of the Pontiffs gave the occasion</translation>

And so that no one may have excuses for their sins, but rather that each one may be moved by the liberality of the Apostolic See and by spiritual benefits to seek the mercy of the Lord, we grant and bestow, for this occasion only, upon all and singular the aforementioned Christian faithful, that they may choose for themselves as confessor a secular priest or a regular <note>member of a religious order</note> of any order; who, having diligently heard their confessions, may be able and empowered, by the plenitude of Apostolic power and trusting in divine kindness and the intercession of the most holy Virgin Mary, Mother of God, and of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, to absolve them from any sins whatsoever, however grave and enormous, even those reserved to the Apostolic See, including those contained in the Bull of the Lord's Supper <note>a papal decree listing excommunicated persons and reserved sins</note>, having imposed upon them a salutary penance; and to commute any vows made by them, with the exception of three, and to grant them a plenary indulgence upon the very reception of the most holy Eucharist. Nevertheless, as satisfaction for their particular penance, we specifically enjoin all the aforementioned Christian faithful, in remission of their sins, that both on the Sunday of receiving communion and on the three days of the aforementioned fast, they are bound to recite the Lord's Prayer and the Angelic Salutation <note>the Hail Mary</note> fifty times each day, imploring the divine clemency with tearful voices, that He may deign to look not upon our transgressions or our ignorances, but upon the wounds of His only-begotten Son, our Redeemer, which He bore for us, who was wounded for our iniquities, that by the bruising of His precious body—if we remain in His love—He might heal all our languors; that He who once heard the prayers of the Ninevites in that three-day penance, and who granted life and the kingdom to the thief at the very point of death, may not spurn our groans, and although we have sinned much, may He cleanse all our crimes by the sprinkling of His most sacred blood. And so that all these things may reach the utility of many, and that the merciful Lord may be entreated by a greater number, we grant and allow to all Patriarchs, Archbishops, Bishops, and other Prelates of the churches, that they may cause these present letters, or a transcript of them signed by the hand of some Prelate or person constituted in ecclesiastical dignity, to be published everywhere throughout their provinces, dioceses, or churches, freely and without any fraud or payment, along with their graces, concessions, faculties, and indulgences; and when these things reach them, we mandate that they be received, even in virtue of the same holy obedience, any Apostolic Constitutions and ordinances or anything else to the contrary notwithstanding.</translation>

Nevertheless, as satisfaction for their particular penance, we specifically enjoin all the aforementioned Christian faithful, in remission of their sins, that both on the Sunday of receiving communion and on the three days of the aforementioned fast, they are bound to recite the Lord's Prayer and the Angelic Salutation <note>the Hail Mary</note> fifty times each day, imploring the divine clemency with tearful voices, that He may deign to look not upon our transgressions or our ignorances, but upon the wounds of His only-begotten Son, our Redeemer, which He bore for us, who was wounded for our iniquities, that by the bruising of His precious body—if we remain in His love—He might heal all our languors; that He who once heard the prayers of the Ninevites in that three-day penance, and who granted life and the kingdom to the thief at the very point of death, may not spurn our groans, and although we have sinned much, may He cleanse all our crimes by the sprinkling of His most sacred blood. And so that all these things may reach the utility of many, and that the merciful Lord may be entreated by a greater number, we grant and allow to all Patriarchs, Archbishops, Bishops, and other Prelates of the churches, that they may cause these present letters, or a transcript of them signed by the hand of some Prelate or person constituted in ecclesiastical dignity, to be published everywhere throughout their provinces, dioceses, or churches, freely and without any fraud or payment, along with their graces, concessions, faculties, and indulgences; and when these things reach them, we mandate that they be received, even in virtue of the same holy obedience, any Apostolic Constitutions and ordinances or anything else to the contrary notwithstanding.

<margin>Constitution of the 16-sided figure. Causes of the day.</margin>
**The passage of the Moon through the angles of the 16-sided figure in daily diseases is the cause of critical, providential, and judicial markers. In monthly diseases, it is the passage of the Sun; in annual ones, the passage of the other planets.**

<note>An ornate initial capital letter 'F'</note>
You should construct the 16-sided figure (as we have said) in such a way that each side is made up of 32 parts and 30 minutes. The fourth and last is in the first part that the Moon held during the disease.

<margin>Against those who attributed critical forces to numbers. Others attribute them to forces of the days.</margin>

### COROLLARIES OF THE RESPONDENT.

#### I.
We assert that the Epistle from Laodicea mentioned in Colossians 4:16 was not written to the Laodiceans, but rather written or sent from Laodicea.

#### II.
And it seems highly probable that by this letter the Apostle denotes the first Epistle to Timothy.

#### III.
In Ephesians 4:24, we believe that <term>ὁσιότητι τῆς ἀληθείας</term> <gloss>holiness of truth</gloss> is better translated as holy</translation>

<translation page="18">zeal for truth, rather than true sanctity.

### IV.

From John 20:19, concerning the <term>θυρῶν κεκλεισμένων</term> <gloss>doors being shut</gloss>, it cannot be concluded that Christ passed through closed doors.

### V.

In Luke 24:31, <term>ἄφαντος</term> <gloss>invisible</gloss> does not note that he became invisible, but that he suddenly withdrew himself from their sight.

### VI.

We are persuaded that the fourth watch of the night in Matthew 14:25 denotes the hours from the third hour of the morning until the sixth by the Evangelist.

### VII.

It is probable that the word Cainan in Luke 3:36 was added by Luke himself.

### VIII.

We maintain that the Gospel according to Mark was written not in Latin, but in Greek.

### IX.

It appears that only the Pentateuch was translated by the Seventy.

### X.

In the New Testament, such a Greek language as that which prevailed among the ancient Greeks is not employed.

Meanwhile, we say that those words do not speak of any descent to the underworld, but rather teach either: (1) that Christ came from the <term>ἀνωτέροις</term> <gloss>superior</gloss> parts, which are the heavens, <term>εἰς τὰ κατώτερα</term> <gloss>to the lower parts</gloss>, which are the earth, at the moment when he was made man and appeared on earth. Or (2) that he not only walked upon the earth, but also, dead and buried, he entered the lower parts of the earth, which men do not enter while they live, as they prefer to breathe the upper air and light.

> May God, who shapes hearts, work within us, so that we do not possess a <term>לב ולב</term> <gloss>double heart</gloss>, but rather may we move away from the Earth:

We assert that the Epistle from Laodicea mentioned in Colossians 4:16 was not written to the Laodiceans, but rather written or sent from Laodicea.

#### II.
And it seems highly probable that by this letter the Apostle denotes the first Epistle to Timothy.

#### III.
In Ephesians 4:24, we believe that <term>ὁσιότητι τῆς ἀληθείας</term> <gloss>holiness of truth</gloss> is better translated as holy

zeal for truth, rather than true sanctity.

### V.

In Luke 24:31, <term>ἄφαντος</term> <gloss>invisible</gloss> does not note that he became invisible, but that he suddenly withdrew himself from their sight.

### VI.

We are persuaded that the fourth watch of the night in Matthew 14:25 denotes the hours from the third hour of the morning until the sixth by the Evangelist.

### VII.

It is probable that the word Cainan in Luke 3:36 was added by Luke himself.

### VIII.

We maintain that the Gospel according to Mark was written not in Latin, but in Greek.

### IX.

It appears that only the Pentateuch was translated by the Seventy.

### X.

In the New Testament, such a Greek language as that which prevailed among the ancient Greeks is not employed.

### XLIX.
Next, the renewal or restoration of the Confraternity belongs to this category, concerning which <person>Carpzovius</person> provides some points in his *Commentary on the Saxon-Hessian Confraternity Pact*, where he prudently warns that it ought to be instituted rarely. One must hold that the solemnity of both the oath and the renewal does not contribute to the constitution of the matter, but rather to the validity and more solemn illustration of what is already constituted. See <person>Herr Hahn</person>, *On the Law of Things*, paragraph 75.

### L.
In place of a concluding summary, the more important effects of the Confraternity must be tasted, at least with the tips of the lips. The primary and more noble effect is that it introduces the Right of Civil Agnatic Succession <note>original: "Jus adgnationis Civilis"</note>. For this is established by that pact, and it is so close that the right of brotherhood is conciliated. If you desire to know its qualities, consider this: it is (1) <term>νῷ καταλαμβανόμενον</term> <gloss>grasped by the intellect</gloss>, as <person>Theophilus</person> often speaks, that is, intellectual. (2) Reciprocal, (3) Conditional, by the argument of Law 54, *On the Signification of Words*, (4) Public (see paragraph 40), (5) Perpetual (the same paragraph), (6) Solemn (see paragraph 48).

The secondary effect is that it grants a right in the thing <note>original: "jus in re"</note>, in some way the same as that which the other party to the pact obtains from the time of the contract. Lest anyone be offended by this as an overstatement, we wish it to be understood with this grain of salt: that one should not think, because we have already established that the right of agnatic succession is conditional, that this real right is assigned to them in the <term>actus secundus</term> <gloss>second act</gloss>, as the philosophers speak, but in the <term>actus primus</term> <gloss>first act</gloss>; insofar as they have the hope that, through the continuation of dominion after the death of the other family, they might obtain the free administration of the goods. are exposed, now the palpitating heart is seen, now the movement of the lungs, which at one moment expand and at the next contract as it receives or returns the breath, presents itself to the eyes; the chest has been laid open by two apertures. <header>HUNGARIA.</header>
<sig>IV.</sig>

This change later provided the cause for great disturbances, when succeeding Kings strove to draw the kingdom back to the laws of a just and ancient empire, while the people had no greater concern than that nothing should be diminished from those prerogatives with which they had been gifted through royal leniency.

<margin>Thuanus, Book I, II, etc. Io. Sambucus, Appendix to Hungarian Affairs. Bonfinius, Decade III, Book I, II. T. Cortese on Matthia Laude.</margin>
XXXI. But Hungary was shaken and struck by more serious turmoils after it began to have foreign Kings following the fate of Andrew III: such as the Bohemians, Bavarians, Angevins, Luxembourgers, and finally the Austrians, who rule today. For since the kingdom underwent such great changes of its Princes, it was inevitable that it be convulsed by many great maladies; while not only were morals and laws dispensed according to the temperament of the masters, but also perpetual tumults and the hatreds of the natives, brought against the new Kings, wretchedly afflicted the Republic. And although John Hunyadi and his son, King Matthias Corvinus, while Hungary fluctuated under foreign rule, made the name of the Hungarians and their kingdom the greatest in Europe with victorious arms, yet soon that greatness collapsed after Muhammad occupied Constantinople in a war shameful to Christians, and, with all barriers broken, poured all his forces into Hungary.

<margin>John Sambucus, Appendix to Hungarian Affairs.</margin>
XXXII. Indeed, through him Bulgaria was seized, and Serbia and Bosnia occupied. Then, in the year 1526, after King Louis was killed at Mohács, while Ferdinand of Austria and John Zápolya, Voivode of Transylvania, contended for the kingdom with the most bitter hatreds, Suleiman used this opportunity to occupy the greater part of Hungary and the very head of the kingdom, Buda. Finally, what remained of Hungary fell to the ruling family of the Austrians, which gathers the remnants of the most noble kingdom from the flames and ruins. It is held to be both greater and narrower than that part of the empire which clings to the jaws of Germany and Italy, and for many ages has boasted of an illustrious name.

<margin>Hieronymus Ortelius, Part II, III of Hungarian Affairs.</margin>
XXXIII. Thus torn into two parts, Hungary is on one side pressed by the Turkish empire, and on the other adheres to the power of the Austrians. This is a most harmful division, since the empire, which could be sustained by one, is lacerated and worn down between two, so that now Hungary is barely to be sought within Hungary itself. For peace between Christians and Turks is always treacherous and exposed to raids, since the treaty is hardly considered broken unless the engines of war are brought out. But the Ottoman dominion is far greater

<summary>This page recounts the internal instability of Hungary following the end of the Arpad dynasty, the subsequent domination by foreign houses, the catastrophic loss at Mohács, and the resulting partition of the kingdom between the Ottoman and Austrian spheres of influence.</summary>
<keywords>Hungary, Andrew III, John Hunyadi, Matthias Corvinus, Muhammad, Suleiman, Mohács, Buda, Ottoman Empire, Austrian Empire</keywords>
</translation>

<header>HUNGARIA.</header>
<sig>C</sig>

<margin>Brietius, Parallelism of Ancient and New Geography, Part 1, Book 1.</margin>
than the Austrian, since out of the 60 counties into which all of Hungary is now divided, twenty-seven obey the Turks and twenty-five the Austrians; the other eight, however, which the Transylvanian has cut off, have also retreated into the client-protection of the Turks. The Turks' primary concern in their rule is that they should press all families of nobility and blood into the same servitude to which they have condemned themselves through base reverence. Hence that great stubbornness of the remaining Hungarians against the Ottoman empire, since the nation recoils from every trace of tyranny; nor are they even faithful to Christian Lords if they are forced by sharp fear and by the crushing of all hope of liberty toward reverence for Princes.

<margin>Barclay in Euphormio’s Satyricon, Chapter viii, Part iv.</margin>
XXXIV. The fortune of those who rest under the mildness of the Austrians is happier and more holy. For the people, though within a kingdom, have great glory of liberty; the Nobles also have immense wealth, by which they hold a faithful multitude of clients in their debt. The Nobles possess an upright mind and a spirit made for magnificence; for them, there is no more important concern than that they possess, intact and safe, their prerogatives and immunities which they obtained from the Kings. And a notable Magistrate, whom they call the Palatine, is said to guard the liberty of the people; hence, as Barclay affirms, many revere him as a defender of liberty, set in opposition to the Kings, just as the Tribunate once set a limit of power upon the Roman Consuls.

<margin>Idem, ibid.</margin>
<margin>Hieronymus Ortelius, Chronicle of Hungarian Affairs, p. 1.</margin>
XXXV. The more serious business of the Kingdom is dispatched in the Diets: here the sacred laws and the greater civil ones, here the arbitration of war and peace, are debated. In these, the people appear through their Delegates, whom they commonly call the Estates. Among whom, the Archbishops and Bishops hold the primary place, whose fortune was once ample and wealthy in riches, before the Turk had erupted into the destruction of many, or those addicted to the new religion had plucked their rich patrimonies. The second order of the Estates is constituted by the Magnates, who, distinguished by the name of hereditary Counts and Barons, prevailed with great authority after the passing of Andrew III. XXXI. But Hungary was shaken and struck by more serious turmoils after it began to have foreign Kings following the fate of Andrew III: such as the Bohemians, Bavarians, Angevins, Luxembourgers, and finally the Austrians, who rule today. For since the kingdom underwent such great changes of its Princes, it was inevitable that it be convulsed by many great maladies; while not only were morals and laws dispensed according to the temperament of the masters, but also perpetual tumults and the hatreds of the natives, brought against the new Kings, wretchedly afflicted the Republic. And although John Hunyadi and his son, King Matthias Corvinus, while Hungary fluctuated under foreign rule, made the name of the Hungarians and their kingdom the greatest in Europe with victorious arms, yet soon that greatness collapsed after Muhammad occupied Constantinople in a war shameful to Christians, and, with all barriers broken, poured all his forces into Hungary.

<margin>John Sambucus, Appendix to Hungarian Affairs.</margin>
XXXII. Indeed, through him Bulgaria was seized, and Serbia and Bosnia occupied. Then, in the year 1526, after King Louis was killed at Mohács, while Ferdinand of Austria and John Zápolya, Voivode of Transylvania, contended for the kingdom with the most bitter hatreds, Suleiman used this opportunity to occupy the greater part of Hungary and the very head of the kingdom, Buda. The Nobles possess an upright mind and a spirit made for magnificence; for them, there is no more important concern than that they possess, intact and safe, their prerogatives and immunities which they obtained from the Kings. And a notable Magistrate, whom they call the Palatine, is said to guard the liberty of the people; hence, as Barclay affirms, many revere him as a defender of liberty, set in opposition to the Kings, just as the Tribunate once set a limit of power upon the Roman Consuls.

Among whom, the Archbishops and Bishops hold the primary place, whose fortune was once ample and wealthy in riches, before the Turk had erupted into the destruction of many, or those addicted to the new religion had plucked their rich patrimonies. ### VII.

Antonius Monachus, a jurist from Turin, in *part 2 of his Treatise on the Correct Interpretation of Feuds* <note>original: "parte 2. Tractatus de Recta Feudorum Interpretatione"</note>, enumerates more modes of acquiring a Feud than anyone else I know. He writes that Feuds are acquired by Investiture, quasi-investiture, Privilege, contract, last will, Donation, Prescription, Sentence, Purchase, arms or military force, succession, and the Right of Accrual. While we have no doubt that he, like the remaining Italians, confuses the modes of constituting and acquiring Feuds, we shall content ourselves with three modes: Investiture, Prescription, and Succession, in agreement with Lord Ludwell and Snobelius. For the others are either easily reduced to these, or they are not modes of acquisition at all.

### VIII.

Petrus de Bella Pertica, Vulteius, and recently Antonius Monachus write that a Feud is acquired by the sentence of a judge. The assertion of Ludwell is more consistent with the law, namely that nothing new is acquired by such a sentence, but only that which already existed is declared. Authors testify that Vulteius finally conceded this in *his Summaries, book 1, chapter 9, number 24 of the latest edition* <note>original: "summaria libro 1, capite 9. numero 24. postremae editionis"</note>.

### IX.

We agree with Lord Suevius, Ludwell, Friderico Lentio in his *Disputations held at Basel* <note>original: "Disputationibus Basileae habitis"</note>, and Setserus that a Feud is acquired by prescription, not only because it is presumed from the lapse of so many years that an investiture has been made,</translation>

<translation page="7">but also in the case where it is evident that someone has not been invested: and thus we maintain that this mode of acquisition is distinct from Investiture, contrary to the Doctors commonly, and among them Vulteius, Niellius, and Lord Struvius.

Alvarottus, Isernia, Zasius, Gothofredus Antonius, Schraderus, Borcholt, Rosenthal, Rittershusius, Molineus, Mynsingerus, Duarenus, Hanneton, Schneidwinus, Fornerius, and Lord Struvius require 40 years for the prescription of a Feud in public or ecclesiastical matters. The former opinion pleases us, which Gothofredus Antonius and Lord Ludwell himself testify is the common one.

### §. XV.

Now we must consider the images of the ancients, which were depictions formed of men, and sketched with colors, and which were preserved either in a more celebrated part of the buildings or in some public place.

### §. XVI.

Most trace their origin to the images of the Gentile gods. Considering that this honor and worship of images was more excellent than others, mortals ensured that such things were erected for themselves, or at least for their deceased friends. (This is almost similar to how our people today build such chapels in cemeteries for themselves and their descendants.) In the past, only those holding office among the Romans were permitted to place images, from which it was called the <term>jus imaginis</term> <gloss>right of the image</gloss>. However, it is certain that this right was not granted absolutely to everyone performing duties in the Senate and public office, but only to those who had presided over those honors with distinction. Therefore, later on, with the authority of the Emperors being added, it was not permitted to place images or statues unless they granted it. *SUETONIUS in TIBERIUS 10.* Yet, *Godescalc Stewech in his Commentary on Book II of VEGETIUS RENATUS, ON MILITARY MATTERS, c. 6*, records that images were also placed for philosophers. He refers to an inscription in Rome on the Aventine Hill dedicated to St. Alexius: TI. CLAVIVS. SECVNDVS. COACTOR. CVM. TI. CLAVDIO. TI. QVIR. SECVNDO. VIATORIBVS. III. VIR. ET IV. VIR SCHOLAM. CVM. IMAGINIBUS. ORNAMENTIS QVE OMNIB. SVA. IMPENSA. FECIT <note>original: "Tiberius Claudius Secundus Coactor, with Tiberius Claudius, son of Tiberius, of the Quirina tribe, Secundus, lictors, one of the three men, and one of the four men, built this school with images and all ornaments at his own expense."</note>.

### §. XVII.

Therefore, when a funeral was to be conducted, the Romans placed the collected images of their ancestors on certain biers and carried them in front of the funeral procession. On feast days, they would also open the cabinet in which it was the custom to store the images, and with various</translation>

ways and rites they would decorate them, having scattered flowers, garlands, and crowns, and having added clothing according to the station of that dignity and the public office which he, whose face the image reflected, had once held. They did not act otherwise than if the person were present alive; they venerated the likeness with honorary titles as well, and they presented and recited the deeds that had been done. For this reason, *MARTIAL, Book V, Epigram 21, verse 7*, calls these images arrogant.

### §. XVIII.

It is certainly highly praiseworthy what is said about these images of the ancients: that they indeed passed on to descendants, yet not so that they themselves could use them for their own honor and praise, but only for the glory of the family, which had grown through the man depicted by the image. And therefore it was conceded that this image of one who had served well should be carried in the funeral of any relative from the family, not equally so that it would belong to all his descendants, unless they had likewise attained the right of the image. *See HÖPPING, who deals with these matters professionally: ON THE LAW OF INSIGNIA, c. The condition of statues was different from that of the images already mentioned. Their origin is the same as that of the images. The primary end of a coin consists in the measurement and estimation of commercial goods a. The coin is indeed necessary
pages.13:
both outside and inside the territory of any well-constituted Republic, with the mutual necessity of commerce so decreeing, for no Republic or Region is so rich in the abundance of all things that it does not need the help of another, so wonderfully and variously has divine providence endowed the parts of this terrestrial globe, so that men might be enticed to friendship and harmony, if not by nature, at least by the mutual need of things b. It is not yet enough to have well constituted the coin in the Republic, the care of the political magistrate [must also be the care] of increasing and preserving it.

<translation page="11">
— V —

Imagination alone can reconstruct the individual acts of the drama that played out in the souls of the masses as they wavered back and forth between <term>Ormuzd</term> <gloss>the supreme god of light in Zoroastrianism</gloss> and the Trinity. We know only the result of the struggle: Mithraism was defeated, and undoubtedly it had to be. Yet its defeat is not to be attributed solely to the superiority of Christian morality or apostolic preaching over the doctrine of the mysteries; it did not perish merely because it was crushed under the inherited burden of a bygone past, but also because its liturgy and theology remained too Asiatic for the Roman spirit to accept without resistance. Conversely, the very same struggle that had erupted at the same time in <term>Irân</term> <gloss>Persia</gloss> between the two rivals remained unsuccessful for the Christians, though not without honor, and in the states of the <term>Sassanids</term> <gloss>the last pre-Islamic Persian dynasty</gloss> Zoroastrianism could never be seriously challenged.

But the defeat of <term>Mithras</term> <gloss>the Persian god of light and truth</gloss> did not mean the end of his power. He had prepared minds for the reception of a new faith that—like himself—came from the banks of the Euphrates and reopened hostilities with altered tactics. <term>Manichaeism</term> <gloss>a dualistic religious movement founded by Mani</gloss> appeared as his heir and continued his work. It was the last onslaught that Persia undertook against the Occident, and it was bloodier than the others; but it, too, was ultimately destined to fail against the resilience of the Christian empire.

This fleeting sketch will, I hope, reveal the importance of the history of Mithraism. As a side-shoot of the ancient Mazdaean stock, it has in many respects preserved the peculiarities of the ancient nature religion of the Iranian tribes and allows us to better understand the much-disputed scope of the Avestan reformation. On the other hand, it has, if not inspired, then at least helped to clarify certain doctrines of the Church,

its method, which is more difficult than all others. But to condense this matter into a few words, we say that it can in no way happen by itself, and experience testifies that love potions have often caused not love but frenzy and insanity, histories of which exist in many places. For love is a desire for a beautiful thing, whether it is truly such or only appears to be. Notice of a thing precedes desire and appetite, and thus no one desires that which they have never known. Therefore, we rightly establish that neither herbs nor any drug possess such power as to compel and force the minds of men so that, against their will, they love that which they never chose.

->84.<-

If, however, such a thing occurs, it happens by accident, and not because of the love potion as such, but primarily because of the interaction with the person who offered the potion. Furthermore, because love potions sometimes excite ardor and venereal appetite (yet that ardor is not directed toward a certain and definite person), the one who took it later becomes, as it were, goaded by the sting of lust and, in a frenzied state, loves the first person they happen upon, and especially the one with whom they have spoken often before.

->85.<-

Retentions, of which mention was made above, can generally cause this malady when all customary evacuations are interrupted, such as suppressed hemorrhoids or menstrual purgations inhibited by obstructions of the veins around the uterus. Even in women, long-term retention has no small influence (as <term>Galen</term> <gloss>Ancient Greek physician</gloss> testifies in *Locis Affectis* book 4). It is to be noted, however, that the suppression of menses is taken here as a prohibited customary evacuation, for if it is taken as an obstruction, it is referred to the number of internal causes.

->86.<-

Finally, among those things which are applied from the outside or happen externally, the constitution of the air and the region can cause this malady if it is cold and dry, such as in autumn, or even if it is too hot or 
</translation>

<translation page="21">
sweltering, which burns up the humors. Likewise, the bite of venomous animals, just as it can induce other afflictions through the peculiar quality of the poison, can also induce this, and other things similar to these. Air in this context is understood insofar as it surrounds us.

### 88.

These things which we have said about these causes should not be accepted simply and absolutely, but with regard to their subjects upon which they act, that is, bodies. Among these, two certain requirements are necessary, as <term>Galen</term> teaches in *On the Causes of Diseases*, chapter 2: namely, time, magnitude, proximity, and the preparation of the body.

### 88.

Having explained the causes, we proceed to the *differences* of Melancholy, some of which are taken from the subject in which they are generated. Thus, one is *Essential and Primary*, which occurs, of course, through a defect of the head itself. Another is through *Consent* or *Accidental*, if it is caused from elsewhere, and this is divided into *Universal and Particular*. It is called *Universal* when it is caused by the whole; *Particular* is that which is called *Hypochondriac* in its species.

### 89.

By reason of magnitude, one is *Strong and Vehement*; another is *Strongest and Most Vehement*, in which all melancholic symptoms appear most strongly; another is *Mild*, in which the symptoms are not seen with such force; another is *Mildest*.

### 90.

On account of the duration of time, one is *Recent*, which is to say, it has not yet begun to afflict for long, but has only just recently begun; another is *Inveterate*, which has lasted for a long period of time and has taken deep roots.

### 91.

On account of the continuity of time, one is *Intermittent*, which is to say, it has periods of exacerbation; another is *Continuous*, which lasts without ceasing.

for the purpose of killing a man, which God approved in his law as just, either expressly or by evident consequence. However, that the proposed case is excepted anywhere in the command of not killing, it is scarce possible to prove with a suitable argument.

### Thesis XV.

Furthermore, they violated the negative precepts of the Law of Nature: *Do not injure anyone*, *Evils must not be done so that goods may result*. And since these precepts, like all negative precepts of the Law of Nature, prohibit what is simply dishonorable, it is sufficiently manifest that no necessity can be found that could place the Dishonorable into the category of licit things, or on account of which it might ever or anywhere be permitted to do dishonorable deeds.

### Thesis XVI.

Moreover, this case seems to partake all the more of the voluntary, the more it is evident that there was a preceding deliberation about the means of procuring sustenance, and a subsequent choice of casting lots, which would separate one from the seven, whose flesh the others would consume.

### Thesis XVII.

Next, the life of a neighbor is not subject to anyone’s arbitrary decision, unless he who is the author and Lord of life, and to whom he has given an express command to kill. Except for these, if anyone takes away the life of another, he sins gravely, while he deprives God of the creature created by Him in His own image, the Republic of a citizen, the family of a head or member, and the one killed of the supreme benefit, which he has from the Divine, and which he can never restore to him.

### Thesis XVIII.

Furthermore, it is certain that they raged against the life of their companion for this purpose, so that it might go well for themselves and their stomachs. If, therefore, no one ought to become richer by the injury of another; how can it be permitted that we procure benefits for ourselves from the disadvantages, injury, and death of others

<summary>This page argues that the killing of the companion violated natural law, as no necessity justifies committing an inherently dishonorable act, and that the deliberative nature of the act underscores its voluntary and sinful character.</summary>
<keywords>Natural Law, negative precepts, deliberation, voluntary homicide, sacredness of life</keywords>
</translation>

by injuring others? If the license to use the goods of another, which can nevertheless be restored, is not granted to anyone even if the possessor himself is held by an equal necessity; what right, therefore, will a starving man have to the life and flesh of another starving man? Rightly says <term>Cicero</term> <gloss>Roman statesman and philosopher</gloss> in book 3 *On Duties*: "Would not," he says, "a wise man, if he were consumed by famine itself, take food away from another man who is of no use to anything? Not at all. For my life is not more useful to me than such an affection of the mind, that I should not violate anyone for the sake of my own benefit."

### TH. XIX.

It does not stand against this that S.P. <note>likely an abbreviation for a contemporary legal commentator</note> denies that the others practiced cruelty against their companion, while he who was dead received the iron in his throat with less pain for the salvation of all, and the other inflicted it. Response: Is it not cruelty, if those who are parents of their own life slaughter their neighbor—whom they are commanded to love not above themselves, nor below themselves, but as themselves—contrary to nature, so that their own life might be preserved?

### TH. XX.

It does not stand against this that S.P. denies that the one killed had reason to fear for his soul. Response: He had to fear for himself as a <term>αὐτόχειρ</term> <gloss>suicide</gloss>. For the one killed had previously consented to his own death, and afterward offered it willingly, although he had received life from the supreme Lord not to be destroyed, nor to satisfy the hunger of another, but to be preserved.

### TH. XXI.

It does not stand against this that the supreme necessity demanded this. Let him who says this hear the response of <term>Aristotle</term> <gloss>Greek philosopher</gloss> in 3 *Ethics* 1: "There are some things of such a kind that perhaps we ought not to be forced to do them by any violence or necessity, so that death should rather be chosen by us, and the most grievous tortures endured."

<margin>

III.
</margin>

### TH. XXII.

It is also asked, *Whether the pardon was rightly granted to the Britons from the ordinary punishment of homicide?* which, with Mr. Röhrenseen, we rightfully affirm.

XLVI. For the brain, beyond those already listed, the following are suitable, as they alter its intemperance.
Amber apples, balm of cinnamon, of cloves, of mace, of nutmeg, of citron.
Oil of cinnamon, of mace, of lavender <note>Latin: "spicae"</note>.
Troches of musk-scented ointment, of musk-scented gallia <note>a perfumed powder or pastille</note>, and of benzoin for incense.

XLVII. Diet follows, which more often accomplishes more than all else; it consists in the legitimate use and application of the six non-natural things <note>a traditional medical category comprising air, food/drink, sleep/waking, exercise/rest, retention/evacuation, and mental affections</note>, in suitable quantity and quality, and finally in opportune time and order.

XLVIII. Therefore, let the air be chosen as temperate and clear, which, if not such by nature, should be prepared by art. This is done by the sprinkling of herbs and flowers of a warming and moistening nature, such as borage, bugloss, violets, and so forth. Spirits may also be refreshed and brightened by fumigations from fragrant gums, such as bdellium, myrrh, storax, or other fragrant things. Rooms decorated with paintings should be avoided, because these objects also disturb the senses.

XLIX. Food that is well-juiced <note>Greek: "euchymon"</note> often has such efficacy that nature, helped by these by itself, if it is fresh, amends this ailment, while good, thin, and clear blood is generated, which corrects all malice of the humors and the habit of the body

<translation page="18">moistens. Let such foods be moderately warming and moistening, easy to digest and nutritious <note>Greek: "eupetoi kai polytrophoi"</note>; such are among the vegetables: borage, bugloss, lettuce, endive, sorrel. Among fruits: sweet and fragrant apples, Corinthian raisins, figs, sweet almonds, pine nuts, pistachios, pomegranates, barley. Among animals: the meat of chicks, hens, kids, lambs, partridges, calves, and rock-fish living in pure waters, fresh and trembling eggs, with pure bread, according to the dictum of the Salernitans:

->*Fresh eggs, red wines, and fatty broths*<-
->*With pure flour are of value to nature;*<-

They are suitable, however, first in moderate quantity, so that nature may gradually accustom itself to them, and the heat may not be overwhelmed by further crudities; for everything that is excessive, says Hippocrates in Aphorism 51 of the second book, is hostile to nature. Among the kinds of drinks, thin wine seasoned with the flowers of borage, bugloss, citron rinds, lemon balm, and elecampane root is suitable, as is barley beer brewed with hops, clear and well-refined. One must, however, abstain from flatulent foods, legumes, and those seasoned excessively with vinegar or salt. 25th thesis proposed.

L. Let bodily movement and exercises be moderate, stimulating the innate heat and sufficient to dissipate excrements, but not such that they dissolve and dry out the body; and as much as possible, rest is to be enjoined upon them above all, for this, as Aëtius says, restores the melancholic.

LI. Sleep is especially beneficial because it moistens, and it contributes not a little to soothing the cause. If it is naturally lacking, it is to be procured by sleep-inducing waters, by the soothing poplar ointment <note>unguentum populeum</note>, and by friction and fomentation of the extremities.

LII. From the affections of the mind, all cares and anxieties and sorrows are to be removed; their spirit must be recalled

### LXXX.

For when a person making a promise <term>constitutor</term> <gloss>the person who formally promises payment for a debt</gloss> simply promises that he will pay what either he himself or another owes, it is manifest that he is bound without the solemnity of words, and that he cannot evade judgment through an exception of a vicious stipulation, provided the plaintiff is satisfied with a simple pact which relies upon the preceding obligation and is clothed with this benefit of the praetor.

### LXXXI.

Hence the diversity of this action from a suretyship is clearly evident, since a surety is bound by a solemn stipulation and cannot be sued without it, as is the more accepted opinion of the <term>Doctors</term> <gloss>learned jurists</gloss> through the law *Blanditus*, Code concerning sureties, and the law of stipulations *Aliae*, paragraph *Satis acceptio*, Digest concerning verbal obligations, with similar laws.

### LXXXII.

The <term>constitutum</term> <gloss>formal promise of payment</gloss> is superior to a <term>novation</term> <gloss>the replacement of an old debt with a new one</gloss>, because this does not extinguish the prior obligation, which that [novation] does; and when one person promises on behalf of another, both are bound, which does not happen in a novation, since that does not change the person.

### LXXXIII.

Furthermore, a bare pact of ecclesiastics, according to the first chapter in the *Extra* concerning pacts, does not lift the utility of this action, since that is not received in the civil forum by the more accepted calculation, and the denunciations of the canons are ignored in many places today. However, where they are still considered, this civil action concurs with said pact and overcomes its associate in the place and manner of proposing it.

### LXXXIIII.

Just as the prior obligation can also be weaker for many reasons than that which arises from the *constitutum*, because this [the *constitutum*] adds something of benefit to the former by reason of place, time, or some other quality and circumstance. And even if sometimes nothing more is achieved in the *constitutum* than in the preceding obligation, its utility nevertheless remains constant in that case as well. It is advantageous for the plaintiff to hold the defendant liable through multiple actions and to be able to choose from them which one he wants.

### LXXXV.

And although mention of "money" is made in the formula, that term now pertains to all things, both movable and immovable, transferred here from the now-antiquated *receptitia* <gloss>the action for money accepted for safe keeping</gloss>, not only to those things which are received in their own kind, to which antiquity had narrowed it, law 2, Code concerning money promised.</translation>

### LXXXVI.

Following the action concerning money promised in <term>Iustinianus</term> <gloss>Justinian's Digest</gloss> is the <term>actio de peculio</term> <gloss>action regarding a fund or small estate</gloss>, which the praetor introduced, moved by natural equity, so that those who contract with slaves or children under parental authority would not be entirely cheated, when their masters or fathers permit them to conduct business using their own <term>peculium</term> <gloss>private fund/small estate</gloss>.

### LXXXVII.

The name *peculium* is derived from *pecunia* <gloss>money</gloss>, as if it were "small money," that is, a small patrimony, in the last paragraph of the Digest on the same subject. But sometimes it is also taken to mean any patrimony of any person, law *Cogit*, Digest to the Trebellian decree. Sometimes also it is used for money set aside for protection, whence it is usually said, "money without a *peculium* is fragile," law *Si chorus*, paragraph 1, Digest concerning legacies 3. In this form of action, however, *peculium* is taken in the meaning which we placed first.

### LXXXVIII.

So that the *peculium* is that which a son under parental authority or a slave has with the permission of the father or master, separated from the paternal or master's accounts, after deducting what is owed to the father, the master, or those who are under their power, guardianship, or curatorship, law *Peculium*, and the following law, last paragraph, Digest concerning the *peculium*.

### LXXXIX.

It is not that we think it necessary that the master or father must always grant a *peculium* to those they have in their power, since by that logic the son of a madman and the slave of a ward or a madman would not have a *peculium*; but we think with Julian that it is sufficient that such persons do not take away the *peculium* from those to whom the previous masters or fathers had already granted it, law *Quam Tuberonis*, Digest concerning the *peculium*.

Although we attribute a *peculium* to both slaves and sons under parental authority, we do not do so in the same way for both; since the *peculium* of slaves is uniform, but that of sons is quadripartite, as it proceeds from different causes: from the father or his intuition, from elsewhere, or simply from elsewhere, or from military industry, or quasi-military.

<translation page="12">he had used that custom, and had tasted both their spirits and their manners, nor did he generally disapprove of them, because many things among them were magnificent in appearance. To know them more deeply, he traveled into Spain, nor did he yield to their splendor; and upon his arrival, he appeared to them as he was, a young man of both first-rate lineage and first-rate arts. Finally, they embraced the noble German knight (for they always show a singular enthusiasm for our people, and seem to bear us more easily), learned first of all, and, which is of value there, well-trained in the equestrian art and in arms. For what should perhaps have been said earlier, he applied himself to those arts from boyhood, and thus he wisely joined music, intended for the spirit, and gymnastics, intended for the body, as the ancients commanded and taught. He incurred heavy expense there, because neither the custom of the nation nor his own dignity demanded otherwise, especially since he had become more familiar with the nobles at the royal court. Although the guest flourished in all things, one very bitter event befell him, in which, however, he conducted himself with moderation, because he lost a strong young man from his household, born of noble rank, when he suddenly fell into a fever from being unaccustomed to the climate and diet. I hold in great esteem the deed of that Appius, who was blind. (Most excellent Fathers and Colleagues.) Having heard that a most serious matter was to be treated in the Senate, he wished to be carried there, so that he might assist his endangered fatherland with his counsel. I would imitate what I praise, were I not hindered by poor health, old age, and a weakness of voice. For my concern for Venice is no less than that of Appius for Rome, nor have I been less involved in the affairs of my Republic than he in his. Sixty years have now passed since I sailed on an honorable embassy to Asia and Egypt. Having been admitted to the Senate not many years later, I strove in my speeches to adorn the youth with my diligence and study. What I have truly achieved, let it be the judgment of others. Certainly, I soon sat in the Council of the Pregadi, and thereafter in the Council of Ten. Nor was I granted any year since to be free from public affairs, having served as an ambassador to Constantinople, England, Germany, France, Spain, and having even traveled as a soldier in Belgium. I have not passed over any famous man in Europe with whom I have not debated, and I have diligently perused both ancient and new writers on the Republic, so that what I could not attain by experience, I might learn by reading. Since some from the most excellent College recently visited me and, in the name of the Great Council, sought my opinion regarding the wars we are now waging, I wished to dictate these brief points to my secretary, so that I might leave behind for the most Serene Republic, my most beloved fatherland, a testament of my judgment as I die.

In principle, I establish that the end of our Republic is that which was once the goal of the Roman: to spare the conquered, to war down the proud, and to acquire the empire of all Italy and—if the fates support our intentions—of the whole world.

Secondly, for achieving this most illustrious end, just as we have many and great resources, so too are great difficulties and obstacles cast in our way, whether by ourselves or others. It is necessary to overcome and remove these by force and art. For that greatness of spirit did not cost the Romans, or anyone who wished to extend the boundaries of an empire and impose a yoke upon their neighbors, a small price. Innumerable myriads of Roman citizens perished in war, and by their own strength, they brought forth greater wars for their descendants, until, having been elevated to the summit of power and the pinnacle of danger, they fell most abruptly and perished miserably. The Macedonian himself, whose country is a neighbor to us, counts more wounds than limbs. What of the Ottomans? Do they not bring security to their empire through domestic blood and the deaths of their brothers? Therefore, the empire of human affairs is sustained at a great cost. The cause of this matter is that many wish to command, while few wish to obey; and because he who strives to grow and dominate others does so to the detriment and insult of others, he is rendered suspect and hateful to all, and is compelled to fear the many whom the many fear. I warn of this, therefore, lest in the shadow and the ferocity of our endeavors we aspire to the empire of the world.</translation>

Thirdly, our goods, wealth, arms, men, and fleets must be compared with those things that stand in our way, with the forces of the enemies, and not only those which appear, but also the arts and councils. If we can prove superior in these, let us bravely wage the war we have begun in Styria, which we have incited in Savoy, and which we suffer in the gulf and the sea betrothed to us, and let us enrich the Republic with the acquisition of new strength. If we are inferior, or if it must be contested at the greatest risk to the Republic, shall we make peace? We will obtain an equitable one while the war has inclined to neither side, while we fear and are feared in turn, and we will find moderate treaties.

For often he who possesses all the elements of victory is cast down by the weak. One betrayal, one word, one stratagem often ruins everything. But nevertheless, let us now look at our defenses. The things that can give us courage are cities, wealth, arms, men, allies, and confederates. While I consider our city, it is most fortified by nature, with riches and splendor; the frequency of its trade surpasses all cities of the whole world, so that by a certain law of nature, the empire of the world seems due to it. Of money, we possess so much that to count the millions would be laborious and difficult. While I gaze upon it, I am accustomed to exclaim:

> How much land and sea could be prepared
> By this, which we hide in the vaults of anxious gold.

The ordinary revenue is two million gold pieces when we act most lightly; if we are more attentive to the matter, we will easily collect as much again. I pass over the extraordinary revenues, which the Turks, Jews, and foreigners are forced to pay, which come from fines, and which arise from the trade of the most Serene Republic. If all these were to fail, we can exact tithes and, by ancestral custom, double or triple them. We can increase the tax on merchandise as much as we like. Other things remain as well; for we can sell magistracies, as our ancestors did after the League of Cambrai; certainly, from that commerce, when they were hard-pressed by the seven-year war, they received five hundred thousand ducats. consequent to the Stoic <term>ἀδιεξάτῳ συμπλοκῇ</term> <gloss>inextricable complication</gloss>, I shall demonstrate the following.

The God of the Stoics is impotent, both regarding his mode of existing and of acting. The former is proved because he so depends on the matter which he informs that he cannot exist outside of it, even for a moment. The latter shines with its own light, since nothing can be accomplished by him that the matter refuses.

Chrysippus is my witness 1): *When [the author of nature] was begetting and bringing forth many great things, very fitting and useful, other things were also generated at the same time, inconvenient things connected to the very things he was making; and these were produced not by nature, but by certain consequences.* I ask, by whose consequences, if not those of matter? Behold the Stoic God, so invalid that he could not fashion a man free from diseases, even though he might have wished to. Matter placed a halter upon him. Go now, miserable Stoic, and lift your hands to heaven, so that your Jupiter, by whom you are afflicted, might ward off disease from you: What answer will you receive but this? I cannot do otherwise for you than what is happening. What, then, is the need for such a bridled God, who can consult neither for himself in the dungeons of his own matter, nor for another who is placed in danger?

->§. II.<-

The Stoics struggle in vain, turning every wickedness into matter so that they may liberate their Jupiter: certainly, while they strive to avoid Charybdis, they cast themselves headlong into Scylla. If every evil owes its birth to matter, why does God take punishment for the <term>ἀνόμοις</term> <gloss>lawless</gloss> actions of men? # Apollo, full of gratitude, sings to the Lion who is exalted among the stars,
### and relates him to the number of the Gods.

<note>An ornate woodcut initial letter 'M' is decorated with scrolling foliage and floral motifs.</note>

Though Your Virtue has drawn me, undeserving, to the ether,
Radiating sight, with tremendous majesty:
The flame-tipped fire, the heat of the celestial point;
That impetus of Yours, the power instilled and innate:
And the hidden vigor, filled with a wondrous magnet,
That genius of Yours, Yours, O Yours, that Spirit of JEHOVAH,
And poured deep through Your limbs:
That hidden and all-powerful four-lettered virtue,
By which You penetrate the clouds, penetrate the adamantine
Firmaments of Heaven, and the two poles; having rejected these with Your claw,
You penetrate that inaccessible conclave of the Gods;
Seeing wonders, stunned by arcana, scrutinizing the great works:
Which are in the fates, and hidden in the Heart of those above.
I repeat myself unworthy, and distant from You by as many windings
As the Earth is distant from the ether in its degrees;
I, even now, am raw iron, a useless weight of the earth:
Yet that magnetic Ardor of Yours, that is Yours.

### LX.
For we establish that both guardianship and curatorship are public duties.

### LXI.
But what we have said regarding children is not to be understood as applying to adopted children, nor to those who have died, but only to living ones or those who have fallen in battle for the republic.

Likewise, he who administers the affairs of the treasury, he who is absent for the sake of the republic, he who holds some other authority, he who is engaged in a lawsuit against the ward or the minor, or he who is burdened by three other guardianships not of his own seeking, deserves an exemption.

An exemption is also granted on account of poverty, poor health, and illiteracy.

Likewise, if a father has appointed someone as guardian in his will on account of enmity, this very fact provides him with an excuse.

Those who wish to excuse themselves do not technically file an appeal, but they must excuse themselves within fifty continuous days from the time they learned that they had been appointed as guardians or curators.

However, those who have not yet reached puberty cannot demand that their guardians be held suspect, but those who have reached puberty can demand this of their curators with the advice of their relatives.

A person is considered suspect, lest anyone err in this regard, who does not manage the guardianship in good faith, even if he is solvent.

<margin>LXXVI.</margin>
Furthermore, before someone even begins to manage a guardianship, he can sometimes be removed as if he were suspect.

<margin>LXXVII.</margin>
A guardian who is removed as suspect becomes infamous if the removal was due to fraud, unless he was a <term>Patronus</term> <gloss>a former master who freed a slave</gloss>; if it was due to negligence, he does not become infamous in the same way.

<margin>LXXVIII.</margin>
If anyone is accused of being suspect, his administration is prohibited until the inquiry is concluded.

The inquiry into a suspect guardian or curator is extinguished by the death of that guardian or curator.

<translation page="15">...tels. And the most prudent legislator wrote laws for his citizens. And under Philistius, the distinguished physician, even more so. Plato, who would not have you believe the astrologers, warned us, mocked, and commanded—thus, as mathematical reason demonstrated—even more so, for Plato would have preferred Cassandra and Archelaus to those who excelled in astronomy. Concerning those previously mentioned, whom you would never trust on the authority of Panaetius, Doychilax of Halicarnassus, who was most learned in all mathematics, rejected the entire genre of divination by the stars. I will come to the moderns. Nicolaus Oresmius, a most acute philosopher and a most learned mathematician, also pursued this astrological superstition with a special commentary, finding it shameful, deeming nothing in the world more fallacious, more detestable, or more contrary to all orders, especially those of princes and great men. Joannes Marlianus, in our own age, was supreme in mathematics and held this view; he not only abstained from these predictions but had also begun to write in his final years about their very falsity, which he did not complete, however, as he was taken by death. He used to say that he was a glorious man, these being the most certain proofs against the astrologers, as others—and his friend Luchinus, a man himself excelling in mathematics—have reported to me more than once. Paul Florentin, learned in medicine and especially in Greek and Latin mathematics, as often as one asked him about that superstition, so often would he assert that it was uncertain and fallacious, providing among other things the evidence of his own experience. When he had already passed his eighty-fifth year, he had found no stellar arrangement in his own nativity that he had examined most diligently. I could cite many others who are still living and who, as astronomers, feel the same. But I do not know if they wish to have envy stirred up against them by men who are powerful by the fate of the heavens. Furthermore, our Marsilius <note>referring to Marsilio Ficino</note> wrote against them, openly following in the footsteps of Plotinus. In interpreting and explaining him, he greatly increased and illustrated Platonic teaching, to such an extent that if some seek to improve their own health by some aids from themselves and the heavens, he believes that it is possible for this to happen, rather than believing [in astrology]. I can bear witness most faithfully to the mind of the man, with whom I am on familiar terms, and I have had no one more diligent and effective in exhorting me against these fallacies. And as often as we were together, there was no better occasion or time for us to laugh than at the vanity of the astrologers, especially if a third party joined us; Politian often joined us, a wonderful mocker of all superstitions. By chance, the judgment of our Nicolaus Leonicenus on this matter should not be concealed. Since he holds mathematics as faithfully as he does all the liberal arts, he judges this divining astrology to be so vain that he does not think that even those who wrote it, especially the more learned, placed faith in what they were writing. If I ask him why, then, they wrote it, he answers partly from greed and partly from the pride of princes. For he says that when those excellent men were laboring day and night on measuring the motions and bodies of the stars, which is what astronomy does, there was no profit for them from that among princes, who cared nothing for the magnitude of the stars or their swift mo...</translation>

<translation page="16">...and their orbital spaces. Having seen this, those men, while searching the heavens, would not again be destitute of earthly things. They devised a clever fallacy that would bind the minds of princes to themselves and make them lovers of their profession. These fictions claimed that all fortunes, but especially those of princes, depended upon these stars: specifically children, life, impious acts, victories, and health. They claimed that it was known and explored thoroughly by them—who had observed the motions and natures of those stars for a long time—what they should promise to each person, or what adverse things they should announce. Furthermore, they added remedies close at hand, by which they could repel evils once they were struck, and confirm good things. For if a happy man noted images crafted from certain material akin to those celestial natures, he could, by wondrous mechanisms, draw down power from the stars, making men very happy; powerful kings would seek these, either by touch or by wearing them, and easily achieve them. To gain more faith for all these things, they added that the more secret mysteries of this art had been revealed to them divinely, just as it is read in Maternus that they received many things from the most powerful divinity of Mercury, and [from] Sesostris and Aesculapius. Then, indeed, princes who were unlettered, curious, and most eager for the things they promised, were easily led to believe them, to foster the professors, and to excite these studies day by day with rewards. This is what our Leonicenus says and thinks seriously about the astrologers, and he is not far from the truth. But one must be careful above all that volumes written by great authors do not slip into our faith, claiming to be by the astrologers. This is common to them with every superstition. For those things that are put forward by them cannot be confirmed by reason, whether they themselves believe them to be true, or want them to be believed by others; they inscribe books of such fables to the most famous and ancient men, and hunt for faith in their error through fictional authors. Of this kind is the book *On the Properties of the Elements*, in which he deals with great conjunctions and secrets, attributed to Aristotle; [this brings] no blame to the philosopher, nor any merit to the man. Just as they circulate books of Plato concerning the magic ox, and those which they call institutions filled with detestable dreams and figments, and no less alien to Plato than these quackeries are to the honesty and wisdom of Plato. Thus, at one time, the heretics called Gnostics showed books of Zoroaster by which they might make their heresy venerable through the antiquity of Zoroaster; Porphyry demonstrated with many arguments that these were new and false, and not of Zoroaster. But it is easily seen that those who are less learned in the humanities are easily deceived and circumvented by these lies; for the otherwise learned, when they see titles of Mary, and Phralim, and Iuola, they immediately recognize the author and distinguish the adulterine from the legitimate. Our astrologers, and the figments of the superstitious arts that are now in our hands, so abhor every semblance of truth that they are obvious from the middle. For who would be led to believe Ovid about the truth of Ovid, in which...</translation>

<summary>Page 15 details the dismissal of astrology by various philosophers and mathematicians, including Nicolaus Oresmius, Joannes Marlianus, and Marsilio Ficino, framing it as a fallacious superstition. Page 16 explains the historical origins of these "fallacies" as cynical inventions by astronomers to secure the patronage of powerful, credulous princes, and warns against falsely attributed texts that claim ancient, authoritative origins.</summary>
<keywords>astrology, divination, superstition, Nicolaus Leonicenus, Plato, Aristotle, Marsilio Ficino, scientific skepticism, patronage</keywords>
