## XVIIII.

It provides not only the necessary qualities, but, if it is a form of a living thing, it also grants a suitable size with the passage of time. Since that size is a certain accident inherent to prime matter, and since prime matter cannot naturally lack a substantial form, it is necessary that along with the addition of size, one substance after another is added and generated, and therefore that nutrition along with augmentation is provided; it is certain that this nutrition is distinguished from generation only by an accidental difference.

## XX.

Some things are nourished by food digested within, others by food prepared outside. Those that digest food within must have a small mouth and a certain crop or stomach. Most perfect animals also possess a ventricle, an intestine, a liver, and veins. The ventricle grasps the food that has fallen from the mouth through the ministry of oblique fibers in such a way that it is necessary for it to rush out of the pylorus, unless providential nature were to prevent this with certain glandular tubercles.

## XXI.

Immediately, the cooking faculty—which is identified with the very substance of the stomach—applies heat as its primary tool and vigorously sets about the concoction, with the liver, spleen, diaphragm, and heart urging the work on from all sides. Once the work is completed, the pylorus opens, and the chyle, entering the duodenum, heads straight for the large intestine and to the extreme part of the large intestine which is called the bowel; it presents itself to be sucked up by the very frequent openings of the mesenteric veins by running through the winding passages of the intestines, so that it retains nothing except feces.

## XXII.

The mesenteric veins carry the juice and flower of the chyle through the mesentery to the portal vein, from which the liver, as each of its parts attracts it, is dissipated in its entirety through multiple and narrow branches; there it undergoes the concoction of the chyme or the four humors, so that from the hotter parts yellow bile is generated, from the colder and more earthy parts black bile is generated, from the more tempered and subtle parts blood is generated, and from the less subtle parts phlegm is generated.

## XXIII.

The four humors, just as they differ in species and nature, are not all deputized to the same task. For yellow bile is received by the gallbladder suspended from the hollow part of the liver, and from there it is poured into the duodenum for the purging of the intestines</translation>

<translation page="10">with its acrimony. The spleen drains the black bile, and partly converts it into itself, and partly vomits it back into the stomach, as some of the more skilled physicians hold—though by what path this occurs is a matter of controversy among physicians. Phlegm acts like a vehicle and carries the blood to the great vena cava.

### XXIIII.

Thence, through the almost innumerable meanderings of the veins, it is carried in an utterly ineffable way to all parts of the body, both heterogeneous and homogeneous, wherever any access lies open, with the phlegm acting as a carrier. For that which is most familiar to any part either swims toward it of its own accord, or is invited and attracted from afar by a drawing virtue.

### XXV.

Meanwhile, the phlegm takes on the nature of blood in part, while the remainder enters the emunctory veins, then the kidneys, and finally the bladder, and is turned into urine. That final concoction, which is exercised in all parts of the living thing and by which the blood leaves its own form and passes into the substance of the animal, is nutrition; if not only augmentation but also rarefaction is a companion to this, the animal will grow into a larger size, otherwise by no means.

### XXVI.

When, however, the parts of a living thing become rarefied, they do not acquire some new quantity, but only where they acquire new material after the old has been cast off; they exhale an excrementitious vapor, relax their pores, and imbibe nourishment more abundantly. Just as a vacuum cannot exist in nature by the forces of nature generally, so neither is it introduced when the parts of a living thing are becoming rarefied.

### XXVII.

Augmentation of a living thing, according to its formal meaning, is the action by which the quantity of food is joined to the quantity of the living thing. It is either an action of the same virtue to which nutrition belongs—which virtue we distinguish from the substance of the living thing only by reason—or of another, which we judge to be identified with the unions of prime matter.

### XXVIII.

Both augmentation and nutrition of individual parts can take place continuously, and indeed throughout the whole time of life, unless diseases and other inconveniences of that kind intervene and, as it were, cut the thread of nutrition and augmentation. Nevertheless, the remaining powers subordinate to nutrition act as much as the obstacles allow when the final <term>lixation</term> <gloss>leaching or washing away</gloss> is vacant, and they flee idleness as a plague.

### XXVIII.

Major diseases almost always arise from a great disturbance of the temperament.</translation>

<translation page="14">
# Corrections.

->E<-

**Echium alterum** <gloss>Another Viper's bugloss</gloss> ] I confess that I do not yet perceive any specific difference between the common Viper's bugloss <term>Echium vulgare</term> and that which grows here and there upon walls among us: let others examine it more strictly.

->G<-

**Geranium malacoides sive columbinum minus** <gloss>Mallow-leaved or lesser dove's-foot crane's-bill</gloss> ] It is not sufficiently clear to me whether the small plant we understand here is entirely the same species as the lesser dove's-foot crane's-bill of Caspar Bauhin.

**Gramen alopecuroides minus spicâ asperâ brevi** <gloss>Lesser foxtail-like grass with a short rough spike</gloss> ] The London botanists call this crested grass, nor would I deny it.

**Gramen caninum** <gloss>Dog grass</gloss> ] This is the same as that which Joannes Bauhinus describes under the cited title: therefore, those things which I noted here must be retracted, for I myself had not observed the panicle before I published the Catalogue: but I believed others rashly.

**Gramen hirsutum majus** <gloss>Greater hairy grass</gloss> ] I now suspect that this grass does not differ specifically from the slender hairy grass, but only in size and other accidents, by reason of the place in which it grows.

->M<-

**Mollugo montana sive Gallium** <gloss>Mountain bastard madder or Bedstraw</gloss> ] These two synonyms, *Rubia sylvatica altera* <gloss>Second wood madder</gloss> of Gesner, and *Matrisylva 2* <gloss>Woodbine 2</gloss> of Tragus, do not belong here, but to the first Mollugo of Dodonaeus, which has a round stem and is erect.

It is not yet entirely certain to me to where this plant, which grows here and there in hedges, ought to be referred; whether to the Mollugo, to which we have referred it here, or to the wood madder. I do not doubt that this is the same plant which Joannes Bauhinus described under the title *Rubia angulosa aspera* <gloss>Rough angular madder</gloss>, and indeed the London botanists name it *Rubia sylvestris* <gloss>Wood madder</gloss>. It seems likely to me that the same plant is described under both titles. Joannes Bauhinus doubts</translation>

<translation page="15">whether it corresponds to his angular madder, or the Mollugo of Clusius, or not. Now indeed the Mollugo of Clusius is the same as the first Mollugo of Dodonaeus, the mountain Mollugo of Gerard, and the more common Mollugo of Parkinson. For the figure is everywhere the same; and both the figure and description correspond to this plant: but the short descriptions of the wood madder in Gerard and Parkinson do not.

Caspar Bauhin incorrectly applies the Mollugo of Clusius and the mountain Mollugo of Gerard to his first or mountain branching broad-leaved Mollugo; since these synonyms pertain to the second no less than the first Mollugo of Dodonaeus.

---

-> O <-

**Origanum vulgare** <gloss>Common marjoram</gloss> ] *The plant that grows in Bowyers close at Cherry-hinton is not this, but* **Clinopodium vulgare** <gloss>Common wild basil</gloss>. *We mistook it when it was young.*

-> P <-

**Polygalon Cortusi** <gloss>Cortuso's milkwort</gloss> ] For this, substitute: **Ferrum equinum Germanicum siliquis in summitate** <gloss>German horseshoe vetch with pods at the summit</gloss> of Caspar Bauhin, whose synonyms you may seek in the Addenda.

-> R <-

**Ranunculus hederaceus rivulorum, et cetera** <gloss>Ivy-leaved brook crowfoot, etc.</gloss> ] The flowers of this plant are white, not yellow as we were conjecturing; and it grows here and there in watery places: therefore the cited synonyms do not correspond to it, unless perhaps it varies in the color of the flower in overseas regions.

-> S <-

**Saxifraga Anglica Occidentalium** <gloss>English western saxifrage</gloss> ] In place of **Saxifragæ Anglicæ alsinefoliæ** <gloss>English chickweed-leaved saxifrage</gloss> of Gerard emaculatus <gloss>the corrected Gerard</gloss>, substitute **Synanchica Lugdunensis page 1125, Gerard emaculatus**, and add the synonyms **Rubia cynanchica** <gloss>Squinancy madder</gloss> of Joannes Bauhinus VI, or **cynanchica** of Caspar Bauhinus.

**Saxifraga graminea pusilla** <gloss>Small grassy saxifrage</gloss> ] *I find upon comparing that this is the same plant described by Johnson upon Gerard under the name of* **Saxifraga Anglicana alsinefolia** <gloss>English chickweed-leaved saxifrage</gloss> *or* **Pearlwort.**</translation>

<summary>This page continues the errata for a botanical catalog, correcting the classification and identification of various plants including grasses, marjoram, and saxifrages, while referencing the works of contemporary botanists like Bauhin, Gerard, and Dodonaeus.</summary>
<keywords>botany, plant identification, John Ray, corrections, taxonomy, flora, England</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page: ...as does the one who, while having it in mind to approach them</meta> he nevertheless perished on the journey itself. In which case, Clement VI, in his Bull, while wishing to signify his clemency toward such men, commands the Angels of Paradise to lead the soul, entirely absolved from Purgatory, into the glory of Paradise; the same grace being granted by Nicholas V, Urban VIII, and Innocent X of this century. Among these, Urban writes thus in his Bull: <note>original: "Quoniam evenire potest, ut ex iis, qui hac de causa iter aggressi fuerint, vel ad Urbem se contulerint, aliqui in via aut etiam in ipsa Urbe, morbo vel alia legitima causa impediti aut morte præventi, præfinitio dierum numero non completo, ac ne quidem fortasse inchoato, præmissa exsequi ac Ecclesiam & Basilicas hujusmodi obire nequeant: nos piæ promptæque illorum Voluntati, quantum in Domino possumus, benigne favere cupientes, eosdem vere pœnitentes & confessos, prædictæ Indulgentiæ & remissionis participes fieri volumus, ac si Ecclesiam & Basilicas prædictas diebus a nobis præscriptis reipsa visitassent"</note> "Since it may happen that among those who have begun the journey for this cause, or have reached the City, some are hindered on the way or even in the City itself by sickness or another legitimate cause, or are forestalled by death, and not having completed the number of days prescribed, or perhaps not even having begun it, are unable to carry out the aforementioned acts and visit the Churches and Basilicas of this kind: we, desiring to favor their pious and prompt will as much as we can in the Lord, wish that those same people, being truly penitent and confessed, become participants in the aforesaid Indulgence and remission, as if they had in reality visited the aforementioned Church and Basilicas on the days prescribed by us," compare Marchantius on the Bull of Urban VIII.

§. 4. As for the absent <term>Jubilatores</term> <gloss>those celebrating the Jubilee</gloss> who do not travel to Rome, the Roman Pontiff, according to the delusions of Marchantius, derives his wells from his own kindness and sends out streams to various provinces, so that all may be able both to wash and to drink, provided they visit the local churches analogous to those in Rome according to the judgment of the Pontiff or his emissaries. This is considered a unique argument for papal beneficence and generosity, which the aforementioned Marchantius praises everywhere; he says "this generosity is provided by the Pontiff to the various regions of the world, so that the kindness of the Father toward his dispersed children, and of the Shepherd toward the sheep that cannot flow together into one place, may shine forth more brightly." Then he says the Pontiff grieves "that these living waters, these streams of grace, cannot be derived to certain provinces and regions because they have cut themselves off from Unity, and like ungrateful children have left their Mother the Church, kicking back after they have sucked her breasts, that is, rebelling against her faith and doctrine, and immersing themselves in the foul waters of perverse and heretical doctrine." This grace, which they estimate as great—namely the Indulgences of the Holy Year—Alexander VI granted even to the most remote provinces to enrich his bastards, as Polydorus writes; and Sixtus IV and Gregory XIII granted them to the Catholics of England, who were both in England and elsewhere and could not reach Rome, according to Frostius. Finally, those who are dead and already burning in Purgatory are to be added to these: even they can be liberated from the flames of Purgatory by an indult of the Roman Pontiff, if the faculty of applying the Jubilee to them is expressly contained in the promulgatory Bull, and if they are helped by the prayers of heirs or friends.</translation>

<translation page="21">
and are aided, to whom <term>Clement VI</term> granted the power, when they had set out to Rome for the sake of the Jubilee, that each might select three or four souls of their choosing; for they would immediately fly from Purgatory into Heaven on account of his Indulgences and their merit. <term>Santarellus</term> is even more bold, saying that the Pontiff, through a most plenary Jubilee, can liberate all the souls of Purgatory in one day (Chap. 3, Dub. 12). But there is no need for us to refute at length that perverse boldness which the Roman Pontiff assumes for himself. Since he is not ignorant of the foundation upon which that Pontifical power rests, which he parades about, and which is not apostolic but anti-Christian, we believe it will not be difficult for him to face judgment for these pompous promises. Let the Pontificials show which Divine Author wished to enrich His Church with such an abundance of grace that the Bishop of Rome could dispense it; if not, what prevents us from saying with the poet:

->What will this promiser bring forth worthy of such gaping?<-

§. 5. The Jubilee of the Papists, therefore, is nothing but a mere fiction; the privileges thereof are sales; the Indulgences are enticements. The reasons that they bring forward here to palliate this simony of their Church are of such a kind that, if you were to recount them, you would already have refuted them. Indeed, regarding what <term>Turecremata</term> dreams here in <term>Jac. de Graff.</term>, <term>Append. aur.</term> Bk. 1, Ch. 8, S. 13:

> "The Jubilee was instituted for the aid of human infirmity, since some men are so weighed down by the burden of sins that they are insufficient in this life to pay the punishments owed; hence, Mother Church, in her piety, acts at a certain time in their life so that the faithful may have the aid of this grace, by means of which they can be absolved from the debts of punishment,"

all of this, since it relies upon a slippery presumption—as if our works could merit any grace from GOD—has an easy refutation in the very words of the Savior:

> "When you have done all those things which you are commanded, say: We are unprofitable servants; we have done that which was our duty to do."

If these things are true of those whom a true love for God impels to walk in the commandments He has prescribed, they will hold all the more in the case of those whose works, dedicated to the study of <term>ἐθελοθρησκείας</term> <gloss>will-worship/voluntary religion</gloss>, the Prophet addresses:

> "Who hath required this at your hand?" (Isaiah 1:12).

Furthermore, if the Pontificials are concerned about this elective worship out of fear of the punishments to be suffered in Purgatory, let them first cast fire onto that chimerical figment, and then we will be concerned about escaping the flames of Purgatory. Nor is that of better quality which the aforementioned <term>Turecremata</term> brings forward for this hypothesis of his, that such an Indulgence was instituted to confirm and strengthen</translation>

<summary>This text critiques the Roman Catholic practice of Jubilees and Indulgences, arguing that they lack biblical foundation and are driven by human pride and monetary greed rather than divine mandate.</summary>
<keywords>Jubilee, Indulgences, Purgatory, Roman Pontiff, Simony, Clement VI, Urban VIII, Turecremata, Papal Authority</keywords>

Mascardus, conclusion 377, because it was done against the law, as said above, and regularly the priest cannot be compelled to reveal or disclose these things, just as Vincentius Carrozius deals with this matter most broadly in his treatise on the revelation of confession, to whom I refer the reader, so that I may not be too long in this undertaking. 

This concludes the dispute regarding the confession of the dying; a certain wounded person in the article of death asserts that Titius inflicted the lethal wound upon him, and thus provided the cause of death; or a certain person, in the crime of poisoning, arson, etc., incriminated and proclaimed other persons as associates at the time of the execution: the question therefore is whether such an assertion or inculpation harms anyone, so that on account of this they could be condemned or tortured? Truly, so that we may also act here by way of referral, the judge should be provident and cautious in these matters, and before all else, according to the usage of the forum, attend to whether other indications concur along with such an inculpation, for example, that the defamed Titius was found in the place where the wound was inflicted, with a sword drawn and bloody; likewise, whether threats and enmities preceded it. These, therefore, if they concur, I think are sufficient not only for inquiry, but also for torture, which the Ordinance of the Empire also proves, chapter 27, paragraph *Zum Sechsten* <gloss>To the sixth</gloss>, there:

> If such a wounded person, for certain (which is to be noted) reasons, accuses someone of the misdeed and dies upon it, etc.

But if other indications or supports are lacking, then although nomination alone makes some presumption and an indication for inquiry, it is not sufficient for torture, nor for imposing an oath of purgation, even if the one confessing is of most approved faith, or the confession was made with an oath. Rather, it is to be rejected *ex post facto* <gloss>from after the fact</gloss>, or it is not to be believed, by law 3, paragraph *Si quis moriens* <gloss>if anyone dying</gloss> 1, in the Digests, On the Senatusconsultum Silanianum, and by article 27 of the Ordinance of the Empire, where it is expressly said that this nomination alone is not a sufficient indication for torture, much less for condemnation. The reason is because such a dying person is not only a sole witness, and in his own cause, and as it were an enemy, but also because the confession of each person should harm only himself, not another, by those things which Mascardus hands down in conclusion 386. Regarding this noble question, after the Doctors in the said law 3, paragraph 1, in the Digests, On the Senatusconsultum Silanianum, and in law *finem* <gloss>the end</gloss> of the Code, On the Julian Law regarding Extortion, see Johann Georg Goedelmann on the point of poisoning, book 3, On Magic, chapter 9, number 5 to the end; Didacus Covarruvias, book 2 of his *Variae* <gloss>Miscellaneous matters</gloss>, chapter 13, number 8; Menochius, book 1 of presumptions, question 89, number 81; Mascardus, conclusion 144 and 1078; Fachineus, book 9 of controversies, chapter 90; Farinaccius, question 46, number 35 and following; Möller, book 3 of his *Semestria* <gloss>six-month courses/studies</gloss>, chapter 8; Polydorus Ripa in the said commentary on actions in the article of death, chapter 16, throughout.</translation>

## Master JOHANN CABES, Candidate in Both Laws <note>i.e., Canon and Civil Law</note>, his Friend.

**The** merchant dares to entrust himself to the waves and to bear the murmurs of the high-sounding sea so that he may pile up wealth. If the goods of Fortune are so often sought with such great labor, which flame or water soon snatches away, why should it be burdensome to seek with study and great labor those goods which will never perish on any day, those which neither flame nor the rapid Ocean can destroy? He who does not seek these goods is not wise.

->Willingly composed by<-
->**JOHANNES GERHARDUS**<-
->**FRAUENBURGUS, Doctor**<-

## Master JOHANN CABES, Candidate in Both Laws and Marriage.

**A** dispute has recently arisen between Themis <note>the personification of Divine law</note> and Venus: she calls you her own, the other calls you her own. One occupies you with honors, the other with loves; to which will you give yourself, so that you might wish to be wholly of one? To neither, I think, JANE. Share the common rights, and in whatever part you can please, do please.

->Poured forth at Altdorf by<-
->**GEORGIUS NOESSLERUS, Doctor and Public Professor**<-
->**Physician to the Palatine Prince and the Republic of Nuremberg.**<-

# XII. IOANNES CONRADVS FINCKHER, CELLENSIS.

## EX LIBRO PHYSICA ASSERTIO XXXV.

<note>An ornamental woodcut initial 'T' features scrolling foliage and floral motifs.</note>

Time, materially and really, is motion itself; formally, it is a passion of motion, consisting first in a divisible, successive, and continuous duration; second, in the nature of a measure that is primarily measured and intrinsic, or a number potentially numbered, which is the aforementioned duration itself, insofar as it renders the motion in which it exists formally apt to be numbered and measured by the duration of another motion; and third, in the nature of an extrinsic and measuring measure, or a numbering number, which measure and number is the same duration of motion, insofar as it is distinguished by the Intellect into certain parts such as days, weeks, months, and so forth, and, being thus distinguished as something better known to us, is applied to discerning the durations of various actions, motions, and things, as they are subject to motions.
<margin>4. Physics, text 131.</margin>

In the first and second modes, the formal nature of Time is a categorical being <note>original: "ens praedicamentale"</note>; in the third mode, it is a being of reason <note>original: "ens rationis"</note>, such that if the soul were removed, Time would not exist. The Aristotelian definition from text 101 can be applied to both of the latter formal natures of Time: "The number of motion in respect to the before and after."

---

## XXXVI.

**H**ence it becomes plain that particular Times are multiplied according to the multitude of motions, since individual numerical motions claim their own durations, which are also called their intrinsic measures. However, a single universal Time is given in number, which is the duration of the first motion, distinguished by the numbering Intellect into certain parts for the purpose of measuring our actions and the motions of things. Duration in reality is nothing other than existence; formally, it differs.

---

## EX LOGICA.

### XXXVII.

<summary>This section defines time as a property of motion, distinguishing between its material reality as motion, its intrinsic measurement as duration, and its extrinsic measurement as a construct of the intellect (a being of reason).</summary>
<keywords>Time, Motion, Duration, Aristotle, Being of Reason, Categorical Being, Physics, Logic</keywords>
</translation>

<translation page="18">
ASSERTIONES

<note>A decorative initial letter D features a small landscape scene with a building and trees.</note>Demonstration comprises both the Demonstration of the "why" <note>original: "Propter quid"</note> and the "that" <note>original: "Quia"</note>. 1 Post. c. 10. For the medium of the demonstration of the "why," and thus for the most perfect demonstration, nothing else is required nor suffices except the causal definition of the property to be demonstrated, which is always simultaneously the proper and proximate cause of the same.

---

## XIII. PHILIPPVS KINE,
->VVANGIANVS.<-

### *EX LIB. DE COELO. ASSERT. XXXVIII.*

<note>A decorative initial letter C within an ornate circular frame depicts a scholar in a landscape setting.</note>Celestial bodies differ from one another in number and essential species, but any given star differs from its orb only by an accidental species, like a denser and brighter part of its orb continued like a knot in wood; and therefore, it does not move within the heaven by its own motion, just as fish do not move in water nor birds in the air <note>implying they are carried by the medium rather than moving independently through it</note>.

## EX LOGICA.

### XXXIX.

<note>A decorative initial letter F features floral and scrollwork ornamentation.</note>The form, which is the internal and essential principle of a syllogism, can be described as a certain complication or disposition of matter apt for inferring a conclusion. If this disposition is the remote matter, that is, of the middle term with the extremes, it is called a Figure; if it is the proximate matter, that is, of the propositions according to a certain essential quantity and quality, it is called a Syllogistic Mood. Conversion, which is the external formal principle of the syllogisms of the 2nd and 3rd Figures, is a formal consequence and therefore necessary, but it is not an argumentation.

<summary>This page addresses the structure of logical demonstration, the nature of celestial motion, and the technical definitions of syllogistic figures and moods.</summary>
<keywords>Demonstration, Causality, Celestial Bodies, Syllogism, Figure, Syllogistic Mood, Conversion, Logic</keywords>
</translation>

<note>A decorative initial letter C within an ornate circular frame depicts a scholar in a landscape setting.</note>Celestial bodies differ from one another in number and essential species, but any given star differs from its orb only by an accidental species, like a denser and brighter part of its orb continued like a knot in wood; and therefore, it does not move within the heaven by its own motion, just as fish do not move in water nor birds in the air <note>implying they are carried by the medium rather than moving independently through it</note>.

<note>A decorative initial letter F features floral and scrollwork ornamentation.</note>The form, which is the internal and essential principle of a syllogism, can be described as a certain complication or disposition of matter apt for inferring a conclusion. ->John of Würzburg<-

Learned man, and much practiced in the Latin muses,
Accept the verses long since vowed to you.

Who is not a master, and who does not even possess a servant.

->A Prognosis on the Venetians in the Year<-
->Fifteen Hundred and Nine<-

The figure of an unknown man was seen by me by chance while I asked
Who he might be; the crowd says he is a Venetian.
A headband bound his hair in the German fashion,
A Gallic crest veiled his Venetian head.
There was a Spanish breastplate, and a Roman garment.
To one asking what this dress meant for him,
He replied, "This plunderer has seized everything, and all
That he holds as empire, what was it but plunder?"
I am a true prophet; may the gods grant that what I say comes to pass:
By the merit of Aesop, the jackdaw will be the fosterer.

<translation page="17">
The German will seize the headband, the Gaul the crest,
The Spaniard the breastplate, and martial Rome the toga.

## Epitaph of Elpis

### Wife of Boethius

I was called Elpis, a foster-child of the Sicilian region,
Whom the love of my spouse drove far from my homeland.
Without him, my days were sorrowful, my nights anxious, my hours tearful.
Not only was there one spirit for the husband and wife;
My light is not extinguished while such a husband remains,
And I shall survive as the greater part of his soul.
In sacred porticos, a pilgrim, I now rest,
Having testified before the throne of the eternal Judge.
Let no hand violate this tomb, lest by chance my spouse
Desire to join these ashes to his own limbs again.

## A Poem by Georgius
## Tiphernus to the Blessed Virgin

Virgin, glory of heaven; Virgin, most holy Virgin,
Who art to be revered above the angelic choirs,
Beautiful one, you surpass the snow-white roses; you surpass the radiant
Lilies; you surpass the stars with your countenance.
Pure like a little dove, whose milky feather knows no
Stain, nor does any blemish sit upon your whole body.
Which of the Sibyls do you not surpass from afar, O Virgin?
What nymph can finally be compared to you?
You are called the beloved mother of God, you are called his bride.

<summary>The page provides an epitaph for Elpis, the wife of Boethius, followed by a devotional poem to the Virgin Mary written by Georgius Tiphernus.</summary>
<keywords>Elpis, Boethius, Georgius Tiphernus, Epitaph, Virgin Mary, Sibyls</keywords>
</translation>

# HYMN OF SAINT ERMI-
# NOLD.

<note>A decorative woodcut initial 'D' with floral and scrollwork ornamentation.</note>

Divine one, whom the work of arduous virtue once carried above the stars, at the annual rite of this day consecrated to you, 
->be present, more gentle.<-

While we celebrate your famous urn with frankincense flames, bringing joyful triumphs and cheerful applause of the ones above, 
->revisit your bones.<-

Bones which have driven away many diseases and severe fevers and various plagues, and white dropsy <note>abnormal accumulation of fluid</note> and everything swelling 
->in the limbs.<-

They have restored the lost use of light to those lacking the power of sight, and at the same time, to those long lame, they have suddenly given 
->a firm knee.<-

Moreover, they have put to flight the horrid shadows and sad Furies <note>avenging spirits of the underworld</note> from the darkness, which often tortured the limbs of 
->men who were suffering.<-

Visit this seat of yours, Father ERMINOLD, which you were the first to cultivate, and look upon the flock prone at your urn 
->with a peaceful light.<-

You who watch over your descendants, destined to be inhabitants of the golden heaven, have mercy on our final life 
->and remove our perils.<-
</translation>

<translation page="14">If you hasten as a pilgrim to other shores,
Who will be the priest, who will be the leader, under whom Germany 
Will be able to preserve the true faith:
For the heretics rejoice now that you are departing,
If you were to stay, they would consume their hearts with excessive grief.
Halt your steps, Martin, and check your pace.
But if you do not leave, then you will save yourself for your friends,
And you will save yourself for God and for the friends faithful to you:
And the Church, performing the duties of its office
Long since omitted, will now enjoy freedom:
And venerable piety will remain at its proper value.
Halt your steps, Martin, and check your pace.
Look where you are going, you will depart for Rome as a German:
Climbing the high summits of the airy mountains,
Then descending as if sent into the depths of the underworld:
Perhaps a thief will also prepare hidden snares,
Who might seek either your wealth or, in the end, your life.
Halt your steps, Martin, and check your pace.
The storm forbids it, the North Wind forbids it, Aeolus, releasing
All the winds enclosed in their prisons from every side,
Dissuades this journey; but if you refuse to obey,
Perhaps you will be forced to meet death and heavy disasters:
But God and fortune will prepare better things for you.
Halt your steps, Martin, and check your pace.

<translation page="17">
# THE PRECEPTS OF THE MOSAIC LAW.
->Reduced to a summary.<-

## FIRST PRECEPT.
### YOU SHALL HAVE NO OTHER GODS
This means the fear of God in love, in true faith, in solid hope, in favorable and adverse circumstances, and finally in one's entire life.

### THE GUILTY OF THIS PRECEPT.
Whoever attributes their life and condition, in every state of fortune, to someone other than God; who relies on themselves or their own, and not on God.

## SECOND PRECEPT.
### YOU SHALL NOT TAKE THE NAME OF YOUR GOD
->In vain.<-
This means to attribute glory, honor, and blessing to God; to worship Him alone; to attribute whatever good you have to Him alone; to call upon Him; to despise oneself. No one doubts that whatever is good is the name of God.

### THE GUILTY OF THIS PRECEPT.
Whoever uses the name of God for anything other than His glory. Whoever flatters themselves with some personal good; who seeks virtue and praise from elsewhere than from God.

## THIRD PRECEPT.
### KEEP THE SABBATH HOLY.
This means to attend to God, to desire and seek His grace alone.

### THE GUILTY.
Whoever does not rest in spirit for God, but persists in work on a holy day; who does not care for divine things, or cares for them coldly; who does not observe the Sabbath as a rest, even from vices.

## FOURTH PRECEPT.
### HONOR YOUR FATHER AND MOTHER.
This means to obey God, and for the sake of God to obey all authority, even up to the point of tyranny; to support parents not only with greetings and nods, but with the diligence of one’s own works, and to assist them especially with acts of kindness.

### THE GUILTY.
<column-break/>
</translation>

<translation page="18">
Whoever flees, despises, and neglects their parents; whoever turns away from and hates magistrates and the law; who does not obey authority, or obeys it unwillingly.

### Fifth Precept.
## YOU SHALL NOT KILL.

This means patience, peace, humanity, mercy, and (to say it in one word) an entire life without the bitterness of malevolence, even toward an enemy, and remaining prompt and beneficial.

### THE GUILTY.

Whoever does not help their brother with counsel, aid, and work; who does not prevent harm from coming to their neighbor.

### Sixth Precept.
## YOU SHALL NOT COMMIT ADULTERY.

This means purity and modesty of mind, speech, and deeds; frugality of living; an undefiled love of heavenly things; contempt for pleasures; the love of God alone.

### THE GUILTY.

Whoever is dissolute in pleasures, or enjoys laughter and joy too immodestly, or does not restrain and bridle them while enjoying them. And whoever allows their soul to care for things other than God.

### Seventh Precept.
## YOU SHALL NOT STEAL.

This means the flight from all avarice, joyful poverty, liberality, and humanity.

### THE GUILTY.

Whoever is unwilling to give to their neighbor as a loan, freely and without interest; who attaches their mind too intemperately to any worldly goods; who bears poverty unwillingly; who denies alms, or does not bestow them in a timely manner; who circumvents their neighbor with deceit and imposture.

### Eighth Precept.
## YOU SHALL NOT BEAR FALSE WITNESS.

This means the naked and simple truth of words and deeds; a tongue that fosters peace, seeks the advantage of one’s brother, desires to compose discord, refutes disparagement, and cleanses and covers the defamation of one’s neighbor.

### THE GUILTY.

<summary>This text provides a summarized interpretation of the Decalogue, defining the ethical demands of each commandment and identifying the behaviors that constitute violations of them.</summary>
<keywords>Mosaic Law, Decalogue, Precepts, Sin, Ethics, God, Charity, Truth</keywords>
</translation>

<meta>continues from previous page: so that they might engage in battle with arms, so that they might not kill me with a cruel death. Pilate speaks again to the crowd with a loud voice: This man is upright in his life, and pure from every crime, for whom you seek a source of harm, and for whom you wish for the gallows. The people pressed further with bitter words: Powerful in sedition, and an open inventor of crimes, who taught impious dogmas with a blasphemous tongue, and filled the whole of the Galilean countryside with tumult. But the Lord kept silent, he added not a single word further, those things seemed wonderful enough to Pilate. But when Pilate, a crafty fox, senses that Herod held JESUS under his jurisdiction, he sent him to that hard and savage tyrant. Herod conceives new joys in his happy spirit, he hopes that this man will perform some miraculous deed, inimitable by anyone. Although he moved words about various matters, he responded nothing, he prepared nothing against him with his voice. The mocker held Christ in contempt <note>original: "naso suspendit adunco", literally "hung by a hooked nose", a classical idiom for mockery or disdain</note>, he sends him back to Pilate dressed in a shining garment. Pilate calls together the first of the nobles and the ignoble crowd, he spoke such things with angry words: You have brought this man as if he were stirring up wars, and dared a crime to be tamed by present death, but I find nothing worthy of death or prison. <note>A decorative initial P appears here.</note>
While Peter opens the stars with apostolic keys,

<note>A decorative initial O appears here.</note>

<translation page="21">that various punishments existed among various nations is, I believe, not unknown to you, and will be explained at some time in its own place and time. Zaleucus also passed a law concerning this, that whoever was convicted of adultery should have both eyes gouged out. But when the son of Zaleucus himself had sinned in this matter and had been found guilty of adultery, and was now to be punished according to his father's law, the whole citizenry professed that they would willingly pardon the son's crime in consideration of the father's virtue and merits. But the father, urging the law and contending that it must be confirmed by his own penalty and that of his kin, when he could not obtain from the people that the son be blinded in both eyes, finally, by an admirable tempering of justice and paternal affection, brought it about that the law was kept inviolate, and that he bestowed upon his son as much paternal affection as the law allowed. For he ordered one eye of the son to be removed, and one of his own. Finally, however, as Suidas noted, he met his death fighting most bravely for his fatherland, to teach others by his own example how sweet and fitting it is to die for one's country.

You have, excellent auditors, what I could learn concerning Charondas and Zaleucus: I earnestly ask that you allow the commemoration of them, whatever its quality, to have been not unwelcome to you, and that you do not regret this time spent.

Concerning myself, and the duties of this office entrusted to me, I would not have you expect me to say anything. For I prefer to demonstrate whatever is in me by the deed itself, for the benefit of the studies of our most flourishing youth and for the adorning of this <term>Sparta</term> <gloss>metaphor for one's assigned task or sphere of duty</gloss>, rather than to promise it at length in words. That I may be able to perform this, I humbly venerate and pray to God, the greatest and best, the author of honest laws and political order, and the fountain of all good.

<translation page="22"><note>An ornamental horizontal band at the top of the page featuring a repeating floral or fleur-de-lis pattern within interlaced circles.</note>

# TO THE BENEVOLENT READER. GREETINGS.

<note>Decorative drop cap 'C' at the start of the text, featuring an ornate floral background with scrollwork.</note>

Since our lawgivers in their prefaces deter men from evil deeds primarily through the mention and consideration of death, because everyone is accustomed to being tormented by the conscience and repentance of those deeds as they draw near to it, but have not added the cause of this thing—which is undoubtedly that a guilty mind has a presentiment of the future judgment and the punishments hanging over it (for what would he fear who believes all things are finished by death?)—so that it may be clear that not even this was unknown to the heathens, it pleases me to append here the most distinguished **IAMBICS OF THE COMIC POET PHILEMON**, which I once rendered from Greek into Latin. The Greek originals are extant partly in Justin Martyr, in his work *On Monarchy*, and partly in Eusebius, in book 13 of the *Evangelical Preparation*, and in Clement of Alexandria, who however attribute these last two to the author **DIPHILUS**. I desire that this work be approved by you, kind reader. V.

> Do you think, Nicostratus, that the dead,
> Who lived in every luxury while they breathed,
> Are thus buried in the earth,
> Only to escape the Divine for all eternity,
> And to hide themselves away in flight?
> The lights of Justice see all these things.
> For we believe there are two paths to the underworld,
> Of which one is for the just, the other for the impious.
> But if the same fortune awaits the pious and the impious,
> Why not kill, steal, and plunder
> Whatever you can, and mingle the depths with the heights?
> What prevents it? An error, my good man, do not let it deceive you:
> Each man's own deeds await him in the underworld,
> Over which will preside the ruler of all, **GOD**:
> Whose tremendous name I could not speak:
> Who often prolongs life for those who sin.
>
> But if any of the mortals, while committing evils
> From day to day, assumes that he is hidden from the Gods,
> He assumes falsely, and enters onto paths of ruin,
> Until the vengeance of **GOD** rests a while.
>
> See for yourselves, you to whom the Gods are but fables:
> God exists, he exists. But if anyone acts wickedly,
> Being of a depraved nature, let him profit for the moment.
> For later, when time has passed, he will pay the penalty.

<summary>The author provides a preface and a poetic translation from Greek sources (Philemon/Diphilus) arguing that ancient pagan writers understood the necessity of divine justice after death to deter wrongdoing.</summary>
<keywords>Philemon, Diphilus, Divine Judgment, Justice, afterlife, ethics</keywords></translation>

While he trusts everything to everyone with a simple mind, he ensures that *Nothing* is trusted to him. The *Politicus* <note>politician</note> prudently despairs of everything, hopes for everything bravely, guards against everything diligently, and thus finally fears *Nothing*. If you are wise, do everything cautiously and quickly, but do *Nothing* rashly or timidly, suddenly or late. Do you ask what you can do without the help of the Best and Greatest **GOD**? *Nothing*. Among Christians, life will condemn some, doctrine others. There are not a few who would defend their religion right up to the fire **EXCLUSIVELY**. It is a marvel that, while pure religion recommends piety, it usually achieves *Nothing*. You will often see men who, their whole life long, are joyful, drinking, and tumultuous. But when a more unfortunate hour strikes, they hurry to their prayer books, and, having first wiped away the dust, they contort their grim faces into devotion, and sighing much, they seek out certain short prayers suitable for their misfortune. Then they count the pages of those prayers, and if they are too long, they either seek out shorter ones or close their books again. Because these people are destitute of harmony between heart and mouth, they deserve to receive *Nothing* from **GOD**. If eyes were plucked out as often as they took scandal and sinned, the entire human race would soon see *Nothing*. On the last day, certain rich men will say that they cast gold, that cursed metal, that incitement to all evils, at the feet of the lyre-player and the flute-player. But to the poor, the friends of Christ, they will cry out that they gave *Nothing* with a religious hand.</translation>

<translation page="11">ORATION.

Praetors and other citizens and wealthy rustics are accustomed to send roosters, capons, geese, thrushes, and other things to the Magnates. But to the poor they give *Nothing*. O madmen! If you wish to send gifts suitable to each person, send food to the poor, and to your patrons either hunger or *Nothing*. Dung, though an excrement, is indeed vile, yet it is not useless. For without it, physicians and farmers possess *Nothing*. <term>Jurisconsults</term> <gloss>lawyers</gloss> love to draw out a litigious case as if it were never to end, and when they have lost the case—and the client his assets—they demand their fee nonetheless, at least because they are shameless. If the client is wise, for the sake of showing gratitude, he gives them *Nothing*. Politicians, who return from Italy and France departing from the customs of our fathers, and who hear all fleas coughing and always rattle off new institutions—not because they are good, but because they are new—they, I say, sometimes seem to imitate <term>Orbilius</term> <note>a Roman grammarian known for his severity</note>, who, intending to reform grammar, did not want his students to say "Sum, Es, Est" <gloss>I am, you are, he/she/it is</gloss>, but "Sum, Sus, Sut." To whom a certain man endowed with old-fashioned faith and morals said in his ear: "Sum, sus, sut, does no good; Sum, es, est, let it remain as it has been." But these same politicians, if they disapprove of everything, worship *Nothing*. There are many <term>Pompeians</term> if Pompey wins. If <term>Caesar</term> wins, they immediately become Caesareans. Do you ask what good princes should expect from these men? *Nothing*. The temple of <term>Ephesian Diana</term> rendered debtors safe from their creditors. Do you ask what provides a safer asylum in this matter? Apart from thrift, *Nothing*. A merchant, if he has lost his property and credit, sings empty-handed before a robber on the road, because he sees that *Nothing* remains for him henceforth. The ancients trusted in coins without a handwritten note, without wax. Now, without both, *Nothing*. I was faithful to <term>Dindymus</term> in both fortunes; he was treacherous to me</translation>

<translation page="13">The bloody TYRANNY struck my spirit, the one with which they strive to expand the Church of Christ, while drunk on the blood of the saints (l). But what they write in the blood of Christians, everyone will read; no future generation will erase it.

For these reasons, therefore, as if by repeated cock-crowing, I was awakened to go out from Babylon, so that the plagues, destined by the just judgment of God, might not rush upon me as well.

*I have departed!* Now I cross over to *You*, who profess the true faith. I have presented my CONFESSION to the leaders of your Church, the summary of which will be read aloud so that it may be known to all. I testify before GOD, before the NURTURING Church, and before ALL OF YOU, solemnly, that I profess this (*m*) with my MOUTH, and believe this with my HEART.

I promise nothing; I am human; but this I hope for with certainty from Divine grace: NOTHING in the world, whether to the right or to the left, will change my resolve.

With this spirit, I PLEDGE MY FAITH to you, and I implore your prayers. Receive me AS A NEWBORN BABE, (*n*) whose desire is to overcome the world through faith. Thus, therefore, I am YOURS, and I shall remain YOURS by the grace of God.

---

(l) Rev. 17:6. (*m*) Rom. 10:9. (*n*) 1 John 5:4, 5.

<translation page="14">Therefore, I lift my eyes to your pinnacle, MOST SERENE PRINCE. You received me, and so that my exile would neither bring shame nor cause want, you sustained me with MAGNIFICENT GENEROSITY. May GOD repay this MERCY to YOU and to YOUR ROYAL FAMILY. I cast myself at your feet; protect me, and use me if I am worth anything. I shall be yours, as long as I live, in faith, prayers, obedience, and service. May God grant You a long life, a lasting Rule, peace to Your lands, victory over the enemy, and through You, the GLORY OF RELIGION, OF YOUR NAME, AND OF YOUR FAMILY.

Now, strengthen me with *Your grace*. Confirm This COVENANT, which I profess in this solemn <term>Synaxis</term> <gloss>assembly/communion</gloss> through the death of YOUR SON, so that it may be for me the certainty of my SALVATION. I HAVE SPOKEN.

> Semiramis of Ninus, who, happy with such a husband,
> Possessed much, but added more to the former,

> Expelled her stepson Trebeta from his ancestral kingdom,

But these are, without doubt, the delusions of idle monks, which we choose to recount rather than refute, along with Philipp Clüver in *Ancient Germany*, Book 2, chapter 14, concerning the Treviri, page 383.

§. 15. Go now, all you who in every way exclude the weaker sex from the keys of power and from the commerce of virtues. We do not hear or approve of everything, without exception, that Bodin, *On the Republic*, Book 6, chapter 5; Arnisaeus, *Political Doctrine*, Book 1, chapter 9, and *Political Relections*, Book 2, chapter 2, section 12; Menochius, *Hierapoliticus*, Book 1, chapter 5; Petilius, *Exarchate*, Book 2, chapters 29 and 30; and Schönborn, *Politics*, Book 2, chapter 12, page 122, have devised for the subversion of <term>Gynaecocracy</term> <gloss>rule by women</gloss>. Virtue is closed to no one; it admits all, and it chooses neither sex nor rank. With Seneca, and the opinion of Tholosanus, *On the Republic*, Book 7, chapter 11; Adam Contzen, *Civil Doctrine*, Book 1, chapter 26; and Danaeus, *Politics*, Book 6, chapter 4, we say, as is fitting: Not always in the narrow breast of women

> Does the fragile mind fluctuate in an easy tide of vices:

And she has that which Schurman replies, saying: Perhaps emulation, or certainly fear, vexes those who think this way, lest that old saying of Ennius should one day come to pass:

> For you men carry womanly spirits,
> That woman, a man.

Alexander the Great was more rightly in admiration of no one than Semiramis and Cyrus; Curtius, Book 7, chapter 6. Julius Caesar also prudently appeals to the empire of Semiramis in Suetonius, §. 23.</translation>

<translation page="16">§. 16. But that the truth of that Maronian <note>referring to Virgil, a native of Mantua (Mantua me genuit)</note> verse might not fail:
->We each endure our own shades;<-
Semiramis also performed magnificent deeds, not only for praise, but for condemnation, as Berosus the monk of Annius of Viterbo says on page 48. Nor is any other vice attributed to her more than lust, for she admitted all the most energetic soldiers to her intimacy, and, after they had been delighted by the use of her body, she removed them from the midst, lest the report of her fornication should spread to the common people. Claudian traces the first eunuchs back to Semiramis; yet Claudius Barthius seems to doubt this due to the silence of Diodorus in his *Annotations on Eutropius*, Book I, page 1325. Ammianus Marcellinus, in Book 14, cited by Henelius in *Wrocław Leisure*, chapter 35, page 274, embraces the side of Claudian when he says: "Wherever anyone walks, seeing the columns of mutilated men, he shall detest the memory of Semiramis, that ancient Queen, who was the first of all to castrate tender males." Pliny writes in his *Natural History*, Book 8, chapter 42, based on Juba, that she had relations with a horse. Indeed, Paulus Orosius testifies in Book 1, chapter 4, that she finally decreed that sexual intercourse and marriages between parents and children should be legally permitted. It is said by Justin and others that, intending to give a specimen of the observance of this law, she sought the bed of her son Ninyas, and was killed by him as he averted such a wicked crime. The history regarding her death is doubtful, however, and it is not sufficiently clear whether she perished from wounds in war or by the crime of her son. Wagner, *Historical Institutions*, Book 3, page 201.

§. 17. The remains of Semiramis are said to have been laid in a tomb which she built for herself while alive in an elevated and conspicuous place in Babylon, with the following inscription added: IF ANY KING IS IN NEED OF WEALTH, LET HIM OPEN THIS MONUMENT AND TAKE AS MUCH AS HE WISHES. When Darius Hystaspis read this, he ordered the sepulcher to be opened, in which he found no gold, but this writing: IF YOU HAD NOT BEEN A WICKED MAN, YOU WOULD NEVER HAVE VIOLATED SEPULCHERS. If you exclude Herodotus, who attributes this tomb to Nitocris, you will hardly find anyone who calls it into doubt. I marvel at the female wit! Semiramis would have been worthy, imposing another epigraph on the living after her funeral, and perhaps such a one as that Felician of Verona has in Camerarius, *Subsecedive Hours*, Century 1, chapter 97, page 455: FELICIAN OF VERONA HAS CONSTRUCTED THIS SACRED MONUMENT FOR HIMSELF. I WHO WAS UNRESTED WHILE ALIVE, NOW AT LAST, DEAD, NOT WILLINGLY
->DO I REST.<-

# XVI.

The external form consists in formalities, *a*, which are either common to a written and a nuncupative <note>oral</note> testament, or proper to one or the other. *b*. Common to both is the summoning of witnesses, *c*. whose quality must also be considered, and they must be invited by a formal request *e*. Finally, the number is defined by law, such that seven must be employed. *f*.

*a*. Donellus, book 6, chapter 7, at the beginning. *b*. Althusius, *Jurisprudence*, book 1, chapter 18, regarding the law *hac consultissima* <gloss>most well-advised law</gloss> 21, at the beginning, and § *per nuncupationem* <gloss>by oral declaration</gloss> 2, *Code on Testaments*, where Sichardus, Covarruvias in chapter *cum esses* 10, number 1, *on Testaments*. *d*. See the following thesis. *e*. Law *heredes* 21, § *in testamentis* <gloss>in testaments</gloss>, law *qui testamenta facere* <gloss>who may make testaments</gloss>, mentioned in the aforementioned law *hac consultissima* at the beginning, *Code on Testaments*. Clarus, in the aforementioned § *testamentis*, question 58. *f*. The aforementioned law *hac consultissima*, final law, *Code on Trusts*; Matantius in *Speculo* § *iudicii tela aggredi* <gloss>to engage in the web of litigation</gloss>, page 2, number 22; Clarus, in the aforementioned §, question 55, number 1, and question 56, number 1. See Mattheus, chapter 18, verse 17; chapter *licet* 23, *on Testaments and Attestations*; Covarruvias in the aforementioned chapter *cum esses*, numbers 7 and 14. Is it asked whether a smaller number of witnesses may be accepted under municipal law? We think it may be, which practice also confirms, and this proceeds to the extent that by the force of a testament thus constructed, the heir also obtains goods situated outside the territory, by argument of § *sed naturalia* 11, *Institutes on the Law of Nature and Nations*, law *si non speciali* 9, law 21, *Code on Testaments*, law 1, at the end, *on the Inspection of the Womb*, law *si fundus* 6, *on Evictions*, law *in hac* 30, *Code on Donations*, joined with the *Institutes* title *on the Lex Fusia*; Gail, book 2, observation 123; Mynsinger, century 5, observation 20. Fachineus, controversy 91, disagrees.

---

# XVIII.

We accept the quality of witnesses such that they are suitable, meaning those who are not prohibited from being witnesses: *a*. for even by the prompting of nature, some are kept away from testimony, such as the pre-pubescent, the insane, the spendthrift, the deaf, the mute, *b*. to whom the blind are rightly added: *c*. and, for another reason, the slave, *d*. the woman, *e*. the infamous person, *f*. the heir instituted, *g*. those of the household of the heir and of the testator himself, *h*. though not the legatee: *i*. the condition of all of whom must be inspected at the time when they are employed. *k*.

*a*. Argument from law *cum Praetor* 12, at the beginning, *on Judgment*. *b*. § *testes* 6, *Institutes on the Ordaining of Testaments*, where the Doctors comment on law *testium* 3, § law 5, law *in testimonium* 20, *on Witnesses*, law 20, § 4, *who may make testaments*. *c*. Argument from law *coram* 209, *on the Signification of Words*; Donellus 6, chapter 7; Clarus, in the aforementioned §, question 59. *d*. The aforementioned § 6; the aforementioned law *qui testamento* 20, § *servus* 7, *Digest*, *Code*, law *quod attinet* 32, *on the Rules of Law*. However, if he is held by everyone to be a free man and is employed as a witness, the testament will not be invalidated for that reason, but see *cum aliquis* 7, *Institutes on the Ordaining of Testaments*, law 1, *Code* on the same.</translation>

<translation page="10">has been approved by the practice of Saxony, as testified by *Carpzovius in Part 2, Constitution 13, Definition 20*. However, it is not rightly argued that a donation made by a man of low birth to a noble woman during marriage is conferred, since all the reasons prohibiting donations between spouses apply equally there, as *Treutler in Volume 2, Disputation 13, Thesis 4, letter b*, and *Bachovius* in that place, believe.

## THES. VII.

The number of Paraphernalia <gloss>extra-dowry property</gloss> is increased by the Wedding Gifts <term>Braut-Taffel Gelder</term> <gloss>nuptial banquet gifts</gloss>, which pertain to the wife for one half part. This is a most equitable opinion, received by *Panormitanus* in *Chapter 2, Extra, concerning donations between husband and wife* and in the Electorate of Saxony in *Part 3, Constitution 22* by way of a special pragmatic sanction. This is true to such an extent that, although by the custom of the region or by reason of the occasion a gift is offered at least to one of the spouses, it is nonetheless common to both and must be divided equally between them by *argument from Law 10, Digest on donations*. This is all the more certain because marriage is held to be a species of partnership (*§ 1, Institutes on paternal power; Law 1, § 3, Digest on Justice and Law; and Law 1, Digest on the Rite of marriage*), the nature of which is such that things donated to the partners so that they may trade better and manage common business, upon the dissolution of the partnership, are divided equally between them and their heirs (*argument from Law 29, Digest on partnership; Carpzovius, Part 3, Constitution 22, Definition 1*). The Academy of Helmstedt supports this opinion, and does not approve of the opinion of *Bartolus*, who, in *Law 10, § 6, Digest on vulgar and pupillary substitution*, attributes to each spouse what the relatives, kinsmen, and friends of each have donated to them, nor the opinion of others who assign everything to the wife, as *Hahn* testifies in his *observations on the paratitla of Wesenbecius, title on the Law of dowries, number 11*, at the end.</translation>

<translation page="11">## THES. VIII.

Let us approach the FORM, of which mention was made above in the explanation of the definition under the term "specific difference," and which consists in the administration of goods brought by the wife being conceded to the husband, whether that concession rests upon express or tacit consent. It is referred to as express if the woman collects the items existing in the husband's house into a document and takes care that it is subscribed by the husband to whom it is offered, as if he had received the items, so that they might be found registered in the dotal instrument as Paraphernalia <gloss>extra-dowry property</gloss> (*Law 9, paragraph last, Digest on the law of dowry; Law last, Code on agreed pacts*), from which it is then fully proven that certain things are Paraphernalia. That concession, however, is tacit if the husband, with the wife’s knowledge and consent, has administered goods brought in addition to the dowry for many years. Although, in the case where a woman has married a husband simply without a fixed dowry being established, we see that doctors argue whether all the goods that the woman possesses ought to be held as dotal or as Paraphernalia. And indeed, they ought to be seen as dotal in cases of doubt, since it is more useful for the wife that her goods be considered dotal than Paraphernalia; for although women have obtained a tacit mortgage <term>hypotheca</term> <gloss>lien/security</gloss> on the husband's goods in place of Paraphernalia, they are nonetheless destitute of the rest of the dowry and lack its privileges, and primarily the benefit of preference <term>praelatio</term> <gloss>priority in claims</gloss>. Since the matter concerns the favor of women, in doubtful cases one must favor them (*Law "in ambiguous cases," Digest on the law of dowry*). It follows that because marriage as a principal thing can be brought about not only by express (*Law 129, Digest on Rules of Law; Novella 22, Chapter 3*) but also by tacit agreement, if the circumstances of the things and persons suggest it, then much more will the same hold true in its accessory, which is the dowry, without which indeed marriage can exist, but the dowry itself can never exist without the marriage.</translation>

<summary>This text discusses the legal classification of spousal property in Saxony, specifically addressing the division of wedding gifts and the distinction between dotal property and paraphernalia based on express or tacit administration.</summary>
<keywords>Paraphernalia, Dowry, Nuptial Gifts, Spousal Partnership, Saxon Law, Legal Administration</keywords>

<translation page="17">## SECTION II.
->proposing<-
## THEOREMS.

1. **IN GOD** there exists an antecedent and a consequent Will. Whether, however, the former is correctly called that of Mercy and the latter that of Justice does not seem to be without doubt, since the consequent Will is also that of Mercy and grace.
2. The object of infinite power is said to be everything possible. And this the created Angel indicates in Luke 1, verse 37, and the uncreated [God] in Genesis 18:14. It is customary to note in this place the Hebraism by which a word is placed for the thing itself. But what if someone raises a doubt as to whether there is a given place in which it is taken in such a way?
3. Creation is correctly attributed to the most holy TRINITY alone and in its entirety. But whether the Son of God is signified by the "saying" <term>τὸ εἰπεῖν</term> <gloss>the saying/the word</gloss> in the History of Creation is altogether doubted, nor are there lacking reasons for doubting, which we shall reserve for a public conflict.
4. Jerome is not wrongly condemned of error, for he denied the Providence of God concerning irrational animals, since sacred scripture testifies evidently that individual animals and the animals themselves are subject to divine Providence. Compare Matthew 10:29. Some philosophers and theologians strive to vindicate Jerome from this injury, but with a vain attempt. See Jerome himself, Commentaries on Habakkuk, chapter 1, page 187.

3. THE WORD which was, the FLESH was not, it BECAME into one, which is and remains both.

# OF IACOBUS LOCHER PHILOMUSUS
## A Decastich.

> Anna, the mother of God rejoices to call you mother,
> And the world always exults in your name.
> Anna, Clavus has sung praises to you, and now
> Prays that you, divine patroness, may bring aid to the miserable.
> The German people hope in you, they consecrate altars to you,
> And as suppliants offer incense and sacred prayers.
> Thus, with your aid, Anna, help the wretched
> And infirm flock that worships at your temples.
> And extinguish various diseases with those sacred remedies
> Which your daughter and your grandson, who is God, bestow upon you.

## OF IOANNES BOEMUS AUBANUS.

> He who wishes to know how clement and how benign
> Blessed Anne is to her own servants,
> Let him read the sweet poem which the venerable Phileremus
> Gave from the highest diligence of his soul.

## TO IOANNES CLAVUS PHILEREMUS, his most beloved brother, Alexander Brassicanus of Tübingen.

> If blessed Anne were to draw breath in our regions,
> She would not wish to be of any more famous a lyre.
> Thus you are able to bend the gods and the dark shades alike.
</translation>

<summary>Page 12 concludes the Sapphic odes, invoking Saint Anne for protection against disease, guidance for scholars, and the promise of heaven. Page 13 contains commendatory verses by Locher, Boemus, and Brassicanus praising Clavus's devotion to Saint Anne.</summary>
<keywords>Saint Anne, Sapphic odes, Humanism, Johannes Clavus, Jacobus Locher, Alexander Brassicanus, devotional poetry, Latin literature</keywords>

<translation page="10">## *Chorus.*

The true prophets are led to their deaths by the command of Jezebel.

## *Scene Four.*

Obadiah urges Elijah to escape the persecution raging against the true prophets of GOD. Elijah, set on fire by the zeal and spirit of GOD, does not flee; instead, he meets King Ahab as he goes to worship Baal. He threatens him with celestial punishments and suddenly departs. The King, driven to a fury, pronounces a sentence of death upon him.

## *Scene Five.*

Elijah, uncertain where to flee, is instructed by an Angel from GOD to travel toward the East and hide in the region of the Jordan by the brook Cherith. Divine Providence accompanies him.

## *Chorus.*

Divine vengeance banishes the signs of water and brings fire upon the Kingdom of Ahab. From these, a famine arises, which the household gods <note>original: "Dij Penates"</note> attempt to subdue, only to be overcome by it.

<note>A horizontal ornamental divider is composed of a repeating row of small floral or star-shaped printer's ornaments.</note>

# ACT TWO.

## *Scene One.*

As the famine intensifies in the Kingdom of Ahab, many die. Some blame Ahab for such a great calamity, while others curse Elijah. Some attack the true prophets, others the false, and threaten them with death unless they obtain rain.

## *Scene Two.*

A raven, summoned by divine Providence, brings food to Elijah.</translation>

<translation page="11">### Scene Three.

Ahab, troubled by the great confusion of his people, orders a search for Elijah throughout all the regions so that he may kill him (as Saint Augustine believes).

### Scene Four.

When the brook Cherith dries up, Elijah is commanded to go to Zarephath of the Sidonians. There, he is to be fed by a widow whom he finds gathering wood with her son. Elijah asks for food, with the promise that the flour will not fail, from which the woman makes him ash-baked bread <note>original: "subcinericium"</note>.

### Scene Five.

The widow of Zarephath joyfully offers Elijah the ash-baked bread. She recounts that the flour has not diminished, blesses the GOD of Elijah, and asks the prophet to deign to lodge in her home.

### Scene Six.

The widow's son falls ill and then dies. Elijah restores him to life and returns him to his mother.

### Chorus.

> Twelve little Sidonian children applaud the son of the woman of Zarephath being restored to life.

<note>A horizontal decorative divider is composed of a sequence of seventeen floral or wheel-like circular ornaments, divided in the center by three horizontal bars.</note>

# ACT THREE.

### Scene One.

**A**hab, lacking counsel, asks his people what must be done in the depth of such scarcity. Finally, he himself and Obadiah depart separately into different regions for the sake of finding food, and Ahab does so in a disguised habit.</translation>

<summary>These pages cover the remainder of the first act and the entirety of the second and third acts, depicting Elijah's confrontation with Ahab, his refuge at the brook Cherith, the miraculous provision of food by the widow of Zarephath, and the eventual search for the prophet during the famine.</summary>
<keywords>Elijah, Ahab, Jezebel, Obadiah, Zarephath, widow, famine, divine providence, persecution</keywords>

<translation page="235">Furthermore, it proceeds from here no differently than the Iliac vein, which is joined to it, toward the foramen of the pubic bone. Before it passes through this, it receives a branch growing from the outer Iliac ramification, and thus it exits the foramen. Once it has departed from there, it is consumed within the muscles, partly those by which the foramen is occluded, and partly those that arise from the pubic bone, just as the internal Iliac vein is consumed. Finally, when it terminates at about the middle of the length of the femur, its extremity meets and unites with the extreme branches of the internal crural muscle, concerning which we speak in the following chapter.

The greater, or exterior [Iliac branch], similarly produces two branches, of which the first is called the External Epigastric, and it arises from the outer part shortly before it perforates the peritoneum; it is reflected upward and ascends along the inner side of the rectus muscle until it is joined by anastomosis with the mammary artery descending around the navel. The other, the Pudendal, which is the interior, small branch, is not divided into as many branches as the vein. Immediately, however, as it departs from the peritoneum, it grows out and is carried transversely along the seam of the pubic bones to the pudendal parts, where it is exhausted into the skin of the penis. The remainder of this trunk passes into the thigh, of which we shall now speak.

<- CHAPTER V ->

<- Branches of the exterior Iliac ramus propagated through the thigh. ->

After the exterior trunk has sent out the aforementioned branches, it departs from the peritoneum and is carried to the groin into the thigh, following the same path as the crural vein, to which it is positioned underneath and is joined as a companion everywhere, and thus it constitutes the Crural trunk (as we always call it). Immediately, however, as soon as it has surpassed the peritoneum, it produces a branch from the outer side, which they call the external crural muscle, which is carried downward and is propagated into the muscles embracing the bone of the thigh on the anterior side. Opposite this sometimes, or more often a little below, but in an internal position nevertheless, another is produced, called the internal crural muscle, which is distributed through the third muscle that flexes the femur, or the <term>Tricipitem</term> <gloss>three-headed muscle/triceps</gloss>, and through those that hold the inner region of the thigh, up to the knee in several branches, the extremities of which are joined with the extremities of the internal Iliac, which we said descends to the thigh through the foramen of the pubic bones. Having sent out these branches, the Crural trunk descends from the groin with the crural vein and is reflected next to the bone of the femur in such a way that, when it reaches the popliteal space, it rests between the two posterior heads of the femur. For skilled Nature always observes this: to lead vessels around that part of the joint where the flexion is, so that they might not be compressed if they went through the part where the joint extends. In this middle journey, as it were, while it descends through the femur, it produces a branch which, divided into several shoots, runs out through the muscles situated in the posterior region of the thigh together with the popliteal vein, and finally descending through the popliteal space (whence it is called the Popliteal), it is digested into the calf in frequent branches. Now resting in the popliteal space, it produces on either side a branch to the sides of the knee joint, buried subsequently deeper, which are exhausted partly in the joint itself and partly in the two <term>Gasterocnemos</term> <gloss>gastrocnemius/calf</gloss> muscles that constitute the calf, whence they are also called the Sural arteries.</translation>
<translation page="236">After the Crural trunk rests in the popliteal space, it brings forth a branch from the outer side, which descends next to the fibula and is hidden between the muscle abducting the foot and the muscles flexing the second tarsus, and it is distributed into the rest of those occupying the anterior part of the tibia, as far as they are fleshy, and they begin to be twisted along the outer malleolus. Shortly below this aforementioned one, another branch is produced from the posterior part of the trunk, which descends as far as the meeting of the tendons of the <term>Gastrocnemiorum</term> <gloss>gastrocnemius/calf muscles</gloss>. Then another from the same posterior part of the trunk, but beneath the second, comes forth, which, descending and crossing the transverse ligament, runs out through the back of the foot, diffused into the muscles abducting the toes. The remainder of the trunk is carried downward through the posterior parts of the tibia and, around the internal malleolus, offers a branch to the foot, which approaches the thumb and creeps along the back of the foot. The trunk itself, lying hidden between the tendons of the muscles of the toes of the foot, is divided into two branches, of which the inner provides two to the thumb, two to the index, and one to the middle toe; the outer, however, bestows two upon the little toe and two upon the toes closest to it, on the lower side. Furthermore, although the progression of the arteries happens for the most part as we have described, that which we said above concerning the veins—that their distribution varies greatly not only according to the diversity of individuals, but also of the sides in the same human—that must also be held regarding the arteries, which behave in one way in some humans and another way in others.

# CHAPTER VI.

*Contains the history of the arterial vein and the venal artery.*

So that this treatment concerning veins and arteries may be perfect and complete in all its parts, we have chosen to append the history of the third vein and the second artery in place of a colophon. The vein is called <term>arterial</term>, and indeed a vein by its office, because the ancients believed it carried blood from the right ventricle of the heart; but arterial from its tunic, similar to the membrane of arteries, since it is not simple, like those of veins, but double. The artery, on the contrary, is called <term>venal</term>, and an artery indeed, because the ancients established that it carries air attracted through the lungs; but venal because its substance corresponds to the body of veins, since its tunic is simple and not very thick. We have relegated the treatment of both to this place in particular so that we might deal with both at once, since they are born from the same viscera and are inserted into the same, and furthermore they enjoy the same distribution. For they arise from the Heart, and the vein indeed from the higher part of the right ventricle; but the artery from the left. And each is implanted and exhausted into the substance of the Lungs; the vein is extended through the right side of the <term>aspera arteria</term> <gloss>trachea/windpipe</gloss>, but the artery through the left. Soon each is cut into two branches, one of which goes to the right and the other to the left part of the lungs, with each again cut in two, and these into other branches, until they are dispersed into the most minute shoots. The larger branches accompany one another, so that the vein perpetually travels with the artery, joined by many <term>anastomoses</term> <gloss>connections between vessels</gloss>, in the middle of which the branches of the <term>aspera arteria</term> run out. These are notable vessels, and far larger than the size of the lungs seems to require, since those parts, as we said in the previous book, which dissipate the most nourishment, require ampler veins, and there is no part that, due to the perpetual... [text breaks off]</translation>

<summary>Pages 235-236 detail the ramification of the crural artery through the thigh, calf, and foot, and provide a anatomical history of the pulmonary vessels known as the arterial vein and venal artery.</summary>
<keywords>Crural artery, Femur, Popliteal space, Gastrocnemius, Arterial vein, Venal artery, Pulmonary circulation, Spigelius, Anatomy</keywords>

Now resting in the popliteal space, it produces on either side a branch to the sides of the knee joint, buried subsequently deeper, which are exhausted partly in the joint itself and partly in the two <term>Gasterocnemos</term> <gloss>gastrocnemius/calf</gloss> muscles that constitute the calf, whence they are also called the Sural arteries.
