After the Crural trunk rests in the popliteal space, it brings forth a branch from the outer side, which descends next to the fibula and is hidden between the muscle abducting the foot and the muscles flexing the second tarsus, and it is distributed into the rest of those occupying the anterior part of the tibia, as far as they are fleshy, and they begin to be twisted along the outer malleolus. Shortly below this aforementioned one, another branch is produced from the posterior part of the trunk, which descends as far as the meeting of the tendons of the <term>Gastrocnemiorum</term> <gloss>gastrocnemius/calf muscles</gloss>. Then another from the same posterior part of the trunk, but beneath the second, comes forth, which, descending and crossing the transverse ligament, runs out through the back of the foot, diffused into the muscles abducting the toes. The remainder of the trunk is carried downward through the posterior parts of the tibia and, around the internal malleolus, offers a branch to the foot, which approaches the thumb and creeps along the back of the foot. The trunk itself, lying hidden between the tendons of the muscles of the toes of the foot, is divided into two branches, of which the inner provides two to the thumb, two to the index, and one to the middle toe; the outer, however, bestows two upon the little toe and two upon the toes closest to it, on the lower side. Furthermore, although the progression of the arteries happens for the most part as we have described, that which we said above concerning the veins—that their distribution varies greatly not only according to the diversity of individuals, but also of the sides in the same human—that must also be held regarding the arteries, which behave in one way in some humans and another way in others.

# CHAPTER VI.

*Contains the history of the arterial vein and the venal artery.*

So that this treatment concerning veins and arteries may be perfect and complete in all its parts, we have chosen to append the history of the third vein and the second artery in place of a colophon. The vein is called <term>arterial</term>, and indeed a vein by its office, because the ancients believed it carried blood from the right ventricle of the heart; but arterial from its tunic, similar to the membrane of arteries, since it is not simple, like those of veins, but double. The artery, on the contrary, is called <term>venal</term>, and an artery indeed, because the ancients established that it carries air attracted through the lungs; but venal because its substance corresponds to the body of veins, since its tunic is simple and not very thick. We have relegated the treatment of both to this place in particular so that we might deal with both at once, since they are born from the same viscera and are inserted into the same, and furthermore they enjoy the same distribution. For they arise from the Heart, and the vein indeed from the higher part of the right ventricle; but the artery from the left. And each is implanted and exhausted into the substance of the Lungs; the vein is extended through the right side of the <term>aspera arteria</term> <gloss>trachea/windpipe</gloss>, but the artery through the left. Soon each is cut into two branches, one of which goes to the right and the other to the left part of the lungs, with each again cut in two, and these into other branches, until they are dispersed into the most minute shoots. The larger branches accompany one another, so that the vein perpetually travels with the artery, joined by many <term>anastomoses</term> <gloss>connections between vessels</gloss>, in the middle of which the branches of the <term>aspera arteria</term> run out. I cannot restrain myself from suggesting a few things regarding a most vexed question: do the Tragedies also acknowledge Seneca the Philosopher as their author? One may read on this matter in Baillet’s *Judgments of the Learned on the Principal Works of Authors*, Volume IV, Part II, page 363, and the authors cited at the end. Truly, the learned feel differently about the Tragedies. They bring forward judgments just stated that they are not by one author; the most illustrious Fabricius also asserts in the cited place, while he claims *Hercules Furens* for M. Annaeus Seneca the Father, *Hippolytus* for Seneca the Philosopher, and so the rest, assigning others to other authors. Olaus Borrichius, a noble name among the Danes, says in his dissertation on poets: *Although it is still argued under the judge whether that illustrious work of Tragedies, which bears his name, should be credited to him (Seneca the Philosopher) himself, most of the learned, if not all, lean toward the view that at least most of these same Tragedies are rightly attributed to him.* That this cannot be denied, writes Borrichius, because L. and when he had finished, he was suddenly struck with consternation, and imploring the aid of those who were present, he died in a pitiable manner and with great pain and groaning. From this, it can be easily understood that divine power was communicated to the divine man. Another example, not unlike the former, is added to this: another William, a Margrave, was treating the aforementioned church of Meissen injuriously. And when the provost of that same church wished to lead the man away from his evil course with great prayers, he not only refused to obey those who were correctly advising him, but also harassed the church itself much more than before. Then the said Provost, being unable to seek help from elsewhere, took refuge in the divine Benno, and prayed to him to save the church. It came to pass that Blessed Benno warned the Margrave three times in his sleep not to plot anything more serious against the church. When he, however, despised this as an empty dream, being severely rebuked a fourth time, he lost one eye, with a more serious danger proposed if he did not desist from his wicked undertaking. William the Margrave, led partly by fear and partly by repentance, restored everything to the church and increased its resources as much as he could, and he also esteemed the divine Benno greatly and venerated him most highly. Indeed, it must not be omitted that there are two districts, in one of which the Margrave hid himself while he was fleeing. In the other, he converted the Vandals from extreme impiety to the Christian faith. In these places, the tracks of his feet are still observed intact; then that hut in which he stayed among the Vandals, even if it is not held together by any more stable structure and had a straw roof, worn away by age, it nevertheless never decayed, nor was it consumed by fire, even though neighboring houses often burned in fires. The episcopal habit, in which his body was committed to the earth, together with the episcopal mitre, lay underground for more than two hundred years, and having been unearthed from the sepulcher without any alteration, it is today seen and shown intact. Many other miracles could be brought forward here; for it is established that many were raised from the dead by the merits of the divine Benno, and many were cured of various 
diseases.

<translation page="15">of the martyrs: more bitter afterward in the conflict with the heretics: most bitter now in the customs of those within the house. Internal and incurable is the wound of the church: and therefore in peace its bitterness is most bitter. Such things and heavier were said by Bernard and not a few others. And Paul: When men say peace and security (for the situation seems to be slipping back, so that barbarism and superstition may prevail again), then suddenly, as pain to a woman with child, so destruction will stand upon them, which they will not escape. For as it happened in the times of Noah, so will the coming of the Son of Man be. And thus, at length, will be the end of superstition. Which indeed the Lord is already destroying by the spirit of his mouth, and will finally abolish completely by the brightness of his coming. Come Lord Jesus, the pious say; may your kingdom come, they ask. Even so, I come quickly, says He who is faithful. The righteous cried, says the Psalmist, and the Lord heard them. <translation page="22">is the vicar of God, and the assistance he provides is piously believed to be brought by God himself indirectly through him, for He wills that all things be done in order and with decency. To the magistrate whom He has given, we owe honor, and from him in turn we expect the duties and protection appropriate to his station. This follows the example of Paul, who regarded the Roman Emperor as a lion in terms of his cruelty <note>original: "2 Timotheum 4.17"</note>, yet in his own time of mortal danger and in a political cause, he rightly appealed to him as an ordinary magistrate <note>original: "Actus 25.10 & 11"</note>.

I also add this: where a divine calling—which is the permission of the supreme magistrate—has joined us with people of a different religion in the same province or city, we can remain there with a clear conscience, provided that it is permitted for us to practice our own religion properly and safely. For then the pious are consoled by that promise of God, by which He pledges that He will be present for everyone in their calling and in their ways <note>original: "Psalmi 91.11, 15"</note>, which can be seen in the case of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob descending into Egypt by His command, and in Daniel and his companions living as captives in Babylon. And to this point I draw that which certain jurists and politicians urge so strongly: that different religions can be tolerated. I concede this, but only by us who are subjects, when the higher magistrate has granted it. Yet, whether a less <term>Orthodox</term> <gloss>correctly believing</gloss> religion ought to be admitted anew in a free Republic, I have thus far seen no one who could prove that from Scripture.

Finally (to omit several other minor objections that can be easily dissolved by what has already been said), the examples of Abraham <note>original: "Genesis 14 & 21"</note> and Isaac <note>original: "Genesis 26"</note> making alliances differ immensely from the present question. For first, there are not lacking (among whom is also our Luther) those who deny that they formed alliances with the impious, the profane, or those alien to the religion of the Patriarchs, which they endeavor to prove by several arguments drawn from the text. I assert that this can be proven quite explicitly from the cited passages: these were not ecclesiastical and mixed alliances, but only political, concerning civil matters; and this was done not so much in defense as in agreement not to offend. Moreover, both were contracted by the Patriarchs at a time when they were not particularly in need of their help—indeed, when Abimelech himself was requesting this from them. What kind of consequence, therefore, is this: that the Patriarchs could—as Luther establishes in his Commentaries on Genesis—contract with their pious neighbors regarding civil matters and non-offense, invited, and so forth?</translation>

For who, from the preceding, does not see that there is a confusion of the most diverse types of alliances, that the principles, objects, ends, and circumstances are diverse here, and that therefore the action cannot be the same?

For this reason, I forgo a more lengthy discussion on a plain matter.

I turn now to merely political alliances, which I affirm to be lawful even with the profane and <term>heterodox</term> <gloss>those of another opinion/sect</gloss> for the following reasons: I. Because they are just and good when viewed from their principle, object, end, and circumstances. II. In this way, all the pious are ordered to intercede with God for kings and all who are in positions of eminence, so that they may lead a tranquil and quiet life with all piety and reverence <note>1 Timothy 2:1-2</note>, and Jeremiah similarly exhorts the captives in Babylon by letter <note>chapter 29:7</note>: "Seek the prosperity of that city to which I have deported you," says Jehovah, "and pray to Jehovah for it; for in its prosperity shall your prosperity be." Yet, whether a less <term>Orthodox</term> <gloss>correctly believing</gloss> religion ought to be admitted anew in a free Republic, I have thus far seen no one who could prove that from Scripture.

Finally (to omit several other minor objections that can be easily dissolved by what has already been said), the examples of Abraham <note>original: "Genesis 14 & 21"</note> and Isaac <note>original: "Genesis 26"</note> making alliances differ immensely from the present question. For first, there are not lacking (among whom is also our Luther) those who deny that they formed alliances with the impious, the profane, or those alien to the religion of the Patriarchs, which they endeavor to prove by several arguments drawn from the text. I assert that this can be proven quite explicitly from the cited passages: these were not ecclesiastical and mixed alliances, but only political, concerning civil matters; and this was done not so much in defense as in agreement not to offend. Moreover, both were contracted by the Patriarchs at a time when they were not particularly in need of their help—indeed, when Abimelech himself was requesting this from them. What kind of consequence, therefore, is this: that the Patriarchs could—as Luther establishes in his Commentaries on Genesis—contract with their pious neighbors regarding civil matters and non-offense, invited, and so forth?

For who, from the preceding, does not see that there is a confusion of the most diverse types of alliances, that the principles, objects, ends, and circumstances are diverse here, and that therefore the action cannot be the same?

Regarding the Calvinists—for I believe that is the only thing remaining in this question—as to whether they differ from us in certain primary and fundamental articles of faith, namely, most significantly in the doctrine concerning the person of CHRIST, Predestination, Baptism, and the Lord’s Supper, etc., I would not believe anyone to be such a stranger to Theology who either ignores this or at least doubts it, since it is sufficiently explained in any Catechetical and Symbolic books, as well as in theological compendia in antithesis, and is otherwise evident from many polemical writings published by both sides over approximately the last eighty years. For this reason, I forgo a more lengthy discussion on a plain matter.

I turn now to merely political alliances, which I affirm to be lawful even with the profane and <term>heterodox</term> <gloss>those of another opinion/sect</gloss> for the following reasons: I. III. Because there are proven examples of the pious: Jacob with Laban <note>Genesis 31:44</note>, David <note>2 Samuel 5:11</note>, and Solomon contracting a political alliance with Hiram, King of Tyre <note>1 Kings 5:12</note>. ### I.

The definition of an <term>Ethical Comet</term>, which Stanislaus Lubieniecius calls and presents as such in his <term>Theatrum Cometicum</term> <gloss>Cometary Theater</gloss>, folio 26, is that it is a supernatural, artificial, arbitrary, doctrinal, indicative, and memorial sign, by which God marks his ways to man, announces good things to the good and evil things to the evil, and man, endowed with reason and the knowledge of the Divine will, and</translation>

*Comets, even if they are not to be feared superstitiously, are not to be held in profane contempt, nor to be mocked sarcastically. They hold the middle ground, as the blessed are fond of saying.*

*The argument is absurd, and natural piety itself hisses at it, by which it is said that comets portend nothing evil because most often, even when such new* Stars *have never been seen, very disastrous times have occurred; or because a most happy state of affairs has followed such phenomena. <translation page="8">or identity, rather, they discussed most shamelessly again and again. Since all of them had justly and by common consent condemned that booklet of Johannes Reuchlin—as being, to the Church of God, more injurious than is credible; to the holy doctors, irreverent; for his own goods, mischievous; for the wicked, suitable; for the very worst, fitting; for the faithful of Christ, scandalous; and finally, too indulgent to Jewish perfidy and savoring of too depraved a heresy—and, by their open letters with their seals appended, had judged it to be cordially condemned and, like deadly poison or a dangerous, spreading plague, to be immediately removed from the use of Christians, then at last the Inquisitor, fortified by the determination, sentence, and authority of such great and learned men, undertook the matter in the diocese and city of Mainz by the consent and exhortation of the Archbishop, inasmuch as it was there that those nefarious booklets were first exposed and publicly sold to all. The Inquisitor himself, that venerable doctor, received therefore from the most reverend lord Archbishop of Mainz four judges from the city of Mainz as his colleagues. To these, the most reverend lord Archbishop of Cologne—a man worthy of all praise and honor—had added, with the consent of the Mainz prince, an official of his court who was truly outstanding and, in all things, remarkable, namely, men who were learned, upright, and excellent, and who in no way deserved to be held suspect by any mortal, however wicked. One of these is the suffragan of Mainz; the second is the magnificent and illustrious rector of that same university; three are doctors of sacred theology; and two others are doctors of canon law. With these excellent and venerable men, the Inquisitor instituted the process of equity and justice there. After the citations were legitimately executed and judicially reproduced (not, indeed, against the person of any specific individual, but generally and specifically against all who considered it to be in their interest to defend the heretical obscenities of the aforementioned booklet), the process—happily and holily begun—continued in accordance with his duty to the faith. Yet, indeed, because the doctor himself at the term of the citation, being more solicitous of his own honor than of the integrity of the Catholic faith and of his own rescue from intolerable scandal, recused the Inquisitor himself (who in no way exulted in this) as suspect through his proctor on the basis of certain frivolous and—if I may say—ineffectual motives, the Inquisitor, sufficiently animated by the cause of justice and distrusting no judge, in order to avoid the multitude of recusations, arbitrations, and appeals (which are disagreeable to every good man) and the frivolous and clearly enervated exceptions that they allege, cast the entire cognizance of the case publicly and judicially upon his colleagues. Wisely exonerating himself from the office of inquiring, judging, and defining, he served only in the office of accuser. Although, however, matters were thus, the proctor of the opposing party nevertheless, during that process without a hearing, interposed a certain childish and clearly inept appeal from the Inquisitor (who had already been recused as judge) to the Holy Apostolic See. And since now, to say much in few words, all terms of law had been duly and legitimately observed with the counsel and assistance (as it is said) of legal experts, and with mature deliberation, the pronouncing of the sentence in this case was—at the prayers of the lords of the cathedral church—suspended for an interval of fifteen days.</translation>

<translation page="9">of Mainz for the aforementioned judges, by the consent of the Inquisitor, had been graciously suspended. And furthermore, a second time, when these fifteen days had elapsed and the aforementioned judges, fully resolved and steadfast in the cause of the faith, were sitting to pronounce judgment from the tribunal, the parties having been legitimately cited and called, there arrived certain letters of the most reverend lord of Mainz, obtained in such a manner—alas, by a man of less than good character—in favor of heretical depravity. By these letters, he had commanded his commissaries or mandataries that unless the Inquisitor suspended the case for an entire month beyond the fifteen days graciously granted, he himself, the Archbishop, would completely revoke the commission given to the judges. And thereafter, if anything were attempted by them within the aforementioned time, he wished it to be entirely void. Thus, everything was inverted and, as you have heard, clearly changed before the prospect. Although that lord of Mainz himself, now deceased and subject to the just Judge, had often at various times added his faithful assistance to the Inquisitor in this, so much so that the lord Inquisitor—seeking the salvation of the Church, as will be clear to everyone under the strict judgment of God—was not a little encouraged by his help and counsel and, trusting in his most pious words, awaited a most happy end, desired by all good men. However, these things having been—as we have heard—sinisterly acted upon by certain ones, good men could easily understand that for the Reverend Inquisitor, in the most pious cause of our Lord Jesus Christ and the most sacred faith, justice itself had not only been manifestly denied but violently snatched from his hands. This is especially true since the aforementioned Archbishop of Mainz neither advocated the case to himself, nor made it ratified or certain by what manner or at what time it was finally to be absolved, nor, now that the month had elapsed, proposed to the Reverend Inquisitor any hope (which ought to have been done otherwise) for the short and total expedition of this cause. Therefore, in the judgment of prudent and learned men, no hope of a good outcome seemed left there for the Inquisitor before the Archbishop, but rather—a thing unworthy to be heard—contempt, derision, and vilification of the Inquisitor. For he did not see to the termination of the cause of Christ as he was bound by law, nor did he take care to transmit it, duly instructed, to the Apostolic See. It is not doubted that this was machinated or, as they say, practiced by the adversary, who was aware of his own guilt, lest perchance, if the Apostolic See were sought out, it would acknowledge—as will undoubtedly happen—the depraved teachings and some intolerable errors of the *Ocular Mirror* and condemn them as quickly as possible with a more severe censure. He knew that the aforementioned judges would undoubtedly pronounce sentence through our Inquisitor against his said scandalous and most pernicious booklets, especially if they had not been revoked by the Archbishop himself and from the office of equity. Hence it is more true and clearer than light that the case, as we have heard, had been completed. Two of those judges, in the name and by the sacred commission of the entire theological faculty of Mainz, delivered the legitimate condemnation of the aforementioned booklets, fortified by the seal of their faculty, when they were legitimately requested to do so, arguing with a sincere heart that they were very sad and clearly groaning that in the causes of the Christian faith things had been dealt with so lightly and captiously. These things having been so done, the adversary himself, in order to impede the rescission of the principal matter—that is, the sentence itself—in any way he could...</translation>

<summary>These pages detail the legal obstruction encountered by the Inquisitor in Mainz during the proceedings against Johannes Reuchlin's "Ocular Mirror." The text describes the formal condemnation by university experts and the subsequent interference by the Archbishop of Mainz, who halted the proceedings through political pressure and bureaucratic delays.</summary>
<keywords>Johannes Reuchlin, Ocular Mirror, Inquisitor, Mainz, heresy, censorship, Church law, academic faculty, legal process, Archbishop of Mainz</keywords>

<translation page="15">After a few days, the state of his body eluded the inexperienced, as it had been changed for the better, as it seemed, by being freed in some part from the burden of the humors through gentle, gradual medicines, and the fever—which had been accompanying the disease at a slow pace—had diminished. But just as a tree does not depart from its root, so the disease could not abandon the infection that was rooted more deeply. The rot, the fever, the sleeplessness, and other symptoms took on strength and increased more and more, and they began to threaten the danger of death more clearly, when Dr. Nicolaus Hannekenius was also called in for consultation. Nature had by then begun to expel the hostile humor through the bowels, along with the rotten masses of blood, the unhappy offspring of a liver already decaying and eroded. Everything that such a great disease and such great symptoms required was attempted. But Nature did not desist from this work of excretion until his strength was utterly cast down, the structure of his body was dissolved along with the parenchyma <note>the functional tissue</note> of the liver, and it was liquefied; and thus a better, eternal origin of life received his diseased, perishable life. So far, the words of the physician.

Thus, we have perceived the origin, progress, vigor, and deeds of this most distinguished man, delineated with a plain mind <note>a classical expression meaning "without artifice"</note>, without the splendor of words. I must finally reach the sad epilogue of his life, alas! I have little to say about this, as no one could inform me further about the manner of his blessed passing, his final words, or other matters that usually happen at this turn and goal of life. Nevertheless, since the most praiseworthy man always lived his life piously and religiously before God, justly toward his neighbor, and temperately toward himself, we neither should nor can doubt that he died well and blessed. This eternal blessedness</translation>

<translation page="16">we congratulate with all our heart upon his blessed soul, wishing for ourselves a similar passing, with a prayer and a desirable sigh: If only he were still living, safe and happy, and could perform this sad duty for many others, and especially for me, who is far more mature for death, which I, by a perverse order of nature, perform for him. But as it pleased the Lord, so it is done. May His holy name be blessed in both favorable and adverse circumstances.

Since it has been decided to commit the remains of his blessed soul to their resting place tomorrow, the 12th of September, the Magnificent Lords Consuls; the Most Noble and Most Learned Lord Syndic; the Most Noble, Most Learned, and also Most Experienced Lords Doctors; the Reverend and Most Distinguished Lords Pastors and Church Ministers; the most illustrious and most prudent Lords Senators and Secretaries; and the other no less honest citizens of this city, and patrons of the school, are requested and invited to be present in great numbers for the funeral procession and obsequies, with the observance, reverence, and diligence that is fitting.

<note>A square woodcut emblem features an hourglass at its center, resting on a flat base. The hourglass is flanked by a stalk of grain on the left and a leafy branch on the right, serving as a memento mori symbol for the passage of time and the cycle of life and death.</note></translation>

For it could not have been obscure to those most grave men that the honorable is by no means to be separated from the useful in the state, nor that anything should be thought honorable which is not useful, nor useful which is not honorable and in agreement with virtue; since these two are connected by a certain natural and most tight bond. However, it is easy to see what utility was understood by them; that, namely, which applies right reason <term>ratio recta</term> <gloss>correct logic/right reason</gloss> to deliberation, by which neither the principles nor the causes of things are neglected, and from which those things that are to follow are accurately weighed and compared with the present. And they judged this alone to be worthy of the name of utility. For utility ceases to be, or is even the greatest ruin, in the estimation of which a man
pages.18:
follows the corrupt judgment of his own passions, choosing a present good that indeed seems joyful and salutary but, if weighed on an even scale, is deceptive, slippery, and inconstant, and is the source and origin of many inconveniences. Many think that great fruits are reaped when faith is not kept, when injury is brought upon the weak, when no pacts are observed, when power and wealth are sought through iniquitous arts, and other things are done which laws and justice want to be sedulously avoided by every race of men. But when those who do these things expect the same from others, who are comparing their own advantages in any way possible, it becomes necessary that, from actions of this kind, separated from the honorable, there can be so little fruit or pleasure for a wise man that, on the contrary, with the order of things confused, they bring the greatest detriment and most severe calamity upon men. Therefore, that which is most profitable is to be looked upon in the republic in such a way that it is conjoined with honorable and praiseworthy things, and that nothing is done or thought that seems to be absent from virtue and the probity of morals. In order that this may be obtained more easily, it will be necessary to observe diligently those things by which the honesty of morals and the pursuit of virtue are helped and promoted. Since not a few of these things have been brought forth by those who, concerned for the most salutary precepts, have weighed such a great matter well in their own minds, we judge, saving the judgments of others, that these three are the most important: religion, discipline, and good laws. To discuss these now in many words, however, is superfluous; since it will come to pass that they will be explained more broadly and more richly by certain youths who will declaim publicly tomorrow. We only add something a little on religion, and we briefly note what the Fathers and Doctors of the Church have felt about it, as it relates to virtues and honorable morals,

# LATER DECLAMATION.

A few days ago, listeners and others, someone appeared in this chair to pursue the infamous pursuit of foreign travel in a speech. You endured the speaker with benevolence and liberal intent, I believe, because in your judgment he had occupied a subject not unworthy of this place, and because it was not tiresome for either your distinguished assembly or the surrounding audience to listen. And so it seemed to me that I had by no means lost the value of my effort, especially in a subject in which one might deservedly test his talent, particularly because it did not at all struggle with sterile poverty. For when the orator had decided, according to the rationale of his plan, to reveal the baseness of this pursuit, it was understood that the subject was presented with such abundance that, in explaining it, talent was more restrained than fatigued by anxious <column-break/>

contemplation. If anyone wished to append other things of that kind that were omitted, he would undoubtedly fill a new speech. <translation page="11">
See Kirchmann, Book I, Chapter IV, on Roman Funerals; this distinction arose from games held in honor of the deceased, which they called funereal, as attested by Rosinus, *Roman Antiquities*, Book V, Chapter XXXIX. The first type is the *Funus indictivum* <gloss>Indictive Funeral</gloss>, so called, according to Festus, because the people were called to it by a herald. Rosinus, loc. laudat. It is named from the calling <term>indicendo</term>, a word the ancients used in this sense (Kirchmann, ibid.). Suetonius in *Caesar*: *The funeral having been announced, a pyre was built on the Campus Martius.* Cicero in his *Oration to the Pontiffs for his House*, and *On Consular Provinces*. The illustrious Scaliger has noted the solemn words of this announcement from the last scene of the fifth act of Terence’s *Phormio*, and Varro, Book IV, *On the Latin Language*. Indictive funerals were the most elaborate, and besides other sumptuous appointments, they were also celebrated with games (Cicero, Book II, *On the Latin Language*; Becman, *On Origins*, p. 706; Rosinus and Kirchmann in the places cited; Scaliger, Book I, *Ausonian Lectures*, Chapter XXVIII), with circus riders also employed (Festus Pompeius, Book XVII; Dempster on Rosinus, *Antiquities*, Book V, Chapter XXIV). The Public funeral can be referred to here, which was sometimes the same as the Indictive, as in Apuleius (Book 11, *Metamorphoses*), sometimes only a part of it, when, for instance, a cessation of business was proclaimed, or public mourning, or expenses were made from the public treasury (Kirchmann, ibid.). This honor was granted to Syphax, King of Numidia (Valerius Maximus, Book V, Chapter 1; Suetonius in *Vitellius*, Chapter III); to Sphaerus, Augustus’s freedman and tutor (Dio, Book XLVIII); to Piso, Urban Prefect (the same, Dio, Book LXIV). Illustrious women were not without a share of this (Idem, Book XLVII; Xiphilinus in *Tiberius*). There were furthermore various kinds of Public Funerals according to the diversity of honors managed by the deceased, such as Praetorian, Consular, Censorial, and Triumphal, as Polybius indicates (Book 6, *Histories*), where, however, Lipsius noted that the triumphal was confused with the censorial under the emperors. The most worthy was the Censorial, by which princes were carried out, such as Claudius (Tacitus, Book XII). Whence Spartianus in *Aelius Verus* calls it an Imperial funeral; in *Opilius Macrinus*, a Royal one. For the Censorship was the most honored among the magistracies (Plutarch in *Cato the Elder*).

## Other Quiet, or *Simpludearia* Funerals. Th. VII.

This is the second type: called by another name, the *Funus Vulgare* <gloss>Common Funeral</gloss> in Capitolinus in *Marcus Antoninus the Philosopher*. Also, the *Funus commune* <gloss>Ordinary Funeral</gloss> (Ausonius, *Parentalia*). Also, the *Plebeian Funeral* (Propertius, Book II, Elegy XIV). The *Funus translaticium* <gloss>Simple Funeral</gloss> (Suetonius, *Nero*, Chapter XXXIII, concerning the death of Britannicus). These funerals were performed without pomp, without a master of ceremonies, without a herald,</translation>

and without proclamation. Seneca, Book 1, *On Tranquility of Mind*, Chapter 1; Ovid, Book 1, *Fasti*, Elegy 3. Indeed, they had no other solemnities, except for games. See Kirchmann, Book I, Chapter IV, on Roman Funerals; this distinction arose from games held in honor of the deceased, which they called funereal, as attested by Rosinus, *Roman Antiquities*, Book V, Chapter XXXIX. The first type is the *Funus indictivum* <gloss>Indictive Funeral</gloss>, so called, according to Festus, because the people were called to it by a herald. Rosinus, loc. laudat. It is named from the calling <term>indicendo</term>, a word the ancients used in this sense (Kirchmann, ibid.). Suetonius in *Caesar*: *The funeral having been announced, a pyre was built on the Campus Martius.* Cicero in his *Oration to the Pontiffs for his House*, and *On Consular Provinces*. The illustrious Scaliger has noted the solemn words of this announcement from the last scene of the fifth act of Terence’s *Phormio*, and Varro, Book IV, *On the Latin Language*. Indictive funerals were the most elaborate, and besides other sumptuous appointments, they were also celebrated with games (Cicero, Book II, *On the Latin Language*; Becman, *On Origins*, p. 706; Rosinus and Kirchmann in the places cited; Scaliger, Book I, *Ausonian Lectures*, Chapter XXVIII), with circus riders also employed (Festus Pompeius, Book XVII; Dempster on Rosinus, *Antiquities*, Book V, Chapter XXIV). The Public funeral can be referred to here, which was sometimes the same as the Indictive, as in Apuleius (Book 11, *Metamorphoses*), sometimes only a part of it, when, for instance, a cessation of business was proclaimed, or public mourning, or expenses were made from the public treasury (Kirchmann, ibid.). This honor was granted to Syphax, King of Numidia (Valerius Maximus, Book V, Chapter 1; Suetonius in *Vitellius*, Chapter III); to Sphaerus, Augustus’s freedman and tutor (Dio, Book XLVIII); to Piso, Urban Prefect (the same, Dio, Book LXIV). Illustrious women were not without a share of this (Idem, Book XLVII; Xiphilinus in *Tiberius*). There were furthermore various kinds of Public Funerals according to the diversity of honors managed by the deceased, such as Praetorian, Consular, Censorial, and Triumphal, as Polybius indicates (Book 6, *Histories*), where, however, Lipsius noted that the triumphal was confused with the censorial under the emperors. The most worthy was the Censorial, by which princes were carried out, such as Claudius (Tacitus, Book XII). Whence Spartianus in *Aelius Verus* calls it an Imperial funeral; in *Opilius Macrinus*, a Royal one. For the Censorship was the most honored among the magistracies (Plutarch in *Cato the Elder*).

The *Funus translaticium* <gloss>Simple Funeral</gloss> (Suetonius, *Nero*, Chapter XXXIII, concerning the death of Britannicus). <margin>How did Pippin break through those obstacles?</margin>
The oath of faith had been established, by which Pippin and the others owed obedience to Childeric. But Pippin easily broke through this by his skill, since the people's veneration for their kings was being turned into contempt through their own sloth and Pippin's arts, and he hoped that the oath could be broken by the authority of the Roman Pontiff, whom he had already obligated to himself through great services. He decided, therefore, to weave his web in the manner explained by Pierre Matthieu in his <term>Genealogia Regum Francorum</term> <gloss>Genealogy of the Kings of the Franks</gloss>, f. m. 50, and by Buffier and others. After he had bound many to himself through benefits, more through promises, and all through his courtesy, and had stirred up old friends with the hope of new things and ignited new ones through the emulation of the old, the talk began to spread everywhere through his arts, first among the courtiers and soon among the common people, that the sloth of the Franks, once the glory of so many kings, was now shameful; that those who were fit to rule neither themselves nor others should be cast out; and that another should be chosen in whose virtue the kingdom might stand, and he need not be sought from afar, for Prince Pippin was at hand, a dwarf in body indeed, but a giant in spirit.

<margin>Pippin proclaims a royal assembly.</margin>
Pippin, therefore, when he noticed that such talk was welcomed by the populace and received by friendly ears, deeming the matter ripe, proclaimed a public convention of the kingdom, having summoned the prelates and the foremost of the nobility, whom he had discovered to be most devoted to his cause.

<margin>What was decreed there?</margin>
In this assembly, having already tested their minds, he proposed the matter and simultaneously carried it; and all went along with his opinion, that they should be sent to the Pontiff to seek release from their oath.

<margin>Legates are sent to Rome to Pope Zacharias.</margin>
III. Sent, therefore, to Zacharias, who at that time presided over the Roman See, were Burchard, Bishop of Würzburg (others name Richard of Bourges), and Volrad, Pippin's so-called chaplain, that is, the prefect <column-break/> of the sacred chambers,</translation>

<translation page="12">
<note>Two small floral woodcut ornaments appear at the top of the page.</note>

<note>A horizontal divider rule with decorative scrollwork terminals.</note>

to whose petition the Pontiff readily assented.

<margin>
What they accomplished there:
Why the Pope assented to Pippin's wishes?
Pippin is anointed King.
Childeric is thrust into a monastery with his wife.
Whence the Bishops of Würzburg hold the title of Duke of Franconia.
</margin>
For the latter, since he feared the Greek Emperors, from whom the Pope had defected, for they were scheming to establish a new empire for themselves and were avengers of Roman treachery, it pleased him at the same time to obligate Pippin—who stood as a threat to the Roman domain, much like the empire of the Greeks—with this new example of treachery, that he might have in him a firm protector against the Greeks and the Lombards. Following this, the task was delegated by Zacharias to Boniface, the Bishop of Mainz, who first introduced the Roman rites of the sacraments and the vanity of dogmas into Germany, which was already imbued with better things in some places, to anoint Pippin as King, whom the Franks themselves had already chosen by their own votes. Therefore, as the legates returned to France, the anointing of Pippin was performed at Soissons by Boniface, and soon Pippin was called King by all, and according to the custom of the people, he was raised upon a shield and placed upon the throne. Finally, he finished the last act to close the scene: the deposition of Childeric, who was led from the rustic villa in which he resided to a monastery at Regensburg (they even destined his wife Gisela for a convent), where, having had his hair shorn and his clothes put aside, he assumed the habit of a monk, with no heavier loss than that of his hair, since he was hardly despoiled of a kingdom he had not possessed, and perhaps losing his wife was a gain. Meanwhile, Burchard, as a reward for his successful embassy, was created Duke of Franconia by Pippin, as Freher notes in his annotations to Bebenburg, page 35. He left this title to his successors.

### IV.

But whether this anointing of Pippin as King is the first among the Kings of the Franks, I see it is doubted, since they allege that Remigius used chrism upon Clovis.

Antonio Pascaligo: Joannes Baptista Benedictus of Cyprus, Jacobus Metius of Chersonesus, Antonius Eudaemonicus of Cydonia, Jacobus Trissinus of Vicenza, Hieronymus Bysantius of Ascruia, and Andreas Calergus of Rethymno were also eager for this praise and desirous of glory, and you ought to consider their memory as one that will never fade. For as long as the Christian and Venetian name endures—which we can promise will be eternal—as long as letters remain, and as long as any place is left for virtue anywhere, the most grateful discourse of men will never fall silent regarding them. For *posterity not only nourishes the life of those who died defending the Fatherland and vindicating the Christian religion, but also, as we have learned from the wisest men, eternity itself always keeps watch over it.* Harmodius and Aristogiton still flourish today in the mouths and minds of all, as do the Horatii, the Decii, and many others, because *they judged it glorious to depart from life for the sake of the Fatherland.* As for those soldiers of yours, who can never be sufficiently praised, who by their own blood brought forth such glory and such a victory for the Christian name, we trust that they have already obtained the reward of their virtues from God, and we see that the honors due to them are being paid today by you and by the entire Christian Republic. This befalls them even more beautifully than it did the Romans or *Athenians*, because those peoples, compelled by their own laws, bestowed praises upon those who had died fighting for the Fatherland; you, whatever you do, bestow it of your own free will and accord upon their virtue, and fulfill the duty of most grateful citizens. And with good reason, indeed. For these excellent men are worthy of having still further unique honors sought out for them by the Senate. Which I, at present,</translation>

<translation page="22">

from the highest lookout of heaven, now seem to see, and to behold your grateful spirits, and therefore to rejoice, because they understand that, through the adornment of words, perennial praise is accustomed to reach those who have performed illustrious deeds among the *Audience*. And since they knew that *this life is a pilgrimage*, they publicly expended their bodies, which they knew to be perishable, so that they might privately acquire a praise that fears no fates of death. I reluctantly pass over the names of other outstanding men who were slain in battle, so that if I were able, I might save them from oblivion. to have sweated over it. However, although I do not have this matter sufficiently settled, I will nonetheless express my opinion without reluctance, so that I may at least provide the more learned an opportunity to dispute such things more fully and subtly. Pliny embraces both the <term>gale</term> <gloss>weasel</gloss> and the <term>ictis</term> <gloss>marten</gloss> under the name of "weasel." For what Aristotle writes, "When the weasel fights the snake, it eats rue," Pliny translated almost word for word when he says, "The weasel, when it is about to fight with serpents, carries rue in its mouth" <note>Natural History, 29.4</note>. And in the same book, those which Aristotle called *Ictides*, he himself also calls weasels. For he writes thus: "There are two kinds of weasels. The other is wild; they differ in size; the Greeks call them *Ictides*." From these passages already cited, it is clear enough that "weasel" is a general name for Pliny, and that in Latin the animal is called a "weasel" which in Greek is called <term>galē</term> <gloss>weasel</gloss> and <term>iktis</term> <gloss>marten</gloss>. 

EUCHARIUS. The language of the Latins is therefore poorer than the Greek. 

ANONYMOUS. The Latins are surpassed by the Greeks not only in the abundance of things, but also in the abundance of words. And just as nothing is lacking to the Greeks, so many things are desired by the Latins. And in my judgment, Cicero <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero</note> exclaims somewhat improperly: "O the impoverished Greek language at times!" 

EUCHARIUS. But what shall we say or do in such great poverty of the Latins? 

ANONYMOUS. We shall borrow names from the common people. For common names are not to be despised, if only Latin ones are lacking.
</translation>

Therefore, I think those weasels which the Greeks call <term>galai</term> <gloss>weasels</gloss> are called by the common people Wisellas, Herminnas, or Hermellas. 

EUCHARIUS. What do you think is the difference between Wisellas and Hermellas? 

ANONYMOUS. Yesterday at the furrier's, we saw the pelts of both animals. The pelt of the Hermella was entirely white, but the pelt of the Wisela was white on the lower part of the belly, while on the upper part of the body it was a dark chestnut color, distinguished with white. And the furrier, as you yourself heard, said that those colors eventually turn white, and that Wisellas become Hermellas. Whether this is so, I leave to the furriers to judge. Certainly, my mind inclines to believe that this happens. For these things are not absurd, since the Wisela and the Hermella do not differ in size, nor in hair, nor in appearance, nor in form; they differ only slightly in color. 

EUCHARIUS. What do the French call Wisellas and Hermellas? 

ANONYMOUS. They call Hermellas almost by the same name, Herminnas. But they call Wisellas *Fouinos* or *Marturellos*. 

EUCHARIUS. Is the <term>fretta</term> <gloss>ferret</gloss> placed among the weasels? 

ANONYMOUS. Certainly. For I believe ferrets are those animals which the French call <term>furones</term> <gloss>ferrets</gloss> and which the Latins call <term>viuerras</term> <gloss>ferrets</gloss>. Boys use ferrets to extract small birds from nests in walls. They are also sent into the hollows of trees, and they bring back small birds from there with their claws. Furthermore, in the hunting of rabbits, they use ferrets. Pliny <note>Natural History, 8.81</note>: "Great [is the utility] of ferrets because of their hunting."
</translation>

### §. XVIII.

Why the ox that was buried was stoned, which is mentioned in Exodus 21, the <note>Weimar interpreters</note> offer this reason in verse 32: *so that the homicide might not remain unavenged.* But <term>Jacobus Bonfrerius</term> does not admit this reason, in his work on this passage, Antwerp, folio 465, writing: *Furthermore, all these things are established against the ox, not because of any guilt, which cannot exist in a brute, but for the greater detestation and horror of homicide.* Similar things are read in <term>Cornelius à Lapide</term>, in his work on this passage, Antwerp edition, Volume 1, page 489, where he comments thus: *If an ox has struck a man or a woman with its horn, and they have died, it shall be overwhelmed with stones, not because of the ox's guilt (for this cannot exist in a brute) but for the terror and example of men, so that by this, of course, men may be more deterred from homicide, whence even today pigs and other beasts are killed if they kill children or men.* Other things pertaining to this stoned ox may be seen in the <term>Mishnah Bava Kama</term>, chapter 4, section 5.

> By what end or period will there ever be a respite from troublesome weariness, when that Firstborn of the Gods, ruling not only the heavens but also the underworld, has now placed a limit? He has driven out the Hebrew Boy, recently shadowed by a prodigious flow and indicated by many sun-dogs, from the seats occupied until now, and has banished the Demons to the Caucasus, nay, to the saddest jaws of Orcus. That heavenly Oil, derived not from a merchant's shop but from the very fountains of Palestine, has filled the prophetic caverns with an unbearable splendor, fragrance, and brightness.

He continues to address Caesar himself:

> You will by no means be able to serve contrary Princes, of Light and Darkness. Since you recently surrendered yourself to his homage, you have spontaneously renounced the service of another with Altar and veneration. The fasces have been submitted to one more eminent, more powerful, and greater. Leave this house which I must shortly abandon; flee our sanctuaries, to be crowned not with Laurel, but with Cypress.

A Hebrew boy, who rules over the blessed gods, commands me to leave this house and return to the underworld; therefore, depart in silence from our altars.

For indeed, Augustus, intending to inquire from the Pythian Demon who would administer the Roman Empire after he himself was taken from human affairs, received this answer from the indignant spirit after repeated sacrifice:

> By what end or period will there ever be a respite from troublesome weariness, when that Firstborn of the Gods, ruling not only the heavens but also the underworld, has now placed a limit? He has driven out the Hebrew Boy, recently shadowed by a prodigious flow and indicated by many sun-dogs, from the seats occupied until now, and has banished the Demons to the Caucasus, nay, to the saddest jaws of Orcus. That heavenly Oil, derived not from a merchant's shop but from the very fountains of Palestine, has filled the prophetic caverns with an unbearable splendor, fragrance, and brightness.

He continues to address Caesar himself:

> You will by no means be able to serve contrary Princes, of Light and Darkness. Since you recently surrendered yourself to his homage, you have spontaneously renounced the service of another with Altar and veneration. The fasces have been submitted to one more eminent, more powerful, and greater. Leave this house which I must shortly abandon; flee our sanctuaries, to be crowned not with Laurel, but with Cypress.

### XXVI.

The <term>jus clientelae</term> <gloss>right of clientage</gloss> is dissolved by the demise and desolation of the thing, for instance, the destruction of the city which one has undertaken to defend <note>argument from 5, § 2; law: "If the usufruct," 21, Digest, By what modes usufruct is lost.</note> The payment of the honorarium established for the sake of defense expires. A great loss of status <note>Law: "Of cognitions," 5, Digest, On extraordinary cognitions</note>, or proscription, or the Imperial Ban, extinguishes clientage in the person of either the patron or the client; for those who are proscribed are stripped of all clientage, faith, and protection, and thus of every liberty and privilege <note>Ordinance of the Chamber, part 2, law 9, § 2; Gail, *On Public Peace*, book 2, chapter 1, number 20; Mynsinger, *century 1, observation 50, and century 3, observation 52*; they fail in agreements, titles, oaths, treaties, and all rights, Bechl., *On Security*, thesis 118 and following.</note> However, it is more true that no one is deprived of that right on account of a change of Catholic or Augustan religion <note>Constitution of the Religious Pacification of the year 55, § "It should also"; Syrinus, *On Religious Peace*, conclusion 37; Besold, *On the Law of Treaties*, chapter 5, number 15.</note> Nor is it lost by major excommunication, as it is by the Ban; for the latter is mortal, as Mager speaks <note>Mager, chapter 16, number 199</note>, whereas the former is medicinal <note>Hopingk, *On the Right of Protection*, thesis 6, letter d</note>.

<translation page="15"># Of the Human Mind.

...and contemplate only the concept and the idea, and set them before ourselves. Judgment, however, is called that by which, from the intuition of those things which we have perceived, we affirm or deny something about the things themselves. This affirmation and negation is threefold: of existence, of essence, and of accidents. For example, when I have affirmed that the mind exists, I have explained what its essence is and what kind of thing it is. I call it an affirmation when judgment attributes the predicate to the subject in an intentional, unitive manner of tending. I call it a negation when it intentionally cuts off and tears away that same predicate from its subject in a divisive manner of tending. Reasoning or discourse is a connection and a certain comparison of many thoughts and judgments, or if you prefer, a passage from one thought to another; since discourse necessarily includes two cognitions in itself, it does not require more. For after the intellect has received an object into itself by simple apprehension, and has passed judgment upon it, soon, by a power implanted in it by nature, it deduces other properties of the object from the already known predicate, and wanders and runs through its many predicates by various acts, as if by steps.

§. 27. But since these four—essence, power, operation, and object—have this order, that power flows from essence, operation from this power, and operation tends toward the object, I must inquire into the object about which the intellect operates in the three ways mentioned, for the sake of its full knowledge. I cannot derive its extension better than from the power implanted in it. My intellect conceives objects infinitely diverse among themselves in number and perfection: impossible, possible, non-existent, immersed in matter, and separated from matter. Although it cannot comprehend God, the creator of all beings, it represents Him as He is in Himself, strengthened by heavenly light, so that no reason appears to me why I should not extend the power of my intellect to every object that falls even under the angelic intellect. Indeed, by exalting its nature, I illustrate the immense goodness of God. Nor is this consideration a small argument for me to believe this: whether I extend the sphere of my intellect or not, and even if I deny it such extension, I find that it must necessarily be attributed to it. For if I hold an affirmation, I must know all those objects; for I cannot affirm anything about any object unless I know it. Without negation...

<summary>This page defines the operations of the mind, specifically distinguishing between simple apprehension, judgment, and reasoning, while asserting that the human intellect possesses the capacity to encompass objects even beyond the material realm.</summary>
<keywords>Simple apprehension, Judgment, Reason, Essence, Intellectual power</keywords></translation>

<translation page="16"># Philosophical Dissertation

...nor can I deny, unless it is what I conceive, so that I conclude: the object of my intellect is also everything that falls under the angelic intellect.

§. 28. The mode by which the intellect operates regarding these objects seems to me twofold. For it perceives some things without a corporeal idea, while others it perceives only with the help of a corporeal idea. I shall call the one who understands in the former way a pure intellect, and the one who understands in the latter way, helped by the senses. I am persuaded that there is a pure intellect in me because I know well that it understands its own thoughts, and it is not plausible to me that any mathematical figures—or rather, any ideas of mathematical figures—or other ideas of the mind (for example, of a thing, substance, truth, goodness, fairness, and common notions, for example, those which agree with a third party, etc.) are drawn by the benefit of the senses, since those ideas contain nothing corporeal or of corporeal affection, nor do they enter into the senses. Rather, it is more plausible that they were implanted in the mind from its very beginning, that is, that the mind was given by God the faculty of exciting and making such forms of concepts. Therefore, I do not think the common saying of <term>Eustachius</term> is universally true: "Nothing is in the intellect, etc." <note>A reference to the Aristotelian dictum: "Nothing is in the intellect that was not first in the senses."</note> For if this adage were universally valid, all knowledge of God would have to be denied entirely. For God was in no way, however you distinguish it, in the senses, since He is not corporeal, and therefore He would never have been in the intellect. For he would foolishly believe in God who knows not even a whit <term>γρὺ</term> <gloss>a tiny amount/a trifle</gloss> about Him. Nor does it follow that God enters into the senses, as some wish, because we arrive at the knowledge of God <term>dianoiticè</term> <gloss>through discursive reasoning</gloss> by the contemplation of His works, which do fall into the senses. For that contemplation does not lead us to know the existence of the supreme Deity in any other way than by exciting us to attend to the idea of the mind, and thus, with that intervening, to conclude the existence of God. But from that, it is not proven that God enters into the senses, which was the matter in question. By the same reasoning, anyone could deny the existence of their own mind, since it does not fall into the senses. And indeed, I do not see how they can prove, through the natural order of the faculties, that the intellect must necessarily contemplate phantasms <term>phantasmata</term> <gloss>mental images or appearances</gloss>. For the connection between the intellect and the fantasy, which they establish as natural, is so great that the intellect cannot grasp a notion of anything without the fantasy accompanying it, experience...

<summary>The author argues for the existence of a "pure intellect" independent of the senses, challenging the scholastic axiom that all knowledge originates in sensory experience by using the existence of God and mathematical concepts as evidence.</summary>
<keywords>Pure intellect, Eustachius, Sensory perception, Phantasms, Knowledge of God</keywords></translation>

<translation page="16">destinies, so that while they render fame immortal, they wear out and weaken the body, the host of a great soul, like iron through vigils and tireless labor; and they become the same color as the dead, who associate too much with the dead. This companionship had been interrupted for our **BLESSED** one for so many years, and although his fame shone more brightly day by day through the attrition of his labors, his strength grew duller day by day, and while he illuminated <term>Cimbria</term> <gloss>Jutland/Denmark</gloss> with his light, he himself seemed to be consumed gradually like a lamp by its own shining.
<margin>Death of his wife.</margin>
Added to this, with his body pressed by such a weight of labors, was a lethal wound, a pain penetrating to the very vitals, from the premature passing of his sweetest wife. The softer his marriage bed had been for so many years without any discord, and the more fruitful it had been with noble offspring emulating his paternal virtues, the more he lamented that his joys were snatched away, all the pleasures of life extinguished with his wife, and that he himself was carried out in the same funeral as she. Forgive, *Auditors*, forgive that I include in these rationalizations the inevitable necessity of fate, or rather of God, the arbiter of life and death, whose commands are not to be moved, by which certain limits are set for us and an immovable goal is fixed by the years—things our mind often perceives falsely, while blind to the rest. These were the decrees of the Fates, to reclaim this deposit of heaven and to insert an immortal head among the stars, which had illuminated *Cimbria* with such great rays. The orbits of the earth seemed too narrow for such a vast mind, therefore it had to be summoned to the wider spaces of the heavens. Although he was always desirous of these, he was not so weary of present things that, had the Fates and God allowed, he would not have indulged us with the use of himself for longer, especially to set the final hand to the divine work he had begun. The sons of the physicians were consulted; everything was sought from everywhere that might strengthen the powers of a body failing day by day, and restore what had collapsed. <margin>Death of his wife.</margin>
Added to this, with his body pressed by such a weight of labors, was a lethal wound, a pain penetrating to the very vitals, from the premature passing of his sweetest wife. The softer his marriage bed had been for so many years without any discord, and the more fruitful it had been with noble offspring emulating his paternal virtues, the more he lamented that his joys were snatched away, all the pleasures of life extinguished with his wife, and that he himself was carried out in the same funeral as she. , [the corruption] always and continuously impeding the healing of the ulcer; finally, from the motion of the discharge, which corresponded to the pulse of the arteries, he could have concluded that there was a very deep injury to the skull. §. XIV. So much for the prognosis: to which it would now be appropriate to append the treatment, if anything other than the name of a plaster and a lancet had become known to us regarding it. Nevertheless, so that it may be clear where reason failed in that regard, it is my intention to set forth briefly the method by which the ulcer was treated by us, and to review it in order, not indeed in a <term>plasmatically</term> <gloss>theoretical/imaginary</gloss> way, but in a tumultuous one, exactly as the course of the history presented itself.

§. XV. Before anything was attempted, it seemed opportune to purge the primary passages with a mild laxative. Although this may seem superfluous to Overkamp and other moderns, it is not without its own utility. Next, since the removal of the hair was extremely necessary both for a more accurate diagnosis of the affected place and for a more suitable application of remedies, and yet the most bitter pain in the reddened skin, rendered fungous by the expansion of the fibers, would not admit the shaving of a razor, the surgeon was forced to trim it with scissors.

§. XVI. A doubt arose concerning the exploration of the depth. For when we measured by means of a stylus how far the edge of the knife ought to be driven, and it stopped against a hard body, and did not immediately descend to the dura mater, we marveled that the skull was not perforated, nor, as we conjectured from the support of the discharge...</translation>

...[supported] by it, that it was perforated. §. XVII. The depth of the wound having thus been revealed, it remained for the skin to be cut down to the skull, and indeed in a crosswise fashion; since both the cavity of the ulcer and the hidden caries indicated incision, and the affected place permitted it, and Hippocrates and Celsus demanded it. That incision is indicated was evident from text 18, in the cited book: *Ulcers which do not have sufficient magnitude of length and breadth for the inspection of the bone, as to whether it has suffered any evil from a projectile, and what kind of evil it has suffered, and how much the flesh is contused, and how much the bone has suffered injury: and again, whether the bone is unharmed by the projectile, and has suffered no evil: and for treatment, what kind of work the ulcer, the flesh, and the affection of the bone require, such ulcers truly require incision.* That incision is permitted, we learned from text 19, because all parts sustain it, except the temples and the vein which runs over the temples, nor, with Celsus as witness, does the skin heal with great difficulty, even if it is cut in vain. Specifically, however, Celsus recommended the incision which takes the shape of the letter X from two transverse lines, so that the skin may then be cut away from each of the preceding angles.

§. XVIII. The opened skin was found to be an inch in thickness, and to have the appearance of a dissected uterus, when in the final months...</translation>

<translation page="13">of which we have made mention until now, show the strength and holiness of the Christian religion only in a general way; furthermore, individual chapters of it, if indeed one must dispute with some pagan, can be defended and declared: but to demonstrate them openly, as we have warned again and again above, is not possible in the same way.

### LXII.

But if such a contest is undertaken with someone who does not reject, alongside the divine Scripture, the authority of the holy Fathers and the universal Church, there is nothing that cannot be proven by that same reasoning.

### LXIII.

Moreover, the office of Theology is not only what we have just explained, namely to defend its principles against those who deny or attack them, and to derive from there, by the force of reason, various other conclusions which serve to protect and illustrate the Christian matter; but it is also to strongly fortify both [the principles and the conclusions] by employing internal and external safeguards and supports of this science.

### LXIIII.

We call the internal and proper safeguards of Theology those arguments which are sought from the Canonical Scripture: from the faithful tradition of Christ and the Apostles: from the authority of the Catholic and Apostolic Church, from the canons of general councils and Roman Pontiffs: and finally, from the monuments of ancient and recent Fathers and Theologians.

### LXV.

<margin>+</margin> External safeguards, and those which might be called borrowed from another’s estate, are those which are taken from the teachings of natural Philosophers, from the responses of Jurists—for they too wish to be counted among the professors of true Philosophy—from the chronicles of history: and finally, from the very resources of human reason.

### LXVI.

For since there is a twofold type of argumentation—one resting on authority, which is proper to the Theologian, and the other instructed by reason, which is peculiar to the Philosopher—if it is not permitted to use the former and proper one, the Theologian seizes what is closest to the former and defends himself by reason in place of authority; yet he often joins both types of proof together.

### LXVII.

From this it is evident that the wisdom of those is foolish who, when they are about to speak on some Theological argument, reject the authority of the Fathers, Councils, and Scriptures as if it were not firm enough, and dispute only with little arguments borrowed from natural Philosophy. For those <term>μωρόσοφοι</term> <gloss>foolish-wise men</gloss> do not understand,</translation>

<translation page="14">a place is so proper to the authority of Theology that it receives almost all the reasons it uses as if they were guests and foreigners.

### LXVIII.

Furthermore, there is this difference among the internal safeguards of Theology: arguments drawn from the authority of the sacred scriptures, from the definition of the Catholic and Apostolic Church, and from the perpetual and constant tradition of that same Church are not only proper and internal, but also necessary. Those taken, however, from the doctrine of some Saint or Father, of whatever order, holiness, or authority he may have been, conclude only probably. Nevertheless, it would be reckless to recede very far from the judgment of many holy Fathers, especially in the interpretation of the Scriptures.

### LXIX.

Therefore, those are proven to err gravely and dangerously who, making Saint Jerome the rule of the canonical Scriptures, wish only those books to be held as canonical to which that same Father, perhaps while busied with something else, applies the name of canonical somewhere.

### LXX.

Truly, a necessary argument is not derived from the authority of Jerome alone, but only a probable one; and not even a probable one always, but only when it does not depart far from the more accepted opinion of the remaining Fathers.

I am unable to repay how much I owe to His Highness in this regard, praying to God that He might graciously reward this care of the Father of the Fatherland. To you also, most Reverend, Most Excellent, and Most Illustrious Men, my tutors and promoters, I devote myself, for I owe it to you. You have dealt with me fatherly, which I always proclaim; you have faithfully confirmed me in the same, having been imbued with the true faith. Therefore, having followed your guidance, I am also most fully persuaded of this:

<margin>Aristotle, Ethics 6.4</margin>
It is better and necessary to set aside one's own concerns for the sake of the preservation of the truth.

You have testified to your benevolent affection; therefore, I hang entirely upon your will. I am yours, as long as I am my own, and I shall remain most observant of all of you, while men, like the blind, grope in more than Cimmerian darkness, knowing neither what they should follow nor what they should decline. Receive your alumnus of the Muses, educated and informed in the Orthodox Lutheran Religion, and one who, by the grace of God, will testify to it until his final breath. Forgive my fall, for even the Saints slip at times, why not the weak? For just as all things situated on a high place have difficult and arduous approaches, so too does that sublime summit of the future life. Hence, it is not within the power of everyone to struggle through the precipices, especially</translation>

<translation page="14">those whose spirits are weighed down by a worldly appetite and whose minds are sluggish, those whom the straits of fortune strike, those whom turbulent movements agitate, those who nearly collapse under the dire waves of persecution, and those who, having read the diverse writings of Heretics, are troubled and distracted in various ways. **XXV.** To the second genus of intellections belongs mental enunciation, which, in order that the Moderns may distinguish it from a proposition—which also pertains to the third operation of the mind and includes virtual discourse—they correctly define as an immediate judgment regarding some thing: that is, one such that it affirms a predicate of a subject because of the connection between the subject itself and the predicate. Whereas, on the contrary, all discourse is a mediate judgment, because it mediately approves the connection of the predicate with the subject. The most powerful property of these acts is formal truth, which is nothing other than the conformity of the judgment with the object; just as, conversely, falsity is the difformity of the judgment with the object. Thus, a true judgment is that which enunciates an object to be as it is in the nature of the thing; a false one is that which does not enunciate it as the object is.

**XXVI.** An enunciation once true can never pass into a false one, nor, conversely, can a false one pass into a true one; for the same cognition always represents the same thing. Therefore, the cognition which represented Adam as writing, with truth, for this instant that the verbal copula designated, represented Adam as writing at this instant for eternity. For just as it is impossible for Adam to have written at this instant A, and not to have written at this instant A, so it is impossible that a cognition which truly represents him as having written at this instant A should ever represent him as not having written; since a proposition speaks for eternity only of this, and of no other instant. Regarding falsity, one must reason in the same way: if a proposition were to represent a time other than that which it had first represented, by this very fact it would not be the same, but another and new representation, and consequently a new cognition.

**XXVII.** To the third and primary genus of the operations of the human intellect belongs formal discourse, or the <term>syllogism</term> <gloss>logical argument</gloss>; which is a statement in which, some things being posited, something else necessarily follows from those which were posited, because these things are so. And essentially it involves not only the conclusion, but also the premises themselves; nor is anyone considered to have constructed a formal syllogism who either infers something without any premises, or, with premises made, infers nothing. But in order that the assent of the conclusion may be distinguished from another immediately judicative assent, it must intrinsically reach the object of the premises as a motive and formal reason for assenting. This is proven from the fact that every act tending toward some material object because of another formal one must reach that formal object. But the formal motive of the conclusion as such is the object of the premises, or the identity of the extremes with a third middle term; therefore, the act of the conclusion as such must reach that object. It is confirmed, because unless the act of the conclusion reaches the formal motive again, in some syllogisms there could not be given a reason why this proposition is a conclusion rather than another of the three, for any of them can be inferred from the others by way of a conclusion.

**XXVIII.** Besides the object of the conclusion and the object of the premises, the goodness of the inference—which is the identity between the object of the premises and the object of the conclusion—must also be reached by the act of the conclusion; for this goodness is also a partial motive, which, together with the object of the premises, moves the intellect to infer the conclusion. For if this unique connection between the object of the premises and the object of the conclusion were removed</translation>

<translation page="12">, however much the object of the premises remains, the intellect would not be moved to the conclusion. Therefore, just as when we love medicine because of health, we also love the connection that medicine has with the repairing of health, because if this connection were excluded we would not love the medicine, so too the intellect, in order to be moved to conclude, must not only reach the object of the premises, but also the goodness of the inference.

**XXIX.** Some doubt whether the judgment concerning the goodness of the inference must be a distinct and intermediate act between the assent of the premises and the assent of the conclusion, through which the intellect reflexively knows that this conclusion is rightly inferred from these premises because those things are identified with each other which are identified with one third. We think it more probable that *a judgment concerning the goodness of the inference is not always necessarily required, distinct from the act of the conclusion*, especially in practiced men to whom that principle is most clearly known, *whatever things are the same as one third, etc.* For such men, after they have seen in the premises that the extremes of the conclusion are identified with one third, immediately infer the act of the conclusion, which hits upon the object of the premises, the goodness of the inference, and the object of the conclusion, all at once. In those men, however, who are not practiced in making syllogisms, and who, even after they have seen two things identified with one third, can still doubt whether those two are identified with each other, we think that a judgment concerning the goodness of the inference that is distinct and precedes the conclusion *does follow*: for the intellect of such men, being imperfect, is not sufficiently determined by the object of the premises to infer the conclusion without any hesitation.

# *Operations of the Human Will.*

**XXX.** That the will is a free spiritual virtue, appetitive of an object, is certain among all; that it is not distinguished from the intellect or from the soul, we suggested above in the third thesis. The *material object* around which it revolves is everything that the intellect can know under the aspect of good or evil. The *formal object*, or that which immediately moves the will, is good and evil; the former moves it toward acts of pursuit, the latter toward acts of flight. The good that moves the will is threefold: *honest, delightful, and useful*. None of these can allure the will unless it is first known; yet that cognition itself is not the motive of the will, but a mere condition applying the motive. The will cannot love *evil as evil*, or that which is proposed solely under the aspect of evil, but it is otherwise if it is presented under the aspect of at least an apparent good.

**XXXI.** Speaking ordinarily, in order for us to love and desire some good for ourselves, it suffices to know that such a good is fitting for us; nor is it necessary that we recognize some goodness in ourselves for the sake of which we are worthy to love such a good for ourselves. But if we love or desire some good for another person, it is required that we apprehend some goodness in that person, for the sake of which we esteem them worthy of such a good. For in order that I may (ordinarily speaking) be able to unite myself through affection with the good of my neighbor, insofar as it is a good for them, I must first unite myself through affection</translation>

It concludes by defining the human will, its formal and material objects, and the conditions under which it pursues or avoids goods.</summary>
<keywords>Mental enunciation, syllogism, formal truth, human intellect, goodness of inference, human will, appetition, moral goodness</keywords>
