For just as it is impossible for Adam to have written at this instant A, and not to have written at this instant A, so it is impossible that a cognition which truly represents him as having written at this instant A should ever represent him as not having written; since a proposition speaks for eternity only of this, and of no other instant. Regarding falsity, one must reason in the same way: if a proposition were to represent a time other than that which it had first represented, by this very fact it would not be the same, but another and new representation, and consequently a new cognition.

**XXVII.** To the third and primary genus of the operations of the human intellect belongs formal discourse, or the <term>syllogism</term> <gloss>logical argument</gloss>; which is a statement in which, some things being posited, something else necessarily follows from those which were posited, because these things are so. And essentially it involves not only the conclusion, but also the premises themselves; nor is anyone considered to have constructed a formal syllogism who either infers something without any premises, or, with premises made, infers nothing. But in order that the assent of the conclusion may be distinguished from another immediately judicative assent, it must intrinsically reach the object of the premises as a motive and formal reason for assenting. This is proven from the fact that every act tending toward some material object because of another formal one must reach that formal object. But the formal motive of the conclusion as such is the object of the premises, or the identity of the extremes with a third middle term; therefore, the act of the conclusion as such must reach that object. It is confirmed, because unless the act of the conclusion reaches the formal motive again, in some syllogisms there could not be given a reason why this proposition is a conclusion rather than another of the three, for any of them can be inferred from the others by way of a conclusion.

**XXVIII.** Besides the object of the conclusion and the object of the premises, the goodness of the inference—which is the identity between the object of the premises and the object of the conclusion—must also be reached by the act of the conclusion; for this goodness is also a partial motive, which, together with the object of the premises, moves the intellect to infer the conclusion. For if this unique connection between the object of the premises and the object of the conclusion were removed

Therefore, just as when we love medicine because of health, we also love the connection that medicine has with the repairing of health, because if this connection were excluded we would not love the medicine, so too the intellect, in order to be moved to conclude, must not only reach the object of the premises, but also the goodness of the inference.

**XXIX.** Some doubt whether the judgment concerning the goodness of the inference must be a distinct and intermediate act between the assent of the premises and the assent of the conclusion, through which the intellect reflexively knows that this conclusion is rightly inferred from these premises because those things are identified with each other which are identified with one third. We think it more probable that *a judgment concerning the goodness of the inference is not always necessarily required, distinct from the act of the conclusion*, especially in practiced men to whom that principle is most clearly known, *whatever things are the same as one third, etc.* For such men, after they have seen in the premises that the extremes of the conclusion are identified with one third, immediately infer the act of the conclusion, which hits upon the object of the premises, the goodness of the inference, and the object of the conclusion, all at once. In those men, however, who are not practiced in making syllogisms, and who, even after they have seen two things identified with one third, can still doubt whether those two are identified with each other, we think that a judgment concerning the goodness of the inference that is distinct and precedes the conclusion *does follow*: for the intellect of such men, being imperfect, is not sufficiently determined by the object of the premises to infer the conclusion without any hesitation.

You have thus far traversed with me, O Auditors, a vast field of the vices by which the learned are accustomed to suffer, but much still remains to be said in that vein, which I willingly omit due to the constraints of time. ### ERROR XIV.
## That the Rational Soul resides in only one part of the Body.

I. Philo the Jew established the Rational Soul in the heart; Parmenides and Epicurus in the whole chest; Strato the Physicist in the bridge of the eyebrows; Erasistratus in the small membranes; Herophilus in the cavity or base of the brain; Hippocrates in the brain; Xenocrates at the crown of the head; others in the whole head as if in a fortress; and finally others elsewhere. Some even placed it in a hidden and obscure spot, from which it would run through the whole body, like a spider catching flies, as opportunity arose.

II. So too, the author of the *Compendium of the Whole of Theological Truth* <note>book 2, Venetian edition, year 1565, chapter 54, page 192</note> says that the soul, placed in the center of the heart, without being extended, gives sensation, life, and movement to the whole body united to it, just like a spider which, residing in the middle of its web, feels any movement made in the web, whether externally or internally; a truly strange opinion for a man.

->C O R R E C T I O.<-

I. The Rational Soul is not in only one part of the body, otherwise it would not substantially inform the others. Rather, it is whole in the whole continuous body, and whole in every part of it, as all sound philosophers and theologians believe, along with the interpreters of Aristotle. *On the Soul 1, text 93*, where the Philosopher says that one cannot even imagine which part (that is, a determined and sole part) the intellect, that is, the Spiritual Soul, has in the body.

II. And although Aristotle, *On Respiration, chapter 1*, expressly says that the soul exists in some particle of the body, it should not be thought that he held the same view as the ancients mentioned, because he immediately adds that it has its virtue in those particles, that is, in certain operations, and that it depends also on certain and determined organs, and has its material virtues or powers residing in and subjected to those particles or organs.

### ERROR XV.
## That the Rational Soul is mortal.

I. Primarily, all Epicureans denied that the Rational Soul is immortal, as witnessed by Ruvius in *On the Separated Soul*. Pliny followed them in *Natural History, book 7, chapter 55*, as did many others, especially the Sadducees, thinking that even the Rational Soul perishes with the body through diseases. Heretics, whom a Castro reports in *Book 2 against heresies, under the entry "Soul"*, are raising this same almost buried error again, and Lucretius in *Book 3* believed the soul was gradually extinguished with the body.

II. Regarding this matter, having weighed many passages on both sides, Aristotle seems to have been at least doubtful, as some note with Scotus in *Book 4, distinction 43, question 2, article 2*. However, some</translation>

<translation page="19">
<header>OF THE RATIONAL SOUL.</header>

of the ancient philosophers, especially the Stoics, thought that the soul does not always endure, but that when freed from the body it is weakened after a long time and finally perishes, though the souls of the wise, however, persevere until the end of the world.

# CORRECTIO.

I. The greater and better part of philosophers, even the ancients, admitted the immortality of the Rational Soul, as can be seen in Eugubinus, *Book 9 on Perennial Philosophy*, and others. Dandinus also, in *Book 1 on the Soul, commentary 39*, says that Pythagoras also acknowledged the immortality of the Rational Soul, for he said, "If you leave the body and are purified and come to the ether, you will be an immortal God, incorruptible, no longer mortal." Saint Thomas also explains Aristotle in this sense in *Against the Gentiles, Book 2, chapter 79*, along with others, as the more common opinion of moderns also holds, especially since he said the Rational Soul comes from without.

II. But whatever may be the case regarding Aristotle, immortality certainly pertains to the Rational Soul by its own nature and is owed to it, just as to the Angels, as witnessed by Ruvius in *On the Separated Soul, question 4, number 52*. Since it is truly created, it has no natural cause of its own corruption; for Christ says in Matthew 10 that they cannot kill the soul. Nor is it an obstacle that in the Epistle of Sophronius, recited in the 11th session of the 6th Council of Constantinople, intellectual beings are said to be immortal only by grace, and not by nature, and that this is approved by the Council. For Sophronius only denied such immortality to the Angels and the Rational Soul as God alone has, who for this reason is said in 1 Timothy 6 to have immortality alone, since he has it from himself and by his own utterly immutable essence.

III. Therefore, since it is certain from the 5th Lateran Council under Leo X, session 8, that immortality belongs to the Rational Soul by itself and by its own nature, some deduce from this that it can also be evidently demonstrated from physical principles, and is known as if from its own terms, at least in itself, even if perhaps not yet as far as we are concerned. For the first Truth cannot lie, nor can the light of nature, which was bestowed upon us by that same Truth to recognize the truth, be repugnant to it; just as Aristotle in the category of quality teaches that the squaring of the circle is expressly demonstrable, although the demonstration by which it might be proved has not yet been discovered.

IV. And indeed, it is at least morally evident that it pertains to divine Providence that the wicked be punished, while the good are affected by a reward worthy of their merit. Since this does not happen in this life, as experience often testifies, one must either concede the immortality of souls, or one must claim that Divine Providence fails in many things and that God is unjust, not treating each one according to merit, which is blasphemous. Saint Chrysostom, in *Homily 4 on Providence*, said that this reasoning is clearer than the midday light regarding the immortality of the Rational Soul.

# After the determination of simple complexions which received their name from the predominance of one element, we are about to speak of the complexion which is mixed from two elements, of which one does not predominate over the other. Such are the Choleric with the Phlegmatic; likewise, the Melancholic with the Sanguine. For it is not repugnant to the possible for contraries to exist in the same thing according to a diminished state, for it is possible for all humors to be gathered in one according to a diminished state, so that one succumbs to another. For as the philosopher writes, for those having a symbol <note>i.e., a shared quality</note>, the transmutation will be easy. For phlegm, on account of the proportion and convenience that it has with melancholy in coldness, is immediately transmuted into it. And the signs of a composite complexion are the same as with the simple, except that you ought to inspect more faithfully. For if you see in a man signs of the phlegmatic and sanguine complexion, such as if he is white and slender in the face, bold, fleshy, not inconstant in mind, and desiring and loving women, then you will say this one is composed of the sanguine and phlegmatic, more so than of the other two, or of one only. With equal confidence, we also proscribe those vulgar external greasy and oily things, which are called "defensives" <term>defensiva</term> <gloss>topical cooling/protective applications</gloss> by a specious and splendid name, and with which they stuff the pores of the skin and not rarely open a door to inflammation. <note>A large ornamental drop cap 'N' begins the section.</note>That perverse method of curing inflammations, which nevertheless clings more deeply in the minds of surgeons <term>Chirurgorum</term> <gloss>surgeons</gloss>, deserves no less severe censure, so that it seems easier to wrest the club from Hercules than to remove these deep-seated prejudices. But what else do they achieve with their repellents, astringents, and refrigerants <term>refrigerantibus</term> <gloss>cooling agents</gloss>, other than to increase obstructions, detain the coarser humors—which, as the more subtle parts evaporate, become acrid and tear or rupture the fibers—whence, with the obstruction increased, a greater tumor follows, and the path to gangrene is made more accessible? To ensure that this danger is averted in time, it will be necessary to direct your cares and thoughts solely toward the obstruction, to which end volatile alkalis, aromatics, and balsamics serve: for example, camphorated spirit of wine, spirit of sal ammoniac, lime water, fumigations, volatile oily salt, diascordium, and the *Theriaca* <gloss>a complex, traditional panacea/antidote</gloss>, which induces new fermentations. Likewise, all those things that temper, invert, or absorb the Stygian acid, to which category the *lac virginis* <gloss>virgin's milk (a milky lead-based lotion)</gloss> is deservedly referred, the chief of which—and one proved by me a hundred times—is that one of Zvölffer prepared from coltsfoot, white rose flowers, elder, wine, vinegar, and so forth. ### Sixth Question.

§. 11. *If Christ were on earth after the Ascension, would he not be our Priest?*

In the Epistle to the Hebrews, chapter 8, verse 4, these words are to be read: *For if he were on earth, he would not be a Priest*. From these, the adversaries <unclear>stealthily</unclear> gather that Christ dwells with his body in the heavens and is not on earth. It is therefore our task to wrest the club from Hercules <note>A proverbial expression meaning to overcome a difficult task or opponent.</note> and to respond soundly: *The first point*: If Christ could not be a Priest (if he were on earth), it would follow that when he was conversing on earth, and offering himself to his Father on the altar of the cross, and showing himself to his disciples for 40 days with many arguments, he was not a priest. The consequent is absurd; therefore, the antecedent is as well. The reason for the connection is evident, because he was on earth at that time. *The second point*: If Christ, because he is a Priest, would not be on earth, he would not be a Priest as God (because he is always on earth just as he is in heaven). The latter is absurd, by the confession of the opposing party; therefore, the former is as well. *The third point*: If Christ, because he is a Priest, would not be on earth, he would not be a Priest according to his human nature, because according to that, by their own admission, he is in Heaven. The latter is absurd, because the Priesthood pertains to his very office, and thus to both Natures; therefore, the former is as well. *Finally*, and *this*, if he were not on earth, he would not be an eternal Priest, because he is to return from Heaven on the last day. This is false, therefore so is that. It is wonderful, then, that the adversaries prop up the building of their opinion on this passage, as if it were some lute-player or a lean-to. But in truth, they act through tunnels <note>Meaning they act deceitfully or by hidden subversion.</note>. For, 1. they insert the words *according to human nature* into the text; 2. they take the words as referring to one or the other nature of Christ, when the Epistle speaks of the whole Christ. Now move the Syllogistic wheel; what will come out? Is it not this?</translation>

...he calmed the disturbances stirred up by unskilled pastors through the untimely changing of rites and absurd clamors about doctrine. He urged the priests with his own voice not to condemn all works without distinction, but to teach the doctrine of law and Gospel, of faith and works—which is necessary for true piety—distinctly and moderately. He urged them not to abolish feast days by their own whim, nor to drive the simple people, not yet illuminated by the true light of the Gospel, toward apostasy and sedition rather than piety, tranquility, and obedience through untimely and overly vehement invectives against the Pope, Cardinals, and Roman Bishops; and finally, not to incite tumults after the manner of fanatic Anabaptists. See his *Historia Arctoa* <gloss>Northern History</gloss>, Book II, p. 220.

### §. XVI.

However, these wicked men did not escape a deadly end. For we have received that *Rinck* <note>original: "Rinckium"</note>, because he did not desist from his errors, was consigned to perpetual imprisonment by the Landgrave of Hesse and thus miserably ended his life. See Seckendorff, *Lutheranism*, Book III, §. XXV, p. 71. But another sustained an even harsher punishment, since he had been an actor in the Münster tragedy. For he was first led before the Princes with other men of the same dregs for the sake of spectacle and mockery. Then, brought to a higher place, he was tied to a stake: two executioners were present, with red-hot pincers; he was torn by many bites, and finally, with a sword thrust through his chest, he died. Once extinguished, he was bound in an iron cage and hung up to be displayed at the highest tower of the city with the rest, the King indeed in the middle, and as great as the stature of a man, higher up. See Sleidanus, *Status Religionis* <gloss>State of Religion</gloss>, Book X, p. 283. It is a wonder to say that this man was hung at the highest tower of the city so that he might be exposed to the eyes of all. We shall say they exist. Many affirm having seen some capable of holding eighty rowers. The use of iron is not found among them. Consequently, our men were filled with great wonder as to how they might construct houses, which they saw were crafted with marvelous skill, or any other things pertaining to their use. But they learned from fame that they are <margin>The incredible savagery of certain men</margin> found in certain riverine regions. They later reported that this was the cause of their fleeing in terror toward our men, for they thought they were Cannibals, or Caribes, as they call those savage men. They leave the islands of these obscene people, situated almost in the middle of the voyage, to the south of these islands. The gentle people themselves complain that their islands are perpetually harassed by the frequent incursions of the Cannibals for the sake of plunder, just as hunters pursue wild beasts through the forests by force and treachery. The boys they capture, they castrate, just as we fatten chickens or pigs that we intend for our meals, so that they become larger and fatter, and they eat them. When they reach mature age, however, when they fall into their hands, they slaughter and divide them. They feast upon the extremities of the limbs while fresh, and they preserve the limbs salted, just as we do with ham, for future times. It is considered an abomination and obscene among them to eat women. If they capture young ones, they keep and guard them for the purpose of procreating offspring, no differently than we do with chickens, sheep, and other animals. They keep old women as slaves for performing menial tasks. In the islands which we can now call our own, both men and women find no safety other than flight when they perceive that the Cannibals are approaching. Although they use sharp-pointed reed arrows, they have found them to be of little use in repressing the violence and fury of the Cannibals; for all the natives admit that ten Cannibals would easily defeat one hundred of the others if they were to clash. What either race worships, besides the sky and its luminaries, they did not have sufficiently explored. Due to the shortness of time and the lack of interpreters, they were not allowed to learn more of the remaining customs of the islands. The gentle people use for food roots of our <margin>Food of the islanders</margin> turnips, similar in size and shape, but sweet in taste and similar to a young chestnut. They call these *ages*, and they have another type of root which they call *iucca* <gloss>yucca</gloss>. From this, they also prepare bread. They use *ages* more often roasted or boiled than for the purpose of making bread. They slice and press the *iucca*, for it is juicy, and bake it into cakes. But this is wonderful: they say the juice of the *iucca* is more lethal than aconite, and kills instantly if drunk; yet everyone has experienced that the bread made from its mass is tasty and healthy. They also prepare bread from a certain panicum grain, of which there is a great abundance among the Infrubes and the Granatenfe Spaniards, without much difference. The ear of this is longer than a span, tapering to a point, and almost the thickness of an arm. The grains are fixed by nature in a wonderful order, and in form and substance they emulate the pea legume. They are white when unripe, and when they have matured, they become very black; when broken, they exceed snow in whiteness. They call this type of grain *maizium* <gloss>maize</gloss>. And gold is of some value among them, for they wear it inserted into pierced earlobes and nostrils, drawn out into very thin laminas. However, since our men had learned that no merchants traveled to them, nor did they know any other shores besides their own, they began to ask them through signs where they obtained that gold. As far as could be gathered from signs, it was obtained from the sands of rivers flowing down from high mountains, and not with great labor; they would compress it into pellets before it was drawn into laminas. It was not, however, in that part of the island which that king held, which later became clear by experiment; for when they had already departed from there, they happened upon a river, and when they leaped onto land for the sake of getting water and fishing, they realized that its sand was mixed with much gold. They say they saw no four-footed animal, except for three types of rabbits. The islands harbor snakes, but they are very harmless. They found wild geese, turtledoves, and ducks, larger than ours and of the whiteness of a swan, with purple heads. Parrots, some of which were green,

# OCEANIC DECADE

<margin>Parrots distinguished by marvelous colors</margin>
C and others yellow over their entire body, others like the Indian ones collared with vermilion, as Pliny says, they brought back forty. But they were most highly distinguished by their most vivid and joyful colors. They have multicolored wings, for with green and yellow feathers, they have certain blue and purple ones mixed in, which variety produces delight. I wished to have recounted these things about the parrots, most illustrious Prince, although the opinion of this Christopher Columbus concerning the magnitude of the sphere and the opinion of the ancients about the circumnavigable world seems to contradict this. Yet, the parrots brought back from there, and many other things, indicate by their proximity or by nature that these islands pertain to the Indian region, especially since Aristotle toward the end of his book *On the Heavens and the World*, Seneca, and other men not ignorant of cosmography, attest that the Indian shores are not distant from Spain by a long stretch of sea toward the west. That land produces by its own nature an abundance of mastic, aloes, cotton, and other things of this kind. From trees, just as among the Seres <gloss>the Chinese</gloss>, fleeces are collected. They brought back certain wrinkled grains of various colors, sharper than Caucasian pepper; also branches from cocifa trees in the shape of cinnamon, but in taste and odor imitating sharp ginger in both the marrow and the bark. Content, therefore, with these signs of the discovered new land and of another unheard-of world, and deciding to return with a prosperous voyage, the zephyrs now blowing because our spring was approaching, he left thirty-eight men with that king of whom we made mention above, to investigate the nature of the places and the times until he himself returned. This king was called Guaccanarillo by the inhabitants, with whom, having struck a bond of singular friendship, he dealt in the ways he could regarding the life, safety, and protection of those he left behind. The king, touched by compassion for our men because they were being abandoned in foreign lands, was seen to shed tears and promised all aid. Thus, having embraced one another, Columbus, about to return to Spain, ordered the sails to be set, taking with him ten men from those [islands], from whom it was discovered that the language of all those islands could be written with our Latin letters <margin>D</margin> without any difficulty. For they call heaven *turei*, house *boa*, gold *cauni*, a good man *tayno*, and nothing *mayani*. They pronounce all other words no less clearly than we do our Latin. You have these things which I considered worthy of memory regarding his first voyage. The King and Queen, whose every thought, even while sleeping, is fixed on the increase of our religion, hoping that so many nations and simple peoples could be easily drawn to the law of Christ, are moved by these reports. They treat the arriving Columbus honorably, as he deserved for such exploits. They had him sit before them in public (which is the greatest sign of love, gratitude, and supreme honor among Spanish kings). They ordered that Columbus henceforth be called the marine prefect. He is known among the Spaniards as Admiral Columbus. They also honored his brother, Bartholomew Columbus, himself skilled in maritime affairs, with the title of prefect of the island of Hispaniola. They commonly call this office *Adelantado*. Therefore, I will sometimes purposely call the Admiral and the Adelantado and the presence of the ships by their common names, so that I may be understood more clearly. Now let us return to our subject. It was believed that the greatest benefits, which all mortals seek with all their strength, would accrue from the islands, just as Columbus himself, now the Marine Prefect, promised in the beginning. Moved by these two reasons, therefore, these two most holy partners order 17 ships to be prepared for the second expedition, three large, reinforced cargo ships, and 12 of the type of ships we wrote are called *caravels* in Spain, without reinforcements. Two of the same type, somewhat larger and suitable for holding reinforcements due to the size of their masts. They entrusted the care of preparing this fleet to Juan de Fonseca, a man of noble birth, Dean of Seville, and a man possessing great talent and spirit. They ordered that more than twelve hundred armed infantry be hired for it, among whom they ordered that craftsmen and artisans of every mechanical art be summoned for pay; they will mix some cavalry with the other armed men. To procreate offspring, they will take mares, sheep, heifers, and many others of their own kind.

They keep old women as slaves for performing menial tasks. In the islands which we can now call our own, both men and women find no safety other than flight when they perceive that the Cannibals are approaching. Although they use sharp-pointed reed arrows, they have found them to be of little use in repressing the violence and fury of the Cannibals; for all the natives admit that ten Cannibals would easily defeat one hundred of the others if they were to clash. What either race worships, besides the sky and its luminaries, they did not have sufficiently explored. Due to the shortness of time and the lack of interpreters, they were not allowed to learn more of the remaining customs of the islands. The gentle people use for food roots of our <margin>Food of the islanders</margin> turnips, similar in size and shape, but sweet in taste and similar to a young chestnut. They call these *ages*, and they have another type of root which they call *iucca* <gloss>yucca</gloss>. From this, they also prepare bread. They use *ages* more often roasted or boiled than for the purpose of making bread. They slice and press the *iucca*, for it is juicy, and bake it into cakes. But this is wonderful: they say the juice of the *iucca* is more lethal than aconite, and kills instantly if drunk; yet everyone has experienced that the bread made from its mass is tasty and healthy. They also prepare bread from a certain panicum grain, of which there is a great abundance among the Infrubes and the Granatenfe Spaniards, without much difference. The ear of this is longer than a span, tapering to a point, and almost the thickness of an arm. The grains are fixed by nature in a wonderful order, and in form and substance they emulate the pea legume. They are white when unripe, and when they have matured, they become very black; when broken, they exceed snow in whiteness. They call this type of grain *maizium* <gloss>maize</gloss>. And gold is of some value among them, for they wear it inserted into pierced earlobes and nostrils, drawn out into very thin laminas. However, since our men had learned that no merchants traveled to them, nor did they know any other shores besides their own, they began to ask them through signs where they obtained that gold. As far as could be gathered from signs, it was obtained from the sands of rivers flowing down from high mountains, and not with great labor; they would compress it into pellets before it was drawn into laminas. It was not, however, in that part of the island which that king held, which later became clear by experiment; for when they had already departed from there, they happened upon a river, and when they leaped onto land for the sake of getting water and fishing, they realized that its sand was mixed with much gold. They say they saw no four-footed animal, except for three types of rabbits. The islands harbor snakes, but they are very harmless. They found wild geese, turtledoves, and ducks, larger than ours and of the whiteness of a swan, with purple heads. Parrots, some of which were green,
pages.34:
# OCEANIC DECADE

<margin>Parrots distinguished by marvelous colors</margin>
C and others yellow over their entire body, others like the Indian ones collared with vermilion, as Pliny says, they brought back forty. But they were most highly distinguished by their most vivid and joyful colors. They have multicolored wings, for with green and yellow feathers, they have certain blue and purple ones mixed in, which variety produces delight. I wished to have recounted these things about the parrots, most illustrious Prince, although the opinion of this Christopher Columbus concerning the magnitude of the sphere and the opinion of the ancients about the circumnavigable world seems to contradict this. Yet, the parrots brought back from there, and many other things, indicate by their proximity or by nature that these islands pertain to the Indian region, especially since Aristotle toward the end of his book *On the Heavens and the World*, Seneca, and other men not ignorant of cosmography, attest that the Indian shores are not distant from Spain by a long stretch of sea toward the west. That land produces by its own nature an abundance of mastic, aloes, cotton, and other things of this kind. From trees, just as among the Seres <gloss>the Chinese</gloss>, fleeces are collected. They brought back certain wrinkled grains of various colors, sharper than Caucasian pepper; also branches from cocifa trees in the shape of cinnamon, but in taste and odor imitating sharp ginger in both the marrow and the bark. Content, therefore, with these signs of the discovered new land and of another unheard-of world, and deciding to return with a prosperous voyage, the zephyrs now blowing because our spring was approaching, he left thirty-eight men with that king of whom we made mention above, to investigate the nature of the places and the times until he himself returned. This king was called Guaccanarillo by the inhabitants, with whom, having struck a bond of singular friendship, he dealt in the ways he could regarding the life, safety, and protection of those he left behind. The king, touched by compassion for our men because they were being abandoned in foreign lands, was seen to shed tears and promised all aid. Thus, having embraced one another, Columbus, about to return to Spain, ordered the sails to be set, taking with him ten men from those [islands], from whom it was discovered that the language of all those islands could be written with our Latin letters <margin>D</margin> without any difficulty. For they call heaven *turei*, house *boa*, gold *cauni*, a good man *tayno*, and nothing *mayani*. They pronounce all other words no less clearly than we do our Latin. You have these things which I considered worthy of memory regarding his first voyage. The King and Queen, whose every thought, even while sleeping, is fixed on the increase of our religion, hoping that so many nations and simple peoples could be easily drawn to the law of Christ, are moved by these reports. They treat the arriving Columbus honorably, as he deserved for such exploits. They had him sit before them in public (which is the greatest sign of love, gratitude, and supreme honor among Spanish kings). They ordered that Columbus henceforth be called the marine prefect. He is known among the Spaniards as Admiral Columbus. They also honored his brother, Bartholomew Columbus, himself skilled in maritime affairs, with the title of prefect of the island of Hispaniola. They commonly call this office *Adelantado*. Therefore, I will sometimes purposely call the Admiral and the Adelantado and the presence of the ships by their common names, so that I may be understood more clearly. Now let us return to our subject. It was believed that the greatest benefits, which all mortals seek with all their strength, would accrue from the islands, just as Columbus himself, now the Marine Prefect, promised in the beginning. Moved by these two reasons, therefore, these two most holy partners order 17 ships to be prepared for the second expedition, three large, reinforced cargo ships, and 12 of the type of ships we wrote are called *caravels* in Spain, without reinforcements. Two of the same type, somewhat larger and suitable for holding reinforcements due to the size of their masts. They entrusted the care of preparing this fleet to Juan de Fonseca, a man of noble birth, Dean of Seville, and a man possessing great talent and spirit. They ordered that more than twelve hundred armed infantry be hired for it, among whom they ordered that craftsmen and artisans of every mechanical art be summoned for pay; they will mix some cavalry with the other armed men. To procreate offspring, they will take mares, sheep, heifers, and many others of their own kind.

<margin>Fruit of the womb of David. Proof. From the testimony of the Psalm.</margin>
Here it suffices that we have proven the only-begotten and natural Son of God is called and is the fruit of the womb of David, as we read in Psalm 132:11. Jehovah swore the truth to David himself, he will not turn away from it, nor deflect, nor depart:

> From the fruit of your womb I will set upon your throne.

### XXXI.

Although many understand this promise only regarding a political kingdom, we, following the divine Luther, believe that God confirmed with an oath that a king would be set from the fruit of the womb of David whose kingdom would be eternal.

### XXXII.

And truly, this is a remarkable promise: because it defines a certain person, and does not allow the succession to wander in an uncertain person.

### XXXIII.

Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob also had the promise concerning Christ, but under an uncertain person if you look at their multiplied posterity.

### XXXIV.

In this promise, however, there is a definite description: a specific person is named, so that even though the whole people were to be led into captivity, as long as the posterity of David remained, they would retain the hope of the kingdom.

### XXXV.

For this family was like a certain star in

<translation page="9">monarchy, we shall see. Behold, since Severus recognized the excellence of separating the duties of administering justice from those of war (see Aelius Lampridius in the life of Alexander Severus), he established salaries for the <term>Assessors</term> <gloss>legal advisors</gloss> of such magistrates. It is said that he was accustomed to grieve that men were promoted to positions other than those who could govern the republic by their own hand in the matters to which they were appointed. He believed that military men should have their own administrations, which they ought to conduct personally, and that the learned should likewise have theirs; and thus, that each should perform what he knows. For this reason, the excellent Prince himself, if a matter of law was being discussed, employed only the learned in his council; but if the matter concerned military affairs, he consulted veteran and aged soldiers, well-deserving and experienced in such locations, inquiring what history recorded the ancient Emperors to have done in similar cases, and so on for each individual matter. To say nothing of what once moved the Persians to laughter, because among the Romans, unlearned men held the office of judge, while the learned stood behind their backs, as attested by Marcellinus, book 23, almost near the end.

Yet we do not entirely disapprove of the institutions of the ancient Emperors, in that they chose military men, distinguished for their fortitude, to govern provinces in their stead. For if men sent to provinces were illustrious in practical experience and civil prudence, who does not see that they could have aptly governed the political state of those places, and preserved and defended them from the assault of enemies? Although they may not have been instructed in an exact knowledge of the laws, they could nevertheless render justice well through the aid of their <term>Assessors</term> <gloss>legal advisors</gloss>. In that same manner, just as in our current time some provinces are governed by Viceroys <note>original: "ProReges"</note> appointed by Princes, in which civil prudence is preeminent, who is there that would require a supreme knowledge of the laws? It is sufficient and necessary that they preside with their own authority, so that the <term>Assessors</term>, who in truth speak the law, are deterred from passing corrupt or evil judgments. Furthermore, this is done so that the authority of the judgment becomes more august and its splendor greater. However, a different standard prevailed, and indeed ought to have prevailed, for other judges whose sole concern was the resolution of forensic</translation>

<translation page="10">controversies. It was necessary for these men to be, above all, learned in the laws and customs of the Roman people during the time of the Emperors. For at that time, because judges were required to render justice based on their own knowledge of the law, it is sufficiently evident that those who were unskilled should not have been placed in charge of the duty of judging. For Alexander replied to the Commanders <note>original: "Capitaneis"</note> that a sentence pronounced against civil law and the constitutions of the Princes is of no moment (*Code, book 2, "When a Challenge is Not Necessary"*), to such an extent that—as Gaius answered in the time of Hadrian and Justinian approved (*Digest, the last book, "On Extraordinary Cognizance," and Institutes, "On Obligations Arising from Quasi-Delict"*)—a judge makes a case his own and begins to be held liable as if from a wrong <note>original: "quasi ex maleficio"</note> if, through imprudence and lack of skill, he judges badly. Not to mention that it is the duty of a judge not only to hear what the litigants bring forward of their own accord, but also to inquire of them whether they wish to bring forward and answer anything certain on their own behalf (*Code, "On Judges," book 9*). From this, those who are learned argue that the door to the courts is closed to the unskilled, because one who is ignorant of jurisprudence and the laws cannot conduct such interrogations. But the Emperor Justinian confirms our view most clearly, as in *Novella 82, preface*, he cuts off all access to an unskilled judge.

> "For we," says the most praiseworthy Emperor, "have not deemed it proper to have the names of certain judges, especially those unlearned in the laws and lacking experience in cases. For our administrators are assisted in all ways by <term>Assessors</term> <gloss>legal advisors</gloss>, who explain what belongs to the laws and fulfill their occupations; since they are detained by many cares which they hold in our service, they rightly supplement the part of the judgments through the presence of their <term>Assessors</term>. But those who possess neither the sword belt <note>original: "cingulum," a symbol of office</note> nor serve us—unless they can know by themselves what is just, but must beg for the honesty of judging from elsewhere—how will it not be the greatest vice for the Republic not to entrust lawsuits to those who know by themselves what ought to be done, but to allow them to seek others from whom it is permitted to learn what they ought to follow in judging? Thus Justinian."</translation>

<summary>The author discusses the historical administration of justice under Roman Emperors, distinguishing between the roles of military governors and specialized judges, while emphasizing the requirement for legal expertise as codified by Justinian.</summary>
<keywords>Roman law, Justinian, Assessors, jurisprudence, judicial competence, Roman Emperors, civil administration</keywords>

A greater doubt arises as to whether this privilege manifests its effect also outside the place of the markets, such that while they last, no arrest can be obtained at all in any place of that province, by which at least the goods of a debtor existing in the markets might be seized when situated outside that place? This question seemed so difficult to Ziegler in the cited place §. 6 and following, that having presented arguments on both sides, he finally suspended his judgment and desired a legislative decision from the supreme Prince. However, we think this knot is not entirely Gordian, such that it cannot be untied by any art. For as far as the inhabitants of the market place are concerned, the words of the often-mentioned Constitution seem to indicate clearly enough that they cannot obtain such arrests by which they might bind the goods of their debtors situated elsewhere; for they expressly prohibit inhabitants from bringing any annoyance upon market-goers under the pretext of a private debt, and they would undoubtedly bring grave annoyance upon them if they sought and obtained arrests on their property elsewhere. We do not hesitate to assert the same regarding outsiders. For the security of market-goers is harmed no less by such arrests obtained by outsiders than by inhabitants, and the very trade in the markets is hindered. To which is added that solemn markets belong not to one city but to the entire province, and therefore the privilege of them must also deservedly be observed in all places of the province or empire. Compare what we said above in §. 20.

### §. XXV.

To this opinion it is primarily objected that the market privilege appears to be local, that is, restricted solely to the place of the markets. For just as the Leipzig markets, for example, cannot be held outside Leipzig, so too, they say, their privilege must be restricted solely to Leipzig, such that it is as if affixed to it. But that market privileges can sometimes be extended also outside the place of the markets is clear even from the fact that Princes very often grant to a certain place the right of prohibition, so that within a few miles</translation>

<translation page="18">
similar markets may not be held. Above also in §. 23 we saw this very privilege of which we speak most rightly extended to the places through which market-goers approach and return; what, therefore, will prevent the same from being done in the present case for the most just reasons?

## §. XXVI.

The effects of this noble privilege are also not ignoble, among which in the very first place the *most complete and total security of those traveling to the markets* stands out; for they are immune from any molestation, vexation, and disturbance by their creditors whatsoever, so much so that all judicial acts undertaken against them are null <term>ipso jure</term> <gloss>by the law itself</gloss>, and are devoid of all value and effect. For that which is done against a prohibiting law cannot but be null <term>ipso jure</term> <gloss>by the law itself</gloss> <note>refers to the Digest/Code of Justinian: Law 5, Paragraph 1, Code concerning Laws</note>. And since this nullity is notorious, the judge proceeding <term>de facto</term> <gloss>as a matter of fact</gloss> is not obeyed with impunity, argument of the final law, ff. on Jurisdiction <note>refers to the Digest of Justinian, usually abbreviated as "ff." or "dig."</note>; nor does the debtor have any need to fear the penalty of contumacy or to appeal from the sentence.

## §. XXVII.

This security is quickly followed by the *distinguished and excellent opportunity for profit*. For he who enjoys present money also enjoys the opportunity of making profit and gain. Debtors would very often certainly emerge from their difficulties if they were not shaken down to the very sack and wallet by inhuman and harsh creditors, and all the nerves for seeking wealth were not cut for them. Especially since an ample opportunity for increasing one's patrimony offers itself in the markets, the Emperors very wisely fortified debtors with the present privilege, by virtue of which they can not rarely not only escape debt, but also restore themselves and their families to a more prosperous state. For who does not know that one happy hour can often repay to a merchant as much as a hundred unfortunate days have taken away?

with the image of God, entrance into the eternal kingdom of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ is abundantly provided; but he who thinks he possesses it, through a reckless abuse of the Gospel, finds that everything is taken away from him. 2 Peter 1:11, Luke 8:18.

### OBSERVATION V.
#### When we speak of the restored image of God, it is not always necessary to add that it is to be understood as begun, and not perfect.

1. The foundation lies in the fact that, although the image of God in this life is not restored in its totality, or in such a way that it attains the perfection of that state which existed before the fall, nevertheless, it is restored in man truly and in reality, so that the conformity with God is no less true than that which existed at the beginning. Now, indeed, whatever things possess absolute truth (that is, things which are not such only by a certain respect or condition, even if they are found to be subject to different degrees regarding perfection), they can also be named by their own right and merit without an added qualification, so that if the inferior condition is not expressed, no one is deceived by the absolute appellation. Just as in natural things, not only those advanced in age and stature, but also infants and the very tender are most correctly called human.

2. Nothing, indeed, can be brought forward to the contrary, unless even a first consideration shows it to be frivolous. For it is most false to say that the image of God, because of the mention of God, cannot be understood as anything but perfect without some qualification; for the common principle itself dictates that predicates are to be understood no otherwise than as the nature of the subjects,
</translation>

or the nature of the underlying argument, permits. The error lies in this, that perfection is wrongly assumed regarding the constitution of any image of God whatsoever, seeing that it pertains to the essence of God; in which there is a notable confusion. But truly, if the image of God, when posited absolutely, is apprehended as nothing but perfect, because God is perfect, then certainly it could not even be said of Adam before the fall, since you might perhaps conceive it as infinite on account of the mention of God, who is infinite. What could be clearer than this objection? Nor is there any inconvenience if there is attributed to the regenerate the same image of God which was created with man and lost by Adam. For if it were declared to be equal, it would not be without error; but to be the same designates nothing except one and the same truth of the image of God. For neither does one who hears that the regenerate have received the image of God which Adam lost think thereby of perfection, because it was perfect, but rather of what is to be understood by the image of God; and so far is such a manner of speaking from insinuating perfection, that there would rather be a need for a new question on the part of the listener: do those who recover it possess it perfectly? This deduction is full of aberration and is therefore null: It is said that the same image of God is received which was lost through Adam; therefore it must necessarily be understood as perfect.

3. And so that the light may shine most openly in this matter, let the dangers be considered which threaten from both extremes. For if it is always urged, whenever the discussion arises regarding the image of God restored in the regenerate, that it is said to be *begun*, and nothing more is to be attributed to the regenerate, the listeners seize an opportunity for sloth, and think there is no conviction other than that the image of God itself is begun, and, when it comes to the zeal of increasing it

<translation page="15">§ XXIX. It is disputed whether both parents, or only the father, must bring this rebellious son to the <term>synedrium</term> <gloss>sanhedrin/council</gloss>. Theodoret, in volume 1 of his works, Paris edition, page 168, believes that both Father and Mother must agree in the accusation of this son before he can be killed. This opinion is approved by a unanimous vote in the <term>Mishnah</term> <gloss>oral law compendium</gloss> regarding the <term>synedria</term> <gloss>councils</gloss>, chapter 8, cited in § 4, where it is said: *If his father wishes (to accuse him) but the mother does not, or if the father does not wish to but the mother does, the son does not become a rebellious and contumacious son until both have willed it.* It is then added: *If one of them (the parents) is maimed, or lame, or mute, or blind, or deaf, the son does not become a rebellious and contumacious son: for it is said: "And his father and his mother shall take hold of him," therefore they must not be maimed; "and they shall bring him out," therefore they must not be lame; "and they shall say," therefore they must not be mute, "this is our son," therefore they must not be blind; "he does not obey our voice," therefore they must not be deaf.*

§ XXX. But a new question arises: whether the verses in Deuteronomy 21:22–23, *And if a man has committed a sin worthy of death, and he is to be put to death, and you hang him on a tree, his body shall not remain overnight on the tree, but you shall surely bury him that day, for he who is hanged is accursed of God, and you shall not defile your land which the Lord your God gives you as an inheritance*, should, I ask, be referred to the rebellious and contumacious son? Certainly, the ancient Hebrews are of the opinion, and they say, if parents spare the son and do not wish to accuse him, that he is then killed by the <term>synedrium</term> <gloss>sanhedrin/council</gloss>, or overwhelmed with stones, and hanged, because if he is a notorious sinner, the senate investigates him. See <term>Jarchii</term> <gloss>Rashi</gloss> on this passage and <term>Elias Misrachi</term>, the most diligent interpreter of <term>Jarchii</term>, in this passage, Cracow edition, folio 304, column 4.

§ XXXI. It remains for us to add something regarding the overnight stay upon the tree. This is certain: that the accused were punished by hanging after death among the ancient Hebrews, as is testified by, among others, <term>Obadias de Saphorno</term> in <term>Biur al Hattora</term> <gloss>Commentary on the Torah</gloss>, Venice edition, folio 73, column 1, where he calls hanging</translation>

<translation page="16">an insult brought upon one after death. <term>Abarbanel</term> agrees with this, who in <term>Per. al. Hattora</term> <gloss>Commentary on the Torah</gloss>, p. 379, col. 2, vigorously defends this opinion. Compare also <term>Aruch</term>, Venice edition, fol. 93, col. 1, at the bottom. It is evident that hanging was the punishment, as <term>Calovius</term> teaches in his notes on Deuteronomy 21. But why the corpses should not have been left upon the tree must be inquired into.

§ XXXII. <term>Jacobus Bolducius</term>, volume 2 on the book of Job, Paris edition, p. 132, relates from <term>Andreas Masius</term> the reason why the law wished for those affected by the punishment of the cross to be buried is this: that from the long spectacle upon the cross, someone might easily be led to the opinion that the soul is extinct, and think less correctly regarding the future resurrection of bodies.

§ XXXIII. But the more potent reason seems to have been that men might not be defiled by the touch of a corpse, especially since the defilement contracted from the dead was the greatest of all defilements among the Hebrew people. This is the direction of the exposition of <term>Lucas Osiander</term> on Deuteronomy 21, at the end.

§ XXXIV. And thus hanging has been examined as it existed among the Jews. Although the wood on which the condemned were hanged can be called a <term>patibulum</term> <gloss>gallows/crossbeam</gloss>, as <term>Jeckutbiel</term> calls it in the German translation of the Bible on Deuteronomy 21, Amsterdam edition, and the word "wood" is also taken for a gallows, as <term>Flacius</term> teaches in <term>Clavis</term> <gloss>Key to the Scriptures</gloss>, under the title "wood," Jena edition, p. 587, nevertheless the punishment of crucifixion was not customary among the Hebrews, because crucifixion is not listed among the punishments as a distinct penalty, but only mention is made of hanging as a subsequent, different punishment. Nor does the word <term>תלה</term> <gloss>to hang/suspend</gloss> precisely signify hanging a living man, or putting him on a cross, since it is also used for those things to which crucifixion does not apply; for example, meat or fish or bread are said to be hung on a wooden peg, which are not said to be crucified. See <term>Nathan Benjechiel</term> in <term>Sepher Herauch</term> <gloss>The Book of the Aruch</gloss>, Venice edition, fol. 162, col. 4.

<translation page="9">Pererius also urges this, saying: 
> Since that translation of Enoch occurred more than six hundred years before the flood, it was possible that Enoch was then led into the earthly Paradise, which we do not deny endured up to the flood: however, one cannot argue from this that Paradise remained untouched by the flood, and that it still exists, and that Enoch and Elijah dwell in it, etc.

What, therefore, have the Adversaries gained from this passage of Ecclesiasticus? I leave it to the kind Readers to decide. I, for my part, cannot grasp what defense they seek here, much less what they find. That the words **INTO PARADISE** were added seems to be gathered also from another place in Sirach, (z) where Enoch is said to be <term>ἀπὸ τῆς γῆς ἀναληφθείς</term> <gloss>taken up from the earth</gloss>, that is, taken up or received upwards from the earth. For <term>ἀναλαμβάνεσθαι</term> <gloss>to be taken up</gloss> is frequently used to mean taken upwards. (α) If, therefore, Enoch was lifted up from the earth, he was not taken into the earthly Paradise, unless you wish to maintain with some, or rather to speak foolishly, that Paradise is closest to the Lunar Sphere, suspended as it were on high, and by no means to be sought on earth. And consequently, if Sirach had written that Enoch was taken into the earthly Paradise, and yet had asserted that he was carried up from the earth to the heights, he would have contradicted himself, or else would have placed that earthly Paradise in the air. But even if he had said that he was taken into Paradise, he would have meant, by the force of another passage, the heavenly Paradise, into which we believe he was truly received, and which some from the very camp of the Papists assert, as we have emphasized in the preceding Dissertation; not to mention the Fathers, who with Ambrose assert that Enoch was raptured into **HEAVEN**, or the heavenly Paradise, to whose statements Cornelius à Lapide indeed tries to respond; (γ) but he satisfies neither the Reader nor himself, as is clear from his own words.

Finally, and thirdly, from the Holy Scriptures, and indeed the canonical book of Genesis, Bellarmine, and with him the Jesuit Jac. Tirinus, (δ) argue that Paradise still remains on earth; because, if the waters of the flood had also devastated Paradise, the dove sent out from Noah’s ark or vessel would not have been able to bring back a branch of green olive. But truly, I would almost call this argument ridiculous. I do not wish to repeat what Pererius himself retorted to this: (ε) I at least urge this, that Moses testifies most evidently that the waters of the flood had already abated or diminished, and that for some days the ark had rested on the mountains of Ararat. Why, then, could an olive tree not emerge at the same time on some high mountain, which, on account of its strength and firmness, especially with God so ordaining, had endured under the waters? Pererius reports from natural philosophers that its leaves never fall, and Pliny testifies (ζ) that it lives for over two hundred years, and that authorities agree on this. And thus we have also brushed away the third <term>ψευδύλλιον πῆμα</term> <gloss>false, deceitful injury</gloss>. The order now requires that, as we promised above, we show with the most solid arguments that an earthly Paradise does not exist even now. But because the thread must be broken here, and we must arrive at the **ONE WHO IS ABOUT TO BID FAREWELL**, we shall defer this part to the following Dissertation. But that one who is about to bid farewell</translation>

<translation page="10">is JOHANNES HEINRICUS AMELONGUS, our fellow citizen or native of Gera, son of the Most Accomplished and Learned Man, Mr. FRIEDRICH AMELONG, <term>τοῦ νῦν μακαρίτου</term> <gloss>the now blessed/departed</gloss>, who, while he lived, was secretary to the Archive and Consistory of Ruthen-Plauen, a man certainly most worthy, in human judgment, of having lived longer, but who perished by a most bitter fate, and not without the mourning of the pious, which is known to everyone. The ratio of this paper does not permit me to explain at greater length or to praise more diffusely with what care he educated this, his younger son, as long as he lived. He spared no vigils and no expenses. For beyond the fact that he ensured his son was polished by public instruction, he always maintained tutors at home who would repeat within the study what had been taught in public, and who took pains that not even a little time would be wasted. And he happened upon those in whom, as far as I recall, he lacked almost nothing. Nor did his excellent mother, who deserves to be mentioned with singular praise because of the outstanding virtues of her sex, neglect anything since the blessed departure of her husband (for I would not easily call it death) that seemed able to contribute to the cultivation of his character. The son himself did not rashly withdraw himself from either public or private readings; rather, he attended diligently, unless he was prevented by ill health, or matters arose at home which, lest he appear to fail his mother, he could not brush aside. He so ordered his way of life that his teachers, whom he always held and revered as parents of his soul, had no need for reproof, especially of a severer kind. He did not provide only one specimen of the progress he made in his studies publicly; rather, he will prove to what extent he has progressed according to his talent in a Farewell Oration, in which he is to speak about the causes for which the most just arbiter of all things, God, permitted so many early victories against the Christians to the most insolent Tyrant of the Turks, who has afflicted the Church with so many disasters; as well as by various <term>εὐχαριστικοῖς</term> <gloss>thanksgiving</gloss> poems. He will appear tomorrow, God willing, around two o'clock in the afternoon, and will recite from the podium what he has worked on at home. Therefore, we ask the Most Venerable and Accomplished INSPECTORS, and other MOST EXALTED MEN, and also the distinguished STUDENTS who now dwell within our walls, <term>καθηκόντως</term> <gloss>dutifully</gloss> or most decorously, that they may deign to listen most benevolently to this son, who does not degenerate from his excellent parent. As we shall always acknowledge and celebrate this with a most grateful heart, so we wish for him who is about to depart all things most prosperous, especially the fatherly grace of God and the most abundant growth in his studies. WOLFGANG WACHTER, of Ebersdorf, <term>Var. P. P.</term> <gloss>various professor</gloss>, will memorize and deliver the <term>Λόγον προσφωνητικὸν</term> <gloss>address of greeting</gloss> on the 17th day before the Kalends of June, 1664.</translation>

<summary>The author continues to debunk the existence of an earthly Paradise by critiquing biblical interpretations concerning Enoch and the aftermath of the flood, then shifts to a valedictory announcement honoring the son of Friedrich Amelong, who is scheduled to present his academic achievements and a lecture on divine providence regarding the Ottoman threat.</summary>

Nor did his excellent mother, who deserves to be mentioned with singular praise because of the outstanding virtues of her sex, neglect anything since the blessed departure of her husband (for I would not easily call it death) that seemed able to contribute to the cultivation of his character. The son himself did not rashly withdraw himself from either public or private readings; rather, he attended diligently, unless he was prevented by ill health, or matters arose at home which, lest he appear to fail his mother, he could not brush aside. He so ordered his way of life that his teachers, whom he always held and revered as parents of his soul, had no need for reproof, especially of a severer kind. He did not provide only one specimen of the progress he made in his studies publicly; rather, he will prove to what extent he has progressed according to his talent in a Farewell Oration, in which he is to speak about the causes for which the most just arbiter of all things, God, permitted so many early victories against the Christians to the most insolent Tyrant of the Turks, who has afflicted the Church with so many disasters; as well as by various <term>εὐχαριστικοῖς</term> <gloss>thanksgiving</gloss> poems. He will appear tomorrow, God willing, around two o'clock in the afternoon, and will recite from the podium what he has worked on at home. Therefore, we ask the Most Venerable and Accomplished INSPECTORS, and other MOST EXALTED MEN, and also the distinguished STUDENTS who now dwell within our walls, <term>καθηκόντως</term> <gloss>dutifully</gloss> or most decorously, that they may deign to listen most benevolently to this son, who does not degenerate from his excellent parent. As we shall always acknowledge and celebrate this with a most grateful heart, so we wish for him who is about to depart all things most prosperous, especially the fatherly grace of God and the most abundant growth in his studies. WOLFGANG WACHTER, of Ebersdorf, <term>Var. P. P.</term> <gloss>various professor</gloss>, will memorize and deliver the <term>Λόγον προσφωνητικὸν</term> <gloss>address of greeting</gloss> on the 17th day before the Kalends of June, 1664.

(q) On which matter let *Reinerius* be read, who is contradictory to himself here, and who attaches not a few errors to the *Waldensians*, *in Flacius, pages 752, 755, 756, and so on*. Compare also *Trithemius, Hirsau Chronicle, folio 145*, and *Binius, in the cited place, folio 563*, enumerating the dogmas and heresies of the *Waldensians*, as he calls them, from *Guido the Carmelite, Bernard of Lutzenburg, Antoninus, and Sanderus*; I pass over the others now, who propose their doctrine with equal—that is, unreliable—faith, and with the harshest words, attaching abominable heresies to them out of hatred.

(r) The writings of the monks are full of such calumnies and fabrications. See *Paris, in the cited place, folio 231; Trithemius, Hirsau Chronicle, folio 179*, and many others. But so that it may be known to some extent with what faith and authority those writers for the most part used when describing the dogmas of the *Waldensians*, I choose to set down the words of *Nauclerus*</translation>

Once their confessions have been diligently heard, these confessors may have the power and ability to absolve them from any sins whatsoever, however grave and enormous, even those reserved to the Apostolic See, including those contained in the Bull <term>In Coena Domini</term> <gloss>the annual papal bull of excommunications</gloss>, after imposing a salutary penance. Nevertheless, for the satisfaction of their particular penance, we specially enjoin upon all the aforementioned faithful of Christ, for the remission of their sins, that on the Sunday of the reception of communion, as well as on each of the three days of the aforementioned fast, they are bound to recite the <term>Oratio Dominica</term> <gloss>Lord's Prayer</gloss> and the <term>Salutatio Evangelica</term> <gloss>Hail Mary</gloss> fifty times, imploring the divine clemency with tearful voices, so that He may deign to look not upon our offenses or our ignorances, but upon the wounds of His only-begotten Son, our Redeemer, which He bore for us, He who was wounded for our iniquities, so that He might heal all our languors by the bruising of His precious body, provided we remain in His love. The efficient causes of a salutary crisis are the virtues and the Sun; the instrumental causes, however, are the provoking humor and the beneficial constitution of the Sun. Conversely, as we have said, in the remaining diseases that are measured by years or by other planets, it is to be judged as follows: the only difference between these and those is that in the former case one observes the Moon, while in the latter one observes the Sun or the other planets.

### The Seventeenth Enunciation.

<margin>Constitution of the 16-sided figure. Causes of the day.</margin>
**The passage of the Moon through the angles of the 16-sided figure in daily diseases is the cause of foreseeable and prognosticative critical days. In monthly diseases, it is the Sun, and in yearly ones, the other planets.**

<note>An ornate initial capital letter 'F'</note>
You should construct the 16-sided figure (as we have said) such that one side is formed from 32 parts and 30 minutes; this number, taken four times, fills the fourth part of the sky, that is, 90 parts. This ratio teaches that sixteen times two and a half degrees, multiplied by sixteen, completes 360 degrees, which is the total circuit of the sky. Therefore, these 16 sides, each constituted from two signs, degrees, and 30 minutes, form the 16-sided figure. Once this is established and the angles of the sides have been properly considered, one will have not only what are called the decretory, but also the prognosticative and provocative <note>days</note> in all diseases. For, as we have said, because of the powers and virtues innate to it, the Moon excites the humors of the body itself and regulates them at its own will. Therefore, the place where the illness began is to be carefully observed, as well as the place opposite to it, and the midpoint of both to the right and left. For since these three places, which the Moon held at the hour of the onset of the illness, strike hostilely with opposing diameters and square rays, when the Moon passes through each of those places, that disease must necessarily produce greater commotions than on other days, due to the degrees of the opposing places to which the Moon belongs. Thus it happens that the passage of the Moon through these angles is the cause of critical commotion, prognosticative expansion, and provocation.

<margin>Lunar passage and causes.</margin>

As we have said regarding the passage of the Moon in daily diseases, so it is in the monthly <note>diseases</note> through the passage of the Sun, and in the yearly ones through the passage of the other planets. For all power is in the passage. This 16-sided figure is described; the strengths and powers of the angles, whence they are, why, and how great, we have stated in the fourteenth enunciation.

### The Eighteenth Enunciation.

**The causes and powers of critical days are from the passage of the Moon through full angles; those of prognosticative days are through passage through semi-full angles; and those of provocative days through passage through halved semi-full angles. Conclude the same regarding other diseases and the passage of the other planets.**

<column-break/>

<note>An ornate initial capital letter 'D' containing a human figure.</note>
<margin>Full angles. Aristotle. Pythagoras.</margin>
A day, in that it is time, is a number; according to Aristotle, no force or power is innate to numbers, whatever Pythagoras may have felt. Therefore, a critical day is not called such because it is held by a certain number, as the ancient physicians wrote under the authority of Pythagoras, but because the force is innate to it from the Moon's passage through the angles. For this day is beneficial because the Moon alters the air with beneficial forces, and it is maleficent because it varies the air with maleficent and destructive powers. Therefore, forces are innate to the days themselves from the passage of the Moon. But just as in the 16-sided figure there are four full angles: the first is constituted in the first part, 90 degrees, as in 15 degrees of Cancer. The second is constituted in the 180th part, as in 15 degrees of Libra. The third is placed in the 270th part, as in 15 degrees of Capricorn. The fourth and last is in the first part that the Moon held at the onset of the disease.

<margin>Against those who attributed critical forces to numbers. Others to the forces of the days.</margin>

<note>An ornate initial capital letter 'F'</note>
You should construct the 16-sided figure (as we have said) such that one side is formed from 32 parts and 30 minutes; this number, taken four times, fills the fourth part of the sky, that is, 90 parts. This ratio teaches that sixteen times two and a half degrees, multiplied by sixteen, completes 360 degrees, which is the total circuit of the sky. Therefore, these 16 sides, each constituted from two signs, degrees, and 30 minutes, form the 16-sided figure. Once this is established and the angles of the sides have been properly considered, one will have not only what are called the decretory, but also the prognosticative and provocative <note>days</note> in all diseases. For, as we have said, because of the powers and virtues innate to it, the Moon excites the humors of the body itself and regulates them at its own will. Therefore, the place where the illness began is to be carefully observed, as well as the place opposite to it, and the midpoint of both to the right and left. For since these three places, which the Moon held at the hour of the onset of the illness, strike hostilely with opposing diameters and square rays, when the Moon passes through each of those places, that disease must necessarily produce greater commotions than on other days, due to the degrees of the opposing places to which the Moon belongs. Look at these words of that greatest falsifier of the Talmudic codex, whom Socinus <note>referring to Fausto Sozzini, an Italian theologian</note>, in the passage you cited above, calls to his aid: he translates the prophet thus: *They shall look toward me, along with him whom they have pierced.* What, I ask you, is to deflect this piercing elsewhere, if this is not? For I truly believed it an impiety to have added even the slightest bit to the text, or to have removed anything from it: but it seemed appropriate to substitute <term>elayv</term> <gloss>to him</gloss> in the Talmudic text, lest our people struggle with the meaning of the prophet. Furthermore, the change in the discourse must be observed, so as not to leave the reader in doubt. And that is the very reason for the word changed in the Talmud: <term>alayv</term> <gloss>upon him</gloss> is immediately added; therefore, so that no one incautiously might think that the persons change, it seemed pleasing for this very reason to assist the text and add some light to it: *I will pour out the spirit of grace upon the house of David and the inhabitants of Jerusalem: they shall look* <term>elayv</term> <gloss>to him</gloss> *whom they have pierced, and they shall mourn* <term>alayv</term> <gloss>for him</gloss> *with the mourning of an only son and they shall be afflicted with bitterness* <term>alayv</term> <gloss>for him</gloss>*, as one is afflicted with bitterness for a deceased firstborn.* I do not even understand what could have cohered more aptly or what I could have brought forward more correctly. L. Remove the veil placed before your eyes. It is not consistent to change the former parts in that scriptural phrase from what follows: but on the contrary, the things which precede confirm us regarding those which follow closely. But if you had wished to sacrifice to the truth and not mix the lowest with the highest, I am mistaken, or this is the exposition you should have prepared: *I will pour out upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem the spirit of grace, and they shall look* <term>elai</term> <gloss>to me</gloss>*, whom they have pierced, and they shall mourn* <term>alayv</term> <gloss>for me</gloss> *with the mourning of an only son, etc.* Now, as for your prattling about the Messiah, son of Joseph, to what does it point? Do you mean our Jesus? No one could ever say that the families of David, Nathan, and Levi mourn him. Men and women do this for him every year, every month, every day.
</translation>

they curse and detest. But if you are turning over some other person in your mind, consult the memory of past times, whether it has produced such a Messiah, who is the progeny of the son of Joseph, whom the Jews have treated most indignantly and pierced, and to whom those things can be attributed which can be assigned to the Messiah from divine oracles, and which most aptly fit our Jesus, the Son of God and Mary. > Rabbi Jochanan said: As for the Messiah, what is his name? The house of Rabbi Shila said: Shila is his name, as it is said: "Until Shila comes" <note>Genesis 49:10</note>. be entered into: because that league was formed long ago, and its leader, the Roman Emperor, was created by common consent. Therefore, all Christians ought to contribute men or money to this common cause according to their means: and I do not see how those who fail to do so can be excused, unless they are kept at home by an inevitable war or a similar evil.

Today, however (alas), there are those found who not only bring no help against the Turk and other impious men, but rather, through the aid of the Turks, bring destruction upon Christians. You would be sufficiently mild toward them if you were to cast the voice of Fulco, the Archimandrite of Reims, spoken to Charles the Simple:

> Who would not be horrified that you desire the friendship of the enemies of God, and that you take up pagan arms and detestable leagues for the slaughter and ruin of the Christian name? For it makes no difference whether one associates oneself with pagans, or, having denied God, worships idols.

What Grotius touches upon here regarding the Roman Emperor, the prince of the Christian league, is abundantly confirmed by the dissertation of Boecler, whose index is *The Holy Roman Empire*, page 7, where he also praises Henry Bebel, who in the previous century demonstrated that our Emperor is rightly called "Most Christian."

Therefore, he would have deserved well of the human race who, with judgment, collected the law of Christian nations, especially regarding war, from the historians and the Fathers of the Church.

For Christians are the *light of the world: the Church is a city set upon a hill.* Therefore, its laws cannot but be illustrious. Although Grotius did not entirely neglect these, he was more fertile in pagan examples, which are often mixed with shadows, and he left many other things worthy of memory to be recorded by others from the clear light of Christianity. Indeed, the fact that in this age so many great men and peoples conduct themselves so irreverently against what is right and wrong, I consider to be primarily for the reason that they read in Christian books the pacts and customs of profane nations more than those of Christian ones. But since, as it has been said, the Emperors are the head of the Christian league, a work of the kind we recommend will rise primarily from their history, and especially from the life of Constantine and Charlemagne (the latter of which Jo. Joach. Franzius has elegantly composed). For almost all other nations, and all the best of Princes, have looked up to that Imperial summit as if it were a Pharos <note>lighthouse</note>; so much so that the Imperial civil law has almost become the law of the world. Aware of this fact, our Emperors show themselves worthy of the guardianship of the Christian World, not so much by sworn law as by the genius of Austrian virtue. And so, to depart from their cultivation and friendship is, in truth, nothing else;
