### XLIX. 
Next, the renewal or restoration of the Confraternity belongs to this class, concerning which <term>Carpzovius</term> provides some points in his *Commentary on the Saxon-Hessian Confraternity Pact*, where he prudently warns that it should be instituted only rarely. It must be held that both the solemnity of the oath and that of the renewal do not contribute to the constitution of the thing, but rather to the validity and more solemn illustration of what is already constituted. See <term>Hahn</term>, *On the Law of Things*, thesis 75.

### L. 
By way of a finishing touch, the more important effects of the Confraternity must be tasted, if only with the lips. The primary and more noble effect is that it induces a <term>Jus adgnationis Civilis</term> <gloss>Civil Right of Agnatic Succession/Relation</gloss>. For this is established by that pact, and it is so close that it cultivates a right of brotherhood. If you desire to know its qualities, consider them as follows: (1) it is <term>νῷ καταλαμβανόμενον</term> <gloss>comprehended by the intellect</gloss>, as <term>Theophilus</term> often says, that is, intellectual; (2) reciprocal; (3) conditional, as argued in law 54 of the *Digest* on the Signification of Words; (4) public (see thesis 40); (5) perpetual (see the same thesis); (6) solemn (see thesis 48).

### LI. 
The secondary effect is that it grants a <term>jus in re</term> <gloss>right in the thing</gloss>, in some way the same as that which the other party to the pact obtains from the time of the contract. Lest this statement, being too strong, offend anyone, we wish it to be understood with a grain of salt, so that from the fact that we have just established that the right of agnatic succession is conditional, one should not think that such a right is assigned to them in the <term>actu secundo</term> <gloss>second act (full realization)</gloss>, as the philosophers say, but in the <term>actu primo</term> <gloss>first act (potentiality)</gloss>: insofar as they have the hope that, through the continuation of the dominion after the death of the other family, they may obtain free administration of the goods. For this reason, there is nothing to prevent the Confratres of the other party from being considered in a certain sense as Lords even while the other family still survives, by the argument of those things which <term>Paulus</term> teaches in law 11 of the *Digest* on children and posthumous heirs. *The constraint of time by which we are encompassed restrains my pen, as I meditate upon further matters; and it urges me to defer the remaining topics to a more convenient time, if God shall grant it. Therefore, the thread being broken, we submit these things which, for the sake of uncovering the truth, it was permitted to record in the present Academic style, to public censure with the modesty that is due, prepared to refute without stubbornness, and to be refuted without anger. If we have erred anywhere, or if anything has been said less aptly or correctly, or not perfectly explained, the difficulty of the subject matter will excuse us, who follow probabilities and cannot advance beyond what appears likely. ### XLIX. 
Next, the renewal or restoration of the Confraternity belongs to this class, concerning which <term>Carpzovius</term> provides some points in his *Commentary on the Saxon-Hessian Confraternity Pact*, where he prudently warns that it should be instituted only rarely. It must be held that both the solemnity of the oath and that of the renewal do not contribute to the constitution of the thing, but rather to the validity and more solemn illustration of what is already constituted. See <term>Hahn</term>, *On the Law of Things*, thesis 75.

### L. 
By way of a finishing touch, the more important effects of the Confraternity must be tasted, if only with the lips. The primary and more noble effect is that it induces a <term>Jus adgnationis Civilis</term> <gloss>Civil Right of Agnatic Succession/Relation</gloss>. For this is established by that pact, and it is so close that it cultivates a right of brotherhood. If you desire to know its qualities, consider them as follows: (1) it is <term>νῷ καταλαμβανόμενον</term> <gloss>comprehended by the intellect</gloss>, as <term>Theophilus</term> often says, that is, intellectual; (2) reciprocal; (3) conditional, as argued in law 54 of the *Digest* on the Signification of Words; (4) public (see thesis 40); (5) perpetual (see the same thesis); (6) solemn (see thesis 48).

### LI. 
The secondary effect is that it grants a <term>jus in re</term> <gloss>right in the thing</gloss>, in some way the same as that which the other party to the pact obtains from the time of the contract. Lest this statement, being too strong, offend anyone, we wish it to be understood with a grain of salt, so that from the fact that we have just established that the right of agnatic succession is conditional, one should not think that such a right is assigned to them in the <term>actu secundo</term> <gloss>second act (full realization)</gloss>, as the philosophers say, but in the <term>actu primo</term> <gloss>first act (potentiality)</gloss>: insofar as they have the hope that, through the continuation of the dominion after the death of the other family, they may obtain free administration of the goods. XXXI. But Hungary was agitated and shaken by more severe turmoil after the fate of Andrew III, when it began to have foreign Kings: such were the Bohemians, Bavarians, Angevins, Luxembourgers, and finally the Austrians, who rule today. For when the kingdom underwent such great changes of its Princes, it was inevitable that it be convulsed by many and great maladies; while not only were customs and laws dispensed according to the character of the lords, but also perpetual tumults and the hatred of the natives—offered up to the new Kings—miserably afflicted the Republic. And although John Hunyadi and his son, King Matthias Corvinus, while Hungary fluctuated under the rule of foreigners, made the name of the Hungarians and their kingdom the greatest in Europe with victorious arms, yet soon such greatness collapsed after Muhammad occupied Constantinople in a war shameful to Christians, and, all barriers broken, poured all his attacks into Hungary.

<margin>John Sambucus, Appendix of Hungarian Affairs.</margin>
XXXII. Indeed, through him Bulgaria was seized, and Serbia and Bosnia were occupied. Then, in the year 1526, when King Louis was killed at Mohács, and Ferdinand of Austria and John Zápolya, Voivode of Transylvania, contended for the kingdom with most sorrowful hatreds, Suleiman used that opportunity to occupy the greater part of Hungary and the very capital of the kingdom, Buda. Finally, what remained of Hungary fell to the reigning Austrian family, which gathers the remnants of the most noble kingdom from the flames and ruins; it is held as greater and narrower than that part of the empire which clings to the jaws of Germany and Italy, and which has boasted a renowned name through many ages.

<margin>Hieronymus Ortelius, Part II and III of Hungarian Affairs.</margin>
XXXIII. than the Austrian, since out of the sixty counties into which all of Hungary is now divided, twenty-seven obey the Turks, and twenty-five the Austrians; while the remaining eight, which the Transylvanian has seized, have also withdrawn into Turkish clientage. The primary concern of the Turks in their rule is to press all families of renown and noble blood into the same servitude to which they have condemned themselves through base reverence. Hence that great stubbornness of the remaining Hungarians against the Ottoman empire, as the people shudder at every trace of tyranny; nor are they faithful even to Christian Lords if they are forced into reverence for Princes by sharp fear and by the crushing of all hope of liberty.

<margin>Barclay, in Euphormio's Satyricon, Chapter VIII, Part IV.</margin>
XXXIV. The fortune of those who rest under the mildness of the Austrians is happier and more sacred. For there is great glory of liberty for the people, even within the kingdom; the Nobles also have vast wealth, by which they hold a faithful multitude of clients in their debt. The nobles have an upright mind and a spirit made for magnificence; they have no greater concern than to possess their prerogatives and immunities, which they obtained from the Kings, intact and safe. And the distinguished Magistrate, whom they call the Palatine, is said to guard the liberty of the people; hence many honor him, as Barclay affirms, as a defender of liberty and one opposed to the Kings, just as the Tribunate once set a limit to the power of the Roman Consuls.

<margin>Ibid.</margin>
<margin>Hieronymus Ortelius, Chronicle of Hungarian Affairs, p. 1.</margin>
XXXV. The more serious business of the Kingdom is dispatched in the Diets: here the sacred and major civil laws, and here the decision of war and peace, are debated. In these, the people appear through their Delegates, whom they commonly call the Estates. Among whom the Archbishops and Bishops hold the primary place, whose fortune was once ample and rich in wealth, before the Turk had erupted into the destruction of many, or those addicted to the new religion had plucked their rich patrimonies. The second order of the Estates is constituted by the Magnates, who, distinguished by the name of hereditary Counts and Barons, prevailed with great authority after the passing of Andrew III. Then there are the Cities and Towns, whose power was great a century or two ago; now the strength of most has been worn away by the Turkish war; many, indeed, buried in their own ruins, can boast of antiquity more than strength.

<summary>This page examines the division of Hungarian territory between Turkish and Austrian powers, the state of civil liberties, and the political structure of the Hungarian Diets and Estates.</summary>
<keywords>Austria, Turkey, Transylvania, Ottoman Empire, Palatine, Roman Consuls, Estates, Magnates, Andrew III</keywords>
</translation>

13. Now, it is also pleasing to pursue the *Offices of the Holy Spirit* from *Chapter III of Genesis*. Since this is the *Chapter* that first opened the *Catholic Workshop of the Holy Spirit* and laid the foundations for the entire Church, it is the *seminary of all the faithful*. In this *Chapter*, the *Holy Spirit* first exercised a most useful and salutary *Office* regarding wretched sinners, and proposed the means of true *penitence*, of *saving faith*, and of *salvation* itself, and practiced them in the *subjects* who were sinning, yet truly *penitent* and believing. In this *Chapter*, the *Pentecostal Holy Spirit* himself first became an *Official*, while he took up and expedited everything that would contribute to the *restoration* of the *Protoplasts* <note>first-formed ones, i.e., Adam and Eve</note> and all their *descendants* in them, and to their *reduction* <gloss>bringing back</gloss> *to God*. We, therefore, with the *Holy Spirit* himself as Leader, or Teacher, or Revealer, or Dictator, will bring forth some things concerning such *Offices* and, as far as can be done, will briefly explain them.

14. We say, moreover, that the *Pentecostal Office of the Holy Spirit*, according to the present *Chapter*, is either *General* or *Special*. It is called *General* because it regards the *fallen man* who is *to be restored* in a general sense, and in this respect, there is not one *General regard*, but (a) another with *respect to God who restores*; (b) another with *respect to Man who is to be restored*; (c) another with *respect to the means of restoration*; (d) another with *respect to the manner of restoration*; (e) another with *respect to the goal, or end, of restoration*.

15. *With respect to God who restores*, a general *Office of the most present Pentecostal manifestation and apparition* is found, because it is said that the *Spirit of the Day* came most presently, manifested himself with a most present arrival, and exhibited himself to the protoplasts as the *Spirit of the Day*, and appeared to them conveniently in his own manner. ### VII.

Antonius Monachus, a jurist from Turin, in *Part 2 of his Treatise on the Correct Interpretation of Feuds* <note>original: "parte 2. Tractatus de Recta Feudorum Interpretatione"</note>, enumerates more modes of acquiring a Feud than anyone else of whom we are aware, when he writes that Feuds are acquired through Investiture, quasi-investiture, privilege, contract, last will and testament, donation, prescription, judicial sentence, purchase, arms or the violence of war, succession, and the right of accrual. While we have no doubt that he, along with the rest of the Italians, confuses the modes of constituting and acquiring Feuds, we shall be content with the three modes of Lord Ludwell and Snobelius: Investiture, prescription, and succession. For the others are either easily reduced to these, or are not modes of acquisition at all.

### VIII.

Petrus de Bella Pertica, Vulteius, and recently Antonius Monachus write that a Feud is acquired by the sentence of a judge. The assertion of Ludwell is more consistent with the law, namely that nothing new is acquired by such a sentence, but rather that which already exists is merely declared. It is testified that Vulteius finally conceded this in his *Summaria, Book 1, Chapter 9, Number 24, of the latest edition* <note>original: "summaria libro 1, capite 9. numero 24. postremae editionis"</note>.

### IX.

That a Feud is acquired by prescription, not only for the reason that it is presumed that investiture has occurred due to the passage of so many years,</translation>

<translation page="7">that it has occurred; but also in the case where it is certain that someone has not been invested: and thus we join Lord Suevus, Ludwell, Fridericus Lentius in his *Disputations held at Basel* <note>original: "Disputationibus Basileae habitis"</note>, and Setserus in asserting that this mode of acquisition is distinct from Investiture, contrary to the Doctors commonly, and among them Vulteius, Niellius, and Lord Struvius.

### X.

Alvarottus, Isernia, Zasius, Gothofredus Antonius, Schraderus, Borcholt, Rosenthal, Rittershusius, Molineus, Mynsingerus, Duarenus, Hanneton, Schneidwinus, Fornerius, and Lord Struvius require 40 years for the prescription of a Feud in a public or ecclesiastical matter. But Nicolaus de Neapoli, Scenkius Baro, Vulteius, Bocerus, Hunnius, Lord Snobelius, and Lord Ludwell judge that 30 years suffice. The former opinion pleases us, which Gothofredus Antonius and Lord Ludwell himself testify to be the common one.

Celsus's surgical <term>fibula</term> <gloss>clasp or surgical pin</gloss> was also a metallic binding, as the force of his words regarding the <term>fibula</term> clearly shows. It also grasps the binding injected into more places; these are added to those that pertain to future <note>suture</note> work, as the needle passes through the body more often. All Latin authors teach that "to bite" (which belongs to a harder object) was proper to the <term>fibula</term>. Virgil:

<margin>Aeneid 12.</margin>
> — — *where the belt, stitched with gold,*
> *is worn, and the* **FIBULA BITES** *the seams of the sides.*

<margin>Book 2, In Eutropium.</margin>
Claudian:
> *Closer to the breasts, the* **FIBULA WAS BITING** *the garments.*

<margin>Book 1.</margin>
Symmachus:
> *I have a* **FIBULA** *that* **BITES** *my military cloak.*

<margin>Book 1, De Pallio.</margin>
Tertullian, on the cloak of Aesculapius: *It rested on the shoulders IN THE BITE OF THE FIBULA*. Jerome, on the woman struck seven times: *She shook off the FIBULA, which was BITING the edges of the cloak, onto the ground.*

<margin>Book 2, Ad Glauc.</margin>
Furthermore, Celsus himself indicated the material and form of his <term>fibulae</term> when he called them <term>ankteres</term> <gloss>hooks</gloss> in Greek. For an <term>ankter</term> is a small metallic hook. Galen also used <term>ankteres</term> in the same sense and usage as our Celsus: hence <term>ankterismos</term>, infibulation; <term>ankterizein</term>, to infibulate; and <term>ankteres epitithenai</term>, to place hooks.
</translation>

<translation page="11">
<header>ACIA EXPLICATA.</header>
<sig>B 2</sig>

or *to place hooks upon* <note>a wound</note>, in the same author.

<margin>Book 7, ch. 7 & 26.</margin>
Finally, Celsus, in other places rendering the <term>ankteres</term> in Latin, spoke of *a sharp hook, blunt hooks, and being seized by small hooks*; these modes of speaking sufficiently indicate that the material of the <term>ankteres</term> was metallic. As Guido clearly teaches, contrary to what Fallopius opined by not understanding the Latin word <term>acia</term> <gloss>a needle or thread/stitch</gloss>: for all <term>fibulae</term>, as Oribasius hands down, were made of bronze, iron, or gold.

<margin>Book on Machines, ch. 4.</margin>
This, therefore, was the placement of the <term>fibulae</term> or hooks according to Celsus. Where a wound was in the flesh and it gaped, and the edges could not easily be drawn together, from which a suture would be inappropriate, <term>fibulae</term> were placed on the wound in this way. With one hook of the <term>fibula</term> (for it consisted of two, one curved inward, the other curved outward, in the shape of a somewhat elongated letter S, and hooked on both sides), the other lip of the wound was grasped with the flesh and skin from the inside, beginning from the flesh. Then, the <term>fibula</term> being drawn back, the opposite lip was seized by the other hook from the outside, biting the skin before the flesh. Thus the edges of the gaping wound, which could not be sewn together because of the distance, were pulled back and held. To almost the same method, Guido says: *The lips of the wound are joined together with hooks, which must be small in proportion to the member; on both sides*
</translation>

We must now consider the images of the ancients, which were effigies of men shaped and outlined with colors, and which were kept either in a more celebrated part of their houses or in some public place.

### §. XVI.

Most people trace their origin to the images of the pagan gods. Considering that this honor and veneration of images was more excellent than others, mortals ensured that such things were erected for themselves, or certainly for their deceased friends. (This is done in nearly the same way as our people today build similar, so to speak, little chapels in cemeteries for themselves and their descendants.) Once upon a time, only those holding the magistracy among the Romans were permitted to set up images, hence the name <term>jus imaginis</term> <gloss>right of the image</gloss>. Yet it is clear that this right was not granted absolutely to everyone performing duties in the public Senate and magistracy, but only to those who had presided over those honors with distinction. For this reason, and later on with the accession of the power of the Emperors, it was not permitted to set up images or statues without their permission. *SUETONIUS in TIBERIUS, 10.* However, *Godescalc Stewech, Commentary on Book II of Vegetius Renatus' ON MILITARY AFFAIRS, ch. 6*, records that images were also set up for philosophers. He refers to an inscription in Rome on the Aventine Hill dedicated to Saint Alexius: TI. CLAVIUS SECVNDUS COACTOR, ALONG WITH TI. CLAVIUS TI. QVIR. SECUNDUS, THROUGH THE TRAVELERS, THE TRIUMVIRS AND QUATTUORVIRS, BUILT THIS SCHOOL WITH IMAGES AND ALL ORNAMENTS AT HIS OWN EXPENSE.

### §. XVII.

Therefore, when a funeral had to be conducted, the Romans placed the collected images of their ancestors on certain biers and carried them before the funeral procession. On feast days, they would also open the cabinet where it was customary for the images to be kept, and in various</translation>

<translation page="10">ways and rites they would adorn them, with scattered flowers, garlands, and crowns, and with clothing added in proportion to the dignity and public office that the man whose face the image represented had once held. They did not act otherwise than if the person were alive; they venerated the likeness with honorary titles, and they proposed and recited their deeds. For this reason, *MARTIAL, Book V, Epigram 21, verse 7*, calls these images "arrogant."

### §. XIIX.

It is certainly highly commendable what is said about these images of the ancients: that they indeed passed on to descendants, yet not so that they themselves could use them for their own honor and praise, but only for the honor of the family, which had increased through the man represented by the image. And therefore it was conceded that this image of the well-deserving person could be carried out at the funeral of any relative from the family, not equally so that it would belong to all his descendants, unless they had likewise acquired the right of the image. *See, dealing with these subjects in a professional capacity: HÖPPING, ON THE LAW OF INSIGNIA, ch. XIX; Gabriel Palæottus, treatise on images; the Antiquities of Rosinus; JACOBUS PONTANUS, Progymnasmata, Book IV; POLYDORE VERGIL, on the Invention of Things, Book VI, ch. 13, who also complains at length about the cult of images as transferred to Christians.*

### §. XIX.

The condition of statues was different from that of the aforementioned images. Naturally, a statue was set up either for a dead or a living person due to outstanding merits toward the Republic in some conspicuous place, as a lasting <term>mnemofynon</term> <gloss>memorial</gloss>; and at first they were fashioned from cypress, cedar, oak, stone, marble, etc.; later, they were made from various metals as well. Their origin is the same as that of images. They were accustomed to be distinguished formerly according to the degree of merit in the Republic, or of dignities, into "equal," "great," "greater," and "greatest": these were those which exceeded the human stature by three times or more; and they were set up for the gods. Monday at Prime.

In the time of Lent, Antiphon. As I live, says the Lord, I do not desire the death of the sinner, but rather that he should be converted, and live.

In the time of the Passion, Antiphon. Deliver me O Lord, and set me beside you, and let the hand of anyone fight against me.

In Paschal time, Antiphon. Alleluia, alleluia, alleluia, alleluia.

In the ferial Office throughout the year, Antiphon. Serve the Lord in fear, and exult to him with trembling.

Chapter. 1 Timothy 1:17.
To the King of ages, immortal and invisible, the only God, be honor and glory, forever and ever. Amen.

R. Thanks be to God.

This Chapter is said on all Solemnities, and Feasts of Saints, and during Octaves, and throughout the whole of Paschal time.

For ferial days only.
Chapter. Zechariah 8:19.
Love peace and truth, says the Lord almighty. R. Thanks be to God.

R. And deliver us for your name's sake.

Lord have mercy. Christ have mercy. Lord have mercy.

Our Father, said in secret until the V. And lead us not into temptation.

I believe in God, in secret until the V. The resurrection of the body.

R. Who made heaven and earth.

The Choir responds.
May almighty God have mercy on you, and having forgiven

— V —

Imagination alone can reconstruct the individual acts of the drama that played out in the souls of the masses as they wavered between <term>Ormuzd</term> <gloss>the supreme god of light in Zoroastrianism</gloss> and the Trinity. We know only the result of the struggle: Mithraism was defeated, and without doubt, it was destined to be. However, its defeat is not to be attributed exclusively to the superiority of evangelical morality or apostolic preaching over the doctrine of the mysteries. It did not perish solely because it was crushed under the inherited burden of a bygone past, but also because its liturgy and theology remained too Asian for the Roman spirit to accept without resistance. Conversely, this very same conflict, which had erupted simultaneously in Iran between the two rivals, remained unsuccessful for the Christians, if not without honor, and in the states of the Sassanids, Zoroastrianism could never be seriously assailed.

But the defeat of Mithras did not mean the end of his power. He had prepared minds for the reception of a new faith which, like himself, came from the banks of the Euphrates and reopened hostilities with changed tactics. Manichaeism appeared as his heir and continued his work. It was the final assault that Persia undertook upon the Occident, and it was bloodier than the others—but it, too, was ultimately to fail against the resilience of the Christian empire.

This brief sketch will, I hope, reveal the importance of the history of Mithraism. As a lateral shoot of the ancient Mazdean stock, it has in many respects preserved the peculiarities of the ancient nature religion of the Iranian tribes and allows us to better understand the controversial significance of the Avestan reformation by comparison. On the other hand, it has, if not inspired, then at least helped to clarify certain doctrines of the Church, such as the conceptions of the infernal powers and the end of the world. Thus, both its rise and its fall contribute to illuminating the origin story of two great religions. In the time of its full strength, it exerted a no less remarkable influence on Roman society and the Roman government. Perhaps Europe was never closer to becoming Asian, not even in the epoch of the Mohammedan invasions, than in the third century of our era; and there was a time when Caesarism seemed on the verge of transforming itself into a Caliphate. People have often pointed to the similarity that exists between the court of Diocletian and that of the Chosroes. The sun cult and especially the Mazdean theories made popular the ideas upon which the deified rulers sought to base their monarchical absolutism. The rapid spread of the Persian mysteries in all classes of the population served in an admirable way the political ambition of the emperors. A tidal wave of Iranian and Semitic ideas broke in, which devoured almost everything that the Greek or Roman spirit had built up through laborious effort; and when the flood finally receded, it left behind in the popular consciousness a strong precipitate of oriental conceptions that never completely disappeared again.

On the other hand, the monuments that have survived are often difficult to interpret, and we are forced to supplement the silence or the insufficiency of the epigraphic and archaeological data with deductions and hypotheses that remain more or less uncertain. it holds: but to reduce this matter to a few points, we say that it can in no way happen by itself, and experience testifies that love potions have often caused not love, but madness and insanity, histories of which exist in many places. For love is a desire for a beautiful thing (whether it is truly such, or only apparently so), and knowledge precedes desire and appetite for a thing; therefore, no one desires what they have never known. For this reason, we rightly establish that there is no such power in herbs or any medicine that can compel and impel the minds of men, so that they love, against their will or despite it, that which they never chose.

->84.<-

If, however, such a thing happens, it occurs by accident, and not because of the love potion as such. It happens firstly because of the interaction with the person who offered the love potion; secondly, because love potions sometimes excite fervor and venereal appetite (yet that fervor is not directed toward a certain and definite person). The person who has taken it, stirred and driven as if by the gadfly of lust, loves the first person they happen upon, and especially someone with whom they have often spoken before.

->85.<-

Retentions, which were mentioned above, generally include all suppressed customary evacuations that can cause this evil, such as suppressed hemorrhoids or menstrual flows inhibited by obstructions in the veins around the uterus. The long-term retention in women has no small power (as <term>Galen</term> testifies in *On Affected Parts, book 4*). Note, however, that the suppression of menses is taken here as a prohibited customary evacuation; if it is taken as an obstruction, it is referred to the number of internal causes.

->86.<-

Finally, among those things that are applied externally or happen from the outside, the constitution of the air and the region can cause this evil, such as a cold and dry one, like the autumn, or also one that is too hot or
</translation>

<translation page="21">
sweltering, which burns up the humors. Likewise, the bite of poisonous animals can induce it, just as it induces other afflictions, through the peculiar quality of the poison; and other similar things. Air, in this place, is understood as that which surrounds us.

### 88.

These things we have said about these causes should not be taken simply and absolutely, but with regard to their subjects upon which they act—that is, the bodies. Among these, two certain requirements are needed, as <term>Galen</term> teaches in *On the Causes of Diseases*, chapter 2: namely, time, magnitude, proximity, and the preparation of the body.

### 88.

Having explained the causes, we proceed to the *differences* of Melancholy, some of which are taken from the subject in which they are generated. Thus, one is *Essential and Primary*, which surely happens by a fault of the head itself; another is through *Consent* or *Accidental*, if it is caused from elsewhere. This is divided into *Universal and Particular*. It is called *Universal* when it is caused by the whole; *Particular* is that which is named *Hypochondriacal* in its species.

### 89.

By reason of magnitude, one is *Strong and Vehement*; another is *Strongest and Most Vehement*, in which all melancholic symptoms appear most strongly; another is *Mild*, in which the symptoms are not observed with such force; another is *Mildest*.

### 90.

Because of the duration of time, one is *Recent*, which is to say it has not afflicted for long, but began quite recently; another is *Inveterate*, which has lasted for a long space of time and has taken deep roots.

### 91.

On account of the continuity of time, one is *Intermittent*, which is to say it has exacerbations by turns; another is *Continuous*, which lasts without intermission.
</translation>

For the local presence does not destroy the personal, nor the personal the local. The one, namely the natural presence, proceeds to the human nature from the property of its essence, which, since it was and remains finite, was circumscribed in one place only in the state of humiliation. The other presence, however, proceeds to the flesh of Christ from the personal union, insofar as the humanity of Christ is exalted and assumed into the unity of the infinite person of the Son of God, above and beyond all creatures. Since, therefore, both are understood according to different modes, they can easily exist together. For it is necessary to confess that the human flesh of Christ exists in a far different manner with Nicodemus in a terrestrial place, and in another manner and ineffably more tightly and closely that the same humanity is united to the <term>λόγος</term> <gloss>Word/Divine Reason</gloss>. It is present to Nicodemus in a terrestrial place and by natural reaching, or physical contact.

But in the person of the <term>λόγος</term>, that the human nature of Christ should subsist in such a physical or local manner would be impious and absurd to say. BETA is a letter with one and the same sound among the Greeks; among the Latins, it is the name of a potherb. And when I say 'lege' <gloss>read</gloss>, the Greek understands one thing and the Latin another in these two syllables. You say: It is the part of a wise man to impose names upon things.* True, but is not the genus of names twofold? ### Thesis XV.

Furthermore, they violated the negative precepts of the Law of Nature: *Do harm to no one*, and *Evils are not to be done, so that good may result*. And since these precepts, like all negative precepts of the Law of Nature, simply prohibit that which is dishonorable, it is sufficiently manifest that no necessity can be found which could place the Dishonorable among the class of lawful things, or for which it may ever or anywhere be permitted to do Dishonorable things.

### Thesis XVI.

Moreover, this case seems to participate more in the nature of a voluntary act, the more it is evident that there was a preceding deliberation concerning the means of obtaining sustenance, and a subsequent choice to cast lots, which would separate one from the seven, whose flesh the others would consume.

### Thesis XVII.

Furthermore, the life of a neighbor is subject to no one's judgment, except for His who is the author and Lord of life, and to whom He has given an express command to kill. Whoever takes away the life of another, besides those so authorized, sins gravely, while they deprive God of His creature, formed by Him in His own image; they deprive the Republic of a citizen; they deprive a family of either its head or a member; and they deprive the one who was killed of the greatest benefit, which he had from the Divine, and which he can never restore to Him.

### Thesis XVIII.

Furthermore, it is certain that they raged against the life of their companion for this end: that it might go well for themselves and their stomachs. If, therefore, no one ought to become wealthier by the injury of another, how can it be lawful for us to obtain advantages from the disadvantages, injury, and death of others</translation>

<translation page="14">If license is not granted to someone to use the property of another, which can at least be restored, if the possessor himself is held by an equal necessity, what right, therefore, will a starving man have to the life and flesh of another starving man? Rightly says *Cicero in book 3 of De Officiis*: "Would not," he says, "a wise man, if he were consumed by hunger itself, take food from another man who is useful for nothing? By no means. For my life is not more useful to me than such a disposition of soul that I would violate no one for the sake of my own advantage."

### TH. XIX.

*Nor does it stand against this that S.P. denies that the rest exercised cruelty toward their companion against Ziegler, since he who died received the steel into his throat with less pain for the safety of all, than the one who drove it in.* Answer: Is it not cruelty, if those who are parents of their own life slaughter their neighbor—whom they are commanded to love not as someone above or below them, but as themselves—against nature, so that their own life might be preserved?

### TH. XX.

*Nor does it stand against this that S.P. denies that the victim had to fear for the danger of his soul.* Answer: He had to fear for himself as a <term>αὐτόχειρι</term> <gloss>suicide</gloss>. For the one killed had previously consented to his own death, and later offered it of his own accord, even though he had received life from the supreme Lord not to destroy it, nor to satisfy the hunger of another, but to preserve it.

### TH. XXI.

*Nor does it stand against this that supreme necessity demanded this.* Let him who says this hear the answer of Aristotle in *Ethics, Book 3, Chapter 1*: There are some things of such a kind that perhaps we should not be compelled to do them by any force or necessity, but rather death should be desired, and the most grievous tortures should be endured.

<margin>
QUESTION
III.
</margin>

### TH. XXII.

*It is also asked, Whether the pardon was rightly granted to the Britons from the ordinary penalty for homicide?* Which we, with Mr. Röhrenseen, rightly affirm.

->TH. XXII.<-</translation>

<summary>The author argues that the killing of the companion was an unlawful act of homicide, violating both divine law and the law of nature, and rejects arguments regarding necessity or the victim's consent; however, he concludes that the state was justified in granting the survivors a pardon.</summary>
<keywords>homicide, Law of Nature, supreme necessity, suicide, pardon, ethics, life and death</keywords>

XLVI. For the brain, in addition to those already listed, the following are suitable and alter its intemperament:
Pomanders of amber, balsam of cinnamon, cloves, mace, nutmeg, citron.
Oil of cinnamon, mace, spike lavender.
Troches of aromatic musk, aromatic gallia, and of benzoin for fumigation.

XLVII. Diet follows, which often accomplishes more than all other things. It consists in the legitimate use and application of the six non-natural things, in suitable quantity and quality, and finally in timely and orderly practice.

XLVIII. Therefore, an air should be chosen that is temperate and clear. If it is not such by nature, it must be prepared by art, which is done by the sprinkling of herbs and flowers of a heating and moistening nature, such as borage, bugloss, violets, and so on. Spirits can also be refreshed and brightened by fumigations from fragrant gums, such as bdellium, myrrh, storax, or other aromatic things. Rooms decorated with paintings should be avoided, because these objects also disturb the senses.

### LXXX.

For when a person who makes a promise <term>constitutor</term> <gloss>one who promises to pay an existing debt</gloss> simply promises that they will pay what either they themselves or another person owes, it is evident that they are bound without the formality of words, and they cannot evade a judgment through the exception of a faulty stipulation, for a simple agreement is sufficient for the plaintiff, which rests upon the preceding obligation and is clothed with this benefit of the praetor.

### LXXXI.

From this, the difference of this action from the surety <term>fideiussoria</term> <gloss>guarantee</gloss> is clearly apparent, since a surety is bound by a formal stipulation and cannot be sued without it, as is the more accepted opinion of the <term>Doctors</term> <gloss>learned jurists</gloss> through the law *Blanditus*, in the <term>Code</term> concerning sureties, and the law of stipulations, section *satis acceptio* in the <term>Digests</term> concerning <term>verbal obligations</term>, along with similar texts.

### LXXXII.

However, the promise <term>constitutio</term> is more powerful than novation, because the former does not extinguish the prior obligation, which the latter does; and when one person promises on behalf of another, both are bound, which does not occur in novation, since that does not change the person.

### LXXXIII.

Furthermore, the bare pact of ecclesiastics, according to <term>chapter one, Extra, concerning pacts</term>, does not diminish the utility of this action, since that is not received in the civil forum by more accepted calculation, and the denunciations of the canons are ignored in many places today. However, where regard is still had for them, this civil action concurs with said pact and overcomes its companion in the place and manner of proposing it.

### LXXXIIII.

Just as the prior obligation can be weaker for many reasons than that which arises from the promise, because this adds some benefit to that one by reason of place, time, or some other quality and circumstance. And although sometimes there is no more in the promise than in the preceding obligation, yet in that case, its own utility remains. For it is advantageous to the plaintiff to hold the defendant liable under multiple actions, and to be able to choose from them whichever one they wish.

### LXXXV.

And although in the formula mention is made only of money, nevertheless that term now pertains to all things, both movable and immovable, transferred here from the now obsolete [actions of] acceptance, not only to those things which in their kind receive a function <note>i.e., things measured by weight, number, or measure</note>, to which antiquity had restricted it, law 2, in the <term>Code</term> concerning money promised.</translation>

### LXXXVI.

Following the action concerning money promised, <term>Iustinianus</term> <gloss>Justinian</gloss> presents the action concerning the <term>peculium</term> <gloss>a slave's or son's separate fund</gloss>, which the praetor introduced, moved by natural equity, so that those who contract with slaves or sons in power might not be entirely mocked, to whom masters or fathers permit the trading of their own peculiar assets.

### LXXXVII.

The name <term>peculium</term> indeed has its origin from *pecunia* <gloss>money</gloss>, as if it were a "small amount of money," that is, a small patrimony, in the last paragraph of the <term>Digests</term> on the same. But sometimes it is also taken for anyone's patrimony, law *cogit*, <term>Digests</term> to the *Trebellianum*. Sometimes it is also [used] for money stored away for the sake of protection, whence it is customary to say "money without a <term>peculium</term> is fragile," law *si chorus*, paragraph 1, <term>Digests</term> concerning legacies 3. In this form of action, however, <term>peculium</term> is accepted in that meaning which we placed first.

### LXXXVIII.

So that the <term>peculium</term> is that which a son in power or a slave has, with the permission of the father or master, separate from the father's or master's accounts, after deducting what is owed to the father or master, or to those who are in their power, guardianship, or care, law *peculium*, and the following law, last paragraph, <term>Digests</term> concerning the <term>peculium</term>.

### LXXXIX.

Not that we think it necessary that the master or father must always grant a <term>peculium</term> to those they have in their power, since by that rule the son of a madman, and the slave of a ward or a madman, would not have a <term>peculium</term>; but because with <term>Iulianus</term> <gloss>Julian</gloss> we think it sufficient that such persons do not take away the <term>peculium</term> from those to whom previous masters or fathers had already granted it, law *quam Tuberonis*, <term>Digests</term> concerning the <term>peculium</term>.

Although we attribute a <term>peculium</term> to both slaves and sons in power, we do not do so in the same way for both; since the <term>peculium</term> of slaves is uniform, but that of sons is quadripartite, as it proceeds from different causes: from the father or his intuition, from elsewhere, or simply from elsewhere, or from military industry, or quasi-military.

<meta>continues from previous page: our Baron, born from this so renowned lineage, had as his father Lord HENRICUS, who, having administered the Republic with singular praise for his prudence, equity, and moderation, and having left behind a clear memory of his piety through the effort by which he ensured the <term>CONFESSIO GERANA</term> <gloss>Gera Confession</gloss> was written and printed, met his end on the 6th day of April in the year 1572. He obtained as a mother DOROTHEA, descended from the illustrious family of the Counts of Solms; she, excelling in the virtues of her sex, was so devoted to piety that she seemed to cultivate it alone, and she studied the Holy Code <note>The Bible</note> so assiduously that she held most exactly everything that contributes to the right conduct of life or the establishment of the pillars of faith.

Therefore, since there were no parents more outstanding in virtue or more eminent in lineage, everyone sees how much ornament and light redounded to our Baron. However, it is of no use to be born from illustrious parents if one degenerates from the virtue of his ancestors. For just as we call those animals whose work is strenuous "noble," so noble men are to be judged by their own and proper virtue, not that which is foreign or acquired. Therefore, his noble mother provided with the greatest care and the greatest industry that her son should not devote himself to any matter unworthy of the customs of his ancestors, but to the most honest</meta> studies of the sciences and to virtue from the very beginning of his age.

</translation>

<translation page="12">
<margin>1527.</margin>
For it matters much with what scents a new vessel is steeped. A mind corrupted from childhood thereafter delights in vices and dreads the sweet scent of virtue; but one steeped in virtue execrates vices and considers nothing prior or more ancient than the sanctity of morals. Thus, our subject was given and committed into the hands of masters and tutors, by whose diligent and accurate instruction he made excellent progress in letters and virtues at home; until at length, as a young man, he was sent to the Academy of Jena <note>original: "Academia Jenensem"</note> as if to a market of higher literature. Where, dwelling for an entire year, he attempted and did nothing but what was worthy of the splendor of his lineage and worthy of his noble character. Then, at the bidding of his noble mother and the Most Illustrious Guardian, Lord Otto, Count of Solms, he departed Jena and went to Strasbourg <note>original: "Argentoratum"</note>, which at that time flourished with a multitude of students and, above all, with the fame of seven Princes and thirty-three Counts and Barons. Here he applied himself diligently to letters for three whole years and also put much effort into the faculty of speaking, so that he gave abundant and bright proofs of his lofty talent and several Orations, which [are in] the second volume of the orations of the most eloquent man, Melchior Junius.

</translation>

<translation page="12">and he had used his customs, and had tasted their spirits and manners, and he did not generally disapprove of them, because most things among them were magnificent in appearance. To understand them more deeply, he crossed into Spain, and he did not yield to their splendor, and upon arriving he appeared to them as he was, a young man of both the first lineage and the primary arts. Finally, they embraced the noble German knight (they always show a unique zeal for our race, and they seem to bear with us more easily), first for his learning, and, what is valued there, for being well-trained in the equestrian art and in arms. For what should perhaps have been said earlier, he applied himself to these arts from boyhood; and he thus wisely combined music, intended for the mind, and gymnastics, intended for the body, as the ancients commanded and taught. § 13. The second corollary is concerning the universality of the future resurrection. Resurrection is distinguished, 1, into the singular, which is Christ’s, which occurred on the third day, Matthew 16, 21; 2, into the particular, of certain pious ones, raised by Christ in each year of his ministry and by the Apostles, of whom the Savior says in Matthew 11, 5: The dead are raised. Such a particular resurrection was that of these saints of ours; 3, into the universal, on the last day, where not only the pious shall rise, but also the impious, according to Scripture, Daniel 12, 2: Many (that is, all, John 5, 28) of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to eternal life, and others to everlasting shame. For the impious shall not rise—that is, they shall not triumph or stand in judgment, Psalm 1, 5. > What has preceded in the head will follow in the body.

I PLACE in high esteem the deed of that Appius, who was blind. <note>The author refers to Appius Claudius Caecus, the Roman statesman who, despite his blindness, spoke in the Senate to oppose peace with Pyrrhus.</note> (Most excellent Fathers and Colleagues.) Having heard that a most serious matter was to be discussed in the Curia, he wished to be carried there so that he might assist his endangered country with his counsel. I would also imitate what I praise, were I not hindered by poor health, old age, and the weakness of my voice. For my concern for Venice is no less than Appius’s was for Rome, nor have I been less involved in the affairs of my Republic than he was in his. It has been sixty years now since I traveled on an honorable embassy to Asia and Egypt; subsequently admitted to the Curia, I strove for many years to enrich the youth with my diligence and study when I expressed my opinion. As to what I have actually achieved, let others be the judge. Certainly, I soon sat in the Council of the Pregadi, and thereafter in the Council of Ten. Nor in any year since was I permitted to be free from public business. I have been an envoy to Constantinople, England, Germany, France, Spain, and even traveled as a soldier in Belgium. I passed over no famous man in Europe with whom I did not dispute, and I diligently studied the ancient and modern writers on the Republic, so that what I could not attain through experience, I might learn through reading. Since some of the most excellent College recently visited me and, in the name of the Grand Council, sought my opinion regarding the wars we are currently waging, I wished to dictate these brief points to my secretary, so that I may leave behind a testament of my judgment to the most Serene Republic, my most beloved country, while I am dying.

In the beginning, I establish that the end of our Republic is the same that once was Rome's: to spare the conquered, to war down the proud, and—if the fates favor our designs—to attain dominion over the whole of Italy and, indeed, the entire world.

Secondly, for the attainment of this most noble end, while we have many and great defenses at our disposal, likewise great difficulties and impediments are placed in our path, either by others or by ourselves. It is necessary to overcome and remove these through force and art. For that greatness of spirit did not come cheaply to the Romans, nor to anyone who wished to extend the borders of their empire and impose a yoke upon their neighbors. Countless myriads of Roman citizens perished in war, and by their own strength, they brought forth greater wars for their descendants, until, having been raised to the pinnacle of power and the height of peril, they fell most abruptly and perished miserably. The Macedonian himself, whose country is a neighbor to us, counts more wounds than limbs. What of the Ottomans? Do they not bring security to their empire through domestic blood and the deaths of brothers? Therefore, the empire of human affairs is costly, the reason for which is that many wish to command and few wish to obey. And because he who tries to grow and dominate others does so to the detriment and insult of those others, he is made suspect and hateful to all, and is compelled to fear the many whom the many fear. I warn of this so that we do not, in the shadow and the ferocity</translation>

<translation page="4">of our own recklessness, aspire to world empire.

Thirdly, therefore, our goods, wealth, arms, men, and fleets must be compared with those that stand against us, with the forces of the enemy; and not only those that appear, but also the arts and councils by which, if we are able to be superior, we may bravely wage the war we have begun in Styria, which we have incited in Savoy, and which we suffer in the gulf and the sea betrothed to us. We should enrich the Republic with the addition of new forces. If we are inferior, or if we must struggle in the utmost peril of the Republic, shall we make peace? We will obtain an equitable one while the war has inclined to neither side, while we fear and are feared in turn; we will find moderate treaties.

Fourthly. Therefore, one must think seriously about the subsidies for war, and that first and foremost, the gamble of Mars is uncertain. For often, he who has all the means of victory is cast down by the weak; one betrayal, one word, one stratagem often ruins everything. But nevertheless, let us now look at our defenses. What can give us courage are cities, wealth, arms, men, allies, and confederates. When I consider our city, it is most fortified by nature, wealth, and splendor; in the frequency of trade, it surpasses all the cities of the entire world, so that by a certain right of nature, the empire of the world seems to be owed to it. The Grand Council, which is the basis of the Republic, has over two thousand five hundred most noble senators, unmixed with any contagion of plebeian blood. We possess so much money that it is laborious and difficult even to count the millions. When I look at it, I am accustomed to exclaim:

> O how much of land and sea could be prepared
> By this, which we hide away in the vaults of anxious gold.

The ordinary revenue is two million gold pieces when we act most lightly; if we are more attentive to the matter, we will not with difficulty collect another amount equal to that. If we judge it by taxes, we will collect four times that. I pass over the extraordinary revenues, which Turks, Jews, and foreigners are compelled to pay, and which accrue from fines and from the commerce of the most Serene Republic. If all these were to fail, we could collect tithes, and by patriotic custom, double or triple them. We can increase the tax on merchandise as much as we wish. Other things also remain; for we can sell magistracies, as our ancestors did after the League of Cambrai. Certainly, from that trade, when they were hard-pressed by that seven-year war, they received five hundred thousand ducats. That which at that time was considered a great price. In the Genoese war, we ennobled three hundred of the wealthier citizens for money received; for if we are in need of money, let us choose a thousand of the wealthiest, and order them to be nobles, and grant them our privileges. Believe me, they will wage a whole year of war for us at their own expense. We have a triple <term>monte</term> <gloss>public bank/fund</gloss>, the old, the new, and the newest (I speak to those who know), from which we dig out gold with less labor, art, and danger than the King of Spain does from the Indies. Our ancestors once also made use of lots and blind fortune. Those things are great, but everything is preceded by what I will add, if you handle the matter with skill: while the Republic is in danger, individual tribes, towns, castles, and villages are compelled to provide and feed a certain number of men. For this is an ancient right. That levy, if it is carried out in the old manner and with rustic simplicity, will be a great help; if any cunning intervenes, it will be the most outstanding of all. For if it is arranged that wealthy and delicate men, who are averse to war, are approached for the levy, however much they may redeem their service with money, we hold armories filled in all places; men also cannot be lacking. In Italy, we hold the most noble cities, Padua, Verona</translation>

Behold the Chrysippean God, so invalid that he could not form a human free from disease, even had he wished it. Matter has cast a halter upon him. Go now, miserable Stoic, and lift your hands to heaven so that your Jupiter, by whom you are afflicted, might ward off disease from you: what response will you receive other than this? I cannot do otherwise for you than what happens. What, then, is the need for a shackled God of this kind, who can provide for neither himself in the prisons of his own matter, nor for another situated in danger?

In vain the Stoics struggle, by rolling all wickedness onto matter, to free their Jupiter: certainly, while they seek to avoid Charybdis, they cast themselves headlong into Scylla. If every evil owes its birth to matter, why does God exact penalties for the <term>ἀνόμοις</term> <gloss>lawless</gloss> actions of humans? He is therefore second to no tyrant in injustice, because he drags the innocent to the harshest of punishments. Guided by sound reason, we surely absolve from blame him who can act no differently than he does. To me, the Jupiter of the Stoics seems like a man constraining a dog with clubs or goads because it does not turn its upturned face to the stars, even though nature fashioned it prone and looking at the ground: yet just as such a mad flagellator would incur the censure of being at least foolish, if not unjust, so the same judgment will await the Stoic Jupiter, who, to a creature as noble as man, [inflicts] thousands of torments [by] the legions.</translation>

# Apollo, in congratulation, sings to the Lion exalted among the stars,
### and recounted among the number of the Gods.

<note>An ornate woodcut initial letter 'M' is decorated with scrolling foliage and floral motifs.</note>

Though Your Virtue, irradiating my sight with tremendous Majesty, 
Has drawn me, undeserving, to the heavens:
The flaming peak of fire, the heat of the celestial point;
That impetus of Yours, the power implanted and innate:
And that hidden vigor, filled with a wondrous magnet,
That Genius of Yours, Yours, O Yours, that Spirit of JEHOVAH,
And diffused deeply through Your limbs:
That hidden and all-powerful four-lettered virtue,
By which You penetrate the clouds, penetrate the adamantine 
Firmaments of Heaven, and both poles; by which, with the claw cast aside,
You penetrate that inaccessible conclave of the Gods;
Seeing wonders, stunned by secrets, scrutinizing great deeds:
Which are in the fates, and hidden in the Heart of the Gods above.
I repeat that I am unworthy, and distant from You by as many turns
As the Earth is distant from the ether in degrees;
I, even now, am but crude iron, a useless weight of the earth:
Yet that Magnetic Ardor of Yours, that is Yours</translation>

<translation page="10">With a mind and body that is, at the same time, weighty (the Nature of the Gods was stunned),
Which is not impenetrable to true touch;

Straightway, O novelty! equipped, so that beneath the stars
I might sing of THEE, for so many acts revealed in so many orbs:
<margin>(g)</margin>
Vienna saved among them by valiant Mars;

O auspicious beginning! they surrendered themselves to their own King:
Thence so often reported, Nitria <note>Nitra</note> is witness,
From enemies slaughtered, driven back, and put to much flight.
Nor is neighboring Posonia <note>Bratislava</note> ignorant of such laurels;
And no one with an unmindful mind will store away that Greatness
Wondrously carried off, worthy of such a Prince, O YOU,
This strength, with hostile and excessive fury repressed,
From Mohaz <note>Mohács</note>, the laurel which was suddenly coined into gold;
After the fortress of Buda was bravely stormed,
And no less successfully obtained, Greek Alba <note>Székesfehérvár</note>.

Hence also in the Hesperian <note>Western</note> lands, with the star turned,
The Gaul was compelled (with combined forces) to render the city
Of Mainz, captured under swift wings with the claw,
Straightway to the ancient Roman Empire;
And what pleases the gods above, to store it again under the wings of Eagles:
Then in related kingdoms, with the star having progressed,
A city recently snatched from the jaws of a kinsman,
And for the snowy triumphs continually to follow;
Thus I cease, having sung with the brief modulation of my reed,
Of one who has merited the heavens, and is placed in a deserved seat,
Residing above the exalted gods on a palm branch.

Aristoxenus, however, says that Pythagoras received many of his moral doctrines from Themistoclea, his sister. Ion of Chios in his *Triaginis* says that Pythagoras, having written a certain poem, attributed it to Orpheus.

Just as some come to it to compete, others to trade, and others to be the best spectators, so too in life, some are born slaves to glory and hunters of desire, while others are students of truth. Plato, who warned us not to trust the astrologers, mocked and commanded this, just as mathematical reasoning demonstrated; even more so, Plato bore more weight than Cassandra and Archelaus, whom he surpassed in astronomy. May you never, by the authority of Panaetius of Rhodes, believe those whom [Doychilax of Halicarnassus] <note>Likely a corruption or variant for a specific scholar or figure in the original text</note>, that most learned man in all of mathematics, rejected regarding the entire art of divination by the stars. I will come to the moderns. Nicolaus Oresme, a most acute philosopher and a most learned mathematician, attacked astrological superstition with a special commentary, indignant, considering nothing more fallacious, nothing more detestable, and nothing more inconsistent with all orders, but especially with those of princes and great men. Joannes Marlianus, in our own age, was supreme in mathematics and astronomy. He not only abstained from these predictions, but had also intended to write about their falsity in his final years; for he was long-lived, yet he did not finish it due to death. He used to say to men—and this is glorious—that he was a most certain demonstrator against the astrologers, and others, including his intimate friend Luchinus, who was himself an outstanding mathematician, related this to me more than once. Paulus Florentinus, learned in medicine and especially in Greek and Latin mathematics, as often as he was asked about that profession, asserted just as often that it was uncertain and fallacious, providing among other things his own evident experiment. For when he had already completed his eighty-fifth year, he found no stellar configuration in his own birth chart, which he had examined most diligently. I could cite many of these, even those who are alive and who, being astronomers, feel the same. But I do not know if they wish to be stirred against those who feel powerful through the fate of the heavens. Furthermore, our Marsilius <note>Marsilio Ficino</note> wrote against them, openly following the footsteps of Plotinus. In interpreting and expounding him, he greatly increased and illustrated Platonic wisdom; if some people, seeking aids for themselves and the heavens, believe that it is possible for such things to be done to soothe human ailments, I can bear witness with the most faithful mind of the man—whom I use familiarly—that he never had a more eager, pleasant, and effective exhortation than to warn against these fallacies. Nor, as often as we were together, was there a more abundant occasion and opportunity for laughter than regarding the vanity of the astrologers, especially if a third party intervened; Politian would intervene, a wonderful mocker of all superstitions. By chance, the judgment of our Nicolaus Leonicenus on this matter should not be concealed. Since he holds mathematics faithfully as do all the liberal sciences, he nevertheless judges this prophesying astrology to be so vain that he does not think that even those who wrote on it, especially the more learned ones, placed any faith in what they were writing. And if I ask him why they wrote, he replies partly due to avarice, partly due to the stupidity of princes. For when, he says, those men who surpassed others in observing the motions and bodies of the stars, which astronomy does mathematically, worked day and night, there was no emolument for them from princes, to whom it mattered nothing what the great stars might be doing, or with what swift motion...</translation>

<translation page="16">...they revolved through the spaces of the heavens. When they had seen this, so as not to be needy of earthly things while exploring celestial ones, they devised a clever fallacy to bind the minds of princes to themselves and to make them lovers of their profession. They claimed that the fortunes of all men, but especially of princes, depended upon these stars: specifically their children, life, piety, victories, and health. But for themselves, who had observed their divine motions and natures, they claimed it was thoroughly known and explored what they promised or announced to each one, whether good or adverse. Furthermore, they held ready at hand remedies by which they might repel evils when struck, and confirm good things. For if a happy man noted images from a certain material more closely related to those celestial natures, he could be forged; by wonderful machines, the power drawn down from the stars would make men most happy, and powerful kings would seek these, either by touching or wearing them, and easily achieve them. To gain more faith for all these things, they added that the more secret mysteries of this art had been revealed to them divinely, just as it is read in Maternus that they received many things from the most powerful divinity of Mercury, and from Pesosiris and Aesculapius. Then indeed, the princes—illiterate, curious, and most desirous of the things they promised—were easily led to believe them, to foster the professors, and to excite these studies daily more and more with rewards. This is what our Leonicenus says and thinks seriously about the astrologers, and not far from the truth. But one must be careful above all that volumes written by great authorities do not creep into our belief, which is common to them with all superstition. For the things that are put forward by them cannot be confirmed by reason. Whether they themselves believe those things to be true, or want them to be believed by others, they inscribe books of such fables to the most famous and ancient men, and hunt for faith in their own error through these fictitious authors. Of this kind is the book *On the Properties of the Elements*, in which he deals with great conjunctions and secrets, which they attribute to Aristotle—no fault of the philosopher, no merit of his—just as they circulate books of Plato concerning magic, and those which they call *Institutions*, filled with execrable dreams and inventions, and no less alien to Plato than these medicines are to the integrity and wisdom of Plato. Thus, the heretics once called Gnostics used to show books of Zoroaster by which they might make their heresy venerable through the antiquity of Zoroaster; Porphyry demonstrated with many arguments that these were new and feigned, not those of Zoroaster. But it is easily seen that those who are less instructed in the humanities are easily deceived and circumvented by these lies, because the learned, as soon as they recognize the authors—Mary, Porphyry, and others—immediately discern the adulterous from the legitimate. And our astrologers, and the figments of superstitious arts that are now in our hands, so abhor every similarity of truth that they lie exposed from their very midst. For who would be led to believe Ovid concerning the truth of Ovid, in which...</translation>

## XVIIII.

It does not merely provide the necessary qualities but, if it is the form of a living thing, it also provides a suitable mass through the passage of time. Since that mass is a certain accident inherent in prime matter, and prime matter cannot naturally lack a substantial form, it is necessary that, along with the accession of mass, one substance after another is added and generated. Consequently, nutrition is necessarily given with augmentation; it is certain that nutrition is distinguished from generation only by an accidental difference.

## XX.

Some things are nourished by food digested internally, others by food prepared externally. Those that digest food internally must have a small mouth and a certain crop or stomach. Most perfect animals also possess a ventricle, an intestine, a liver, and veins. The stomach embraces food that has fallen from the mouth through the ministry of oblique fibers, in such a way that it would necessarily escape through the pylorus <note>the opening from the stomach into the small intestine</note> if provident nature did not prevent it with certain glandular tubercles.

## XXI.

Immediately, the cooking faculty, which is identified with the substance of the stomach itself, applies heat as its primary instrument and works diligently at digestion, with the liver, spleen, diaphragm, and heart urging the work on from all sides. When the work is finished, the pylorus opens, and the chyle <note>a milky fluid consisting of lymph and emulsified fats</note>, entering the duodenum, heads straight for the large intestine and to the extreme part of the large intestine, which is called the bowel. By running through the winding passages of the intestines, it presents itself to be sucked up by the very frequent openings of the mesenteric veins, so that it retains nothing except feces.

## XXII.

The mesenteric veins carry the juice and flower of the chyle through the mesentery to the portal vein, from which the liver, as any part of it attracts, immediately dissipates it through multiple and narrow branches throughout the whole; there it undergoes the concoction of chyme or the four humors, such that from the hotter parts yellow bile is generated, from the colder and more earthy parts black bile, from the more temperate and subtle parts blood, and from the less subtle parts phlegm.

# Corrections.

->E<-

**Echium alterum** <gloss>Another Viper's bugloss</gloss> ] I confess that I do not yet perceive any specific difference between common Viper's bugloss and that which grows here and there among us on walls: let others examine it more strictly.

->G<-

**Geranium malacoides sive columbinum minus** <gloss>Mallow-leaved or lesser dove's-foot crane's-bill</gloss> ] It is not sufficiently certain to me whether the small plant we understand here is entirely the same species as the lesser dove's-foot crane's-bill of Caspar Bauhin.

**Gramen alopecuroides minus spicâ asperâ brevi** <gloss>Lesser foxtail-like grass with a short rough spike</gloss> ] The London botanists call this crested grass, and I would not deny it.

**Gramen caninum** <gloss>Dog's grass</gloss> ] This is the same thing that Johannes Bauhinus describes under the cited title: therefore, what I noted here must be retracted, for I had not observed the panicle myself before I published the Catalogue, but had rashly believed others.

**Gramen hirsutum majus** <gloss>Greater hairy grass</gloss> ] I now suspect that this grass does not differ specifically from the slender hairy grass, but only in size and other accidents, by reason of the place in which it grows.

->M<-

**Mollugo montana sive Gallium** <gloss>Mountain bastard madder or Bedstraw</gloss> ] These two synonyms, *Rubia sylvatica altera* <gloss>second wood madder</gloss> of Gesner, and *Matrisylva 2* <gloss>woodbine 2</gloss> of Tragus, do not belong here, but to the first Mollugo of Dodonaeus, which has a round stem and is erect.

It is not yet fully discovered to me to what this plant, which grows here and there in the hedges, should be referred; whether to the Mollugo, to which we have referred it here, or to the wood madder. I do not doubt that this is the same plant which Johannes Bauhinus described under the title *Rubia angulosa aspera* <gloss>rough angular madder</gloss>, and indeed the London botanists name it *Rubia sylvestris* <gloss>wood madder</gloss>. It is likely to me that the same plant is described under both titles. He doubts</translation>

<translation page="15">
whether the Mollugo of Clusius corresponds to his *Rubia angulosa* or not. But truly the Mollugo of Clusius is the same as the first Mollugo of Dodonaeus, the mountain Mollugo of Gerard, and the more common Mollugo of Parkinson. For the figure is everywhere the same, and both the figure and the description correspond to this plant: but the short descriptions of the wood madder in Gerard and Parkinson do not.

Caspar Bauhin incorrectly applies the Mollugo of Clusius and the mountain Mollugo of Gerard to his first or broad-leaved branching mountain Mollugo; since these synonyms pertain to the second no less than the first Mollugo of Dodonaeus.

---

-> O <-

**Origanum vulgare** <gloss>Common Marjoram</gloss> ] *The plant that grows in Bowyers close at Cherry-hinton is not this, but* **Clinopodium vulgare** <gloss>Common Wild Basil</gloss>. *We mistook it when it was young.*

-> P <-

**Polygalon Cortusi** <gloss>Cortuso's Milkwort</gloss> ] For this, substitute **Ferrum equinum Germanicum siliquis in summitate** <gloss>German horseshoe vetch with pods at the summit</gloss> of Caspar Bauhin, the synonyms of which look for in the Addenda.

-> R <-

**Ranunculus hederaceus rivulorum, et cetera** <gloss>Ivy-leaved crowfoot of the streams, etc.</gloss> ] The flowers of this plant are white, not yellow as we conjectured; and it grows here and there in watery places: therefore the cited synonyms do not correspond to it, unless perhaps it varies in the color of the flower in overseas regions.

-> S <-

**Saxifraga Anglica Occidentalium** <gloss>English Saxifrage of the Westerners</gloss> ] In place of **Saxifragæ Anglicæ alsinefoliæ** <gloss>English chickweed-leaved saxifrage</gloss> of Gerard emaculatus <gloss>amended Gerard</gloss>, substitute **Synanchica Lugdunensis page 1125 Gerard emaculatus** and add the synonyms **Rubia cynanchica** <gloss>dog-strangling madder</gloss> of Johannes Bauhinus VI, or **cynanchica** of Caspar Bauhinus.

**Saxifraga graminea pusilla** <gloss>Small grassy saxifrage</gloss> ] *I find upon comparing that this is the same plant described by Johnson upon Gerard under the name of* **Saxifraga Anglicana alsinefolia** <gloss>English chickweed-leaved saxifrage</gloss> *or* **Pearlwort.**</translation>

<summary>This page continues the list of botanical corrections and synchronicities, refining the classification of various grasses, madder-like plants, and saxifrages by reconciling observations with the works of Bauhin, Gerard, and other contemporary naturalists.</summary>
<keywords>botany, taxonomy, John Ray, corrections, Bauhin, plants, synonyms</keywords>

Enjoy, therefore, the auxiliary favors of your most brave Patroness, Rhenish Nation; you who were once renowned for triumphal fortitude, when already the Euphrates and Tigris, the Propontis and Nile, the Seine and Rhone, the Volga and Dnieper, the Guadalquivir <note>original: "Bætis"</note> and Thames had served the Tiber, and when you alone dared to fight for the Rhine against the encroaching power of the Romans. And having already overcome Pyrrhus, defeated Antiochus, routed Hannibal, subjugated Mithridates, put Pharnaces to flight, curbed Asia, tamed Africa, and reduced Europe—which had been brought almost to the necessity of ignominious submission—to the slaughter inflicted upon the Varian army <note>referring to the Battle of the Teutoburg Forest</note>, you dared to rise up against a people victorious over nations.
