<meta>continues from previous page: while having it in mind to approach them</meta> he nevertheless died on the journey. In this case, Clement VI, in his Bull, while wishing to signify his Clemency toward such men, commands the Angels of Paradise to lead the soul, thoroughly absolved from Purgatory, into the Glory of Paradise, granting the same Grace to them as did Nicholas V, Urban VIII, and Innocent X of this century: among whom Urban writes thus in his Bull: *Since it can happen that of those who have set out on a journey for this cause, or have betaken themselves to the City, some may be hindered by illness or other legitimate cause on the way or even in the City itself, or prevented by death, and being unable to complete the prescribed number of days, or perhaps not even having begun it, are unable to carry out the aforementioned acts and visit the Church and Basilicas of this kind: we, wishing to favor their pious and prompt Will as much as we can in the Lord, wish for them, being truly penitent and confessed, to be made participants in the aforesaid Indulgence and remission, as if they had actually visited the Church and the Basilicas mentioned on the days prescribed by us*, compare Marchantius on the Bull of Urban VIII.

§. 4. Regarding the absent Jubilators who do not approach Rome, the Roman Pontiff, according to the raving of Marchantius, derives his wells from his own kindness and sends out rivulets to diverse provinces, so that all may both wash and drink, provided they visit their local churches that are analogous to those in Rome according to the judgment of the Pontiff or his envoys. This is believed to be a singular Argument of papal beneficence and generosity for them, which the aforementioned Marchantius proclaims everywhere, saying *that this generosity is bestowed by the Pontiff upon various regions of the world, so that the kindness of the Father toward his dispersed children, and of the Shepherd toward his sheep who cannot gather together in one place, may shine forth more brightly*. From this, he says the Pontiff grieves *that these living waters, these rivulets of Grace, cannot be derived to certain provinces and regions, because they have cut themselves off from Unity, and like ungrateful children have left their Mother Church, kicking out after they have sucked her breasts, that is, rebelling against her faith and Doctrine, and immersing themselves in the foul waters of perverse and heretical Doctrine*. Alexander VI granted this Grace, which they estimate to be the Indulgences of the Holy Year, even to the most remote provinces to enrich his bastards, as Polydorus writes, and Sixtus IV and Gregory XIII granted them to the Catholics of England, both in England and elsewhere, who could not approach Rome, according to Frostius. Finally, those who are dead and already burning in purgatory must be added to these: even they can be liberated from the flames of purgatory by the indulgence of the Roman Pontiff, if the faculty to apply the Jubilee to them is expressly contained in the promulgatory bull, and if they are helped by the suffrages of heirs or friends</translation>

<translation page="21">
<meta>continues from previous page: helped by the suffrages of heirs or friends</meta>, to whom Clement VI, when they had set out for Rome for the sake of the Jubilee, granted the power that each could select three or four souls, whomever they wished; for those souls, because of his Indulgences and their Merit, would immediately fly from purgatory into Heaven. Santarellus, even bolder, says that the Pontiff, through a most plenary Jubilee, can liberate all the souls of purgatory in one day, Chap. 3, Dub. 12. But there is no reason for us to refute at length that perverse Audacity which the Roman Pontiff takes upon himself: since we are not ignorant of the foundation upon which that Pontifical power rests, which he parades, and which is not Apostolic but Anti-Christian, we believe it will not be difficult to form a judgment on these pompous promises. Let the Pontificians show which Divine Author wished to enrich his Church with such an abundance of Grace that the Bishop of Rome could dispense it; if not, what prevents us from saying with the poet:

->What will this boaster produce worthy of such gaping?<-

§. 5. The Jubilee of the Papists is therefore nothing but a mere Fabrication; its Privileges are acts of trafficking; its Indulgences are lures. The reasons which they bring forward here to palliate this Simony of their Church are of such a kind that if you list them, you have already refuted them. Indeed, what Turecremata <note>original: "Turec."</note> dreams here in Jac. de Graffiis <note>original: "Jac. de Graff."</note>, *Appendix aurea, Book 1, Chap. 8, Sec. 13:*

> That the Jubilee was instituted to aid human infirmity, since some men are so burdened by the weight of their sins that they are insufficient in this life to pay the punishments owed; hence, the pious Mother Church commonly acts at a certain time in their life so that the faithful may have the help of this grace, by means of which they may be absolved from the debts of punishment,

all of which, since it feeds on slippery Presumption, as if our Works could merit any grace from GOD, has an easy refutation through the very words of the Savior:

> When you have done all those things which are commanded you, say: We are unprofitable servants: we have done that which was our duty to do.

If these things are true of those whom a true Love toward God impels to walk in the commandments prescribed by Him; they will hold all the more with respect to those about whose works, dedicated to the study of <term>ἐθελοθρησκεία</term> <gloss>will-worship/self-imposed religion</gloss>, the Prophet says:

> Who hath required this at your hand? Is. 1:12.

Furthermore, if the Pontificians are anxious about this elective Worship for fear of the punishments to be suffered in Purgatory, let them first apply fire to that chimerical invention, and then we will worry about escaping the flames of purgatory. Nor is what the cited Turecremata brings forward for this hypothesis of his of any better stock, namely that such an Indulgence was instituted to confirm and strengthen</translation>

<summary>This section critiques the Roman Catholic Jubilee as a man-made fabrication, refuting the validity of Indulgences for the living and the dead, and challenging the authority of the Roman Pontiff to dispense divine grace through such rituals.</summary>
<keywords>Jubilee, Indulgences, Purgatory, Roman Pontiff, Simony, Clement VI, Turecremata, Christian doctrine</keywords>

The nutritive and augmentative power are only formally distinguished, but in reality, they are one and the same power.

<margin>XXXIIII.</margin>
Although the power of generating and altering is not in the thing that arises or changes, the power of augmenting must necessarily be in that which grows.

<margin>XXXV.</margin>
The augmentation of a whole living being is not, strictly speaking, a single motion. For the unity of motion requires the unity of the object moved, the term, and the time, as is written in Book 5 of the *Physics*, Text 34; if these are taken strictly, they are lacking in this increment.

<margin>XXXVI.</margin>
The augmentation of all parts of a living being, taken together, is not a continuous motion.

<margin>XXXVII.</margin>
The augmentation of no single particle is continuous by a proper continuity.

<margin>XXXVIII.</margin>
Augmentation can be called continuous in the same way as alteration, namely, when no instant passes in which it could happen, without it actually happening.

<margin>XXXIX.</margin>
The augmentation of a living being is sought by nature, in itself and primarily, for the convenience of the living being itself. The augmentation of metals, stones, and similar things, however, looks rather to the benefit of the species than to that of any particular individual.</translation>

<translation page="12">Although, due to the variety of complexions, locations, nourishment, and other things, a certain number of years cannot be assigned during which the augmentation of men is perfected, nevertheless, if we speak of a man who is reasonably well-constituted, and of what usually happens for the most part, we must agree with the ancient philosophers and physicians that growth in length continues up to the 24th year, and growth in width continues up to the 30th year, more or less. After the 30th year, however, up to the 35th or 40th, no augmentation occurs, nor any diminution; but from the 40th up to the 60th, a certain faint diminution follows, to which eventually, until death, an open loss of parts succeeds. <translation page="18">it proves nothing, in the said chapter *Si sacerdos* <gloss>if a priest</gloss> 2. Mascardus, conclusion 377, because it is done against the law, as said above, and regularly the priest cannot be compelled to reveal or open it, just as Vincentius Carrozius deals with that matter most extensively in his treatise on the revelation of confession, to whom, so that I may not be too long in this institution, I remit myself.

Closing this Disputation: the confession of a dying person. If some wounded man in the article of death asserts that Titius inflicted the lethal wound upon him, and thus caused his death; or if someone in the crime of poisoning, arson, etc., at the time of punishment accused and proclaimed other persons as his associates: the question therefore is, whether such an assertion or accusation harms anyone, such that for this reason they can be condemned or tortured? Truly, so that we may deal with this by way of remission, the judge in these matters ought to be provident and cautious, and above all, from the usage of the court, attend to whether, together with such an accusation, other indications concur; for instance, that the defamed Titius was found at the place where the wound was inflicted, with a sword unsheathed and bloody; likewise, whether threats and enmities preceded. If these, therefore, concur, I think it is sufficient not only to investigate, but also to torture, which the Ordinance of the Empire also proves in chapter 27, paragraph "To the sixth" <note>German text follows: "If such a wounded person, for certain (which is to be noted) reasons, accuses someone of the misdeed and dies thereupon, etc."</note>.

But if other indications or supporting evidence are lacking, then although the nomination alone makes some presumption and indication for investigation, it is not, however, sufficient for torture, nor for imposing the oath of purgation, even if the confessor is of the most approved faith, or if the confession was made with an oath. But it must be rejected *ex post facto* <gloss>from after the fact</gloss>, or it is not to be believed, by law 3, paragraph *Si quis moriens* <gloss>if anyone dying</gloss> 1, in the Digests *ad Senatusconsultum Silanianum* <gloss>regarding the Silanian Decree of the Senate</gloss>, and by article 27 of the Ordinance of the Empire, where it is expressly said that this nomination alone is not a sufficient indication for torture, much less for condemnation. The reason is that such a dying person is not only a sole witness, and in his own cause, and as it were an enemy, but also because one's own confession ought to harm oneself, not another, by those things which Mascardus hands down in conclusion 386. Regarding this noble question, after the Doctors, in the said law 3, paragraph 1, in the Digests *ad Senatusconsultum Silanianum* and in law "the end" in the Code *ad Legem Iuliam repetundarum* <gloss>regarding the Julian Law on Extortion</gloss>, see Iohannes Georgius Goedelmannus on the point of poisoning, book 3 of *De Magis* <gloss>On Wizards</gloss>, chapter 9, number 5, up to the end; Didacus Covarruvias, book 2 of *Variarum* <gloss>Various Matters</gloss>, chapter 13, number 8; Menochius, book 1 of *Presumptions*, question 89, number 81; Mascardus, conclusion 144 and 1078; Fachineus, book 9 of *Controversies*, chapter 90; Farinaccius, question 46, number 35, with the following; Möller, book 3 of *Semestria* <gloss>Semester treatises</gloss>, chapter 8; Polydorus Ripa in the said commentary on actions in the article of death, chapter 16, throughout.</translation>

->To the Most Outstanding and Most Learned MAN<-

## To Master JOHANN CABES, Candidate in Both Laws <note>Both Laws refers to Canon and Civil law.</note>, his friend.

**As** the merchant ventures to entrust himself to the waves to pile up wealth, and to bear the murmurs of the deep-sounding sea; if the goods of Fortune are very often sought with such great labor, which the flame or the wave soon snatches away; why should it be wearisome to seek with zeal and great labor those goods which are not going to perish on any day, which neither flame nor rapid Ocean can destroy? He who does not seek these goods, he is not wise.

->Willingly composed by<-
->**JOHANNES GERHARDUS**<-
->**FRAUENBURGUS, Doctor**<-

<note>A horizontal divider ornament composed of linked geometric and scrolled typographical elements.</note>

->To the Most Outstanding and Most Learned MAN<-

## To Master JOHANN CABES, Candidate in Both Laws and Marriage.

**A** dispute recently arose between Themis <note>Goddess of divine law and custom.</note> and Venus <note>Goddess of love and marriage.</note>: she calls you her own, and she calls you her own. One occupies you with honors, the other with loves; to which one will you give yourself, that you might wish to be entirely of one? To neither, JANE <note>Addressing Johann Cabes in the vocative case.</note>, I think. Divide the common rights, and in whatever part you can please, please.

->Poured forth at Altdorf by<-
->**GEORGIUS NOESSLERUS, Doctor and Public Professor**<-
->**Physician of the Palatine Principality and the Republic of Nuremberg.**<-

# XII. IOANNES CONRADUS FINCKHER, OF CELLE.

## FROM THE BOOK ON PHYSICS, ASSERTION XXXV.

<note>An ornamental woodcut initial 'T' features scrolling foliage and floral motifs.</note>
Time, materially and realistically, is motion itself; formally, it is a property of motion, consisting in a continuous, divisible, and successive duration. It consists also in the account of a measure, primarily that which is measured and intrinsic, or a number in potentiality, which is that very duration already mentioned, insofar as it renders the motion it inhabits formally fit to be numbered and measured by the duration of another motion. Finally, it consists in the account of an extrinsic and measuring measure, or a numbering number, which measure and number is the same duration of motion, insofar as it is distinguished by the intellect into certain parts such as days, weeks, months, and so forth, and once so distinguished, as if it were something better known to us, is applied to discerning the durations of various actions, motions, and things, as they are subject to motion.
<margin>4. Physics, text 131.</margin>
In the first and second ways, the formal account of Time is a categorical being <note>original: "ens praedicamentale"</note>; in the third way, it is a being of reason <note>original: "ens rationis"</note>, such that if the soul were removed, Time would not exist. To both of these latter formal accounts of Time, the Aristotelian definition can be applied, from text 101: "The number of motion in respect to the prior and the posterior."

---

## XXXVI.

**H**ence it becomes plain that particular Times are multiplied according to the multitude of motions, since individual numerical motions claim their own durations, which are also called their intrinsic measures. However, Universal Time is given as unique in number, which is the duration of the first motion, distinguished by the numbering intellect into certain parts to measure our actions and the motions of things. Duration in reality is nothing other than existence; it differs formally.

---

## FROM LOGIC.

### XXXVII.

<summary>This page defines Time as both motion and a property of motion, distinguishing between its internal measure and the extrinsic measure applied by the human intellect, and notes the distinction between particular times and universal time.</summary>
<keywords>Time, Motion, Duration, Aristotle, Being of Reason, Categorical Being, Physics, Logic, Ioannes Conradus Finckher</keywords>
</translation>

For the medium of a demonstration "on account of which," and consequently the most potent [form of proof], nothing else is required or suffices, besides the causal definition of the property to be demonstrated, which is always simultaneously the proper and proximate cause of the same.

---

## XIII. PHILIPPUS KINE,
->OF WANGEN.<-

### FROM THE BOOK ON THE HEAVENS. ASSERTION XXXVIII.

<note>A decorative initial letter C within an ornate circular frame depicts a figure, likely a scholar or celestial observer, in a landscape setting.</note>Celestial bodies differ among themselves in number and in essential species, yet every star differs from its sphere only by an accidental species, just as a denser and more luminous part of its own sphere, continued like a knot in wood; and therefore, it does not wander through the heavens by its own motion, just as fish do not [move] through the water and birds through the air [by the motion of the elements themselves].

## FROM LOGIC.

### XXXIX.

<note>A decorative initial letter F features floral and scrollwork ornamentation.</note>The form, which is the internal and essential principle of a syllogism, can be described as a certain complication or disposition of the matter fit to infer a conclusion. This disposition, if it is the remote matter or the middle [term] with the extremes, is called a Figure; if it is the proximate matter, namely of the propositions according to a certain quantity and essential quality, it is called a Syllogistic Mode. Conversion, which is the formal extrinsic principle of the syllogisms of the 2nd and 3rd Figure, is a formal and therefore necessary consequence, but not an argumentation.

<summary>This page covers the nature of demonstration in logic, the accidental difference between stars and their celestial spheres, and the formal structure of the syllogism, including the concepts of figure, mode, and conversion.</summary>
<keywords>Demonstration, Philippus Kine, On the Heavens, Logic, Syllogism, Figure, Syllogistic Mode, Conversion</keywords>
</translation>

Who he might be: the commoners said he is a Venetian.
A headband bound his hair in the German manner,
A Gallic crest veiled the Venetian's head.

To one asking what this dress meant for him,
He replied: "This predator has snatched everything, and all
That holds power: what was it if not plunder?"
I am a true prophet: if only the gods of the born would favor me,
By Aesop's merit, the jackal will be the nourisher.

## Epitaph of Elpis
### Wife of Boethius

I was called Elpis, a foster-child of the Sicilian region,
Whom the love of my husband took far from my fatherland.
Without him, the day is sad: the night anxious, the hour tearful;
There was not only one spirit for the husband and wife.
My light is not extinguished, with such a husband remaining,
And I shall survive in the greater part of my soul.
Now, as a pilgrim, I rest in the sacred porticoes,
Bearing witness to the throne of the eternal Judge.
Let no hand violate the tomb, lest by chance my husband
Desire to join these ashes to his limbs again.

## A Poem to the Blessed Virgin
## by Georgius Tiphernus

Virgin, glory of heaven, most holy Virgin,
Who art to be venerated above the angelic choirs,
Beautiful one, you surpass the snowy roses: you surpass the white
Lilies: you surpass the stars with your countenance.
Pure, like a little dove, whom no milky
Feather does not know: nor does a blemish rest on the whole body.
Which Sibyls do you not excel, O Virgin,
And what nymph can finally be compared to you?
You are called the beloved mother of God: you are called his bride.

# HYMN OF SAINT ERMI-
# NOLD.

<note>A decorative woodcut initial 'D' with floral and scrollwork ornamentation.</note>

Divine one, whom the work of arduous virtue once carried above the stars, in the annual rite of the day consecrated to you, be more gentle.

While we celebrate your famous urn with frankincense flames, bringing joyful triumphs and cheerful applause to the gods above, revisit your bones.

Bones which have driven away many diseases and severe fevers, and various plagues, and the white dropsy <note>edema</note>, and every swelling in the limbs.

They restored the lost enjoyment of light to those lacking the power of sight, and at the same time they suddenly gave the long-lame their steps with firm knees.

Moreover, they put to flight the horrid shadows and sad Furies from the underworld, often tormenting the limbs of men with the madness of the guilty.

Visit this seat of yours, Father ERMINOLD, which you first cultivated, and gaze with a calm light upon the flock prone before your urn.

You who have considered your descendants, written in golden notes, as future inhabitants of heaven, taking pity on their final life, remove their perils.
</translation>

<translation page="20">
> Let us therefore sing praises to the Divinity, which is one in equal Deity, and which is not enclosed by persons nor by temporal age.

Who will be the priest, who will be the leader by whom
Germany will be able to preserve the true faith in safety?
For the heretics rejoice now that you are leaving;

Halt your steps, Martin, and check your pace.
But if you do not leave, then you will save yourself for your friends,
And you will save yourself for God and for the friends faithful to you;
And the Church, performing the duties of its office,
Which has long been abandoned, will now enjoy freedom;
And venerable piety will remain in its own esteem.
Halt your steps, Martin, and check your pace.
Look where you are going: you, a German, will depart for Rome,
Climbing the airy summits of the mountains,
Descending again as if sent down into the depths of hell.
Perhaps a robber will prepare hidden traps,
To seize either your riches or, ultimately, your life.
Halt your steps, Martin, and check your pace.
The storm prevents you, the North Wind forbids you, Aeolus,
Releasing all the winds from their prison,
Dissuades this journey; but if you refuse to obey,
You may be forced to meet death and grave misfortunes.
But may God and fortune prepare better things for you.
Halt your steps, Martin, and check your pace.

<translation page="17">
# THE PRECEPTS OF THE MOSAIC LAW.
->Reduced to a summary.<-

## FIRST PRECEPT.
### YOU SHALL HAVE NO OTHER GODS
This is to fear God in true faith, solid hope, in favorable and adverse circumstances, and indeed in your entire life.

### THE GUILTY OF THIS PRECEPT.
Whoever ascribes their life and condition, in every state of fortune, to another rather than to God, and trusts not in God but in themselves or their own possessions.

## SECOND PRECEPT.
### YOU SHALL NOT TAKE THE NAME OF YOUR GOD
->In vain.<-
This is to refer glory, honor, and blessing to God, to worship Him alone, to credit whatever good you possess to Him alone, to call upon Him, and to detest oneself. No one doubts that whatever is good is the name of God.

### THE GUILTY OF THIS PRECEPT.
Whoever uses the name of God for anything other than His glory. Whoever flatters themselves with any personal good, and seeks virtue and praise from somewhere other than from God.

## THIRD PRECEPT.
### YOU SHALL KEEP THE SABBATH HOLY.
This is to attend to God, to desire and seek only His grace.

### THE GUILTY.
Whoever does not rest the mind in God, but persists in work on the sacred day: whoever does not care for divine things, or cares for them coldly: and whoever does not keep the Sabbath by resting from vices.

## FOURTH PRECEPT.
### HONOR YOUR FATHER AND MOTHER.
This is to obey God, and for the sake of God, to obey every authority, even unto tyranny; to support parents not only with greetings and nods, but with the diligence of your deeds, and to honor them especially with benefits.

### THE GUILTY.
</translation>
<translation page="18">
Whoever flees, despises, and neglects their parents, who is averse to and hates magistrates and the law. Whoever does not obey authority, or obeys reluctantly.

### Precept V.
## YOU SHALL NOT KILL.

This is patience, peace, humanity, mercy, and (to speak in one word) an entire life without the bitterness of malice, even ready and beneficial toward an enemy.

### THE GUILTY.

Whoever does not help a brother with advice, aid, and work, and does not prevent evil from reaching a neighbor.

### Precept VI.
## YOU SHALL NOT COMMIT ADULTERY.

This is purity and modesty in thoughts, speech, and deeds, frugality in living, an uncorrupted love of heavenly things, contempt for worldly pleasures, and the love of God alone.

### THE GUILTY.

Whoever is dissolute in pleasures, enjoys laughter and joy immodestly, or does not restrain and curb those who do. And those who allow their soul to be occupied with the care of things other than God.

### Precept VII.
## YOU SHALL NOT STEAL.

This is the flight from all avarice, joyful poverty, generosity, and humanity.

### THE GUILTY.

Whoever is unwilling to give a loan to a neighbor for free and without interest, who attaches their mind too intemperately to any of the world's goods, who bears poverty unwillingly, who denies alms or does not bestow them in a timely manner, and who circumvents a neighbor with deceit and imposture.

### Precept VIII.
## YOU SHALL NOT BEAR FALSE WITNESS.

This is the naked and simple truth of words and deeds, a tongue fostering peace, seeking the benefit of a brother, desiring to compose discord, refuting detraction, and clearing and covering the defamation of a neighbor.

### THE GUILTY.
</translation>

<summary>This passage presents a concise moral summary of the Ten Commandments, defining each precept alongside the actions that constitute a violation of those laws.</summary>
<keywords>Mosaic Law, Decalogue, Precepts, Sin, Morality, Duty to God, Duty to Neighbor</keywords>

<note>A decorative initial P begins the section.</note>

<note>A decorative initial O begins the section.</note>

For by this reasoning, they do not so much insult the Scripture as they do its primary author, the best and greatest God, with a notable indignity.

<translation page="21">that various punishments existed among various nations, is not, I suppose, unknown to you, and will be explained in its own place and time. Zaleucus had also passed a law regarding this same matter, that whoever was convicted of adultery should have both eyes gouged out. When, however, the son of Zaleucus himself had sinned in this, and had been convicted of adultery, and was now to be punished according to his father's law, the entire citizenry professed that they would gladly forgive the son's crime for the sake of the father's virtue and merits. But the father, urging the law and contending that it must be confirmed even by his own punishment and that of his family, yet being unable to obtain from the people that the son should be blinded in both eyes, finally achieved this by an admirable temperament of justice and paternal affection, that the law was kept inviolate, and, as far as the law allowed, he provided paternal affection to his son. For he ordered one of the son's eyes to be put out, and one of his own. Finally, however, as Suidas noted, he met his death while fighting most bravely for his country, in order to teach others, by his own example as well, how sweet and fitting it is to die for one's country.

You have, excellent listeners, what I was able to learn concerning Charondas and Zaleucus: I ask vehemently that you allow this commemoration, such as it is, to have been not unwelcome to you, and that you do not regret this time spent.

Concerning myself, and the parts of this task entrusted to me, I would not wish for you to wait for me to say anything. For I prefer to contribute whatever is in me by deed itself, for the benefit of the studies of the flourishing youth and for the adorning of this <term>Sparta</term> <gloss>the duty or role one has undertaken</gloss>, rather than to promise it profusely with words. That I may be able to achieve the former, I humbly pray and beseech God, the greatest and best, the author of honest laws and political order, and the fountain of all good.

<translation page="22">
<note>An ornamental horizontal band at the top of the page featuring a repeating floral or fleur-de-lis pattern within interlaced circles.</note>

# TO THE BENEVOLENT READER. GREETINGS.

<note>Decorative drop cap 'C' at the start of the text, featuring an ornate floral background with scrollwork.</note>

Since our lawgivers in their prefaces deter men from evil deeds chiefly by the mention and regard for death, because each one is accustomed to being tortured by the conscience and repentance of those deeds while near to it: yet they do not add the cause of this thing, which is undoubtedly that a mind conscious of evil foresees the future judgment concerning itself and the impending punishments (for what would he fear, who believed that all things are ended by death?): that it may be established that not even this was unknown to the heathens, I am pleased to set forth here the most excellent **IAMBICS OF PHILEMON THE COMIC**, which I once translated into Latin from the Greek. The Greek versions exist partly in Justin Martyr, in his *On Monarchy*, partly in Eusebius, in book 13 of the *Preparation for the Gospel*, and in Clement of Alexandria, who however attribute these two later ones to the author **DIPHILUS**. I desire, friendly reader, that this work be approved by you.

> Do you believe, Nicostrate, that the dead,
> Who lived in every luxury while they breathed,
> Are thus covered by the earth,
> So that the Deity might remain hidden from them for all eternity,
> And they might escape from Him by flight?
> These are the lights of Justice that see all things.
> For we believe there are two ways to the underworld,
> Of which one is for the just; the other for the impious.
> But if the same fortune awaits the pious and the impious,
> Then go, slaughter, steal, and plunder
> Whatever you can, and mix the lowest with the highest.
> What stops you? An error, good man, lest it bewitch you:
> Each man's own deeds await him in the underworld,
> Over which will preside the ruler of all, **GOD**:
> Whose tremendous name I could not speak:
> Who often prolongs life for those who sin.
> 
> If, however, any of mortals, while he commits
> Evils day by day, imagines that he is hidden from the gods,
> He imagines falsely, and brings himself onto paths,
> Until **GOD**'s vengeance rests for a little while.
> 
> Look to yourselves, for whom the gods are but fables:
> There is, there is a **GOD**. But if anyone does wickedly
> By a perverse nature, let him seize time for himself.
> For afterward, when time has elapsed, he will pay the penalty.

<summary>The author presents Greek iambics by Philemon (or Diphilus) concerning divine judgment and the afterlife, translated into Latin to demonstrate that pagan writers acknowledged the fear of God's justice.</summary>
<keywords>Philemon, Diphilus, divine judgment, afterlife, justice, ethics, God</keywords></translation>

<translation page="10">ORATION.

tells things that should be kept silent to a friend, whom he then adjures by all that is sacred and profane to bury what he has heard in eternal silence. Do you wish, O *Corydon*, that others be silent? Be silent yourself, and say *Nothing*. The *Ardelio* <note>busybody</note> wanders through the city all day long, always asking, "What is new? What is good?" While he trusts everyone with everything with a simple mind, he causes *Nothing* to be trusted to him. The *Politicus* <note>politician/schemer</note> prudently despairs of everything, hopes for everything courageously, and diligently guards against everything, and thus, in the end, he fears *Nothing*. If you are wise, do everything cautiously and quickly, but do *Nothing* rashly or timidly, suddenly or late. Do you ask what you can do without the help of the Best and Greatest **GOD**? *Nothing*. Among Christians, life will condemn some, and doctrine will condemn others. There are not a few who would defend their religion even to the fire **EXCLUSIVELY**. It is a wonder that, while pure religion encourages piety, it usually achieves *Nothing*. You will often see men who are happy, bibulous, and boisterous throughout their entire lives. Yet, when a more unfortunate hour arrives, they hasten to prayer books, and after wiping away the dust, they contort their grim faces into devotion, and sighing heavily, they search for certain short prayers suited to their misfortune. Then they count the pages of those prayers, and if they are too long, they either look for shorter ones or close the books again. Because these men are destitute of harmony between heart and mouth, they deserve to receive *Nothing* from **GOD**. If eyes were dug out as often as they took offense and sinned, the entire human race would soon see *Nothing*. On the final day, certain rich men will say that they cast gold—that cursed metal, that incitement to all evils—at the feet of the singer and the flute player. Yet they will shout to the poor, the friends of Christ, that they gave *Nothing* with a religious hand.</translation>

<translation page="11">ORATION.

Praetors and other wealthy citizens and rustics are accustomed to sending cocks, capons, geese, thrushes, and other things to the magnates. Yet to the poor, they give *Nothing*. O fools! If you wish to send gifts suitable to each person, send food to the poor, and to your patrons, either hunger or *Nothing*. Dung, though it is a vile excrement, is nevertheless not useless. For without it, physicians and farmers would possess *Nothing*. <term>Jurisconsults</term> <gloss>lawyers</gloss> love to drag out a litigious matter as if it were never to end, and when they have lost the case—and the client his property—they nonetheless demand their fee, at least for the sake of shame. If the client is wise, he gives them *Nothing* as a testament to his gratitude. The politicians who, returning from Italy and France, depart from the customs of our fathers, and hear every flea cough, and are always rattling off new institutions—not because they are good, but because they are new—they, I say, sometimes seem to imitate <term>Orbilius</term> <gloss>a harsh schoolmaster</gloss>, who, intending to reform grammar, did not want his students to say "Sum, Es, Est" <gloss>I am, you are, he is</gloss>, but "Sum, Sus, Sut." To whom a certain man endowed with old-fashioned faith and character said in his ear: "Sum, sus, sut, does no good; Sum, Es, Est, let it remain as it has been." <translation page="13">The bloody TYRANNY moved my spirit, by which, of course, they strive to expand the Church of Christ, drunk on the blood of the saints (l). But what they write in the blood of Christians, everyone shall read; no posterity will erase it.

Therefore, for these reasons, as if by repeated cock-crows, I was awakened to go out from Babylon, so that the plagues, destined by the just Divine judgment, might not fall upon me as well.

I have come out! Now I pass on to *You*, who profess the true faith. I have presented my CONFESSION to the leaders of your Church, the sum of which will be read out so that it may be known to all. I testify before GOD, before the NUTRITION <note>The author uses the Latin term *Nutritio*, likely referring to the church leadership as a sustainer or nourisher of the faithful.</note> of the Church, and before YOU ALL, solemnly, that I profess this with my MOUTH and believe this in my HEART (m).

I promise nothing; I am a human being; but I certainly hope this from Divine grace: NOTHING in the world, whether to the right or to the left, will change my opinion.

With this mind, I GIVE MY FAITH to you, and I implore your prayers. May you receive me as a NEWBORN (n), whose desire it is to overcome the world through faith. Thus, therefore, I am YOURS, and I shall remain YOURS by the grace of God.

---

(l) Rev. 17:6. (m) Rom. 10:9. (n) 1 John 5:4-5.

<translation page="14">Wherefore, I lift my eyes to your pinnacle, MOST SERENE PRINCE. Since he knew, therefore, that his mother was hostile to him, he built a fleet and set out from Asia to Europe; he is recorded to have settled in Gaul by way of the Rhine and Moselle, and to have built a most flourishing city, calling it Treves after his own name. They say that in the year 1200, a poem was found engraved on stone, such as this:

> Semiramis, wife of Ninus, who was happy with such a spouse,
> Possessed much, but added more to what she had before,
> Not content with her own, nor with the entire bounds of the world,
> She expelled her stepson Trebeta from his ancestral kingdom;
> He, an exile, founded our distinguished city.
> Treves stood twelve hundred years before Rome.

But these are without a doubt the delirious ravings of an idle monk, which we wish to record, not refute, along with Philip Cluver in *Ancient Germany*, Book 2, chapter 14, concerning the Treviri, page 383.

§. 15. Go now, all you who in every way exclude the weaker sex from the keys of power and from commerce with the virtues. We do not hear or approve of everything, without exception, that Bodin in *On the Republic*, Book 6, chapter 5; Arnisæus in *Political Doctrine*, Book 1, chapter 9, and *Political Relections*, Book 2, chapter 2, section 12; Menochius in *Hierapol*, Book 1, chapter 5; Petilius in *Exarch*, Book 2, chapters 29 and 30; and Schönborn in *Politics*, Book 2, chapter 12, page 122, have devised for the subversion of <term>Gynaecocracy</term> <gloss>government by women</gloss>. Virtue is closed to no one; it admits all, and chooses neither sex nor rank. We, embracing the opinion of Tholosanus in *On the Republic*, Book 7, chapter 11; Adami Conzeni in *Civil Doctrine*, Book 1, chapter 26; and Danaeus in *Politics*, Book 6, chapter 4, as much as is appropriate, say with Seneca:

> ...in a narrow breast
> The fragile mind does not always fluctuate in an easy tide of vices:

And there is that which Schurman replies, saying: Perhaps emulation disturbs those who think this way, or certainly fear, lest that old saying of Ennius one day come to pass:

> You indeed, young men, possess womanly spirits,
> She, the virago, possesses those of a man.

Alexander the Great more correctly admired no one more than Semiramis and Cyrus; Curtius, Book 7, chapter 6. Julius Caesar also prudently appeals to the rule of Semiramis, according to Suetonius, §. 23.</translation>

<translation page="16">§. 16. But that the truth of that Maronian <note>i.e., Virgilian</note> sentiment might not fall:
->Each of us suffers his own ghosts;<-
Semiramis also performed magnificent deeds that lead to disparagement, not only to praise, as Berosus the monk of Annius of Viterbo says on page 48. Nor is any other fault given to her more than lust, for she admitted every vigorous soldier to her intimacy, and, after they were enjoyed by the use of her body, she removed them from the midst, so that the rumor of fornication might not spread to the common people. Claudian traces the first eunuchs back to Semiramis; yet Claudius Barthius seems to doubt this due to the silence of Diodorus in his *Annotations on Eutropius*, Book I, page 1325. Ammianus Marcellinus, Book 14, as cited by Henelius in *Wrocław Leisure*, chapter 35, page 274, adopts the position of Claudian when he says: Wherever anyone walks, seeing the crowds of mutilated men, he will execrate the memory of Semiramis, that ancient Queen, who was the first of all to castrate tender males. That she had relations with a horse, Pliny writes from Juba in *Natural History*, Book 8, chapter 42. Indeed, she finally commanded that fornication and marriage between parents and children should be permitted, as Paulus Orosius testifies in Book 1, chapter 4. It is said by Justin and others that she sought the bed of her son Ninyas to provide an example of the observance of this law, and was killed by him because he rejected so nefarious a crime. Yet the history of her death is doubtful, and it is not sufficiently clear whether she perished from wounds in war or by the crime of her son. Wagner, *Historical Institutions*, Book 3, page 201.

§. 17. The remains of Semiramis are said to have been placed in a tomb, which she built for herself while alive in an elevated and conspicuous place in Babylon, with this inscription attached: IF ANY KING IS IN NEED OF MONEY, LET HIM OPEN THIS MONUMENT AND TAKE AS MUCH AS HE WISHES. When Darius Hystaspis had read this, he ordered the sepulcher to be opened, in which he found no gold, but this written: UNLESS YOU WERE A WICKED MAN, YOU WOULD NEVER HAVE VIOLATED THE SEPULCHERS. If you exclude Herodotus, who attributes this tomb to Nitocris, you will hardly find anyone who calls it into doubt. I marvel at the female wit! Semiramis would have been worthy, imposing an epigraph upon the living after her funeral, and perhaps one such as that which Felicianus the Veronese has in Camerarius’s *Historical Meditations*, Century 1, chapter 97, page 455: FELICIANUS THE VERONESE HAS SET UP THIS SACRED MONUMENT TO HIMSELF. I, WHO WAS RESTLESS WHILE ALIVE, NOW AT LAST, DEAD, AM UNWILLINGLY
->AT REST.<-

<translation page="8"># XVI.

The external form consists in the solemnities <note>formal requirements</note>, which are either common to both written and oral testaments, or proper to one or the other. Common to both is the bringing in of witnesses, whose quality must be considered, and who must be invited by a formal request; finally, the number is defined by law, so that seven are to be brought in.

<note>Supporting citations include: Donellus, Althusius, the Code of Justinian (on testaments), Sichardus, Covarruvias, and Clarus. Regarding whether a smaller number of witnesses may be accepted by local law, we believe they may, and custom confirms this. This proceeds to the extent that, by virtue of a testament so established, an heir may also obtain goods situated outside the territory, supported by the Institutes (on the law of nations), the Digest, the Code, and works by Gail and Mynsinger. Fachineus dissents.</note>

# XVIII.

We understand the quality of witnesses such that those who are not prohibited from being witnesses are considered suitable. For nature itself warns that some are restrained from testifying, such as the prepubescent, the insane, the prodigal, the deaf, and the mute, to whom the blind are rightly added. For other reasons, slaves, women, the infamous, the heir instituted, and the domestics of the heir or of the testator himself are also excluded, though a legatee <note>one who receives a specific legacy</note> is not. The condition of all these is to be examined at the time they are brought in.

<note>Supporting citations include: the Digest, the Institutes (on the ordering of testaments), and commentaries by the Doctors, Donellus, and Clarus. If someone is held by all to be a free man and is brought in as a witness, the testament is not on that account invalidated.</note></translation>
<translation page="9">But it is not without reason that one doubts whether that case may be extended to another defect in the witnesses, such as if an infamous person were brought in who was unknown to be such at the time the testament was established. We affirm this, based on the Digest (on ignorance of law and fact), the Code (on sacrosanct churches and on testaments), and the works of Clarus, Covarruvias, Decius, Beust, and the Institutes (on the ordering of testaments).

->XVIII.<-

It is also a common requirement that, in the execution of either type of testament, each part must be performed in a continuous sequence, with the witnesses remaining together, and no extraneous act intervening. It is not inappropriate to examine what must be determined concerning the common question: Can contracts be constituted by a testament? Many deny this, along with Viglius, but we shall demonstrate that their opinion is not entirely straightforward.

<note>Supporting citations include: the Digest (on the ordering of testaments), the Code, commentaries by Duarenus, Clarus, Wesenbeccius, Everardus, Viglius, and Bronchorst.</note>

->XIX.<-

These things are proper to a written testament: that the will of the testator be reduced to writing and offered to the witnesses, who shall subscribe their names and affix their seals. Proper to an oral <note>original: "nuncupativo"</note> testament is the declaration of the supreme will made by the testator openly and intelligently; if this is reduced to writing by a notary (as is the custom today), it is nonetheless called an oral testament.

<note>Supporting citations include: the Institutes (on the ordering of testaments), the Digest, the Code, and works by Duarenus, Donellus, Cujacius, and Hotomanus.</note></translation>

<summary>This text details the legal formalities required for written and oral testaments, focusing on the qualification, number, and status of witnesses, as well as the procedural requirements for the continuous execution of testamentary acts.</summary>
<keywords>testamentary law, witnesses, solemnities, Roman law, inheritance, oral testament, written testament</keywords>

## CONTROVERSIA IV. GENERAL
->CONCERNING<-
# PENANCE.

### THESIS LXXVI.

Penance is not a sacrament properly so called.
Against Bellarmine, Book I on Penance, chapter VIII. Council of Trent, Session XIV, canon I.

### THESIS LXXVII.

Contrition is not an action, nor is it free, nor evangelical.
Against Bellarmine, Book II on Penance, chapter I, Proposition II.

### THESIS LXXIIX.

The enumeration of all sins, even if probable, is not necessary by divine law, nor to obtain remission.
Against Bellarmine, Book III on Penance, chapter II, § I. Council of Trent, Session XIV, chapter V.

### THESIS LXXIX.

When the guilt is remitted, no temporal punishment of this life or the next remains to be paid.

### THESIS LXXX.

Therefore the fiction of satisfaction, for this punishment, through good works, falls away.
Against the same, in the same place.

### MELETEMATA <note>meditations/studies</note>

->*On the three lights by which GOD, the Thrice Greatest and Best, offers himself to be known.*<-

<note>A decorative initial letter P starts the section.</note>

The Father of lights (James 1:17) manifests himself under three lights: under the light of nature, for the intelligent alone; under the light of grace, for the holy alone; under the light of glory, for the elect alone. The light of nature is great, the light of grace is greater, the light of glory is the greatest. The former shines in the <term>Macrocosm</term> <gloss>the universe</gloss> and <term>Microcosm</term> <gloss>man as a world in miniature</gloss>; the latter shines in the visible and invisible Church; this last glows in the seat and assembly of the blessed and the Angels. These three lights are subordinate to one another. For the light of nature is kindled to the end that we may be led to the light of grace and the light of glory.</translation>

<translation page="17">## SECTION II.
->proposing<-
## THEOREMS.

1. IN GOD there is an antecedent Will and a consequent Will. Whether, however, the former is rightly called the Will of Mercy and the latter the Will of Justice does not seem to be without doubt, since the consequent Will is also one of Mercy and grace.
2. The object of infinite power is said to be everything possible. And the created Angel hints at this in Luke 1, verse 37, and the uncreated [God] in Genesis 18:14. It is customary to note the Hebraism in this place, by which the word is used for the thing itself. But what if one should raise a doubt whether a place exists in which it is taken in such a way?
3. Creation is rightly attributed solely and entirely to the Most Holy TRINITY. Whether, however, by the *τὸ* <gloss>the</gloss> [neuter article] "to say" in the History of Creation the SON OF GOD is signified is altogether doubted, nor are there lacking reasons for doubting, which we shall reserve for public debate.
4. Jerome is not unjustly condemned of error for having denied God's Providence over irrational animals, since sacred scripture evidently testifies that individual animals and all animals are subject to divine Providence. Compare Matthew 10:29. Some philosophers and theologians alike strive to clear Jerome of this injustice, but with failed effort. Let Jerome's own Commentaries on Habakkuk, chapter 1, page 187, be consulted.

---

## on John 1:14.

1. THE WORD, which gave counsel and brought aid, BECAME FLESH; where there is a complaint, there is the remedy, remaining what it was, assuming what it was not.

3. THE WORD that was, the FLESH that was not, BECAME into one, which is and remains both.
4. THE WORD: behold the Divinity! FLESH: behold the humanity! IT BECAME: behold the Unity of the Person!</translation>

# OF IACOB LOCHER PHILOMUSUS
## Decastichon <note>a poem of ten lines</note>.

> Anne, the mother of God rejoices to call you mother,
> And the world always exults in your name.
> Anne, Clavus sang praises to you, and now prays
> That you, divine patroness, may bring aid to the miserable.
> The German people hope in you, they consecrate altars to you,
> And as suppliants offer incense and sacred prayers.
> Thus, with your aid, Anne, assist the wretched
> And infirm flock that worships in your temples.
> And extinguish various diseases with sacred remedies,
> Which your daughter and your grandson, God, bestow upon you.

## OF IOANNES BOEMUS AUBANUS.

> Whoever wishes to know how clement and how benign
> Blessed Anne is to her servants,
> Let him read the sweet poem which the venerable Phileremus
> Produced from the greatest diligence of his heart.

## TO IOANNES CLAVUS PHILEREMUS, his most beloved brother, Alexander Brassicanus of Tübingen.

> If blessed Anne were to draw breath in our regions,
> She would wish for no clearer lyre than yours.
> Thus you are able to sway the gods, and also the dark shades of the underworld.
</translation>

<summary>These pages conclude a series of Sapphic odes praising Saint Anne and contain laudatory epigrams from contemporaries of Johannes Clavus, including Jacob Locher, Ioannes Boemus Aubanus, and Alexander Brassicanus.</summary>
<keywords>Saint Anne, Johannes Clavus, Humanist Latin poetry, Jacob Locher, Alexander Brassicanus, Christian piety, devotion</keywords>

> Anne, Clavus sang praises to you, and now prays
> That you, divine patroness, may bring aid to the miserable.
> The German people hope in you, they consecrate altars to you,
> And as suppliants offer incense and sacred prayers.
> Thus, with your aid, Anne, assist the wretched
> And infirm flock that worships in your temples.
> And extinguish various diseases with sacred remedies,
> Which your daughter and your grandson, God, bestow upon you.

## OF IOANNES BOEMUS AUBANUS.

> Whoever wishes to know how clement and how benign
> Blessed Anne is to her servants,
> Let him read the sweet poem which the venerable Phileremus
> Produced from the greatest diligence of his heart.

## TO IOANNES CLAVUS PHILEREMUS, his most beloved brother, Alexander Brassicanus of Tübingen.

> If blessed Anne were to draw breath in our regions,
> She would wish for no clearer lyre than yours.
> Thus you are able to sway the gods, and also the dark shades of the underworld.

Moreover, from this point, just like the Iliac vein which is joined to it, it tends toward the foramen of the pubic bone. Before it crosses through, it receives a branch growing from the outer Iliac ramus, and thus exits the foramen. Once it has departed from there, it is consumed within the muscles—partly those by which the foramen is closed, and partly those which arise from the pubic bone—just as the internal Iliac vein is consumed. Finally, when it terminates at approximately the middle of the length of the femur, its extremity meets and is united with the extreme branches of the internal crural muscle, which we discuss in the following chapter.

The larger or outer [branch] similarly produces two offshoots, of which the first is called the External Epigastric. It arises from the outer side a little before it perforates the peritoneum, reflects upward, and ascends along the inner side of the rectus muscle until it is joined by anastomosis with the descending mammary artery around the navel. The other, the Pudendal, which is a small inner branch, is not divided into as many rami as the vein. As soon as it has departed from the peritoneum, it arises and is carried transversely along the commissure of the pubic bones to the pudendal parts, being exhausted into the skin of the penis. The remainder of this trunk goes into the leg, of which we shall now treat.

<- CHAPTER V. ->

<- The branches of the outer Iliac ramus propagated through the leg. ->

After the outer trunk has led out the branches described, it departs from the peritoneum and is carried to the groin into the leg, along the same path as the crural vein, to which it is placed underneath and is joined as a companion throughout. Thus, it constitutes the crural trunk (which we always call by this name). Immediately upon passing the peritoneum, it leads out an offshoot from the outer side which they call the outer crural muscle. Carried downward, it is propagated into the muscles embracing the bone of the thigh on the anterior side. In the same region, sometimes directly opposite, but more often a little below—though in an inner position—another is led out, called the inner crural muscle. This is distributed through the third flexor of the femur, or the triceps, and through those that occupy the inner region of the thigh, as far as the knee, by several branches whose extremities are joined with the extremities of the internal Iliac, which we said descends to the leg through the foramen of the pubic bones. Having led out these branches, the crural trunk descends from the groin with the crural vein and is reflected next to the thigh bone in such a way that, when it reaches the ham <note>the popliteal fossa</note>, it rests between the two posterior heads of the femur. For skilled Nature always observes this: it leads vessels around that part of a joint where the flexion is, lest they be compressed if they were to pass through the part where the joint extends. However, almost exactly in the middle of its path while it descends through the thigh, it leads out a branch which, broken into many twigs, runs out through the muscles situated in the posterior region of the thigh, together with the popliteal vein, and finally, descending through the ham (whence it is called the popliteal), is divided into the calf by frequent branches. Standing now in the ham, it leads out a branch on both sides to the sides of the knee joint, buried deeper one after another, which are exhausted partly into the joint itself and partly into the two gastrocnemius muscles that constitute the calf, <pb n="258"/> from which they are also called the sural arteries. After the crural trunk stops in the ham, it brings forth an offshoot from the outer side which descends next to the fibula, and is hidden between the muscle abducting the foot and the muscles flexing the second tarsus, and is distributed into the remaining ones occupying the anterior part of the tibia, as far as they are fleshy and begin to twist along the outer malleolus. A little below this mentioned one, another is led out from the posterior site of the trunk, which descends as far as the junction of the tendons of the gastrocnemii. Then another comes forth from the same posterior site of the trunk, but below the second, which descending and passing through the transverse ligament, runs out through the dorsum of the foot, diffused into the muscles abducting the toes. The rest of the trunk is carried downward through the posterior parts of the tibia and, around the inner malleolus, offers a little branch to the foot which approaches the thumb <note>the big toe</note> and creeps across the dorsum of the foot. The trunk itself, lying hidden between the tendons of the muscles of the toes of the foot, is divided into two rami: the inner one distributes to the thumb two, to the index two, to the middle one; the outer one, however, distributes to the little toe two, and two to the toes next to it, on the lower side. Moreover, even if the progress of the arteries occurs for the most part as we have described, nevertheless, what we said above regarding the veins—that their distribution varies greatly not only due to the diversity of individuals but also of the sides in the same human—that must also be held regarding the arteries, which behave differently in other humans.

<- CHAPTER VI. ->

<- Contains the history of the arterial vein and the venal artery. ->

So that this treatise on veins and arteries may be perfect and absolute in all its parts, we have chosen to append the history of the third vein and the second artery in place of a concluding flourish. The vein is called the arterial vein—the word 'vein' from its function, because the ancients believed it carried blood from the right ventricle of the heart; but 'arterial' from its tunic, which is similar to the membrane of the arteries, since it is not simple as that of the veins, but double. The artery, on the contrary, is called the venal artery—'artery' because the ancients determined it carried air drawn through the lungs; 'venal', however, because its substance corresponds to the body of the veins, since it is a simple and not very thick tunic. We have deferred the treatment of both to this place in particular so that we might treat both together, since they are born from the same viscera, are inserted into the same, and furthermore, enjoy the same distribution. For they arise from the heart: the vein from the higher seat of the right ventricle, and the artery from the left. Both are implanted and exhausted into the substance of the lungs; the vein is stretched through the right side of the trachea <note>original: "asperae arteriae"</note>, and the artery through the left. Soon, each is cut into two rami, of which one goes to the right part of the lungs and the other to the left, with each again cut in two, and these into other rami, until they are dispersed into the most minute twigs. The larger rami accompany one another so that the vein always proceeds with the artery, joined by many anastomoses, in the middle of which the rami of the trachea run out. These are significant vessels, and far larger than the size of the lungs would seem to require, since those parts, as we said in the previous book, which dissipate the most nourishment, require larger veins, and there is none which, for the lungs' perpetual [motion...]

</translation>

<pb n="97"/>Manuscript in Ecclesiastical Theology 8; he himself, however, cites Theophilus Raynaud on good and evil books, page 119, Possevin in the *Apparatus* Volume II, page 389, and from our own, Varenius in the *Rational of the First Century*, page 150. Whatever objection Jacobus Faber Stapulensis raises—who, in his commentary on the epistles of Paul, asserts that Seneca stooped to such simplicity of style so that he might not be recognized by his own, and thus incur the hatred of his own people—see the most distinguished M. Goetz's *Sketch regarding the Supposititious and Lost Writings of Paul*. There are other, more certain matters which are rightly attributed to the philosopher Lucius Annaeus Seneca, and which we know were only recently ascribed to him by that most distinguished man, Johannes Albertus Fabricius, in his *Latin Library*. Specifically: the three books *On Anger*, the book *On Consolation to his mother Helvia*, the book *On Consolation to Polybius*, the book *On Consolation to Marcia*, *On the Tranquility of the Mind*, *On the Constancy of the Wise*, *On Clemency*, *On the Shortness of Life*, *On the Happy Life*, *On Leisure or the Retirement of the Wise*, the seven books *On Benefits*, the 124 letters *To Lucilius*, the seven books of *Natural Questions*, and the most delightful satire *The Pumpkinification of Claudius Caesar* <note>original: "ἀποκολοκύνθωσις"</note>, regarding which I would wish for you to compare what is found, beyond Fabricius's observations, in the *Introduction to Ecclesiastical History* by the blessed Sagittarius, historian of Jena, on page 602. Held as supposititious, however, are the book *On the Cardinal Virtues*, *On Morals*, *On Poverty*, the eight letters *To Paul*, and others. I cannot restrain myself from suggesting a few things regarding a most vexing question: do the Tragedies also acknowledge the philosopher Seneca as their author? For it is known how three men distinguished by the name Seneca are commonly enumerated: M. Annaeus the Rhetorician, L. Annaeus Seneca the Philosopher, and finally Seneca the Tragedian. One may read about this in Baillet's *Judgments of the Learned on the Principal Works of Authors*, Volume IV, Part II, page 363, and the authors cited at the end. Truly, the learned hold differing opinions regarding the Tragedies. They offer the judgments cited above, arguing that they are not by a single author; the most distinguished Fabricius also asserts in the cited place that he vindicates *Hercules Furens* for M. Annaeus Seneca the father, *Hippolytus* for Seneca the philosopher, and the others for various other authors. Olaus Borrichius, a noble name among the Danes, states in his dissertation on poets: *Although it is still contested under judgment whether that illustrious work of Tragedies, which bears his name, should be attributed to him (Seneca the Philosopher), nevertheless, most of the learned, if not all, incline to the belief that at least most of these Tragedies are justly attributed to him.* That this cannot be denied, writes Borrichius, because L. Annaeus Seneca the philosopher was skilled in the poetic art, is proven by the epitaph which Seneca the philosopher is said to have composed for himself, and which is annotated by Lilius in Book VII of *Poetic History*, Volume II of his works, folio 317.

> *Care, labor, merit, honors taken for the duty,*
> *Depart, from now on trouble other souls.*
> *GOD calls me far from you, at once, having performed*
> *My earthly deeds, farewell, hospitable earth.*
> *Yet, greedy one, receive the body into solemn stones,*
> *For we return the soul to heaven, the bones to you.*

Unless the Lord Cellarius, professor at Halle, has some <unclear>value</unclear> when he appends these words in the continuation of the Faber-Buchner Lexicon: *I could never be led to believe that Seneca wrote these verses. Let those who have a deeper investigation therefore judge.* For at present, our subject is not with the writer of the Tragedies (if there was such a person, a son, brother, or nephew through a brother of the philosopher), but with the philosopher himself, whose name, lineage, and books we have enumerated, and we shall not be slow to annotate what seems to the learned to be his style of speaking.

<pb n="98"/>How Aulus Gellius—who in book 12, number 2, not only cites judgments about Seneca but also, if we take note of his common and colloquial usage, his learning—is thrashed by Muretus and others is well known. He judges it with the reason of a more elegant mind in these words:

> A more sublime diction
> which might descend more deeply into the hearts; an oration so concise
> in the weight of thoughts and most combative in arguments, with great force
> everything conforms to the brow of all, thus it cannot seem surprising.

When Quintilian in book 10 speaks of breaking oneself with weight, this is without doubt from envy, as Rabner conjectures, because the rhetorician preferred the Laconic parsimony of words. Maresius in Book I, Epistle 1, is less than friendly, because he wrote letters about philosophy to a friend, but the historian in Book I, Chapter 23, says it quite well:

> Nothing is more scriptural
> and sententious, which I would persuade to be unrolled and unrolled again,
> than a hodgepodge of various maxims in unity.

**Erasmus** in Seneca criticizes base words, but he is defended by Buchanan. That Seneca gave excellent precepts, everyone admits. It breathes nothing else, nor does he differ more regarding virtue than he asserts and inculcates. **Wilkins**, in the introduction to his translation of Cicero's *On Duties* <note>original: "Offic. Cic."</note>, page 16, praises his moral, paraenetic philosophy. **Lord Kirchmayer, Doctor**, dealt with Lucius Annaeus Seneca and his natural piety at Wittenberg in the year 1690; yet he does not support the opinions that are sometimes rejected, as if he were affected by the errors of Stoic philosophy. For he acts very insanely in Epistle 70: *Let him go out, from where he took the impulse, whether by iron or some potion occupying the veins, let him proceed, and break the chains of servitude.* He praises the adolescent who, because of a troublesome disease, fasted. Time prevents me from discussing these individual things more prolixly now, or from explaining the instruction by which he taught Nero, and more; especially where the holidays are discussed by **Lord Ziegler** in the cited book. Also excellent are the seven books *On Benefits*, from which one may extract most elegant maxims and examine them according to logical rules. A passage is taken from the same to be read in Book II, Chapter 9: *They advise that some benefits should be given openly, some secretly, etc.*, which four students of our Gymnasium have taken to treat themselves, so that they might be matters for an oration. For thus it was thought that the solemn custom might be satisfied, and that benefits received might be rightly acknowledged with a most grateful mind. I request that you, most honored men, if it is convenient for you and your affairs, attend for the honor of GOD and the Patrons of the School, in a panegyrical manner <note>original: "πανηγυρικῶς"</note>, at Schleusingen, in a manner observant, dutiful, and friendly. From the Gymnasium at Schleusingen, regarding the philosopher Lucius Annaeus Seneca, in the year of the Christian era 16... <note>original text ends abruptly here</note>

<note>A schema of the students to be heard follows:
- Friedericus Abraham Müller will discourse on benefits in a Greek oration.
- Joh. Christoph. Steltzner on benefits given openly.
- Joh. Nicol. Jungglaß will show gratitude for benefits received, and show the same to our MOST SERENEST LORDS, in the Hebrew idiom.
- Joh. Fridericus Kern on the prologues and epilogues.</note>

<note>From the printing house of GOEBEL.</note>

</translation>

<pb n="13"/>he had finished; he is suddenly struck with terror and, imploring the help of those who were present, dies in a miserable manner and with great pain and groaning. From this it can be easily understood that divine power was communicated to the divine man. Another example, not unlike the former, is added to this. Another Margrave, William, was treating the aforementioned church of Meissen injuriously. And when the provost of the same church wished to lead the man away from his evil intent with great prayers, he not only refused to obey those who were rightfully warning him, but also troubled the church itself much more than before. Then the said Provost, since he could not seek help from elsewhere, fled to the divine Benno and prayed to him to save the church. It happened that Blessed Benno warned the Margrave three times in his sleep not to plot anything more serious against the church. When he despised this as an empty dream, being vehemently rebuked the fourth time thereafter, he lost one eye, with a more serious danger proposed if he did not desist from his wicked project. Margrave William, led partly by fear and partly by repentance, restored everything to the church and increased its resources as much as he could, and he also esteemed the divine Benno highly and honored him greatly. Indeed, one must not pass over the fact that there are two regions; in one of which the Margrave hid himself while he was fleeing. In the other, however, he converted the Vandals from extreme impiety to the Christian faith. In these regions, the footprints of his feet are still observed intact, and that hut in which he stayed among the Vandals—even if it is not secured by any stable structure and had a roof of straw, finished by age—nevertheless never suffered damage nor was it consumed by fire, although the neighboring houses frequently burned in fires. The episcopal habit, in which his body was commended to the earth, along with the episcopal miter, lay underground for over two hundred years, and having been dug out of the sepulcher without any alteration, it is seen and displayed today in its entirety. <pb n="15"/> of the martyrs: more bitter later in the conflict with heretics: most bitter now in the conduct of those within. Internal and incurable is the plague of the church, and therefore in peace its bitterness is most bitter. Such things and graver ones were said by Bernard, and not a few others. And Paul says: When men say peace and security (for the situation seems to be reverting to that, so that barbarism and superstition may prevail once again), then suddenly as pain to a woman in labor, so destruction will come upon them, from which they will not escape. For as it happened in the times of Noah, so will be the coming of the Son of Man. And so at length will be the end of superstition, which indeed the Lord is already destroying with the spirit of His mouth, and will at last utterly abolish by the brightness of His coming. Come Lord Jesus, say the pious: let your kingdom come, they pray. I will indeed come soon, says He who is faithful. The righteous cried out, says the Psalmist, and the Lord heard them. But He will arrive all the more promptly as the pious are more desirous. And again, He will come the more hastily as the wicked are more numerous. For impiety draws on plagues, as the <term>Caecias</term> <gloss>a northeast wind</gloss> draws clouds. Since, therefore, these men draw them on, and on the other hand the pious strive with all their might for the same, the Lord will hasten twofold, according to that word in Luke 18: Amen I say to you, the Lord will vindicate His elect from their enemies, and that SHORTLY. An excellent word, and most consolatory to those praying for the end. But the evil servant, thinking in his heart that his master delays his coming, beats his fellow servants, eats and drinks with the drunkards, wages war against those who obey the commands of God and have the testimony of Jesus Christ, changes times and law, and establishes new cycles, which he extends into many centuries. Yet the Lord will come on a day he does not expect, and at an hour unknown, and will cut him asunder, and set his portion with the hypocrites, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. The Lord does not delay His promise, as some interpret tardiness: but the Lord is indeed slow toward us, not wishing for anyone to perish, <pb n="16"/> but for all to return to health. I say the day of the Lord will come as a thief in the night, and as it happened in the time of Noah. Even so, Come Lord Jesus: may His grace be with all those who piously desire His coming. Amen.

<pb n="12"/>all, just as <term>Thomas Hobbes</term> described their natural state in his *book On the Citizen, chapter 1, §§. 10 & 11, pages 12, 13, and following*. For citizens, in order to forestall the oppression of their superiors, would be anxious about an occasion to rebel against their future oppressors; among spouses, some disagreement and suspicion would quickly arise, by which one might remove the other from the midst by poison or another way; in the household and domestic society, a fearful danger would be present, against which, however, no small precaution is taken through piety or the frequent exercise of it <note>compare <term>Pufendorf</term> <gloss>Samuel von Pufendorf, jurist</gloss>, *On the Duty of Man and Citizen*, book 1, chapter 4, §§. 9, pages 53, 54, 55; as well as the dissertation of the most distinguished Master <term>Pritius</term> on Atheism, both in itself foul and harmful to the human race, art. 18</note>. This utility is also observed, to be silent about more, in homages and alliances, as well as in the passing of laws, so that the minds of citizens may be restrained within the bounds of what is right and just. For it is the custom of human nature that human counsels, laws, or edicts are likely to have scarcely any weight unless they are corroborated by the consensus and will of the Divine <note>compare <term>Masius</term>, loc. cit., chapter 1, §§. 3, 4, 5 and following</note>. See how excellently <term>Pufendorf</term> shows in his *On the Habitude of Religion to Civil Life, §. 5 and following*, that without reverence for the Divine, no faith in pacts, and without religion and the fear of the Supreme Judge, no authority of an earthly judge is kept whole and safe.

### §. XI.

This can be seen in very many Republics, where piety and religion have produced much convenience. Although the cults of the <term>Romans</term> were quite superstitious, religion nevertheless urged them to keep faith and treaties, and to subject themselves to the laws and the Magistrate, because they believed that God would punish those who did otherwise <note><term>Arnis</term>, book 2, Politics, chapter 5</note>. Hence it is that <term>Numa Pompilius</term> feigned that he had nocturnal meetings with the Goddess <term>Egeria</term>, and said that by her admonition he was instituting what was acceptable to the Gods <note><term>Livy</term>, book 1, History</note>. And perhaps there is no legislator <pb n="13"/>that ever existed who did not borrow the authority of his laws from that same origin, or at least base his statutes upon religion, even if it were false and feigned. Thus, <term>Philip</term>, the father of <term>Alexander the Great</term>, made use of such excellent reverence for the Gods and religion that, when there was need, he was believed by all of <term>Greece</term> to be the avenger of sacrileges and the sole champion of piety and the Gods, and, what is greater than all these things, he would overthrow an enemy by the consciousness of impiety as if by a machine <note>compare the dissertation of the most distinguished <term>Sagittarius</term>, Professor at Jena, on Religion, §. 19. Regarding the connection between religion and the civil state of the <term>Jewish</term> Republic, <term>Masius</term> discourses in the same place, chapter 6</note>.

Moreover, the consensus of political thinkers is on our side, among whom is not the least <term>Septalius</term>, who vigorously calls piety—if it be neither feigned nor simulated—the foundation of Empire and Reason of State <note>*Reason of State*, book 2, chapter 10; and <term>Verulamius</term> <gloss>Francis Bacon</gloss>, Fabr. Fort., page 346</note>. Regarding the saying of the Savior from *Matthew VI, verse 33*, cited above, he exclaims, "O corner-stone of theology and philosophy!", implying the happiness resulting from a diligently sought piety <note><term>Weis</term> on Political Fortune, chapter 2, §§. 30</note>. I add from our own authors the most excellent <term>Bosius</term> in his *Synopsis of Politics*, <term>Lipsius</term>-<term>Bernegger</term> edition, Exercitation 1, §. 4 and following, where he says as follows:

> Although the rudder of prudence properly governs civil life, it does not do so, however, without the use and aid of this magnet, namely virtue; and for that reason it is rightly placed before the former. I consider this virtue to be highly necessary in a prince, and one which he ought by right to embrace. Whether you consider the excellence of virtue itself, as it surpasses all others and is alone in its own power; or its beauty, than which nothing is more lovable and nothing more proper to it than to win for itself the minds of men and to attach them to its own uses; or its own happiness, to whom, if he cultivates it properly, all things will be good; or finally the happiness of his subjects resulting from it, who, being endowed with that goodness and virtue, are for the most part of good and virtuous nature.
</translation>

<summary>This text argues that piety and religion are essential foundations for the stability of a Republic, serving to restrain citizens and rulers alike by invoking divine authority over human laws and social contracts.</summary>
<keywords>Piety, Religion, Reason of State, Political Philosophy, Thomas Hobbes, Samuel von Pufendorf, Numa Pompilius, civil duty, virtue</keywords>

For indeed, while we observe lymphatic vessels exiting from all the glands, we conclude firmly that lymph and other humors are secreted from the blood in them: for nothing is secreted from another thing to which it is intimately admixed, unless by some aid and secretory principle.
