<pb n="22"/>is the vicar of God, and it is piously believed that the assistance he provides is brought about indirectly by God himself, who wills that all things be done decently and in order; and toward the magistrate whom he himself has given, we must show the honor due to him, and in turn, we must expect from him the services and protection appropriate to his office. We follow the example of Paul, to whom, in matters of cruelty, the Roman Emperor was a lion <note>reference to 2 Timothy 4:17, where Paul speaks of being delivered from the lion's mouth</note>, yet in matters of life and political concern, he rightly appeals to him as an ordinary magistrate, Acts 25:10–11.

I also add this: where a divine calling—which is the permission of the supreme magistrate—has joined us with people of a different religion in the same province or city, there we may remain with a clear conscience, provided it is permitted for us to practice our religion duly and safely. For then the pious are comforted by that promise of God, by which He promises that He will be present to everyone in their calling and their ways, Psalm 91:11, 15; this can be seen in Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, who descended into Egypt at His command, and in Daniel and his companions, who lived as captives in Babylon. And to this point I bring what certain jurists and politicians urge so strongly, that different religions can be tolerated. I concede this, but only from us who are subjects, when the superior magistrate has granted it. But whether a less <term>Orthodoxa</term> <gloss>orthodox</gloss> religion should be admitted anew in a free Republic, I have seen no one prove from Scripture.

Finally (to omit other minor objections, which can be easily dissolved from what has already been said), the examples of Abraham in Genesis 14 and 21, and Isaac in Genesis 26, entering into covenants, are vastly different from the present question. First, there are not lacking (among whom is also our Luther) those who deny that those with whom they confederated were impious, profane, or alien to the religion of the Patriarchs, which they attempt to prove by several arguments taken from the text. I assert that this can be proven quite clearly from the cited passages: these were not ecclesiastical and mixed covenants, but only political, concerning civil matters; and this was done not so much by defending as by not offending, and both were contracted by the Patriarchs when they themselves were not particularly in need of their help, or indeed, when Abimelech sought this from them. Therefore, what sort of consequence is this? The Patriarchs were able to contract with their pious neighbors (as Luther decides in his Commentaries on Genesis) concerning civil matters and non-offense, being invited, etc., <pb n="23"/>covenants. Ergo, we too can enter into a covenant of defense with men who are either entirely impious or blasphemous against God and His word, even granting them the free exercise of their religion, inviting them, and enticing them by all means. For who, from the preceding, does not see that the most diverse types of covenants are being confused? That the principles, objects, ends, and circumstances are different here, and therefore the action cannot be the same?

As for the Calvinists (for I believe that is the only thing remaining in this question), whether they dissent from us in certain primary and fundamental articles of faith—namely, most especially in the matter concerning the person of CHRIST, Predestination, Baptism, and the Lord's Supper, etc.—I would not believe anyone is such a stranger to Theology that they would either ignore this or at least doubt it, since it has been sufficiently explained in all Catechetical and Symbolic books, as well as in Compendiums of Theology in the antithesis, and is otherwise evident from many polemical writings published by both sides for about eighty years; for which reason I supersede a more lengthy commentary on a plain matter.

And I proceed to purely Political covenants, which I affirm are lawful even with the profane and <term>heterodoxis</term> <gloss>those of another opinion</gloss>, for the following reasons: I. Because they are just and good, viewed from the principle, object, end, and circumstances; II. Because they are not only permitted by God, but even commanded. Psalm 34:13, Romans 12:18, Hebrews 12:14. Likewise, all the pious are commanded to intercede with God for kings and all those constituted in eminence, so that they may lead a tranquil and quiet life with all piety and veneration, 1 Timothy 2:1–2; and Jeremiah so exhorts the captives in Babylon by letter, chapter 29:7: "Seek the prosperity of that city to which I have deported you," says Jehovah, "and pray for it to Jehovah; for in its prosperity, there shall be prosperity for you." III. Because approved examples of the pious exist, such as Jacob with Laban in Genesis 31:44, David in 2 Samuel 5:11, and Solomon in 1 Kings 5:12, contracting a political covenant with Hiram, king of Tyre. IV. Because God severely punished the violators of them: Saul and his descendants in 2 Samuel 21:1–2, etc. Compare Joshua 9 and 1 Samuel 28:3, 9. Ladislaus, King of Hungary, breaking the political covenant entered into with Amurath at the instigation of the Roman Pontiff (book 3 of Carion's Chronicle). And it is worth noting what the chronicles of the Silesians report, that Amurath, already almost put to flight with his men, after he had looked upon the image of the crucified Christ carried by the Christians</translation>

# COROLLARIES
## Added.

### I.

The ethical definition of a Comet, which Stanislaus Lubieniecius presents and exhibits in his *Theatrum Cometicum* <gloss>Theater of Comets</gloss>, folio 26, is that it is a supernatural, artificial, arbitrary, doctrinal, indicative, and memorial sign, by which God marks his ways to man, announces good things to the good and evils to the bad, and man, being endowed with reason and knowledge of the Divine will, and obedient to its <pb n="14"/>intention and institution, suffers and rejoices to have his duties recalled to his memory; on the contrary, he who is negligent of his duties fears and shudders at the threatened punishments, and in doing so, he sins against *Moral Philosophy*.

## II.

*Comets, although they are not to be feared superstitiously, are not to be contemned profanely, nor ridiculed sarcastically. They hold the middle ground, as the blessed are fond of saying.*

## III.

*That reasoning is inept, and even natural piety hisses at it, by which comets are said to portend nothing evil, because it has often happened that even when such new Stars were never seen, most calamitous times occurred, or that a most happy state of affairs followed such phenomena. This contradicts partly the* Divine *liberty, and partly* Divine *goodness and the promise in Jeremiah 18.*

<pb n="8"/>have held the most impudent identities over and over again. After they had all unanimously and justly condemned that booklet of Johannes Reuchlin—as being injurious to the Church of God beyond what is credible, irreverent toward holy doctors, suitable for the wicked, fit for the worst, scandalous to Christ-believers, and ultimately too indulgent toward Jewish perfidy and tasting of too depraved a heresy—and had judged by their open letters, with the attachment of their seals, that it should be heartily condemned and soon removed from the use of Christians like a mortal poison and a dangerous spreading plague, only then did the Inquisitor, fortified by the determination, judgment, and authority of such great and learned men, set upon the matter itself in the diocese and city of Mainz with the consent and exhortation of the Archbishop, as it was there that those wicked booklets had been first exposed and publicly sold to all. Therefore, the Inquisitor, a venerable doctor, accepted from the most reverend Lord Archbishop of Mainz four judges from the city of Mainz as his colleagues. To these, the most reverend Lord Archbishop of Cologne—a man worthy of all praise and honor—had added, with the consent of the Prince of Mainz, an official of his own court, distinguished and remarkable in all things, truly most learned men, of the utmost integrity, and the best, who by no merit of any mortal, even the most wicked, should be held as suspicious in the slightest. One of these is the Suffragan of Mainz, the second is the magnificent Rector of that same illustrious university, three are doctors of sacred theology, and two others are doctors of canon law. With these excellent and venerable men, the Inquisitor instituted the process of equity and justice there. Later, the citations (not for any effect upon the person of anyone, but generally and specifically against all who might consider it their concern to defend the heretical obscenities of the said booklet) were lawfully executed and judicially (to use the common term) reproduced; the process, happily and holily begun, continued in accordance with his duty to the faith. But indeed, because at the deadline of the citation that doctor—more concerned with his own honor than the integrity of the Catholic faith and fearing he would be cut down by an intolerable scandal—recused the Inquisitor himself through his proctor on the basis of certain frivolous and void (so to speak) motives (though he did not exult in this alone). Therefore, the Inquisitor, sufficiently animated by the cause of justice and distrusting none of the judges, to avoid the unpleasant and—to every good man—abhorrent plurality of recusations, arbitrations, and appeals, and to avoid what they call frivolous and clearly enervated exceptions, referred the entire cognizance of the cause publicly and judicially to his colleagues, and wisely exonerating himself from the office of hearing, judging, and defining, he served merely in the office of accuser. Although the matter stood thus, the proctor of the adverse party nonetheless, in that same process without a hearing, interposed a certain childish and clearly inept appeal from the Inquisitor—who had already been recused as a judge—to the Holy Apostolic See. And since now, to say much in few words, all legal terms had been duly and lawfully observed with the counsel and assistance (as it is said) of legal experts, the pronouncement of the sentence in this case, after mature deliberation, had been suspended by a delay of fifteen days at the request of the lords of the major church, <pb n="9"/>of Mainz, with the consent of the Inquisitor, to the aforementioned judges. And furthermore, second, when these fifteen days had now elapsed and the aforementioned judges, fully resolved and steadfast in the cause of the faith, were sitting to pronounce judgment from the tribunal, the parties having been lawfully cited and called, there arrived certain letters from the most reverend Lord of Mainz, obtained in some manner by a less than good man in favor, alas, of heretical depravity, by which he had commanded his commissaries or mandate-holders that unless the Inquisitor suspended the cause for one whole month beyond the fifteen gracious days already granted, the Archbishop himself would entirely revoke the commission given to the judges. And further, if anything were attempted by them within the aforementioned time, he wished it to be entirely void. *Leeches* <term>Hirudines</term> are conveniently applied to those accustomed to the flow of hemorrhoids, if the malady has received its fuel from that source.

*Fontanels* <term>Fonticuli</term> <gloss>small artificial ulcers or setons for drainage</gloss>, when properly raised, contribute to preservation.

*Frictions* <term>Frictiones</term> for the purpose of revulsion and discussion; *Blistering agents* <term>Vesicantia</term> are sometimes admitted for the sake of evacuation; but *Cautery* <term>Ustio</term> and the excision of veins find scarcely any place in the modern age.

### II.

From the *PHARMACEUTICAL* <term>PHARMACEUTICO</term> supply of various evacuating and altering medicines, both simple and composite, of the ancients and the moderns, is drawn. Since this is treated quite prolixly by practitioners, and their almost countless volumes are filled with prescriptions and formulas, yet since one must not absolutely insist on such things in the cure, but must before all else look to the circumstances and accidents which the present state of the arthritic patient demands: it has pleased [me] to report only a very few from that genus of medicines pertaining here.

As for *Purgatives* <term>Purgantia</term>, they cannot be used safely either in the beginning or in the augmentation of pains (unless they are very mild); since, by the strong agitation of the humors, the paroxysm is further exacerbated. They must therefore be taken before or after the invasion, with *lenitives* and *preparatives* having been administered first.

Let a lenitive be prescribed such as this:

| | | |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Recipe. | Alexandrian Senna leaves, <term>f. s.</term> <gloss>according to art</gloss> | 1 ounce |
| | Indian Rhubarb root | 1/2 ounce |
| | Polypody <term>polypod.</term> | 1/2 ounce |
| | Anise and Fennel seeds, of each | 2 drams |
| | Small raisins | 2 ounces |

Let them be boiled in a closed vessel with 2 pounds of spring water to the consumption of a third part. Let 3 drams be taken then in the morning hours<pb n="19"/> so that the dose may be repeated until the bowels are gently moved. More, if necessity demands, can be compounded from crystals of <note>Alchemical symbol for Tartar</note> <term>Tartar</term>, <term>Mecchoacan</term>, <term>Cassia</term>, <term>solutive syrups</term>, and many others.

*Aloetic* preparations can be used in every gout as a preservative and if the bowels are constipated. Examples are the *aloëphanginae* <gloss>aromatic aloe</gloss> and *Frankfurt* pills.

*Lenitive clysters* are also conveniently admitted, the supply of which is well known.

For the *Preparation* and cutting of humors, it is customary to take the salts of *germander*, *ground pine*, *volatile spirit of amber*, *juniper*, or *restharrow*, mixed with sugar, in a dose of 16 or 18 grains.

*Stronger purgatives* taken from the cabinets of the chemists are *Antimonials* and <note>Alchemical symbol</note> *mercurials*, though properly prepared. The ancients, following the dogmatics, used *Scammony*, *Gratiola*, *Hellebore*, *Turpeth*, etc. The *hermodactyl* pills are praised, which *Paracelsus* also approves. Yet milder ones are generally recommended, e.g.

> <note>Recipe symbol (℞)</note> *magistery of jalap,*
> *crystals of* <note>Alchemical symbol for Tartar</note> *tartar, of each 9 grains.*
> *oil of anise and fennel, of each 2 drops.*
> *Mix, make a powder.*

*Sudorifics* <gloss>sweat-inducing medicines</gloss> are considered very useful in this affliction, provided they are not too hot. Coming into use here are *Magistery of calcined philosopher's Hartshorn and Spirit. Bezoardic tincture. Diaphoretic mercury <note>original: "☿ diaphoret."</note>. Extract of sarsaparilla root.* The decoction of china root and sarsaparilla was once in great use among the Spaniards. Provided, however, that they are not given while the body is impure.

*Diuretics* are likewise beneficial. In which case it is better to employ spirit of juniper and rose hip fruit tempered with parsley water. Medicines prepared from turpentine promise the same. *Spirit of* <note>Alchemical symbol for Salt</note> *Salt. Spirit of* <note>Alchemical symbol for Vitriol</note> *Vitriol. Spirit of* <note>Alchemical symbol (circle with vertical line)</note> *Nitrate impregnated with volatile salt of urine. Tincture of* <note>Alchemical symbol for Tartar</note> *Tartar, etc.*

Regarding the salivatory cure by <term>mercury</term> <note>original: "υδράργυρον"</note>, it is left to each to hold his own opinion.

<pb n="15"/> After a few days, the state of the body deceived the inexperienced, seeming to have changed for the better, partly liberated from the burden of the humors by gentle remedies, and with the fever, which had already been accompanying the illness, decreasing at a slow pace. But just as a tree does not depart from its root, so the disease could not abandon the infection that was rooted more deeply. The rot, fever, sleeplessness, and other <term>symptomata</term> <gloss>symptoms</gloss> took strength and increased more and more, and they began to threaten the danger to his life more clearly, when Lord Dr. Nicolaus Hannekenius was also called in for consultation. By then, nature had already begun to expel the hostile humor through the bowels, as well as the putrid masses of blood, the unfortunate offspring of a liver already rotting and consumed. Everything that such a great disease and such great symptoms required was attempted. But nature did not cease from this work of excretion before the strength was completely cast down, the frame of the body was dissolved along with the <term>parenchyma</term> <gloss>functional tissue</gloss> of the liver, and liquefied, and thus the source of a better, eternal life might take up this diseased, frail life. So far the words of the Physician.

I have thus perceived the origin, progress, vigor, and deeds of this most distinguished man, described with simple effort <note>original: "rudi minerva," a classical idiom meaning a humble or unpolished attempt</note> without the splendor of words. It is finally necessary for me to approach the sad epilogue of his life itself, alas, of which I must speak very briefly, since no one could inform me further about the manner of his blessed passing, his final words, and other things that usually occur around this turning point and end of life. However, since the most praiseworthy man lived his life never otherwise than piously and religiously toward God, justly toward his neighbor, and temperately toward himself, we neither ought to nor can doubt that he died well and blessedly. Which eternal blessedness <pb n="16"/> we congratulate with all our hearts to his blessed spirit, wishing for ourselves a similar passing, with a prayer and a desirable sigh: if only he were living, safe and joyful, and could perform this sad duty for many others, and especially for me, who is far more ripe for death, which I, by a perverse order of nature, perform for him. But as it pleased the Lord, so it is done. May His holy name be blessed in both favorable and adverse things.

Since it has been decided to commit the remains of his blessed soul to their resting place <note>original: "Conditorio," literally a storehouse or tomb</note> tomorrow, the 12th of September, the Magnificent Lords Consuls, the most noble and most learned Lord Syndic, the most noble, most learned, and also most experienced Lords Doctors, also the Reverend and most distinguished Lords Pastors and Ecclesiasts, as well as the most distinguished and most prudent Lords Senators and Secretaries, and the other no less honest citizens of this city, and patrons of the School, are requested and invited, with the observance, reverence, and diligence that is proper, to attend the funeral procession and obsequies in great numbers.

And after a night, if any other in my life, was sadder and completely sleepless, at the first light of the next day I decided that something must be attempted immediately. I gave my effort there and then with all my strength, so that this University at least might intercede, since otherwise it was not possible, by a Public Protestation, an Obtestation, and a Supplication; both before the Orders <note>original: "Ordines"</note> (as they were called) of the Republic, and before the Great Military Council <note>original: "Concilium Militare"</note> which alone held dominion. I wrote out what I intended in formal words; I offered myself, undeterred by all things, as a prepared Messenger and <pb n="10"/> Actor. This, if it might not stop the unspeakable and execrable undertaking, would certainly testify to the present and future age that this University abhorred such great impiety and brutality. This we owed to God, and to the religion we profess, to the best King, to the Fatherland, and finally to ourselves. For these things, *Listeners*, I gave all the diligent effort (as I said) that I could; but oh grief! oh shame! it was empty effort: *I sing to the deaf*. What times were among us then must remain silent. And so that summary of all our evils proceeded, the detestable and uninterrupted investigation—before Traitors regarding Treason, before Tyrants regarding Tyranny, before Murderers and Parricides regarding Murder—of the cause of the most innocent and most pious Prince. An investigation, *Listeners*? Oh, most wickedly shameless investigators!

business. This indeed cannot be called a conversation of a man, nor one directed toward a man. And yet there are not lacking, which is not a little to be wondered at, some among the moderns who, seduced by those vain arguments of the ancients, shamelessly teach that only utility and an abundance of those things which fortune provides ought to be cared for in the state, and that those who have been set apart for the hope of managing the republic and great duties need not have any regard for what is honest and lawful. For who is unaware of the impious voice of Machiavelli in chapter XV of <italic>The Prince</italic>, where he thinks it is *necessary for the safety of the Prince that he not be good*, and by this very thing, he not only recommends evil arts to him who governs regions, but even persuades him that they are most necessary for establishing a Principality and preserving an empire? We omit other Doctors who even today attempt to defend the same most pestilential error to the immense damage of states. But this foul opinion has long since been refuted and condemned by ancient writers of great name, whose authority is not to be despised, by suitable arguments. For it could not have been obscure to those most grave men that the honest is by no means to be separated from the useful in a state, nor should anything be thought honest that is not useful, or useful that is not honest and in agreement with virtue; since these two are connected by a certain natural and most tight bond. However, it easily appears what utility was understood by them; that, namely, which applies right reason <term>ratio recta</term> <gloss>correct logic/straight judgment</gloss> to deliberation, by which neither the principles nor the causes of things are neglected, and from which the things that are to follow are accurately weighed and compared with present ones. And they judged this alone to be worthy of the name of utility. For utility ceases to be, or is even the greatest ruin, in which a man <pb n="18"/> follows the corrupted judgment of his own passions, and chooses a transient good that indeed seems joyful and salutary, but, if weighed in an equal scale, is painted over, slippery, and inconstant, and is the source and origin of many inconveniences.

Many think that great fruits are gathered when faith is not kept, when injury is brought upon the weak, when no treaties are observed, when power and wealth are sought through unjust arts, and when other things are done which laws and rights desire to be carefully avoided by all kinds of men. But since it is necessary that those who do these things expect the same from others, who seek their own advantages from whatever matter, there can be so little fruit or joy for a wise person from actions of this kind, separated from the honest, that on the contrary, with the order of things confused, they bring the greatest detriment and most serious calamity upon men. Therefore, that which is most profitable in a republic must be regarded in such a way that it is joined with honest and praiseworthy things, and nothing is done or thought that seems to be absent from virtue and the probity of morals. In order that this may be obtained all the more easily, it will be necessary to observe diligently those things by which the honesty of morals and the pursuit of virtue are helped and promoted. Since not a few of these have been brought forth by those who, anxious about the most salutary precepts, have weighed such a great matter well in their own minds, we judge, with the opinions of others preserved, that these three are the principal ones: religion, discipline, and good laws. But it is superfluous to speak of these at greater length now; since it will be the case that they will be explained more broadly and abundantly by some young men who are to speak publicly tomorrow. We add only a little concerning religion, and we note briefly what the Fathers and Doctors of the church have felt about it, when related to virtues and honest morals.
</translation>

The author identifies religion, discipline, and good laws as the essential pillars for cultivating such morality in the citizenry.</summary>
<keywords>Political science, Machiavelli, Natural Law, Virtue, Utility, Public Policy, Ethics, Religion, Civic Duty</keywords>

In order that this may be obtained all the more easily, it will be necessary to observe diligently those things by which the honesty of morals and the pursuit of virtue are helped and promoted. Since not a few of these have been brought forth by those who, anxious about the most salutary precepts, have weighed such a great matter well in their own minds, we judge, with the opinions of others preserved, that these three are the principal ones: religion, discipline, and good laws. But it is superfluous to speak of these at greater length now; since it will be the case that they will be explained more broadly and abundantly by some young men who are to speak publicly tomorrow. We add only a little concerning religion, and we note briefly what the Fathers and Doctors of the church have felt about it, when related to virtues and honest morals.

# LATER DECLAMATION.

<pb n="5"/>There appeared in this chair in recent days, O auditors and others, one who would pursue the infamous pursuit of foreign travel in an oration. You supported the speaker with goodwill and generous interest, I believe, because in your judgment he had occupied a subject not unworthy of this present place; nor was it wearisome to listen to your illustrious assembly, or the rest of the gathering gathered round. In this favor of minds and tongues, after others, as was fitting, when I too had prepared myself to be free in mind and ears for the speaker: what he accomplished in others, I may conjecture; for myself, I can affirm clearly that my mind was so led that I began to abhor these customs and detest the madness of such studies. Therefore, I did not seem to myself to have wasted the effort, especially in a subject in which one might rightly test his talent, and one which by no means labored under a sterile scarcity. For when the orator had determined to expose the disgrace of this pursuit according to the plan of his purpose, it was understood that the subject was represented with such an abundance that in explaining it, one’s talent would be suited to be restrained rather than wearied by anxious <pb n="6"/> meditation. If anyone wished to append other things of that kind that were omitted, he would undoubtedly fill a new oration. Truly, I will not dissemble that the desire then entered my mind to experiment with what could be brought forward by me in the same genre. But the palm is placed in the midst for all; let whoever pleases make the attempt. I, having debated the matter more diligently with myself, since I chose to be a reserve in this arena, thought it better, rather than being equipped from the same arsenal, to take up new weapons with which I might fight against that most vain pursuit; and I determined to show that, just as it is judged base and infamous, so it must also be held harmful to both public and private interests. In which I am persuaded that the logic of my plan has not escaped me much. For, as for contributing something of talent to the former, I saw that the main points had already been vanquished; I understood that if this latter type of argument were omitted, the censure would be imperfect. Add that the minds of men are so constituted that they are little moved by the mere proposal of a thing's baseness: if you demonstrate that something is joined with destruction, you will draw them, terrified, wherever you wish, even if unwilling. Therefore, let this pursuit of foreign travel be base, because it is for the ungrateful, it is servile, insane, and finally inept; I will strive to effect this, so that it may appear that it is rightly called a plague to private property, and thence a ruin to the public.</translation>

<summary>This text introduces a speaker's intention to critique the habit of foreign travel, arguing that while previous orators have addressed its moral disgrace, it is necessary to further demonstrate its practical harm to both private and public affairs.</summary>
<keywords>Declamation, foreign travel, moral critique, public interest, private property, oratory.</keywords>

<pb n="11"/> in Gruter, page 628, in which the <term>Quaestor Urbanus</term> <gloss>city treasurer</gloss>, who holds the treasury province, is ordered to pay the salary to the scribes. But observe the words:

> THE URBAN QUAESTOR WHO HOLDS THE TREASURY PROVINCE
> SHALL PAY THAT SALARY.
> AND THE QUAESTOR WHO SHALL HOLD THE TREASURY PRO-
> VINCE
> SHALL PAY THAT MONEY TO THAT SCRIBE, TO THE SCRIBES,
> OR TO HIS HEIR.
> AND IT SHALL BE PERMITTED FOR HIM TO DO THIS WITHOUT
> ANY WRONGDOING ON HIS PART,
> PROVIDED IT IS DONE WITHOUT
> EVIL EMBEZZLEMENT. AND IT SHALL BE PERMITTED FOR THOSE
> MEN TO RECEIVE THAT MONEY.

However, since these scribes were often compelled to go into the provinces with their patrons (for in the retinue of the governors going into the provinces, there were all those assistants, ministers, and companions whom the usage and rationale of the province, as well as the dignity of the magistrates and the Republic itself, demanded; for example, legates, military tribunes, centurions, prefects, <term>decuriones</term> <gloss>decurions</gloss>, and others, the assistants and ministers of military works and accounts; furthermore, scribes, <term>accensi</term> <gloss>attendants</gloss>, heralds, lictors, interpreters, messengers, <term>aruspices</term> <gloss>diviners</gloss>, chamberlains, physicians, and <term>contubernales</term> <gloss>companions/messmates</gloss>, and the rest), these <term>decuriae</term> <gloss>divisions</gloss> were often sold by the scribes and bought by others. Regarding this matter, Reinefius speaks again in the cited letter. Cicero mentions such a purchase in his speech against Varus: *Recall me to those scribes, if you please, he says; do not gather these men who, having collected money from the wealth of spendthrifts and from the gratuities of actors, when they have bought a <term>decuria</term> <gloss>division</gloss>, say they have come from the first rank of the rejected to the second rank of the citizenry. I will have those scribes as judges of this crime with you, who take it ill that these men are scribes. Although, when we see many in that order who are unsuitable, which order is intended for industry and dignity, shall we wonder that some shameful men are in it, to which anyone is permitted to arrive for a price?* Sigonius indicates that the power of electing scribes into the <term>decuriae</term> <gloss>divisions</gloss> lay primarily with the praetors, quaestors, and aediles, and indeed from the <pb n="12"/> Cluentiana of Cicero, where these things occur: *Lately, when I had defended a modest man, the aedilician scribe Decimus Matrinius, before the praetors Marcus Junius and Quintus Publicius, and the curule aediles Marcus Plaetorius and Caius Flaminius, I persuaded them to elect him as a sworn scribe, whom those same censors had left in the treasury.* Livy has things akin to this. In the forty-fifth book, the praetor urbanus Quintus Petillius took those books from the scribe Lucius Petillius. And there was a familiar usage, because the quaestor Quintus Petillius had elected him as a scribe into the <term>decuria</term> <gloss>division</gloss>.

->§. XI.<-

The duties of the public scribes were primarily these: (1) To serve the magistrates, which, besides those things we have already cited, is also confirmed by a passage of Plutarch in his *Life of Cato*, which, when translated into the Latin language, sounds as follows: *Cato, when he had entered the quaestorship, restrained the ministers and scribes who, handling public records and laws, having found young men as the magistrates whom they were serving, because those men were dependent on their masters due to lack of knowledge, did not yield their power, but were themselves the magistrates. Cato, however, treated them in the place of servants, as they were, when he accused some of fraud and others of ignorance.* (2) To read publicly to the people everything that the magistrate wished to be published from a document, and to submit it to the herald to be proclaimed, concerning which Philip Beroaldus writes in the ninth book of Apuleius. (3) They countersigned, collected, and entered into records those things which were published from the proceedings, whence Isidore, in the cited passage, writes that they were called <term>Tabelliones</term> <gloss>notaries/scribes</gloss> because they wrote those things which were published in the proceedings. (4) The records of the magistrates were committed to them, which Cicero testifies in the cited passage: *It is truly an honorable order, because the public records and the records of the magistrates are committed to the faith of these men.* But what is understood here by "records of the magistrates," Barthius explains: *What Cicero says in these words, that the records of the magistrates were committed to the scribes, teaches which instruments, contracts, agreements, pacts, or last wills, or other such things that were to be credited to the public faith, had been deposited with the scribes.* (5) To have the laws somewhat in their hands and from them to suggest the law to the magistrates, which can be gathered from the passage of Cicero in the third book *De Legibus*: *I observe everyone in magistracies by ignorance*</translation>

<summary>This text details the selection process, professional status, and specific duties of Roman public scribes, including their role in managing treasury records, provincial administration, and the judicial functions of magistrates.</summary>
<keywords>Roman scribes, public administration, quaestor, decuriae, magistrates, public records, Cicero, legal history</keywords>

### §. II.

Festus provided this Apostle, standing before the tribunal of Caesar at Caesarea, with the opportunity to appeal to Caesar, as has already been stated in *Section I, §. VI, page 7*. For he, desiring to curry favor with the Jewish accusers, had asked in *verse 9 of Chapter XXV*, whether Paul wished to be judged at Jerusalem. But the Apostle, when he perceived the intention of this question, quite opportunely and prudently *appealed to Caesar*: for, just as a wise man, to speak with Gregory of Nazianzus, *avoids all heavy and dangerous things, just as a shipmaster avoids storms*, so too Paul, taught by experience that he would never and nowhere be safe in Judea, cautiously and diligently avoids these snares of Jewish deceit, especially since he dreaded (1) **THE JEWS**, of whom very many—as is sufficiently evident from the *Evangelical and Apostolic History*—were most bitter enemies of the Christian doctrine, which he, inflamed by pious emulation and divine zeal, was propagating, and (2) **THE CITY OF JERUSALEM**, where the prophets were slaughtered and the apostles were stoned; *Matthew XXIII, v. 37, compared with Acts VII, v. 52*, indeed, where he had already previously been received with dire lashes by the Jews striving to kill him, *Acts XXI, v. 31, 32*, and (3) **THE JOURNEY**, on account of the ambushes of slaughter intended to be set for him by assassins on the road. *Acts XXV, v. 3, compared with Acts XXIII, v. 12-15.*

### §. III.

Regarding the *crimes* of which the Jews were laboring to accuse Paul gravely before Festus, they are generally called *πολλά καὶ βαρέα αἰτιάματα* <gloss>many and heavy accusations</gloss> in *Acts XXV, v. 7*. But what those *accusations* were, and how great they were specifically, the *Pauline Apology* in the following verse, 8, indicates not obscurely, since <pb n="15"/> from it, it is gathered that there were three main heads of accusation: *namely, that Paul had sinned against the law and the temple of the Jews, and against Caesar. Confer also the assertion of Festus, Acts XXV, v. 18, 19.* Paul, however, well aware of his own innocence and not paling from any guilt of those crimes, vigorously denied *that anything had been sinned by him, either against the law and temple of the Jews, or against the majesty of Caesar*; and rightly so, since, as is read in the said Chapter, v. 7, *the accusers could not prove their charges brought against Paul.*

### §. IV.

Wherefore Paul, compelled by such necessity, appealed to Caesar, which was lawful for him (1) as a MAN, (2) as a ROMAN CITIZEN, (3) as a CHRISTIAN, and (4) as an APOSTLE. It was lawful, I say, for Paul, as a MAN, through the benefit of *Appeal* to avert the death intended for him by the Jews: *for the defense and preservation of oneself*, to which MEN are led by a certain natural instinct and by a most sharp desire, as it were, is lawful, just as those who have handed down the sounder precepts of the *Law of Nature* regarding the duties of a MAN toward himself assert. And surely, one must be the less doubtful about this assertion, the more certainly it is evident that our supreme and provident Deity wills that the HUMAN RACE be preserved for its end, and that for this cause lawful remedies, conducive to preserving the same, be applied in time, lest anyone rashly neglect the protection of his own body or make light of the preservation of his own life, but rather protect and defend the same in every way. Therefore, Paul not only here before Festus, through the benefit of the *Appeal*, sought to secure his life
</translation>

<pb n="11"/> Kirchmann (Book 1, Chapter IV, *On Roman Funerals*), that distinction arose from the games held in honor of the deceased, which were called funeral games, as attested by Rosinus (Book V, *Roman Antiquities*, Chapter XXXIX). Now, the first kind is the *Funus Indictivum* <gloss>Indictive Funeral</gloss>; it is so named, according to Festus, because the people were called to it by a herald (Rosinus, the aforementioned location). It is named from the *indicendo* <gloss>proclaiming</gloss>, a term the ancients used in this sense (Kirchmann, ibid.). Suetonius in *Caesar*: *The funeral having been proclaimed, a pyre was built in the Campus Martius.* Cicero in his *Orations, For His Own House to the Pontiffs* and *On the Consular Provinces*. The illustrious Scaliger long ago noted the formal words of this proclamation, drawn from the final scene of Act V of Terence's *Phormio* and Book IV of Varro’s *On the Latin Language*. Indictive funerals, moreover, were most elaborate, and besides other sumptuous equipment, were also celebrated with games (Cicero, Book II, *On the Latin Language*; Becmann, *On Origins*, p. 706; Rosinus and Kirchmann, in the cited places; Scaliger, Book I, *Ausonian Lectures*, Chapter XXVIII), also employing circus riders (Festus Pompeius, Book XVII; Dempster on Rosinus, *Antiquities*, Book V, Chapter XXIV). The Public funeral can be referred to here, which was sometimes the same as the Indictive, as in Apuleius (Book 11, *Metamorphoses*), and sometimes only a part of it, as when a cessation of business was proclaimed, or public mourning, or expenses were made from the public treasury (Kirchmann, ibid.). This honor was granted to Syphax, King of Numidia (Valerius Maximus, Book V, Chapter 1; Suetonius in *Vitellius*, Chapter III); to Sphaerus, Augustus’s freedman and tutor (Dio, Book XLVIII); and to Piso, Urban Prefect (the same, Dio, Book LXIV). Illustrious women were not without a share of this (Idem, Book XLVII; Xiphilinus in *Tiberius*). There were furthermore various kinds of Public Funerals according to the diversity of honors managed by the deceased, such as Praetorian, Consular, Censorial, and Triumphal, as Polybius indicates (Book 6, *Histories*), where, however, Lipsius noted that the triumphal was confused with the censorial under the emperors. The most worthy was the Censorial, by which princes were carried out, such as Claudius (Tacitus, Book XII). Whence Spartianus in *Aelius Verus* calls it an Imperial funeral; in *Opilius Macrinus*, a Royal one. For the Censorship was the most honored among the magistracies (Plutarch in *Cato the Elder*).

## *Other Silent, or "Simpludearian" Funerals. Thesis VII.*

This is the second kind: called by another name the Common funeral in Capitolinus in *Marcus Antoninus the Philosopher*, also the Public funeral (Ausonius, *Parentalia*), also the Plebeian funeral (Propertius, Book II, Elegy XIV), and the *translatitium* <gloss>transferred/simple</gloss> funeral (Suetonius, *Nero*, Chapter XXXIII, concerning the death of Britannicus). These funerals were performed without pomp, without a master of ceremonies, <pb n="12"/> a herald, and a proclamation. Seneca, Book 1, *On Tranquility*, Chapter 1; Ovid, Book 1, *Fasti*, Elegy iii; indeed, with no solemnities other than games. Dempster in *Paralipomena* to Book V, Chapter XXIV of Rosinus’s *Roman Antiquities*; Scaliger on Festus, and Book 1, *Ausonian Lectures*, Chapter XXIII. Hence it is called *Simpludearium*, as if *Simpliludiarium*, because simple *ludii* <gloss>players/performers</gloss> were used, that is, dancers or tumblers, or servants whom Festus calls *corbitores* <gloss>basket-carriers</gloss> (Rosinus, Chapter XXXIX, Book 1, *Roman Antiquities*; Becmann, *On Origins*, page 706). To these funerals also belong the *Acerba* <gloss>untimely funerals</gloss>, that is, those of persons who died before the day of their coming-of-age and before the assumption of the manly toga (Kirchmann, Book 1, Chapter IV, *On Roman Funerals*). The most famous Philippus Camerarius, son of the great Joachim, observed what *Larvata* <gloss>masked/ghostly</gloss> funerals are in Book 1 of his *Historical Meditations*, Chapter XCVI. Polybius describes Imaginary Funerals in the book that is now the sixth. Capitolinus in *Pertinax*.

->*Thus in the division: it follows in the enumeration of the rites.*<-

### Th. VIII.

## **Those which precede the funeral, and concern the dying people themselves.**

When every hope of life seemed to have failed in the sick person, friends and the nearest in blood were accustomed to kiss the dying person and to embrace his body (Seneca, *On the Shortness of Life*). *He departed in their embrace and kisses* (Ausonius, *Parentalia*, poem 23).

> That hand died between the kisses of the mother and the father.
> And the rest.

Thus, the author Suetonius in his life of Augustus Caesar (Chapter XC) says that he died in the kisses of Livia. Kirchmann has the causes of this custom in Chapter V of Book 1, *On Roman Funerals*. Next, if the sick person was dying at home, when he had begun to breathe his last, those who were closest would catch his spirit with their mouths and wished to transfer it into themselves: a thing which the ancients, in a womanly fashion, thought could be done (Cicero in the *Verrines* V; Virgil, Book IV of the *Aeneid*).

> — — — If any last breath lingers above,
> I shall catch it with my mouth — — —

For the ancients believed that the soul, about to depart from the body, exited through the mouth as if through some gate (Seneca, *Epistle* XXX, and in *Hercules Furens*, lines 1310). Furthermore, it was also customary for rings to be drawn off the dying.
</translation>

<summary>This text discusses the various types of Roman funeral rites, distinguishing between the public "indictive" funerals, which were proclaimed by a herald and included games, and the "silent" or "simpludearian" funerals, which lacked elaborate ceremony. It also details the traditional rituals performed at the moment of death, such as kissing the dying, catching their last breath, and removing rings.</summary>
<keywords>Funus Indictivum, Funus Publicum, Funus Simpludearium, Roman funeral rites, Kirchmann, Rosinus, death rituals, mourning customs</keywords>

This is the second kind: called by another name the Common funeral in Capitolinus in *Marcus Antoninus the Philosopher*, also the Public funeral (Ausonius, *Parentalia*), also the Plebeian funeral (Propertius, Book II, Elegy XIV), and the *translatitium* <gloss>transferred/simple</gloss> funeral (Suetonius, *Nero*, Chapter XXXIII, concerning the death of Britannicus). These funerals were performed without pomp, without a master of ceremonies,
pages.12:
a herald, and a proclamation. Seneca, Book 1, *On Tranquility*, Chapter 1; Ovid, Book 1, *Fasti*, Elegy iii; indeed, with no solemnities other than games. Dempster in *Paralipomena* to Book V, Chapter XXIV of Rosinus’s *Roman Antiquities*; Scaliger on Festus, and Book 1, *Ausonian Lectures*, Chapter XXIII. Hence it is called *Simpludearium*, as if *Simpliludiarium*, because simple *ludii* <gloss>players/performers</gloss> were used, that is, dancers or tumblers, or servants whom Festus calls *corbitores* <gloss>basket-carriers</gloss> (Rosinus, Chapter XXXIX, Book 1, *Roman Antiquities*; Becmann, *On Origins*, page 706). To these funerals also belong the *Acerba* <gloss>untimely funerals</gloss>, that is, those of persons who died before the day of their coming-of-age and before the assumption of the manly toga (Kirchmann, Book 1, Chapter IV, *On Roman Funerals*). The most famous Philippus Camerarius, son of the great Joachim, observed what *Larvata* <gloss>masked/ghostly</gloss> funerals are in Book 1 of his *Historical Meditations*, Chapter XCVI. Polybius describes Imaginary Funerals in the book that is now the sixth. Capitolinus in *Pertinax*.

->*Thus in the division: it follows in the enumeration of the rites.*<-

### Th. VIII.

## **Those which precede the funeral, and concern the dying people themselves.**

When every hope of life seemed to have failed in the sick person, friends and the nearest in blood were accustomed to kiss the dying person and to embrace his body (Seneca, *On the Shortness of Life*). *He departed in their embrace and kisses* (Ausonius, *Parentalia*, poem 23).

> That hand died between the kisses of the mother and the father.
> And the rest.

Thus, the author Suetonius in his life of Augustus Caesar (Chapter XC) says that he died in the kisses of Livia. Kirchmann has the causes of this custom in Chapter V of Book 1, *On Roman Funerals*. Next, if the sick person was dying at home, when he had begun to breathe his last, those who were closest would catch his spirit with their mouths and wished to transfer it into themselves: a thing which the ancients, in a womanly fashion, thought could be done (Cicero in the *Verrines* V; Virgil, Book IV of the *Aeneid*).

> — — — If any last breath lingers above,
> I shall catch it with my mouth — — —

For the ancients believed that the soul, about to depart from the body, exited through the mouth as if through some gate (Seneca, *Epistle* XXX, and in *Hercules Furens*, lines 1310). Furthermore, it was also customary for rings to be drawn off the dying.

<margin>How did Pippin break through those [barriers]?</margin>
The oath of faith had been sworn, by which Pippin and the others owed obedience to Childeric. But Pippin easily broke through this with his skill, since the people's veneration for their kings was turning into contempt through their sloth and Pippin's arts, and he hoped that the oath could be severed by the authority of the Roman Pontiff, whom he had already obligated with great services. He decided to weave the web, therefore, in the manner explained by Pierre Matthieu in his <term>Genealogia Regum Francorum</term> <gloss>Genealogy of the Kings of the Franks</gloss> (f. 50), by Buffier, and others. After he had bound many through benefits, more through promises, and all through his courtesy, had aroused old friends with the hope of new things, and had inflamed new ones with the emulation of the old, the conversation started here and there through his machinations by his intimates. It emanated first to the courtiers, then to the common people, that the sloth of so many kings was now a disgrace to the glory of the Franks, that those who were equal to governing neither themselves nor others should be cast aside, and that another should be chosen whose virtue would uphold the kingdom; and he need not be sought from afar, for there was at hand Prince Pippin, a dwarf in body but a giant in spirit.

<margin>Pippin proclaims a royal assembly.</margin>
Pippin, therefore, when he noticed that such talk was welcomed by the common people and received by friendly ears, deeming the business ripe, proclaimed a public assembly of the kingdom, having summoned the prelates and the leading men of the nobility whom he had found to be most devoted to him:

<margin>What was decreed there?</margin>
in which gathering, having tested their spirits, he proposed the matter and simultaneously prevailed, and it was agreed by all to send to the Pontiff to seek a release from their oath.

<margin>Legates are sent to Rome to Pope Zachary.</margin>
III. Therefore, there were sent to Zachary, who then presided over the Roman See, Burchard, Bishop of Würzburg (others name Richard of Bourges), and Fulrad, the chaplain—as they call him—of Pippin, that is to say, the official in charge of the sacred treasury, <pb n="12"/><note>Two floral ornaments are positioned at the top of the page.</note>
<note>A horizontal divider rule with decorative scrollwork terminals.</note>
whose request the Pontiff readily granted.

<margin>What they accomplished there: Why the Pope assented to Pippin's wishes. King Pippin is anointed. Childeric is thrust into a monastery with his wife. Whence the Bishops of Würzburg have the title of Duke of Franconia.</margin>
For the Pope, fearing the Greek Emperors from whom he had defected and who were plotting a new empire for themselves as avengers of Roman perfidy, and at the same time wishing to obligate to the Roman domain Aistulf, King of the Lombards, who was threatening it just as the empire of the Greeks did, decided it would please him to use this new example of perfidy by Pippin, in whom he would have a firm defense against the Greeks and the Lombards. Following this, the task of anointing Pippin as King—whom the Franks themselves had already chosen by their own votes—was entrusted by Zachary to Boniface, the Bishop of Mainz, who had been the first to introduce the Roman rites of the sacred offices and the folly of dogma into Germany, which was already imbued with better things in some places. Therefore, when the legates returned to France, the anointing of Pippin was performed at Soissons by Boniface, and soon Pippin was called King by all, and according to the custom of the people, he was carried on a shield and placed upon the throne. Finally, to close the scene, he completed the act of Childeric's deposition. He was led from the country villa where he was living to a monastery at Regensburg (they also intended his wife Gisela for a monastery), his hair was shorn, and having laid aside his robes, he assumed the habit of a monk, with no heavier loss than that of his hair, since he was not despoiled of the kingdom which he had not possessed, and perhaps losing his wife was a gain. Meanwhile, Burchard, as a reward for his successful legation, was created Duke of Franconia by Pippin, as Freher notes in his notes to Bebenburg on page 35, and he left this title to his successors.

### IV.

But whether this anointing of Pippin as King is the first among the kings of the Franks, I see it is doubted, since they claim that Remigius used chrism on Clovis.</translation>

<summary>This passage describes how Pippin the Short orchestrated a political campaign to displace the last Merovingian king, Childeric III, by questioning the royal family's competence and securing Papal support. It details the diplomatic mission to Pope Zachary, Pippin's subsequent anointing by Saint Boniface, and the forced tonsuring and monastic confinement of Childeric.</summary>
<keywords>Pippin the Short, Childeric III, Pope Zachary, Boniface of Mainz, Merovingian dynasty, Carolingian succession, political legitimacy, deposition, anointing of kings</keywords>

<pb n="21"/>
<header>ORATION ON THE ECHINADES.</header>

ANTONIO PASCALIGO: Joannes Baptista Benedictus, a Cypriot; Jacobus Metius, from the Chersonese; Antonius Eudaemonicus, from Cydonia; Jacobus Trissinus, from Vicenza; Hieronymus Bysantius, from Ascruia; and Andreas Calergus, from Rethymno, were also eager for this praise and desirous of glory. You ought to consider that the memory of all these men will never perish. For as long as the Christian and Venetian name endures, which we can promise will be eternal, as long as literature remains, and as long as any place is left anywhere for virtue, the most grateful discourse of men will never be silent about them. For <note>original: "vitam earum, qui Patriam defendendo, Christianamque Religionem vindicando obierunt, non modo alit posteritas, sed etiam, ut a sapientissimis Viris accepimus, ipsa aeternitas semper intuetur."</note> "posterity not only nourishes the life of those who died defending their Fatherland and vindicating the Christian Religion, but also, as we have learned from the wisest men, eternity itself always contemplates it." Harmodius and Aristogiton still flourish today in the mouths and minds of all, as do the Horatii, the Decii, and many others, because <note>original: "de vita exire pro Patria gloriosum judicarint."</note> "they judged it glorious to depart from life for the sake of the Fatherland." However, we trust that these soldiers of yours, who have never been praised enough, and who by their own blood have produced such glory and such a victory for the Christian name, have already obtained the reward of their virtues from GOD; and we see that today the honors owed to them are being paid by you and by the entire Christian REPUBLIC. This happens to them even more splendidly than it did to the Romans or the *Athenians*, because those peoples, compelled by their laws, adorned with praises those who had died fighting for their country; but you, whatever you do, attribute it freely and spontaneously to their virtue, and you fulfill the duty of most grateful citizens. And rightly so. For these excellent men are worthy of even further unique honors to be sought by the Senate. These, in the present <pb n="22"/> <header>ON THE VICTORY OF THE CHRISTIANS</header>

I seem to see already from the highest watchtower of heaven, I seem to perceive your grateful spirits, and therefore I rejoice, because they understand that, through the embellishment of words, perennial praise is accustomed to reach those who have performed illustrious deeds among the *Audience*. For they themselves indicated that they were more studious of this glory than of life, when they died for their Fatherland, more desirous of this light than of hostile punishment. And since they knew that *this life is a pilgrimage*, they publicly expended their bodies, which they knew to be perishable, so that privately they might obtain a praise that fears no fates of death. Therefore, parents ought to use this consolation, that since they knew <note>original: "se natos genuisse, non inmortalteis, sed quos bonos atque illustreis fore optabant"</note> "that they had given birth not to immortals, but to those whom they hoped would be good and illustrious," they have now fully obtained both, since they have produced such guards of the **REPUBLIC**. *Children*, because they will be provided with domestic examples of virtue. *Spouses*, because they are deprived of husbands whom they should praise rather than mourn. Finally, all people, because they understand that those who met death have obtained immortality in place of the mortal condition of life, since it must be most firmly believed that the defenders of the *Fatherland and of Christian Piety*, migrating from here to the seat of the celestial minds from which we have our imparted souls, have flown away, where they enjoy eternal time and perpetual happiness. Unwillingly, I pass over the names of other excellent men who were slain in the line of battle, so that if I were able to do anything, I would save them from oblivion. But since your *Commanders* have not yet written down the matter one by one as it happened, and you have ordered me to deliver this oration almost extemporaneously, I am forced to pass over them in silence for now. But you, **Most Serene PRINCE**, **Most Illustrious LEGATES AND FATHERS**
</translation>

<summary>This passage commemorates the soldiers and leaders who died at the Battle of Lepanto, framing their sacrifice as a path to eternal glory and divine reward for their service to the Venetian Republic and the Christian faith.</summary>
<keywords>Battle of Lepanto, Christian virtue, martyrdom, Venetian Republic, immortality of fame, sacrificial death for the Fatherland</keywords>

<translation>
<pb n="9"/>XXIII. There is no doubt that excommunicated persons and even heretics possess this right of sending Legates. For excommunication pertains to ecclesiastical discipline, whereas an embassy pertains to civil and secular affairs. Furthermore, a mission, which exists by the law of nations, looks to and considers men according to the law of nations, in that they are merely men among us, not by the law and custom of any region or religion. And the rights of peace are not abolished by diversity of religion; much less are the mutual dealings of an embassy abolished by a contradiction of faith: says <term>Kirchnerus</term> <note>original: "Kirchnerus"</note> in book 1, chapter 3, whose words it pleased me to insert here.

XXIV. Although there are some who ascribe the right of embassies to the free nobles and Hanseatic cities dwelling in France, Swabia, and the Rhine tract, nevertheless, since they are not estates of the Empire, are not found in the register of the Empire, and are not summoned to the diets, we deny that they possess that right, along with <term>Kirchnerus</term> in book 1, chapter 3, number 56, and <term>Heiden</term> <note>original: "Heiden"</note> on Embassies. For the free cities contained within the Hanseatic league cannot communicate or impart their own right to others, and even to certain foreign cities.

XXV. We also deny the right of sending Legates to Queens, if they are married and the rule resides with the husband: for then they send only messengers, not Legates, since according to the law "Woman" 2 of the Pandects on Rules of Law, they are barred from the entire administration of public offices: Except, however, those who hold supreme power and exercise the highest rule, whether they be unmarried, as was Elizabeth of England, and is still today Christina, Queen of Sweden, or if they are indeed joined in marriage, but have retained the rights of Majesty and Empire for themselves and have not communicated them to their husband, examples of which we have in Isabella of Castile, Mary, Queen of Hungary, and Mary of England. <term>Kirchnerus</term>, book 1, chapter 3; <term>Bodinus</term> <note>original: "Bodinus"</note>, book 6 of the Republic, chapter 5.

XXVI. Pontiffs, Bishops, Clerics, and in those churches that profess the Apostolic doctrine, Superintendents, and the Bishops of Denmark, Sweden, and England, in so far as they are occupied with ecclesiastical affairs and do not possess secular rule, <pb n="10"/>do not possess the right of sending Legates: Because, however, they are secular Princes and Dukes, and exercise political rule, we cannot deny that the same right belongs to them as to other Princes. Meanwhile, this right cannot be ascribed to academics under any title, since they are in the position of subjects. <term>Kirchnerus</term>.

XXVII. Furthermore, we bar from this right of sending Legates rebels, who, with no pre-existing just cause, tear themselves by force from the jurisdiction of their masters—over whom the Prince’s right and authority always remains intact—who, setting aside divine and human laws, dissolve civil society and tear asunder every bond of humanity. To these we also add the proscribed. For they, since they lose all privileges, rights of dignities, and royal prerogatives, cannot possess that right within that empire from which they are proscribed. They may, however, send to foreigners.

XXVIII. But those who, compelled by extreme necessity, defend their life, reputation, wives, children, possessions, the freedom of the Fatherland, and the exercise of Religion against a Tyrannical Prince, and thus defect, are excused by law from rebellion, and possess this right of Embassy.

XXIX. And since the greatest consideration is placed in the choice of Legates, the one sending, with the female sex excluded from this, should provide for himself such a Legate who is primarily most instructed in the gifts of mind and intellect; and secondarily, who also possesses the goods of body and fortune.

XXX. We require the goods of the mind above all because of the gravity of the business, so that the Legate may have the most exquisite knowledge of all things, the keenest judgment, and dexterity of wit: And in short, let him be conspicuous in all virtues. But since no man is so absolute and perfect in all respects, the Prince should select from many one who surpasses others in doctrine, fidelity, silence, and diligence. See also other requirements in <term>Albericus Gentilis</term> <note>original: "Albericus Gentilis"</note>, book 3 on Embassies, and <term>Magirus</term> <note>original: "Magirus"</note>, book 2 on Embassies.

XXXI. That doctrine ought not to be vulgar, but from the most approved</translation>

It concludes with the necessary virtues and qualifications of a diplomat.</summary>

XXIII. There is no doubt that excommunicated persons and even heretics possess this right of sending Legates. For excommunication pertains to ecclesiastical discipline, whereas an embassy pertains to civil and secular affairs. Furthermore, a mission, which exists by the law of nations, looks to and considers men according to the law of nations, in that they are merely men among us, not by the law and custom of any region or religion. And the rights of peace are not abolished by diversity of religion; much less are the mutual dealings of an embassy abolished by a contradiction of faith: says <term>Kirchnerus</term> <note>original: "Kirchnerus"</note> in book 1, chapter 3, whose words it pleased me to insert here.

XXIV. Although there are some who ascribe the right of embassies to the free nobles and Hanseatic cities dwelling in France, Swabia, and the Rhine tract, nevertheless, since they are not estates of the Empire, are not found in the register of the Empire, and are not summoned to the diets, we deny that they possess that right, along with <term>Kirchnerus</term> in book 1, chapter 3, number 56, and <term>Heiden</term> <note>original: "Heiden"</note> on Embassies. For the free cities contained within the Hanseatic league cannot communicate or impart their own right to others, and even to certain foreign cities.

XXV. We also deny the right of sending Legates to Queens, if they are married and the rule resides with the husband: for then they send only messengers, not Legates, since according to the law "Woman" 2 of the Pandects on Rules of Law, they are barred from the entire administration of public offices: Except, however, those who hold supreme power and exercise the highest rule, whether they be unmarried, as was Elizabeth of England, and is still today Christina, Queen of Sweden, or if they are indeed joined in marriage, but have retained the rights of Majesty and Empire for themselves and have not communicated them to their husband, examples of which we have in Isabella of Castile, Mary, Queen of Hungary, and Mary of England. <term>Kirchnerus</term>, book 1, chapter 3; <term>Bodinus</term> <note>original: "Bodinus"</note>, book 6 of the Republic, chapter 5.

XXVI. Pontiffs, Bishops, Clerics, and in those churches that profess the Apostolic doctrine, Superintendents, and the Bishops of Denmark, Sweden, and England, in so far as they are occupied with ecclesiastical affairs and do not possess secular rule,
pages.10:
do not possess the right of sending Legates: Because, however, they are secular Princes and Dukes, and exercise political rule, we cannot deny that the same right belongs to them as to other Princes. Meanwhile, this right cannot be ascribed to academics under any title, since they are in the position of subjects. <term>Kirchnerus</term>.

XXVII. Furthermore, we bar from this right of sending Legates rebels, who, with no pre-existing just cause, tear themselves by force from the jurisdiction of their masters—over whom the Prince’s right and authority always remains intact—who, setting aside divine and human laws, dissolve civil society and tear asunder every bond of humanity. To these we also add the proscribed. For they, since they lose all privileges, rights of dignities, and royal prerogatives, cannot possess that right within that empire from which they are proscribed. They may, however, send to foreigners.

XXVIII. But those who, compelled by extreme necessity, defend their life, reputation, wives, children, possessions, the freedom of the Fatherland, and the exercise of Religion against a Tyrannical Prince, and thus defect, are excused by law from rebellion, and possess this right of Embassy.

XXIX. And since the greatest consideration is placed in the choice of Legates, the one sending, with the female sex excluded from this, should provide for himself such a Legate who is primarily most instructed in the gifts of mind and intellect; and secondarily, who also possesses the goods of body and fortune.

XXX. We require the goods of the mind above all because of the gravity of the business, so that the Legate may have the most exquisite knowledge of all things, the keenest judgment, and dexterity of wit: And in short, let him be conspicuous in all virtues. But since no man is so absolute and perfect in all respects, the Prince should select from many one who surpasses others in doctrine, fidelity, silence, and diligence. Although these things are not denied, yet it cannot be said absolutely and simply that an ass was not buried; and that the burial of an ass is an unburied burial, since the firstborn of an ass, having been struck by a hatchet and not redeemed with money, had to be buried according to the laws of the Hebrews, as was demonstrated in § 6.

### §. XVIII.

As to why the ox that was buried was stoned, which is mentioned in Exodus 21, the *Weimar interpreters* give this reason in verse 32, that homicide might not remain unavenged. But *Jacob Bonfrère*, in his commentary on this passage (Antwerp, folio 465), does not accept this reason, writing: "Furthermore, all these things are decreed against the ox, not because of any guilt, which cannot exist in a brute, but for the greater detestation and horror of homicide." Similar things are read in *Cornelius à Lapide*, in his commentary on this passage (Antwerp edition, Vol. 1, p. 489), where he comments as follows: "If an ox has struck a man or woman with its horn, and they have died, it shall be overwhelmed with stones, not because of the ox's guilt (for this cannot exist in a brute) but for the terror and example of men, so that men may be the more deterred from homicide, whence even today pigs and other beasts are killed if they kill or destroy children or men." Other matters pertaining to this stoned ox may be seen in the *Mishnah Bava Kamma, chapter 4, section 5*.

### §. XIX.

But another question is still raised regarding the stoned and buried ox: if the heirs were willing, could the owner of the ox, who was guilty of death, redeem its life with silver? *Grotius* affirms this question in Exodus 22, verse 29. But *Varenius* opposes Grotius, because he followed *Rashi* and *Ibn Ezra*, and believes that the owner of the brute could redeem his life only <pb n="13"/> if he could not be soundly convicted of gross negligence.

This opinion of *Varenius* is also embraced by other men of great name. But the most learned *L'Empereur* resolves this dispute and suitably combines both opinions, so that the *Hebrew* literalists might not be branded without cause, nor should he teach that one must cling only to them. His words in his *singular book on the forensic laws of the Hebrews* (Leiden edition, p. 82) are these: "Therefore, in verses 29 and 30 (of Exodus), the law proposes two cases distinct from the first: either the knowledge which the owner possesses is certain, or it is uncertain, and the negligence is either grave or light, or the friends of the slain man urge the strictest law, or they remit it. But if the knowledge was certain, the negligence grave, and the friends pursue their right, the words and circumstances show that the guilty party is to be punished with death; if, however, the knowledge is uncertain, or the negligence is lighter, or the hand of the friends is more lenient, I would think that verse 30 (concerning redemption) should be followed."

Furthermore, if something is promised in place of an annual honorarium, that too must be paid by the client. However, regarding the payment of contributions which are levied by reason of superiority and jurisdiction, Caspar Glocken, <note>original: "de contributionibus Imperij thesi 6. litera a. & b."</note> since the simple right of protection does not grant this, Wehner and Besold on the words "Protection and Shelter" <note>original: "Schutz und Schirm"</note>; Gail, Book 2, Observation 54, [say that] if a people is free, nothing should prejudice their liberty, Law: "I do not doubt," 7, of the Digest, On Captives and Postliminy, [and] the clients are by no means bound. Similarly, neither can the right of patronage properly so called—since this is annexed to spiritual matters, Chapter "When," 3, On Judgments; Chapter "On the right," 16, On the right of patronage—be arrogated to himself, nor can the Protector change anything regarding religion, since protection is a merely temporal right. <note>original: "Synz. thesi 22."</note>

### XXVI.

The Right of Clientage is dissolved by the death and desolation of the thing, such as the destruction of the city which one has undertaken to defend, by the argument of Law 5, § 2, Law: "If the usufruct," 21, of the Digest, On by what means usufruct is lost. The payment of the honorarium established for the sake of defense expires. A great loss of status, Law: "Of cognitions," 5, of the Digest, On extraordinary cognitions, or proscription or Imperial ban, in the person of either Patron or Client, extinguishes the clientage; for those who are proscribed are stripped of all clientage, faith, and protection, and thus of every liberty and privilege. <note>original: "Ordinatio Camerae parte 2. lege 9. §. 2. Gailius de Pace Publica libro 2. capite 1. numero 20. Mynsingerus centuria 1. observatione 50. & centuria 3. observatione 52. Pactis, nominibus, juramentis, foederibus, juribus omnibus excidunt Bechl. de Securitate thesi 118. & sequentibus."</note> However, it is truer that no one is deprived of that right because of a change in the Catholic or Augsburg religion. <note>original: "Constitutio Pacificationis religiosa de anno 55. §. Es sol auch. Syrinus de pace religiosa conclusione 37. Besoldus de jure foederibus capite 5. numero 15."</note> Nor is it lost by major excommunication as it is by a ban, because the latter is mortal, as Mager says <note>original: "capite 16. numero 199."</note>, while the former is medicinal. <note>original: "Hopingk de jure protectionis thesi 6. litera d."</note>

### XXVII.

When the strength of the Patron is exhausted and rendered useless for defense, <pb n="15"/> it is truer that the right of defense does not perish <note>argument: see Chapter "Briefly," Extra, On Oaths; Chapter "Fact," Legally, On the Rule of Law, in the Sext; Law: "In ambiguous cases," § "It is not new," Digest, On the same</note>, for a completed contract is not immediately vitiated, although it has come to a case from which it could not have begun <note>Law: "The penultimate, § Even if," Digest, On the meaning of words</note>. And it is easier for something to be preserved by civil law than to be newly granted <note>argument: Law 3, Digest, On the new work</note>. Yet, in extreme necessity and with the Patron suffering from poverty, so that no hope of better fortune or restitution remains, it could be conceded that the cliental right also dies.

### XXVIII.

Clientage contracted for a day is dissolved when that day arrives. Because any contracts and agreements stipulated for a certain time of duration are dissolved and cease when that time has elapsed <note>argument: Law: "If one," § 1, Digest, On Pacts; Law: "Of obligations," 44, § "It pleases," Digest, On Obligations and Actions</note>. It is also dissolved by the mutual consent and will of the parties <note>Law: "Nothing is so natural," 35, Digest, and there Gothofredus, On the Rule of Law</note>. However, the dissent of one party—since the matter is no longer intact and the interest of the other has already begun—does not remove it <note>Law 5, Code, On Obligations and Actions</note>. # On the Human Mind.

<note>from the previous page: ...we contemplate only the image and concept, and set it before ourselves.</note> Judgment, however, is that by which, from the intuition of those things which we have perceived, we affirm or deny something about the things themselves. This affirmation and negation is threefold: of existence, of essence, and of accidents. For example, when I have affirmed that the mind exists, I have explained what its essence is and what kind of thing it is. I call it an affirmation when judgment attributes a predicate to a subject in an intentional way through its unitive mode of tending. I call it a negation when it intentionally severs and removes the same predicate from its subject through a divisive mode of tending. Reasoning or discourse is a connection and a certain comparison of multiple thoughts and judgments, or, if you prefer, a passage from one thought to another, since discourse necessarily encompasses two cognitions within itself, but does not require many. For after the intellect has received an object within itself through simple apprehension, and has passed sentence on it by means of an elicited judgment, it soon, by a power implanted in it by nature, deduces other properties of the object from the predicate already known, and through its many other predicates, it wanders and runs forth through various other acts, like footsteps.

§. 27. Since these four—essence, power, operation, and object—have this order, that power flows from essence, operation from this, and operation tends toward an object, the object concerning which the intellect operates in the three reviewed ways must be investigated by me for its full knowledge. I cannot derive its extension better than from the power implanted in it. My intellect, however, conceives objects that are infinitely diverse among themselves in number and perfection, such as impossibles, possibles, non-existents, those immersed in matter, and those torn away from matter. It even represents God, the creator of all beings, in the way He is in Himself—strengthened by celestial light—even if it cannot comprehend Him, so that no cause appears to me why I should not extend the power of my intellect to every object that falls even under the angelic intellect; indeed, by elevating its nature, I illustrate the immense goodness of God. Nor is this consideration a small argument to me for believing this: that whether I thus extend the sphere of my intellect or do not extend it, and deny it such an extension, I will nevertheless find that it must necessarily be attributed to it. For if I maintain an affirmation, it is necessary that I know all those objects; for I cannot affirm anything about any object unless I know it. Without <pb n="16"/> negation, I also cannot deny, unless it be that which I conceive, so that I may conclude that the object of my intellect is also everything that falls under the angelic intellect.

§. 28. The mode, however, by which the intellect operates concerning these objects seems twofold to me. For it perceives some things without a corporeal idea, while others it perceives only by the help of a corporeal idea. One who understands by the former mode I shall call the pure intellect; one who understands by the latter, I shall call the intellect aided by the senses. I am persuaded that a pure intellect is given in me by the fact that I know well that it understands its own thoughts, and it does not seem likely to me that any mathematical figures—or rather any ideas of mathematical figures—or other ideas of the mind, <term>for example</term> of thing, substance, true, good, equal, and common notions, <term>for example</term> that things which agree with a third thing agree with each other <term>etc.</term>, were drawn by the benefit of the senses, since those ideas contain nothing corporeal or of corporeal affection, nor do they even fall into the senses. Rather, it is more likely that they were implanted in the mind from its very beginning, <term>that is</term>, the capacity given to the mind by God for exciting and making such forms of concept. Therefore, I do not think that the common saying is universally true, as Eustachius holds: "There is nothing in the intellect <term>etc.</term>" For if this statement were universally valid, all knowledge of God would have to be denied entirely. For God was in no way, however you may distinguish it, in the sense, since He is not corporeal, and consequently would never have been in the intellect. For he would foolishly believe in God who does not know even a <term>crumb</term> <gloss>Greek: γρῦ, a trifle or the smallest amount</gloss> about Him. Nor does it follow that God falls into the senses, as some wish, because we arrive <term>dianoetice</term> <gloss>by way of discursive reasoning</gloss> at the knowledge of God through the contemplation of His works, which do fall into the senses. For that contemplation does not lead us to know the existence of the supreme Divinity in any other way than by exciting us to attend to the idea of the mind, and thus, with that intervening, to conclude the existence of God. But it is not proven from there that God falls into the senses, which was the matter in question. For the same reason, anyone could deny the existence of his own mind, since it does not fall into the senses. And indeed, I do not see how they can prove through the natural order of powers that the intellect must necessarily contemplate phantasms. <summary>This passage defines the operations of the human mind, distinguishing between simple apprehension, judgment, and reasoning, while arguing that the intellect possesses a capacity for pure, non-corporeal cognition that reaches beyond sensory experience to the knowledge of God.</summary>
<keywords>human mind, judgment, intellect, essence, power, operation, pure intellect, sensory cognition, existence of God, phantasms</keywords>
