<pb n="16"/>fates, that while they render a reputation immortal, they wear down and weaken the body, the host of a great soul, like iron through vigils and tireless labor; and they become similar in color to the dead who converse too much with the dead. This companionship had been interrupted for our **BLESSED** one for so many years, and although his reputation shone more brightly day by day through the attrition of his labors, his strength nevertheless grew dull day by day, and while he illuminated <term>Cimbria</term> <gloss>the region of Schleswig-Holstein</gloss> with his light, he himself seemed to be consumed little by little like a lamp burning out.
<margin>Death of his wife.</margin>
There was added, to a body pressed by such a weight of labors, a lethal wound and a pain penetrating to the very vitals, from the premature death of his Sweetest Wife: the more tender the bed that had been for him for so many years without any strife, the more fruitful in noble offspring and those who emulated their father’s virtues, the more he lamented her snatched-away joys, and all the pleasures <note>original: "Veneres"</note> extinguished with his wife, and himself carried out in the same funeral procession as she. Forgive, *Auditors*, forgive me for including in my reasoning the inevitable necessity of fate, or rather of God, the arbiter of life and death, whose dictates are not to be moved, by which fixed limits are set for us and the goal is immovably fixed for years, which our mind often perceives falsely, being blind to the rest. These were the decrees of the Fates, to reclaim this deposit of heaven and to insert this immortal head among the stars, which had illuminated *Cimbria* with such great rays. The orbits of the earth seemed too narrow for such a vast mind, therefore he had to be summoned to the wider spaces of the heavens. Though he was always desirous of these, he was nevertheless not so disdainful of the present that, had fate and God permitted, he would not have granted us more of his use, especially in order to lay the final hand to the divine work he had begun. The sons of the physicians were consulted; everything was sought from all sides that might strengthen the forces of his body, which was failing day by day, and restore what had collapsed. But human counsels are in vain where Divine ones are contrary! Earth keeps in vain while heaven summons. Among the <margin>Journey to the Spadan springs.</margin>
wonders of nature are the Acidulae <note>mineral springs</note>, the Spadan springs <note>modern Spa, Belgium</note> gushing through mountain ducts by hidden paths, which bountiful Mother Nature, or rather the great father of nature, God, seems to have produced as if in aid of failing art and human assistance. Through these medicated springs, the languor of torpid bodies was often shaken off, fevers extinguished, pains driven away, pristine vigor returned to the year, and strength restored to the limbs. Thither, therefore, the great researcher of nature hastened, hoping for a more benign treatment from her whose mysteries he had long interpreted! But he experienced her as a stepmother, and the waters that had been healthy for others so often were lethal to him. *Cimbria* followed him as he went there with a thousand prayers, and, as if prescient of the future, unwillingly let go of such an ornament, never to return. ### LXII.

But if indeed such a struggle has been undertaken with someone who does not reject, alongside the divine Scripture, the authority of the holy Fathers and of the universal Church, there exists no point which cannot be proven by that same reasoning.

### LXIII.

Moreover, the task of Theology is not only that which we have just explained, namely, to defend its principles against those who deny or attack them, and to deduce from there, by the force of reason, other conclusions which serve to protect and illustrate the Christian matter; but also to fortify both strongly by employing internal and external protections and aids of this science.

### LXIIII.

We call the internal and proper protections of Theology those arguments which are sought from the Canonical Scripture: from the faithful tradition of Christ and the Apostles: from the authority of the Catholic and Apostolic Church, and from the canons of general councils and of the Roman Pontiffs: and finally, from the monuments of ancient and recent Fathers and Theologians.

### LXV.

<margin>+</margin> Those can be called external, and as it were borrowed from an alien field, which are taken from the tenets of natural Philosophers, from the opinions of legal scholars—for they too wish to be counted among the professors of true Philosophy—from the commentaries of historical events, and finally from the resources of human reason itself.

### LXVI.

For since there is a twofold kind of argumentation—the one resting on authority, which is proper to the Theologian, and the other instructed by reason, which is peculiar to the Philosopher—if it is not granted to use the former and proper one, the Theologian seizes upon what is next to the former, and defends himself by reason in place of authority; yet he often joins both kinds of proof together.

### LXVII.

From this it is clear that the wisdom of those who, about to speak on any theological argument, reject the authority of the Fathers, Councils, and Scriptures as if it were not firm enough, and dispute only with little arguments borrowed from natural Philosophy, is foolish. For those <term>μωρόσοφοι</term> <gloss>foolish-wise men</gloss> do not understand 
<pb n="14"/>that the place is so proper to the authority of Theology that it receives almost all the reasons it uses as guests and foreigners.

### LXVIII.

Furthermore, there is this difference among the internal protections of Theology: that arguments drawn from the authority of the sacred letters, the definition of the Catholic and Apostolic Church, and the perpetual and constant tradition of that same Church, are not only proper and internal, but also necessary; whereas those taken from the doctrine of any Saint or Father, of whatever order, holiness, or authority he may be, conclude only with probability. Nevertheless, it would be rash to depart too far from the judgment of many holy Fathers, especially in the interpretation of the Scriptures.

### LXIX.

They are therefore convicted of erring gravely and dangerously who, making Saint Jerome the rule of the testamentary Scriptures, wish only those books to be held among the Canonical which the same Father, perhaps busied with something else, calls by the name of Canonical somewhere.

### LXX.

Truly, a necessary argument is not drawn from the authority of Jerome alone, but only a probable one; and not even that is always probable, but only when it does not depart far from the more accepted opinion of the remaining Fathers.

where the mode of personal subsistence, or <term>suppositalitas</term> <gloss>the state of being a subject</gloss>, is really distinguished from the substance. But in divine things, the mode and the substance do not differ really, nor is any distinction of essence in the divine persons to be admitted, unless only of reason, lest some composition of essence and person be established in God. They are, therefore, infinitely distant, just as the finite essence and the finite person are; the finite essence is individual because of unity and incommunicable to multiple persons because of finiteness. The infinite, even if it is supremely individual because of supreme unity, is nevertheless truly communicable to multiple persons because of infinity. In finite things, one person is distinguished from another no less by the singularity of being than by the incommunicability of subsisting. But in the mystery of the <term>Trinitas</term> <gloss>Trinity</gloss>, the persons are distinguished from each other at least by the incommunicability of subsisting, but not indeed by the singularity of essence; the one is not the other, yet it is of the same numerical essence as the other. There, any person is entirely distinct from another person and separated, and they have no intrinsic connection. Here, although the persons are distinguished really, they cannot, however, be separated in being, but by reason of it, one is in the other, nor can it exist outside the other because of the identity of essence. Briefly: *Finite persons are distinguished by time, will, virtue, operation, and place.* But in the divine persons, because of the <term>homoousian</term> <gloss>consubstantiality</gloss> of the essence, there is co-eternity, one will, one virtue, one operation, and where one is, there is the other. And so much for the definition of a Person; the application follows.

### XXI. The <term>Photiniani</term> <gloss>followers of Photinus</gloss> <term>apotomos</term> <gloss>sharply/stubbornly</gloss> deny that the HOLY SPIRIT is a Person, asserting that the same is a *Virtue*, or an *Attribute* of **GOD**, or indeed some quality intermediate between the virtue of **GOD** and the faculties excited in man. *Crellius, book 1, on the One God the Father, Section III, chapter 8.* To <term>Socinus</term>, the Holy Spirit is a virtue and power naturally residing in God. To whom we oppose the following argument. Whatever is attributed to all those things which, conceived under the reason of a person, are appropriate to things subsisting by themselves, that thing truly subsists, <pb n="18"/>
<note>A row of fleurons or ornamental typographical marks appears above and below the page number 14.</note>

and is designated by the name of a person. But all those requisites are attributed to the HOLY SPIRIT, which are [attributed to] others, and so on. Therefore, the HOLY SPIRIT truly subsists, and is designated by the name of a person. The major premise is of manifest truth. The minor is proven from a sufficient enumeration of (1) names, (2) idioms, (3) works, (4) apparitions, which cannot belong except to a subsisting thing.

XXII. (1) By reason of names, the Holy Spirit is called <term>kyrios</term> <gloss>Lord</gloss>, 2 Corinthians 3:17, 1 Corinthians 12:4, or <term>parakletos</term> <gloss>Advocate</gloss>, John 16:26, chapter 15:26, chapter 16:7. I conclude: He who is Lord, Advocate, and Paraclete truly subsists and is a Person. For who ever read in the scriptures that the Virtue and attributes of GOD are called Lord and Advocate? Furthermore, he is called a witness with the Father and the Son, 1 John 5:7. Hence, I argue thus: That of which the name of witness is properly predicated is a person. But the name of witness is properly predicated of the HOLY SPIRIT. Therefore, the major is manifest and is conceded by Gossavius against Keckermann, page 1, chapter 4, page 50; for the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are joined together as witnesses in heaven. Therefore, just as the Father and Son is a witness, so is the Holy Spirit. But they are properly witnesses, as cannot be denied. Moreover, from verse 9, it is clear that the testimony of the three witnesses in heaven is compared with the testimony of men, of whom the law says that every truth consists in the mouth of two or three, to which the Apostle seems to refer; as therefore the three witnesses among men are persons, so also those three who are said to testify in heaven are brought forward as three persons. Finally, that the HOLY SPIRIT is not an attribute or virtue of God, but rather an <term>hypostasin</term> <gloss>a subsisting reality</gloss>, is gathered most openly from that very passage. For if it were the virtue of the Father, and not something subsisting distinct from the Father, it could not be introduced as a third witness distinct from the Father and the Son. Truly, there is one and the same attestation of essence and virtue, since, as the adversaries themselves concede, a virtue could not properly be said to testify, and much less to be contradistinguished from other distinct witnesses.

### §. XV.

That was the condition of the elder man, whom we recall as having flourished at another time with favor entrenched at Caesar’s court above the rest of his friends. Why, therefore, should it be a wonder if the sons were in a much worse position? Certainly, Archelaus had reason to fear the Prince, whose will initially diminished his dignity, and later openly prostrated him in his anger, when Vienna was chosen for the bearing of the bitterness of exile. <note>Noldius, p. 229.</note> Josephus did not pass over the imperious voice of the Prince, <note>Antiquities, book 17, chapter 15.</note> so that we may easily agree with Spanheim, the defender of the Evangelist, who does not limit the term <term>βασιλεύειν</term> <gloss>to rule as a king</gloss> to such narrow boundaries that it does not sometimes encompass a power inferior to royal authority in its meaning. <note>vol. 2, Dubia Evangelica 86, compare to the same work.</note>

### §. XVI.

Why, therefore, would the Tetrarchs, confined to the coast of Palestine, be angry with us if we point out that they obtained only a precarious rule? They undoubtedly lay stricken whenever they appeared to the Prince to have plotted anything against him. As happened to Antipas, spurred on by Herodias; not so to Philip, a composed man, who took wiser counsel for himself, even though both men otherwise testified to their obedience to the Prince with many services. <note>Antiquities, 18, chapter 9.</note> I omit the fates of Lysanias, and of Zenodorus, and of others, whom it was necessary to experience grave calamity if they caused, by their crimes or by their zeal for factions, the anger of their master to be kindled. <note>Antiquities, 15, chapter 13.</note>

### §. XVII.

I am little moved by the honorary titles of kingdoms, regarding which, what should be decided, those hesitating are unable to be sufficiently instructed from the previous mention. But having contemplated the taxes imposed, the descriptions of the borders, and the freely distributed dignities, I am finally compelled to admit that it is an ill-timed endeavor for anyone who might perhaps struggle to support their supreme right or to defend an absolute power. <note>See Noldius, same work; Selden, On the Law of Nature and Nations, book 6, chapters 17 and 18.</note>

<pb n="11"/>

### §. XVIII.

Thus, we have viewed the Tetrarchs in general, with the title of the rulers of a fourth part expressed with appropriate brevity. Now, nothing prevents or forbids us from looking at each individual. The first according to Luke is indeed Antipas, more powerful in authority, even if younger in age. Josephus describes his incest, his foul dissimulation, his envy, and his tyrannical cruelty, along with the ruin of his fortunes, gravely in many places, and the Evangelists do not consider these things to be entirely passed over for themselves. We, leaving many things to history, shall have fulfilled our duty with a brief review. However, one should not be silent about the earlier intention of his father, in which, if he had persisted, he would not have been a <term>τετράρχης</term> <gloss>tetrarch</gloss>, but a king. <note>Antiquities, 17, chapter 8.</note> Even that wickedness and criminality is shown by the fact that he was rebuked by John for many crimes, whose freedom he indeed curbed with chains at first, but finally extinguished it completely by the sword of the executioner. <note>Chemnitz, Harmony of the Gospels, chapter 31; Josephus, Antiquities, book 18, chapter 7.</note>

### §. XIX.

The name of Herod, with which Luke distinguished him, was neither unusual in this family, just as it was for the Scythians and their Parthian kings; nor was it so hated by foreign nations that it was not frequently used. But I do not agree with Schotanus, who denied that it was genuine. As for his origin, I fear that Salmasius does not derive it correctly, and therefore he calls him a little Greek.
</translation>

The author challenges the idea of their absolute sovereignty and provides historical context for their political and moral failures, including the execution of John the Baptist.</summary>
<keywords>Tetrarchs, Herod, Antipas, Archelaus, Roman authority, Josephus, sovereignty, political history</keywords>

<pb n="11"/>XXV. The second genus of intellections pertains to mental enunciation, which—so that the Moderns may distinguish it from a proposition, which also looks toward the third operation of the mind and includes virtual discourse—they correctly define as an immediate judgment regarding some thing: that is, such that it affirms a predicate of a subject because of the connection between the subject itself and the predicate. Whereas, on the contrary, all discourse is mediate judgment, because it mediately approves the connection of the predicate with the subject. The most powerful property of these acts is formal truth, which is nothing other than the conformity of the judgment with the object; just as, conversely, falsity is the difformity of the judgment with the object. Thus, a true judgment is one that enunciates the object as being such as it is on the part of the thing itself; a false one is that where the object is not such as it is enunciated to be.

XXVI. An enunciation once true can never pass into a false one, nor conversely can a false one pass into a true one. For the same cognition always represents the same thing; therefore, the cognition that with truth represented Adam as writing for this instant, which the verbal copula designated, represented for eternity Adam writing at this instant. For just as it is impossible for Adam to have written at this instant A, and not to have written at this instant A, so it is impossible that the cognition which truly represents him as having written at this instant A could ever represent him as not having written, since a proposition speaks for eternity only of this, and of no other, instant. The same must be reasoned concerning falsity, that if a proposition were to represent a time other than that which it had first represented, by this very fact it would not be the same, but another and new representation, and consequently a new cognition.

XXVII. To the third and primary genus of operations of the human intellect belongs formal discourse, or the syllogism; which is an oration in which, certain things being posited, something else necessarily follows from these things that were posited, because they are. And it essentially involves not only the conclusion, but the very premises themselves, nor is anyone considered to have constructed a formal syllogism who either infers something without any premises, or, having made the premises, infers nothing. But in order for the assent of the conclusion to be distinguished from another immediately judicative assent, it ought intrinsically to attain the object of the premises as the motive and formal reason for assenting. This is proven therefrom, because every act tending into some material object because of another formal one ought to attain that formal object; but the formal motive of the conclusion as such is the object of the premises, or the identity of the extremes with a third medium; therefore the act of the conclusion, as such, ought to attain that object. It is confirmed, because unless the act of the conclusion again attains the formal motive, in some syllogisms there could be no reason given why this proposition is a conclusion rather than another of the three, for any of them can be inferred by way of a conclusion from the others.

XXVIII. Beyond the object of the conclusion, and the object of the premises, there must also be attained by the act of the <pb n="12"/> conclusion the goodness of the inference, which is the identity between the object of the premises and the object of the conclusion: for this goodness is also a partial motive, which, together with the object of the premises, moves the intellect to infer the conclusion; for with this unique connection between the object of the premises and the object of the conclusion removed, however much the object of the premises might remain, the intellect would not be moved to the conclusion. Just as, therefore, when we love medicine for the sake of health, we also love the connection that medicine has with restoring health, because with this connection excluded we would not love the medicine, so also the intellect, in order to be moved to conclude, must not only attain the object of the premises, but also the goodness of the inference.

XXIX. Some doubt whether the judgment concerning the goodness of the inference must be a distinct and intermediate act between the assent of the premises and the assent of the conclusion, through which the intellect reflexively knows that this conclusion is rightly inferred from these premises, because those things are identified among themselves which are identified to one third. We think it more probable that *a judgment concerning the goodness of the inference distinct from the act of the conclusion is not necessarily always required*, especially in practiced men to whom that principle is most clearly known, *whatever things are the same as one third, etc.* For such men, after they have seen in the premises that the extremes of the conclusion are identified to one third, immediately infer the act of the conclusion, which simultaneously and at once attains the object of the premises, and the goodness of the inference, and the object of the conclusion. In those men, however, who are not practiced in making syllogisms, and who even, after they have seen that two things are identified to one third, can still doubt whether those two things are identified among themselves, we think it entirely follows that *a judgment concerning the goodness of the inference is distinct, and precedes the conclusion itself*: for the intellect of such people is so imperfect that it is not sufficiently determined by the object of the premises to infer the conclusion without any hesitation.

### Operations of the Human Will.

XXX. That the will is a free spiritual virtue, appetitive of an object, is certain among all: that it is not distinguished from the intellect, nor from the soul, we hinted above in the third thesis. The *material object* about which it is concerned is everything that the intellect can know under the aspect of good or evil. The *formal object*, or that which immediately moves the will, is the good and the evil; the former moves to acts of pursuit, the latter to acts of avoidance. The good, which moves the will, is threefold: *honest, delightful, useful*. None of these can allure the will unless it is first known: yet the cognition itself is not the motive of the will, but a mere condition applying the motive. *Evil as evil*, or proposed only under the aspect of evil, the will cannot love, otherwise than if it is presented under the aspect of at least an apparent good.

XXXI. Ordinarily speaking, in order for us to love and desire some good for ourselves, it suffices to know that this good is suitable to us; nor is it necessary that we recognize in ourselves any goodness, because of which we might be worthy to love such a good for ourselves. But if we love or desire some good for another person, it is required that we apprehend in them some goodness, because of which we estimate them worthy of such a good. For in order (ordinarily speaking) that I may be able to join myself through affection with the good of my neighbor, insofar as it is a good for him, I ought first to join myself through affection

<pb n="13"/> and the monsters of the most grievous errors. Behold that sad dialogue of <term>Flacius Illyricus</term>, a man otherwise not unlearned, held at Weimar with <term>Strigelius</term>. Oh, immortal God! How many pernicious storms did it stir up for this world? Because he, inflamed by the spirit of contention and with a confused sharpness of mind, had thoughtlessly vomited forth that most absurd of all things: *that Original Sin is the very substance of man*, which he later sustained by every means, lest he appear vanquished. Greater still is that other, certainly more tragic and fateful, example which stands in writing regarding <term>Arminius</term>. For because of the controversies stirred up concerning certain hidden chapters of theology, not only did the whole of Belgium, but almost the entire of Europe, begin to be split into factions, and <term>Arminius</term> himself, consumed by grief, having fallen into a slow and grave illness and having been extinguished by it, is said to have followed this epitaph:

> *That subtle man, powerful in speech,*
> *But whose primary care was always for morals,*
> *Calls to all, here lying Arminius,*
> *Lest they prefer to dispute rather than to live.*

You have traveled with me so far, O Auditors, through the spacious field of the vices from which the learned are accustomed to suffer, but many things sufficiently worthy of mention still remain in that category, which I willingly omit due to the narrowness of time. Certainly, the insatiable greed of certain learned men, the immoderate luxury of others, and the seething lust of some would still need to be touched upon. Yet, since I perceive that it is the nature of these vices that many other men, not a few, are agitated by the same goads, and that the aforementioned stains do not flow from the abuse of learning itself, we refrain from examining them more fully. Nothing remains but that I should address with friendly exhortation those who desire to be esteemed by the name of learned; let them, by the very sacred things of their studies, by the inviolable altar of <term>Pallas</term> <gloss>goddess of wisdom</gloss> to which they have sworn, and by the excellence of the name of the learned, which is venerable above all others, act solicitously so that, not being ensnared by the soft depravity of the vices reviewed thus far, they might fall from their dignity; but rather let them contend to strive so that, in a most sweet harmony, the praise of refined doctrine and the splendor of virtues may most amicably conspire in their own breasts. Let all, however, beware diligently, lest because of those flaws by which we have warned that many learned men have been contaminated, they hold the most useful care of learning and letters in contempt, and do not attribute the origin of foul vices to learning, which is the foster-mother of all virtues; remembering well that there is nothing so innocent and holy that it cannot be corrupted by another's fault, if it is led into perverse uses. I now proceed to carry out that which <pb n="14"/> for the sake of which I have most especially allowed this task of speaking to be demanded of me today; namely, that I should take upon myself today the duty of offering part of the pious vows and most humble thanksgivings that are heard everywhere from all learned men for the subsidies of studies bestowed by the **MOST SERENE PRESERVER OF LETTERS, OUR MOST CLEMENT LORD**, for the benefit of the literary republic. Nor can I do otherwise, while I perceive my own studies most liberally aided and confirmed by His Most Munificent Hand. But from where am I to lead the beginning of this speech of mine, I am utterly hesitant and doubtful? For what hope have I to encompass, with the narrow and thin supplies of my oratory, matters greater than any eulogy? What, then, shall I do, when both my piety bids me speak, and the awareness of my weakness bids me be silent? I will certainly strive that what I cannot express in words, I may supply with my soul and silent vows. My soul, therefore, overflowing with the most humble devotion, inclines itself at Your feet, **MOST SERENE PRESERVER AND CONSERVATOR OF THE MUSES**. Kindly cast Your eyes upon this most profound humility, which was not once displeasing even to the Gods, and accept this chaste vow which is offered here at Your footstool. And since You have thus far proved Yourself a Great **PROTECTOR** in the affairs of both peace and war, remain also hereafter the most certain safeguard of the literary republic, which You have been until now, and may You be heard as the Happy and Invincible Restorer of studies, religion, and the good arts; by which reliance, under Your gentle rule, the literary republic may always grow with the sweetest peace, firm security, and most joyful abundance, and may it flourish, triumph, and be eternal for all time! May Your life be long, **MOST BENIGN FATHER OF THE FATHERLAND**. May You live happy, and may You live for a very long time, together with Your **MOST SERENE SPOUSE and the PRINCE OF YOUTH**, the hope and Pillar of the future happiness of <term>Brandenburg</term> <gloss>a region in Germany</gloss>; and may future centuries forever adore and venerate the splendor of Your Most Serene Name. Finally, I also recognize with a grateful mind that excellent kindness, O Auditors most highly to be observed, which you have not refused to show me until now by your diligent listening, and I shall take care to respond to that diligence and benevolence of yours <it>with a certainly grateful and mindful spirit.</it>

<header>PHILOSOPHICAL DISPUTATION.</header>

### ERROR XIV.
## That the Rational Soul resides in only one part of the body.

I. Philo the Jew placed the Rational Soul in the heart; Parmenides and Epicurus in the whole chest; Strato the Physicist in the bridge of the eyebrows; Erasistratus in the small membranes; Herophilus in the cavity or base of the brain; Hippocrates in the brain; Xenocrates at the crown; others established it in the whole head as if in a fortress; others finally elsewhere, and some indeed in a hidden and obscure place, from which, like a spider, it would run throughout the whole body to catch flies, according to the opportunity of things.

II. So too does the author of the *Compendium of the Whole of Theological Truth* (book 2, Venetian edition, year 1565, ch. 54, p. 192) say that the soul, placed in the center of the heart without its own extension, gives sense, vivifies, and moves the whole body united to it, just like a spider, which, residing in the middle of its web, feels any movement made in the web, whether externally or internally; a truly strange opinion of a man.

->C O R R E C T I O.<-

I. The Rational Soul is not in only one part of the body; otherwise, it would not inform the others substantially. Rather, it is whole in the whole continuous body, and whole in any part of it, as all sound philosophers and theologians hold, along with the interpreters of Aristotle (*On the Soul*, book 1, text 93), where the Philosopher says that one cannot even imagine which part (that is, determinate and sole) the intellect, that is, the Spiritual Soul, has in the body.

II. And although Aristotle (*On Respiration*, ch. 1) expressly says that the soul exists in some particle of the body, he is not to be considered as having thought the same as the mentioned ancients, for he immediately adds that it has its virtue in particles, that is, in certain operations, and that it depends on certain determinate Organs, and that it has its virtues or material powers residing in those particles or Organs and subjected to them.

### ERROR XV.
## That the Rational Soul is mortal.

I. The Epicureans, as witnessed by Ruvius in *On the Separated Soul*, denied that the Rational Soul was immortal first of all; Pliny followed them (*Natural History*, book 7, ch. 55) and many others, especially the Sadducees, thinking that even the Rational Soul perishes with the body through diseases. Heretics, whom a Castro reports in *Against Heresies*, book 2, under the word "Soul," revive this same error, which was almost buried; and Lucretius (*On the Nature of Things*, book 3) believed the Soul is gradually extinguished with the body.

<margin>II
II II
II II
II II
II II</margin>
II. Regarding this matter, having weighed the many passages on both sides, Aristotle seems at least to have been doubtful, as some note with Scotus in *Sentences*, book 4, distinction 43, question 2, article 2; but some 

<pb n="19"/>
<header>OF THE RATIONAL SOUL.</header>

among the ancient philosophers, especially the Stoics, judged that the Soul does not always endure, but that when released from the body it is weakened after a long time and finally perishes, though the souls of the wise persevere until the end of the World.

# CORRECTIO.

I. The greater and better part of the philosophers, even the ancients, admitted the immortality of the Rational Soul, as can be seen in Eugubinus, book 9 of *On Perennial Philosophy*, and others. Dandinus also, in book 1 of *On the Soul*, commentary 39, says that Pythagoras also recognized the immortality of the Rational Soul; for he used to say that if you leave the body and come purified to the ether, you will be an immortal God, incorruptible, no longer mortal. Saint Thomas also explains Aristotle in favor of this opinion in *Summa contra Gentiles*, book 2, chapter 79, as does the more common opinion of the moderns, especially since he said the Rational Soul comes from without.

II. But whatever may be the case regarding Aristotle, immortality certainly pertains to and is owed to the Rational Soul by its own nature, as it is to the Angels, as witnessed by Ruvius in *On the Separated Soul*, question 4, number 52. Since it is truly created, it has no natural cause for its own corruption; for Christ says in Matthew 10 that they cannot kill the soul. Nor is it an objection that in the Letter of Sophronius, recited in the 11th session of the 6th Council of Constantinople, intellectual beings are said to be immortal only by grace, not indeed by nature, and that this is approved by the Council. For Sophronius only denied such immortality to Angels and the Rational Soul as God alone has, who therefore is said in 1 Timothy 6 to have immortality alone, since he has it from himself and through his own altogether immutable essence.

III. Hence, since it is certain from the Fifth Lateran Council under Leo X, session 8, that immortality belongs to the Rational Soul by itself and from its own nature, some therefore deduce that it can also be evidently demonstrated from physical principles, and is known, as it were, from its terms, at least in itself, even if perhaps not yet as far as we are concerned. For the primary Truth cannot lie, nor can the light of nature conflict with it, which was bestowed upon us by that same Truth for the sake of knowing the truth, just as Aristotle in the *Categories* teaches that the squaring of the circle is expressly demonstrable, even though the demonstration by which it might be proved has not yet been discovered.

IV. And truly it is at least morally evident that it pertains to divine Providence that the wicked be punished, and that the good be affected by a reward worthy of their merit. Since this does not happen in this life, as experience bears witness, one must either concede the immortality of souls, or else conclude that Divine Providence fails in many things and that God is unjust, not treating each one according to merit, which is blasphemous. This reasoning, Divus Chrysostom said in homily 4 *On Providence*, is clearer than the midday light in demonstrating the immortality of the Rational Soul.

The author affirms the soul's immortality and its presence throughout the entire body, citing Aristotle, Church Councils, and various historical philosophers.</summary>

### Sixth Question.

### §. 11. If Christ were on earth after the Ascension, would he not be our Priest?

In the Epistle to the Hebrews, chapter 8, verse 4, one may read these words: "For if he were on earth, he would not be a priest." From these, the adversaries <unclear>stealthily</unclear> gather that Christ dwells with his body in the heavens and is not on earth. It is therefore our task to wrest the club from Hercules <note>an allusion to the proverb "to take the club from Hercules," meaning to overcome a powerful opponent</note> and to answer soundly. The first point: If Christ could not be a Priest (if he were on earth), it would follow that when he lived on earth, offered himself to his Father on the altar of the cross, and showed himself to his disciples for forty days with many proofs, he was not a priest. The conclusion is absurd. Therefore the antecedent is also. The reason for this connection is manifest, because he was on earth at that time. Second: If Christ, because he is a Priest, would not be on earth, he would not be a Priest as God (because he is always on earth just as he is in heaven). The latter is absurd, by the confession of the opposing party. Therefore the former is also. Third: If Christ, because he is a Priest, would not be on earth, he would not be a Priest according to his human nature, because by their own admission, he is in Heaven according to that nature. The latter is absurd, because the priesthood pertains to his office, and thus to both Natures. Therefore the former is also. Finally, this point: If he were not on earth, he would not be an eternal Priest, because he is to return from Heaven on the last day. This is false, therefore that is too. It is therefore a wonder that the adversaries prop up the building of their opinion on this passage, as if on a wooden support or some eaves-bracket; but in truth, they work through tunnels. For first, they insert the words "according to human nature" into the text; second, they take the words as referring to one or the other of Christ's natures, when the Epistle speaks of the whole Christ. Now move the syllogistic wheel; what will emerge? Is it not this?

we shall say they exist. Many affirm they have seen ships capable of holding eighty rowers. No use of iron is found among them. Consequently, our men were filled with great wonder as to how they built either the houses, which they saw were fashioned with marvelous skill, or any other things pertaining to their use. But from certain river <margin>The incredible savagery of certain men</margin>
dwellers, they learned by hearsay the cause of why they fled so fearfully to help our men; they later reported that they believed them to be <term>Canibales</term> <gloss>Cannibals</gloss>, or as they call those ferocious ones, <term>Caribes</term>. They left the islands of these obscene people roughly in the middle of the journey toward the islands to the south. The gentle people of these islands complain that they are perpetually harassed by the frequent raids of the Cannibals for prey, just as hunters in the woods pursue wild beasts by force and ambush. The boys they capture, they castrate to raise as fatter and more tender, just as we do with chickens or pigs intended for food. When they reach mature age and fall into their hands, they divide them after they are killed. They feast upon the fresh outer parts of the limbs, and they preserve the limbs salted, as we do with pork hams, for future times. It is forbidden and obscene to eat women among them. If they capture young women, they care for and guard them for procreating offspring, just as we do with hens, sheep, and other animals. The old women they keep as slaves to perform chores. Both men and women of the islands, which we can now call ours, when they sense that the Cannibals are arriving, find no salvation other than flight. Although they use sharp-tipped reed arrows, they have found they are of little use for repelling the force and fury of the Cannibals. For all the natives admit that ten Cannibals would easily defeat one hundred of the others if they clashed. What each nation worships, besides the sky and its lights, they did not have sufficiently explored. Because of the brevity of time <pb n="34"/> and the scarcity of interpreters, the rest of the customs of the islands were not allowed to be known. These gentle people use for food roots <margin>Island foods</margin>
the size and shape of our turnips, but sweet in taste, similar to chestnuts that are still tender. They call these <term>ages</term> <gloss>a type of yam</gloss> themselves. There is another type of root they call <term>iucca</term> <gloss>cassava</gloss>; from this, they also make bread. They use the <term>ages</term> more roasted or boiled than for the purpose of making bread. They grate the <term>iucca</term> and press it, for it is juicy, and bake it into cakes. But this is wonderful: they say the juice of the <term>iucca</term> is more deadly than aconite, which kills instantly if swallowed, yet everyone has experienced that bread made from its mass is tasty and healthy. They also make bread from a certain panic-grass, which is in great abundance among the people of the <term>Infrubes</term> <gloss>referring to local peoples</gloss> and the <term>Granatenses</term> <gloss>people of Granada</gloss> Spaniards, without much difference. The stalk of this is longer than a span, tapering to a point, almost the thickness of an arm. The grains, fixed by nature in a wonderful order, emulate the form and body of the pea legume in shape. They are white when bitter, but when they have ripened, they become very black. When crushed, they surpass snow in whiteness. They call this type of grain <term>maizium</term> <gloss>maize</gloss>. Gold is of some estimation among them, for they wear it inserted into pierced earlobes and nostrils, drawn out into very thin leaves. However, since our men learned that merchants do not travel to them, nor did they themselves know any shores other than their own, they began to ask them through signs where they obtained that gold. As much as could be gathered from signs, it was from the sands of rivers flowing down from high mountains, and it was obtained without great labor. They would tighten it into pellets before it was drawn into leaves. Yet, it was not in that part of the island which that king held, which was later revealed by experience. For when they had departed from there, they chanced upon a river, which they perceived to have much gold mixed in the sand when they had jumped out onto the land for the sake of getting water and fishing. They say they saw no quadruped animal, except for three types of rabbits. The islands harbor snakes, but they are very harmless. They found wild geese, turtledoves, and ducks, larger than ours and with the whiteness of a swan, with a purple head. They found parrots, of which some were green, <margin>Parrots distinguished by wonderful colors</margin>
others yellow over their whole body, others similar to the Indian ones collared with cinnabar, as Pliny says. They took forty, but they were remarkably vivid and bright in color. They have multicolored wings, for with green and yellow feathers, they have some blue and purple mixed in, which variety produces delight. I wanted to recount this about the parrots, most illustrious Prince. Although the opinion of this Christopher Columbus seems to oppose the magnitude of the sphere and the opinion of the ancients about the non-navigable world, the parrots brought from there, and many other things, indicate by either their proximity or their nature that these islands taste of the Indian land. Especially since Aristotle, toward the end of his book <term>De coelo et mundo</term> <gloss>On the Heavens and the World</gloss>, Seneca, and other experts in cosmography testify that the Indian shores are not distant from Spain by a long stretch of sea across the west. That land produces by its own nature an abundance of mastic, aloes, cotton, and other things of this kind. Fleeces are collected from trees, just as among the Seres. They brought certain wrinkled grains of various colors, sharper than Caucasian pepper; they also brought twigs from coconut trees in the form of cinnamon, but with a taste and smell imitating sharp ginger, both in pith and, as I wrote in the previous book. Content, therefore, with these signs of a newly discovered land and another unheard-of world, and with the west winds already blowing for a prosperous return, intending to return because our spring was approaching, he left thirty-eight men with the king of whom we made mention above, to inquire into the nature of the places and times until he himself returned. That king was called by the inhabitants Guaccanarillus. Having struck a pact of singular friendship with him, he took care, in all ways he could, for the life, safety, and protection of those he left behind. Touched by mercy toward our men because they were to be left in foreign lands, the king seemed to have shed tears and promised all aid. Thus, having embraced one another, Columbus, about to return to Spain, ordered the sails to be set. He took with him ten men from among those from whom it was discovered that the language of all those islands could be written with our Latin letters without any difficulty. For they call heaven <term>turei</term>, house <term>boa</term>, gold <term>cauni</term>, a good man <term>tayno</term>, nothing <term>mayani</term>. They pronounce all other words as clearly as we do our Latin. These things you have, which I have thought worthy of mention concerning his first voyage. The King and Queen, all of whose thoughts, even while sleeping, are set on the increase of our religion, hoping that so many nations and simple peoples could easily be drawn to the law of Christ, were moved by hearing these things. They treated the arriving Columbus honorably, as he deserved for such ventures. They had him sit before them in public, which is the greatest sign of love, gratitude, and supreme respect among the Spanish kings. They ordered Columbus to be called the Admiral of the Sea from then on. He is titled <term>Almirantus</term> <gloss>Admiral</gloss> Columbus among the Spaniards. They also adorned his brother, Bartholomew Columbus, who was himself skilled in naval affairs, with the title of Prefect of the island of Hispaniola. They commonly call this office <term>Adelantatus</term> <gloss>Governor/Lieutenant</gloss>. Therefore, the titles of Admiral, Governor, and the presence of ships, and other things of this kind, I will sometimes call by their common names on purpose, so that I may be understood more clearly. Now let us return to the plan. It was believed that from the islands, as Columbus himself—now the Admiral of the Sea—had promised at the beginning, the greatest benefits would arise, which all mortals pursue with all their might. Moved, therefore, by these two reasons, these two most holy partners ordered seventeen ships to be prepared for the second expedition: three large hold-laden cargo ships, and twelve of the kind of ships we wrote are called <term>Carauelas</term> <gloss>caravels</gloss> among the Spaniards, without holds. Two of the same kind, somewhat larger, and suitable for sustaining holds because of the size of their masts. They entrusted the care of preparing this fleet to Juan Fonseca, a man of noble birth, Dean of Seville, and possessed of great talent and spirit. They ordered that over twelve hundred armed infantry be hired for him, among whom they ordered craftsmen and workers of all mechanical arts to be recruited with pay. They mixed some cavalrymen among the other armed men. To procreate offspring, they took mares, sheep, heifers, and many others along with those of their kind.

<summary>This passage details the inhabitants and natural resources of the newly discovered islands, describes the encounters with the cannibalistic tribes, and outlines the preparations for Columbus's second expedition to the Indies under the patronage of the Spanish monarchs.</summary>
<keywords>Canibales, iuccam, maizium, Columbus, Guaccanarillus, Hispaniola, Adelantatus, Juan Fonseca</keywords>

<pb n="12"/>

### XXIX.

<margin>Properly.</margin>
But in this place it is taken properly: since the word <term>pará</term> <gloss>fruit/offspring</gloss> is general, pertaining to the fruit-bearing of anything. Whence it is joined with various words: as may be seen in many sayings of the Scripture.

### XXX.

<margin>Fruit of the womb of David. Proof. From the testimony of the Psalm.</margin>
Here it suffices, where we have proven that the one and natural Son of God is called, and is, the fruit of the womb of David: as we read in Psalm 132:11. Jehovah swore truth to David himself, he will not turn away, or deflect, or depart from it:

> Of the fruit of your womb I will set upon your seat, or throne.

### XXXI.

Although many understand this promise only regarding a political kingdom: yet we, having followed the divine Luther, believe that God confirmed by an oath that a king should be set from the fruit of the womb of David, whose kingdom might be eternal.

### XXXII.

And truly this is a notable promise: because it defines a certain person; nor does it allow the succession to wander in an uncertain person.

### XXXIII.

Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob also had a promise concerning Christ. But under an uncertain person: if you look to the multiplied posterity.

### XXXIV.

In this promise, however, there is a certain description, because a certain person is named: so that, although the whole people were to be led away captive; yet, as long as the posterity of David survived, they retained hope of the kingdom.

### XXXV.

For this family was, as it were, a certain star in <pb n="13"/> this people: whose posterity, as long as it was seen, left behind a certain hope of future liberation through Christ, even in the Babylonian captivity and all other dangers, and so forth.

### XXXVI.

<margin>From concordances.</margin>
In the Latin Bibles, concordances are added to this verse: which themselves also show that the Psalmist speaks here of Christ.

### XXXVII.

Such is that saying in 2 Samuel 7:12. When your days are completed and you sleep with your fathers, I will raise up your seed after you, which shall go forth from your womb: and I will establish his kingdom. Luke 1:55. Just as he spoke to our fathers, to Abraham, and to his seed forever.

### XXXVIII.

In the margin of the German version, Psalms 89 and 110 are cited, which explicitly—which can be easily demonstrated—speak of Christ.

### XXXIX.

<margin>From the authority of the orthodox.</margin>
In a similar way, Urbanus Regius in his Dialogue, Pomeranus, and other faithful and orthodox interpreters declare this passage.

### XL.

<margin>Fruit of the loins of David.</margin>
Peter refers to this without any doubt in Acts 2:30, where he calls Christ the fruit of the loins of David, saying that David, since he was a Prophet, knew: that God had sworn to him with an oath, that of the fruit of his loin he would sit upon his seat.

### XLI.

<margin>Fruit of the earth.</margin>
Isaiah, in chapter 4:2, names him—to bring forward his true humanity—the fruit of the earth: since in Genesis 3:19, man is earth: as the Seventy <note>the Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note> interpret:
</translation>

<summary>This text provides theological evidence from the Psalms and the Book of Samuel to establish Jesus as the "fruit of the womb" of David, linking this lineage to the promise of an eternal kingdom. It also cites reformers and biblical interpreters to support the interpretation of these passages as prophecies of Christ.</summary>
<keywords>Jesus, David, Psalms, Luther, prophecy, genealogy, fruit of the womb, incarnation, Urbanus Regius, Pomeranus, Septuagint</keywords>

He believed that military men should have their own administrations, which they ought to manage themselves, and that the learned should have theirs; thus, each man ought to handle the affairs he knows. Hence, this excellent Prince, if matters of law were being discussed, employed only the learned in his council; if, however, the matter was military, he employed veteran soldiers, men of merit, and those experienced in the terrain. He would inquire what history recorded the ancient Emperors to have done in similar cases, and so on for each matter. To say nothing of what once moved the Persians to laughter, because among the Romans, uneducated men held the office of judges while the learned stood behind them, as Marcellinus testifies in book 23, near the end.

Yet, we do not entirely disapprove of the institutions of the ancient Emperors, provided that they chose military men, distinguished for their courage, to rule the provinces in their place. For if the men sent to the provinces were renowned for their experience in affairs and for civil prudence, who does not see that they could aptly govern their political state, preserve them, and defend them from the assault of enemies? Although, therefore, they might not have been instructed in the exact science of the laws, they were nevertheless able to render justice well through the aid of their assessors. This is certainly for the same reason that, in our own time, some provinces are governed by viceroys <term>ProReges</term> <gloss>viceroys/governors</gloss> appointed by Princes. In these cases, where civil prudence shines, who is it that requires the highest science of the laws? It is sufficient, and it is necessary, for them to preside with their authority so that the assessors, who in truth pronounce the law, are deterred from passing bad judgments due to corruption; furthermore, it makes the authority of the judgment more august and its splendor greater. But a different standard held, and indeed had to hold, for other judges, upon whom rested the sole care of resolving forensic 
<pb n="10"/>controversies. These men had to be most learned in the laws and customs of the Roman people during the time of the Emperors. For then, because judges were required to render justice based on their own knowledge of the laws, it is clear enough that they ought not to have been appointed to the office of judging if they were unskilled. C. quando provoc. non est neces."</note>). This was carried so far that, as Gaius responded in the time of Hadrian and Justinian approved (as found in *Digest, Book on Extraordinary Cognition and Institutes on Obligations arising from quasi-delicts* <note>original: "l. ult. ff. d. extraord. cognit. & pr. Instit. d. oblig. quæ ex quasi malef."</note>), a judge made the lawsuit his own and began to be held liable as if for a crime <term>quasi ex maleficio</term> <gloss>as if from a crime</gloss> if he judged poorly through imprudence and lack of skill. Not to mention that it is the office of a judge not only to hear what the litigants bring forward of their own accord, but also to inquire from them whether they wish to bring forward or answer anything specifically regarding the matter (*Codex, Title: Judges* <note>original: "l. judices 9. C. d. judic."</note>). From this, the learned argue that the door to judicial office is closed to the unskilled, because one who is unskilled in jurisprudence and the laws cannot conduct such interrogations. But Emperor Justinian confirms our opinion most clearly; in the *Novellae 82, preface*, he cuts off all access to an unskilled judge.

> "For we did not think," says the most lauded Emperor, "that it was proper to have the names of certain judges, especially those unlearned in the laws and, furthermore, lacking experience in cases. For our administrators are accompanied in all ways by assessors, who explain matters of law and fulfill their duties. Since they are occupied with the many cares they have under us, they rightfully fulfill the role of judges through the presence of their assessors. But those men who hold no official belt <term>cingulum</term> <gloss>belt (symbol of office)</gloss> and do not serve us, if they cannot know by themselves what is just, but must beg for the honor of judging from others, how will it not be a great vice for the republic not to entrust lawsuits to those who know by themselves what should be done, but to allow them to seek others from whom they might learn what they ought to follow in judging?" These are the words of Justinian.</translation>

### §. XXIV. 17

A greater doubt exists as to whether this privilege exerts itself with this effect also outside the place of the markets, such that while they are in progress no arrest can be obtained in any place of that province, so that at least the goods of a debtor existing in the markets might be seized when situated outside that place. This question seemed so difficult to Ziegler in the cited place §. 6 and following, that having presented arguments on both sides he finally suspended his judgment and desired a decision by the supreme Legislator. But we think this knot is not entirely Gordian, such that it cannot be untied by any art. For as far as it concerns the inhabitants of the market place, the words of the often-remembered Constitution seem to clearly intimate that they cannot obtain such arrests, by which they might seize the goods of their debtors situated elsewhere; for they expressly forbid the inhabitants from bringing any annoyance upon market-goers under the pretext of a private debt, and they would undoubtedly bring a grave annoyance upon them if they were to seek and obtain arrests elsewhere against their goods. We do not hesitate to assert the same regarding foreigners. For the security of market-goers is damaged no less by such arrests obtained by foreigners than by those obtained by inhabitants, and commerce itself within the markets is hindered. To which is added that solemn markets are not of one city but of the whole province, and therefore their privilege ought deservedly to be observed in all places of the province or empire. Compare those things which we said above in §. 20.

### §. XXV.

To this opinion it is primarily objected that the market privilege appears to be local, that is, restricted solely to the place of the markets. For just as, for example, the Leipzig markets cannot be held outside Leipzig, so too they say that the privilege of them must be restricted solely to Leipzig, such that it is as if it were affixed to it. But that market privileges can sometimes be extended also outside the place of the markets is evident from the fact that Princes frequently grant to a certain place the right of prohibition, lest within a few miles <pb n="18"/> similar markets be held. Above also in §. 23 we saw this very privilege of which we speak most correctly extended to the places through which market-goers approach and return; what, therefore, will prevent the same from being done in the present case for the most just reasons?

## §. XXVI.

The effects of this noble privilege are also not ignoble, among which in the very first place stands out the *most full and total security of those coming to the markets*; for they are immune from all harassment, vexation, and disturbance by their creditors, so that all judicial acts undertaken against them are also void by the law itself, and are destitute of all value and effect. By this method, the contentions of the parties will be removed, and just punishment will come to the accused. This is my decree, Aeacus, unless you, in your wisdom, think otherwise. 

AEAC. Surely, justice and manifest reason command me to think otherwise than either of you. For the crimes of these two are greater than to be able to be chastised according to their merit by such light evils, such as you yourselves have decreed. No pigsty of Orcus, no stable of Augeas, no dung-heap of Cerberus is enough to atone for the filth of Luther and the curses of Calvin. And although you might tear and rend both of them into small pieces and scraps through the crossroads of Hell, it will still be nothing compared to their merit. For they would be removed by only one kind of death, whereas it would be just for them to die a thousand deaths, and that distribution of members could stir up a tumult among the spirits, with these ones demanding this part contentiously, and those ones demanding another. It is also to be feared that these men, whom you strive to slaughter for their disgrace and ignominy, might think themselves affected by you with honor and a kind of triumph, when they understand that their limbs and bones are to be distributed one by one like the remains and venerable relics of great saints and demigods. Therefore, another method must be entered upon by us, so that, while the laws of Hell are kept safe, the crimes of Luther and Calvin may be paid for with punishments as just as can possibly be. First, indeed, you must establish, judges, that no heresy has been devised by anyone anywhere since the foundation of the world that is as harmful and pestilent to the human race as that which Luther and Calvin brought in with ill-omened birds <note>a classical idiom for bad luck or disastrous consequences</note>. No Manichaeism, no Arianism, no Macedonianism, no Nestorianism, Eutychianism, or Pelagianism (and yet these were capital sects among all) produced such a slaughter of souls, nor did they cast as many peoples into Orcus as Lutheran-Calvinism. Look, if you please, at the vast spaces of the underworld, run your eyes over the columns of the damned, review the ranks of the spirits living among us, count the Manichaeans, Arians, Macedonians, survey the Nestorians, Eutychians, Monothelites, weigh the Pelagians, Donatists, Albigenses, then recite the Lutherans and Calvinists, and when you have called each individual group to the account, compare these last ones with all the others, number by number, sum by sum, and by the immortal God, see if they do not exceed all those others by far. 

RHAD. You speak the truth, Aeacus. But what could be the cause of this so clear slaughter? For truly, if we weigh the ancient errors, some of them are indeed much more hideous than those which Luther and Calvin fashioned. 

AEAC. Even if there are some errors among the ancients that departed further from the truth of faith, they <pb n="22"/> were either of short duration or confined to small spaces of the earth, and they did not scatter their poison very widely. 

MIN. But there were others whose contagion flowed most profusely and infected almost the entire world. Arianism embraced the rising and setting sun in such a way that it left almost nothing sound at all. Nestorianism and Eutychianism occupied all of Asia, and Africa, Egypt, Abyssinia, and the entire shores of the Orient of India, and, propagated through so many centuries, it endures to this very day.

MIN. That I desire to understand from you, how it came to be. For that it happened, both the matter itself speaks, and Hell, filled with the multitude of spirits arriving here from there, testifies abundantly, but how it happened is not equally clear to me. 

AEAC. Yet this matter is not of very deep investigation. Come, tell me, does the eternal salvation of the faithful not depend for the greater part upon the use of the sacraments?

### OBSERVATION V.
#### When we speak of the restored image of God, it is not always necessary to add that it is understood as begun, and not perfect.

1. The foundation is laid in the fact that, although the image of God is not restored totally in this life, or in such a way that it attains the perfection of the state which existed before the fall, nevertheless, it is restored in man really and truly, so that there is no less a true conformity with God than that which existed at the beginning. Now, whatever things possess absolute truth (that is, things which are not such only by a certain respect or condition, even if they are found to be subject to different degrees regarding perfection), they can also, by their own right and merit, be designated without an added qualifier, so that, even if an inferior measure is not expressed, no one is deceived by the absolute appellation. Just as in natural things, not only those advanced in age and stature, but also infants and those of the most tender age are called men most correctly.

2. Indeed, nothing can be brought forward to the contrary, unless even the first consideration shows it to be frivolous. For the claim that the image of God cannot be understood as anything but perfect, without some qualifier, on account of the mention of God, is most false; because common reason dictates that predicates are not to be taken otherwise than as the reason of the subjects, or of the underlying argument, permits. <pb n="15"/>§ XXIX. Whether both parents, or only the father alone, ought to bring this rebellious son to the <term>synedrium</term> <gloss>council of elders/Sanhedrin</gloss> is a matter of dispute. Theodoretus, in the first volume of his works, Paris edition, page 168, believes that both Father and Mother must have concurred in the accusation of this son before he could be put to death. This opinion is approved with a white ballot <note>a classical expression for a favorable or unanimous vote</note> in the *Mishnah on the Sanhedrin, chapter 8, cited § 4*, where it is said: *if his father wishes to accuse him but the mother does not, or if the father does not wish to but the mother does, the son does not become a rebellious and stubborn son until both have wished it.* Then it is added: *If one of them (the parents) is maimed, or lame, or mute, or blind, or deaf, the son does not become a rebellious and stubborn son; because it is said: "And his father and mother shall take hold of him," therefore they must not be maimed; "and bring him out," therefore they must not be lame; "and they shall say," therefore they must not be mute, "this our son," therefore they must not be blind; "he does not listen to our voice," therefore they must not be deaf.*

§ XXX. But a new question arises: whether Deuteronomy 21, verses 22 and 23, *And if a man has committed a sin worthy of death, and he is put to death, and you hang him on a tree, his body shall not remain overnight on the tree, but you shall surely bury him on that day, for he who is hanged is accursed of God, and you shall not defile your land, which the Lord your God is giving you as an inheritance*, whether, I ask, those verses ought to be referred to the rebellious and stubborn son? Truly, the ancient Hebrews are of that opinion, and they say that if the parents spare the son and do not wish to accuse him, he is then put to death by the <term>synedrium</term> <gloss>Sanhedrin</gloss>, or overwhelmed with stones, and suspended, because if he is a notorious sinner, he is investigated by the senate. See *Jarchii on this passage and Elias Misrachi, the most diligent interpreter of Jarchii, in this place, Cracow edition, folio 304, column 4.*

§ XXXI. It remains for us to add something regarding the remaining overnight on the tree. This is certain: that among the ancient Hebrews, the guilty were punished by suspension after death, as is testified by, among others, Obadias de Saphorno in the *Biur al Hattora*, Venice edition, folio 73, column 1, where he calls suspension <pb n="16"/> an indignity brought upon the body after death. Abarbanel agrees with this, who in the *Perusch al Hattora*, page 379, column 2, vigorously defends this opinion. Compare also the *Aruch*, Venice edition, folio 93, column 1, at the bottom. For it is evident that suspension was a penalty, as Calovius teaches in *Deut. 21*. But why the corpses should not have been left on the wood is to be inquired.

§ XXXII. Jacobus Bolducius, Vol. 2, in the Book of Job, Paris edition, page 132, reports the reason from Andrea Masio as to why the law wanted those who suffered the punishment of the cross to be buried: namely, because from a long display upon the cross, one could easily be led to the opinion that the soul was extinguished, and think less correctly about the future resurrection of bodies.

§ XXXIII. But a better reason seems to have been that men might not be defiled by the touch of the corpse, especially since the uncleanness contracted from the dead among the Hebrew people was the greatest among all uncleannesses. The exposition of Lucae Osiandri in *Deut. 21, at the end*, tends toward this.

§ XXXIV. And thus the nature of suspension as it existed among the Jews has been examined. Although the wood upon which the guilty were suspended can be called a <term>patibulum</term> <gloss>gallows/crossbeam</gloss>, as Jeckutbiel calls it in his German version of the Bible on *Deut. 21, Amsterdam edition*, and the word "wood" is also taken to mean the gallows, as Flacius teaches in *Clavis, title "lignum," Jena edition, page 587*, nevertheless the punishment of crucifixion was not customary among the Hebrews, because crucifixion is not listed as a peculiar punishment, but only the mention of suspension is introduced, as a subsequent punishment. Nor does the word <term>talah</term> <gloss>to hang/suspend</gloss> precisely signify suspending a living man, or putting him on a cross, since it is also used for those things upon which crucifixion does not fall; for example, meat, fish, or bread are said to be suspended on a wooden peg, which are not said to be crucified. See *Nathan Benjechiel in the Sepher Herauch, Venice edition, folio 162, column 4.*

->TO GOD ALONE BE THE GLORY.<-
</translation>

For all things that truly exist in all of nature are either absolute forms devoid of matter, separated from all material concretion, divine, eternal, immutable, distinct, and not grasped by any sense, such as the first cause or the divinity above the heavens; Metaphysics, or first Theology, considers these. Or they are things composed of form and matter, and that matter is either ethereal and peculiar and proper, or elemental, in which there is privation, subject to motions and changes; Physics considers these. Or they are Accidents, which are in things composed of matter and form, of which those that are proper to matter or form, such as qualities, actions and passions, and the genera of motions and changes, <pb n="14"/>and are called <term>ἐνεργήτικα</term> <gloss>energetic/active</gloss>, are also considered by Physics. Those, however, which are common to both matter and form, such as magnitudes, numbers, figures, place, time, and local motion, are inquired into by Mathematics.

### XV.

The distinctions of all arts and sciences are rightly accustomed to be made according to the subjects about which they are occupied and exercised, and the ends toward which every performance or contemplation of them is directed, and to which all the precepts taught in them are referred. Parents should be more fearful regarding their children <note>referring to Law 8, section 3, Digest on that which is done because of fear</note>. Nor is it surprising, since they are parts of our own body and affection, for whom we often labor no less than for ourselves, and frequently even more, as VVesenbecius states in his paratitles on the Digest, On that which is done because of fear, number 8. To this point, the notable deed of Charlemagne seems relevant; when he understood that a father and son, accused of a crime, refused to confess even when questioned, he ordered both to be hanged, having proven that one of them had truly committed the murder. Therefore the father, seeing no hope of redemption while being led to execution, and terrified more by his own son’s death than his own, confessed to the crime in order to save his son from punishment. From this appears to follow that which is read in 3 Kings, chapter 3, concerning Solomon judging between the women contending with one another over a child.

### XXXI.
Or by craftiness or deceit; which we call evil not as an epithet, but for the sake of distinction and difference. For the ancients spoke also of "good deceit," and used this name for cleverness, such as when one plots against an enemy or a bandit <note>referring to Law 1, section 3, Digest on evil deceit; it is permitted if one’s word is kept; Law 26, Digest on captives and those who have returned from postliminy; canon 2, "Lord," 23, question 2</note>. For "deceit" is a middle term, which can be taken in a good or a bad sense, just like poison <note>referring to Law 3, section 2, Digest on the Cornelian Law against assassins; Law "who poison," 236, Digest on the meaning of words</note>. Yet, used simply and without addition, it denotes evil deceit.

### XXXII.
Or by age; yet not any age at all, but that which begins in the 14th year for males and the 12th for females, and lasts until the twenty-fifth year, without distinction of sex; for although females mature more quickly in body, they do not do so in judgment and counsel. Now, the praetor assists those under 25 years of age, following natural equity, since it is agreed among all that the judgment of such an age is fragile and weak, prone to many deceptions, and exposed to the plots of many <note>referring to Law 1, principle, Digest on minors</note>. The praetor assists these individuals, whether they are sons under power or heads of households <note>referring to Law 3, section 4, Digest on minors</note>, but not those who are of age, per the said Law 3, section 4. Except if something was done with a person of age, the disadvantage of which pertains to the minor <note>referring to the final law, Code on if against a decided matter, because from that an action on a decided matter is given against a minor; Law 4, principle, with the following section, Digest on a decided matter</note>.

### XXXIII.
Excluded from this, therefore, will also be infants, who <pb n="12"/>since they do not understand what they are doing, are obligated by no transaction; and where there is no obligation, the praetor certainly ought not to interpose himself <note>Law 16, section 3, Digest on minors</note>. Likewise, this aid is denied to wards who contract without their tutor’s authority, whether or not they have become richer; for in this case they are protected by the law itself, and therefore do not need this extraordinary aid <note>Law 16, principle and following sections, Digest on minors</note>. But when they are not held liable except to the extent that they have become richer (in which case they are civilly obligated and an action is given against them <note>citing Law 1, section 15, Digest of deposit; Law 5, section 1, Digest on the authority of tutors; Law 3, principle, Digest of loan for use; Law 3, section 4, Digest on business managed</note>), no prejudice is generated against them by denying this aid, since one certainly ought not to become richer through another’s loss <note>Law 14, Digest on the condition of indebitum</note>. It is another matter, however, if they have done something with the tutor’s authority that could harm them, as in the case of <note>Law 2 and 3, Code if a tutor or curator intervenes</note>, of which we have already spoken above.

### XXXIV.
Or by the *capitis diminutio* <gloss>reduction of status</gloss> of the person with whom a matter was previously transacted or a contract made <note>Law 2, section 1, Digest on capitis diminutio</note>. Now, *capitis diminutio* is a change of status <note>Law 1, Digest on capitis diminutio; principle of the Institutes of the same</note>. Just as status is threefold—of liberty, of citizenship, and of family (for these are the three things that we possess, not indeed by our own act and contract, but by public benefit, as the principles of the remaining rights that can belong to us <note>final law, on capitis diminutio; Locamerus on the beginning of the Institutes of the same</note>)—so too is its change threefold: maximum, by which liberty is changed; intermediate, by which citizenship is changed; and minimum, by which the family is changed <note>the said final law, in which the whole title of the Institutes of the same is found</note>. What each is, when, and in what ways they occur is explained therein. Ulpian teaches that this aid, or this restitution, pertains to the minimum *capitis diminutio* in <note>Law 2, principle, Digest on capitis diminutio</note>.

Or by absence; not just any absence, but a just one, if the absent person, or one who was absent, acts against one who is present.
