Pererius also urges this, saying:
> Since that translation of Enoch occurred more than six hundred years before the flood, it is possible that Enoch was led then into the earthly Paradise, which we do not deny lasted until the flood: however, one may not argue from this that said Paradise remained intact after the flood, and still exists, and that Enoch and Elijah dwell therein, etc.

What, therefore, have the Adversaries gained by this passage of Ecclesiasticus? I leave it to the benevolent readers to judge. I, for one, cannot grasp what defense they seek here, much less what they find. Moreover, that the words **INTO PARADISE** were added seems to be gatherable from another passage of Sirach, (z) where Enoch is said to have been taken **FROM THE EARTH**, <term>ἀπὸ τῆς γῆς ἀναληφθείς</term> <gloss>taken up from the earth</gloss>, that is, taken up or received up from the earth. For <term>ἀναλαμβάνεσθαι</term> <gloss>to be taken up</gloss> frequently means to be taken up. (α) If, therefore, Enoch was taken up from the earth, he was not taken up into the earthly Paradise, unless you wish to maintain with some—or rather, to talk nonsense—that Paradise is next to the Lunar Sphere, suspended as it were on high, and not to be sought on earth at all. Consequently, if Sirach had written that Enoch was taken up into the earthly Paradise, and yet had asserted that he was taken up from the earth into the heights, he would have contradicted himself, or would have located that earthly Paradise in the air. But even if he had said that he was taken up into Paradise, he would have understood, by the force of another passage, the heavenly Paradise, into which we believe he was truly received—as some from the very camp of the Papists assert, as we inculcated in the preceding Dissertation; not to mention the Fathers who, with Ambrose, assert that Enoch was snatched into **HEAVEN**, or the heavenly Paradise. To these statements, Cornelius à Lapide (γ) indeed tries to respond, but he satisfies neither the reader nor himself, as is evident from his own words.

Finally, and for the third time, from the Holy Scriptures—and indeed from the canonical book of Genesis—Bellarminus and with him the Jesuit Jac. Tirinus (δ) reason that Paradise survives on earth, because if the waters of the flood had devastated even Paradise, the dove sent out from the ark, or Noah’s vessel, could not have brought back a branch of green olive. But I would call this argument almost ridiculous. I do not wish to repeat what Pererius himself retorted to this; (ε) I urge at least this: that Moses most evidently testifies that the waters of the flood had already abated, or diminished, and that the ark had stood for several days on the mountains of Ararat. Why, then, could an olive tree not have emerged at the same time on some high mountain, which, because of its strength and firmness—especially with God ordaining it so—endured under the waters? Pererius also reports from naturalists that its leaves never fall, and Pliny testifies (ζ) that it lives for over two hundred years, and that this is agreed upon among authors. And thus we have also brushed away this third <term>ψευδύλλιον πῆμα</term> <gloss>false, little mischief</gloss>. Order now demands that, as we promised above, we show through the most solid arguments that an earthly Paradise does not exist even now. But because the thread must be broken here, and we must reach the one who is **ABOUT TO BID FAREWELL**, we shall defer this part to the following Dissertation. That one who is about to bid farewell <pb n="10"/> is JOHANNES HEINRICUS AMELONGUS, a local from Gera, the son of that most distinguished and learned man, FRIDERICUS AMELONGUS, <note>the recently deceased</note>, who, while he lived, was a secret secretary to the Archive and Consistory of Rutheno-Plavia, a man certainly most worthy, in human judgment, of having lived longer, but who, by a most bitter fate and not without the mourning of the pious—which escapes no one—has passed away. With what great care he educated this younger son of his, as long as he lived, the limits of the paper do not permit me to explain at length or to praise in detail. He certainly spared no vigils and no expenses. For beyond the fact that he ensured his son was polished through public instruction, he always maintained tutors at home who would repeat within the study what had been publicly inculcated and who took care that not even a little time was wasted. And he found those in whom, as far as I remember, he missed almost nothing. Nor did his excellent mother, who must be commemorated with singular praise for the outstanding gifts of her sex, neglect anything after the blessed departure of her husband (for I would not easily call it death) that seemed capable of contributing to the cultivation of his character. The son himself did not rashly absent himself from either public or private lectures; rather, he attended diligently, unless he was prevented by ill health or if matters arose at home that he could not remove from his own shoulders, lest he appear to fail his mother. He ordered his way of life in such a way that his teachers, whom he always held and respected as the parents of his mind, had no need for censure, especially not severe censure. He has publicly produced not just one specimen of the progress he made in his studies, and he will prove how far he has advanced according to the measure of his ability through his Valedictory Oration, in which he is to speak of the causes for which the most just arbiter of all things, God, has permitted so many victories against Christians to the most powerful Tyrant of the Turks, who has afflicted the Church with so many disasters, as well as through various <term>εὐχαριστικῶν</term> <gloss>thanksgiving</gloss> poems. He will appear tomorrow, God willing, around two o'clock in the afternoon, and will recite from the chair that which he has labored over at home. Therefore, we most fittingly ask the Most Venerable and Distinguished INSPECTORS, and OTHER HIGHEST MEN, and also the Excellent STUDENTS who now dwell within our walls, to deign to listen most benevolently to this son, who does not degenerate from his Excellent Parent. As we shall always recognize and celebrate this with the most grateful heart, so we wish for him, as he is about to depart, all things most prosperous, especially the fatherly grace of God, and the most abundant growth in his studies. VVOLFGANGUS WACHTER will deliver the <term>Λόγον προσφωνητικὸν</term> <gloss>speech of greeting</gloss> from memory. / Ebersd. Var. P. P. June 16, 1664.

<term>Arcas</term> <gloss>Hermes</gloss>, and the lyre that gives spirit to human minds,

Lyre with your fingers and ivory plectrum, so that we may modulate the festive
Song of gladness with a docile throat.
You also, <term>Pierides</term> <gloss>the Muses</gloss>, lean deities of poets, Muses;
Whether you leap toward the waves of the <term>Aganippaean</term> <gloss>of the spring sacred to the Muses</gloss> fountain,
Or play in the leafy fields of <term>Helicon</term> <gloss>mountain sacred to the Muses</gloss>,
Or tread the flowering ridges of the <term>Pimplaean</term> <gloss>of the Muses' birthplace</gloss> mountain,
Sweep the ground with a garment saturated in Tyrian purple,
And bind your yellow hair with the Parnassian laurel;
Let your left hand hold the lyre, distinguished by jewels and Indian ivory,
Let the other hand hold the plectrum, bend your sweet-sounding voices
In sweet song, and strike the resounding strings with a tender thumb,
And draw forth joyful songs with an eloquent quill.
The beautiful fortress lies where the <term>Mulda</term> <gloss>Mulde River</gloss> beats with rapid storms,
And roars around <term>Grima</term> <gloss>Grimma, a town in Saxony</gloss> with swollen waves;
Solemn marriage rites are prepared there for the noble
Bride and groom; the ample house resounds with the sound of the lyre,
Everything shines, decorated with glowing curtains,
And poured balms moisten the covered tables;
Even the earth, sprinkled, holds its own ornament.
<pb n="10"/>
For it bears various flowers: blueberries, marigolds,
Threads of saffron, rue, and stalks of green nard;
All things are dedicated to joy, and all things to the bride and groom.
<note>A small horizontal floral ornament follows.</note>
And now the groom, whom all await, is famously present.
Grimma, open your doors; come, Grimma, open your thresholds,
And throw back your gates; for no Babylonian
Concubine comes, nor a savage prefect of the Iberian realm,
But a hero, rich in the gifts of the Muses, seeks entry,
And is illustrious, born from a noble lineage;
I add that a wonderful skill in the Ausonian <note>Latin</note> tongue
Commends the young man, as well as his prudence in law.
Enter, excellent hero, with happy fates;
Who would forbid entry? Who would not admit to the city
A man worthy of praise? Who, unless they were lacking in mind,
Would not joyfully welcome the sweet pupil of the Muses?
For you (as the Muses keep in their memory)
Did not add yourself, in the green flower of your youth,
To those whose cold blood around their hearts
Blocked their talent, whom the <term>Camoenae</term> <gloss>the Muses</gloss>,
And Pallas and Phoebus drive away, whom the swift <term>Tegeatic</term> <gloss>Hermes, as god of thieves/tricksters</gloss> looks upon with a stern,
Unlucky light at his birth.
You did not imitate, in the years of your first downy beard,
Those Centaurs who become brutal with excessive luxury,
Competing with set wine, whose custom it is to wear out their strength by drinking,
Whom reckless gambling strips bare,
Whom Venus enervates, whom nightly drinking
Has cast out from their ancestral homes, whom poverty oppresses,
Whom swords and quarrels delight, whom Lethean <note>forgetful</note> sloth,
Given over to sleep, exercises with no cares.
But because both God and a better mind called you—
Secretly apart from the dull common crowd—to better things,
Deeming it shameful to have remained among ancestral hearths,
Which Phoebus provides here and there on Teutonic shores,
You took up goblets full of the Pimplaean liquor.</translation>

<summary>This passage invokes the gods, the Muses, and natural elements to celebrate the wedding in Grimma, praising the groom's noble heritage, his eloquence in Latin, and his commitment to intellectual pursuits over the vices of youth.</summary>
<keywords>Grimma, Mulde River, marriage, Muses, Apollo, Pallas, education, nobility, virtue</keywords>

<pb n="590"/>Look at those words, and consider that greatest of all falsifiers of the Talmudic codex, whom Socinus—in the passage you cited earlier—calls upon for support. He renders the prophet thus: *They shall look toward me, along with him whom they have pierced.* What, I ask, is this but to deflect this piercing elsewhere? For my part, I have considered it a sin to add even the slightest bit to the text, or to remove anything from it. Yet, in the Talmudic text, it seemed proper to substitute <term>elayv</term> <gloss>to him</gloss>, lest our people struggle with the prophet's meaning. Why? Because a change in discourse must be observed to avoid leaving the reader in doubt. And that is finally the reason for the changed word in the Talmud; <term>alayv</term> <gloss>upon him</gloss> is immediately subjoined. Therefore, lest some imprudent person think the persons change, it was decided to help the text in this specific way and add some light to it: *I will pour out the spirit of compassion upon the house of David and the inhabitants of Jerusalem: they shall look* <term>elayv</term> <gloss>to HIM</gloss> *whom they have pierced, and they shall mourn* <term>alayv</term> <gloss>for him</gloss> *with the mourning for an only child, and they shall be bitter* <term>alayv</term> <gloss>for him</gloss>*, as one is bitter for a deceased firstborn.* I do not even understand what could be more fittingly connected or what I could have brought forward more correctly. L. Remove the veil placed before your eyes. It is not consistent to change the former parts of that scriptural phrase from what follows. On the contrary, the preceding words confirm what immediately follows. But if you had wished to sacrifice to the truth and not mix the low with the high, I am mistaken, or this is the exposition you should have adorned: *I will pour out upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem the Spirit of compassion, and they shall look* <term>elai</term> <gloss>to me</gloss>*, whom they have pierced, and they shall mourn* <term>alayv</term> <gloss>for me</gloss> *with the mourning of an only child, and so on.* Now, as for your prattling about the Messiah, son of Joseph, toward what does it look? Do you mean our Jesus? No one would ever say that the families of David, Nathan, and Levi mourn him. Men and women curse and detest him every year, every month, every day <pb n="591"/>and execrate him. If you are turning some other person over in your mind, consult the memory of past ages. Has it ever produced such a Messiah, who is an offspring of the son of Joseph, whom the Jews treated most indignantly and pierced, and to whom could be attributed those things which can be assigned to the Messiah from divine oracles, and which fit most aptly upon our Jesus, the Son of God and Mary? For I do not believe you are still awaiting another Messiah who is celebrated by the name of the son of Joseph.

But even setting aside these words, let us finally look upon Isaiah, who by Jerome's account is more of an Evangelist than a prophet. It would be superfluous if I were to attempt to recount his words from chapter 53, since they fall so manifestly upon the Messiah and our Jesus. J. I am not moved at all. I am entirely convinced that whatever the prophet sang there is to be understood regarding the Israelite people. For what else does the eighth verse cry out, where the prophet explicitly says in the name of God: <term>Mi-pesha' 'ammi nega' lamo</term> <gloss>For the transgression of my people, the blow (was) TO THEM</gloss>. How, I ask, were you able to convince yourself to take this as referring to an individual person? For <term>lamo</term> <gloss>to them</gloss> involves many who have suffered evils. L. I am amazed that your mind is so fascinated that you unwillingly concede what your ancestors freely granted. J. I do not quite grasp which ancestors you could be preaching to me who are opposed to this opinion. P. By the immortal God! It was not tiresome to turn through the <term>Sanhedrin</term> <gloss>Jewish judicial assembly/tractate</gloss> so many times, nor was it permissible to ignore those things observed in the memory of your forebears! Read at least the final chapter, titled <term>Heleq</term> <gloss>Portion</gloss>. J. I have observed nothing of the sort, I confess. L. Yet we have long read these things:

> Rabbi Jochanan said: What is the name of the Messiah? The school of Rabbi Shila said: Shila is his name, as it is said (Genesis 49:10): "Until Shilo comes." The school of Rabbi Jannai said: Yinnon is his name, as it is said (Psalm 72:17): "May his name endure forever; while the sun exists, Yinnon will be his name." The school of Rabbi Chanina said: Chanina is his name, as it is said (Jeremiah 16:13): "Where I will not show you Chanina." And some say: Menachem, son of Hezekiah, is his name, as it is said (Lamentations 1:16): "For the Comforter (Menachem) who should restore my soul is far from me." And the Rabbis say: The Leper of the house of the Rabbi is his name, as it is said (Isaiah 53:4): "Truly he has borne our sicknesses and carried our pains," and so on.
</translation>

<summary>The interlocutors debate the interpretation of Zechariah 12:10 and Isaiah 53, arguing over whether these texts refer to the Christian Messiah or the collective suffering of the Jewish people, while also citing Talmudic passages regarding the name of the Messiah.</summary>
<keywords>Messiah, Zechariah 12:10, Isaiah 53, Talmud, Sanhedrin tractate, Piercing of the Messiah, Jewish-Christian polemics, Messianic names</keywords>

### COROLLARIES OF THE RESPONDENT.

#### I.
We assert that the Epistle from Laodicea <note>original: "Τὴν ἐκ Λαοδικείας"</note> (Colossians 4:16) was not written to the Laodiceans, but written or sent from Laodicea.

#### II.
And it seems highly probable that by this, the Apostle denotes the First Epistle to Timothy.

#### III.
In Ephesians 4:24, we believe that <term>hosiotēti tēs alētheias</term> <gloss>holiness of truth</gloss> is better translated as holy <pb n="18"/> pursuit of truth than as true holiness.

### IV.

From John 20:19, it cannot be concluded from <term>thyrōn kekleismenōn</term> <gloss>the doors being shut</gloss> that Christ passed through closed doors.

### V.

In Luke 24:31, <term>aphantos</term> <gloss>vanished</gloss> does not denote that he became invisible, but that he suddenly withdrew himself from their sight.

### VI.

We are persuaded that by the fourth watch of the night in Matthew 14:25, the hours from the third hour of the morning until the sixth are noted by the Evangelist.

### VII.

It is probable that the name Cainan in Luke 3:36 was added by Luke himself.

### VIII.

We maintain that the Gospel according to Mark was not written in Latin, but in Greek.

### IX.

The Pentateuch alone appears to have been translated by the Septuagint.

### X.

In the New Testament, such Greek language as prevailed among the ancient Greeks is not employed.

<pb n="21"/> of union be entered into, because a treaty was already long ago established, and its prince was created Roman Emperor by common consent. Therefore, all Christians ought to contribute men or money to this common cause according to their strength. I do not see how they can be excused for not doing so, unless they are held back at home by an inevitable war or a similar evil.

Today, however, alas, there are found those who not only do not offer help against the Turk and other impious men, but of their own accord provide the Turks with the means to destroy Christians. You would be mild enough towards them if you were to cast at them the utterance of Fulco, Archbishop of Rheims, spoken to Charles the Simple:

> Who would not shudder that you wish for the friendship of the enemies of God, and that you undertake detestable pagan arms and treaties for the slaughter and ruin of the Christian name? For it makes no difference whether one allies oneself with pagans, or denies God to worship idols.

What Grotius touches upon here regarding the Roman Emperor, the prince of the Christian confederacy, is amply confirmed by the dissertation of Boëcler, titled *The Holy Roman Empire*, page 7, where he also praises Heinrich Bebel, who in the previous century demonstrated that our Emperor is rightly called "Most Christian."

Therefore, he would have done a service to the human race who, with discernment, collected the law of Christian nations, especially that of war, from historians and the Fathers of the Church. For Christians are the *light of the world: the Church is a city set upon a hill.* Its laws, therefore, cannot fail to be illustrious. Although Grotius did not entirely neglect these, he was more fertile in pagan examples, which are not rarely mixed with shadows, and he left many things regarding the clear light of Christianity to be recorded by others as being worthy of memory. Indeed, the reason why so many and such great men and peoples behave so irreverently against right and wrong in this age is, I think, primarily because they read in Christian books about the pacts and customs of profane nations rather than Christian ones. But since, as has been said, the Emperors are the head of the Christian alliance, a work such as the one we recommend will rise primarily from their history, and especially from the lives of Constantine and Charlemagne (the latter of which Jo. Joach. Franzius has elegantly composed). For almost all other nations, and all the best of the Princes, have looked up to that Imperial summit as if it were a lighthouse, to such an extent that the Imperial Civil Law <note>original: "jus civile Caesareum"</note> has almost become the law of the world. Aware of this, our Emperors show themselves worthy of the protection of the Christian World <note>original: "Orbis Christiani"</note>, not more by sworn law than by the genius of Austrian virtue. And so, to depart from their cultivation and friendship is, in truth, nothing else; <pb n="22"/> than to turn away from the light and protection of the whole Christian order.
</translation>

<summary>This text advocates for a unified Christian response against external threats and argues that the legal and ethical framework for such cooperation should be derived from the history of Christian leaders and the Church rather than from pagan precedents.</summary>

<keywords>Christian unity, Roman Empire, law of nations, war, historical precedents, Church Fathers, Imperial Civil Law</keywords>

### XLIX.
Furthermore, the renewal or restoration of a Confraternity belongs to this class. Concerning this, Carpzovius provides some notes *on the pact of the Saxon-Hessian Confraternity*, where he prudently warns that it should be established only rarely. One must hold that both the solemnity of the oath and the solemnity of the renewal do not pertain to the constitution of the thing itself, but rather to the validity and more solemn illustration of what is already constituted. See Lord Hahn, *On the Law of Things*, thesis 75.

### L.
In place of a concluding summary, the more important effects of the Confraternity must be tasted, at least with the lips. The primary and more noble effect is that it introduces the Right of Civil Agnition <gloss>legal recognition of kinship</gloss>. For this is established by that pact, and it is so close that the right of brotherhood is conciliated. If you desire to know its qualities, hold them as follows: it is (1) <term>νῷ καταλαμβανόμενον</term> <gloss>grasped by the intellect</gloss>, as Theophilus speaks throughout, that is to say, intellectual; (2) reciprocal; (3) conditional, by the argument of law 54 *On the Meaning of Words*; (4) public (see thesis 40); (5) perpetual (see the same thesis); (6) solemn (see thesis 48).

### LI.
The secondary effect is that it grants a right in the thing <term>jus in re</term>, the same in a certain way as that which the other party to the pact obtains from the time of the contract. So that this, as an overstatement, may not offend anyone too harshly, we wish it understood with a grain of salt, so that one does not think that this real right is assigned to them in the second act <term>actu secundo</term>, as the philosophers speak, but in the first act <term>actu primo</term>: insofar as they have the hope that, through the continuation of the dominion after the death of the other family, they may obtain the free administration of goods. For which reason, nothing prevents the Confratres, even while the other family still survives, from being considered in a certain way as Lords, by the argument of those things which Paul teaches in law 11, *Digest on children and posthumous heirs*. Through this continuation of a right in the thing, which is proposed to the contracting parties, <pb n="24"/> I think it comes about that our pact is considered irrevocable.

*The narrowness of the time by which we are circumscribed puts a brake on my pen, even as I ponder more; and it urges me to put off what remains to be said to a more convenient time, if God shall grant it. Therefore, with the thread broken, we submit to public censure with due modesty those things which it was permitted to record at present with an Academic style for the sake of uncovering the truth, prepared both to refute without stubbornness and to be refuted without anger. If in any place there has been a wandering, or if anything has been said less fitly or correctly, or not perfectly explained—we who follow the probable, and cannot advance beyond what seems likely—the difficulty of the subject matter will excuse it. Just as in a game of ball, it is for one person to throw well, and for the other to receive as beautifully as possible, even if something was thrown amiss, and to correct it with art; so it is thought to be the duty of a fair Reader to bend certain things toward a more benign interpretation.*

I think it comes about that our pact is considered irrevocable.

*The narrowness of the time by which we are circumscribed puts a brake on my pen, even as I ponder more; and it urges me to put off what remains to be said to a more convenient time, if God shall grant it. Therefore, with the thread broken, we submit to public censure with due modesty those things which it was permitted to record at present with an Academic style for the sake of uncovering the truth, prepared both to refute without stubbornness and to be refuted without anger. If in any place there has been a wandering, or if anything has been said less fitly or correctly, or not perfectly explained—we who follow the probable, and cannot advance beyond what seems likely—the difficulty of the subject matter will excuse it. Just as in a game of ball, it is for one person to throw well, and for the other to receive as beautifully as possible, even if something was thrown amiss, and to correct it with art; so it is thought to be the duty of a fair Reader to bend certain things toward a more benign interpretation.*

this change later provided the cause for the greatest disturbances, as succeeding Kings strove to draw the kingdom back to the laws of a just and ancient rule, while the people had no greater concern than that nothing should be lost of those prerogatives with which they had been gifted through royal leniency.

<margin>Thuanus <note>Jacques-Auguste de Thou</note>, books I, II, etc. Io. Sambucus, Appendix to Hungarian Affairs. Bonfinius, decade III, books I, II. T. Cortese on Matthias Corvinus.</margin>
XXXI. But Hungary was agitated and shaken by more serious troubles after it began to have foreign Kings following the fate of Andrew III: such were the Bohemians, Bavarians, Angevins, Luxembourgers, and finally the Austrians, who rule today. For since the kingdom was undergoing such great mutations of its Princes, it was inevitable that it should be torn apart by many great ills: while not only were customs and laws dispensed according to the character of the masters, but also, for the new Kings, perpetual tumults and the hatreds of the natives were brought to bear, miserably afflicting the Republic. And although John Huniades and his son, King Matthias Corvinus, while Hungary fluctuated under the rule of foreigners, made the name of the Hungarians and the kingdom the greatest in Europe with victorious arms, such magnitude soon collapsed after Mohammed <note>Mehmed II</note>, in a war shameful to Christians, occupied Constantinople and, breaking all barriers, poured all his forces into Hungary.

<margin>Io. Sambucus, Appendix to Hungarian Affairs.</margin>
XXXII. Indeed, through this man, Bulgaria, Serbia, and Bosnia were seized: then, in the year 1526, with King Louis <note>Louis II of Hungary</note> killed at Mohács, while Ferdinand of Austria and John Szapolyai, Voivode of Transylvania, contended for the kingdom with the saddest hatreds, Suleiman, using this occasion, occupied the greater part of Hungary and the capital of the kingdom itself, Buda. Finally, what remained of Hungary fell to the reigning Austrian family, which gathers from the flames and ruins the remnants of a most noble kingdom: held as a part of that empire which is greater and narrower, which clings to the jaws of Germany and Italy, and has boasted of a renowned name through many ages.

<margin>Hieronymus Ortelius, Hungarian Affairs, parts II, III.</margin>
XXXIII. Thus, torn into two parts, Hungary is pressed there by the Turkish empire, while here it adheres to the power of the Austrians; a most harmful division, since the empire, which could be sustained by one, is lacerated and worn away between two, so much so that now Hungary is sought within Hungary itself. For peace between Christians and Turks is always treacherous and prone to incursions, since the treaty is not considered broken unless the engines of war are brought forth. But the Ottoman dominion is far greater 

<pb n="19"/>
than the Austrian, since out of the sixty counties into which all of Hungary is now divided, twenty-seven obey the Turks and twenty-five the Austrians: however, the remaining eight, which the Transylvanian <note>the Prince of Transylvania</note> has carved off, have also retreated into Turkish clientage. The Turks' principal concern of domination is that they might press all families of clarity and blood into a single servitude, to which they have condemned themselves through base reverence. Hence that great stubbornness of the remaining Hungarians against the Ottoman empire, as the people shudder at every trace of tyranny; nor are they even faithful to Christian Lords if they are compelled by sharp fear and pressure upon every hope of liberty to the reverence of Princes.

<margin>Barclay in *Euphormionis Satyricon*, book VIII, part IV.</margin>
XXXIV. More joyful and sacred is the fortune of those who rest under the gentleness of the Austrians. For there is great glory of liberty for the people, even though in a kingdom: and for the Nobles, there are vast riches, by which they hold a faithful multitude of clients in subjection. The Nobles have an erect mind and a spirit made for magnificence: for whom there is no greater care than to possess their prerogatives and immunities, which they obtained from the Kings, intact and safe. And the distinguished Magistrate, whom they call the Palatine, is said to defend the liberty of the people: whence, as Barclay affirms, many revere him as the avenger of liberty and an opposition to the Kings, just as the Tribunate once imposed a limit of power upon the Roman Consuls.

<margin>Ibidem.</margin>
<margin>Hieronymus Ortelius, Chronicle of Hungarian Affairs, p. 1.</margin>
XXXV. The more serious matters of the Kingdom are expedited in the Diets: here the sacred and greater civil laws are debated, here the judgment of war and peace. In these, the people appear through their Delegates, whom they commonly call the Estates. Among whom the Archbishops and Bishops hold the leading place, whose fortune was once ample and wealthy in riches, before the Turk had poured out into the destruction of the many, or those addicted to the new religion had stripped their rich patrimonies. The Magnates constitute the second order of the Estates, who, distinguished by the name of hereditary Counts and Barons, excelled with great authority after the passing of Andrew III. Then there are the Cities and Towns, whose power was great a century or two ago: now the strength of most is worn away by the Turkish war: many, even buried in their own ruins, can boast more of antiquity than of strength.</translation>

<summary>This text traces the political decline of Hungary following the death of Andrew III, the subsequent partitioning of the kingdom between the Ottoman and Austrian empires, and the resulting shift in the governance and social structure of the Hungarian Estates.</summary>
<keywords>Andrew III, John Huniades, Matthias Corvinus, Ottoman Empire, Austrian Empire, Palatine, Diets, Hungarian Estates, Transylvania, Buda, Mohács</keywords>

ought to investigate divine praises more studiously, and must use all things equally, which are in the creatures, for the sanctification, celebration, and glorification of the Name, which we could certainly demonstrate to the eye with many <term>Psalms</term> <gloss>songs of praise</gloss>, if we wished now to add more to the preceding points.

13. It is now also pleasing to pursue the <term>Offices of the Holy Spirit</term> <gloss>duties or functions of the Holy Spirit</gloss> from the *Third Chapter of Genesis*. Indeed, this is that *Chapter* which first opened the *Catholic Workshop of the Holy Spirit* and laid the foundations for the entire Church, the *seminary of all the faithful*. In this *Chapter*, the *Holy Spirit* first exercised a most useful and most salutary *Office* regarding miserable sinners, and proposed the means of true *repentance*, of *saving faith*, and of *salvation itself*, and exercised them in the sinful, truly *penitent*, and believing *subjects*. In this *Chapter*, the *Pentecostal Holy Spirit* first became an *Official* <gloss>administrator or functionary</gloss>, while he undertook and facilitated all things that would contribute to the *restoration of the Protoplasts* <gloss>the first created beings, Adam and Eve</gloss>, and all their *descendants* in them, and to their *reduction* <gloss>bringing back</gloss> *to God*. We, therefore, with the *Holy Spirit* himself as our Guide, or Teacher, or Revealer, or Dictator, will bring forth some things about such *Offices*, and, as far as it is possible, will explain them briefly.

14. We say, however, that the *Pentecostal Office of the Holy Spirit*, according to the present *Chapter*, is either *General* or *Special*. It is called *General* because it regards the *fallen man* in general who is to be *brought back*; and in this manner, there is not one *General respect* given, but (a) one *respecting God who is restoring*; (b) another *respecting Man who is to be restored*; (c) another *respecting the means of restoration*; (d) another *respecting the mode of restoration*; (e) another *respecting the goal or end of restoration*.

15. *Respecting God who is Restoring*, the *Office of the most present Pentecostal manifestation and appearance* is found to be general, because it is said that the *Spirit of the Day* came in the most present way, manifested himself by a most present arrival, and exhibited himself to the protoplasts as the *Spirit of the Day*, and appeared to them in his own convenient way. Where the *symbols of this manifestation and appearance* are to be noted first of all, <pb n="20"/> <header>ON THE MYSTERY OF THE OFFICE OF THE HOLY SPIRIT.</header>
such as: (a) the *Symbol of the Spirit*, (b) the *Symbol of the Day*, because the Holy Spirit made himself known to them as the *Spirit of the Day*, and instituted the Pentecost of Paradise as such. In this manner, *such symbols are*: (1) *Symbols that are primarily inchoative* <gloss>beginning or initiating</gloss>, because the Pentecostal <term>εργοδιώκτης</term> <gloss>taskmaster or executor of the work</gloss> appeared to them partly as the *Spirit*, who might move all corrupt things causally toward the cessation of corruption and toward the restitution of perfection; for as long as they lie fallen or corrupt, and remain in their corruption and are foul, no hope is seen in them, and no good is detected in them; but as soon as they are moved from the fall toward resurrection, and are moved from corruption toward restitution, then a new hope arises, and the first indication of the lost perfection to be restored is said to occur. Our *Protoplasts* lay fallen after the fall, and were *groaning* under the dominion of the serpent, they were *hiding* in the thickest part of the trees, and were *foul* in corruption, and conceived nothing of hope, and nothing of the thing, for their own restitution; they knew nothing of it, and were able to do nothing. But as soon as the *active Spirit of the Day* approaches and institutes his mystical motion, the old is suddenly exchanged for a new state. A dead body is not moved without the Spirit: but when the Spirit comes and truly moves, the dead is brought to life, is gifted with the Spirit, and is animated toward vital, animal, and rational motions. Partly as the *Spirit of the Day*, because through the fall, the shadows of mere death, the mere mists of sins, and a mere spiritual night were obscuring the <term>Macrocosm</term> <gloss>the universe</gloss>, but most especially were totally occupying and deforming the <term>Microcosm</term> <gloss>the human individual</gloss>, the most miserable sinner. Therefore, the *Spirit of the Day* wished to drive away the shadows, to reject the mists, to invert the night, and to promote the Day of the Kingdom of Grace, so that a new light might arise, a new lamp might be scattered, a new illumination might be initiated by the *Spirit of the Day*, and the whole Kingdom of Grace, and the faithful within it, might be illuminated. (2) *Symbols that are always continuative*, because the Pentecostal guest began to use these symbols for his office, namely both *Spirit*, or motion, and day, or light, or the act of illumination; thus he also continued the Kingdom of Grace through all centuries by *these same Symbols* in all the faithful, especially in the *Prophets* and other *Ministers of the Church*, which [he did] through all things.
</translation>

<summary>This text explores the Pentecostal Office of the Holy Spirit as revealed in Genesis Chapter 3, framing it as the initial restorative work of God following the Fall. It identifies the Holy Spirit as the active agent who uses symbols of spirit, light, and day to transform the fallen protoplasts and continue the work of illumination throughout history.</summary>
<keywords>Holy Spirit, Genesis 3, Restoration, Pentecostal Office, Protoplasts, Macrocosm, Microcosm, Kingdom of Grace, Symbols</keywords>

Antonius Monachus, a jurisconsult from Turin, in the second part of his *Treatise on the Correct Interpretation of Feuds* <note>original: "parte 2. Tractatus de Recta Feudorum Interpretatione"</note>, enumerates more modes of acquiring a Feud than anyone else we know, as he writes that Feuds are acquired by Investiture, quasi-Investiture, Privilege, contract, last will, Donation, Prescription, Sentence, Purchase, arms or the violence of war, succession, and the Right of Accretion. For the others are either easily reduced to these, or they are not modes of acquisition at all.

### VIII.

Petrus de Bella Pertica, Vulteius, and recently Antonius Monachus write that a Feud is acquired by the sentence of a judge. The assertion of Ludwell is more consistent with the law, namely that nothing new is acquired by such a sentence, but rather that which already exists is merely declared. It is testified that Vulteius eventually conceded to this in his *Summary, book 1, chapter 9, number 24 of the final edition* <note>original: "summaria libro 1, capite 9. numero 24. postremae editionis"</note>.

### IX.

That a Feud is acquired by Prescription, not only because it is presumed from the lapse of so many years that an Investiture has taken place, <pb n="7"/> but also in the case where it is certain that someone has not been invested, and thus that this mode of acquisition is distinct from Investiture, contrary to the common opinion of the Doctors and among them Vulteius, Niellius, and Lord Struvius, we shall agree with Lord Suevius, Ludwell, Fridericus Lentius in his *Disputations held at Basel* <note>original: "Disputationibus Basileae habitis"</note>, and Setserus.

### X.

For the prescription of a Feud in public or ecclesiastical property, Alvarottus, Isernia, Zasius, Gothofredus Antonius, Schraderus, Borcholt, Rosenthal, Rittershusius, Molineus, Mynsingerus, Duarenus, Hanneton, Schneidwinus, Fornerius, and Lord Struvius require 40 years. But Nicolaus de Neapoli, Baron Scenkius, Vulteius, Bocerus, Hunnius, Lord Snobelius, and Lord Ludwell judge that 30 years are sufficient. The former opinion pleases us, which Gothofredus Antonius and Lord Ludwell himself also testify to be the common one.

The bowels are excellently softened by turpentine mixed with <term>Iva arthetica</term> <gloss>ground pine</gloss>, specifically 1 dram of turpentine and 1 scruple of ground pine; or one may also mix in parts of rhubarb. Above all, I prefer pills of washed aloe, at 1 or 1 and a half scruples, for they excellently strengthen the stomach. Customary evacuations (namely the flow of the menses, hemorrhoids, and nosebleeds) should be procured, and if they do not flow of their own accord, they must be aided by art so that nature may be relieved.

### LIX.

With this regimen established, in those where blood abounds, bloodletting is beneficial, especially in the autumn and spring, in the manner we mentioned above. In weaker persons, scarification and leeches have their place; scarifications may be repeated every three months. In gout, they should not be applied to the feet, lest more [humor] be attracted. When blood and melancholic humor abound, some greatly praise leeches applied to the hemorrhoids in the autumn. Nor are <term>fonticuli</term> <gloss>small artificial ulcers or setons for drainage</gloss> without their merit (based on experience) on the arms or legs, and so forth. Likewise, vomit-inducing and sweat-inducing agents are beneficial; the most illustrious practitioners prefer induced vomiting to all types of purges, alongside Avicenna, and it should be excited every month, especially when an attack is to be feared. Regarding diaphoretics and diuretics, see above. For those with <term>cacochymia</term> <gloss>depraved or corrupt humors</gloss>, purges should be applied, especially in spring and autumn before the equinox. Regarding purgatives, besides those we noted above, the following <term>Pilulae Magistrales</term> <gloss>Master Pills</gloss> are excellent: Take half an ounce of washed aloes, 1 and a half drams of white hermodactyls, 1 and a half drams of turbith, and the same amount of agaric, 6 grains each of mastic, Indian salt, and ginger, with syrup of roses and juice of wormwood. Let pills be made. The gout powder ascribed to Crollius Paracelsus is praised, differing little from <term>Caryocostinum</term> <gloss>a medicinal electuary of cloves and costus root</gloss>.

### LX.

Truly, in treatment and preservation, before using purgatives, administer preparations such as syrup from an infusion of roses, betony, myrtle, and stoechas <gloss>French lavender</gloss>; or syrup of sorrel juice, sugar, syrup of lemon peel, betony water, syrup of borage, lemon balm water, and sorrel or plantain water. Quercetanus's <term>Hydromel Antipodagricum</term> <gloss>anti-gout honey-water</gloss> is excellent.

### LXI.

The use of specifics and anti-gout remedies should also not be neglected, of which the ancients, such as Aetius, Trallianus, and others, as well as <pb n="17"/> those following them, Sennertus in his specific treatise on arthritis, and also Horstius the Elder in the second part of his *Observations*, book 3, and Crato from time to time, make mention. What Paracelsus also promises regarding black hellebore is read in his own treatise on <term>Contractura</term> <gloss>contraction of the limbs</gloss>, which Helmontius also recommends for these uses. The spirit of quicklime, first described by Basilius Valentinus but since then revived by certain empirics with additives, provides a sufficiently safe and not-to-be-neglected prophylactic.

### LXII.

Finally, the affected parts must be strengthened, for which the <term>Emplastrum Diachalciteos</term> <gloss>a lead-based plaster</gloss> is recommended, from which a shoe covering the foot may be made, or it may even be worn during the day, removed at night, dried, and put back on in the morning. Urine of young boys [is recommended]; hence fullers are less frequently troubled by gout. Grape skins, to which may be added an ointment of earthworms and marshmallow root. Herbs and flowers (of which we spoke above regarding anodynes) should be boiled in false chalybeate water <note>water infused with iron</note> and the vapor received. Moderate exercise on an empty stomach is beneficial, as is frequent friction with false oil. Frequent cleansing with a dry sponge, or one lightly moistened with a decoction, can be done. Fumigation is praised by others, made from sandarach, frankincense, cloves, cinnamon, and nutmeg, pulverized and mixed with gum tragacanth. Omphacine oil of roses with added yellow powder of roses is proven. It is excellent if the affected part is protected with hare skins. Crato suggests placing mugwort and wormwood under the soles of the feet. A dog skin may be anointed with costus oil. The intemperance of the principal parts must also be corrected. For strengthening the stomach, <term>Elixir Proprietatis</term> <gloss>a medicinal tincture of aloe, myrrh, and saffron</gloss> is beneficial. Paracelsi</translation>

<header>OF CORNELIUS CELSUS</header>

The surgical <term>fibula</term> <gloss>clasp/pin</gloss> of Celsus was also a metallic fastener, as the force of his words regarding the <term>fibula</term> clearly shows; it also bites into several places where the fastener is inserted, which are situated beneath those that pertain to the suture, where the needle passes through the body more frequently. That it was characteristic of a <term>fibula</term> to bite (which is a property of a harder substance), all Latin authors teach. Virgil:

<margin>12. Aeneid</margin>
> — — *where the belt, sewn with gold,*
> *is worn, and the* **FIBULA BITES** *the joinings of the sides.*

<margin>2. In Eutropium</margin>
Claudian:
> *Closer to the breasts the* **FIBULA BIT** *the garments.*

<margin>Book 1</margin>
Symmachus:
> *I have a* **FIBULA** *that bites my military cloak.*

<margin>Book 1, On the Mantle</margin>
Tertullian, on the mantle of Aesculapius: *It rested on the shoulders IN THE BITE OF THE FIBULA*. Jerome on the woman struck seven times: *He shook onto the ground the* <term>fibula</term> <gloss>clasp</gloss>, *which was BITE-ing the edges of her mantle*.

<margin>2. To Glaucus</margin>
Furthermore, Celsus himself indicated the material and form of his <term>fibulae</term> when he said they were called <term>ἀγκτῆρας</term> <gloss>hooks/clasp-hooks</gloss> by the Greeks. For an <term>ἀγκτὴρ</term> <gloss>clasp-hook</gloss> is a small metallic hook: and Galen used <term>ἀγκτῆρας</term> in the same sense and usage as our Celsus: whence <term>ἀγκτηριασμός</term> <gloss>infibulation</gloss>; <term>ἀγκτηριάζειν</term> <gloss>to infibulate</gloss>; and <term>ἀγκτῆρας ἐπιτιθֵναι</term> <gloss>to attach clasp-hooks</gloss>, 
<pb n="11"/>
<header>ACIA EXPLICATED.</header>
<sig>B 2</sig>

or *to place hooks upon*, in the same author.

<margin>Book 7. ch. 7. & 26</margin>
Finally, Celsus in other places, rendering <term>τοὺς ἀγκτῆρας</term> <gloss>the clasp-hooks</gloss> in Latin, said *a sharp little hook, blunt hooks, and to be seized by little hooks*: which formulas of speaking sufficiently indicate that the material of the <term>ἀγκτῆρας</term> was metallic; as *Guido* clearly teaches, contrary to what *Fallopius* judged, not having understood the Latin word <term>ACIA</term> <gloss>thread/suture</gloss>: for all <term>fibulae</term>, as *Oribasius* relates, were made of bronze, iron, or gold.

<margin>Book on Mechanics, ch. 4.</margin>
This, therefore, was the placing of the <term>fibulae</term> or hooks according to *Celsus*. Where there was a wound in the flesh, and it was gaping; and the edges could not easily be drawn together, whence a suture was unsuitable; <term>fibulae</term> were placed on the wound in this manner. With one hook of the <term>fibula</term> (for it consisted of two, one curved, the other re-curved, in the shape of a somewhat elongated letter S, and hooked on both sides), the other lip of the wound was seized with the flesh and skin from within, beginning from the flesh. Then, with the <term>fibula</term> retracted, the opposite lip was seized by the other hook from the outside, biting the skin before the flesh: and thus the edges of the gaping wound, which could not be sewn together because of the distance, were drawn back and held. In almost the same way, *Guido* says: *The lips of the wound are brought together in turn with hooks, which ought to be small in proportion to the member; on both sides*
</translation>

<summary>This text examines the historical and medical definition of the "fibula" as a metallic surgical device (clasp or hook) used by Celsus for closing wounds, contrasting this technical usage with its common application as a garment fastener.</summary>
<keywords>Celsus, fibula, surgical hooks, ancient medicine, medical philology, infibulation, Guido, Fallopius, Oribasius</keywords>

### §. XV.

We must now consider the images of the ancients, which were effigies of men shaped and shadowed with colors, and were preserved either in a more prominent part of their buildings or in some public place.

### §. XVI.

Most trace their origin to the idols of the heathen gods. Mortals, considering this honor and worship of images to be superior to others, ensured that such things were erected for themselves, or at least for their deceased friends. (This is almost similar to how our contemporaries nowadays build such chapels in cemeteries for themselves and their descendants.) Once upon a time among the Romans, it was permitted only for those holding magistracies to place images, whence it was called the <term>jus imaginis</term> <gloss>right of the image</gloss>. However, it is clear that this right was not granted absolutely to everyone performing functions in the Senate and magistracy, but only to those who had served with distinction in those honors. Therefore, even subsequently, with the authority of the Emperors increasing, it was not permitted to place images or statues except by their permission. *Suetonius in Tiberius 10*. Yet Godescalc Stewechius, in his commentary on Book II of Vegetius Renatus’s *De Re Militari* ch. 6, records that images were also placed for philosophers. He refers to an inscription in Rome on the Aventine Hill at the church of Saint Alexius: TI. CLAVIVS. SECVNDVS. COACTOR. CVM. TI. CLAVDIO. TI. QVIR. SECVNDO. VIATORIBVS. III. VIR. ET IV. VIR SCHOLAM. CVM. IMAGINIBVS. ORNAMENTIS QVE OMNIB. SVA. IMPENSA. FECIT <note>original: A Latin inscription noting that Tiberius Claudius Secundus, along with others, constructed a school with images and all ornaments at his own expense.</note>.

### §. XVII.

Therefore, when a funeral was to be conducted, the Romans placed the collected images of their ancestors on certain biers and carried them in front of the funeral procession. On feast days, they would also open the cabinet in which it was customary to reserve the images, and with various <pb n="10"/> ways and rites they would decorate them, scattering flowers, garlands, and crowns, and adding clothing in proportion to the dignity and public office that the individual whose face the image reflected had once held. They did not act otherwise than if the person were present alive; they venerated the likeness with honorific titles, and proposed and recited their achievements. Wherefore *Martial, Book V, Epigram 21, line 7*, calls these images "haughty."

### §. XIIX.

It is certainly most praiseworthy what is said regarding these images of the ancients: that they passed to their descendants, yet not so that they themselves could use them for their own honor and praise, but only for the glory of the family, which had increased through the man depicted by the image. And therefore it was conceded that this image of one who had deserved well could be brought out at the funeral of a relative from the family, not equally so that it might belong to all his descendants, unless they had likewise acquired that right of the image. See Hopping, who deals with these matters professionally: *De Jure Insign.* <gloss>On the Law of Insignia</gloss>, ch. XIX; Gabriel Paleotti’s treatise *On Images*; Rosinus’s *Antiquities*; Jacob Pontanus’s *Progymnasmata*, Book IV; and Polydore Vergil’s *De Rerum Inventoribus*, Book VI, ch. 13, who also complains at length about the worship of images translated to Christians.

### §. XIX.

The condition of statues was different from that of the aforementioned images. Indeed, a statue was placed for the dead or the living on account of outstanding merits for the Republic in some conspicuous place, as a lasting <term>mnemofynon</term> <gloss>memorial</gloss>. At first, they were fashioned from cypress, cedar, oak, stone, marble, etc., and subsequently, they were made from various metals as well. Their origin is the same as that of images. They used to be distinguished according to the degree of one's merits in the republic, or of their dignities, into equal, great, greater, and greatest: these were those that exceeded the human stature three times or more, and they were placed for the gods. Hence, the Exchange, <term>der Wechsel</term> <gloss>the exchange</gloss>, of which Hieronymus Pistor, book 3, question, and Berandutius [write] more.

### EIGHTH ASSERTION.

To have established a coin in a well-constituted Republic is not yet enough; the care of the political magistrate also [concerns] increasing and preserving...

<translation>
<pb n="52"/>
# Monday at Prime.

In the Time of Lent, Antiphon: As I live, says the Lord, I desire not the death of the sinner, but rather that he may be converted, and live.

In the Time of Passion, Antiphon: Free me O Lord, and set me beside you, and let any man's hand fight against me.

In Paschal Time, Antiphon: Alleluia, alleluia, alleluia, alleluia.

In the ferial <term>Officium</term> <gloss>office/liturgy</gloss> throughout the year, Antiphon: Serve the Lord in fear, and exult to him with trembling.

Chapter. 1 Tim. 1:17.
To the King of ages, immortal and invisible, the only God, be honor and glory, for ever and ever. Amen.

R. Thanks be to God.

This Chapter is said on all Solemnities, and Feasts of Saints, and throughout the Octaves, and throughout the entire Paschal time.

For weekdays only.
Chapter. Zech. 8:19.
Love peace and truth, says the Lord almighty. R. Thanks be to God.

V. Arise, O Christ, help us.
R. And deliver us for your name's sake.

Lord, have mercy. Christ, have mercy. Lord, have mercy.

Our Father, in silence until the V. And lead us not into temptation.
R. But deliver us from evil.

The following Prayers are not said on Doubles, nor within Octaves: but then, having said the Our Father, it is said, The Lord <column-break/> be with you. And the Prayer.
Lord God almighty, as below.

But when the Prayers at Prime and Compline are said with bended knees, they are recited according to the general Rubrics regarding Prayers and genuflection.

PRAYERS.
I believe in God, in silence until the V. The resurrection of the flesh.
R. Life everlasting. Amen.

V. Our help is in the name of the Lord.
R. Who made heaven and earth.

Then the <term>Hebdomadarius</term> <gloss>priest presiding for the week</gloss> makes the Confession.

I confess to almighty God, to blessed Mary ever Virgin, to blessed Michael the Archangel, to blessed John the Baptist, to the holy Apostles Peter and Paul, to blessed Benedict, and to all the Saints, and to you brothers: that I have sinned exceedingly in thought, word and deed: through my fault, through my fault, through my most grievous fault. Therefore I beseech blessed Mary ever Virgin, blessed Michael the Archangel, blessed John the Baptist, the holy Apostles Peter and Paul, blessed Benedict, all the Saints, and you brothers, to pray for me to the Lord our God.

The Choir responds.
May almighty God have mercy on you, and having forgiven <pb n="53"/>
your sins, bring you to life everlasting. Amen.
Then the Confession is repeated, and where it says "you brothers" and "you brothers," it is said "thee father" and "thee father."
The Confession having been made by the Choir, the Hebdomadarius says:
May almighty God have mercy on you, and having forgiven your sins, bring you to life everlasting.
R. Amen.
May the almighty and merciful Lord grant us indulgence, absolution, and remission of our sins.
R. Amen.
And he continues the V. Vouchsafe, O Lord, this day.
R. To keep us without sin. V. O Lord, hear my prayer. R. And let my cry come unto thee.
V. The Lord be with you.
R. And with your spirit.
Let us pray. Prayer.
Lord God almighty, who have brought us to the beginning of this day: save us today by your power; so that in this day we may decline to no sin; but always that our words may proceed, and our thoughts and works may be directed, to the doing of your justice. Through our Lord, etc. R. Amen.
V. The Lord be with you.
R. And with your spirit.

<column-break/>

V. Let us bless the Lord.
R. Thanks be to God.
This being said, Prime of the Blessed Mary is said, if it is to be said.
Then in the Choir the <term>Martyrologium</term> <gloss>list of martyrs/saints</gloss> is read immediately.
Afterwards the Hebdomadarius says the V. Precious in the sight of the Lord.
R. Is the death of his Saints.
And absolutely, without "Let us pray."
Prayer.
May holy Mary and all the Saints intercede for us to the Lord, that we may merit to be helped and saved by him, who lives and reigns for ever and ever.
R. Amen.
V. O God, come to my assistance. R. O Lord, make haste to help me.
And it is said three times: at the last is added Glory be to the Father.
As it was in the beginning.
Lord, have mercy. Christ, have mercy. Lord, have mercy.
Our Father, in silence. V. And lead us not into temptation.
R. But deliver us from evil. V. Look upon your servants, O Lord, and upon your works, and direct their children.
R. And let the brightness of the Lord our God be upon us, and direct the works of our hands over us, and the work of our hands direct.
Glory be to the Father. As it was.
Let us pray.
</translation>

<summary>This text details the liturgical order for Monday Prime within the Benedictine monastic office, including the specific antiphons, chapters, the Confiteor, and concluding prayers.</summary>
<keywords>Benedictine liturgy, Prime, Confiteor, daily office, monastic prayer</keywords>

<translation>
<pb n="11"/>— V —

Imagination alone can reconstruct the individual acts of the drama that played out in the souls of the masses as they wavered between Ormuzd and the Trinity. We know only the result of the struggle: Mithraicism was defeated, and without doubt it was destined to be. However, its defeat is not to be attributed solely to the superiority of evangelical morality or apostolic preaching over the doctrine of the mysteries; it did not perish merely because it was weighed down by the inherited burden of a bygone past, but also because its liturgy and theology had remained too Asiatic for the Roman spirit to accept without resistance. Conversely, that same struggle, which had ignited at the same time in Iran between the two rivals, remained without success for the Christians, though not without honor, and in the states of the Sassanids, Zoroastrianism could never be seriously challenged.

But the defeat of Mithras did not mean the end of his power. He had prepared the spirits for the reception of a new faith which, like himself, came from the banks of the Euphrates and reopened hostilities with changed tactics. Manichaeism appeared as his heir and continued his work. It was the last assault that Persia undertook against the Occident, and it was bloodier than the others, but it, too, would eventually fail against the resilience of the Christian empire.

This fleeting sketch will, I hope, reveal the importance of the history of Mithraicism. A side-shoot of the old Mazdean stock, it has in many respects preserved the peculiarities of the ancient nature religion of the Iranian tribes and allows us to better understand, by comparison, the much-disputed significance of the Avestan reformation. On the other hand, it has, if not inspired, at least <pb n="12"/>helped to define certain doctrines of the Church, such as the conceptions of the infernal powers and the end of the world. Thus, its rise and its fall contribute to illuminating the history of the origins of two great religions. During the time of its full strength, it exerted a no less remarkable influence on Roman society and the Roman government. Perhaps Europe was never closer to becoming Asiatic, even in the era of the Mohammedan invasions, than in the third century of our era; and there was a time when Caesarism seemed on the verge of transforming itself into a Caliphate. Attention has often been drawn to the similarity that exists between the court of Diocletian and that of the Chosroes. The sun cult, and specifically Mazdean theories, made popular the ideas upon which the deified rulers sought to base their monarchical absolutism. The rapid spread of the Persian mysteries in all classes of the population served in an admirable way the political ambition of the emperors. A storm tide of Iranian and Semitic thoughts broke in, which devoured almost everything that the Greek or Roman spirit had built up through laborious effort; and when the flood finally receded, it left behind in the popular consciousness a strong precipitate of oriental conceptions that never completely disappeared.

I believe I have sufficiently shown to what extent the subject I have attempted to treat deserved a more detailed examination. — V —

Imagination alone can reconstruct the individual acts of the drama that played out in the souls of the masses as they wavered between Ormuzd and the Trinity. We know only the result of the struggle: Mithraicism was defeated, and without doubt it was destined to be. However, its defeat is not to be attributed solely to the superiority of evangelical morality or apostolic preaching over the doctrine of the mysteries; it did not perish merely because it was weighed down by the inherited burden of a bygone past, but also because its liturgy and theology had remained too Asiatic for the Roman spirit to accept without resistance. Conversely, that same struggle, which had ignited at the same time in Iran between the two rivals, remained without success for the Christians, though not without honor, and in the states of the Sassanids, Zoroastrianism could never be seriously challenged.

But the defeat of Mithras did not mean the end of his power. He had prepared the spirits for the reception of a new faith which, like himself, came from the banks of the Euphrates and reopened hostilities with changed tactics. Manichaeism appeared as his heir and continued his work. It was the last assault that Persia undertook against the Occident, and it was bloodier than the others, but it, too, would eventually fail against the resilience of the Christian empire.

This fleeting sketch will, I hope, reveal the importance of the history of Mithraicism. A side-shoot of the old Mazdean stock, it has in many respects preserved the peculiarities of the ancient nature religion of the Iranian tribes and allows us to better understand, by comparison, the much-disputed significance of the Avestan reformation. On the other hand, it has, if not inspired, at least

<translation>
<pb n="20"/>has: but to compress this matter into few words, we say that this cannot happen by itself in any way, and experience testifies that philtres, or love potions, have rarely caused love but rather frenzy and insanity, the histories of which exist in many places. For love is a desire for a beautiful thing (whether it is truly such, or only appears to be so), and knowledge of a thing precedes desire and appetite; thus, no one desires that which they have never known. Therefore, we rightly establish that neither herbs nor any drug possess such power that it could compel and impel the minds of men, so that they, against their will, would love that which they have never chosen.

If, however, such a thing happens, it occurs by accident, and not because of the philtre insofar as it is such, but firstly because of interaction with the person who presented the philtre, and then also because philtres sometimes excite heat and venereal appetite (yet that heat is not directed toward a certain and definite person) in the one who has consumed it; subsequently, however, that person, as if stung by the gadfly of lust and frenzied, loves the first person they happen upon, especially if it is someone with whom they have spoken often before.

Retentions, which were mentioned above, generally can cause this evil if all habitual evacuations are interrupted, such as suppressed hemorrhoids or menstrual purgations inhibited by obstructions in the veins around the uterus; and the long-term retention in women has no small power (as <term>Galen</term> testifies in *On Affected Parts, book 4*). Note, however, that the suppression of menses is taken here as a prohibited habitual evacuation; for if it is taken as an obstruction, it is referred to the number of internal causes.

Finally, among those things that are applied externally or happen from the outside, the constitution of the air or the region can cause this evil, if it is cold and dry, such as autumn, or even overly hot or <pb n="21"/>sweltering, which burns up the humors; likewise, the bite of venomous animals, just as it can indirectly induce other affections through the peculiar quality of the poison, can do the same, and other things similar to these. Air in this place is taken insofar as it surrounds us.

### 88.

These things which we have said about these causes are not to be taken simply and absolutely, but with regard to their subjects upon which they act, that is, the bodies, among which two certain requirements are demanded, as <term>Galen</term> teaches in *On the Causes of Diseases*, chapter 2: namely time, magnitude, proximity, and the preparation of the body.

### 88.

Having explained the causes, we proceed to the *differences* of Melancholy, some of which are taken from the subject in which they are generated; thus, one is *Essential and Primary*, which occurs, to be sure, through a specific defect of the head. Another is by *Consent* or *Accidental*, if it is caused from elsewhere, and this is divided into *Universal and Particular*. It is called *Universal* when it is caused by the whole; *Particular* is what is named *Hypochondriac* in its species.

### 89.

By reason of magnitude, one is *Strong and Vehement*; another is *Strongest and Most Vehement*, in which all the melancholic symptoms appear most strongly; another is *Mild*, in which the symptoms are not seen with such force; another is *Mildest*.

### 90.

Because of the duration of time, one is *Recent*, which clearly has not begun to afflict for long, but only very recently; another is *Inveterate*, which has lasted for a long space of time and has struck deep roots.

### 91.

Because of the continuity of time, one is *Intermittent*, which clearly has exacerbations by turns; another is *Continuous*, which lasts without ceasing.</translation>

Since, therefore, each is understood according to different modes, they can easily exist together. It assists Nicodemus in a terrestrial place and by natural reaching or physical contact.

Since the union is not physical nor local, but personal, it is exempt from all laws of nature and the conditions of this age, so that no creature can intervene that could tear apart the natures personally united in Christ.

Nor indeed does the Apostle Paul conflict with these things said, who writes that Christ according to his humanity now, after the ascension into the heavens, Fills All Things. And as was said above, from the personal union Christ has the state of being omnipotent, but from the session at the right hand, the state of manifesting that majesty everywhere, and reigning as Lord established everywhere over all the works of the hands of God; which majesty of governing all things omnipresently, the Apostle calls filling all things, not implying a naked presence but showing a full administration.

<pb n="13"/> for the purpose of killing a man, which God in His law approved as just, either by express command or by evident consequence. However, that the proposed case is excepted anywhere in the command against killing is scarcely possible to prove with a suitable argument.

### Thesis XV.

Furthermore, they violated the negative precepts of the Law of Nature: *Do no harm to anyone*, *Evils are not to be done so that goods may result*. And since these precepts, like all negative precepts of the Law of Nature, prohibit that which is simply dishonorable, it is sufficiently manifest that no necessity can be found which could place the Dishonorable among the class of permitted things, or for the sake of which it may ever or anywhere be permitted to perform dishonorable acts.

### Thesis XVI.

Moreover, this case seems to participate all the more in the voluntary, the more the preceding deliberation concerning the means of obtaining food, and the subsequent choice of casting lots to separate one from the seven whose flesh the others would consume, is manifest.

### Thesis XVII.

Next, the life of one’s neighbor is not subjected to the judgment of anyone, unless to Him who is the author and Lord of life, and to whom He has given an express command to kill. Whoever takes the life of another, besides those so authorized, sins gravely: by slaying a creature made by God in His own image, a citizen of the Republic, or a member of a family—whether head or limb—he deprives that person of the supreme gift received from the Divine, which can never be restored to him.

### Thesis XVIII.

Furthermore, it is certain that they raged against the life of their companion for this end: that it might be well with themselves and their own stomachs. If, therefore, no one ought to be made richer by the injury of another, how can it be permissible that we obtain advantages from the misfortunes, injuries, and death <pb n="14"/> of others? If a license is not granted to anyone to use the goods of another, which can nevertheless be restored, if the possessor himself is held by an equal necessity, what right, therefore, will a starving man have over the life and flesh of another starving man? *Cicero* rightly says in *Book 3 On Duties*: "Would a wise man, if he were consumed by famine himself, take food from another man who is of no use to anything? By no means. For my life is not more useful to me than such a disposition of mind, that I may harm no one for the sake of my own advantage."

### TH. XIX.

*And it does not stand against this that S.P. denies that the survivors exercised cruelty against their companion, while the one who died received the steel into his throat with less pain, and the other inflicted it.* Answer: Is it not cruelty if those who are parents of their own lives slay, contrary to nature, the life of their neighbor—whom they are commanded to love not as someone above or below them, but as themselves—so that their own life might be preserved?

### TH. XX.

*And it does not stand against this that S.P. denies that the one killed had to fear for the peril of his soul.* Answer: He had to fear for himself as a <term>αὐτόχειρι</term> <gloss>suicide</gloss>. For the one who was killed had previously consented to his own death and later offered it of his own free will, even though he had received life from the supreme Lord not to be destroyed, nor to satisfy the hunger of another, but to be preserved.

### TH. XXI.

*And it does not stand against this that supreme necessity demanded this.* Let him who says this hear the response of *Aristotle* in *Ethics, Book 3, Chapter 1*: "There are some things of such a kind that we perhaps ought not to be compelled to do them by any force or necessity, such that death and the most grievous tortures should be chosen instead."

III.
</margin>

### TH. XXII.

*It is also asked, whether the pardon from the ordinary punishment for homicide was rightly granted to the Britons?* which, with Mr. Röhrenseen, we deservedly affirm.

*With pure flour, are of avail to nature;*

Rhosny <note>likely Maximilien de Béthune, Duke of Sully</note>, so that it might be sufficient for governing a very great kingdom. <note>Warem. de subs. reg. c. 6. n. 19. p. 93.</note> Some people quite rightly call such men **Practiken-Reichmacher** <gloss>schemers for riches/practitioners of accumulation</gloss>. The Prince should therefore be warned not to trust them blindly when they assert that he must shear his subjects thoroughly so that they submit their spirits and do not, relying on their wealth, desire novelties. They also argue that it is his own affair, and that the subjects have no reason to complain if they are left just enough to drag their miserable lives along; and that willows are pruned every three years so that they may strive upward all the more vigorously. Furthermore, they claim that if another excuse is lacking, one may be invented. Finally, they contend that all the goods of the subjects belong to the Prince, and that they possess nothing except by his favor and pleasure. And they argue that this right of the king is proven by the divine scriptures <note>1 Samuel 8:11 and following</note>. But who would believe these things to be true, when they are clearly lies? Poverty often does not break spirits so much as it inflames them, and history writers teach that the worst crimes are often begun by the most destitute. Even Catiline, surrounded by every necessity, is said to have joined to himself men "who had the greatest necessity, the most audacity, and abundance of all evils," but neither property nor any good hope. <note>Sallust, Catiline, p. 37; see more in Clapm., b. 2, ch. 23, p. 112; Scipio Ammirato, disc. 6 on Tacitus, lib. 17, p. 550; Forstner on Tacitus, p. 303.</note> If, however, property is taken from the subjects along with their very dust, who will wonder whence one might take more when nothing remains? A gardener cutting herbs from the root will expect fruit in vain. Not everything belongs to the Prince as the subjects' own, although in a sense everything is his. Things are his by reason of protection, jurisdiction, and administration; they are not his by reason of ownership, for these things are defined for individual masters. <note>Arnisaeus, on the Rights of Majesty, minor, b. 3, ch. 1, n. 4, p. 448; Seneca, On Benefits, b. 7, ch. 3, p. 173.</note> But as for what is said in Samuel regarding royal right, it appears to one examining it correctly that it is not to be understood as true and genuine right (of which Deuteronomy 17 speaks), but as usurped right. <note>Wilh. Zepperus, in Explanation of Mosaic Laws, b. 3, ch. 8, p. 215; Carpzovius, on the Law of the Realm, ch. 1, sect. 5, n. 14, p. 26; Ad. Contzen, b. 6, ch. 2, § 9, p. 336. Compare Gerhard, T. 6, Theological Commonplaces, on the Political Magistrate, n. 125, p. 760 ff.</note> Nor is it, however, a matter of bare fact, but one that has some effect of law, that is, an obligation of non-resistance. <note>H. Grotius, On the Law of War and Peace, b. 1, ch. 4, n. 3, p. 90.</note> (d) The matter therefore returns to this, that one may say: I have never seen better counsel given, but there is something <pb n="14"/> else that drives these men off course, namely the sweet scent of profit. These eloquent men—or should I say loquacious men—increase their own wealth in the Prince's name, and if you attend more closely, you will see that they especially advise those things from which they hope that either a Quaestorship or large windfalls will accrue to them. Therefore, the public evil nourishes these men, and quiet matters are a profit to them when disturbed, just as for fishermen, for whom the eel is not a prize unless the water is troubled. <note>Faust. ab Aschaffenburg, On the Treasury, Cons. 64, Ord. DCLVII, p. 312.</note>

Such men are especially assumed from abroad, whom the Prince is accustomed to prefer over the natives, but wrongly so. For their mind cannot but be foreign to a foreign Republic, in which they always think: "Here, nothing is sown or reaped for me." <note>Lipsius, in notes to b. 3 of Politics, ch. 6, p. 574.</note> Concerning the natives, however, we believe they would not dare such things, mindful of the land that bore and nourished them, although experience cries out that this does not always hold true. (e) Let the Prince avoid these men like a reef, <note>Bodin, On the Republic, b. 6, ch. 2, p. 1037.</note> and keep away those who are the true reefs of his safety. For if the subjects feel that they are exposed to the plunder of these few greedy courtiers, will they not accuse his rule as unjust? Will not the populace, having found a leader, seize these men to be torn to pieces? Will they not approach him with arms? The common people of France were moved in the year 1316, during the reign of Philip V, because he—relying more on physical strength than on strength of mind—allowed his advisors to act too liberally through his own negligence; for they, being insolent, wielded dominion. <note>Serres, on Philip V, R. G.</note>

These counsels, however, since they are uncertain in themselves and not without danger, are the worst for the advisor. <note>Drexeler, in Phaethon, book C, ch. 8, § 1, p. 188.</note> Even otherwise, if you have counseled something well, it is done under the Prince’s auspices; but all adverse things, and those that turn out poorly, are imputed to the one who gave the counsel. Alva had written to the King of Spain from Belgium that he had found a vein most fertile in gold, implying the tithes. Because of this, and because he had invaded the province with iron and flame when the army was brought up (whence arose the greatest disturbances), he was hated by the King and never afterwards softened his mind. Even the statue which he had set up for himself in Antwerp was pulled down. <note>Meteranus, part 1, b. 3, to the year 1571, p. 134, where shortly before it is seen cast in bronze. Compare Pet. Matthieu, History of France, b. 1, nar. 4, num. 6.</note> When he died, the King appeared in public, showing no sadness of mind. This is different from the ways of the ancients.
