<pb n="17"/>### LXXX.

For since the one promising payment <term>constitutor</term> <gloss>one who enters into a formal promise of payment</gloss> simply promises that he will pay what either he himself or another owes, it is manifest that he is obligated without the formality of words, nor can he evade the judgment through the exception of a faulty stipulation, since the simple agreement is sufficient for the plaintiff, which relies upon the preceding obligation and is clothed with this benefit of the praetor.

### LXXXI.

Hence the diversity of this action from the suretyship action clearly shines forth, since a <term>fideiussor</term> <gloss>surety/guarantor</gloss> is obligated by a solemn stipulation, and cannot be sued without it, as is the more accepted opinion of the <term>Doctors</term> <gloss>learned jurists</gloss> through the law <term>Blanditus</term> in the <term>Code</term> concerning sureties, and the law of stipulations, other sections, paragraph "the acceptance is sufficient," in the <term>Digests</term> concerning <term>verbal obligations</term> with similar ones.

### LXXXII.

The <term>constitutio</term> <gloss>formal promise of payment</gloss> is, however, more potent than <term>novatio</term> <gloss>the replacement of an old obligation with a new one</gloss>, because the latter does not annul the prior obligation, which the former does. And when one constitutes for another, both are obligated, which does not fall under <term>novation</term>, since that does not change the person.

### LXXXIII.

A bare pact of ecclesiastics from <term>chapter one, outside of the title on pacts</term>, does not elevate the utility of this action, since that is not received in the civil forum by a more accepted calculation, and the denunciations of the canons are in many places despised today. But where account is still taken of them, this civil action concurs with said pact and overcomes its associate in the place and manner of proposing.

### LXXXIIII.

Just as also the prior obligation can be weaker for many reasons than that which arises from the <term>constitutum</term>, because the latter adds something to the former either by reason of place, or time, or some other quality and circumstance of profit. And although sometimes nothing more is achieved in the <term>constitutum</term> than in the preceding obligation, yet even in that case its utility stands for itself. It is advantageous for the plaintiff to hold the defendant liable by more actions and to be able to choose from them which one he wishes.

### LXXXV.

And although in the formula mention is made only of money, yet that appellation now pertains to all things, both movable and immovable, having been transferred here from the <term>receptitia</term> <gloss>action regarding the safe-keeping of property</gloss>, now obsolete, and not only to those which receive function in their own genus, to which antiquity had narrowed it, <term>law 2</term>, <term>Code</term> concerning money promised.

<pb n="18"/>### LXXXVI.

Following the action concerning money promised in <term>Justinian</term>, there is the action concerning <term>peculium</term> <gloss>property held by a son or slave with the owner's permission</gloss>, which the praetor, moved by natural equity, introduced so that those who contract with slaves or sons in power would not be entirely defrauded, to whom owners or fathers permit trading in <term>peculiar</term> property.

### LXXXVII.

The name <term>peculium</term> is derived from <term>pecunia</term> <gloss>money</gloss>, as if it were "small money," that is, a small patrimony, in the last paragraph of the <term>Digests</term> of the same title. But sometimes it is taken also for any patrimony of anyone, <term>law Cogit</term>, <term>Digests</term> on the <term>Trebellian Senate Consult</term>. Sometimes also for money laid aside for the sake of protection, whence it is usually said, "money without a <term>peculium</term> is fragile," <term>law Si Chorus</term>, paragraph 1, <term>Digests</term> on <term>legacies 3</term>. In this form of action, however, <term>peculium</term> is accepted in that meaning which was placed by us in the first position.

### LXXXVIII.

So that a <term>peculium</term> is that which a son in power or a slave has as his own by the permission of his father or master, separate from the paternal or master's accounts, that having been deducted which is owed to the father or master, or to those who are in their power, guardianship, or care, <term>law Peculium</term>, and the following law, last paragraph, <term>Digests</term> on the <term>peculium</term>.

### LXXXIX.

Not that we think it necessary that the master or father always grant a <term>peculium</term> to those they have in their power, since by that contract the son of a madman and the slave of a ward or a madman would not have a <term>peculium</term>; but because we think with Julian that it is enough that such persons do not take away the <term>peculium</term> from those to whom former masters or fathers had previously granted it, <term>law Quam Tuberonis</term>, <term>Digests</term> on the <term>peculium</term>.

### LXXXX.

Although we attribute a <term>peculium</term> to both slaves and sons in power, we do not do so in the same way for both. For the <term>peculium</term> of slaves is uniform, but that of sons is fourfold, according to whether it proceeds from different causes: from the father or his intent, from elsewhere, or simply from elsewhere, or from military industry or the like.

### LXXXXI.

Nor, however, is this action accommodated to all these species, but only to the <term>profectitium</term> <gloss>peculium derived from the father's estate</gloss>, since in the <term>castrense</term> <gloss>military property</gloss> or its like, the son in power</translation>

<pb n="11"/>renowned lineage, our Baron had as his father Lord <term>Henricus</term> <gloss>Henry</gloss>, who, having administered the Republic with singular praise for his prudence, equity, and moderation, and having left behind a brilliant memory of his piety through the zeal with which he saw to the drafting and printing of the <term>Confessio Gerana</term> <gloss>Gera Confession</gloss>, met his end on the 6th day of April in the year 1572. He had as his mother <term>Dorothea</term>, born of the illustrious family of the Counts of <term>Solms</term> <gloss>Solmensium</gloss>; she, excelling in the virtues of her sex, was so devoted to piety that she seemed to cultivate it alone, and she studied the Holy Scriptures so assiduously that she grasped with the utmost precision those things which pertain to living a righteous life or establishing the principles of faith.

Since there was nothing more excellent in virtue or more eminent in lineage than these parents, everyone sees how much distinction and light redounded to our Baron. Yet it is of no avail to be born of noble parents if one degenerates from the virtue of one's ancestors; for just as we call those animals "generous" whose work is strenuous, so noble men are to be judged by their own inherent virtue, not by that which is alien or adventitious. Therefore, his noble mother provided with the greatest care and the greatest industry that her son would not devote himself to anything unworthy of the traditions of his ancestors, but rather to the most honorable <pb n="12"/><margin>1527.</margin>studies of learning and to virtue from the very beginning of his life. For it matters much with what scents a fresh vessel is imbued. A mind corrupted from childhood thereafter delights in vices and fears the sweet scent of virtue; but one imbued with virtue loathes vices and considers nothing prior or more important than holiness of character. Therefore, our subject was handed over and entrusted to tutors and teachers, under whose diligent and accurate instruction he made excellent progress in letters and virtues at home; until at length, as a youth, he was sent to the Academy of <term>Jena</term> <gloss>Jena University</gloss> as if to a market of higher learning. There, dwelling for an entire year, he attempted and did nothing that was not worthy of the splendor of his lineage and worthy of his noble character. Then, by the command of his noble mother and his most illustrious guardian, Lord <term>Otto</term>, Count of <term>Solms</term>, he departed from <term>Jena</term> and went to <term>Strasbourg</term> <gloss>Argentoratum</gloss>, which was flourishing at that time with a multitude of students and, above all, with the fame of seven Princes and thirty-three Counts and Barons. Here he applied himself diligently to his studies for three full years and also devoted much effort to the faculty of oratory, so that he produced abundant, clear evidence of his lofty intellect, and some Orations, which are included in the second volume of the orations of that most eloquent man, <term>Melchior Junius</term>
</translation>

<keywords>Henricus, Dorothea of Solms, Gera Confession, Otto of Solms, Melchior Junius, education, genealogy, nobility</keywords>

Finally, they embraced this noble German knight—for they always show a singular zeal for our people, and they seem to bear with us more easily—who was learned in the first place, and, which is held in high value there, was well-practiced in the equestrian art and in arms. For, as it perhaps should have been said earlier, he had applied himself to these arts from boyhood; and he so wisely combined music, intended for the mind, and gymnastics, intended for the body, as the ancients used to command and speak of them. He incurred heavy expenses there, as neither the custom of the nation nor his own dignity demanded otherwise, especially since he had become quite familiar with the nobles at court. While he flourished among all as a guest, one very bitter event happened to him, in which, however, he conducted himself with moderation: he lost a brave young man from his household, born of noble station, when, unaccustomed to the climate and diet, he had suddenly fallen into a fever. In other respects, he was fortunate, especially in this: that hardly any other guest was more pleasing to that people at that time. <pb n="13"/>From Spain, he crossed into Gaul. Whence Jerome in letter 51 to Pammachius: Christ the Lord was not yet dead, and the athlete of the Church saw his Redeemer rising from the underworld. Compare Psalm 16, 10; Acts 2, 31. Since, therefore, we are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses, why should we not grant faith to them, especially because these saints of ours could clearly not have risen to eternal life if Christ had not risen, since our resurrection depends solely and most tightly upon the resurrection of Christ and his efficacy, as the Apostle teaches at length in 1 Corinthians 15, as will soon be said.

§ 13. The second [corollary] concerns the universality of the future resurrection. Resurrection is distinguished 1. into the singular, which is that of Christ, which occurred on the third day, Matthew 16, 21. 2. into the particular, [the resurrection] of certain pious ones, raised by Christ in the individual years of his ministry and by the Apostles, of whom the Savior says in Matthew 11, 5: The dead rise again. Such a particular resurrection was also that of our saints. 3. into the universal [resurrection], on the last day, where not only the pious will rise, but also the impious, according to Scripture, Daniel 12, 2: Many (that is, all, John 5, 28) of those sleeping in the dust of the earth shall awaken, some to eternal life, others to everlasting reproach. However, a distinction must be made between resurrection and resurrection to glory. The latter only, not the former, is denied to the impious. For the impious shall not rise—that is, they shall not triumph or stand in the judgment, Psalm 1, 5. These things are argued against the <term>Photinians</term> <gloss>a sect denying the divinity of Christ</gloss> and the Jews, who deny that the impious will rise.

§ 14. The third [corollary], therefore, is regarding the diversity of the meritorious cause of the resurrection of the pious and the impious. The resurrection of the pious <pb n="10"/> is owed solely to the merit of Christ, John 6, 39, 40; 1 Corinthians 15, 20. Christ is called the firstfruits of those who sleep, who, being raised from the dead, has obtained this for us, so that a full harvest might follow this offering of firstfruits—that is, the universal resurrection of the pious. For the harvest is the end of the age, Matthew 13, 39. Whence Tertullian calls the resurrection of Christ the example of our hope, the key to our sepulchers, and the pledge of our resurrection. And Augustine piously says:
> What has preceded in the head will follow in the body.

§ 15. The resurrection of the impious, however, even taken generally as mere vivification, does not depend upon the merit of Christ, but upon his just judgment and omnipotence, insofar as he is divinely established as the Judge of the living and the dead, John 5, v. 27–28; Hebrews 9, v. 27. For that unhappy resurrection of the impious would have been [future] even if Christ had neither suffered nor been resurrected, because it would not satisfy divine justice through the punishment and damnation of the soul alone, but [rather] of body and soul together: Genesis 2, 17. Because the whole man had sinned, hence the body also had to be resurrected.

§ 16. But one may object to this opinion of ours with the passage of the Apostle in 1 Corinthians 15, v. 22:
> *Just as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive.*

Where some believe that this verse and the whole chapter deal with the resurrection of both the pious and the impious together, since 1. the sign of universality, «all», proves this; 2. the subject [proves this]; 3. the scope of the Apostle [proves this].

§ 17. But it is more rightly established if it is said that this place, with the whole chapter, deals directly and immediately only with the resurrection of the pious, not also of the impious. For 1. the sign «all» is restricted by the Apostle himself to particularity, v. 1, 3, 18, 19, 20: the firstfruits of those who sleep.

I PLACE in high regard the deed of that Appius who was blind. <note>original: "FACTUM Appii illius, qui caecus fuit"</note> (Most excellent Fathers and Colleagues.) Having heard that a matter of the gravest importance was to be debated in the <term>Curia</term> <gloss>Senate/Council</gloss>, he wished to be carried there so that he might assist his endangered country with his counsel. I would imitate what I praise, were I not hindered by infirm health, old age, and a weakness of voice. For my concern for Venice is no less than Appius's was for Rome, nor have I been less involved in the affairs of my Republic than he was in his. Sixty years have now passed since I sailed on an honored embassy to Asia and Egypt. Having been admitted to the <term>Curia</term> <gloss>Senate</gloss> not many years later, I strove in expressing my opinion to adorn the youth with my diligence and study. But whatever I have achieved, let others be the judge. Certainly, I soon sat in the Council of the <term>Pregadi</term> <gloss>Venetian Senate</gloss>, and thereafter in the Council of Ten. Nor was I granted any year of respite from public business; I served as ambassador to Constantinople, England, Germany, France, Spain, and even traveled as a soldier in Belgium. I passed by no famous man in Europe with whom I did not dispute, and I diligently studied the ancient and modern writers on the Republic, so that what I could not attain through experience, I might learn by reading. But when some from the most excellent College visited me recently and, in the name of the Great Council, sought my opinion on the wars we are now waging, I wished to dictate these brief points to my secretary, so that I might leave behind for the Most Serene Republic, my most beloved homeland, a testament to my judgment as I die.

In principle, I determine that the end of our Republic is that which was once the end of the Roman: to spare the submissive and vanquish the proud, and—if the fates support our designs—to gain dominion over all of Italy and the entire world.

Secondly, for the achievement of this most noble end, while we possess many and great resources, so too are great difficulties and obstacles cast in our path, either by ourselves or by others. It is necessary to overcome and remove these with force and skill, for that magnanimity did not come cheaply to the Romans, nor to anyone who wished to extend the boundaries of their empire and impose a yoke upon their neighbors. Countless myriads of Roman citizens perished in war, and their own strength brought forth greater wars for their descendants, until, having been raised to the pinnacle of power and the summit of danger, they fell most abruptly and perished miserably. The Macedonian himself, whose homeland is a neighbor to us, counts more wounds than limbs. What of the Ottomans? Do they not, with domestic bloodshed and the deaths of brothers, bring security to their empire? Therefore, dominion over human affairs is costly. The reason for this is that many wish to command, few wish to obey, and because he who strives to grow and rule over others does so to the detriment and insult of others, he is therefore rendered suspect and hateful to all, and is forced to fear the many whom the many fear. I warn of this, therefore, so that we do not, in the shadow and frenzy <pb n="4"/> of our savagery, aspire to the empire of the world with our light vessels.

Thirdly, we must therefore weigh our goods, wealth, arms, men, and fleets against those which stand in our way, and against the enemy's forces, and not only those which are apparent, but also the arts and councils by which, if we can render ourselves superior, we may bravely wage the war we began in Styria, which we instigated in Savoy, and which we suffer in the gulf and sea betrothed to us, and thus enrich the Republic with the addition of new forces. If we are inferior, or if we must contend at the greatest risk to the Republic, should we make peace? We will obtain an equitable one while the war has inclined to neither side, while we fear and are feared in turn, and we will find moderate treaties.

Fourthly, one must therefore think seriously about the subsidies for the war, and especially this: that the gamble of Mars is uncertain. For often, he who has all the ingredients for victory is struck down by the weak. One betrayal, one word, one stratagem often ruins everything. But nevertheless, let us now see our defenses. The things, therefore, that can give us courage are cities, wealth, arms, men, allies, and confederates. When I consider our city, it is most fortified by nature, wealth, and splendor. In the frequency of its trade, it surpasses all the cities of the entire world, so that by a certain right of nature, the dominion of the earth seems owed to it. The Great Council, which is the basis of the Republic, holds more than two thousand five hundred most noble Senators, unmixed with any contagion of plebeian blood. We possess so much money that it is laborious and difficult to count the millions. When I look upon that, I am accustomed to exclaim:

> How much of land and sea could be prepared
> By this, which we hide in the vaults as anxious gold.

The ordinary revenue is two million gold pieces when we act most lightly; if we are more attentive to the matter, we will not find it difficult to collect as much again. If we judge by taxes, we will collect four times as much. I pass over the extraordinary revenues, which the Turks, Jews, and foreigners are forced to pay, and which come from fines and from the trade of the Most Serene Republic. If all these were to fail, we could demand tithes and, by paternal tradition, double or triple them. We could increase the tax on goods as much as we like. Other things also remain; for we can sell offices as our ancestors did after the League of Cambrai. Certainly, from that trade, when they were hard-pressed by that seven-year war, they received five hundred thousand ducats. That which was considered a high price at that time. During the Genoese War, we ennobled three hundred of the richer citizens after receiving money; for if we are in need of money, let us select a thousand of the wealthiest, and command them to be nobles, and grant them our privileges. Believe me, at their own expense they will wage an entire year's war for us. We have the triple mountain—the old, the new, and the newest (I speak to those who know)—from which we dig gold with less labor, art, and danger than the King of Spain does from the Indies. Our ancestors once also made use of lots and blind fortune. These are great things, but what I will add precedes them all, if you handle the matter with skill: while the Republic is in danger, each tribe, town, castle, and village is forced to provide and feed a certain number of men. For this is an ancient right. If that levy is carried out with the old custom and rustic simplicity, it will be a great aid; if some cunning intervenes, it will be the most outstanding of all. For if it is done so that wealthy, delicate men, averse to war, are touched by the levy, however much they redeem their exemption with money, we hold our arsenals full in every place, and men cannot be lacking. In vain do the Stoics strive, by revolving every depravity into matter, to liberate their Jupiter; certainly, while they seek to avoid Charybdis, they cast themselves headlong into Scylla. ### and translated into the number of the Gods.

<note>An ornate woodcut initial letter 'M' decorated with scrolling foliage and floral motifs.</note>

Although your Virtue dragged me, unworthy as I am, to the ethers,
Radiating Vision, with tremendous Majesty:
The flaming peak of fire, the heat of the Celestial point;
That impulse of yours, the power instilled, and innate:

That genius of yours, Yours, O that Yours of JEHOVAH
Spirit, and deeply diffused through your limbs:
That hidden, and all-powerful four-lettered <note>referring to the Tetragrammaton</note> Virtue,
By which you pierce the Clouds, you pierce the adamantine
Firmaments of Heaven, and the two Poles; by which, once they are cast off,
You pierce that inaccessible Inner Chamber of the Gods;
Seeing wonders, stupefied by mysteries, Scrutinizing the Great Works:
Which are in the fates, and hidden in the Heart of the Gods above.
I repeat that I am unworthy, and distant from You by as many windings
As the Earth is distant in degrees from the ether;
I, even now, am but crude iron, a useless weight of the earth:
Nevertheless that of yours, that Magnetic Ardor of yours <pb n="10"/>

With a mind and at the same time a grave body (the Nature of the Gods was stupefied),
Which in truth is not impenetrable to the touch;
As the wind snatched it to the heights of the Celestial Colossus,
Immediately, O Novelty! instructed, as below among the stars
THEE, for so many countless deeds made manifest in the orbs:
<margin>(g)</margin>
Vienna saved among them by valiant War;
And soon Your fort, happy Strigonia <note>Esztergom</note>, ordered to be so;
O auspicious beginning! they gave themselves to their own King:
Thence so often brought back, You know, O Nitria <note>Nitra</note>, as witness,
From the enemy slaughtered, driven back, and much put to flight.
Nor does neighboring Posonia <note>Bratislava</note> ignore such great Laurels;
Nor will anyone with an unmindful mind store away that so Great
Wonderfully carried off, by You, O Prince, worthy of so much
Strength, with hostile and excessive fury repressed,
From Mohaz <note>Mohács</note>, the Laurel, which suddenly was struck into gold;
After the fortress of Buda was bravely stormed,
And no less happily obtained Greek Alba <note>Székesfehérvár</note>.

Hence also in the Hesperian <note>Western</note> Lands, with the star turned,
The Frenchman having been compelled (with joined forces) to the City
Of Mainz <note>Moguntina</note>, captured by the swift feather of the claw,
Immediately to return it to the ancient Roman Empire;
And what pleases the gods above, to store it under the feathers of the Eagles:
Then in kindred Kingdoms, with the star having progressed,
The City recently snatched from the jaws of a relative,
And for the snowy Triumphs always about to follow;
Thus, I, having sung in the short modulation of my pen of him,
Deserving of the gods above, and placed also in a deserved seat,
Residing above the high gods with a palm branch, I conclude.

<note>(g) A series of memorable deeds accomplished by the fearless Lion.</note>
</translation>

<pb n="277"/>PYTHAGORAS. BOOK VIII.

<margin>A</margin>When Pythagoras set out to write about nature, he said this at the beginning: "I shall not admit any disparagement of this discourse, not by the air I breathe, nor by the water I drink." Pythagoras wrote three volumes: *On Instruction*, *On Statesmanship*, and *On Nature*. However, the work that is read under the name of Pythagoras is by <term>Lysis of Tarentum</term>, a Pythagorean who, having fled to Thebes, was the teacher of <term>Epaminondas</term>. <term>Heraclides</term>, son of <term>Serapion</term>, reports in the *Epitome of Sotion* that he also wrote in verse *On the Totality*. Likewise, he wrote a *Sacred Discourse*, which begins:

<margin>B</margin>> *O youths, cultivate these pious rites in silent peace.*

The third is *On the Soul*; the fourth, *On Piety*; the fifth, *Helothales*, father of the comic poet <term>Epicharmus</term>; the sixth, *Croton*, and others. Furthermore, they say the *Mystic Discourse* was by <term>Hippasus</term>, who wrote it to the injury of Pythagoras; likewise, many things written by <term>Aston of Croton</term> are ascribed to Pythagoras. <term>Aristoxenus</term> says that Pythagoras received many of his moral doctrines from <term>Themistoclea</term>, his sister. <term>Ion of Chios</term> says in his *Triagmos* that when Pythagoras wrote a certain poem, he attributed it to <term>Orpheus</term>. <margin>C</margin> They also say that the *Scopias* is his, the beginning of which is: "Do not be a king in need of anything." <term>Sosicrates</term> in his *Successions* says that when asked by <term>Leon</term>, the tyrant of the Phliasians, who he was, he replied, "A philosopher." He said that the present life was very similar to a festival. For just as some come to this gathering to compete, others to trade, and others to be the best spectators, so too in life some are born as slaves to glory and hunters of desire, <margin>312</margin> while others are students of truth. And these things are so. But as for those three little works of Pythagoras that we mentioned, the following are generally reported. He does not allow <margin>D</margin> anyone to pray for himself, because he does not know what is expedient for him. He calls drunkenness a separate destruction, and he rejects everything in excess, saying that no one should exceed the measure in either labors or food. And concerning sexual matters, he says: sexual acts should be done in winter, not in summer; in autumn and spring, more lightly. At all times, however, they are burdensome and little suited to health. When asked when <pb n="278"/> one should have intercourse, he said: "When you wish to become weaker than yourself." He divides the human lifespan thus: a boy completes twenty years, an adolescent twenty, a young man twenty, and an old man twenty. Moreover, these ages correspond to the seasons of the year: the boy to spring, the adolescent to summer, the young man to autumn, and the old man to winter. By adolescent he understands the pubescent, by young man the adult male. He was the first, according to <term>Timaeus</term>, to say that all things are common among friends and that friendship is equality. His disciples deposited all their wealth in one place and made it common property, <margin>B</margin> and they were silent for five whole years, hearing only what was said, and never seeing Pythagoras until they were approved. From that point on, they were admitted to his house and his presence. They abstained from the cypress coffin, because the scepter of <term>Jupiter</term> was said to be made from it, as <term>Hermippus</term> says in the second book *On Pythagoras*. It is also handed down that he was of an extremely beautiful form, so much so that his disciples supposed him to be the <term>Apollo</term> who had come from the <term>Hyperboreans</term>. There is a report that his thigh was once bared and appeared golden, and there were those who said that the river <term>Nessus</term> called out to him as he was crossing it. <term>Timaeus</term> also says in the tenth book of his *Histories* that he said those things that dwell with men are considered under the names of the gods as <term>kórai</term> <gloss>maidens</gloss> and nymphs, and subsequently are called mothers. <term>Anticlides</term> is the authority in his second book *On Alexander* that he perfected geometry, whereas <term>Moeris</term> had previously discovered the principles of its elements, and that Pythagoras was most occupied with the arithmetic aspect of it, and discovered the rule which is derived from one string. Nor did he neglect medicine. <term>Apollodorus</term> the calculator reports that he sacrificed a <term>hecatombe</term> <gloss>a sacrifice of one hundred oxen</gloss> when he discovered that the side of the triangle (which they call <term>orthogonium</term> <gloss>right-angled</gloss>) subtending the right angle has the same power as those which contain it. And there is an epigram that goes thus:

<margin>C</margin>
<margin>313</margin>

<margin>D</margin>> *Pythagoras once made a noble sacrifice to the gods,*
> *Because that celebrated letter was discovered by him.*

He is also reported to have been the first to feed athletes with meat, whereas previously (as <term>Favorinus</term> says in his third *Commentaries*), they were accustomed to nourish their bodies with dried and soft figs and wheat, as he says.
</translation>

…in regard to children, following the example of other public duties.

### LX.
For we also establish that guardianship and curatorship are public duties.

### LXI.
But what we have said regarding children we do not accept in such a way as to say that adopted children count, or those who have died, but only the survivors or those who have fallen in battle for the republic.

### LXII.
Likewise, he who administers the affairs of the treasury, he who is absent for the sake of the republic, he who holds some other power, he who conducts a lawsuit against a ward or adult, or he who is burdened by three responsibilities of guardianship not of his own seeking, deserves an excuse.

### LXIII.
But an excuse is also granted on account of poverty, poor health, and illiteracy.

### LXIIII.
Likewise, if a father has appointed someone as guardian by testament due to enmity, this very fact provides him with an excuse.

### LXV.
However, the excuse of one who relies solely on the fact that he was unknown to the father of the wards will not be admitted.

### LXVI.
Furthermore, mortal enmities which someone has exercised against the father of the wards or adults, if no reconciliation has occurred, are accustomed to provide an excuse.

### LXVII.
As is also a controversy of status which one has suffered at the hands of the father of the wards.

### LXVIII.
On account of age, those older than seventy years are excused, and those younger than twenty-five are prohibited, as are soldiers.

### LXIX.
Likewise, at Rome, grammarians, rhetoricians, and physicians, who <pb n="12"/> in their own country practice these arts, if they are within the prescribed number, have an exemption from guardianship and curatorship.

<margin>LXX.</margin>
Those, however, who wish to excuse themselves do not technically file an appeal, but must excuse themselves within fifty continuous days from the time they learned they were appointed as guardians or curators.

<margin>LXXI.</margin>
If anyone, however, has obtained an excuse from guardianship through false allegations, the excuse will be invalid from the beginning.

<margin>LXXII.</margin>
Finally, this must not be overlooked, that all guardians can be accused of being suspect, and that the accusation of being suspect is open to all.

<margin>LXXIII.</margin>
To the extent that women are also admitted to this, who, not overstepping the modesty of their sex, out of a certain sense of duty cannot bear the injury done to wards.

<margin>LXXIIII.</margin>
However, those who have not reached puberty themselves cannot petition against their guardians as suspect, but those who have reached puberty may do so against their curators with the advice of their relatives.

<margin>LXXV.</margin>
A person is suspect—lest anyone err in this matter—who does not manage the guardianship in good faith, even if he is solvent.

<margin>LXXVI.</margin>
But also, before one begins to manage a guardianship, one may sometimes be removed as if suspect.

<margin>LXXVII.</margin>
A removed suspect, if he is infamous due to fraud, is marked, unless he was a patron; if it was due to negligence, he is not marked to the same degree.

<margin>LXXVIII.</margin>
If anyone is accused as suspect, administration is forbidden to him until the inquiry is finished.

<margin>LXXIX.</margin>
The inquiry into a suspect is extinguished by the death of the guardian or curator.

teles. But the most prudent legislator wrote laws for his citizens. And Philistio, the distinguished physician, did more. Plato, whom you would not believe to be a supporter of astrologers, warned us against them and mocked them. He commanded this, just as mathematical reasoning also demonstrates it. Furthermore, Plato, who excelled in astronomy, would certainly hold it in higher regard than the aforementioned <note>referring to those who rely on astrology</note>. You will never find among the authors from whom you take your cues—Panaetius, Doychilax of Halicarnassus, whom I consider most learned in all mathematics—that he repudiated this entire kind of divination by the stars. I will come to the moderns. Nicolaus Oresmius, a very acute philosopher and a most learned mathematician, indignant at the peculiar superstition of astrology, attacks it. He deems nothing more fallacious, nothing more detestable, nothing more contrary to all orders, especially to the principles of <unclear>men of rank</unclear>. Joannes Marlianus, who was supreme in mathematics in our age and held it in high regard, not only abstained from these predictions himself, but had even begun to write about their falsity in his final years; for he was long-lived, though he did not finish it due to being intercepted by death. This man, glorious in his own right, used to say that he had the most certain demonstrations against the astrologers, and Luchinus, another of our friends who is himself a distinguished mathematician, has reported this to me more than once. Paul Florentinus, learned in medicine and especially in Greek and Latin mathematics, as often as one asked him about that wretched practice, would as often assert that it was uncertain and fallacious, offering as one of his proofs his own experience. When he had already completed eighty-five years, he had found no stellar arrangement in his own birth chart that he had examined most diligently. I could cite many of these, even those who live now and are astronomers, who feel the same way. But I do not know if they would wish to be summoned against those who are powerful in the celestial sciences. Furthermore, our Marsilius <note>Ficino</note> wrote against them, openly following the footsteps of Plotinus. In interpreting and explaining him, he greatly increased and illustrated the Platonic teachings. If he <note>the astrologer</note> corrupts some people who are eager for health by promising them certain aids from himself and from heaven, he <note>Marsilius</note> would rather believe that such things can happen than that they are true; this I can testify most faithfully, for I know his mind well, nor have I had anyone more earnest and effective in urging me to avoid these fallacies. And as often as we were together, there was no better opportunity or reason for us to laugh than at the vanity of the astrologers, especially if a third party intervened—and Politian often intervened, a wonderful ridiculer of all superstitions. Perhaps I should not leave unmentioned the judgment of our Nicolaus Leonicenus on this matter. Since he faithfully holds to mathematics, as you know, like all the liberal arts, he nevertheless judges this prophetic astrology to be so vain that he does not believe even those who wrote it, especially the more learned ones, placed any faith in what they were writing. And if I ask him why they wrote it, he answers that it was partly due to greed and partly to the fear of princes. For, he says, when those men, who excelled in measuring the motions and bodies of the stars—which is what mathematics does—labored day and night, they gained no profit from it among princes, who, naturally, cared nothing for how great the stars were or with what swift motion 
<pb n="16"/>
they revolve through the spaces of the heavens. When those men saw this, fearing that while scrutinizing celestial things they would remain destitute of earthly ones, they devised a clever fallacy to bind the minds of princes to themselves and make them lovers of their profession. They claimed that the fortunes of all men, but especially those of princes—that is, their children, their impious lives, their victories, and their health—depended on those stars. They claimed they had deeply known and explored what should be promised or what adverse events should be announced to each individual, having observed their long motions and natures. Furthermore, they added that they had remedies at hand by which evils could be repelled and goods confirmed. For if a man were fortunate, they would note that images could be fashioned from certain materials having an affinity to those celestial natures, and by marvelous machines, the power drawn down from the stars would make men most fortunate, such that powerful kings, either by touch or by wearing them, would easily attain whatever they desired. To gain more faith for all these things, they added that the more secret mysteries of this art had been revealed to them by divinity, just as it is read in Maternus that they received many things from the most powerful god Mercury, and from Pesosiris and Aesculapius. Then, indeed, illiterate and curious princes, most eager for the things they promised, were easily led to believe them, to foster the professors of such arts, and to excite these studies daily more and more with rewards. Our Leonicenus speaks and thinks of the astrologers in all seriousness, and not far from the truth. We must, however, take the greatest care that volumes of falsehoods written by great authors do not creep in to gain our belief. This is common to them along with all superstition. For the things that are put forth by them cannot be confirmed by reason, whether they themselves believe them to be true or whether they wish them to be believed by others; they inscribe books of such fables to the most famous and ancient men, and thus fish for faith in their error and their feigned authors. Of this kind is the book *On the Properties of the Elements*, in which he deals with the great conjunctions and secrets, which they attribute to Aristotle—a book for which the philosopher is in no way to blame, and in which he has no merit—just as they circulate books of Plato concerning magic, and those which they call *Institutions*, filled with execrable dreams and figments, and no less foreign to Plato than these remedies are to the honesty and wisdom of Plato. Thus, the heretics once called Gnostics showed the books of Zoroaster, by which they sought to make their heresy venerable through the antiquity of Zoroaster. Porphyry demonstrated with many arguments that these were new and feigned, and not by Zoroaster. But it is easily seen that those who are less versed in the humanities, though otherwise learned, are easily deceived and circumvented by these lies, because when they recognize the authors of such works—Marcellus, Phranza, and Iuvencus—they immediately distinguish the adulterated from the legitimate. Our astrologers, and the figments of superstitious arts now in circulation, are so abhorrent to all semblance of truth that they are exposed from their very midst. ## XVIIII.

Nor does it only gather the necessary qualities; truly, if it is the form of a living thing, it also provides a suitable bulk with the passage of time. Since that bulk is a certain accident inherent in prime matter, and prime matter cannot naturally be without a substantial form, it is necessary that along with the addition of bulk, another substance succeeds and is generated, and therefore that nutrition along with augmentation is provided; it is certain that this nutrition is distinguished from generation only by an accidental difference.

## XX.

Some things are nourished by food digested within, others by food prepared outside. Those that digest food within must have a small mouth and a certain crop or stomach. Most perfect animals also possess a ventricle, an intestine, a liver, and veins. The ventricle gathers the food that has fallen from the mouth through the ministry of oblique fibers, so that it would be necessary for it to rush out undigested from the pylorus, if provident nature did not prevent it with certain glandular tubercles.

## XXI.

Immediately the cooking faculty, which is identified with the very substance of the stomach, having applied heat as its primary instrument, sets to work diligently on digestion, while the liver, spleen, diaphragm, and heart urge the work on from all sides. Once the work is completed, the pylorus opens, and the chyle, entering the duodenum, heads straight to the large intestine and to the extreme part of the large intestine, which is called the colon, and offers itself to be sucked up by the most frequent mouths of the mesenteric veins while running through the winding passages of the intestines, so that it retains nothing except feces.

## XXII.

The mesenteric veins carry the juice and flower of the chyle through the mesentery to the portal vein, from which it is immediately dissipated through the whole liver by the attraction of any part of the liver through multiple and narrow branches. There it undergoes the confection of chyme or the four humors, so that from the hotter parts yellow bile is generated, from the colder and more earthy parts black bile, from the more temperate and subtle parts blood, and from the less subtle parts phlegm.

## XXIII.

Nor does it only gather the necessary qualities; truly, if it is the form of a living thing, it also provides a suitable bulk with the passage of time. ## XX.

Some things are nourished by food digested within, others by food prepared outside. Those that digest food within must have a small mouth and a certain crop or stomach. Most perfect animals also possess a ventricle, an intestine, a liver, and veins. The ventricle gathers the food that has fallen from the mouth through the ministry of oblique fibers, so that it would be necessary for it to rush out undigested from the pylorus, if provident nature did not prevent it with certain glandular tubercles.

# Corrections.

->E<-

**Echium alterum** <gloss>Another viper's bugloss</gloss> ] I confess that I do not yet perceive any specific difference between the common Viper's bugloss and that which grows here and there on walls among us: let others examine it more strictly.

->G<-

**Geranium malacoides sive columbinum minus** <gloss>Mallow-leaved or lesser dove's-foot crane's-bill</gloss> ] It is not sufficiently certain to me whether the small plant we understand here is entirely the same species as the lesser dove's-foot crane's-bill of Caspar Bauhin.

**Gramen alopecuroides minus spicâ asperâ brevi** <gloss>Lesser foxtail-like grass with a short rough ear</gloss> ] The London botanists call this crested grass, and I would not deny it.

**Gramen caninum** <gloss>Dog's grass</gloss> ] This is the same thing that Johannes Bauhinus describes under the cited title: and therefore what I noted here must be retracted, for I myself had not observed the panicle before I published the Catalogue: but I believed others rashly.

**Gramen hirsutum majus** <gloss>Greater hairy grass</gloss> ] I now suspect that this grass does not differ specifically from the slender hairy grass, but only in size and other accidents, by reason of the place in which it grows.

->M<-

**Mollugo montana sive Gallium** <gloss>Mountain bastard madder or bedstraw</gloss> ] These two synonyms, *Rubia sylvatica altera* <gloss>other wild madder</gloss> of <term>Gesnerus</term> and *Matrisylva 2* <gloss>woodbine 2</gloss> of <term>Tragus</term>, do not belong here, but to the first Mollugo of <term>Dodonaeus</term>, which has a round stem and is erect.

It is not yet entirely clear to me to where this plant, which grows here and there in hedges, should be referred; whether to the Mollugo, to which we have referred it here, or to wild madder. I do not doubt that this is the same plant which Johannes Bauhinus described under the title *Rubia angulosa aspera* <gloss>rough angular madder</gloss>, and indeed the London botanists call it *wild madder*. It is likely to me that the same plant is described under both titles. <term>Clusius</term> doubts <pb n="15"/> whether his angular madder corresponds to the Mollugo of Clusius or not. But indeed, the Mollugo of Clusius is the same as the first Mollugo of Dodonaeus, the mountain Mollugo of <term>Gerard</term>, and the more common Mollugo of <term>Parkinson</term>. For the figure is everywhere the same, and both the figure and the description suit this plant: but the short descriptions of wild madder in Gerard and Parkinson do not.

Casparus Bauhinus incorrectly applies the Mollugo of Clusius and the mountain Mollugo of Gerard to his first, or mountain, branching, broad-leaved Mollugo, since these synonyms pertain to the second no less than the first Mollugo of Dodonaeus.

---

-> O <-

**Origanum vulgare** <gloss>Common marjoram</gloss> ] *The plant that grows in Bowyers close at Cherry-hinton is not this, but* **Clinopodium vulgare** <gloss>Common basil-thyme</gloss>. *We mistook it when it was young.*

-> P <-

**Polygalon Cortusi** <gloss>Cortuso's milkwort</gloss> ] For this, substitute **Ferrum equinum Germanicum siliquis in summitate** <gloss>German horseshoe vetch with pods at the top</gloss> of <term>Casparus Bauhinus</term>, whose synonyms seek in the Addenda.

-> R <-

**Ranunculus hederaceus rivulorum, et cetera** <gloss>Ivy-leaved crowfoot of the brooks, etc.</gloss> ] The flowers of this plant are white, not yellow as I was conjecturing; and it arises here and there in watery places: therefore the cited synonyms do not correspond to it, unless perhaps it varies in the color of the flower in foreign lands.

-> S <-

**Saxifraga Anglica Occidentalium** <gloss>English saxifrage of the westerners</gloss> ] In place of **Saxifragæ Anglicæ alsinefoliæ** <gloss>English chickweed-leaved saxifrage</gloss> of <term>Gerard emaculatus</term> <gloss>the updated edition of Gerard's Herball</gloss>, substitute **Synanchica Lugdunensis** <gloss>Lyons squinancy-wort</gloss>, page 1125 of <term>Gerard emaculatus</term>, and add the synonyms **Rubia cynanchica** <gloss>squinancy madder</gloss> of <term>Joannes Bauhinus VI</term>, or **cynanchica** <gloss>squinancy-wort</gloss> of <term>Casparus Bauhinus</term>.

**Saxifraga graminea pusilla** <gloss>Small grassy saxifrage</gloss> ] *I find upon comparing that this is the same plant described by Johnson upon Gerard under the name of* **Saxifraga Anglicana alsinefolia** <gloss>English chickweed-leaved saxifrage</gloss> *or* **Pearlwort.**

</translation>

whether his angular madder corresponds to the Mollugo of Clusius or not. <pb n="20"/>having, yet died on the very journey. In such a case, Clement VI, in his Bull, while wishing to signify his clemency toward such men, commands the Angels of Paradise to introduce the soul, completely absolved from Purgatory, into the glory of Paradise; the same grace was imparted to them by Nicholas V, Urban VIII, and Innocent X of this century. Among these, Urban writes thus in his Bull: <note>original: "Quoniam evenire potest, ut ex iis, qui hac de causa iter aggressi fuerint, vel ad Urbem se contulerint, aliqui in via aut etiam in ipsa Urbe, morbo vel alia legitima causa impediti aut morte præventi, præfinitio dierum numero non completo, ac ne quidem fortasse inchoato, præmissa exsequi ac Ecclesiam & Basilicas hujusmodi obire nequeant: nos piæ promptæque illorum Voluntati, quantum in Domino possumus, benigne favere cupientes, eosdem vere pœnitentes & confessos, prædictæ Indulgentiæ & remissionis participes fieri volumus, ac si Ecclesiam & Basilicas prædictas diebus a nobis præscriptis reipsa visitassent"</note> "Since it can happen that of those who have undertaken a journey for this cause, or have betaken themselves to the City, some are hindered by sickness or other legitimate cause, or prevented by death, on the road or even in the City itself, the number of days prescribed not being completed, and perhaps not even begun, and thus are unable to fulfill the aforementioned requirements and visit the Churches and Basilicas of this kind: we, desiring to favor their pious and ready will as much as we can in the Lord, wish those same truly penitent and confessed persons to become participants in the aforesaid Indulgence and remission, as if they had in fact visited the aforementioned Church and Basilicas on the days prescribed by us," compare Marchantius on the Bull of Urban VIII.

§. 4. As regards the absent <term>Jubilatores</term> <gloss>those celebrating the Jubilee</gloss>, who do not approach Rome, the Roman Pontiff, according to the delusions of Marchantius, derives his wells to them also out of his kindness, and sends out rivulets to various provinces so that all may be washed and may drink, provided they visit the churches of their native lands that are analogous to those Roman ones according to the judgment of the Pontiff or his emissaries. This is believed by them to be a singular argument of papal beneficence and generosity, which the aforementioned Marchantius proclaims everywhere, saying "this generosity is performed by the Pontiff toward the various regions of the world, so that the kindness of the Father toward dispersed sons, and of the Shepherd toward his sheep, who cannot gather together into one place, may shine more brightly." He says that the Pontiff grieves "that these living waters, these rivulets of grace, cannot be derived to certain provinces and regions, because they have cut themselves off from Unity, and like ungrateful sons have left Mother Church, kicking back after they have sucked at her breasts, that is, rebelling against her faith and doctrine, and immersing themselves in the foul waters of perverse and heretical doctrine." Alexander VI granted this great grace, as they esteem it—the Indulgences of the Holy Year—even to the most remote provinces to enrich his base-born ones, as Polydorus writes; Sixtus IV and Gregory XIII granted them to the Catholics of England, both those existing in England and elsewhere, who could not approach Rome, according to Frostius. Finally, to these must be added the dead, already burning in Purgatory: even they can be freed from the flames of Purgatory by an indult of the Roman Pontiff, if the power to apply the Jubilee to them is expressly held in the promulgatory Bull, and if they are assisted by the intercessions of heirs or friends, <pb n="21"/>to whom Clement VI, when they had set out to Rome for the sake of the Jubilee, granted the power to choose individually three or four souls, whomever they wished; for those souls, because of his Indulgences and their merit, were to fly forth immediately from Purgatory into Heaven. Santarellus, still more audacious, says that the Pontiff, through the most plenary Jubilee, can liberate all the souls of Purgatory in one day (Chapter 3, Doubt 12). But there is no reason for us to refute at length that preposterous audacity which the Roman Pontiff assumes for himself; he who is not ignorant of the foundation upon which that Pontifical power rests, which he parades and which is not Apostolic but Anti-Christian, will find judgment on these pompous promises not difficult. Let the Pontificians show which Divine Author desired to enrich his Church with such an abundance of grace that the Roman Bishop could dispense it; if not, what prevents us from saying with the poet:

->What will this promiser produce worthy of such great gaping?<-

§. 5. Therefore, the Jubilee of the Papists is nothing but a mere invention; its privileges are acts of peddling; its Indulgences are enticements. The reasons that they bring forward here to gloss over this simony of their Church are of such a kind that, if you list them, you have already refuted them. Indeed, what Turecremata dreams here (in Jac. de Graff., *Append. aur.*, Book 1, Ch. 8, S. 13):

> The Jubilee was instituted to aid human infirmity, since some men are so weighed down by the burden of sins that they are insufficient in this life to pay the penalties owed, whence the pious Mother Church acts commonly at a certain time in their life, so that the faithful may have the aid of this grace, by means of which they can be absolved from the debts of penalties,

all that, since it is a manifestation of slippery presumption, as if our works could merit any grace from GOD, has an easy refutation through the very words of the Savior:

> When you have done all those things which are commanded you, say: we are unprofitable servants: we have done that which was our duty to do.

If these things are true of those whom a true love toward God impels to walk in the commandments prescribed by Him, they will apply much more to those concerning whose works, dedicated to the zeal of <term>ethelothreskeia</term> <gloss>will-worship/self-invented religion</gloss>, the Prophet says:

> Who hath required this at your hand? (Isaiah 1:12).

Furthermore, if the Pontificians are concerned about this elective worship out of a fear of penalties to be suffered in Purgatory, let them first throw the fire onto that chimerical invention, and then we shall be concerned about escaping the flames of Purgatory. Nor is it of better quality what the aforementioned Turecremata brings forward for this hypothesis of his, that such an Indulgence was instituted to confirm and strengthen</translation>

<keywords>Jubilee, Indulgences, Purgatory, Roman Pontiff, Papal Bull, Simony, Turecremata, Clement VI, Urban VIII</keywords>

Who has not heard of the excellent virtue of Ulpian, whose supreme praises are proclaimed because of his love of justice and the innocence of his life? For this reason, he was so dear to the Emperor Alexander Severus that the emperor used only his counsel in all matters and, apart from him alone, admitted no one to conversation. Truly, I wish this concern would also affect our own leaders who sit at the helm of state. The condition of the Republic would be much happier, and there would be a greater reverence for laws, if those who must utter them—and who are the voice of the law—shone for others by their own example. For the poet rightly says:

->Thus is censure sought, and thus are examples prepared,<-
->When the judge himself does what he advises others to do.<-

But to speak of our Papinian, there were in him supreme virtues: integrity of life and morals, <pb n="17"/>probity, faithfulness, candor, moderation in councils and deliberations, chastity, and a love of justice and truth. He showed constancy in the defense of justice and the laws, the sources of which he embraced in his writings. Because of these virtues, he was dear to the Emperor Severus and his friend. He lived in the year 200 after the birth of Christ and was a defender of the sacred laws and their most fierce champion. Because of his love for virtue and probity, Severus raised Papinian to the highest pinnacle of honor, such that he held the second position under the prince. For Papinian succeeded Severus in the administration of the treasury <term>fiscus</term> <gloss>imperial treasury</gloss>, and when he was already in his thirtieth year of life, he was called to the office of the prefecture. He was powerful in the court, even more than he wished. For this reason, he often attempted to lay down his burden, but since his wisdom, probity, and faithfulness were known to Severus, he could not obtain it.

Severus, even while paying his own debt to nature, commended his sons to him as if to a most faithful parent and teacher. But see what rewards he earned by his virtue and his good deeds.

<meta>continues from previous page: ...The efficient cause of augmentation is not the gravity</meta> and lightness of the elements, as Empedocles <note>a Greek pre-Socratic philosopher</note> supposed, nor the heat of fire, but the soul acting through heat and other powers, as if through instruments.

<margin>XXXIII.</margin>
The nutritive and augmentative power are distinguished only formally, but in reality, they are one and the same power.

<margin>XXXIIII.</margin>
Although the power of generating and altering are not in the thing which is rising or changing, yet the power of growing must necessarily be in that which is growing.

<margin>XXXV.</margin>
The augmentation of the whole living being is not, strictly speaking, a single motion. For the unity of motion requires the unity of the mobile object, the term, and the time, as is written in the 5th book of *Physics*, Text 34; these, if taken strictly, are missing in this increment.

<margin>XXXVI.</margin>
The augmentation of all parts of a living being, taken together, is not a continuous motion.

<margin>XXXVII.</margin>
The augmentation of no particle is continuous by a proper continuity.

<margin>XXXVIII.</margin>
Augmentation can be called continuous in the same way as alteration, specifically when no instant passes in which it could happen, without it actually happening.

<margin>XXXIX.</margin>
The augmentation of a living being is sought by nature in itself and primarily for the benefit of the living being itself. However, the augmentation of metals, stones, and similar things looks rather to the benefit of the species than to any particular individual.

<pb n="12"/>Although, on account of the variety of temperaments, locations, nourishment, and other things, a certain number of years cannot be assigned by which the augmentation of humans is completed, yet if we speak of a human who is reasonably well-constituted, and of what usually happens for the most part, it must be determined, with the ancient philosophers and physicians, that growth in length continues up to the 24th year, but in width up to the 30th year, more or less. However, after the 30th year and up to the 35th or 40th, no augmentation occurs; and from the 40th up to the 60th, a certain faint diminution follows, to which, finally, up to death, an open loss of parts succeeds. In our own age, however, due to the corrupt and foul life of certain men, and the weakness of nature itself, which is now aging, these things are sometimes accustomed to happen a little differently.

->PRAISE BE TO GOD.<-</translation>

<summary>This section concludes the discussion on the mechanics of biological growth, distinguishing between formal and nutritive powers, and providing an empirical timeframe for human physical maturation and decline.</summary>
<keywords>augmentation, nutritive power, biological growth, human development, physiology, natural philosophy, Aristotle</keywords>

Mascardus, conclusion 377, because it was done against the law, as said above, and regularly the priest cannot be compelled to reveal or disclose those things, as Vincentius Carrozius deals with most extensively in his treatise on the disclosure of confession. To him, so that I may not be verbose in this undertaking, I refer myself.

We conclude this Disputation regarding the confession of the dying: A person wounded at the point of death asserts that Titius inflicted the lethal wound upon him, and thus was the cause of his death; or someone, in a crime of poisoning, arson, etc., at the time of his execution accused and proclaimed other persons as his accomplices: therefore, the question is whether such an assertion or inculpation harms anyone, such that they could be condemned or tortured on account of it? Truly, so that this may also be handled with restraint, the judge ought to be provident and cautious in these matters, and before all else, according to the custom of the forum, look to whether other indications concur with such an inculpation, for instance, that the defamed Titius was found at the place of the inflicted wound with a drawn and bloody sword; likewise, whether threats and enmities preceded it. If these things concur, I believe it is sufficient not only to conduct an inquiry, but even to apply torture, which the Ordinance of the Empire, chapter 27, paragraph *Zum Sechsten* <gloss>to the sixth</gloss>, also proves, where it says: 

> If such a damaged person, for certain (which is to be noted) reasons, accuses someone of the crime and dies thereof, etc.

But if other indications or supporting evidence are lacking, then although the mere naming creates some presumption and an indication to proceed with an inquiry, it is not sufficient for torture, nor for imposing the oath of purgation, even if the person confessing is of the most approved faith, or if the confession was made with an oath. But it is to be rejected *ex post facto* <gloss>after the fact</gloss>, or not to be believed, by law 3, paragraph *Si quis moriens* <gloss>if anyone dying</gloss> 1, Digest on the Senatus Consultum Silanianum, and by article 27 of the Ordinance of the Empire, where it is expressly said that this naming alone is not a sufficient indication for torture, much less for condemnation. The reason is that such a dying person is not only a sole witness, and in his own cause, and as it were an enemy, but also because one's confession ought to harm only oneself, not another, by what Mascardus teaches in conclusion 386. Regarding this noble question, after the Doctors in the said law 3, paragraph 1, Digest on the Senatus Consultum Silanianum and in law *finem* <gloss>the end</gloss>, Code on the Julian Law regarding Extortion, see Johannes Georgius Goedelmannus on the point of poisoning, book 3, *De Magis* <gloss>on wizards/sorcerers</gloss>, chapter 9, number 5 to the end; Didacus Covarruvias, book 2 of his *Variae* <gloss>Varied [Researches]</gloss>, chapter 13, number 8; Menochius, book 1 of presumptions, question 89, number 81; Mascardus, conclusion 144 and 1078; Fachineus, book 9 of controversies, chapter 90; Farinaccius, question 46, number 35 and the following; Möller, book 3 of his *Semestria* <gloss>six-month reports</gloss>, chapter 8; Polydorus Ripa in the said commentary on actions at the point of death, chapter 16, throughout.

<pb n="19"/><note>A decorative headpiece features symmetrical floral scrolls and stylized leaf patterns.</note>

->To the Most Excellent and Learned Man<-

## Master JOHANN CABES, Candidate of Both Laws <note>i.e., Canon and Civil Law</note>, his friend.

**Just** as the merchant emboldens himself to trust his wealth to the waves, and to bear the roar of the deep-sounding sea. If the goods of Fortune are sought so very often with such great labor, which flame or wave soon steals away. Why should it be a burden to seek with study and great labor those goods which are not to perish on any day, which neither flame nor the rapid Deep can destroy, he who does not seek these goods, he is not wise.

->Willingly composed by<-
->**JOHANN GERHARDUS**<-
->**FRAUENBURGUS, Doctor**<-

---

->To the Most Excellent and Learned Man<-

## Master JOHANN CABES, Candidate of Both Laws <note>Canon and Civil Law</note> and of Matrimony.

**A** lawsuit has lately arisen between Themis <note>the goddess of divine law and order</note> and Venus <note>the goddess of love and beauty</note>: the former calls you hers, the latter calls you hers. The one occupies you with honors, the other with loves; to which will you give yourself, that you might wish to be entirely the one's? I think to neither, JANE. Divide the common laws, and in whatever part you can please, please.

->Poured forth at Altdorf by<-
->**GEORGIUS NOESSLERUS, Doctor and Public Professor**<-
->**Physician of the Palatine Principality and the Republic of Nuremberg.**<-

### T H E  E N D.
</translation>

PHILOSOPHICA.
# XII. IOANNES CONRADVS FINCKHER, CELLENSIS.
## EX LIBRO PHYSICA ASSERTIO XXXV.
<note>An ornamental woodcut initial 'T' features scrolling foliage and floral motifs.</note>
Time, materially and really, is motion itself; formally, it is the <term>passio</term> <gloss>affection or attribute</gloss> of motion, consisting first in a divisible, continuous, successive duration; second, in the <term>ratio</term> <gloss>concept/nature</gloss> of a measure, primarily the measured and intrinsic <term>ratio</term>, or the number of the potential numbered, which is the aforementioned duration itself, insofar as it renders the motion in which it exists formally apt to be numbered and measured by the duration of another motion; and third, in the <term>ratio</term> of an extrinsic, measuring measure, or the numbering number, which measure and number is the same duration of motion, insofar as it is distinguished by the Intellect into certain parts—such as days, weeks, months, etc.—and, being thus distinguished as something more known to us, is applied to discerning the durations of various actions, motions, and things, as they are subject to motion. <margin>4. Physics, text 131.</margin> 
In the first and second ways, the formal <term>ratio</term> of Time is a categorical being, but in the third way, it is a being of reason, such that if the soul were removed, Time would not exist. To both of the latter formal <term>ratio</term>s of Time, the Aristotelian definition can be applied (text 101): "The number of motion in respect to the prior and the posterior."

## XXXVI.
<note>An ornamental decorative initial letter 'H' begins the paragraph.</note>
Hence it becomes plain that particular Times are multiplied to the multitude of motions, since individual numerical motions claim their own durations, which are also called their intrinsic measures; however, a Universal Time is given that is unique in number, which is the duration of the first motion distinguished by the numbering Intellect into certain parts to measure our actions and the motions of things. Duration in reality is nothing other than existence; it differs formally.

## EX LOGICA.
### XXXVII.
<pb n="16"/>
ASSERTIONES
<note>A decorative initial letter 'D' features a small landscape scene with a building and trees.</note>
Demonstration proximately contains the Demonstration <term>propter quid</term> <gloss>of the reasoned fact</gloss> and <term>quia</term> <gloss>of the fact</gloss>. 1 Posterior Analytics, chapter 10. The medium of a demonstration <term>propter quid</term>—and thus the most potent kind—requires and suffices for nothing other than the causal definition of the property to be demonstrated, which is always simultaneously the proper and proximate cause of the same.

## XIII. PHILIPPVS KINE,
->VVANGIANVS.<-

### EX LIB. DE COELO. ASSERT. XXXVIII.
<note>A decorative initial letter 'C' within an ornate circular frame depicts a figure in a landscape setting.</note>
Celestial bodies differ among themselves in number and essential species, but any given star differs from its sphere only by an accidental species, like a denser and more luminous part of its own sphere, continuous like a knot in wood; and therefore, it does not wander through the heaven by its own motion, just as fish do not [wander] through the water, nor birds through the air.

## EX LOGICA.
### XXXIX.
<note>A decorative initial letter 'F' features floral and scrollwork ornamentation.</note>
The form, which is the internal and essential principle of the syllogism, can be described as a certain complication or disposition of matter apt for inferring a conclusion. This disposition, if it be remote matter or the middle [term] with the extremes, is called Figure; if it be proximate matter—namely, of the propositions according to a certain quantity and essential quality—it is called a Syllogistic Mood. Conversion, which is the extrinsic formal principle of the syllogisms of the 2nd and 3rd Figure, is a formal and therefore necessary consequence, but not an argumentation.
</translation>

<summary>This text defines the nature of time as a measurement of motion, distinguishes between specific and universal time, explains the causal requirements of demonstration in logic, describes the relationship between celestial bodies and their spheres, and classifies the formal principles of syllogisms, including figures and moods.</summary>
<keywords>Time, Physics, Logic, Aristotle, Demonstration, Syllogism, Celestial Bodies, Duration, Motion, Formal Causality</keywords>

The figure of an unknown man was seen by me by chance, asking
Who he might be: the crowd says, "He is a Venetian."
A headband bound his hair in the German custom,
A Gallic crest covered the Venetian’s head.
And there was a Spanish breastplate, and a Roman garment.
To one asking what this dress meant for him,
He replied, "A plunderer has seized everything, and everything
Which holds power: what was it if not plunder?"
I am a true prophet: if only the gods favor the things born,
By the merit of <term>Aesop</term> <gloss>the fable writer</gloss>, the jackdaw will be the fosterer.

<pb n="17"/>The German will snatch the headband, the Gaul the crest,
The Spaniard the breastplate, and warlike Rome the toga.

## Epitaph of Elpis

### Wife of Boethius

I was called Elpis, a foster-child of the Sicilian region,
Whom the love of a spouse led far from my homeland.
Without him, the day was mournful, the night anxious, the hour tearful;
Not only for my husband was there one soul.
My light is not extinguished while such a husband remains,
And I shall survive in the greater part of my soul.
In sacred porticoes, I, a pilgrim, now rest,
Having witnessed the throne of the eternal judge.
And let no hand violate my tomb, lest my husband
Desire to join these limbs to his ashes once again.

## A Poem of Georgius
## Tiphernus to the Blessed Virgin

Virgin, glory of heaven, most holy Virgin,
You who are to be venerated above the angelic choirs,
Beautiful one, you surpass snowy roses, you surpass
White lilies: you surpass the stars with your countenance.
Pure, like a little dove whom no milky
Feather knows, nor does a flaw sit upon your whole body.
Which of the <term>Sibyls</term> <gloss>prophetesses of antiquity</gloss> do you not far excel, O Virgin?
What nymph can finally be compared to you?
You are called the beloved mother of God: you are called his spouse.
</translation>

<summary>This text contains verses by Eobanus Hessus, including a cryptic prediction about Venice in 1509, followed by an epitaph for Elpis (wife of Boethius) and a devotional poem to the Virgin Mary by Georgius Tiphernus.</summary>
<keywords>Eobanus Hessus, Venice, 1509, Elpis, Boethius, Georgius Tiphernus, Virgin Mary, Latin poetry, prophecy</keywords>

# HYMN TO ST. ERMINOLD

<note>A decorative woodcut initial 'D' with floral and scrollwork ornamentation.</note>

Divine one, whom the work of steep virtue once carried above the stars, be present more gently, I pray, on this day consecrated to you by annual rite.

While we celebrate your famous urn with frankincense flames, bringing back happy triumphs and cheerful applause of those above, visit your bones.

Bones that drove away many diseases, and heavy fevers, and various plagues, and dropsy <note>edema</note> with white-swollen limbs, and all other ailments.

They gave back the lost use of sight to those lacking a sharp eye, and at once gave back steps to those who had been lame for a long time, with firm knees.

Moreover, they have often put to flight horrible shadows and sad Furies driven from Erebus <note>the underworld</note>, which were tormenting the limbs of guilty men with fury.

Visit this seat of yours, Father ERMINOLD, which you first cultivated, and watch over the assembly prostrate at your urn with a placid light.

You who have seen your descendants, written in the golden registers of heaven, as future inhabitants, pitying our final life, remove our perils.

<pb n="20"/>Let us therefore sing praises to the Divinity, which is one in equal Deity, and in persons is not bounded by any temporal age.

-> AMEN. <-

---

# TO THE BLESSED ERMINOLD
## FROM THE PEOPLE OF PRÜFENING <note>original: "Brunfeningenses"</note>

<note>An ornamental decorative initial 'D' featuring floral motifs.</note>

Divine Father, why now, with the star setting low, is the nurturing presence of your sacred body absent from the tomb? There was once no one more celebrated in the Bavarian region, whom everyone did not call upon for the great help of ERMINOLD. Have the many crimes of our life recently offended you? Or has the honor of your worship perhaps been scorned? Alas, what help remains for us if our Defender is angry? There will be no one to whom we can flee. Ah, splendor of the heavens, leader and author of monks, ah, let your wrath be softened toward our evils. Behold, we weep for our sins and prostrate ourselves at the urn, help us, Divine one, even in this final time.

-> Praise to GOD and to the Virgin Mother Mary. <-

-> With the permission of the Superiors. <-

<pb n="14"/>But if you hasten as a pilgrim to other shores,
Who will be here as priest, who will there be, under whose leadership
Germany will be able to preserve the true faith in safety?
For the heretics rejoice that you are now departing,
If you were to remain, they would consume their breasts with excessive grief.
Halt your steps, Martin, and check your pace.
But if you do not depart, then you will save yourself for your friends,
And you will save yourself for God and for the friends loyal to you:
And the Church, performing the duties of its office,
Freed from a long absence, will enjoy freedom again:
And venerable piety will remain in its own value.
Halt your steps, Martin, and check your pace.
See whither you are going, you will depart, a German, to Rome:
Climbing the airy peaks of the highest mountains,
Descending again as if sent down into the underworld:
Perhaps even a robber will prepare hidden ambushes,
To snatch either your riches or, finally, your life.
Halt your steps, Martin, and check your pace.
The storm prohibits it, the North Wind forbids it, Aeolus,
Releasing all the winds from their prisons on every side,
Dissuades this journey; but if you refuse to obey,
Perhaps you will be forced to meet death and heavy accidents:
But God and fortune will prepare better things for you.
Halt your steps, Martin, and check your pace.
<pb n="15"/>But if you are swayed neither by prayers nor by any words,
Go, seek the Roman citadels with happy fates,
And plant the kisses to be given to the feet of the sacred Pontiff:
And, as you are accustomed, manage the entrusted business
Of Duke Albert, than whom no other is more excellent.

# PRECEPTS OF THE MOSAIC LAW.
->Reduced to a summary.<-

## PRECEPT I.
### YOU SHALL HAVE NO OTHER GODS.
It is the fear of God in love, true faith, solid hope, in favorable and adverse circumstances, and finally in one's entire life.

### GUILTY OF THIS PRECEPT.
He who attributes his life and condition, in every state of fortune, to another rather than to God; he who trusts in himself or his own, not in God.

## PRECEPT II.
### YOU SHALL NOT TAKE THE NAME OF YOUR GOD
->In vain.<-
It is to refer glory, honor, and blessing to God, to worship Him alone, to refer whatever good you have as received from Him alone, to call upon Him, and to detest oneself. No one doubts that whatever good there is, it is the name of God.

### GUILTY OF THIS PRECEPT.
He who uses the name of God for anything other than His glory. He who flatters himself with some good of his own, seeking virtue and praise from elsewhere than from God.

## PRECEPT III.
### KEEP THE SABBATH HOLY.
It is to attend to God, and to seek and inquire after His grace alone.

### GUILTY.
Whoever does not rest in his soul for God, but insists on working during the holy light: he who does not care for divine things, or cares for them coldly: he who does not observe the Sabbath as a rest from vices.

## PRECEPT IV.
### HONOR YOUR FATHER AND MOTHER.
It is to obey God, and for the sake of God to obey every authority, even to the point of tyranny; it is to assist parents, not only with greetings and nods, but with the diligence of one’s deeds, and to pursue them, especially with benefits.

### GUILTY.
<pb n="18"/>
He who flees, despises, and neglects his parents; he who is averse to and hates magistrates and the law; he who does not obey authority, or obeys it unwillingly.

### Precept V.
## YOU SHALL NOT KILL.

It is patience, peace, humanity, mercy, and (to say it in one word) an entire life without the bitterness of malevolence, prompt and beneficial even toward an enemy.

### GUILTY.

He who does not aid a brother with counsel, help, and work; he who does not prevent evil from his neighbor.

### Precept VI.
## YOU SHALL NOT COMMIT ADULTERY.

It is purity and modesty of souls, speech, and deeds; frugality of living; undefiled love of heavenly things; contempt of pleasures; the love of God alone.

### GUILTY.

Whoever is dissolved in pleasures, who enjoys laughter and joy immodestly, or does not restrain and bridle those who are enjoying them. And whoever permits their soul to take care of things other than God.

### Precept VII.
## YOU SHALL NOT STEAL.

It is the flight from all avarice, cheerful poverty, liberality, and humanity.

### GUILTY.

Whoever is unwilling to give a loan to a neighbor freely and without interest; those who apply their mind too intemperately to any worldly goods; those who bear poverty unwillingly; those who deny alms, or do not distribute them in a timely manner; those who circumvent their neighbor with deceit and imposture.

### Precept VIII.
## YOU SHALL NOT BEAR FALSE WITNESS.

It is the naked and simple truth of words and deeds; a tongue fostering peace, seeking the benefit of a brother, desiring to compose discord, refuting disparagement, and purging and covering the defamation of a neighbor.

### GUILTY.
</translation>

<summary>This text provides a summarized interpretation of the Mosaic Law, defining each of the first eight commandments and identifying the behaviors that render one guilty of violating them.</summary>
<keywords>Mosaic Law, Decalogue, Ten Commandments, Christian ethics, divine obedience, moral conduct</keywords>
