<pb n="21"/>various punishments existed among various nations, which is not unknown to you, I believe, and will be explained in its own place and time. Zaleucus also enacted a law regarding this same matter, that whoever was convicted of adultery should have both eyes gouged out. When, however, even the son of Zaleucus himself had sinned in this regard and was accused of adultery, and was now to be punished according to his father's law, the entire citizenry professed that they would not unwillingly pardon the son's crime in consideration of the father's virtue and merits. But the father, urging the law and contending that it ought to be confirmed even by his own and his family's punishment, when he could nevertheless not obtain from the people that his son should be deprived of both eyes, finally achieved this by an admirable temperament of justice and paternal piety, so that the law was kept inviolate, and, as far as could be done while preserving the law, he displayed paternal affection toward his son. For he ordered one eye of his son to be removed; and the other for himself. Finally, however, as Suidas has noted, while fighting most bravely for his fatherland, he met his death, so that by his own example he might also teach others how sweet and becoming it is to die for one's country.

You have, most excellent listeners, what I have been able to learn about Charondas and Zaleucus: I earnestly ask that you allow their commemoration, whatever it may be, to have been not unwelcome to you, and that you may not regret this time.

Since our legislators, in their prefaces, chiefly deter men from evil deeds by the mention and consideration of death, because everyone is accustomed to being tormented by the conscience and repentance of those deeds as they draw near to it: but since they do not add the cause of this, which is without doubt that a mind conscious of evil foresees the judgment to come upon itself and the impending punishments (for what would one fear, who believed that all things are ended by death?): that it may be clear that not even this was unknown to the heathens, it pleases me here to append the most distinguished **IAMBICS OF THE COMIC POET PHILEMON**, which I once rendered into Latin from the Greek. However, the Greek originals exist partly in Justin Martyr, in his *On Monarchy*, and partly in Eusebius, in the 13th book of his *Preparation for the Gospel*, and in Clement of Alexandria, who, however, attribute these two later ones to the author **DIPHILUS**. I desire, friendly reader, that this deed be approved by you.

> Who wallowed in all manner of delights while they lived,
> Are thus buried in the earth,
> To remain hidden from the Divine for all eternity,
> And to escape from this?
> All these things the lights of Justice behold.
> For we believe in two paths to the underworld,
> Of which one belongs to the just; the other to the impious.
> But if the same fortune awaits the pious and the impious,
> Why not kill, steal, and plunder
> Whatever you can, and mix the lowest with the highest?
> What stands in the way? Do not let error, my good man, bewitch you:
> Each person's own judgments await them in the underworld,
> Over which **GOD**, the ruler of all, will preside:
> Whose tremendous name I could not utter:
> Who often prolongs life for those who sin.
> 
> But if any mortal, while he commits evils day by day,
> Assumes that he is hidden from the Gods,
> He assumes falsely, and leads himself into ruin,
> Until **GOD**'s vengeance rests for a little while.
> 
> See for yourselves, you to whom the Gods are but fables:
> There is, there is a **GOD**. But if anyone does evil
> Because of a depraved nature, let him take profit for himself.
> For later, when time has elapsed, he will pay the penalty.

# ORATIO.

what ought to be kept secret, he tells to a friend, whom he then adjures by all things sacred and profane to keep what he has heard in eternal silence. Do you wish, oh *Corydon*, that others be silent? Be silent yourself, and say *Nothing*. The *Ardelio* <gloss>busybody</gloss> wanders the city all day, always asking, what is new? what is good? While he trusts all things to everyone with a simple mind, he ensures that *Nothing* is trusted to him. The *Politicus* <gloss>politician</gloss> prudently despairs of everything, hopes for everything bravely, guards everything diligently, and thus finally fears *Nothing*. If you are wise, do all things cautiously and quickly, but rashly or timidly, suddenly or late, *Nothing*. Do you ask what you can do without the help of the Best and Greatest **GOD**? *Nothing*. Among Christians, life will condemn some, and doctrine will condemn others. There are not a few who would defend their religion even to the fire **EXCLUSIVELY**. It is strange that while pure religion indeed urges piety, it often achieves *Nothing*. You will often see men who, throughout their lives, are joyful, drinking, and rowdy. Yet, when a more unhappy hour strikes, they hurry to their prayer books, and having first wiped away the dust, they contort their stern faces into devotion, and sighing deeply, they look for certain little prayers suited to their misfortune. Then they count the pages of those prayers, and if they are too long, they look for shorter ones or close the books again. Because these men are devoid of harmony between heart and mouth, they deserve to receive *Nothing* from **GOD**. If eyes were plucked out as often as they took offense and sinned, the entire human race would soon see *Nothing*. On the last day, some rich men will say that they threw gold, that cursed metal, that incitement of all evils, at the feet of the lyre-player and the flute-player. Yet to the poor, the friends of Christ, they will cry out that they gave *Nothing* with a religious hand.

<pb n="55"/>
# O R A T I O.

Praetors and other citizens and wealthy rustics are accustomed to send roosters, capons, geese, thrushes, and other things to the magnates. But to the poor, they give *Nothing*. Oh, madmen! If you wish to send gifts suitable for each person, send food to the poor, and either hunger or *Nothing* to your patrons. Dung, indeed, is vile excrement, yet it is not useless. For without it, physicians and farmers possess *Nothing*. <term>Jurisconsults</term> <gloss>lawyers</gloss> love to drag out a litigious matter as if it were never to be finished, and when they have lost the case, and the client his property, they demand their fee nonetheless, at least because they are ashamed. If the client is wise, for the sake of showing gratitude, he gives them *Nothing*. Politicians, who, returning from Italy and France, depart from the customs of our fathers, and hear every flea coughing, and are always rattling off new institutions, not because they are good, but because they are new; these men, I say, sometimes seem to imitate <term>Orbilius</term> <gloss>a Roman schoolteacher known for severity</gloss>, who, when about to reform grammar, did not want his students to say "Sum, Es, Est" <gloss>I am, you are, he is</gloss>, but "Sum, Sus, Sut". To whom a certain man, endowed with faith and ancient morals, whispered in his ear: "Sum, sus, sut, does no good; Sum, Es, Est, let it remain as it has been." But these same politicians, if they disapprove of everything, venerate *Nothing*. Many are <term>Pompeians</term> if Pompey is winning. If <term>Caesar</term> is winning, they become Caesarians on the spot. Do you ask what good princes should hope for from these men? *Nothing*. The temple of <term>Diana</term> of Ephesus made debtors safe from their creditors. Do you ask what provides a safer asylum in this matter? *Nothing* besides frugality. If a merchant has lost his property and credit, he sings empty-handed before a highwayman, because he sees that he has *Nothing* left henceforth. The ancients believed in coins without a written document or wax. Now, without both, *Nothing*. I was faithful to <term>Dindymus</term> in both fortunes, but he was perfidious to me
</translation>

More rightly, Alexander the Great admired no one more than Semiramis and Cyrus; Curtius, Book 7, Chapter 6. Julius Caesar also prudently appeals to the rule of Semiramis in Suetonius, §. 23. <pb n="16"/> §. 16. But so that the truth of that Maronian line might not fail:

->Each of us suffers his own ghost;<-

Semiramis also conducted herself in a way that leads to vituperation, not just praise, as Berosus the monk of Annius of Viterbo says on page 48. Nor is any other vice attributed to her more than lust, for she admitted all the most energetic soldiers to her intimacies, and having been delighted by the use of their bodies, she removed them from the midst, so that the reputation for fornication would not spread to the common people. Claudian traces the first eunuchs back to Semiramis; yet Claudius Barthius seems to doubt this due to the silence of Diodorus in his *Notes on Eutropius*, Book I, page 1325. Ammianus Marcellinus, in Book 14, cited by Henelius in *Wrocław Leisure*, Chapter 35, page 274, embraces Claudian’s view when he says: Wherever anyone goes, seeing throngs of mutilated men, he will detest the memory of Semiramis, that ancient Queen who was the first of all to castrate tender males. Pliny writes from Juba in his *Natural History*, Book 8, Chapter 42, that she had relations with a horse. Indeed, Paulus Orosius testifies in Book 1, Chapter 4, that she finally decreed that illicit relationships and marriages between parents and children could take place lawfully. It is handed down by Justin and others that, as an example of the observance of this law, she sought the embrace of her son Ninyas, and was killed by him when he averted such a wicked crime. However, the story of her death is uncertain, and it is not sufficiently clear whether she perished from wounds in war or by the crime of her son. Wagner, *Historical Institutions*, Book 3, page 201.

§. 17. The remains of Semiramis are said to have been laid in a tomb which she built for herself while alive in an elevated and conspicuous place in Babylon, with the following inscription attached: IF ANY KING IS IN NEED OF MONEY, LET HIM OPEN THIS MONUMENT AND TAKE AS MUCH AS HE WISHES. When Darius Hystaspis had read this, he ordered the tomb to be opened, in which he found no gold, but this writing: UNLESS YOU HAD BEEN A WICKED MAN, YOU NEVER WOULD HAVE VIOLATED A TOMB. # XVI.

The external <note>form</note> consists of formalities <note>original: "solemnitatibus"</note>, which are either common to both the written and the nuncupative <note>oral</note> testament, or proper to one or the other. Common to both is the summoning of witnesses, whose quality <note>legal standing/fitness</note> must be regarded, and they must be invited by a formal request. Finally, the number is defined by law, such that seven must be employed.

<note>Supporting citations include: Donellus (Book 6, chapter 7); Althusius (Jurisprudence, Book 1, chapter 18); the law "Hac consultissima" (21) in the Code on Testaments; Sichardus; Covarruvias (on the chapter "Cum esses," 10, no. 1, on Testaments). Regarding the quality of witnesses, see the following thesis. Regarding the formal request, see the law "Heredes" (21, § "In testamentis"); the law "Qui testamenta facere"; and the aforementioned law "Hac consultissima" in the Code on Testaments. Is a smaller number of witnesses permissible by municipal law, it is asked? We believe it is possible, which both usage confirms and it proceeds to such an extent that, by the force of a testament thus constructed, the heir obtains even goods situated outside the territory, by the argument of the law § "Sed naturalia" (11) in the Institutes on the Law of Nature and Nations; law "Si non speciali" (9); law (21) in the Code on Testaments; law (1) at the end on the inspection of the belly; law "Si fundus" (6) on evictions; law "In hac" (30) in the Code on Donations, joined with the title in the Institutes on the Lex Fusia; Gail (Book 2, observation 123); Mynsinger (century 5, observation 20). <pb n="10"/>the custom of Saxony has approved, as Carpzovius testifies in Part 2, Constitution 13, Definition 20. However, it is not correctly considered that a donation is made by a low-born husband to a noble woman during the marriage, since all the causes prohibiting donations between spouses apply equally in that instance, as Treutler thinks in Volume 2, Disputation 13, Thesis 4, letter b, and Bachovius there as well.

## THES. VI. <note>Note: The input identifies this as THES. VI. but the content follows the logic of the previous pages.</note>

Indeed, they increase the number of Paraphernalia <gloss>property held by a wife outside her dowry</gloss> with Wedding Gifts, <term>Braut-Taffel Gelder</term> <gloss>wedding table money/wedding feast gifts</gloss>, which belong to the wife for one half. This is a very equitable opinion, received by Panormitanus in Chapter 2, Extra, on donations between husband and wife, and in the Electorate of Saxony in Part 3, Constitution 22, by way of a special pragmatic sanction. This is true to such an extent that, although by regional custom or by reason of the occasion a gift may be offered to only one of the spouses, it nevertheless remains common to both and must be divided equally between them by the argument of Law 10, Digest on donations. This is all the more certain because marriage is considered a species of society/partnership (Institutes, Section 1, on paternal power; Law 1, Section 3, Digest on Justice and Law; and Law 1, Digest on the Rites of Marriage), the nature of which is such that things donated to the partners so that they might better negotiate and handle common business, once the partnership is dissolved, are divided equally between them and their heirs by the argument of Law 29, Digest on partnership, and Carpzovius in Part 3, Constitution 22, Definition 1. The Helmstadiensis Academy favors this opinion, and does not approve the opinion of Bartolus—who, in Law 10, Section 6, Digest on vulgar and pupillary substitution, grants to each spouse what the relatives, kinsmen, and friends of each have donated to them—or of others who assign everything to the wife, as Hahn testifies in his observations on the paratitla of Wesenbecius, title on the Law of Dowries, number 11, at the end.

<pb n="11"/>

## THES. VIII.

Let us proceed to the FORM, of which mention was made above in the explanation of the definition under the term "specific difference," and which consists in the administration of goods brought by the wife being conceded to the husband, whether that concession relies on express or tacit consent. It is referred to as express if the woman places the things existing in the husband's house into a book and causes it to be offered to the husband and signed by him, as if he had received the things, just as if the paraphernal things were found recorded in the dotal instrument (Law 9, last paragraph, Digest on the Law of Dowry; Law last, Code on agreed pacts), from which it is then fully proven that some things are paraphernal. But that concession is tacit if the husband, with the wife knowing and allowing it, has administered the goods brought in addition to the dowry for many years. Although in that case, where a woman has married a husband without any certain dowry being established, we see that doctors argue whether all the goods the woman possesses ought to be considered as dotal or as Paraphernal. And indeed, in doubt, they ought to be considered dotal, since it is more useful for the wife that her goods be considered dotal than Paraphernal; for although women have obtained a tacit mortgage <gloss>security interest</gloss> on the husband's goods in place of Paraphernalia, they are nevertheless deprived of and lack the privileges of a dowry, and especially the benefit of preference <gloss>priority in repayment</gloss>. Thus, where it is a matter of the favor due to women, in doubtful cases, one must favor them (Law "in ambiguous," Digest on the Law of Dowry). It follows that because marriage, as a principal, can be introduced not only by express (Law 129, Digest on Rules of Law; Novella 22, Chapter 3) but also by tacit agreement if the circumstances of the things and persons persuade it, then much more in its accessory, such as the dowry, the same will hold valid, without which a marriage, while the dowry itself without the same is never...
</translation>

<keywords>Paraphernalia, Dowry, Spousal Property, Saxon Law, Legal Administration, Marriage Partnership</keywords>

## *Chorus.*

The true prophets are led to their deaths by the command of Jezebel.

## *Scene Four.*

Obadiah urges Elijah to decline the persecution raging against the true prophets of GOD by fleeing. Elijah, inflamed with zeal and the spirit of GOD, not only refuses to take flight, but meets King Ahab as he goes to worship Baal, threatens him with heavenly punishments, and suddenly flees. The King, driven to fury, pronounces a death sentence upon him.

## *Scene Five.*

Elijah, uncertain where to flee, is warned by an Angel from GOD to set out towards the East, and to lie hidden in the region of the Jordan beside the brook of Cherith. Divine Providence becomes his companion.

## *Chorus.*

Divine vengeance puts to flight the water-signs and brings forth fiery ones upon the Kingdom of Ahab; from these a famine arises, which the household gods <term>Penates</term> <gloss>Roman household gods</gloss> attempt to subdue, only to be overcome by it.

<note>A horizontal ornamental divider composed of a repeating row of small floral or star-shaped printer's ornaments.</note>

# ACT TWO.

## *Scene One.*

As the famine gains strength in the Kingdom of Ahab, many die, with some cursing Ahab as the cause of such a great calamity, and others cursing Elijah. Some attack the true prophets, others the false ones, and threaten them with death if they do not obtain rain.

## *Scene Two.*

Summoned by divine Providence, a raven brings food to Elijah.

<pb n="11"/>

### Scene Three.

Ahab, disturbed by the great confusion of his people, orders a search for Elijah throughout all the regions, so that he may kill him (as Saint Augustine believes).

### Scene Four.

The brook of Cherith having dried up, Elijah is ordered to go to Zarephath of the Sidonians; there he is to be fed by a widow woman, whom he finds gathering wood with her son. Elijah asks for food, with the promise that the flour will not fail, from which the woman makes him an ash-baked bread <term>subcinericium</term> <gloss>bread baked under ashes</gloss>.

### Scene Five.

The widow of Zarephath joyfully offers Elijah the ash-baked bread. She tells of the flour having in no way diminished, blesses the GOD of Elijah, and asks the prophet to deign to lodge in her home.

### Scene Six.

The widow’s son falls ill and then dies; Elijah restores him to life and returns him to his mother.

### Chorus.

> Twelve little Sidonian children applaud the son of the woman of Zarephath having been called back to life.

<note>A horizontal decorative divider composed of a sequence of seventeen floral or wheel-like circular ornaments, divided in the center by three horizontal bars.</note>

# ACT THREE.

### Scene One.

**A**hab, destitute of counsel, asks his own men what should be done in this great scarcity of resources. Finally, he himself and Obadiah set out separately into various regions to procure food, with Ahab traveling in a disguised habit.

<pb n="13"/><meta>continues from previous page: He had scarcely finished these words</meta> when he was suddenly struck down; imploring the help of those who were present, he died in a pitiable manner with great pain and groaning. From this it can easily be conceived that divine power was communicated to the holy man. To this is added another example, not unlike the first: another Margrave <gloss>a military governor or nobleman</gloss> named William was treating the aforementioned church of Meissen injuriously. When the provost of the same church wished to lead the man away from his evil intent with great entreaties, he not only refused to obey those giving right counsel, but even harassed the church much more than before. Then the said provost, since he could not seek help from elsewhere, fled to Saint Benno and prayed to him that he might preserve the church. As a result, Blessed Benno warned the Margrave three times through his sleep <note>meaning through dreams or visions</note> that he should not attempt anything further against the church. When the Margrave despised this as an empty dream, he was subsequently rebuked vehemently a fourth time and lost one eye, with a more serious danger proposed unless he desisted from his wicked purpose. Margrave William, led partly by fear and partly by repentance, restored everything to the church and increased its resources as much as he could; he also valued Saint Benno highly and honored him greatly. Indeed, it must not be passed over that there are two villages, in one of which the Margrave hid himself while fleeing; in the other, Benno converted the Vandals from the greatest impiety to the Christian faith. In these places, the prints of his feet are perceived even today as still intact, as is that hut in which he stayed among the Vandals. Even though it is secured by no stable structure and had a roof of straw consumed by age, it has never suffered any defect nor been consumed by fire, even though the neighboring houses have frequently burned with fire. Also, the episcopal garment in which his body was committed to the earth, together with the episcopal miter, lay hidden under the earth for over two hundred years; having been dug out of the tomb without any alteration, it is seen and displayed today in its entirety. Many other miracles could be brought forward here; for it is well known that many were raised from the dead by the merits of Saint Benno, and many <pb n="14"/> cured of various diseases. Finally, whoever made a vow, there is no one who has not felt his benefit. On account of these things, our most dear son in Christ, Charles, the Catholic King of the Romans and of the Spains, already elected Emperor <note>Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor</note>; and our beloved sons, Albert, etc., Priest of Saint Peter in Chains, and Matthew, Deacon of Saint Angelus, Cardinals of the Holy Roman Church; and our venerable brothers, Richard of Trier and Hermann of Cologne, Archbishops, through their letters patent; as well as our beloved sons, the noble men Ferdinand, Archduke of Austria, and George and Henry, biological brothers, Dukes of Saxony, Landgraves of Thuringia and Margraves of Meissen, have caused a humble supplication to be made to us through our venerable brother, John, Bishop of Meissen, their messenger and orator sent to us by them, and through our beloved son, William van Enckevoirt, Bishop-elect of Tortosa <term>dertusensem</term>, our Datary <gloss>an official of the Roman Curia</gloss> and domestic Prelate, also their orator and manager of business with us and the Apostolic See. They requested that, having diligently investigated and explored the premises, we might deign to proceed to the canonization of the blessed man. Although we wished to grant their prayers willingly, and we rejoiced exceedingly that such a canonization should happen in our times by a certain divine ministry, and it seemed just to us that the same Blessed Benno—whom God had already made worthy of the choir of saints in heavenly grace, as He had shown by very many and manifest signs and miracles—should not be defrauded on earth of the honor due to saints; yet, we decided that a matter of such weight and moment should not be done immediately, but must be considered slowly and maturely according to ancient and laudable custom. Therefore, after a threefold inquiry duly performed regarding this matter, first from the commissions of Alexander VI of recordable memory, and then of Julius II, and successively of Leo X, our predecessors, finally the same Leo X [entrusted it] to three Cardinals of the Holy Roman Church from their three orders, namely our venerable brothers Bernardino of Ostia, of the Holy <note>The text likely continues to mention the Holy Cross.</note>
</translation>

And Paul: When men shall say peace and security (for matters seem to be sliding back to the point where barbarism and superstition prevail again) then suddenly, as labor pains come upon a woman carrying a child, destruction will press upon them, which they shall not escape. For as it happened in the times of Noah, so shall be the coming of the Son of Man, and so at last shall be the end of superstition. Indeed, the Lord has already begun to consume it by the breath of his mouth, and will at last utterly abolish it by the brightness of his coming. Come Lord Jesus, say the pious: let your kingdom come, they ask. Surely I come quickly, says He who is faithful. The righteous cried out, says the Psalmist, and the Lord heard them. He will arrive all the sooner as the pious are more eager. And again, He will come all the more hastily as the ungodly are more numerous. For impiety draws plagues as the <term>Caecias</term> <gloss>the Northeast wind</gloss> draws clouds. Since therefore the former draw them, and on the other hand the pious strive for the same with all their might, the Lord will hasten doubly, according to that saying in Luke 18: Truly I say to you, the Lord will avenge his elect from their enemies, and that QUICKLY. An excellent Word, and one most consoling to those praying for the end. But the evil servant, thinking in his heart that his master delays his coming for a long time, beats his fellow servants, eats and drinks with drunkards, and brings war upon those who obey the commands of God and hold the testimony of Jesus Christ; he changes the times and the law, and establishes new <term>cycles</term> <gloss>calendrical or historical periods</gloss> which he extends into many centuries. Yet the Lord will come on a day when he does not expect, and at an unknown hour, and will cut him asunder, and place his portion with the hypocrites, where there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth. The Lord is not slow concerning his promise, as some interpret slowness: but the Lord is indeed patient toward us, not wishing that any should perish, <pb n="16"/> but that all should return to health. The day of the Lord, I say, will come like a thief in the night, and just as happened in the time of Noah. Even so, Come Lord Jesus: may whose grace be with all who piously desire his coming. Amen.

And Paul: When men shall say peace and security (for matters seem to be sliding back to the point where barbarism and superstition prevail again) then suddenly, as labor pains come upon a woman carrying a child, destruction will press upon them, which they shall not escape. For as it happened in the times of Noah, so shall be the coming of the Son of Man, and so at last shall be the end of superstition. Indeed, the Lord has already begun to consume it by the breath of his mouth, and will at last utterly abolish it by the brightness of his coming. Come Lord Jesus, say the pious: let your kingdom come, they ask. Surely I come quickly, says He who is faithful. The righteous cried out, says the Psalmist, and the Lord heard them. He will arrive all the sooner as the pious are more eager. And again, He will come all the more hastily as the ungodly are more numerous. For impiety draws plagues as the <term>Caecias</term> <gloss>the Northeast wind</gloss> draws clouds. but that all should return to health. The day of the Lord, I say, will come like a thief in the night, and just as happened in the time of Noah. Even so, Come Lord Jesus: may whose grace be with all who piously desire his coming. Amen.

For citizens, in order to prevent the oppression of superiors, would then be anxious for an opportunity to rebel against their future oppressors; among spouses, some discord and suspicion would more quickly arise, by which one might remove the other by poison or another way; in masterly and domestic society, a similar danger would be feared, which is nonetheless not a little guarded against through piety or its frequent exercise <note>compare Pufendorf, *On the Duty of Man and Citizen*, book 1, chapter 4, section 9, pages 53, 54, 55; as well as Master Pritius's *Dissertation on Atheism, both Foul in Itself and Noxious to the Human Race*, article 18</note>. This utility is also seen—to say nothing of more examples—in homages and treaties, as well as in the passing of laws, so that the minds of citizens may be restrained within the boundaries of what is right and just. For the nature of men tends to be such that human counsels, laws, or edicts will have scarcely any weight unless they are strengthened by the consent and will of the Divine Power <note>compare Masius, in the place cited, chapter 1, sections 3, 4, 5, etc.</note>. See how excellently <term>Pufendorf</term> demonstrates in *On the Nature of Religion in Relation to Civil Life*, section 5 and following, that without reverence for the Divine Power no faith in pacts is kept, and without Religion and fear of the Supreme Judge, no authority of an earthly judge is preserved safe and sound.

### §. XI.

This may be seen in very many Republics where piety and Religion brought forth much benefit. Although the cults of the Romans were quite superstitious, Religion nevertheless compelled them to keep faith and treaties, and to subject themselves to the laws and the Magistrate, because they believed that those who did otherwise would be punished by God <note>Arnisaeus, book 2 of *Politics*, chapter 5</note>. Hence it is that Numa Pompilius feigned that he had nightly meetings with the Goddess <term>Egeria</term>, and by her advice he said he instituted those things which were acceptable to the Gods. <note>Livy, book 1 of the *Histories*</note>. And perhaps there <pb n="13"/> was never any Legislator who did not borrow the authority of his laws from that same origin, or at least spread Religion, even if false and feigned, beneath his statutes. Thus also Philip, the father of Alexander the Great, employed an extraordinary reverence for the Gods and Religion so that he was believed by all Greece, when there was need, to be the avenger of sacrileges and the unique champion of piety and the Gods; and what is greater than all these things, he overthrew the enemy by their own conscience of impiety as if by a siege engine. <note>Compare B. Sagittarius, Professor at Jena, *Dissertation on Religion*, section 19</note>. **Masius, in the cited work, chapter 6, discusses the connection between Religion and the civil state of the Jewish Republic.**

---

->§. XII.<-

Furthermore, the consensus of Political writers supports us, among whom not the least is <term>Septalius</term>, who vigorously calls piety—if it be neither feigned nor simulated—the foundation of Empire and of the Reason of State <note>Septalius, *On the Reason of State*, book 2, chapter 10</note>; and <term>Verulamius</term> <gloss>Francis Bacon</gloss> in *The Smith of Fortune*, page 346, concerning the saying of the Savior from Matthew 6, verse 33, alleged above, exclaims: *O angular stone of Theology and Philosophy!* hinting at the happiness resulting from diligently sought Piety <note>Weise, *On Political Fortune*, chapter 2, section 30</note>. I add from our own countrymen the most excellent <term>Bosius</term> in his *Synopsis of Politics*, based on Lipsius and Bernegger, Exercise 1, sections 4 and following, where he speaks thus:

> Although the helm of prudence properly guides civil life, it does not do so without the use and help of this magnet, namely, virtue: and therefore it is rightly placed before it. Which I judge to be most greatly necessary in a prince, and which he ought deservedly to embrace. Whether you look at the excellence of virtue itself, as it stands out before all others and is alone in its own power; or its beauty, than which nothing is more lovable, nothing more proper to it than to win over the minds of men and join them to its uses; or its own happiness, in whose possession, if he cultivates it uprightly, all things will be good; or finally the happiness proceeding from it to his subjects, who, being endowed with that good and virtue, for the most part will be of good and of virtue

<pb n="21"/><meta>continues from previous page</meta> will be permitted for everyone to assert: Today there is no doubt regarding the <term>conglomerate glands</term> <gloss>glands composed of several smaller lobes with a shared duct</gloss>, since their lymph or secreted juice is set before our eyes, as is sufficiently manifest regarding the salivary glands, the pancreatic gland, and others. This is also proved by that peculiar duct into which the smallest glands connected there deposit their lymph. This lymph is also collected by certain experiments if a glass vessel is conveniently attached according to the method of <term>Graaf</term> <gloss>Regnier de Graaf, a Dutch physician known for studying the pancreas and reproductive organs</gloss>.

§. 58. Regarding certain others, the matter still seems obscure, but from the explanation of each it will be evident that what we have said is most true: that these same glands secrete a certain liquid, which whether you call it lymph or liquor is all the same to me; for different glands secrete different humors.

§. 59. For while we see that the glands under the armpits and in the groins secrete a foul-smelling humor, the prostates an oily one, those in the membrane of the palate a viscous one, those in the ears a bilious one, and the tonsils a pituiteous <note>phlegm-like</note> one, it will likewise be permitted to argue the same concerning all others.

§. 60. For it seems better thus to trust in experiments and <term>autopsy</term> <gloss>personal observation or "seeing for oneself"</gloss> rather than in mere reasons, although reasons are not lacking to confirm this opinion.

§. 61. Indeed, while we observe the lymphatic vessels departing from all glands, we firmly conclude that lymph and other humors are secreted from the blood within them. For nothing is separated from another thing to which it is intimately mixed except by some aid and secretive principle. One may also conveniently argue from the conglomerate glands to the rest, since they are composed of <term>conglobate</term> <gloss>simple, smooth-surfaced</gloss> glands. Therefore, what they do when they are united and many are connected to one another, the solitary ones will also perform, following the example of the testes and the kidneys.

§. 62. Doubt only seems to remain concerning the gland of the mesentery, called the pancreas by <term>Wharton</term> <gloss>Thomas Wharton, an English anatomist</gloss>, into which the <term>lacteal</term> <gloss>milk-carrying</gloss> and lymphatic vessels are inserted, as is commonly believed; whether it primarily secretes <pb n="22"/> anything is deservedly doubted. But in truth it also secretes something, and I judge, perhaps not ineptly, that in this gland a peculiar <term>ferment</term> <gloss>a chemical agent of transformation</gloss> is secreted to be mixed with the chyle. This is certain: that neither the lacteal nor the lymphatic vessels are inserted into the actual substance of this gland. Instead, they deposit the chyle and lymph into a certain cistern or wider duct behind the gland, from which an entirely different use must be assigned to this gland—namely, the same use as in others: to secrete something.

§. 63. And while I have thus established that the proper action of glands is to secrete humors from the blood, I simultaneously assert that, as a consequence, they purify the blood mass. For some glands secrete useful humors, others even useless ones; indeed, while even the useful ones are secreted, the blood mass is purified. For instance, while the liver secretes bile and the pancreas its own liquid, the blood is simultaneously purified by that very action, since those particles, when accumulated in the blood, often excite many disturbances if they are not secreted in the proper manner. How often is salivation instituted to purify the blood in the <term>venereal disease</term> <gloss>syphilis</gloss>? I will not even mention how all purgatives and sudorifics <note>medicines that induce sweating</note> stimulate the glands to secrete; while they do this, they simultaneously lead out humors that are faulty not only in quantity, but also in quality and substance.

<note>A woodcut illustration depicts a small, leafy tree or shrub growing from a mound of earth, serving as a decorative tailpiece at the end of the section.</note>
</translation>

<keywords>glands, secretion, lymph, blood purification, Regnier de Graaf, Thomas Wharton, anatomy, humors, mesenteric gland</keywords>

<translation>
<pb n="22"/><meta>continues from previous page: provided that he is in these lands</meta> is the deputy of God, and whatever assistance he provides, it is piously believed that God himself has brought it through him mediately, since God wills that all things be done decently and in order; and toward the magistrate whom he himself has given, we should exhibit the honor due to him, and in turn expect from him the duties and defense fitting for a magistrate. This follows the example of Paul, for whom, regarding cruelty, the Roman Emperor is a Lion <note>2 Timothy 4:17</note>; and yet, in danger of life and in a political cause, he rightly appeals to him as the ordinary magistrate <note>Acts 25:10-11</note>.

I also add this: where a divine calling has joined us with people of a different religion in the same province or city, which is by the permission of the highest magistrate, there we can remain with a clear conscience, provided it is permitted for us to practice our religion rightly and safely. For then that promise of God consoles the pious, by which he promises that he will be present with each one in his calling and his ways <note>Psalm 91:11, 15</note>. This can be seen in Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob descending into Egypt by his command, and in Daniel and his captive companions living in Babylon. And to this I draw what certain legal scholars <term>Jurisconsulti</term> and politicians urge so greatly: that diverse religions can be tolerated. I concede this, but for us who are subjects, when the superior magistrate has granted it. Truly, whether a less orthodox religion ought to be admitted anew in a free Republic, I have so far seen no one who could prove this from Scripture.

Finally, to omit many other minor objections which can be easily dissolved from what has already been said, it is immense how much the examples of Abraham <note>Genesis 14 and 21</note> and Isaac <note>Genesis 26</note> striking treaties <term>foedera</term> differ from the present question. First, there are those (among whom is our own Luther) who deny that those they allied with were impious, profane, or alien to the religion of the Patriarchs, which they themselves attempt to prove with several arguments taken from the text. I say this can be sufficiently and clearly shown from the cited passages: these were not ecclesiastical and mixed treaties, but only political ones regarding civil matters. And this was not so much for defending as for not offending <note>non-aggression</note>; both were contracted by the Patriarchs when they themselves did not greatly stand in need of their help, but rather when Abimelech requested this from them. What, therefore, is this conclusion? The Patriarchs were able to contract with their pious neighbors (as Luther establishes in his commentaries on Genesis) concerning civil matters and non-offending, being invited and so forth. <pb n="23"/> Therefore, we too can enter into a treaty of defense with people who are either plainly impious or blasphemous against God and his word—even granting them the free exercise of their own religion—by inviting them and enticing them by all means. For who does not see from the preceding points that very different types of treaties are being confused? That the principles, objects, ends, and circumstances here are different, and therefore it cannot be the same action?

Truly, as for what concerns the Calvinists (for I think this one thing remains in this question), whether they dissent from us in certain principal articles of faith, and those fundamental, namely and especially in the topic of the person of Christ, predestination, baptism, and the Lord’s Supper, etc.; I would believe no one is such a stranger to theology as to be either ignorant of it or at least doubt it. For these things are sufficiently explained in any Catechetical and Symbolic books, likewise in Compendiums of theology in the antitheses, and it is otherwise established from many polemical writings published by both sides for about eighty years now; for which reason I refrain from a more prolix commentary on a plain matter.

And I come to purely political treaties, which I affirm to be lawful even with profane and heterodox <note>those of differing beliefs</note> people, for the following reasons. I. Because they are just and good, viewed from their principle, object, end, and circumstances. II. Because they are not only permitted by God, but even commanded <note>Psalm 34:13; Romans 12:18; Hebrews 12:4</note>; just as all the pious are ordered to intercede with God for kings and whoever is placed in eminence, so that they may lead a tranquil and quiet life with all piety and reverence <note>1 Timothy 2:1-2</note>. And Jeremiah thus exhorts the captives in Babylon by letter <note>Chapter 29:7</note>: "Seek the prosperity of that city where I have deported you," says Jehovah, "and pray for it to Jehovah; for in its prosperity shall be your prosperity." III. Because approved examples of the pious exist: Jacob with Laban <note>Genesis 31:44</note>, David <note>2 Samuel 5:11</note>, Solomon contracting a political treaty with Hiram king of Tyre <note>1 Kings 5:12</note>. IV. Because God severely punished those who violated them: Saul and his descendants <note>2 Samuel 21:1-2, etc.; compare Joshua 9 and 1 Samuel 28:3, 9</note>. And Ladislaus, King of Hungary, breaking a political treaty entered into with Amurath <note>Murad II</note> at the instigation of the Roman Pontiff <note>Chronicle of Carion, book 3</note>. And it is worth noting what the annals of the Silesians record: that Amurath, when he was already almost driven into flight with his men, after he had looked upon the image of the crucified Christ displayed by the Christians...
</translation>

<summary>Tarnow argues that while ecclesiastical alliances with those of differing faiths are unlawful, purely political and civil treaties are permissible and even commanded by Scripture. He distinguishes between religious fellowship and civil cooperation, citing biblical examples and historical consequences of broken treaties.</summary>

<keywords>political treaties, Calvinists, Lutherans, religious tolerance, magistrate, Abimelech, Amurath, Ladislaus of Hungary, biblical precedents</keywords>

Therefore we shall pluck only very few things from the aforementioned Authors, yet we shall see whether we might not also be able to add some things of our own. Indeed, we shall repeat this purification itself from Numbers 5:12 and following, and from it we shall briefly contemplate both the *subject*, who especially had to undergo that purification, and also the *formal act* itself by which this purification was performed. And that former part is described clearly enough for us in verse 12 and following, namely that it was a woman living in the marital state who, having turned away from her true husband, conversed familiarly with some other in secret, and there either formally committed adultery or at least gave no light suspicion to the husband that she had done something of that kind, and thus supplied the occasion for him to demand from her the purification of chastity. Where the Talmudic writers accurately observe that it was not necessary for this purification to be undertaken indiscriminately by every married woman, and that nothing concerning this Law of God intervened for any betrothed Virgin or a widow, or even one awaiting a <term>Levir</term> <gloss>a brother-in-law required to marry a widow</gloss>, if they were caught having some clandestine business contrary to the precept of the fiancé or the Levir with him whose familiarity they were forbidden, as taught in chapter 4 <pb n="9"/> of the <term>Sota</term> <gloss>the tractate on the suspected adulteress</gloss>, <term>Mishnah</term> <gloss>codification of Jewish oral law</gloss> 1, in Mr. Wagenfeil in *Sota*, page 550, whom you may also consult on page 381: just as he alleges that very same thing also from the <term>Yalkut</term> <gloss>collection of midrashic commentaries</gloss>, folio 207, column 3 and folio 208, column 3; Chaskuni at the words "besides a man" <note>original: מבלעדי איש</note>; <term>Mincha Betula</term> folio 136 a; <term>Kiddushin</term> <gloss>the tractate on betrothal</gloss> chapter 1, folio 27 b; <term>Sifrei</term> <gloss>halakhic midrash</gloss> folio 4, column 4; and <term>Rabboth</term> <gloss>the Great Midrash</gloss> folio 230, column 4, middle. Mr. Acoluthus, in the cited place, folio 135, deduces from the writings of the Rabbis on page 137 and following, that besides these just-mentioned women, far more still, who were either blind, or deaf, or mute, stood immune from this purification, concerning which Mr. Wagenfeil also deserves to be read in the cited place, page 587. Therefore, only the remaining women, into whom none of these conditions fitted, could be driven to the purification of chastity, so that the wives of Priests and Eunuchs, likewise freedwomen and proselytes, were altogether subjected to this, as <term>Mishnah</term> 4, chapter 4 of the <term>Sota</term> confesses, as does Mr. Wagenfeil in the cited place, page 581. Moreover, the occasion for this purification was not only a crime committed by the wife, but even the bare suspicion of the husband alone, and sometimes even rashness and a wandering desire to separate from their wives, so that if the husband wished, he could demand this purification from his wives at any time and place. Therefore, in the said case, if he had seen her even once talking familiarly with another, and he himself wished to be separated from his wife, he seized this occasion of freeing himself from her either through a bill of divorce or even, if she would not consent to this, through the purification of chastity, and for that reason he brought her to the Priest, where she had to undergo this purification. # COROLLARIES
## Added.

### I.

The ethical definition of a comet, which Stanislaus Lubieniecki <note>a Polish astronomer and historian</note> so names and presents in the *Conclusion of the Cometic Theater* <note>original: "Theatri Cometici Exitu"</note> on leaf 26, is that it is a supernatural, artificial, arbitrary, doctrinal, indicative, and memorial sign, by which God marks His ways to man, announcing good things to the good and evil to the evil; and man, endowed with reason and knowledge of the Divine will, and obedient to His <pb n="14"/><note>The top of the page features floral ornaments surrounding the page number.</note> *intention and institution, allows and rejoices that his duties are recalled to his memory; on the contrary, if he is negligent of his duties, he fears and dreads the announced threats: he sins against* moral philosophy.

## II.

*Although comets are not to be feared superstitiously, they are nevertheless not to be profanely despised or sarcastically mocked. The blessed ones, as they love to say, have held the middle ground.*

*The reasoning is inept, and one which even natural piety hisses at, which claims that* comets *portend no evil because most often most calamitous times have occurred even without such new* stars *ever being seen, or because a most happy state of affairs has followed such phenomena. <translation>
<pb n="8"/>...the same impudent pattern or identity I encountered again and again. Because everyone, by unanimous consensus, had most justly rejected that booklet of Johannes Reuchlin as being injurious to the Church of God beyond what is credible, irreverent toward the holy doctors, suitable for his own ends but wicked, fit for the worst men, scandalous to Christians, and finally too indulgent toward Jewish perfidy and savoring too much of depraved heresy, they judged it—by their open letters with the attachment of their seals—as something to be heartily condemned and soon removed from the use of Christians like a deadly poison and a burgeoning, dangerous plague. Then at last the Inquisitor, fortified by the determination, opinion, and authority of such great and most learned men, undertook the matter itself in the diocese and city of Mainz with the consent and exhortation of the Archbishop; especially since those wicked booklets had first been displayed there and publicly sold to everyone. Therefore, the Inquisitor himself, a venerable doctor, received from the Most Reverend Lord Archbishop of Mainz four judges from the city of Mainz as his colleagues. To these, the Most Reverend Lord Archbishop of Cologne—worthy of all praise and honor—had also added his own official of the court, an outstanding man visible in all things, with the consent of the Prince of Mainz. These were indeed most learned, upright, and excellent men, who should be held suspect in the slightest degree by no mortal, even the most wicked. One of them is the Suffragan of Mainz; the second is the magnificent Rector of the famous university there; three are doctors of Sacred Theology, while two others are doctors of Pontifical Law. With these distinguished and venerable men, the Inquisitor instituted there a process of equity and justice. After citations were lawfully executed and judicially reported (as we commonly say)—not indeed for any effect on any person's individual character, but generally and specifically against all those who thought it in their interest to defend the heretical obscenities of the said work—he continued the process happily and holily begun for the sake of his office of the faith. But in truth, at the deadline of the citation, that doctor <note>Johannes Reuchlin</note>, more concerned for his own honor than for the integrity of the Catholic faith and for cutting off the intolerable scandal, refused the Inquisitor himself as suspect through his procurator, based on certain frivolous and (if I may say so) invalid motives, exulting in this alone. Wherefore the Inquisitor, sufficiently encouraged by the cause of justice and distrusting none of the judges, wisely unburdened himself from the duty of investigating, judging, and defining, in order to avoid the plurality of refusals, arbiters, and appeals—and the frivolous and plainly weak exceptions (as they call them)—which are unpleasant to every good man. He rejected the entire judicial recognition of the case publicly and judicially upon his colleagues and performed only the duty of the accuser. However, although things stood thus, the procurator of the opposing party nevertheless interposed a certain childish and plainly inept appeal to the Holy Apostolic See against only the Inquisitor as a judge already refused, without even seeing the process. And now, to say much in few words: when all the legal terms had been observed rightly and lawfully, also with the counsel and assistance (as it is said) of legal experts, and the proclamation of the sentence in this case, following mature deliberation, <pb n="9"/> had been kindly suspended for an interval of fifteen days at the prayers of the lords of the Great Church of Mainz <note>the Cathedral Chapter</note> and with the consent of the Inquisitor. And furthermore, for a second time, when these fifteen days had already elapsed and the aforementioned judges, fully resolved and constant in the cause of faith, sat for the purpose of pronouncing judgment from the tribunal—the parties having been lawfully cited and called—there arrived certain letters from the Most Reverend Lord of Mainz, obtained somehow or other from a less-than-good man in favor (alas!) of heretical depravity. In these letters, he commanded his commissioners or delegates that unless the Inquisitor suspended the case for one entire month beyond the aforementioned fifteen gracious days already granted, the Archbishop himself would utterly revoke the commission given to the judges. And thereafter, if anything were attempted by them within the prescribed time, he wished all of it to be void. Thus all things were overturned and (as you have heard) plainly changed before they could be seen through. Although the Lord of Mainz himself, now deceased and subject to the Just Judge, had often added his faithful service to the Inquisitor in this matter at various times—so much so that the Lord Inquisitor, seeking the salvation of the Church (as will be open to everyone at the strict judgment of God), was not a little encouraged by his help and counsel and, trusting in his most pious words, expected a most happy end desired by all good men. Moreover, as we have heard these things were done so sinisterly by certain people, good men might easily understand that justice itself was not only manifestly denied to the Reverend Inquisitor in the most pious cause of our Lord Jesus Christ and the most sacred faith, but was violently snatched from his hands. Especially since the aforementioned Archbishop of Mainz neither called the case to himself, nor made it certain or settled in what way or at what time it should finally be concluded; nor, once the month had passed, did he propose any hope (as ought to have been done otherwise) of a brief and total expedition of this case to the Reverend Inquisitor. Therefore, in the judgment of prudent and learned men, no hope of a good outcome seemed left to the Inquisitor there with the Archbishop, but rather (what is unworthy to hear) contempt, mockery, and disparagement of the Inquisitor. This was because the Archbishop cared neither to terminate the cause of Christ as he ought to by law, nor to transmit it, duly prepared, to the Apostolic See. It is not doubted that this was devised or (as they say) practiced by the adversary, who was ill-prescient of his own case, lest perhaps if the Holy Apostolic See should recognize the depraved teachings of the *Ocular Mirror* and certain intolerable errors (as will undoubtedly happen), it would condemn them as quickly as possible with a more severe censure. He surely knew that the above-written judges, through our Inquisitor, were undoubtedly going to pronounce a sentence against his said scandalous and most pernicious booklets, especially if they had not been recalled by the Archbishop himself and from the office of equity. Hence it is truer and clearer than light that the case was concluded as we have now heard. Two of those judges, in the name and by the sacred commission of the entire faculty of theology at Mainz, delivered a lawful condemnation of the previously noted booklets, fortified with the seal of their faculty as lawfully required, declaring with a sincere heart that they were greatly saddened and plainly groaned because the causes of the Christian faith had been dealt with so lightly and captiously. These things having been so conducted, the adversary himself, in order to cut off the principal matter—that is, to impede the sentence itself by any means—
</translation>

<summary>This passage describes the legal and ecclesiastical proceedings in Mainz against Johannes Reuchlin's book, the Ocular Mirror. It details how the Inquisitor, supported by several universities, faced procedural delays and an appeal to Rome orchestrated by Reuchlin's side and the Archbishop's intervention.</summary>

<keywords>Johannes Reuchlin, Ocular Mirror, Speculum Oculare, Inquisition, Mainz, University of Cologne, heresy, ecclesiastical law, Archbishop of Mainz, theological faculty</keywords>

*Little Fountains* <gloss>Fonticuli/Issues</gloss> <note>surgically created sores kept open to drain ill humors</note> correctly excited contribute to preservation.

*Frictions* for the sake of revulsion and dispersal, and *Blistering agents* <gloss>Vesicantia</gloss> by way of evacuation, are sometimes admitted; however, *Cautery* <gloss>Ustio</gloss> and the excision of veins find scarcely any place in the modern age.

### II.

From the **PHARMACEUTICAL** source, a store of various evacuating and altering medicines, both simple and compound, ancient and modern, is drawn. Since this is treated quite at length by practitioners, and their almost innumerable volumes are filled with prescriptions and formulas, one must not insist absolutely on such things in the cure, but look above all to the circumstances and accidents which the present state of the arthritic patient requires: it has pleased me to record only a very few from this class of relevant medicines.

Regarding *Purgatives*, they can be safely administered neither in the beginning nor during the increase of the pains <note>unless they are very mild</note>; since the paroxysm is further exacerbated by a strong agitation of the humors. They must therefore be taken before or after the onset, after *lenients and preparatives* have been sent before.

Let such a lenient be prescribed:

| | | |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Take. | Alexandrian Senna leaves, <term>f. s.</term> <gloss>without stalks</gloss> | one ounce. |
| | Indian Rhubarb root | half an ounce. |
| | Polypody <note>a type of fern</note> | half an ounce. |
| | Anise and Fennel seeds, of each | two drachms. |
| | Smaller Raisins <gloss>Passul. minor.</gloss> | two ounces. |

Let them be boiled in a closed vessel with two pounds of spring water until a third part is consumed. Then let three drachms be taken in the morning hours, <pb n="19"/> and let the dose be repeated until the bowels are gently moved. More, as necessity requires, can be composed from crystals of Tartar <note>original: alchemical symbol for Tartar</note>, *Mechoacan, cassia, laxative syrups*, and many others.

*Aloetics* <note>medicines containing aloes</note> can be used in every case of gout <gloss>podagra</gloss> as a preservative and if the bowels are constricted. Examples are the *aloëphangine* and *Frankfurt* pills.

Lenient *Enemas* <gloss>Clysteres</gloss> are also conveniently admitted, the supply of which is well known.

For the *Preparation* and cutting of the humors, it is customary to take *salts of wall-germander, ground-pine, volatile salt of amber, juniper*, or *rest-harrow* <gloss>resta bovis</gloss>, mixed with sugar, in a dose of 16 or 18 grains.

*Stronger purgatives* sought from the chests of the chemists are *Antimonials* and Mercurials <note>original: alchemical symbol for Mercury/mercurials</note>, provided they are correctly prepared. The ancients among the dogmatics used *Scammony, Hedge Hyssop, Hellebore, Turbith*, etc. The *hermodactyl pills* are praised, which even *Paracelsus* approves. However, milder things are generally commended, for example:

> Take <note>original: ℞ symbol</note> *magistery of jalap,*
> *crystals of Tartar <note>original: alchemical symbol for Tartar</note> of each 9 grains.*
> *oil of anise and fennel of each 2 drops.*
> *Mix to make a powder.*

*Sudorifics* <gloss>sweat-inducing agents</gloss> are esteemed very useful in this affection, provided they are not too hot. Coming into use here are *Magistery of Hartshorn, philosophically calcined, and Spirit. Bezoardic tincture. Diaphoretic Mercury* <note>original: ☿ symbol</note>. *Extract of sarsaparilla root.* A decoction of china root and sarsaparilla was once in great use among the Spaniards. Yet let these not be given while the body remains impure.

*Diuretics* are likewise beneficial. In which case it is better to administer spirit of juniper and of rose-hips <gloss>cynosbati</gloss> tempered with parsley water. Medicines prepared from turpentine promise the same. *Spirit of Salt* <note>original: symbols for Salt and Vitriol</note>. *Vitriol* <note>original: symbol for Vitriol</note> impregnated with the volatile salt of urine. *Tincture of Tartar* <note>original: symbol for Tartar</note> etc.

Concerning the salivary cure by means of mercury <term>hydrargyrum</term>, it is left to each man’s own preference.
</translation>

<pb n="15"/><meta>continues from previous page: He omitted nothing that he could do for the preservation of the Eximite Man, his most dear friend.</meta> After a few days, the state of the body deceived the inexperienced; the burden of humors having been gradually liberated by mild medicines, it changed for the better, as it seemed, and there was a decrease in the fever that had accompanied the disease at a slow pace. Truly, just as a tree does not depart from its root, so also the disease could not abandon its more deeply rooted fuel. The putrefaction, fever, sleeplessness, and other symptoms took on more and more strength and increase, and began to more clearly threaten the danger of death, when Lord Doctor Nicolaus Hannekenius was also called into counsel. Nature had already then begun to drive out the hostile humor through the bowels, and the putrid masses of blood, the unhappy offspring of the now rotting and eroded liver <note>original: "Hepatis"</note>. All things were attempted which such a great disease and such great symptoms required. But Nature did not desist from this work of excretion until the strength was utterly cast down, and the framework of the body was dissolved along with the parenchyma <note>the functional tissue of an organ</note> of the liver, and liquefied; and thus the source of a better, eternal life took the place of this diseased, fleeting life. Thus far the words of the Physician.

Thus we have perceived the origin, progress, vigor, and deeds of this Most Illustrious Man, sketched with a rough hand <note>original: "rudi minerva", a Latin idiom for a simple or unrefined style</note> without the splendor of words. It is necessary that I finally approach the, alas, sad epilogue of his life itself, concerning which I must deal very briefly, since there is no one who could teach me more regarding the manner of his blessed passing, or likewise concerning his last words, and other things which are accustomed to happen around this turn and goal of life. Nevertheless, since this most praised man always lived his life piously and religiously toward God, justly toward his neighbor, and temperately toward himself, we neither ought to nor can doubt that he died well and blessedly. Which eternal happiness <pb n="16"/> we congratulate his blessed departed spirit from our heart, wishing for ourselves a similar passing, with a desirable vow and sigh: Would that he were living safe and joyful, and that he could perform this sad duty for many others, and especially for me—being much riper for death—which I, by a perverse order of nature, perform for him. But as it pleased the Lord, so it was done. May His holy name be blessed in favorable as well as adverse circumstances.

Since it has been decided to commit the remains of his blessed soul to his burial vault tomorrow, the 12th of September, for the leading forth of the funeral and the funeral rites, the Magnificent Lords Burgomasters <note>original: "CONSULES"</note>; the most Noble and Learned Lord Syndic; the most Noble, Learned, and likewise most Experienced Lord Doctors; the Reverend and also Most Illustrious Lords Pastors and Ecclesiastics; the most Distinguished and Prudent Lords Senators and Secretaries, and no less the other most honorable Citizens of this City, Patrons of the School, that they might wish to be present in large numbers, with that observance, reverence, and diligence which is fitting,

<pb n="9"/>the accusation was brought forward. While these preparations were underway, the rumor of this monstrous affair reached here. I heard, I was struck down, <unclear>my heart failed</unclear>:

And after a night that was the most sorrowful and entirely sleepless of any in my life, I resolved at first light to attempt something immediately. I labored there and then to the best of my ability so that this University at least might intercede in whatever way it could, since no other way was granted, by a Public Protest, Entreaty, and Supplication; both before the Ranks <note>original: "Ordines"</note> of the Commonwealth (as they were called), and before the Great Military Council, which alone held absolute power. I drafted in formal words what I desired; I offered myself, unafraid of anything, as a ready Messenger and <pb n="10"/>Agent. This, if it could not stop that unspeakable and cursed endeavor, would certainly testify to the present and future age that this University shrinks from such great impiety and brutality: that we owe this to God, to the religion we profess, to the Best of Kings, to our Country, and finally to ourselves. To all these things, *Listeners*, I gave (as I said) my diligent effort; but oh, the grief! oh, the shame! a vain effort: *I sing to the deaf*. What the times were like among us then must be kept silent. And so that summary of all our evils proceeded: the detestable and uninterrupted trial <note>original: "causae cognitio," literally a judicial investigation or hearing</note> of the most Innocent and most Pious Prince, before Traitors concerning Treason, before Tyrants concerning Tyranny, before Homicides and Parricides concerning Homicide. <translation>
<pb n="17"/><meta>continues from previous page: ...employ justice and equity in all their dealings.</meta> Indeed, such a discourse should be called neither of man nor for man. Yet there is no lack of those among the more recent writers—which is no small cause for wonder—who, seduced by those vain arguments of the ancients, shamelessly teach that in the state <note>original: "politia"</note> one must care only for utility and the abundance of those things which fortune supplies. They argue that those who are set apart for the hope of administering the republic and for great cares should have no regard for what is honorable and lawful. For who has missed the impious voice of Machiavelli in the fifteenth chapter of *The Prince*, where he judges it necessary for the safety of a Prince that he be not good? By this very principle, he not only commends but even persuades the one who governs regions that evil arts are most necessary for stabilizing a Princedom and preserving an empire. We omit other Doctors who even today attempt to defend the same most pestilential error to the immense loss of states. But this foul opinion has long since been refuted and condemned with suitable arguments by ancient writers of great name, whose authority is not to be despised. For it could not be obscure to those most grave men that the honorable <note>original: "honestum"</note> must in no way be severed from the useful in a state, nor should anything be thought honorable which is not useful, or useful which is not honorable and consistent with virtue; since these two are connected by a certain natural and most tight bond. It easily appears, however, what utility was understood by them: namely, that which employs right reason in its counsel, by which neither the principles nor the causes of things are neglected, and those things which are to follow are accurately weighed and compared with the present. And they judged this alone to be worthy of the name of utility. For utility ceases to be such, or is even the greatest destruction, in the estimation of which a man <pb n="18"/>follows the corrupt judgment of his own affections, and chooses such a good which indeed seems joyful and salutary, but, if weighed in an equal balance, is counterfeit, slippery, and inconstant, and is the source and origin of many inconveniences. Many think that great fruits are reported when faith is not kept, when injury is brought upon the weak, when no agreements are observed, when power and wealth are sought by unjust arts, and other things are done which the laws and rights require to be sedulously avoided by every kind of man. When, however, those who do these things expect the same from others who procure their own advantages from any matter whatsoever, it must necessarily follow; from actions of this kind, separated from the honorable, there can be so little fruit or pleasantness for a wise man that, on the contrary, with the order of things confused, they bring the greatest detriment and most grave calamity to men. Thus, therefore, that which is most profitable must be so regarded in the republic that it be joined with honorable and laudable things, and that nothing be done or thought which seems to be far from virtue and the probity of morals. In order that this may be more easily obtained, it will be very necessary that those things by which the honesty of morals and the study of virtue are aided and promoted be diligently observed. While not a few such things have been brought forward by those who, solicitous for the most salutary precepts, have well weighed such a great matter in their minds; yet we judge that these three are the chief: religion, discipline, and good laws—saving the judgments of others. However, to deal with these now in more words is superfluous; since they will be explained more broadly and abundantly by certain youths who are to declaim publicly tomorrow. We add only something concerning religion and briefly note what the Fathers and Doctors of the Church have felt concerning it, in relation to virtues and honorable morals.
</translation>

<keywords>Machiavelli, The Prince, utility vs. honor, political virtue, right reason, statecraft, religion, discipline, laws, Church Fathers</keywords>

# THE SECOND DECLAMATION.

In recent days, there came forth to this platform, Listeners and others, one who would pursue in speech the infamous passion for foreign travel <term>peregrinitatis</term> <gloss>the practice of wandering or traveling abroad</gloss>. You supported the speaker with benevolence and a liberal interest, I believe, because in your judgment the subject he had taken up was not unworthy of this present place; nor was it something that your renowned assembly or the rest of the gathered crowd <note>original: "concionem"</note> would be reluctant to hear. Amidst this favor of minds and tongues, after the others, as was fitting—since I had also prepared myself to devote my mind and ears to the speaker—I can only guess what effect he had on others; but of myself, I can plainly affirm this: my mind was so swayed that I began to abominate these customs and detest the insanity of such pursuits. Therefore, I felt that I had by no means wasted my effort, especially on a subject where one’s intellect <note>original: "ingenium"</note> might deservedly be put to the test, and because the topic suffered very little from a sterile lack of material. Indeed, when the orator, according to the method of his plan, had determined to expose the baseness of this study, it was understood that the subject was represented with such abundance that, in explaining it, the intellect had to be restrained rather than exhausted by anxious <pb n="378"/> meditation. But if someone wished to add the other points of that kind which were omitted, he would undoubtedly fill a whole new speech. Truly, I will not hide that a desire then entered my mind to test what could be brought forward by me in the same vein. But the palm of victory is placed in the center for all; anyone who wishes may make the attempt. For my part, having debated the matter more diligently with myself, since I have chosen to be a substitute <note>original: "succenturiatus"</note> in this arena <term>palaestra</term> <gloss>wrestling school or place of debate</gloss>, I considered it better, rather than being equipped from the same armory, to take up new weapons with which to fight against this most vain pursuit. I have decided to show that, just as that pursuit is judged base and infamous, it must also be held as harmful to both public and private interests. In this, I am persuaded that the logic of my plan has not strayed far. For even if I were to contribute some bit of wit to what came before, I saw that the principal points had already been exhausted; yet I understood that the condemnation <note>original: "vituperatio"</note> would be imperfect if this latter part of the argument were omitted. Add to this that human temperaments are so constituted that they are little moved by the mere demonstration of a thing's baseness; but if you demonstrate that something is joined with ruin, you will drag them, terrified, wherever you wish, even against their will. Therefore, let this passion for foreign travel be base, because it belongs to the ungrateful, the servile, the insane, and finally the inept; I shall strive to bring this about: that it may appear that *it is rightly called, on one hand, a plague to the family estate, and on the other, a subversion of the public good,* 
</translation>

<summary>This declamation argues against the "infamous" practice of traveling abroad, shifting the focus from the moral baseness of the habit to its practical and economic destructiveness. The speaker intends to prove that such wandering ruins family fortunes and undermines the stability of the state.</summary>

<keywords>foreign travel, declamation, social critique, family estate, public good, Georg Steinhagen, rhetoric, peregrinitas</keywords>

Furthermore, since these Scribes were quite often forced to go into the provinces with their Patrons (for in the retinue of Governors going into the provinces, they were all those assistants, servants, and companions whom the usage and reason of the province, as well as the dignity itself of the magistrates and the republic demanded; for example: Legates, Military Tribunes, Centurions, Prefects, Decurions, and other assistants and servants of military works and accounts; and additionally, Scribes, attendants, heralds, lictors, interpreters, couriers, soothsayers, chamberlains, physicians, and companions, and so forth), for that reason those <term>decuriae</term> <gloss>squadrons or official divisions</gloss> were quite often sold by the Scribes, and indeed bought by others. On which matter Reinefius again speaks in the cited Letter. Cicero mentions such a purchase in his speech against Verres <note>original: "in Varum", likely a transcription error for "in Verrem"</note>: *Recall me to those Scribes, if you please; do not collect these men who, having scraped together small coins from the goods of their grandsons and from the gifts of actors, say that they have come from the first rank of the rejected into the second rank of the state when they bought a <term>decuria</term>. I shall have those Scribes as judges of this crime who are annoyed that those others are Scribes at all. Although, when we see many in that rank who are not suitable—an order which was established for industry and dignity—shall we wonder that some shameful men are in that rank, which anyone is allowed to reach for a price?* Moreover, Sigonius indicates that the right of choosing Scribes into the <term>decuriae</term> was chiefly in the hands of the Praetors, Quaestors, and Aediles, and indeed from Cicero's <pb n="12"/>speech for Cluentius <note>original: "Cluentiana"</note>, where these things occur: *Recently, when I defended a man of small means, an aedilician scribe named Decimus Matriniius, before the Praetors Marcus Junius and Quintus Publicius and the Curule Aediles Marcus Plaetorius and Gaius Flaminius, I persuaded them that they, being under oath, should choose as a scribe a man whom those same Censors had left as an <term>aerarius</term> <gloss>a citizen reduced to a lower rank but still paying taxes</gloss>.* Livy has things related to these. In the Fortieth Book, Quintus Petillius, the Urban Praetor, took those books from Lucius Petillius the scribe. And there was a familiar use of him, because the Quaestor Quintus Petillius had chosen him into the <term>decuria</term> as a scribe.

### §. XI.

The duties of the Public Scribes were chiefly these: (1) To attend upon the Magistrates; which, besides those things we have already brought forward, is also confirmed by a passage of Plutarch in his life of Cato, which, translated into the Latin language, sounds thus: *When Cato had entered the quaestorship, he restrained the servants and scribes who, handling the public tablets and laws, did not yield their power when they encountered young men who were the magistrates they attended, because those magistrates lacked experience and needed teachers; instead, they themselves were the magistrates. But Cato treated them as attendants, as they were, since he accused some of fraud and others of ignorance.* (2) To read aloud publicly to the people and to submit to the herald for proclamation all those things which the magistrate wished to be made public from writing. On which see Philippus Beroaldus in the Ninth Book of Apuleius. (3) They signed, recorded, and entered into the tablets those things which were made public from the acts and were reported into them; whence Isidore, in the place cited, writes that they were called <term>Tabelliones</term> <gloss>notaries/secretaries</gloss> because they wrote those things which were made public by the acts.
