<pb n="14"/>### §. II.

The occasion for appealing to Caesar was given to this Apostle, standing before the tribunal of Caesar at Caesarea, by Festus, as has already been stated in *Section I, §. VI, page 7.* For he, greatly desiring to find favor with the Jewish accusers, had asked, in *Chapter XXV, verse 9*, whether Paul wished to be judged at Jerusalem? But the Apostle, when he perceived the intent of this question, quite opportunely and prudently *appealed to Caesar*: for, just as a wise man, to speak with Gregory Nazianzen, *avoids all heavy and dangerous things, just as a pilot avoids storms*, so also Paul, taught by experience that he would never and nowhere be safe in Judea, cautious and diligent, avoids these snares of Jewish deceit; especially since he dreaded (1.) **THE JEWS**, most of whom, as is abundantly clear from *Gospel and Apostolic History*, were most bitter enemies of the Christian doctrine which he was propagating, kindled by pious emulation and divine zeal; and (2.) **THE CITY OF JERUSALEM**, where the Prophets were slaughtered and the Apostles were stoned; *Matthew XXIII, v. 37 compared with Acts VII, v. 52*; indeed, where he had already before been received with dire beatings by Jews seeking to kill him, *Acts XXI, v. 31, 32*; and (3.) **THE JOURNEY** on account of the ambushes for his murder to be prepared by assassins on the road. *Acts XXV, v. 3 compared with Acts XXIII, v. 12–15.*

### §. III.

As for the *crimes* of which the Jews were laboring to heavily accuse Paul before Festus, these are called <term>polla kai barea aitiāmata</term> <gloss>many and heavy charges</gloss> in general in *Acts XXV, v. 7.* What kind, however, and how great those <term>aitiāmata</term> <gloss>charges</gloss> were specifically, the *Pauline Apology* in the following *Verse 8* indicates clearly enough, since <pb n="15"/> indeed it is gathered from it that there were three primary heads of accusation: namely, that *Paul had sinned against the law and the temple of the Jews, and against Caesar. Compare also the assertion of Festus, Acts XXV, v. 18, 19.* Paul, however, being well aware of his own innocence and not turning pale with any guilt for those crimes, strenuously denied that *anything had been committed by him against either the law and temple of the Jews, or against the majesty of Caesar*; and rightly so, because, as is read in verse 7 of said chapter, *the accusers were not able to prove their charges brought against Paul.*

### §. IV.

Wherefore Paul, compelled by such necessity, appealed to Caesar, which was permitted to him (1.) as a MAN, (2.) as a ROMAN CITIZEN, (3.) as a CHRISTIAN, and (4.) as an APOSTLE. It was permitted, I say, to Paul as a MAN, through the benefit of *Appeal*, to turn away the death intended for him by the Jews: for *self-defense and preservation*, toward which MEN are carried by a certain natural instinct and a most sharp desire, as it were, is permitted, just as those who have handed down the sounder precepts of the *Law of Nature* concerning the duties of MAN toward himself assert. And truly, one should doubt this assertion all the less, because it is more certainly evident that our supreme and provident Deity wills that the HUMAN RACE be preserved for its end, and that for this cause, permitted remedies conducive to the preservation of the same be employed in time, lest anyone rashly neglect the protection of his own body, or hold the preservation of his life in indifference, but rather protect and defend it in every way. Therefore, Paul not only here before Festus, by the benefit of *Appeal*, [defended] his life
</translation>

<pb n="11"/>Kirchmann, Book I, Chapter IV, *On Roman Funerals*, notes that this distinction arose from the games held in honor of the deceased, which they called "funeral games," as witnessed by Rosinus, Book V, *Roman Antiquities*, Chapter XXXIX. Now, the first kind is the Indictive Funeral: so named, according to Festus, because the people were summoned to it by a herald. Rosinus, in the place cited. It is named from "indicting" <gloss>proclaiming</gloss>, a term the ancients used in this sense, as Kirchmann notes in the same place. Suetonius in *Caesar*: *A funeral having been indicted, a pyre was built in the Field of Mars.* Cicero in his *Speech for his House to the Pontiffs* and *On the Consular Provinces*. Moreover, the illustrious Scaliger has already observed the solemn words of this proclamation from Terence’s *Phormio*, Act V, last Scene, and Varro’s Book IV, *On the Latin Language*. These Indictive Funerals were most magnificent, and besides other costly preparation, they were also celebrated with games. Cicero, Book II, *On the Laws*; Beckman, *On Origins*, page 706; Rosinus and Kirchmann in the cited places; Scaliger, Book I, *Ausonian Readings*, Chapter XXVIII; with circus riders <term>desultores</term> also employed. Festus Pompeius, Book XVII; Dempster on Rosinus, *Antiquities*, Book V, Chapter XXIV. The Public funeral can be referred to here, which was sometimes the same as the Indictive, as in Apuleius, Book XI, *Metamorphoses*; sometimes only a part of it, when, for instance, a cessation of business <term>justitium</term> was proclaimed, or public mourning, or expenses were made from the public treasury. Kirchmann, ibid. This honor was granted to Syphax, King of Numidia (Valerius Maximus, Book V, Chapter I; Suetonius in *Vitellius*, Chapter III); to Sphaerus, Augustus’s freedman and tutor (Dio, Book XLVIII); to Piso, Urban Prefect (the same, Dio, Book LXIV). Illustrious women were not without a share of this (Idem, Book XLVII; Xiphilinus in *Tiberius*). There were furthermore various kinds of Public Funerals according to the diversity of honors managed by the deceased, such as Praetorian, Consular, Censorial, and Triumphal, as Polybius indicates (Book VI, *Histories*), where, however, Lipsius noted that the triumphal was confused with the censorial under the emperors. The most worthy was the Censorial, by which princes were carried out, such as Claudius (Tacitus, Book XII). Whence Spartianus in *Aelius Verus* calls it an Imperial funeral; in *Opilius Macrinus*, a Royal one. For the Censorship was the most honored among the magistracies (Plutarch in *Cato the Elder*).

## Other Silent, or Simpludearian Funerals. Thesis VII.

This is the second kind: called by another name the Common funeral in Capitolinus, *Life of Marcus Antoninus the Philosopher*. Likewise the Shared funeral, Ausonius, *Parentalia*. Also the Plebeian funeral, Propertius, Book II, Elegy XIV. The Ordinary funeral, Suetonius, *Nero*, Chapter XXXIII, regarding the death of Britannicus. These funerals were held without pomp, without a funeral director <term>designator</term>, without a herald <pb n="12"/>and without a proclamation. Seneca, Book I, *On Tranquility*, Chapter I; Ovid, Book I, *Fasti*, Elegy III. Indeed, they were held with no other solemnities except games. Dempster in his *Additions* to Book V, Chapter XXIV of Rosinus's *Roman Antiquities*; Scaliger on Festus; and Book I of *Ausonian Readings*, Chapter XXVIII. From this it was called "Simpludearian" as if "Simple-play-ian" <term>Simpliludiarium</term>, because simple players <term>ludii</term> were employed—that is, dancers, or tumblers <term>cernuatores</term>, or servants whom Festus calls "basket-bearers" <term>corbitores</term>. Rosinus, Chapter XXXIX, Book I, *Roman Antiquities*; Beckman, *On Origins*, page 706. To these funerals also belong "Bitter Funerals" <term>acerba funera</term>, that is, those of people who died within the day of their initiation <term>tirocinium</term> and before taking up the toga of manhood. Kirchmann, Book I, Chapter IV, *On Roman Funerals*. The most distinguished Philippus Camerarius, son of the great Joachim, observed what "Masked Funerals" <term>larvata funera</term> are in Book I, *Historical Meditations*, Chapter XCVI. Polybius describes "Imaginary Funerals" in the book which is now the sixth; so does Capitolinus in his life of *Pertinax*.

->So much for the division: what follows is the enumeration of the rites.<-

### Thesis VIII.

## Regarding things that precede the burial, and concern the dying men.

When all hope of life seemed to have failed in the sick man, friends and those closest by blood used to kiss the dying person and embrace his body—Seneca, *On the Brevity of Life*. *In her embrace and kisses he perished*, Ausonius, *Parentalia*, Poem XXIII:

> He died between the hands of his mother
> and the kisses of his Father, etc.

Thus Augustus Caesar died in the kisses of Livia, as the author Suetonius states in his life, Chapter XC. Kirchmann gives the reasons for this custom in Chapter V, Book I, *On Roman Funerals*. Then, if the sick person died at home, when he began to breathe out his soul, those who were closest caught his breath with their mouth and wished to transfer it into themselves: which the ancients, in a womanish way, thought could be done. Cicero in the *Verrines*, V; Virgil, *Aeneid*, IV:

> — — — If any last breath wanders above,
> let me catch it with my mouth — — —

For the ancients thought that the soul, about to depart from the body, went out through the mouth as if through a door. Seneca, Letter XXX. And in *Hercules Furens*, verse 1310. Furthermore, rings were also usually removed from the dying...
</translation>

It describes the cultural practice of catching a dying relative's final breath and the removal of rings to facilitate the soul's departure.</summary>

To these people, nothing seems more anxious or wretched, because they know their enemies can scent and track their return, drag them from their hiding places, hand them over to custody, afflict them with many injuries, and cast them into dim and murky places—these true worshippers of the Christian faith, bound with chains and burdened with iron. The heretics do not even permit food to be brought in to them, except for a little dark bread, and that not often but only when it pleases them, and when they know for certain they are about to die, unless something is given to retain the soul, which they seem scarcely to draw in their chests, exhausted by hunger and near to death itself. But why do I recount the miseries of the English Catholics? Since the Christian faith has been cast out from its borders, there are no temples, no altars, no religious sacrifices; no images of the saints are seen. If any are found, they are cast into corners, covered in dust, covered in filth, trampled by sacrilegious feet, ruined, worn away, and broken into pieces; others are without heads or form, like stones clinging to walls or lying on the ground in the ruins of buildings, confused and mixed among the rest of the masonry. Many temples lie prostrate on the ground <pb n="12"/> with their walls cast down and roofs overturned, leveled with the citadels; a multitude of porters and the infirm flock there, wishing to attend to their needs.

Many have been converted into cookshops, overflowing with the smoke and stench of gluttony; many have been changed for the use and habitation of heretics. There, the most wicked gluttons and low tradesmen <note>original: "cerdonesque"</note> bring in their secret gatherings, their nefarious rites, and the most pestilential poison of their sermons on fixed days to fill themselves with food and wine. Thus, no sacrifice of divine matters is performed in England; no prayers, whether recited or chanted, are heard; the temples of the Catholics are filled with no assemblies of the heralds of the divine word, but with the discordant and horrid shouts of heretics. Confessions have been taken from the kingdom, the sacraments removed, and the most holy host cast down and trampled. No obedience or deference is shown to the Roman Pontiff; in short, no worship is granted to the Divine Majesty.

Heresy, with neck erect and drawn sword, breathing death and cruelty, dominates far and wide. The Catholics have no one to whom they may turn except the Catholic King. They have implored the help of Philip; they have [sought] the faith of Philip.
</translation>

The heretics do not even permit food to be brought in to them, except for a little dark bread, and that not often but only when it pleases them, and when they know for certain they are about to die, unless something is given to retain the soul, which they seem scarcely to draw in their chests, exhausted by hunger and near to death itself. But why do I recount the miseries of the English Catholics? Since the Christian faith has been cast out from its borders, there are no temples, no altars, no religious sacrifices; no images of the saints are seen. If any are found, they are cast into corners, covered in dust, covered in filth, trampled by sacrilegious feet, ruined, worn away, and broken into pieces; others are without heads or form, like stones clinging to walls or lying on the ground in the ruins of buildings, confused and mixed among the rest of the masonry. Many temples lie prostrate on the ground
pages.12:
with their walls cast down and roofs overturned, leveled with the citadels; a multitude of porters and the infirm flock there, wishing to attend to their needs.

Many have been converted into cookshops, overflowing with the smoke and stench of gluttony; many have been changed for the use and habitation of heretics. There, the most wicked gluttons and low tradesmen <note>original: "cerdonesque"</note> bring in their secret gatherings, their nefarious rites, and the most pestilential poison of their sermons on fixed days to fill themselves with food and wine. Thus, no sacrifice of divine matters is performed in England; no prayers, whether recited or chanted, are heard; the temples of the Catholics are filled with no assemblies of the heralds of the divine word, but with the discordant and horrid shouts of heretics. Confessions have been taken from the kingdom, the sacraments removed, and the most holy host cast down and trampled. No obedience or deference is shown to the Roman Pontiff; in short, no worship is granted to the Divine Majesty.

Heresy, with neck erect and drawn sword, breathing death and cruelty, dominates far and wide. The Catholics have no one to whom they may turn except the Catholic King. They have implored the help of Philip; they have [sought] the faith of Philip.

<pb n="11"/><meta>continues from previous page: ...and religion and</meta> the oaths of fidelity were established, by which Pippin and the others owed obedience to Childeric. But Pippin easily broke through these with his cleverness, since the people's veneration for the Kings was turned into contempt through their own sloth and Pippin's arts; he hoped that the oath could be severed by the authority of the Roman Pontiff, whom he had already bound to himself with great services. He decided, therefore, to weave the web in this way, as Pierre Matthieu in his <term>Genealogy of the Kings of France</term> <gloss>Genealogia Regum Francorum</gloss>, page 50, Buffier, and others explain. After he had bound many to himself by good deeds, more by promises, and everyone by his courtesy—having excited old friends with new hope and inflamed new ones by emulation of the old—a conversation was started everywhere by his associates through his maneuvers. It emanated first among the courtiers, then to the common people, that the sloth of so many kings was now a shameful thing to the glory of the Franks; that those who were equal neither to governing themselves nor others ought to be cast aside, and another should be chosen by whose virtue the kingdom might stand. Nor was such a person to be fetched from afar: Prince Pippin was ready at hand, a dwarf in body indeed, but a giant in soul.

<margin>Pippin proclaims a council of the kingdom.</margin>
Therefore, when Pippin noticed that such talk was pleasing to the common people and received by friendly ears, thinking the business was ripe, he proclaimed a public assembly of the kingdom, summoning the prelates and the chief men of the nobility whom he had found to be most supportive of him.

<margin>What was decreed there?</margin>
In this gathering, having already tested their dispositions, he proposed the matter and simultaneously won them over; it was agreed by everyone that messengers should be sent to the Pope to request release from the oath of allegiance.

<margin>Legates are sent to Rome to Pope Zacharias.</margin>
III. There were sent, therefore, to Zacharias, who then presided over the Roman See, Burchard, Bishop of Würzburg (others name Richard of Bourges), and Wolrad, Pippin’s chaplain, as they call him—that is, the overseer of the <pb n="12"/> chapel—to whose request the Pontiff easily assented.

<margin>
What they accomplished there:
Why the Pope assented to Pippin's wishes?
Pippin is anointed King.
Childeric is thrust into a monastery with his wife.
The origin of the title of Duke of Franconia for the Bishops of Würzburg.
</margin>
For the Pope, since he feared the Greek Emperors (from whom the Popes had revolted to strive for a new power for themselves) as avengers of Roman perfidy, and at the same time feared Aistulf, King of the Lombards, who was threatening the Roman territory just as he had the Greek empire, he chose to bind Pippin to himself by this new example of bad faith, in whom he might have a firm defense against the Greeks and Lombards. Following this, the task of anointing Pippin as King—whom the Franks themselves had already chosen by their votes—was entrusted by Zacharias to Boniface, Bishop of Mainz, who was the first to introduce Roman sacred rites and a vanity of dogmas into Germany, which was already imbued with better things in some places. Therefore, upon the legates' return to France, the anointing of Pippin was performed by Boniface at Soissons, and soon Pippin was called King by all; according to the custom of the nation, he was carried around on a shield and placed upon the throne. Finally, to close the scene, he performed the last act: the deposition of Childeric. Led from the rustic villa in which he lived to a monastery in Regensburg (they also destined his wife, Gisela, for a nunnery), his hair was shorn, his royal garments were laid aside, and he put on the habit of a monk. He suffered no heavier loss than that of his hair, since he was hardly despoiled of a kingdom which he had never truly held; and to lose a wife is perhaps even a gain. Meanwhile, Burchard, as a reward for his successful embassy, was created Duke of Franconia by Pippin, as Freher notes in his notes to Bebenburg, page 35. He left this title to his successors.

### IV.

However, whether this anointing of Pippin as King was the first among the Kings of the Franks, I see is doubted, since they claim that Remigius used the Chrism on Clovis.
</translation>

<pb n="21"/>Antonius Pascaligo: also eager for this praise and desirous of glory were Joannes Baptista Benedictus, a *Cypriot*, Jacobus Metius of *Chersonesos*, Antonius Eudaemonicus of *Cydonia*, Jacobus Trissinus of *Vicenza*, Hieronymus Bysantius of *Ascrivium* <note>Modern Kotor</note>, and Andreas Calergus of *Rethymno*, the memory of all of whom you ought to believe will never perish. For as long as the Christian and Venetian name shall endure—which we can promise will be everlasting—as long as letters remain, as long as any place for virtue is left anywhere: the most grateful speech of men regarding them shall never be silenced. For *the life of those who have died defending the Fatherland and vindicating the Christian Religion is not only nourished by posterity, but, as we have learned from the wisest men, eternity itself always gazes upon it.* Even today Harmodius and Aristogiton <note>Famous tyrannicides of ancient Athens</note> live on in the mouths and minds of all; the Horatii live on, the Decii live on, and many others, because *they judged it glorious to depart from life for the sake of the Fatherland.* Furthermore, these soldiers of yours, never sufficiently praised, who by their own blood brought forth such great glory for the Christian name and such a great victory, we trust have already attained the reward of their virtues from God; and we see today the honors due to them being paid by you and by the entire Christian Republic. This happens even more splendidly for these men than for the Romans or *Athenians*; because those people, compelled by their laws, adorned with praises those who had died fighting for the Fatherland; you, whatever you do, you grant it of your own accord and spontaneously to their virtue, and you fulfill the duty of most grateful citizens. And rightly so. For these excellent men are worthy for whom other singular honors should also be sought from the Senate. Whom I, in this present <pb n="22"/> moment, already seem to see from the highest watchtower of heaven, looking upon your grateful souls, and therefore rejoicing because they understand that through the adornment of words, perennial praise is accustomed to reach those who have performed illustrious deeds among the *listeners*. For they themselves showed that they were more studious of this glory than of life, when they died for the Fatherland more desirous of the enemy's punishment than of this light <note>Meaning the light of life</note>. And since they knew that *this life is a pilgrimage*, they expended the body, which they knew to be frail, for the public good, so that they might acquire privately a praise that fears no fates of death. Wherefore parents ought to use this consolation: that although they knew *they had fathered sons who were not immortal, but whom they hoped would be good and illustrious*, now they have entirely attained both, since they have fathered such great protections for the **REPUBLIC**. Their *children* have consolation because they will provide them with domestic examples of virtue. Their *wives*, because they belonged to private men whom they should praise rather than mourn. Everyone, finally, because they understand that those who met death have attained immortality in exchange for the mortal condition of life; since it must be especially believed that the defenders of the *Fatherland and of Christian Piety*, migrating from here, have flown away to the seat of celestial minds—from which we have our souls drawn—where they may enjoy everlasting age and perpetual happiness. Unwillingly I pass over the names of other outstanding men who were slain in the battle line, so that if I were able to do anything, I might rescue them from destruction. But since your *Commanders* have not yet written down the matter in detail as it was carried out, and you have commanded me to deliver this oration almost extemporaneously: I am now forced to pass over those things in silence. But you, **Most Serene PRINCE**, **Most Illustrious AMBASSADORS and FATHERS**
</translation>

He offers theological and patriotic consolation to the grieving families, asserting that those who died for the Christian faith have earned eternal life and heavenly joy.</summary>

<keywords>Battle of Lepanto, Venetian Republic, martyrdom, funeral oration, patriotism, afterlife, Augustus Barbadicus, Christian victory, naval warfare</keywords>

<pb n="9"/>XXIII. There is no doubt that even excommunicated persons and heretics possess this right of sending legates. For excommunication pertains to ecclesiastical discipline, whereas an embassy relates to civil and secular matters. Likewise, the sending of envoys, which exists by the law of nations <note>original: "jure gentium"</note>, regards and considers men according to that law, insofar as they are merely humans among us, and not according to the law and custom of any particular region or religion. The rights of peace are not nullified by a diversity of religion; much less are the mutual dealings of embassy abolished by a contradiction of faith: so says Kirchner <note>Hermann Kirchner, 1562–1620, a German jurist and poet</note> in book 1, chapter 3, whose words it was pleasing to include here.

XXIV. Although there are some who ascribe the right of embassies to the free nobles living in Franconia, Swabia, and along the Rhine, and to the Hanseatic cities, nevertheless, since they are not Estates of the Empire, are not found in the Imperial Register <note>the "Reichsmatrikel," a list of the constituent states of the Holy Roman Empire</note>, and are not called to the diets, we deny that they possess that right, agreeing with Kirchner, book 1, chapter 3, number 56, and Heiden, On Embassies <note>original: "de Legationibus"</note>. For the free cities contained within the Hanseatic League cannot communicate or rub off <note>original: "affricare," meaning to transfer or bestow</note> their own right onto others or even onto certain foreign cities.

XXV. We also deny the right of sending legates to Queens if they are married and the power of command rests with the husband: for then they send only messengers <note>original: "nuncios"</note>, not legates, since according to the law "a woman," 2nd <term>Pandects</term> <gloss>the Digest of Justinian</gloss> on the Rules of Law, they are barred from all administration of public offices. Excepted, however, are those who hold supreme power and exercise supreme command, whether they be unmarried, as was Elizabeth of England and today still Christina, Queen of Sweden, or if they are indeed entangled in marriage, they have nevertheless retained the rights of Majesty and Empire for themselves and have not shared them with a husband, examples of which we have in Isabella of Castile, Mary Queen of Hungary, and Mary of England. Kirchner, book 1, chapter 3; Bodin <note>Jean Bodin, 1530–1596, French political philosopher</note>, book 6, On the Republic, chapter 5.

XXVI. Popes, bishops, clerics, and in those churches professing Apostolic doctrine, Superintendents, and the bishops of Denmark, Sweden, and England, insofar as they are occupied with ecclesiastical business and do not hold secular command, do <pb n="10"/>not have the rights of sending legates. Because, however, they are secular princes and dukes and exercise political command, we cannot deny that the same right belongs to them as to other Princes. Meanwhile, this right can be ascribed to academics by no title, since they are in the position of subjects. Kirchner.

XXVII. We furthermore bar from this right of sending legates those rebels who, with no just cause existing beforehand, snatch themselves by force from the jurisdiction of their Lords, over whom the Prince’s right and authority always remains intact; who, having neglected divine and human laws, shatter civil society and tear apart every bond of humanity. To these we also add the proscribed <note>those placed under an imperial ban</note>. For since they lose all privileges, rights of dignity, and regalia, they cannot have that right within the empire from which they were proscribed. They can, however, send to foreigners.

XXVIII. However, those who, driven by extreme necessity, defend their life, reputation, wives, children, resources, the liberty of their Fatherland, and the exercise of Religion against a Tyrannical Prince, and thus defect, are by right excused from rebellion and possess this right of embassy.

XXIX. And since the greatest consideration is placed in the choice of legates, the sender—the female sex being excluded from this—should provide for himself such a legate who is primarily most well-equipped with the gifts of mind and character; secondarily, he should also excel in the goods of the body and fortune.

XXX. Indeed, we require the goods of the mind most of all because of the gravity of the business, so that the legate may have the most exquisite knowledge of all things, the sharpest judgment, and dexterity of character: and in short, that he be conspicuous for all virtues. Truly, since no human being is so absolute and perfect in all respects, the Prince should select such a one from the many who stands above the rest in learning, loyalty, silence <note>discretion or secrecy</note>, and diligence. See other requirements in Alberico Gentili <note>1552–1608, a founder of the science of international law</note>, book 3, On Embassies; Magirus, book 2, On Embassies.

<pb n="14"/>have toiled much. However, even if I do not have this matter fully proven, I will nonetheless offer my opinion without hesitation, so that I may at least provide the more learned an opportunity for discussing such things more extensively and precisely. Pliny, under the name of Weasel <note>original: "Mustella"</note>, includes both the <term>galē</term> <gloss>common weasel</gloss> and the <term>ictis</term> <gloss>marten</gloss>. For what Aristotle writes—the <term>galē</term> <gloss>weasel</gloss>, when it fights a snake, eats rue—Pliny translated almost word for word when he says: the Weasel, about to fight with serpents, carries rue in its mouth. And in Book 29, Chapter 4, those which Aristotle called <term>Ictides</term>, he himself also calls Weasels. For he writes thus: There are two kinds of Weasels. One is the wild kind, they differ in size, and the Greeks call them <term>Ictidas</term>. From these places already cited, it is sufficiently clear that "weasel" is a general name for Pliny, and that the animal which is called <term>galē</term> and <term>iktis</term> by the Greeks is called a weasel by the Latins. 

EUCHARIUS. Here, then, the language of the Latins is poorer than the Greek. 

ANONYMOUS. The Latins are surpassed by the Greeks not only in the abundance of things, but also in the abundance of words. And just as the Greeks lack nothing, so many things are found wanting for the Latins. And in my own judgment, Cicero <note>original: "Tullius"</note> exclaims somewhat improperly: "O, how the Greek language is sometimes impoverished!" 

EUCHARIUS. But what shall we say or do in such a great poverty of Latin? 

ANONYMOUS. We shall borrow names from the common people. For common names are not to be despised <pb n="15"/> if Latin ones are lacking. <margin>Wisela, Wisel. Herminna, herminne. Hermella, Hermelle.</margin> Therefore, those weasels which the Greeks call <term>galas</term>, I believe are named by the common people as Wisellas, Herminnas, or Hermellas. 

EUCHARIUS. What difference do you think there is between Wisellas and Hermellas?

ANONYMOUS. For Hermellas, they use almost the same name, <term>Herminnas</term>. But they call Wisellas <term>Fouinos</term> or <term>Marturellos</term>.

<pb n="14"/><note>based on the argument from Law 10, section 1 and Law 12 at the end of the Digest, On managing affairs; and Law 1, section 10 of the Digest, On extraordinary proceedings.</note> Furthermore, if any annual sum was promised by way of an honorary gift, that too must be paid by the client. However, regarding the payment of taxes <note>original: "collectas"</note> which are imposed by reason of sovereignty and jurisdiction, Caspar Glocken states <note>On Imperial contributions, thesis 6, letters a and b</note> that the simple right of protection does not grant such authority, as noted by Wehner and Besoldus under the terms <term>Schutz und Schirm</term> <gloss>Protection and Defense</gloss> <note>Gail, Book 2, Observation 54</note>. But if the people are free, it should in no way prejudice their liberty <note>Law: "I do not doubt," 7, Digest, On captives and postliminy</note>; the clients are by no means held to such payments. Similarly, the right of patronage properly so called <note>original: "jus patronatus"</note> cannot be claimed by the protector, nor can he change anything regarding religion, since this is annexed to spiritual matters <note>chapter: "When," 3, On Judgments; chapter: "On the law," 16, On the law of patronage</note> and protection is a purely temporal right <note>Synz. thesis 22</note>.

### XXVI.

The Right of Clientship <note>original: "Jus Clientelae"</note> is dissolved by the destruction and desolation of the thing, such as the destruction of a city which one has undertaken to defend <note>based on the argument from section 5, paragraph 2; Law: "If the usufruct," 21, Digest, In what ways a usufruct is lost</note>. And the payment established for the sake of the defense fee expires. A great loss of status <note>Law: "Of inquiries," 5, Digest, On extraordinary proceedings</note>, or outlawry <note>original: "Proscriptio"</note>, or an Imperial Ban <note>original: "Bannum Imperiale"</note>, whether in the person of the Patron or the Client, extinguishes the clientship. For those outlawed are stripped of all clientship, faith, and protection, as well as all liberty and privileges <note>Ordinance of the Chamber, part 2, Law 9, section 2; Gail, On the Public Peace, book 2, chapter 1, number 20; Mynsinger, century 1, observation 50, and century 3, observation 52</note>. They fall away from all agreements, names, oaths, treaties, and rights <note>Bechl. On Security, thesis 118 and following</note>. However, it is truer that no one is deprived of this right because of a change to the Catholic or Augsburg religion <note>Constitution of the Religious Peace of the year 1555, section "It shall also"; Syrinus, On the religious peace, conclusion 37; Besoldus, On the law of treaties, chapter 5, number 15</note>; nor is it lost by a major excommunication as it is by the Ban. For the latter is mortal, as Magerus says <note>chapter 16, number 199</note>, while the former is medicinal <note>Hopingk, On the law of protection, thesis 6, letter d</note>.

### XXVII.

When the resources of the Patron are worn down and rendered useless for defense, <pb n="15"/>it is truer that the Right of defense does not collapse <note>argument from chapter: "Briefly," Extra, On the law of oaths; chapter: "Legitimately done," On the Rule of Law, in the Sext; Law: "In ambiguous matters," section "It is not new," Digest, ibid.</note>. For a perfected contract is not immediately voided, even if it reaches a state from which it could not have begun <note>Law: "The penultimate," section "Even if," Digest, On verbal obligations</note>. And something is more easily preserved by civil law than granted anew <note>argument from Law 3, Digest, On the report of a new work</note>. Yet, if the Patron is struggling in such extreme necessity and poverty that no hope of better fortune or restitution remains, it could be conceded that the cliental right also dies out.

### XXVIII.

A clientship contracted for a specific day <note>or period</note> is dissolved when that day arrives. Because any contracts and pacts agreed upon for a certain duration of time are dissolved and cease when that time has elapsed <note>argument from Law: "If one," section 1, Digest, On Pacts; Law: "Of obligations," 44, section "It is agreed," Digest, On Obligations and Actions</note>. It is also dissolved by the mutual consent and will of the parties <note>Law: "Nothing is so natural," 35, Digest, and Gothofredus on the same, On the Rule of Law</note>. However, the dissent of one party does not remove it when the matter is no longer untouched <note>original: "integra"</note> and it has already begun to concern the interest of the other <note>Law 5, Code, On Obligations and Actions</note>. Except when the law of the convention has been fulfilled by one side: for then the party that has fulfilled it, even against the will of the other and before the other fulfills it, can withdraw from the contract and change their mind without penalty <note>Law: "If money," in the beginning, and Digest, On the recovery of what was given for a cause; where Gothofredus notes this applies even if the convention was sworn, chapter: "It reached us," On the law of oaths; chapter: "In vain," On the Rule of Law, in the Sext, where Peckius and the Commentators agree</note>.

### XXIX.

A civil obligation arises from this contract <note>Law 5, section 1, Digest, On words used in a prescriptive sense</note>. An equitable action <note>original: "utilis actio"</note> is also granted <note>Law 3, section 4, Digest, On the recovery of what was given for a cause</note> to the Client, to the effect that the promise of protection be fulfilled, or that what was given for the sake of protection be restored <note>Last law, Code, On the recovery of what was given for a cause</note>. Or let there be provided as much as it concerns the Client that the contract was not fulfilled <note>Law 7, Digest, On words used in a prescriptive sense</note>. To the Protector
</translation>

<summary>This section discusses the financial and religious limitations of a protector's rights, clarifying that protection is a temporal rather than spiritual authority. It details the conditions under which a cliental relationship is dissolved, including the destruction of a city, the Imperial Ban, or the expiration of a fixed-term contract.</summary>
<keywords>Imperial Ban, Religious Peace of 1555, jus clientelae, civil obligation, contract law, patronage, jurisdiction</keywords>

pages.14:
<note>based on the argument from Law 10, section 1 and Law 12 at the end of the Digest, On managing affairs; and Law 1, section 10 of the Digest, On extraordinary proceedings.</note> Furthermore, if any annual sum was promised by way of an honorary gift, that too must be paid by the client. However, regarding the payment of taxes <note>original: "collectas"</note> which are imposed by reason of sovereignty and jurisdiction, Caspar Glocken states <note>On Imperial contributions, thesis 6, letters a and b</note> that the simple right of protection does not grant such authority, as noted by Wehner and Besoldus under the terms <term>Schutz und Schirm</term> <gloss>Protection and Defense</gloss> <note>Gail, Book 2, Observation 54</note>. But if the people are free, it should in no way prejudice their liberty <note>Law: "I do not doubt," 7, Digest, On captives and postliminy</note>; the clients are by no means held to such payments. Similarly, the right of patronage properly so called <note>original: "jus patronatus"</note> cannot be claimed by the protector, nor can he change anything regarding religion, since this is annexed to spiritual matters <note>chapter: "When," 3, On Judgments; chapter: "On the law," 16, On the law of patronage</note> and protection is a purely temporal right <note>Synz. thesis 22</note>.

### XXVI.

The Right of Clientship <note>original: "Jus Clientelae"</note> is dissolved by the destruction and desolation of the thing, such as the destruction of a city which one has undertaken to defend <note>based on the argument from section 5, paragraph 2; Law: "If the usufruct," 21, Digest, In what ways a usufruct is lost</note>. And the payment established for the sake of the defense fee expires. A great loss of status <note>Law: "Of inquiries," 5, Digest, On extraordinary proceedings</note>, or outlawry <note>original: "Proscriptio"</note>, or an Imperial Ban <note>original: "Bannum Imperiale"</note>, whether in the person of the Patron or the Client, extinguishes the clientship. For those outlawed are stripped of all clientship, faith, and protection, as well as all liberty and privileges <note>Ordinance of the Chamber, part 2, Law 9, section 2; Gail, On the Public Peace, book 2, chapter 1, number 20; Mynsinger, century 1, observation 50, and century 3, observation 52</note>. They fall away from all agreements, names, oaths, treaties, and rights <note>Bechl. On Security, thesis 118 and following</note>. However, it is truer that no one is deprived of this right because of a change to the Catholic or Augsburg religion <note>Constitution of the Religious Peace of the year 1555, section "It shall also"; Syrinus, On the religious peace, conclusion 37; Besoldus, On the law of treaties, chapter 5, number 15</note>; nor is it lost by a major excommunication as it is by the Ban. For the latter is mortal, as Magerus says <note>chapter 16, number 199</note>, while the former is medicinal <note>Hopingk, On the law of protection, thesis 6, letter d</note>.

### XXVII.

When the resources of the Patron are worn down and rendered useless for defense,
pages.15:
it is truer that the Right of defense does not collapse <note>argument from chapter: "Briefly," Extra, On the law of oaths; chapter: "Legitimately done," On the Rule of Law, in the Sext; Law: "In ambiguous matters," section "It is not new," Digest, ibid.</note>. For a perfected contract is not immediately voided, even if it reaches a state from which it could not have begun <note>Law: "The penultimate," section "Even if," Digest, On verbal obligations</note>. And something is more easily preserved by civil law than granted anew <note>argument from Law 3, Digest, On the report of a new work</note>. Yet, if the Patron is struggling in such extreme necessity and poverty that no hope of better fortune or restitution remains, it could be conceded that the cliental right also dies out.

### XXVIII.

A clientship contracted for a specific day <note>or period</note> is dissolved when that day arrives. Because any contracts and pacts agreed upon for a certain duration of time are dissolved and cease when that time has elapsed <note>argument from Law: "If one," section 1, Digest, On Pacts; Law: "Of obligations," 44, section "It is agreed," Digest, On Obligations and Actions</note>. It is also dissolved by the mutual consent and will of the parties <note>Law: "Nothing is so natural," 35, Digest, and Gothofredus on the same, On the Rule of Law</note>. However, the dissent of one party does not remove it when the matter is no longer untouched <note>original: "integra"</note> and it has already begun to concern the interest of the other <note>Law 5, Code, On Obligations and Actions</note>. Except when the law of the convention has been fulfilled by one side: for then the party that has fulfilled it, even against the will of the other and before the other fulfills it, can withdraw from the contract and change their mind without penalty <note>Law: "If money," in the beginning, and Digest, On the recovery of what was given for a cause; where Gothofredus notes this applies even if the convention was sworn, chapter: "It reached us," On the law of oaths; chapter: "In vain," On the Rule of Law, in the Sext, where Peckius and the Commentators agree</note>.

### XXIX.

A civil obligation arises from this contract <note>Law 5, section 1, Digest, On words used in a prescriptive sense</note>. An equitable action <note>original: "utilis actio"</note> is also granted <note>Law 3, section 4, Digest, On the recovery of what was given for a cause</note> to the Client, to the effect that the promise of protection be fulfilled, or that what was given for the sake of protection be restored <note>Last law, Code, On the recovery of what was given for a cause</note>. Or let there be provided as much as it concerns the Client that the contract was not fulfilled <note>Law 7, Digest, On words used in a prescriptive sense</note>. To the Protector

Judgment, however, is said to be that by which, from the intuition of those things we have perceived, we affirm or deny something about the things themselves; and this affirmation and negation is threefold: regarding existence, essence, and accidents, just as when I affirmed that the mind exists, I explained what its essence is and of what kind it is. I call it affirmation when the judgment, by its unitive mode of reaching out, intentionally attributes a predicate to a subject. I call it negation when the judgment, by its divisive mode of reaching out, intentionally cuts away and tears the same predicate from its subject. Reasoning or discourse is a certain connection and comparison of several thoughts and judgments, or if you prefer, a transition from one thought to another, since discourse necessarily encloses two cognitions within itself and does not require more. For after the intellect has received an object into itself by simple apprehension and has passed sentence on it through an elicited judgment, it soon, by a power implanted in it by nature, deduces other properties of the object from the already known predicate, and through its several predicates, it ranges and runs forward by various acts, as if by steps.

§. 27. Since, however, these four—essence, power, operation, and object—have this order, such that power flows from essence, operation from power, and operation tends toward the object, I must inquire into the object about which the intellect operates in the three reviewed ways for a full knowledge of it. I cannot better derive its extension than from the power inherent in it. Moreover, my intellect conceives objects infinitely diverse among themselves in number and perfection: the impossible, the possible, the non-existent, those immersed in matter, and those torn away from matter. It represents even God himself, the founder of all beings, though it cannot comprehend him, yet strengthened by heavenly light as he is in himself. Thus, no cause appears to me why I should not extend the force of my intellect to every object that falls even under the angelic intellect; indeed, by extolling its nature, I illustrate the immense goodness of God. Nor is this consideration a small argument for me to believe this: that whether I extend the sphere of my intellect in this way or do not extend it and deny it such an extension, I find that it must necessarily be attributed to it. For if I hold to affirmation, I must know all those objects; for I cannot affirm anything about any object unless I know it. If negation <pb n="16"/> I also cannot deny anything except that which I conceive, so that I conclude: the object of my intellect is also everything that falls under the angelic intellect.

§. 28. The mode by which the intellect operates concerning these objects seems to me to be twofold. For it perceives certain things without a bodily idea, but others only with the help of a bodily idea. I shall call the one that understands in the former way the pure intellect, and the one in the latter way, aided by the senses. I am persuaded that a pure intellect exists in me from the fact that I well know that it understands its own thoughts; nor does it seem likely to me that any mathematical figures—or rather any ideas of mathematical figures—or other ideas of the mind, <term>verbi gratia</term> <gloss>for example</gloss> of a thing, substance, truth, goodness, fairness, and of common notions, <term>verbi gratia</term> <gloss>for example</gloss> those which agree in a third thing <term>et cetera</term> <gloss>and so forth</gloss>, are drawn in by the benefit of the senses. Since those ideas contain nothing bodily or of a bodily affection, nor do they even run into the senses; but rather it is more likely they are implanted in the mind from its first origin, <term>hoc est</term> <gloss>that is</gloss> the faculty of exciting and making such forms of concepts was given to the mind by God. Therefore, I do not think that well-worn saying of Eustachius <note>likely Eustachius a Sancto Paulo, a Cistercian philosopher</note> is universally true: "There is nothing in the intellect <term>et cetera</term> <gloss>which was not first in the senses</gloss>." For if this dictum were universally valid, all knowledge of God would have to be entirely denied. For God, in no way—whatever you may distinguish—was in the sense, since he is not bodily, and accordingly he never was in the intellect. For he who knows not even a <term>γρὺ</term> <gloss>grunt/whit</gloss> <note>a Greek idiom for the smallest possible thing</note> about him would foolishly believe in God. Nor does it follow that God runs into the sense, as some wish, because we arrive <term>dianoitice</term> <gloss>through discursive reasoning</gloss> at a knowledge of God through the contemplation of his works, which do run into the senses. For that contemplation leads us to know the existence of the supreme Deity in no other way than by exciting us to attend to the mind's idea, and thus, with that intervening, we conclude the existence of God. But from that, it is not proved that God runs into the senses, which was the point in question. By like reason, anyone could deny the existence of their own mind, since it does not run into the senses. And truly I do not see how, through the natural order of powers, they can prove that the intellect must necessarily behold <term>phantasmata</term> <gloss>mental images</gloss>. For a natural connection of the intellect with the imagination of the kind they establish—so great that the intellect cannot grasp a notion of any thing without the imagination accompanying it—is [contrary to] experience.
</translation>

<summary>Johann Grafft defines the operations of the human intellect, including simple apprehension, judgment, and reasoning. He argues for the existence of a pure intellect capable of conceiving abstract and divine concepts independent of sensory input, challenging the Aristotelian-Thomistic principle that all knowledge begins in the senses.</summary>

<keywords>intellect, judgment, reasoning, pure intellect, innate ideas, Eustachius a Sancto Paulo, cognition of God, sensory perception, mental images, logic</keywords>

<pb n="16"/>fates are such that, while they render fame immortal, they wear down and weaken the body—the lodging of a great soul—like iron through vigils and tireless labor; and those who converse too much with the dead become the same color as the dead. This had been a never-interrupted fellowship for our **BLESSED** <note>Daniel Georg Morhof</note> one for so many years, and although his fame shone brighter day by day from the wearing away of his works, his strength grew duller daily, and while he illuminated *Cimbria* <note>The Cimbrian Peninsula, modern Jutland and Schleswig-Holstein</note> with his light, he himself seemed to be gradually consumed like a burning lamp.
<margin>The Death of his Wife.</margin>
Added to this, with his body pressed by such a mass of labors, was a lethal wound and a pain penetrating to his very vitals from the premature death of his Sweetest Wife. For just as his bed had been softer for so many years without any chill, and more fruitful with a noble offspring emulating their father's virtues, so much the more did he lament that his joys were snatched away, all charms extinguished with his Spouse, and that he himself was carried out in the same funeral with her. Forgive me, *Auditors*, forgive me, for including under reasons—blinding myself to the rest—the inevitable necessity of fate, or rather the unshakeable commands of God, the arbiter of life and death, by which certain limits are placed for us and a fixed goal is set for our years, which our mind, looking at the rest with blindness, often perceives falsely. These were the decrees of the Fates: to demand back this heavenly deposit and to insert among the stars that immortal head which had illustrated *Cimbria* with such great rays. The spheres of the earth seemed too narrow for so vast a mind; therefore, it had to be summoned to the wider spaces of the heavens. Though he was always desirous of these, he was not so disdainful of present things that he would not have indulged us further in his use, had the fates and God allowed, especially so that he might place the final hand upon the divine work he had begun. The Sons of Physicians <note>The medical profession</note> were consulted; things were sought from everywhere to strengthen the daily failing powers of his Body and restore those that had collapsed. But human counsels are in vain where Divine ones are contrary! In vain does the earth hold back while heaven summons. Among the 
<margin>Journey to the springs of Spa.</margin>
wonders of nature are the Acidulae, the springs of Spa <note>Mineral springs in Belgium</note>, bubbling forth through mountain conduits by secret paths, which nurturing mother Nature, or rather God the great father of nature, seems to have produced as if in aid of failing art and human help. By these medicinal springs, sluggishness has often been shaken from listless bodies, fevers extinguished, pains driven away, and former vigor and the strength that had belonged to the limbs returned to the year. Hither, therefore, the great explorer of nature hurried, hoping for that more kindly nature for himself, of whose secrets he had long been the interpreter! But he experienced her as a stepmother, and those waters which had so often been healthy for others were lethal for him. *Cimbria* followed him as he stretched toward that place with a thousand vows and, as if a prophetess of future things, unwillingly let go of such a great ornament, never to return. 
<margin>He returns to Lübeck.</margin>
Heaven indeed seemed to nod to the vows when he was brought to *Lübeck* by a hurried return. But soon the hope of the fatherland was disturbed, and the vows he had made were all frustrated when, 
<pb n="17"/>after a few days had intervened—namely, on the day before the Kalends of July of the previous year <note>June 30, 1691</note>—that most brilliant star of the fatherland was submerged in the fatal shadows. Unhappy springs of *Spa*! O most bitter waters of *Pyrmont*! Did nature lead you down to this, so that like *Lethean* waves the light of *Cimbria* might be extinguished? Do we find by experience that things healthy for others are fatal for great Names? Were the *Rhine* once and now the *Warnow* <note>River in Rostock</note> sufficient in being made mournful, without *Cimbria* being added? Still mindful of its own slaughter, *Lyon* and the manes of the great *Salmasius* <note>Claude Saumaise</note> demand restitution from you: *Rostock* demands it, and *Cimbria* demands it too, so that the wound might not be simple, but rather that he who had been the companion of *Morhof* on his journey should also be the companion of his death. Let others complain of their own pains, let others mourn their own wounds: *Lyon* its *Scaligers*, *Amsterdam* its *Barlaeuses*, *Helmstedt* its *Conrings*, *Jena* its *Bosiuses*; as *Cimbria* was once more fortunate than these, so now she heaves deeper groans. We shall eternally weep for your fates, Divine Poet! We ascribe your funerals to the great Muses of *Wasmuth* and the illustrious *Gudius* and others, of whom even now the most bitter sense remains! Your mind, indeed, drunk with heavenly nectar, now looks down upon the *Castalian* springs, but we complain that these have been muddied for us by Your death. Your tongue now sounds something higher, and you sing much greater things, mixed in the choir not of Muses but of heavenly spirits; but to us you leave *Elegies* and broken plectrums. No longer does the *Laurel* bind your brow, which was once your honor, but we look up at your head inserted among the stars and your crown gleaming with rays; yet we complain of a wilting *Laurel* and a *Helicon* made funereal with *Cypress*. Who now will clear the muddied springs of the *Muses*? Who will replace the broken strings? Who will reanimate the *Lyre* <note>term: Chelyn</note> falling sadly silent, and rouse the numbed *Muses*? Who will complete the structure of the mass he began, of which

Who will vindicate the merits of the *Germans* in letters by your example to mortals? Who will follow with a divine mind that which is divine in the sciences? Who will meditate on the <term>ἰσογέμεια</term> <gloss>equivalence/equal weight</gloss> of Roman jurisprudence now that You, the *Polyhistor*, have been snatched away? Who will comment on the mystery of the *North*, on the *Mannus* <note>mythical founder of the Germanic peoples</note> of the *Germans*, on the *Pileus* <note>the felt cap of liberty</note>, on the *Nail* <note>referring to his work on the 'Golden Nail'</note>, and other things, now that Your hand is failing? These things had once been destined for his restless industry, the hope of all of which is buried with You in the same tomb; and so the wound is greater than any soothing, the funeral greater than any eloquence. Nor is this disaster for *Cimbria* alone; almost the whole world is drawn into its portion: mother *Germany* mourns the citizen snatched from her, so great an ornament whom she had hoped would be the vindicator of her glory and merits. *Belgium* and the neighboring *Briton* groan together for the extinguished star of their age, once a most welcome guest; *Padua* mourns its advocate and the manes of *Livy* as if...

<summary>This passage laments the death of the polymath Daniel Georg Morhof in 1691, attributing his decline to overwork and grief over his wife's death. It describes his failed search for health at the mineral springs of Spa and lists the unfinished scholarly works left behind at his passing.</summary>

<pb n="13"/><meta>continues from previous page</meta> of which we have made mention so far, show only in a general way the firmness and sanctity of the Christian religion. Furthermore, the individual heads of that religion, if indeed one must dispute with some pagan, can be defended and declared; but they cannot be openly demonstrated, as we have repeatedly warned above.

### LXII.

But if a contest of this kind is undertaken with one who does not refuse the authority of the holy Fathers and the universal Church in addition to the divine Scripture, there is nothing that cannot be proven by that same reasoning.

### LXIII.

Moreover, the duty of Theology is not only that which we have just set forth—namely, to defend its principles against those who deny or attack them, and to gather from there, by the force of reason, various conclusions which serve to protect and illustrate the Christian matter—but also to strongly fortify both with the internal and external protections and aids of this science.

### LXIIII.

We call the internal and proper protections of Theology those reasons which are sought from the Canonical Scripture; from the faithful tradition of Christ and the Apostles; from the authority of the Catholic and Apostolic Church; from the Canons of the general Councils and the Roman Pontiffs; and finally, from the monuments of the ancient and recent Fathers and Theologians.

### LXV.

<margin>+</margin> The external protections, and those as if begged from another's estate, can be said to be those which are taken from the decrees of the natural Philosophers; from the responses of the Jurisconsults <note>legal experts</note>—for they too wish to be counted among the Professors of true Philosophy; from the commentaries of historical events; and finally from the resources of human reason itself.

### LXVI.

For since there are two kinds of arguing—one resting on authority, proper to the Theologian; the other furnished with reason, peculiar to the Philosopher—if it is not permitted to use the former and proper kind, the Theologian, seizing upon what is closest to the former, defends himself by reason instead of authority; yet he often joins both kinds of proof together.

### LXVII.

Hence it is clear that the wisdom of those is foolish who, being about to speak on some Theological argument, reject the authority of the Fathers, Councils, and Scriptures as if they were insufficiently firm, and dispute only with petty reasons begged from natural Philosophy. For those <term>mōrosophoi</term> <gloss>foolish-wise men</gloss> do not understand <pb n="14"/> that the place of authority is so proper to Theology that it receives almost all the reasons it uses as if they were foreigners and traveling guests.

### LXVIII.

Furthermore, there is this difference among the internal protections of Theology: that arguments drawn from the authority of the sacred writings, the definition of the Catholic and Apostolic Church, and the perpetual and constant tradition of the same Church, are not only proper and internal, but also necessary. But those taken from the doctrine of any Saint or Father—of whatever order, sanctity, or authority he may have been—conclude only with probability. Nevertheless, it would be rash to depart too far from the judgment of many Holy Fathers, especially in the interpretation of the Scriptures.

### LXIX.

Accordingly, they are convicted of erring gravely and dangerously who, making Saint Jerome the rule of the testamentary Scriptures, wish only those books to be held among the Canonical ones to which the same Father, perhaps while doing something else, somewhere applies the name of Canonical.

### LXX.

Indeed, a necessary argument is not drawn from the authority of Jerome alone, but only a probable one; and not even always a probable one, but only then, when it does not depart far from the more accepted opinion of the rest of the Fathers.

->PRAISE BE TO GOD.<-

<note>An ornamental initial A</note>
*Friendly Reader, lest any space should remain in so small a work, it pleased me to add in this place what Saint Augustine hands down somewhere concerning the obscurity of the sacred writings, so that from this also the utility of Theological study and the vanity of the Sectarians might become more manifest.*

<note>An ornamental initial C</note>
> When I read (said Honoratus) I understood it by myself. Is it so? (said Augustine). Imbued with no poetic discipline, you would not dare to touch Terentianus Maurus <note>a Latin grammarian</note> without a teacher. Asper, Cornutus, Donatus, and countless others are required so that any poet can be understood, whose poems even seem to capture the applause of the theater; do you rush without a guide into those books which, whatever their nature, are proclaimed to be holy and full of divine matters by the confession of almost the entire human race, and about them without <note>continued on next page: a teacher</note>
</translation>

It argues that theology primarily rests on authority and tradition rather than human reason alone, specifically critiquing those who rely solely on individual Fathers like Jerome or their own private interpretation.</summary>

<pb n="17"/><meta>continues from previous page: ...essence of which it is the mode,</meta> where also the personal mode of subsisting <note>subsistentia</note> or personhood <term>suppositalitas</term> <gloss>the state of being a self-subsisting individual</gloss> is really distinguished from the substance. But in divine things, mode and substance do not differ really, nor should a distinction of essence in the divine persons be admitted, except only according to reason, lest any composition of essence and person be established in God. Therefore, finite and infinite essence and person are distant by an infinite degree. A finite essence is individual because of its unity and incommunicable to multiple persons because of its finitude. Although the infinite essence is supremely individual because of its supreme unity, it is nevertheless truly communicable to multiple persons because of its infinity. In finite things, one person is distinguished from another no less by singularity of being than by incommunicability of subsisting. But in the mystery of the <term>Trinitatis</term> <gloss>Trinity</gloss>, the persons are distinguished from one another at least by the incommunicability of subsisting, but truly not by singularity of essence; one is not the other, yet it is of the same numerical essence as the other. In the former case, any person is entirely distinct from another person and separate, and they have no intrinsic connection. In the latter, although the persons are distinguished really, they cannot be separated in being; rather, by reason of being, one is in the other, nor can it be outside the other because of the identity of essence. Briefly: *Finite persons are distinguished by time, will, power, operation, and place:* But in the divine persons, because of the <term>homoousian</term> <gloss>consubstantiality; being of the same essence</gloss> of the essence, there is coeternity, one will, one power, one operation, and where one is, there is the other. So much for the definition of the Person; the application follows.

### XXI. The PHOTINIANS <note>Followers of Photinus who denied the personality of the Holy Spirit</note> <term>apotomos</term> <gloss>sharply/curtly</gloss> deny that the HOLY SPIRIT is a Person, asserting that He is a *Power* or *Attribute* of **GOD**, or indeed some intermediate quality between the power of **GOD** and the faculties stirred up in man. *Crellius, book 1, On the One God the Father, Section III, chapter 8.* To Socinus, the Holy Spirit is a power and potency naturally residing in God. To these we oppose the following argument: To whomsoever all those things are attributed which belong to things subsisting by themselves and conceived under the reason of a person, that being truly sub- <pb n="18"/>-sists and is indicated by the name of person. But to the Holy Spirit are attributed all those requirements, etc. Therefore, the HOLY SPIRIT truly subsists and is indicated by the name of person. The major premise is of manifest truth. The minor is proved from a sufficient enumeration of (1) names, (2) properties, (3) works, and (4) appearances, which cannot belong except to a subsisting thing.

XXII. (1) By reason of Names, the Holy Spirit is called Lord <term>kyrios</term> <gloss>Lord</gloss> in 2 Corinthians 3:17 and 1 Corinthians 12:4; or advocate <term>paraklētos</term> <gloss>Paraclete; one called alongside to help</gloss> in John 16:26, chapter 15:26, and chapter 16:7. I conclude: He who is Lord, Advocate, and Paraclete truly subsists and is a Person. For who has ever read in the scriptures that the Power and attributes of GOD are called Lord and Advocate? Furthermore, He is called a witness with the Father and the Son in 1 John 5:7. Hence I argue thus: He of whom the name "witness" is properly predicated is a person. But the name "witness" is properly predicated of the HOLY SPIRIT. Therefore, the Major premise is manifest and is conceded by Gossavius against Keckermann, page 1, chapter 4, page 50; for the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are joined together as witnesses in heaven. Therefore, as the Father and Son are witnesses, so also is the Holy Spirit. But those are properly witnesses, as cannot be denied. Furthermore, in verse 9 it is established that the testimony of the three witnesses in heaven is compared with the testimony of men, concerning whom the law says that every truth stands in the mouth of two or three; to which the Apostle seems to look back. Thus, just as the three witnesses among men are persons, so also those three who are said to testify in heaven are brought forward as three persons. Finally, that the HOLY SPIRIT is not an attribute or power of God, but rather a <term>hypostasin</term> <gloss>hypostasis; a distinct individual subsistence</gloss>, is gathered most clearly from the passage itself: For if He were the power of the Father, and not something subsisting distinct from the Father, He could not be introduced as a third witness distinct from the Father and the Son. Surely there is one and the same testifying of the essence and the power, since properly a power could not be said to testify (as the adversaries themselves concede), much less be distinguished from other distinct witnesses.

XXIII. (2) The properties of a subsisting thing, which [are attributed] to the HOLY SPIRIT...
</translation>

He emphasizes the distinction between finite human persons and the infinite, consubstantial persons of the Trinity who share a single essence.</summary>

<keywords>Holy Spirit, Trinity, Divine Personhood, Photinians, Socinians, Consubstantiality, Paraclete, Hypostasis, Subsistence</keywords>

But in divine things, mode and substance do not differ really, nor should a distinction of essence in the divine persons be admitted, except only according to reason, lest any composition of essence and person be established in God. Therefore, finite and infinite essence and person are distant by an infinite degree. A finite essence is individual because of its unity and incommunicable to multiple persons because of its finitude. Although the infinite essence is supremely individual because of its supreme unity, it is nevertheless truly communicable to multiple persons because of its infinity. In finite things, one person is distinguished from another no less by singularity of being than by incommunicability of subsisting. But in the mystery of the <term>Trinitatis</term> <gloss>Trinity</gloss>, the persons are distinguished from one another at least by the incommunicability of subsisting, but truly not by singularity of essence; one is not the other, yet it is of the same numerical essence as the other. In the former case, any person is entirely distinct from another person and separate, and they have no intrinsic connection. In the latter, although the persons are distinguished really, they cannot be separated in being; rather, by reason of being, one is in the other, nor can it be outside the other because of the identity of essence. Briefly: *Finite persons are distinguished by time, will, power, operation, and place:* But in the divine persons, because of the <term>homoousian</term> <gloss>consubstantiality; being of the same essence</gloss> of the essence, there is coeternity, one will, one power, one operation, and where one is, there is the other. I conclude: He who is Lord, Advocate, and Paraclete truly subsists and is a Person. For who has ever read in the scriptures that the Power and attributes of GOD are called Lord and Advocate? Furthermore, He is called a witness with the Father and the Son in 1 John 5:7. Hence I argue thus: He of whom the name "witness" is properly predicated is a person. But the name "witness" is properly predicated of the HOLY SPIRIT. Therefore, the Major premise is manifest and is conceded by Gossavius against Keckermann, page 1, chapter 4, page 50; for the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are joined together as witnesses in heaven. Therefore, as the Father and Son are witnesses, so also is the Holy Spirit. But those are properly witnesses, as cannot be denied. Furthermore, in verse 9 it is established that the testimony of the three witnesses in heaven is compared with the testimony of men, concerning whom the law says that every truth stands in the mouth of two or three; to which the Apostle seems to look back. Thus, just as the three witnesses among men are persons, so also those three who are said to testify in heaven are brought forward as three persons. <pb n="10"/>Such was the condition of the old man <note>referring to Herod the Great</note>, whom we remember once flourished in lasting favor with Caesar above all other friends. Why then should it be surprising if his sons were in a much worse position? Certainly Archelaus had reason to fear the Prince <note>the Emperor</note>, whose will initially diminished his dignity and whose anger later utterly overthrew him, choosing Vienna as the place for him to endure the bitterness of exile. <note>Noldius, page 229.</note> Josephus did not overlook the imperious voice of the Prince, <note>Antiquities, book 17, chapter 15.</note> so that we may easily agree with Spanheim, a defender of the Evangelist, who does not circumscribe the word <term>basileuein</term> <gloss>to reign as a king</gloss> within such narrow limits that it cannot sometimes encompass a power lower than royal authority within its meaning. <note>volume 2, Doubt 86; compare the previously cited location.</note>

### §. XVI.

Will the Tetrarchs, confined to the coast of Palestine, therefore be angry with us if we declare that they obtained only a precarious command? They undoubtedly lay struck down whenever they appeared to have attempted anything against the Prince. This happened to Antipas, incited by Herodias; though not to Philip, a composed man who consulted his own interests more wisely, even if both otherwise testified to their obedience to the Prince through many services. <note>Antiquities, book 18, chapter 9.</note> I pass over the fates of Lysanias, and Zenodorus, and others, who were necessarily made to feel heavy calamity if they occasionally brought about the masters' anger through their crimes or party zeal. <note>Antiquities, book 15, chapter 13.</note>

### §. XVII.

I am little moved by the honorary titles of kingdoms, concerning which those who are hesitating <pb n="11"/> cannot be sufficiently instructed as to what ought to be decided. Indeed, having contemplated the imposed taxes, the descriptions of borders, and the dignities freely distributed, I am ultimately compelled to confess that it is an untimely zeal by which someone perhaps endeavors to support their supreme right or defend their absolute power. <note>see Noldius in the cited place; Selden, On the Law of Nature and Nations, book 6, chapters 17 and 18.</note>

### §. XVIII.

Thus we have looked at the Tetrarchs in general, expressed with suitable brevity as the dynasts of quarters; now nothing hinders or forbids us from looking at them individually. The first in Luke’s account is Antipas; more powerful in command as well, although younger in age. His incest, foul hypocrisy, envy, and tyrannical cruelty, along with the ruin of his fortunes, which Josephus describes weightily in many places, the Evangelists did not think they should entirely overlook. Leaving much to history, we shall have performed our duty with a brief review. However, we must not remain silent about the Parent's <note>Herod the Great's</note> prior plan, in which if he had persisted, Antipas would not have been a <term>tetrarches</term> <gloss>tetrarch</gloss>, but a king. <note>Antiquities, book 17, chapter 8.</note> Even this shows him to be wicked and criminal: that he was rebuked by John for many outrages, whose liberty he initially restrained with chains, but finally extinguished entirely with the executioner’s sword. <note>Chemnitz, Harmony, chapter 31; Josephus, Antiquities, book 18, chapter 7.</note>

### §. XIX.

The name of Herod, by which Luke designated him, was neither unusual in this family—just as the Scythians and Parthians had their own names for kings—nor was it so hated by foreign nations that it was not frequently used. But I do not agree with Schotanus, who denied it was his true name; just as I fear Salmasius does not rightly trace its origin when he calls him a little Greek <note>original: "Graeculum"</note>
</translation>

It argues that their titles did not reflect absolute sovereignty, as they remained subject to the Emperor's will and Roman taxation.</summary>
