<pb n="11"/>XXV. To the second genus of intellections belongs the mental enunciation, which, so that the Moderns may distinguish it from the proposition (which also pertains to the third operation of the mind and includes a virtual discourse), they correctly define as an immediate judgment concerning some thing: that is, such that it affirms a predicate of a subject on account of the connection between the subject and predicate themselves. Since, on the contrary, every discourse is a mediate judgment, because it mediately approves the connection of the predicate with the subject. The most powerful property of these acts is formal truth, which is nothing other than the conformity of the judgment with the object, just as on the contrary falsehood is the disconformity of the judgment with the object; so that, accordingly, a true judgment is that which enunciates the object to be just as it is in reality: a false one, if the object is not as the judgment enunciates it.

XXVI. An enunciation once true can never pass into a false one, nor conversely a false one into a true one; for the same cognition always represents the same thing, therefore the cognition which represented with truth that Adam is writing for this instant, which the verbal copula designated, represented for eternity that Adam is writing at this instant. For just as it is impossible for Adam to have written at this instant A and not to have written at this instant A, so it is impossible that the cognition which truly represents him to have written at this instant A should at some time represent him as not having written: since the proposition for eternity speaks only of this, and of no other instant. Regarding falsehood, one must reason in the same way, for if the proposition represented another time from that which it first represented, by this very fact it would not be the same, but another and new representation, and consequently a new cognition.

XXVII. To the third and primary genus of the operations of the human intellect belongs the formal discourse, or <term>syllogism</term> <gloss>a logical argument</gloss>; which is a speech in which, certain things being posited, something else necessarily happens from these things that were posited, because these things are so. And essentially it involves not only the conclusion, but also the premises themselves; nor is anyone judged to have constructed a formal syllogism who either infers something without any premises, or, having made premises, infers nothing. However, so that the assent of the conclusion can be distinguished from another immediately judicative assent, it ought intrinsically to attain the object of the premises as the motive and formal reason for assenting. This is proved from the fact that every act tending toward some material object on account of something else formal must attain that formal object: but the formal motive of the conclusion as such is the object of the premises, or the identity of the extremes with a third middle <note>this refers to the middle term in a syllogism which links the major and minor terms</note>, therefore the act of the conclusion, as such, ought to attain that object. This is confirmed because unless the act of the conclusion attains the formal motive again, in some syllogisms no reason could be given why this proposition should be the conclusion rather than another of the three, for any of them can be inferred by way of a conclusion from the others.

XXVIII. In addition to the object of the conclusion and the object of the premises, the goodness of the inference must also be attained by the act of the conclusion, which is the identity between the object of the premises and the object of the conclusion: for this goodness is also a partial motive, which together with the object of the premises moves the intellect to infer the conclusion; for if this single connection between the object of the premises and the object of the conclusion were taken away, <pb n="12"/> however much the object of the premises might remain, the intellect would not be moved to the conclusion. Just as, therefore, when we love medicine for the sake of health, we also love the connection which medicine has with restoring health, because if this connection were excluded we would not love the medicine, so also the intellect, so that it can be moved to conclude, ought not only to attain the object of the premises, but also the goodness of the inference.

XXIX. Some doubt whether the judgment concerning the goodness of the inference ought to be a distinct and intermediate act between the assent of the premises and the assent of the conclusion, through which the intellect reflexively knows that this conclusion is rightly inferred from these premises, because those things are identified with each other which are identified with one third thing. We judge it more probable that *a judgment concerning the goodness of the inference distinct from the act of the conclusion is not necessarily always required*, especially in practiced men, to whom that principle is very clearly known: *whatever things are the same as one third thing, etc.* <note>referring to the logical principle: things which are equal to the same thing are equal to each other</note> For such persons, after they have seen in the premises that the extremes of the conclusion are identified with one third thing, immediately infer the act of conclusion, which simultaneously and at once attains the object of the premises, the goodness of the inference, and the object of the conclusion. In those men, however, who are not practiced in making syllogisms, and who even after they have seen that two things are identified with one third can still doubt whether those two are identified with each other, we think it altogether follows that *a judgment concerning the goodness of the inference is distinct and precedes the conclusion itself*: for the intellect of these people is so imperfect that it is not sufficiently determined by the object of the premises to infer the conclusion without any hesitation.

# *Operations of the human Will.*

XXX. That the will is a free spiritual virtue, appetitive of an object, is certain among all: we have suggested above in the third thesis that it is distinguished neither from the intellect nor from the soul. The *material object* with which it is occupied is everything that the intellect can know under the aspect of good or evil. The *formal object*, or that which immediately moves the will, is good and evil; the former moves to acts of pursuit, the latter to acts of flight. The good which moves the will is threefold: *the honorable, the pleasurable, the useful*. None of these can entice the will unless it is first known: yet the cognition itself is not the motive of the will, but a mere condition applying the motive. *Evil as evil*, or proposed only under the aspect of evil, the will cannot love, otherwise than if it is presented under the aspect of at least an apparent good.

XXXI. Ordinarily speaking, so that we may love and desire some good for ourselves, it suffices to know that the good is suitable for us; nor is it necessary that we recognize in ourselves some goodness on account of which we are worthy to love such a good for ourselves. If truly we love or desire some good for another person, it is required that we apprehend in them some goodness on account of which we estimate them worthy of such a good. For (ordinarily speaking) so that I may join myself through affection with the good of my neighbor, insofar as it is a good for him, I ought first to join myself through affection
</translation>

<pb n="13"/><meta>continues from previous page</meta> and the monsters of the most grave errors. Consider that sad colloquy held at Weimar between <term>Flacius Illyricus</term> <gloss>Matthias Flacius, a Lutheran reformer</gloss>, a man otherwise not unlearned, and <term>Strigel</term> <gloss>Victorinus Strigel</gloss>. O immortal God! How many and how ruinous the storms this man stirred up in the world? Because, inflamed by a spirit of contention and with the vision of his mind clouded, he thoughtlessly vomited out that most absurd of all notions: *that Original Sin is the very substance of man*, which he then chose to defend by every means, lest he should seem defeated. Even greater than this, and certainly more tragic and fatal, is the example regarding <term>Arminius</term> <gloss>Jacobus Arminius</gloss> that stands in literature. For because of the controversies stirred up concerning certain hidden chapters of Theology, not only all of Belgium, but nearly all of Europe began to be split into factions; and Arminius himself, overcome by grief, when he had fallen into a slow and heavy illness and had been exhausted by it, is said to have earned the following epitaph:

->*He who was subtle in perception and powerful in speech,*<-
->*But whose first care was always for morals,*<-
->*Arminius, lying here, calls out to all,*<-
->*That they should not prefer to dispute, rather than to live.*<-

Thus far, O Distinguished and Most Honorable Auditors, you have traversed with me the spacious field of the vices by which the Learned are accustomed to suffer; but quite many things in that category remain to be said, which, shut out by the narrowness of time, we willingly pass over. To be sure, one would still have to touch upon the insatiable greed of certain scholars, the immoderate luxury of others, and the seething lust of some. However, since I perceive it to be the nature of these vices that not a few other men are also driven by the same stings, and that they do not flow from the abuse of learning itself like the previously mentioned stains, we refrain from examining them more at length. Nothing remains but that I should compel those who wish to be counted under the name of the learned with a friendly exhortation: that they may wish, by the very sacred rites of study, by the inviolable altar of <term>Pallas</term> <gloss>Athena, goddess of wisdom</gloss> to which they have sworn, and by the excellence of the name of the learned, which is venerable above all others, to act solicitously, lest, enticed by the soft depravity of the vices reviewed thus far, they fall from their dignity. Rather, let them strive to exert themselves so that, in a most sweet harmony, both the praise of refined learning and the splendor of virtues may most amicably conspire within their breasts. Indeed, let everyone diligently beware lest, on account of those blemishes with which we have warned many learned men are contaminated, they hold the most useful care of learning and letters in contempt; nor should they attribute the birth of such foul vices to learning, which is the patroness of all virtues. They should be rightly mindful that nothing is so innocent and holy that it cannot be corrupted by the fault of another, if it is led down into perverse uses. I come now to fulfill that for which <pb n="14"/> I chiefly allowed this duty of speaking to be demanded of me today; namely, that I might claim for myself today a part in offering those pious vows and most humble thanks which are heard everywhere from all the learned on account of the subsidies for studies bestowed by the **MOST SERENE ESTABLISHER OF LETTERS, OUR MOST CLEMENT LORD** <note>This refers to the ruling Prince or Elector providing patronage</note>, for the benefit of literary affairs. Nor indeed can I do otherwise, while I find my own studies most liberally aided and confirmed by His Most Munificent Hand. But from where I shall draw the beginning of this speech of mine, I hang entirely wavering and doubtful. For how can I hope to encompass matters greater than all praise with the narrow and thin furniture of my oratory? What then shall I do, when both my piety bids me speak, yet the consciousness of my thinness bids me keep silent? This at least I will strive for: that what I cannot express in words, I may supply with my mind and silent vows. Therefore, an inner spirit overflowing with most humble devotion bows itself at Your feet, **MOST SERENE ESTABLISHER and PRESERVER OF THE MUSES**. Graciously impart Your eyes to this most profound submission, not unpleasing even to the Gods of old, and receive the pure vow which is brought here to Your cushion. And since thus far You have shown **YOURSELF** Great in the business of both peace and war, may You remain hereafter the most certain protection of literary affairs, as You have been until now; and may You be called the Happy and Unconquered Restorer of studies, religion, and the good arts. Relying upon this under Your mild rule, may the Republic of Letters grow with the sweetest peace, firm security, and the most joyful increases perpetually, and may it flourish, triumph, and be eternal for all time! May your life be long-lasting, **MOST BENIGN FATHER OF THE FATHERLAND**. May You live happy and live for a very long time, together with Your **MOST SERENE CONSORT and THE PRINCE OF YOUTH** <note>The hereditary prince</note>, the hope and Pillar of the destined eternal happiness of <term>Brandenburg</term>, and may future ages perpetually adore and venerate the splendor of the Most Serene Name. Finally, I acknowledge with a grateful mind that distinguished benefit, *Auditors most greatly to be respected*, which you have not refused to show me thus far by your diligent listening; I shall give effort continually to respond to that zeal and benevolence of Yours

->with a certainly grateful and mindful spirit.<-

O immortal God! How many and how ruinous the storms this man stirred up in the world? Because, inflamed by a spirit of contention and with the vision of his mind clouded, he thoughtlessly vomited out that most absurd of all notions: *that Original Sin is the very substance of man*, which he then chose to defend by every means, lest he should seem defeated. Even greater than this, and certainly more tragic and fatal, is the example regarding <term>Arminius</term> <gloss>Jacobus Arminius</gloss> that stands in literature. For because of the controversies stirred up concerning certain hidden chapters of Theology, not only all of Belgium, but nearly all of Europe began to be split into factions; and Arminius himself, overcome by grief, when he had fallen into a slow and heavy illness and had been exhausted by it, is said to have earned the following epitaph:

->*He who was subtle in perception and powerful in speech,*<-
->*But whose first care was always for morals,*<-
->*Arminius, lying here, calls out to all,*<-
->*That they should not prefer to dispute, rather than to live.*<-

Thus far, O Distinguished and Most Honorable Auditors, you have traversed with me the spacious field of the vices by which the Learned are accustomed to suffer; but quite many things in that category remain to be said, which, shut out by the narrowness of time, we willingly pass over. To be sure, one would still have to touch upon the insatiable greed of certain scholars, the immoderate luxury of others, and the seething lust of some. However, since I perceive it to be the nature of these vices that not a few other men are also driven by the same stings, and that they do not flow from the abuse of learning itself like the previously mentioned stains, we refrain from examining them more at length. Nothing remains but that I should compel those who wish to be counted under the name of the learned with a friendly exhortation: that they may wish, by the very sacred rites of study, by the inviolable altar of <term>Pallas</term> <gloss>Athena, goddess of wisdom</gloss> to which they have sworn, and by the excellence of the name of the learned, which is venerable above all others, to act solicitously, lest, enticed by the soft depravity of the vices reviewed thus far, they fall from their dignity. Rather, let them strive to exert themselves so that, in a most sweet harmony, both the praise of refined learning and the splendor of virtues may most amicably conspire within their breasts. Indeed, let everyone diligently beware lest, on account of those blemishes with which we have warned many learned men are contaminated, they hold the most useful care of learning and letters in contempt; nor should they attribute the birth of such foul vices to learning, which is the patroness of all virtues. They should be rightly mindful that nothing is so innocent and holy that it cannot be corrupted by the fault of another, if it is led down into perverse uses. I come now to fulfill that for which
pages.14:
I chiefly allowed this duty of speaking to be demanded of me today; namely, that I might claim for myself today a part in offering those pious vows and most humble thanks which are heard everywhere from all the learned on account of the subsidies for studies bestowed by the **MOST SERENE ESTABLISHER OF LETTERS, OUR MOST CLEMENT LORD** <note>This refers to the ruling Prince or Elector providing patronage</note>, for the benefit of literary affairs. Nor indeed can I do otherwise, while I find my own studies most liberally aided and confirmed by His Most Munificent Hand. But from where I shall draw the beginning of this speech of mine, I hang entirely wavering and doubtful. For how can I hope to encompass matters greater than all praise with the narrow and thin furniture of my oratory? What then shall I do, when both my piety bids me speak, yet the consciousness of my thinness bids me keep silent? This at least I will strive for: that what I cannot express in words, I may supply with my mind and silent vows. Therefore, an inner spirit overflowing with most humble devotion bows itself at Your feet, **MOST SERENE ESTABLISHER and PRESERVER OF THE MUSES**. Graciously impart Your eyes to this most profound submission, not unpleasing even to the Gods of old, and receive the pure vow which is brought here to Your cushion. And since thus far You have shown **YOURSELF** Great in the business of both peace and war, may You remain hereafter the most certain protection of literary affairs, as You have been until now; and may You be called the Happy and Unconquered Restorer of studies, religion, and the good arts. Relying upon this under Your mild rule, may the Republic of Letters grow with the sweetest peace, firm security, and the most joyful increases perpetually, and may it flourish, triumph, and be eternal for all time! May your life be long-lasting, **MOST BENIGN FATHER OF THE FATHERLAND**. May You live happy and live for a very long time, together with Your **MOST SERENE CONSORT and THE PRINCE OF YOUTH** <note>The hereditary prince</note>, the hope and Pillar of the destined eternal happiness of <term>Brandenburg</term>, and may future ages perpetually adore and venerate the splendor of the Most Serene Name. <translation>
<pb n="18"/>### ERROR XIV.
## That the Rational Soul resides in only one part of the Body.

I. Philo the Jew placed the Rational Soul in the heart, Parmenides and Epicurus in the whole chest, Strato the Physician in the middle of the eyebrows, Erasistratus in the membranes, Herophilus in the hollow or base of the brain. Hippocrates placed it in the brain, Xenocrates in the crown of the head, others in the whole head as if in a citadel, and finally others elsewhere; some even in a certain hidden and obscure place, from which it might run through the whole body like a spider to catch flies as opportunity arose.

II. Thus also the Author of the *Compendium of the Whole Theological Truth* <note>original: "Compendii totius Theologicae veritatis"</note>, Venice edition, Year 1565, book 2, chapter 54, page 192, says the soul is placed in the center of the heart without any stretching of itself, and it gives sensation, life, and motion to the whole body united to it; like a spider which, residing in the middle of its web, feels every motion made in the web, whether externally or internally: a truly remarkable opinion from the man.

->CORRECTION.<-

I. The Rational Soul is not in only one part of the Body, otherwise it would not substantially inform the others; rather, it is whole in the whole continuous body, and whole in any part of it, as all sound Philosophers and Theologians feel, along with the Interpreters of Aristotle. In *On the Soul* <note>original: "de Anima"</note>, book 1, text 93, where the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> says it cannot even be imagined what part (namely a specific and solitary one) the intellect—that is, the Spiritual Soul—occupies in the body.

II. And although Aristotle in *On Respiration* <note>original: "de respir."</note>, chapter 1, expressly says that the soul exists in some small particle of the body, he is not to be judged to have felt the same as the aforementioned ancients, because he immediately adds that it has its power in the particles—that is, in certain operations it depends on certain and determined Organs—and has its material powers or faculties residing and subjected in those particles or Organs.

### ERROR XV.
## That the Rational Soul is mortal.

I. All Epicureans denied that the Rational Soul was immortal, as witnessed by Ruvius in *On the Separated Soul* <note>original: "de Anim. separ."</note>, whom Pliny followed in book 7, chapter 55 of the *Natural History* <note>original: "histor. natur."</note>, and many others, especially the Sadducees, thinking that even the Rational soul perishes through diseases along with the body. Heretics whom Castro mentions in *Against Heresies* <note>original: "aduers. haeres."</note>, book 2, under the word "Soul," revive this nearly buried error again; and Lucretius in book 3 believed the Soul was gradually extinguished with the body.

II. In this matter, having weighed many passages on both sides, Aristotle at least seems to have been doubtful, as some note with Scotus in book 4, distinction 43, question 2, article 2; while some <pb n="19"/> among the ancient philosophers, especially the Stoics, judged that the Soul does not last forever, but once released from the body, it is weakened after a long time and finally perishes, though the Souls of the Wise persist until the end of the World.

# CORRECTION.

I. The greater and better part of the Philosophers, even the ancients, admitted the immortality of the Rational soul, as can be seen in Eugubinus, book 9, *On Perennial Philosophy* <note>original: "de perenni philosophia"</note>, and others. Dandinus also, in book 1 of his commentary on *On the Soul*, says that Pythagoras also recognized the immortality of the Rational Soul; for he used to say, "If you leave the body and come purified to the heavens, you will be an immortal God, incorruptible, no longer mortal." For this opinion, Saint Thomas, in *Against the Gentiles* <note>original: "contra Gentes"</note>, book 2, chapter 79, explains Aristotle along with others, as the more common opinion of the moderns also holds, especially since he said the Rational Soul comes from the outside.

II. But whatever the case may be regarding Aristotle, immortality certainly belongs and is due to the Rational Soul from its own nature, just as to the Angels, as Ruvius witnesses in *On the Separated Soul*, question 4, number 52. Since it is truly created, it does not have a natural cause of its own corruption; for Christ says in Matthew 10 that they "cannot kill the Soul." Nor does it stand in the way that in the Letter of Sophronius, recited in the 6th Synod of Constantinople, session 11, Intellectual things are said to be immortal only through grace, not truly through nature, and that this is approved by the Council. For Sophronius only denied such immortality to the Angels and the Rational Soul as God alone possesses, who therefore in 1 Timothy 6 is said to be the only one to have immortality, since he has it from himself and through his own entirely immutable essence.

III. Since it is certain from the 5th Lateran Council under Leo X, session 8, that immortality belongs to the Rational Soul in itself and from its own nature, some deduce from this that it can also be evidently demonstrated from physical principles, and is known as if from its very terms, at least according to itself, even if perhaps not yet as far as we are concerned. For the first Truth cannot lie, nor can the light of nature—which was granted to us by that same Truth for the purpose of knowing what is true—contradict it, just as Aristotle in the category of Quality teaches expressly that the squaring of the circle is demonstrable, even though the demonstration by which it may be proven has not yet been found.

IV. And indeed, it is at least morally evident that it pertains to Divine Providence that the evil be punished and the good be affected with a deserved and worthy reward; since this often does not happen in this life, as experience witnesses, one must either grant the immortality of souls or assert that Divine Providence fails in many things and that God is unjust, not treating each person according to merit, which is blasphemous. Saint Chrysostom, in his 4th homily *On Providence*, said this reason is more evident than the light of midday for the immortality of the Rational Soul.

<note>A small typographic ornament consisting of three decorative fleurons at the bottom right margin.</note>
</translation>

<summary>These pages refute the errors that the rational soul resides in only one specific organ and that it is mortal, arguing instead that the soul is present throughout the entire body and possesses inherent immortality by its very nature.</summary>
<keywords>Rational Soul, immortality, Aristotle, location of the soul, divine providence, Lateran Council, Saint Thomas Aquinas, Philo Judaeus, Epicureans, Stoics</keywords>

<translation>
<pb n="12"/><meta>continues from previous page: corrupt and...</meta> extremely weak, or least robust and less warm, the woman has conceived a sperm that is indeed able to attract nourishment and attempts to undertake the business of conformation and to fashion the membranes. But while it intends to perfect the work begun further, the distinction of the parts is hindered by the predominance of blood. We experience this happening especially when the seed is, as I said, small and diseased, in which the formative faculty labors under an evident weakness, and is joined, or rather confounded, with abundant menses, with blood that is at that time impure, endowed with a dreggy thickness, and therefore by no means suitable for nourishing. Thus, in place of an animal, which was the first intention of nature, at least an unformed flesh is generated, having certain principles of life, but so weak that they are immediately extinguished and annihilated.

XXXII. A <term>mola</term> <gloss>mole; a mass of unformed flesh in the uterus</gloss> is also sometimes begotten from a parched condition of the female, which happens in seed that is too salty, sharp, and corrupt, such as those with <term>scurvy</term> <gloss>scorbutici</gloss> and <term>cachexia</term> <gloss>cachectici; a wasting syndrome</gloss> possess. In this state, the generative spirit suffers dissipation and resolution; the seed, deprived of this benefit and strength, since it cannot achieve the goal of forming an animal, devises an unformed body of flesh, and thus wanders from the path of nature.

XXXIII. Here also it must be observed, concerning the generation of a <term>mola</term>, that its origin becomes even easier if the woman has intercourse with a man during the very flow of the menses, or if she has not yet been fully purged from them. For then the seed, if it happens to be conceived, is overwhelmed by them and greatly weakened and diluted. Nor am I unaware that there are some among the most distinguished men who deny that widows should be excluded from the occurrence of a <term>mola</term>, but by no means concede it to virgins. I do not wish to be troublesome to them with an ambition for contrary opinions, because I trust I have sufficiently demonstrated that it is just as impossible for a virgin or a widow to conceive a <term>mola</term> without the congress and companionship of a man as it is a fetus.

XXXIV. Thus far concerning the causes of the <term>mola</term> and the manner of its generation. Now follow the differences, which must not be neglected for a better light on indications <pb n="13"/> and its cure. However, what we mean by a true <term>mola</term>, understood strictly and properly, and what we mean by one improperly taken or not true—such as that which is watery and flatulent or windy—has already been proposed and declared above. If the surgeon is ignorant of these things, as all those are who are especially unrefined in physics <note>meaning natural philosophy or the physical sciences</note>, he will not infrequently lead the patient into the most immediate danger. Hence, I indeed proceed by a path plainly new and unusual to the ancients, and I exhibit wound-decoctions not with full cheeks and in such great quantity, but by the spoonful, especially in the first days, so that I may be made more certain of the state of the blood and the degree of acidity, which will not be difficult once the sign is taken from what helps and what harms. To these things the most celebrated Wedel adds his vote and weight when he writes thus in his <term>Amoenitates</term> <gloss>Delights</gloss>: "Just as it is a certain, constant, and faithful assertion that wound-remedies for internal use are most beneficial for external healing—under which name we have found the most expert traumatic essence described in Hagendorn's <term>Tractatus de terra Japonica</term> <gloss>Treatise on Catechu</gloss>, not to mention crab's stones <note>small calcium deposits from the stomachs of crayfish, used as antacids</note> used alone with success—so that other point is also certain, that traumatics must be varied according to the nature of the affections and effects, and so forth."

### VIII.

With equal confidence, we also proscribe those common external greasy and oily things which are called "defensives" by a plausible and splendid name, and with which they stuff the pores of the skin and not infrequently throw wide the door to inflammation. And I, for my part, do not see under what pretext we can expect any comfort from them; rather, I am persuaded that it would be not only more consistent with reason and experience, but also more profitable for the affected part itself, if it were fostered either with a small bag filled with warm sand or with warm wine, <pb n="12"/>or if it were washed more frequently with camphorated spirit of wine. See Blankaart's <term>Cartesiana Academia</term> <gloss>Cartesian Academy</gloss>.

# IX.

<note>Large ornamental drop cap N at the start of the section.</note>
Nor does that perverse method of curing inflammations deserve less severe animadversion, which nevertheless sticks so deeply in the minds of surgeons that it seems easier to wrest the club from Hercules than to remove these rooted prejudices. For what else do they achieve with their repellents, astringents, and refrigerants <note>cooling agents</note> than to increase obstructions and retain the thicker humors? When the more subtle parts evaporate, these humors, having become sharper, tear or break the fibers, whence from the increased obstruction a greater tumor supervenes, and the way to gangrene is rendered more expedited. So that this danger may be averted in time, it will be necessary for you to direct your cares and thoughts solely toward the obstruction, for which purpose volatile alkalis, aromatics, and balsamics serve: for example, camphorated spirit of wine, spirit of sal ammoniac, quicklime water, fumigations, oily volatile salt, diascordium <note>an electuary made from water germander</note>, and Theriac <note>a complex herbal jam used as a universal antidote</note>, which induces new fermentations. Likewise, all those things which temper, invert, or absorb stygian acid <note>a metaphorical term for corrosive or destructive acids</note>, to which the <term>Epithemata</term> <gloss>lotions or poultices</gloss> called "virgin's milk" are rightly referred. The chief of these, and proved by me even a hundred times, is that of Zwelfer prepared from coltsfoot, white rose flowers, elder, wine, vinegar, and so forth. Nor are those of less efficacy which Mr. Muys has in his observations; for he is the first who, in surgery, broke the ice frozen by the frost of ignorance, and of whom they hold out hope that he will publish an entire Surgery illustrated from the principles of the great Descartes for the benefit of the sick and the solace of the wounded.

# X.

<note>Large ornamental drop cap E at the start of the section.</note>
Worthy of the same censorial rod are those vehement errors which many see being committed daily on the field of Mars <note>the battlefield</note>, not without [danger to] life...

And from this have been born those "golden" emblems of theirs: "By as great an interval as Heaven is distant from the earth, so great is his body distant from us." "He ascended into the heavens, therefore he is not present on the earth, in the Church, or in the Supper"; "Therefore he is contained by heaven," namely, based on a passage miserably twisted and depraved by them in the manner of the <term>cubici</term> <gloss>those who confine God to a cube or specific space</gloss> <note>Acts 3, verse 21</note>. But truly, where will Christ be when that Heaven perishes <note>Psalm 102, verse 27</note>, and when their elect will not remember them <note>Isaiah 65, verse 17; 2 Peter 3, verse 13</note>? Truly, Christ ascended into that heaven from which God looks down upon the children of men <note>Psalm 144, verse 2</note>. Will God then be from afar and not near <note>Acts 17, verse 27</note>? Will he not be near to all who call upon him in truth <note>Psalm 145, verse 18</note>? Fourthly, others attack the Pauline passage in Ephesians 4, verse 10, and say that Christ indeed ascended above the airy and starry heaven, but not above the third heaven, in which his body is contained as if in a place and most august palace; and thus they say the Apostle is speaking not of all the Heavens, but only of the visible heavens. I respond: They achieve nothing, because Paul speaks of all the Heavens without distinction or restriction. Now, the airy and starry heavens are not all the Heavens, because a third is given <note>2 Corinthians 12, verse 2</note>; indeed, Christ ascended even above the third Heaven, being placed and highly exalted at the right hand of God, which is certainly so sublime that the heavens of heavens cannot contain it <note>Ephesians 1, verse 20</note>, and so high that it fills all things, <pb n="11"/> Ephesians 4, verse 10, and so powerful that all things are subject to it <note>Hebrews 2, verse 8</note>.

### Sixth Question.

#### §. 11. If Christ were on earth after the Ascension, would he not be our Priest?

In the Epistle to the Hebrews, chapter 8, verse 4, one may read these words: "For if he were on earth, he would not be a priest." From these words, the adversaries <unclear>furtim</unclear> <note>clandestinely/stealthily</note> gather that Christ dwells with his body in the heavens and is not on the earth. It is therefore our task to "wrest the club from Hercules" <note>a proverb meaning to perform a nearly impossible feat of strength or logic</note> and respond solidly. First: if Christ could not be a Priest (if he were on earth), it would follow that when he lived on earth, offered himself to his Father on the altar of the cross, and showed himself to his disciples by many proofs for forty days, he was not a priest. The consequence is absurd; therefore, so is the antecedent. The reason for the connection is obvious, because he was then on the earth. Second: if Christ, because he is Priest, were not on earth, then as God he would not be a Priest (since as God he is always on earth as he is in heaven). The latter is absurd by the admission of the opposing side; therefore, so is the former. Third: if Christ, because he is Priest, were not on the earth, he would not be a Priest according to his human nature, because according to that nature—by their own admission—he is in the Heavens. The latter is absurd, because the Priesthood belongs to his office, and thus to both Natures; therefore, so is the former. Finally: if he were not on the earth, he would not be an eternal Priest, because on the last day he is to return from Heaven. This is false; therefore, so is that. It is a wonder, then, that the adversaries prop up the building of their opinion with this passage as if with a pillar or a support; but truly, they conduct the matter through tunnels <note>undermining logic</note>. For 1. they insert the words "according to his human nature" into the text; 2. they take the words as referring to one or the other of Christ's natures, whereas the Epistle speaks of the whole Christ. Now set the syllogistic wheel in motion: what will come forth? Will it not be this?
</translation>

"He ascended into the heavens, therefore he is not present on the earth, in the Church, or in the Supper"; "Therefore he is contained by heaven," namely, based on a passage miserably twisted and depraved by them in the manner of the <term>cubici</term> <gloss>those who confine God to a cube or specific space</gloss> <note>Acts 3, verse 21</note>. But truly, where will Christ be when that Heaven perishes <note>Psalm 102, verse 27</note>, and when their elect will not remember them <note>Isaiah 65, verse 17; 2 Peter 3, verse 13</note>? Truly, Christ ascended into that heaven from which God looks down upon the children of men <note>Psalm 144, verse 2</note>. Will God then be from afar and not near <note>Acts 17, verse 27</note>? Will he not be near to all who call upon him in truth <note>Psalm 145, verse 18</note>? Fourthly, others attack the Pauline passage in Ephesians 4, verse 10, and say that Christ indeed ascended above the airy and starry heaven, but not above the third heaven, in which his body is contained as if in a place and most august palace; and thus they say the Apostle is speaking not of all the Heavens, but only of the visible heavens. I respond: They achieve nothing, because Paul speaks of all the Heavens without distinction or restriction. Now, the airy and starry heavens are not all the Heavens, because a third is given <note>2 Corinthians 12, verse 2</note>; indeed, Christ ascended even above the third Heaven, being placed and highly exalted at the right hand of God, which is certainly so sublime that the heavens of heavens cannot contain it <note>Ephesians 1, verse 20</note>, and so high that it fills all things,
pages.11:
Ephesians 4, verse 10, and so powerful that all things are subject to it <note>Hebrews 2, verse 8</note>.

### Sixth Question.

#### §. 11. If Christ were on earth after the Ascension, would he not be our Priest?

In the Epistle to the Hebrews, chapter 8, verse 4, one may read these words: "For if he were on earth, he would not be a priest." From these words, the adversaries <unclear>furtim</unclear> <note>clandestinely/stealthily</note> gather that Christ dwells with his body in the heavens and is not on the earth. It is therefore our task to "wrest the club from Hercules" <note>a proverb meaning to perform a nearly impossible feat of strength or logic</note> and respond solidly. First: if Christ could not be a Priest (if he were on earth), it would follow that when he lived on earth, offered himself to his Father on the altar of the cross, and showed himself to his disciples by many proofs for forty days, he was not a priest. The consequence is absurd; therefore, so is the antecedent. The reason for the connection is obvious, because he was then on the earth. Second: if Christ, because he is Priest, were not on earth, then as God he would not be a Priest (since as God he is always on earth as he is in heaven). The latter is absurd by the admission of the opposing side; therefore, so is the former. Third: if Christ, because he is Priest, were not on the earth, he would not be a Priest according to his human nature, because according to that nature—by their own admission—he is in the Heavens. The latter is absurd, because the Priesthood belongs to his office, and thus to both Natures; therefore, so is the former. Finally: if he were not on the earth, he would not be an eternal Priest, because on the last day he is to return from Heaven. This is false; therefore, so is that. It is a wonder, then, that the adversaries prop up the building of their opinion with this passage as if with a pillar or a support; but truly, they conduct the matter through tunnels <note>undermining logic</note>. For 1. they insert the words "according to his human nature" into the text; 2. they take the words as referring to one or the other of Christ's natures, whereas the Epistle speaks of the whole Christ. Now set the syllogistic wheel in motion: what will come forth? Will it not be this?

<pb n="33"/> we will say they are. Many affirm to have seen most of them capable of holding eighty rowers. No use of iron is found among them; therefore, the greatest admiration gripped our men as to how they fashioned either their houses, which they saw worked with wonderful skill, or anything else pertaining to their use. But they learned by rumor that they are sharpened <margin>The incredible cruelty of certain men</margin> from certain river stones. They later reported this as the reason why they fled in such trembling to seek refuge with our men: they thought they were Cannibals, for so they call those fierce ones, or Caribs. They left the islands of these filthy people to the south, almost in the middle of the journey to these islands. Their own peaceful islands were complained of as being perpetually harassed by frequent incursions from the Cannibals for the sake of prey, not unlike how hunters chase wild beasts through the groves by force and by snares. They castrate the boys they capture, just as we do with young chickens or pigs we wish to raise fatter and more tender for food; when they have become older and fat, they eat them. When they come into their hands at a mature age, they partition them after they are killed; they feast on the extremities of the limbs while fresh, and preserve the limbs seasoned with salt, as we do with swine hams, for later times. It is considered a crime and a filthiness among them to eat women: if they capture young ones, they care for and guard them for the procreation of offspring, not differently than we do with hens, sheep, and other animals; they keep the old women for performing services as slaves. When the men as well as the women of the islands which we can now call ours sense the Cannibals approaching, they find no safety other than flight; although they use very sharp reed arrows, they found them to be of little use in restraining the violence and rages of the Cannibals. Indeed, all the natives admit that ten Cannibals would easily overcome a hundred from the others if they should clash. What either race adores besides the sky and its lights, they did not have sufficient opportunity to explore. Regarding the other customs of the islands, the brevity of time <pb n="34"/> and the lack of interpreters did not permit us to know more. <margin>Food of the islanders</margin> These peaceful people use for food certain roots similar to our turnips in both size and shape, but in a sweet taste like tender chestnuts. They themselves call these <term>ages</term>, and another kind of root they call <term>yucca</term>, and from this they also make bread. They use <term>ages</term> more often roasted or boiled than for the purpose of making bread. They grind the <term>yucca</term>, cut and pressed (for it is juicy), and bake it into cakes. But this is wonderful: they say the juice of the <term>yucca</term> is more deadly than aconite, for if drunk it kills instantly; yet everyone has experienced that bread made from its mass is tasty and healthy. They also make bread from a certain panic-grain <note>a type of millet</note>, of which there is a very great abundance among the Insubres and the Spaniards of Granada, with not much difference. The head of this is longer than a span, tapering to a point, almost the thickness of an arm. The grains, fixed by nature in a wonderful order, rival the pea legume in shape and body; they are white when unripe, and when they have matured they are made very black; when broken, they surpass snow in whiteness: they call that kind of grain <term>maize</term>. And gold is of some estimation among them, for they wear it inserted into the lobes of their ears and perforated nostrils, drawn out into very thin plates. However, since our men had learned that no merchants traveled to them, nor did they themselves know any shores besides their own, they began to ask them through signs from where they prepared that gold for themselves. As much as could be gathered by signs, it was obtained without great labor from the sands of rivers sliding down from high mountains: they bound it into small balls before it was drawn into plates. However, this was not in that part of the island which that king held, as later became clear by experiment; for when they had already departed from there, they happened upon a river whose sand they perceived was mixed with much gold when they had jumped onto the land for the sake of watering and fishing. They say they saw no quadruped animal except for three kinds of rabbits. The islands nourish serpents, but they are not at all harmful. They found wild geese, turtledoves, ducks larger than ours and of swan-like whiteness with a purple head. They brought back forty parrots, of which some were green, <margin>Parrots marked with wonderful colors</margin> others yellow over the whole body, others similar to the Indian ones collared with vermilion, as Pliny says, but with very vivid and joyful colors. They have multicolored wings, for with green and yellow feathers, they have some mixed blue and purple: which variety produces delight. I wished to have recited these things about the parrots, most illustrious prince, although the opinion of this Christopher Columbus seems to oppose the magnitude of the sphere and the opinion of the ancients concerning the sub-navigable world; nevertheless, the parrots brought from there, and many other things, indicate by either proximity or nature that these islands savor of the Indian soil: especially since Aristotle near the end of the book On the Heaven and the Earth, Seneca, and other not ignorant cosmographers attest that the Indian shores are not distant from Spain by a long tract of sea through the west. That land produces by its own nature an abundance of mastic, aloes, cotton <note>gosampij</note>, and other things of this sort. Fleeces are collected from trees, just as among the Seres <note>the Chinese</note>. They brought back certain wrinkled grains of various colors, sharper than Caucasian pepper; also branches from cinnamon-like trees, but imitating sharp ginger in taste and smell both in the marrow and the outer part. Content therefore with these signs of a discovered new land and of another unheard-of world of lands, intending to return with a prosperous return, with the zephyrs now blowing because of our approaching spring, he left thirty-eight men with that king of whom we made mention above, who were to investigate the nature of the places and times until he himself should return. That king was called Guaccanarillus by the inhabitants: with whom, a treaty of singular friendship having been struck, he dealt in whatever ways he could concerning the life and safety and protection of those whom he was leaving there. Touched by mercy toward our men because they were being carried to foreign lands, the king was seen to have shed tears and promised all help. Thus having embraced one another, Columbus, about to return to Spain, orders the sails to be given: taking away with him ten men from those people, from whom it was discovered that the language of all those islands could be written with our Latin letters without any distinction. For they call the sky <term>turei</term>, a house <term>boa</term>, gold <term>cauni</term>, a good man <term>tayno</term>, and nothing <term>mayani</term>. They utter all other words no less clearly than we do our Latin ones. You have these things which I thought worthy of mention concerning his first navigation. The King and Queen, all of whose thoughts even while sleeping are placed in the increase of our religion, hoping that so many nations and simple peoples could easily be drawn to the law of Christ, were moved by these reports. They treat Columbus arriving honorably, as he deserved for such daring deeds. They made him sit publicly before them (which is the greatest sign of love and gratitude and supreme service among Spanish kings). They command Columbus to be called the Marine Prefect henceforth. He is named Admiral Columbus among the Spaniards. They also adorned his brother, Bartholomew Columbus, himself skilled in marine affairs, with the title of the prefecture of the island of Hispaniola. They commonly call this magistrate the <term>Adelantado</term>. Therefore, I will sometimes call the Admiral and the <term>Adelantado</term> and the present names of ships, and other things of this sort, by their common names for the sake of being understood more clearly. Now let us return to the undertaking. From the islands, as Columbus himself, now the Marine Prefect, promised in the beginning, it was believed that the greatest advantages of those things which all mortals pursue with all their strength would come. Moved therefore by these two causes, these two most holy consorts <note>Ferdinand and Isabella</note> order seventeen ships to be prepared for the second expedition: three large decked merchant ships, and twelve of that kind of ship which we wrote are called <term>Caravels</term> among the Spaniards, without decks. Two of the same kind were somewhat larger, and fit for sustaining decks on account of the magnitude of the masts. They hand over the care of preparing this fleet to Juan Fonseca, a man of noble birth, Dean of Seville, prevailing in talent and spirit. They command more than twelve hundred armed foot-soldiers for him, among whom they order countless smiths and artisans of all mechanical arts to be summoned for pay: they mix certain horsemen with the rest of the armed men. For the procreating of offspring, they brought mares, sheep, heifers, and many other things with those of their kind...

Moved therefore by these two causes, these two most holy consorts <note>Ferdinand and Isabella</note> order seventeen ships to be prepared for the second expedition: three large decked merchant ships, and twelve of that kind of ship which we wrote are called <term>Caravels</term> among the Spaniards, without decks. Two of the same kind were somewhat larger, and fit for sustaining decks on account of the magnitude of the masts. They hand over the care of preparing this fleet to Juan Fonseca, a man of noble birth, Dean of Seville, prevailing in talent and spirit. <margin>Literally.</margin>
But truly <note>original: "Verùm"</note> in this place it is taken literally: since the word <term>pará</term> <gloss>to bear/bring forth</gloss> is general, pertaining to the reproduction of anything. Whence it is joined with various words: as can be seen in many sayings of scripture.

### XXX.

<margin>Fruit of the womb of David. Proof. From the testimony of the Psalm.</margin>
It suffices here, when we have proved, that the only and natural son of God is called, and is, the fruit of the womb of David: just as we read in Psalm 132:11. Jehovah swore the truth to David himself, he will not turn away, or deflect, or depart, from it:

> Of the fruit of your womb I will set upon your seat, or your throne.

### XXXI.

Although many understand this promise only concerning a political kingdom: nevertheless, following the divine Luther, we believe that God confirmed by an oath, that a king be placed from the fruit of the womb of David; whose kingdom shall be eternal.

### XXXII.

And indeed this promise is remarkable: because it defines a certain person; nor does it allow the succession to wander into an uncertain person.

### XXXIII.

Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob also held the promise concerning Christ. But under an uncertain person: if you look back at the multiplied posterity.

### XXXView.

In this promise, however, there is a certain description, because a certain person is named: so that, although the entire people were to be led away captive; nevertheless, as long as the posterity of David survived, they would retain the hope of the kingdom.

### XXXV.

For this family was like a certain star in <pb n="13"/>this people: as long as its posterity was visible, it left a certain hope of future liberation through Christ even in the Babylonian captivity and all other dangers, and so forth.

### XXXVI.

<margin>From the concordances.</margin>
In the Latin Bibles, concordances are added to this verse: which themselves show that the Psalmist is speaking here about Christ.

### XXXVII.

Such is that saying of 2 Samuel 7:12. When your days are fulfilled and you sleep with your fathers, I will raise up your seed after you, which shall go forth from your womb: and I will establish his kingdom. Luke 1:55. As he spoke to our fathers, to Abraham, and to his seed forever.

### XXXVIII.

In the margin of the German version, Psalms 89 and 110 are cited, which openly, as can be easily demonstrated, speak of Christ.

<margin>From the authority of the orthodox.</margin>

<margin>Fruit of the loins of David.</margin>

### XLI.

<margin>Fruit of the earth</margin>
Isaiah in chapter 4:2. names him, to assert his true humanity, the fruit of the earth: since in Genesis 3:19. Man is earth: as the Seventy <note>the Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> interpret it:

<pb n="9"/><meta>continues from previous page</meta> monarchy, we shall see. Behold, since Severus <note>Severus Alexander, Roman Emperor</note> felt most correctly that the duties of rendering justice and performing military service should be kept separate <note>original: "vide Aelius Lampridius in Alexandro Severo"</note> by establishing salaries for the <term>Assessors</term> <gloss>legal advisors</gloss> of such magistrates, he is said to have often lamented that any others were promoted than those who could handle the affairs of the republic entirely by themselves in the matter to which they were appointed: namely, that military men should have their own administrations which they ought to perform themselves, and that the learned should have theirs likewise: and thus everyone ought to do what he knows. For this reason, the excellent Prince himself, if legal matters were being discussed, admitted only the learned into his council; but if the matter concerned military affairs, he admitted veteran soldiers and well-deserving old men who were experts in various locations: inquiring what history recorded the ancient Emperors had done in similar cases, and so on for individual matters. Let us remain silent about how this once moved the Persians to laughter, because among the Romans unlearned men held the office of judges while the learned stood behind them as assistants, as witnessed by Marcellinus in book 23, near the end.

However, we do not altogether reject the institutions of the ancient Emperors when they chose military men noted for their bravery to rule provinces in their stead. For if the men sent into the provinces were famous for their experience in affairs and for civil prudence, who does not see that they could aptly govern the political state of those provinces, and preserve and defend them from the attacks of enemies? Although they were not equipped with an exact knowledge of the laws, they could nevertheless render justice well with the help of <term>Assessors</term>. Truly, by the same reasoning, just as in our own present time several provinces are governed by Princes and Viceroys, in whom civil prudence is prominent, who is there who would require the highest knowledge of the laws? It is sufficient and necessary that they preside with their own authority, so that the <term>Assessors</term>, who actually pronounce the law, are deterred from judging poorly through corruption; indeed, it is so that the authority of the judgment may be made more venerable and its splendor greater. But a different rule prevailed, and ought to have prevailed, in the case of the other judges, upon whom only the care of resolving forensic <pb n="10"/> controversies was incumbent. It was necessary for these men to be excellently learned in the laws and customs of the Roman people during the time of the Emperors. At that time, because judges were required to render justice according to their own knowledge of the law, it is clear enough that unskilled men should not have been appointed to the office of judging. Indeed, the Emperor Alexander <note>Severus Alexander</note> wrote back to the Captains that a sentence delivered against the civil law and the constitutions of the Princes is of no significance <note>original: "l. 2. C. quando provoc. non est neces."</note>; so much so that (as Gaius answered in the time of Hadrian and Justinian approved <note>original: "l. ult. ff. d. extraord. cognit. & pr. Instit. d. oblig. quæ ex quasi malef."</note>) a judge "made the case his own" and began to be held liable as if from a <term>malfeasance</term> <gloss>quasi ex maleficio</gloss> if he judged poorly through imprudence and lack of skill. Let us not fail to say that it is the duty of a judge not only to hear what the litigants bring forward of their own accord, but also to inquire from them whether they wish to bring forward or answer anything regarding certain specific matters <note>original: "l. judices 9. C. d. judic."</note>. From this, the experts argue that the door of the courts is closed to the unskilled, because one unskilled in justice and the laws cannot employ such interrogations. But most clearly of all, the Emperor Justinian confirms our opinion, who in <term>Novel 82</term> cut off all access to the unskilled judge.

> For, says the most praised Emperor, we have not thought it proper to have the names of certain judges, especially those unlearned in the laws, nor those who lack experience in cases. For <term>Assessors</term> are present with our administrators in every way, both explaining the matters of the law and fulfilling their duties; since they are detained by many cares which they have in our service, they deservedly fulfill the role of the courts through the presence of their <term>Assessors</term>. But those others, neither wearing the official belt <note>the "cingulum" was a mark of high office or military rank</note> nor serving us, unless they are able to know by themselves what is just, but must beg for the integrity of judging from elsewhere; how will it not be the greatest vice of the republic not to hand over lawsuits to those who know from themselves what ought to be done, but to allow them to seek others from whom they may learn what they themselves ought to follow in judging. Thus spoke Justinian.
</translation>

<summary>The author examines the role of legal advisors in the Roman provincial administration and contrasts it with the requirements for professional judges. He cites Emperor Justinian to argue that while high officials might rely on advisors, dedicated judges must possess personal legal expertise to avoid judicial errors and liability.</summary>
<keywords>Severus Alexander, Justinian, Assessors, legal education, Roman provincial government, judicial liability, civil law, Novel 82</keywords>

### §. XXIV.

A greater doubt exists as to whether this privilege exerts itself with this same effect even outside the place of the markets; so that while they are lasting, no arrest <note>original: "arrestum"</note> at all can be obtained in any place in that province, by which at least the goods of a debtor present at the markets, but situated outside the location of those markets, might be seized? This question seemed so difficult to Ziegler <note>Caspar Ziegler (1621–1690), a prominent German jurist</note> in the cited location, §. 6 and following, that after bringing forth arguments for both sides, he finally suspended his judgment and desired a legislative decision from the Sovereign Prince. However, we think this knot is not entirely Gordian, such that it cannot be untied by any skill. For as far as it concerns the inhabitants of the market location, the words of the often-mentioned Constitution <note>likely referring to the imperial or local statutes governing market rights</note> seem to imply clearly enough that they cannot obtain such arrests by which they bind the goods of their Debtors located elsewhere; since the words expressly forbid the inhabitants from bringing any trouble upon the market-goers under the pretext of a private debt, and they would undoubtedly bring grave trouble upon them if they sought and obtained arrests elsewhere upon their goods. We do not hesitate to assert the same regarding outsiders. For the security of the market-goers is no less harmed by such arrests obtained by outsiders than by inhabitants, and commerce itself in the markets is hindered. To this is added the fact that solemn markets belong not to one City but to the whole province, and therefore their privilege ought deservedly to be observed in all places of the province or empire. Compare those things which we said above in §. 20.

### §. XXV.

The primary objection to this opinion is that the market privilege seems to be local, that is, restricted only to the place of the markets. For just as the markets of Leipzig, for example, cannot be held outside of Leipzig, so also their privilege, they say, must be restricted to Leipzig alone, as if it were fixed to it. But it is clear that market privileges can sometimes be extended even outside the place of the markets from the fact that Princes very often grant to some place the right of prohibition <note>original: "jus prohibendi"</note>, so that within several <pb n="18"/> miles similar markets may not be held. Above in §. 23, we also saw that this very privilege of which we speak is most rightly extended to the places through which the market-goers approach and return; what, therefore, will prevent the same from being done in the present case for the most just reasons?

## §. XXVI.

The effects of this noble privilege are also not ignoble, among which, in the very first place, <term>the most full and all-encompassing security of those traveling to the markets</term> <gloss>plenissima & omnimoda ad nundinas commeantium securitas</gloss> raises its head; since they are immune from every single demand, harassment, and disturbance by their Creditors, so much so that all judicial acts undertaken against them are null by the law itself, and are deprived of all value and effect. For it cannot be otherwise than null by the law itself, that which is done against a prohibiting law <note>citing the Code of Justinian: "l. 5. §. 1. C. de LL." (De legibus et constitutionibus principum)</note>. And since this nullity is notorious, for this reason a Judge proceeding against the facts is not obeyed with impunity <note>arguing from the Digest: "l. fin. ff. de Jurisd." (De jurisdictione)</note>, nor does the Debtor need to fear the penalty of contumacy or to appeal from the sentence.

## §. XXVII.

Following closely on the heels of this security is <term>a distinguished and excellent opportunity for profit</term> <gloss>preclara egregiaque lucrandi occasio</gloss>. For he who enjoys ready money also enjoys the ready opportunity of making profit and gain; very often Debtors would surely emerge from their difficulties, were they not shaken out even to their sack and pouch by inhuman and harsh Creditors, and all the nerves <note>the "sinews" or essential resources</note> for seeking wealth cut off from them. Especially in the markets, since an ample opportunity for increasing one's inheritance offers itself, the Emperors most wisely fortified Debtors with the present privilege, by the virtue of which they can not infrequently not only struggle out of debt, but even restore themselves and their families to a more prosperous state. For who does not know that one happy hour can often repay a Merchant as much as a hundred unlucky days have taken away.

## §. XXVIII.

And this opportunity for seeking and increasing wealth in the markets is a magnet, which attracts men from all places of the earth to them and...
</translation>

<summary>This section discusses whether market privileges (protection from arrest for debt) extend beyond the physical boundaries of the market to the entire province or to the journey itself. It emphasizes that such protections are essential for the security of merchants and the economic prosperity that markets provide.</summary>

<keywords>market privilege, nundinae, arrest of debtors, debt immunity, commercial law, Leipzig markets, Caspar Ziegler, legal nullity, merchant security, profit opportunity</keywords>

<translation>
<pb n="21"/>the breast for the Aetians, the feet for the Petrobrusians, the arms for the Albigenses; let the Nestorians, Eutychians, Pelagians, and finally all other wanderers obtain their own portion from Luther and Calvin, whether chance provides it or the Urn of the judges decrees it. By this reasoning, both the disputes between parties will be removed and a just punishment will befall the guilty. Thus I resolve, Aeacus, unless you, according to your wisdom, feel otherwise. **AEAC.** Manifest equity and reason command me to feel quite differently from both of you. For the crimes of these two are too great to be able to be chastised according to their merit by such light evils as you have indeed decreed. No pigsty of Hell, no Augean stable, no dung-pit of Cerberus is enough for purging the filth of Luther and the curses of Calvin. And even if you tear and pull both of them apart, cut into small strips and pieces through the crossroads of hell, it will still be nothing compared to their merit. For they would be removed by only one kind of death, whom it would be right to die a thousand deaths; and that scattering of limbs could stir up a tumult among the Shades, with these men contentiously demanding that part, and those demanding another. It is also to be feared lest these whom you strive to slaughter for the sake of propriety and ignominy should think themselves affected by you with honor and a kind of triumph, when they realize that their limbs and bones are to be distributed man by man like certain remains <note>original: "lipsana"</note> and venerable relics of great saints and demigods. Therefore, we must enter upon another plan, so that, while the laws of hell remain intact, the crimes of Luther and Calvin may be weighed with equal punishments, as far as that can be done. First, indeed, you ought to establish, judges, that no heresy has ever been devised by anyone since the founding of the world that is equally harmful and pestilential to the race of mortals as that which Luther and Calvin introduced under ill-omened birds <note>under bad omens</note>. No Manichaeism, no Arianism, no Macedonianism, no Nestorianism, Eutychianism, or Pelagianism (and yet these were the capital sects among all) produced such a slaughter of souls, nor cast so many peoples headlong into Hell as Luther-Calvinism. Behold, if you please, the vast spaces of the lower world, run your eyes through the wedges of the damned, review the ranks of the ghosts dwelling among us, count the Manichaeans, Arians, Macedonians, survey the Nestorians, Eutychians, Monothelites, weigh the Pelagians, Donatists, Albigenses, then recite the Lutherans and Calvinists; and when you have called the individual bands to the reckoning, compare these last to all the others, number to number, sum to sum, and by the immortal God see whether these do not by far exceed all those. **RHAD.** You speak most truly, Aeacus. But what could be the cause of such a brilliant <note>glaring or conspicuous</note> disaster? For indeed, if we weigh the ancient errors, there are some of them much more foul than those which Luther and Calvin forged. **AEAC.** Although there may be some among the ancient errors which have receded further from the truth of the faith, they nonetheless <pb n="22"/>were either of short duration or confined to small spaces of land; they did not scatter their poison very widely. **MIN.** But there were others whose contagion flowed most extensively and infected almost the whole world. Arianism embraced the rising and the setting sun in such a way that it left behind almost nothing healthy. <pb n="21"/><meta>continues from previous page: together with the image of God</meta> an entrance into the eternal kingdom of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ is abundantly supplied; but whoever thinks he possesses it, by a reckless abuse of the Gospel, even what he has shall be taken away from him. 2 Peter 1:11, Luke 8:18.

### OBSERVATION V.
#### When we speak of the restored image of God, it is not always necessary to add that it is understood as incomplete rather than perfect.

1. The foundation is situated in this: although the image of God in this life is not restored totally, or in such a way that it reaches the perfection of that state which existed before the fall; nevertheless, it is restored in man realistically and truly, so that there is a conformity with God no less true than that which existed in the beginning. Now indeed, whatever things possess absolute truth <note>that is, things which are not such only in a certain respect or condition, even if they are found subject to different degrees regarding perfection</note> those also can be named by their own right and merit without an added qualifier; so that, if the lower degree is not expressed, no one is deceived by an absolute designation. Just as in natural things, not only those advanced in age and stature, but even infants and the most tender ones are most correctly called men.

2. Indeed, nothing can be brought against this unless it is something so frivolous that even the first consideration would expose it. For it is utterly false to claim that the image of God, without some added qualifier, can only be understood as perfect because of the mention of God; for common reason itself dictates that predicates are not to be understood otherwise than the nature of the subjects or the underlying argument permits. An error lurks in this: that perfection is wrongly assumed regarding every constitution of the image of God, as if it must match the essence of God; in this there is a notable confusion. But truly, if the image of God, when stated absolutely, is apprehended only as perfect because God is perfect, certainly it could not even have been said of Adam not yet fallen, since similarly, on account of the mention of God, who is infinite, you might perhaps conceive of an infinite image. What could be clearer than this instance? Nor is there any disadvantage if the same image of God that was created within man and lost by Adam is attributed to the reborn. If it were preached as equal <note>in degree</note>, it would not be without error; but to say it is the same designates nothing except the one and the same truth of the image of God. For he who hears that the reborn have received the image of God which Adam lost does not by that very fact think of perfection <pb n="22"/> or that it must be perfect, but rather of what is to be understood by the "image of God" itself. So far is it from the case that a speech of this kind suggests perfection, that instead the listener would need a new question: whether those who recover it possess it in a perfect state? This consequence is full of wandering and is therefore void: "The same image of God is said to be received which was lost through Adam; therefore it must necessarily be understood as perfect."

3. And so that light may shine most clearly in this cause, let the dangers that threaten from both extremes be considered. For if it is always urged, wherever a discourse occurs concerning the image of God restored among the reborn, that it is spoken of as *incomplete, and that nothing more is to be attributed to the reborn; the listeners seize the opportunity for sluggishness, and they think that any level of persuasion is the incomplete image of God itself; and when it comes to the zeal for increasing it* <note>the text breaks off mid-sentence as it moves toward a discussion of spiritual growth</note>
</translation>

<summary>This section argues that the "image of God" restored in believers is real and true in essence, even if it has not yet reached the degree of perfection seen before the Fall. The author warns against requiring constant qualifiers like "incomplete," which might lead to spiritual laziness.</summary>

<keywords>image of God, imago Dei, restoration, perfection, Adam, rebirth, regeneration, theology of sanctification</keywords>

<pb n="51"/>§ XXIX. It is disputed, however, whether both parents, or only the father alone, ought to bring this rebellious son to the <term>synedrium</term> <gloss>council or court</gloss>. <note>Theodoret, Volume 1 of his works, Paris edition, page 168</note> considers that both the Father and the Mother must have agreed in the accusation of this son before he could be put to death. This opinion is approved with a white stone <note>A metaphor for a favorable or confirming vote</note> in the <term>Mishnah</term> <gloss>Jewish oral law</gloss> regarding the <term>Sanhedrin</term> <gloss>the supreme council</gloss> in the cited eighth chapter, section 4, where it is said: *if his father wishes to accuse him but the mother does not wish to, or if the father did not wish to but the mother wishes to, he does not become a rebellious and stubborn son until they both wish it.* Then it is added: *If one of them <note>the parents</note> is maimed, or lame, or mute, or blind, or deaf, he does not become a rebellious and stubborn son; because it is said: "and his father and mother shall lay hold of him," therefore they must not be maimed; "and they shall bring him out," therefore they must not be lame; "and they shall say," therefore they must not be mute; "this our son," therefore they must not be blind; "he does not hear our voice," therefore they must not be deaf.*

§ XXX. But a new Question arises: whether verses 22 and 23 of Deuteronomy 21—*And when there shall be in a man a sin that deserves death, and he is put to death, and you hang him on a tree, his corpse shall not remain overnight on the tree, but you shall surely bury him on that day, because he who is hanged is cursed by God, and you shall not defile your land, which Jehovah your God gives to you as a possession*—whether, I say, those verses ought to be referred to the rebellious and stubborn son? Certainly the ancient Hebrews are of that opinion, and they say that if the parents spare the son and do not wish to accuse him, he is then put to death by the council, either crushed by stones or hanged, because if he is a notorious sinner, he is investigated by the senate. <note>See Jarchi in this place and Elias Mizrachi, a most diligent interpreter of Jarchi, in this place, Cracow edition, folio 304, column 4.</note>

§ XXXI. It remains for us to add something regarding the staying overnight on the tree. This is certain: that among the ancient Hebrews, guilty persons were punished by hanging after death, as among others <pb n="52"/> <term>Obadiah de Sforno</term> testifies in the <term>Biur al Hattora</term> <gloss>Commentary on the Law</gloss>, Venice edition, folio 73, column 1, where he calls hanging an insult inflicted after death. With whom <term>Abarbanel</term> agrees, who in <term>Perush al Hattora</term> <gloss>Commentary on the Law</gloss> page 379, column 2, strongly defends this opinion. Compare also the <term>Aruch</term> <gloss>Talmudic lexicon</gloss>, Venice edition, folio 93, column 1, at the bottom. For it is clear that the punishment was hanging, as <term>Calovius</term> teaches on Deuteronomy 21. However, the reason why the corpses ought not to have been left on the tree must be investigated.

§ XXXII. <term>Jacques Bolduc</term>, Volume 2 on the book of Job, Paris edition, page 132, reports from <term>Andreas Masius</term> the reason why the law wanted those affected by the punishment of the cross to be buried: it was because from the long-lasting spectacle on the cross, someone might easily be seen as led into an opinion of an extinguished soul, and think less correctly about the future resurrection of bodies.

§ XXXIII. But a stronger reason seems to have been lest men be defiled by the touch of a corpse, especially since uncleanness contracted from the dead was the greatest among all types of uncleanness for the Hebrew people. The exposition of <term>Lucas Osiander</term> on the end of Deuteronomy 21 tends toward this.

§ XXXIV. And thus the nature of hanging among the Jews has been examined. Although the wood on which the guilty were hung can be called a <term>patibulum</term> <gloss>gallows or yoke</gloss>, as <term>Yekuthiel</term> calls it in the German version of the Bible in Deuteronomy 21, Amsterdam edition; and "wood" is also taken for "gallows" as <term>Flacius</term> teaches in the <term>Clavis</term> under the title "wood," Jena edition, page 587; nevertheless, the punishment of crucifixion was not customary among the Hebrews. This is because crucifixion is not reckoned as a specific punishment among the penalties, but mention is only inserted of hanging as a consequence of another punishment. Nor does the word <term>talah</term> <gloss>to hang</gloss> precisely signify hanging a living man or driving him onto a cross, since it is also used for those things to which crucifixion does not apply; for example, meat or fish or loaves of bread are said to be "hung" on a wooden nail, which are not said to be "crucified." See <term>Nathan Ben Jehiel</term> in <term>Sefer He-Arukh</term> <gloss>The Lexicon</gloss>, Venice edition, folio 162, column 4.
