->XIII.<-

For all things which truly exist in all of nature are either absolute forms devoid of matter, free from all material concretion, divine, everlasting, immutable, separate, and grasped by no sense, such as the first cause or the divinity above the heavens; these are considered by Metaphysics or primary Theology. Or they are things composed of form and matter, and that matter is either ethereal and peculiar and its own, or elementary and subject to privation, liable to motions and changes; these are considered by Physics. Or they are Accidents, which are present in things composed of matter and form. Of these, those which are proper to matter or form, such as qualities, actions, and passions, and the types of motions and <pb n="14"/>changes, and are called <term>energetika</term> <gloss>active/energetic</gloss>, are also considered by Physics. However, those which are common to both matter and form, such as magnitudes, numbers, figures, place, time, and local motion, are investigated by Mathematics.

### XV.

The distinctions of all arts and sciences are rightly accustomed to be made according to the subjects about which they are occupied and exercised, and the ends toward which every execution or contemplation of them is directed, and to which all the precepts taught in them are referred. For the adjuncts and the subjects are related and mutually explain one another; and just as every art or discipline comprised within the scope of Philosophy is a certain habit of the intellect tending toward some end regarding a subject, from which it takes its beginning, and on account of which it has its own precepts separate from the precepts of the remaining arts, so also it is accustomed to be valued by its end and subject, distinguished from other arts and named, so that one is learned as <term>theoretike</term> <gloss>theoretical</gloss>
</translation>

<pb n="11"/>conquers. According to the final law of the Code on curators for the insane and prodigals, parents are more terrified regarding their children. According to law 8, the final paragraph of the Digest on that which is done because of fear, it is no wonder, since they are a part of their body and affection, and for whom we labor no less than for ourselves, often even more, as Wesenbeck <note>Matthaeus Wesenbeck (1531–1586), a prominent jurist</note> says in the summaries of the Digest on that which is done because of fear, number 8. To this point the remarkable deed of Charlemagne seems to apply: when he understood that a father and son accused of a crime were unwilling to confess even when tortures were applied, having proven that one of them had truly committed the homicide, he ordered both to be hanged. Therefore the father, when already led to the execution and seeing no hope of redemption, was more terrified by the death of his son than his own, and to free his son from the execution, he confessed the crime. In this he seems to have followed what is read in the 1st Book of Kings, chapter 3, concerning Solomon judging between the women contending with each other over the son.

### XXXI.
Or because of craftiness or <term>dolus</term> <gloss>deceit</gloss>; which we call "evil" not as an epithet, but for the sake of distinction and difference; for the ancients also spoke of "good deceit," and took this name for ingenuity, such as occurs if one plots against an enemy or a robber, according to law 1, paragraph 3, of the Digest on evil deceit, which is permitted while keeping faith. See law 26 on captives and those returned by <term>postliminium</term> <gloss>right of return</gloss>; canon 2, "the master," question 2, cause 23. For deceit is a neutral word, which can be taken in both a good and a bad sense, just like "poison." See law 3, paragraph 2, of the Digest on the Cornelian law regarding assassins; law "he who poison," 236, of the Digest on the Signification of Words; however, when placed simply and without addition, it denotes "evil deceit."

### XXXII.
Or because of age; yet not just any age, but that which begins in the 14th year for males and the 12th for females, and lasts until the twenty-fifth year, without distinction of sex; for although females mature earlier in body, they do not mature earlier in judgment and counsel. Moreover, the praetor assists those younger than 25 years, following natural equity, since it is agreed among all that the counsel of such an age is fragile and weak, and liable to many deceptions, and exposed to the snares of many, according to law 1, the beginning, of the Digest on minors. The praetor assists these people whether they are <term>filiisfamilias</term> <gloss>sons under paternal power</gloss> or <term>patribusfamilias</term> <gloss>heads of households</gloss>, according to law 3, paragraph 4, of the Digest on minors; but not truly those of age, through the said law 3, paragraph 4. Exception is made if something was done with one of age, whose disadvantage pertains to a minor; see the final law of the Code on if against a matter judged, because from there an action of a judged matter is given against a minor, according to law 4, the beginning with the following paragraph, of the Digest on judged matters.

### XXXIII.

<pb n="9"/>Pererius also urges this point, saying:
> Since that translation of Enoch took place more than six hundred years before the flood, it could have happened that Enoch was then led into the earthly Paradise, which we do not deny lasted until the flood: however, one cannot argue from this that that Paradise remained untouched by the flood, and still exists, and that Enoch and Elijah dwell in it, and so forth.

I leave it to be discussed by the kind readers what the Adversaries <note>The Roman Catholic theologians</note> have therefore gained from this passage of Ecclesiasticus. I certainly cannot grasp what protection they seek here, much less what they find. Furthermore, that the words **INTO PARADISE** were added seems also possible to gather from another passage of Siracides, (z) where Enoch is said to have been taken up **FROM THE EARTH** <term>apo tēs gēs analēphtheis</term> <gloss>original Greek: ἀπὸ τῆς γῆς ἀναληφθείς</gloss>, that is, taken up or received upwards from the earth or out of the earth. For the term <term>analambanesthai</term> <gloss>ἀναλαμβάνεσθαι</gloss> frequently means to be taken upwards. (α) If, therefore, Enoch was lifted upwards from the earth, he was not lifted into an earthly Paradise, unless you wish to determine with certain people, or rather to play the fool, that Paradise is closest to the Lunar Sphere, suspended as if on high, and by no means to be sought on earth. And accordingly, if Siracides had written that Enoch had been lifted into an earthly Paradise, and yet asserted that he was carried upwards from the earth, he would have contradicted himself, or placed that earthly Paradise in the air. But even if he had said most emphatically that he was taken into Paradise, he would have understood it, by the force of the other passage, as the heavenly Paradise, into which we believe he was truly received, and as several from the Papal camps themselves assert, as we emphasized in the preceding Dissertation; to say nothing of the Fathers who, with Ambrose, assert that Enoch was snatched into **HEAVEN**, or the heavenly Paradise, to whose words Cornelius à Lapide indeed tries to respond; (γ) but he neither satisfies the reader, nor himself, as is evident from his own words.

Finally and thirdly, from the Holy Scriptures, and indeed the Canonical book of Genesis, Bellarmine and with him Jacobus Tirinus, a Jesuit, (δ) reason that Paradise survives on earth; because, if the waters of the flood had also devastated Paradise, the dove sent out from the ark or vessel of Noah could not have brought back a branch of green olive. But truly I would almost call this argument ridiculous. I do not wish to repeat what Pererius himself replied to it: (ε) I only urge this, which Moses most evidently testifies: that the waters of the flood had already been alleviated or diminished, and the ark had stood for several days on the mountains of Ararat. Why then could an olive tree not emerge at the same time on some high mountain, which because of its strength and firmness, especially with God so disposing it, endured under the waters. Pererius also reports from the Naturalists that its leaves never fall, and Pliny testifies (ζ) that it lives over two hundred years, and that this is agreed upon among authors. And so we have wiped away this third "petty, deceptive pain" <note>original Greek: ψευδύλλιον πῆμα</note>. Order now requires that, as we promised above, we show by the most solid arguments that an earthly Paradise does not still exist. But because the thread must be broken off here, and we must come to the one who is about to **SAY FAREWELL**, we shall defer this part to the following Dissertation. The one who is about to say farewell <pb n="10"/> is JOHANNES HEINRICUS AMELONGUS, one of our own, or from Gera, son of the most distinguished and learned man, Master FRIDERICUS AMELONGUS, <term>tou nyn makaritou</term> <gloss>of blessed memory</gloss>, who, while he lived, was secretary for the Archives and Consistory of Reuss-Plauen, a man certainly most worthy in human judgment to have lived longer, but extinguished by a most bitter fate, and not without the grief of the pious, as is known to everyone. With what great care he educated this his younger son as long as he lived, the nature of this paper does not permit me to explain more at length or praise more diffusely. He certainly spared no vigils and no expenses. For besides the fact that he took care to have his son polished by public instruction, he always maintained tutors at home who would repeat within the study what had been instilled publicly, and would give effort so that not even the smallest amount of time would be wasted. And he always obtained those in whom, as far as I remember, he found almost nothing lacking. Nor should the excellent mother be passed over without singular praise for the distinguished virtues of the weaker sex, who since the blessed departure of her husband (for I would not easily call it a death) neglected nothing that seemed able to contribute anything to the cultivation of his talent. The son himself did not rashly withdraw himself from either public or private lectures; but rather was present assiduously, except when his health did not permit, or those things happened at home which he could not push away from his neck lest he seem to fail his mother. He so established his way of life that his teachers had no need for notice, especially of the more severe kind, whom he always held as parents of the mind and respected. Of the progress which he made in his studies, he has published more than one specimen, and how far he has progressed according to the nature of his talent, he will prove in his Valedictory speech, in which he will treat the causes for which the most just judge of all things, God, has permitted so many victories against the Christians to the most powerless Tyrant of the Turks, who has afflicted the Church with so many slaughters; as well as in various poems of thanksgiving. He will come forward tomorrow, God willing, around two o'clock in the afternoon etc., and will recite from the chair those things he has worked out at home. Therefore, we most dutifully or most decently ask the Very Reverend and Distinguished Gentlemen INSPECTORS, and OTHER GREAT MEN, also the Excellent STUDENTS of the Master, who are now present within our walls, that they deign most kindly to listen to this son who is not degenerate from his Excellent Parent. As we shall always acknowledge and celebrate this with a most grateful mind; so we wish for the one about to depart all things most prosperous, especially the paternal grace of God, and the most abundant increases of studies. WOLFGANG WACHER of Ebersdorf will deliver the greeting from memory. May 16, 1664.

---

### §. VIII.

Therefore, although the doctrine of the Waldensians was simple and sincere for the state of those times, the Inquisitor monks nevertheless traduced it with monstrous calumnies and accused them of the most execrable heresies that ever existed. They called them <term>Gnostics</term>, <term>Cathars</term>, <term>Nicolaitans</term>, as well as <term>Manichaeans</term> and <term>Arians</term>, and attributed many errors to them regarding due obedience to Magistrates, legitimate oaths, infant baptism <note>original: "Paedobaptismum"</note>, the resurrection of the bodies, and so forth. (q) Most especially, the monks falsely attributed to these innocent men (r) the foul heresy of the <term>Adamites</term> concerning the lawful promiscuous use of women and incestuous pollutions, just as the pagans once did to the Christians, (s) unjustly ascribing to them the most shameful outrages and enormous crimes of incestuous minglings. Indeed, they even falsely attributed execrable blasphemies against Christ and the saints out of hatred and envy, simply to render them hateful to Christian Princes and to expose them to the fury of the ignorant common people under this specious pretext.

(q) On this matter, let <term>Reinerius</term> be read, who is here contradictory to himself, ascribing not a few errors to the Waldensians, in <term>Flacius</term> page 752, 755, 756, and so forth. Compare also <term>Trithemius</term> in the *Chronicle of Hirsau* <note>original: "Chronicon Hirsaugiense"</note> folio 145, and <term>Binius</term> in the place cited, folio 563, who enumerates the doctrines and heresies of the Waldensians, as he calls them, from <term>Guido the Carmelite</term>, <term>Bernard of Luxembourg</term>, <term>Antoninus</term>, and <term>Sanderus</term>. I pass over the rest for now, who set forth their doctrine with equal faith—namely, unreliable—and with the harshest words, ascribing abominable heresies to them out of hatred.

(r) The writings of the Monks are full of calumnies and fictions of this sort. See <term>Paris</term> in the place cited, folio 231, <term>Trithemius</term> in the *Chronicle of Hirsau* folio 179, and several others. In order that it may become known to some extent with what faith and authority these writers for the most part acted in describing the doctrines of the Waldensians, I am pleased to include the words of <term>Nauclerus</term> <pb n="16"/> which are found in his *General Chronography* 41, folio 211 a, in the Tubingen edition of the year 1516. In these days, he says, in the province of Narbonne, many despisers of Christian purity appeared from Albi <note>original: "ex Albigesio"</note> and so forth, whose doctrine, however, no writer known to this day has left behind. And since they call them heretics and authors record that they were exterminated for that fault, yet they pass over the type of heresy; I think, as far as I can reach by conjecture, that they followed a secret plague, and also indulged in foul loves and male cohabitations, and therefore condemned legitimate marriage and the eating of flesh. Thus far <term>Nauclerus</term>. A truly remarkable specimen of the monastic lust for inventing whatever they please at will! He relies here on mere conjectures, yet he does not fear to brand innocent men with such a mark of ignominy without further scrutiny of the truth and without trustworthy and suitable witnesses, and to ascribe altogether abominable outrages to them. But the name of heretic alone was once so powerful that upon hearing it, men would imagine all the worst things for themselves, being wretchedly bound to the Pope by the strongest bond of blind obedience, as if he were unable to deceive. On this matter, <term>Abraham Bzovius</term>, a monk, should be consulted regarding the *Impieties and Sacrileges of the Albigensians*, which he is said to have collected from all sides from monastic fictions of this kind, according to <term>Spanheim</term> in the place cited, page 574.

<pb n="21"/>The efficient causes of a salutary crisis are the bodily virtues and the Sun; the instrumental causes, however, are the provoking humors and the beneficial constitution of the Sun. For ruinous crises, the opposite is true, as we have said. Likewise, in other diseases measured by years, one must judge by the other planets: the only difference between these and those <note>daily diseases</note> is that there the Moon is observed, while here the Sun or other planets are observed.

### The Seventeenth Enunciation.

<margin>The construction of the sixteen-sided figure. On the causes of the day.</margin>
**The passage of the Moon through the angles of a sixteen-sided figure in daily diseases is the cause of predictable critical and indicative days; likewise the passage of the Sun in monthly diseases, and of the other planets in annual ones.**

<note>An ornate initial capital letter F.</note>
You should construct the sixteen-sided figure, as we have said, so that out of every thirty-two parts and thirty-six minutes <note>of the zodiac</note>, one side is formed. This number, multiplied by four, fills a quarter of the sky, which is ninety degrees; this calculation shows that two degrees and six minutes multiplied sixteen times complete three hundred and sixty degrees, which is the total circuit of the heavens. These sixteen sides, therefore, established from every two signs, degrees, and thirty minutes, make the sixteen-sided figure. Once this is constructed and the angles of the sides are properly considered, one will have the keys to all diseases, not only those called decretory <note>critical</note> but also the indicative and provocative days. For, as we said, the Moon—certainly because of the powers and potencies inherent to it—stirs the humors of our bodies and moderates them at will. Therefore, its location must be diligently inspected at the hour anyone begins to fall ill; likewise, the place opposite to this, and the midpoint of both to the right and left. Since these three places, which the Moon held at the hour of illness, strike with hostility by opposite rays—or as the Greeks say, by diameters and quadrangular rays—whenever the Moon passes through any of those places, it is necessary for that disease to cause greater commotions than on other days, due to the degrees of the opposing places to which the Moon pertains. Thus it happens that the passage of the Moon through these angles is the cause of critical commotion, indicative intensification, and provocation.
<margin>The passage of the Moon and its causes.</margin>

-> Day 21. -> Day 17. <-

<note>A complex square astrological diagram titled "Figure of sixteen sides and critical days." It features a central square rotated 45 degrees within a larger square, subdivided into various triangular and quadrilateral sections. These sections contain astrological signs (Capricorn, Aquarius, Sagittarius, Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, Virgo, Libra, Scorpio), degrees, and "day" numbers. The diagram marks the "Beginning and end" point on the left side.</note>

<columns>2</columns>

As we have said regarding the passage of the Moon in daily diseases, so it is in monthly ones with the passage of the Sun and in annual ones with the passage of the other planets. For by every powerful passage, this sixteen-sided figure is described; we have stated in the fourteenth enunciation what the strengths of the angles and powers are, and from where and how great they are.

### The Eighteenth Enunciation.

**The causes and powers of critical days arise from the passage of the Moon through the full angles. Those of the indicative days arise from the passage through the half-full angles; and those of the provocative days from the passage through the quarter-full angles. Gather the same for other diseases and the passage of the other planets.**

<column-break/>

<note>An ornate initial capital letter D containing a human figure.</note>
<margin>Full angles. Aristotle. Pythagoras.</margin>
Insofar as a day is a time, and as time is a number, no inherent force or power is in numbers according to Aristotle, whatever Pythagoras might have thought. Therefore, a critical day is not a "warrior" simply because it is held by such a number, as the ancient physicians wrote under the authority of Pythagoras. Rather, its power is inherent to it from the passage of the Moon through the angles. For this day is beneficial because in it the Moon alters the air with beneficial powers; and it is harmful because it spoils the air with harmful and ruinous powers. Therefore, the powers born in the days themselves are inherent from the Moon's passage. Just as in the sixteen-sided figure there are four full angles: the first is established at the first ninety-degree part, such as 15 degrees of Cancer. The second is established at the one-hundred-and-eightieth part, such as 15 degrees of Libra. The third is placed at the two-hundred-and-seventieth part, such as 15 degrees of Capricorn. The fourth and last is in the first part which the Moon held in the disease <margin>Against those who attributed critical powers to numbers. Others <note>attribute it</note> to the powers of the days.</margin> <pb n="22"/> at the beginning, such as in the 15th part of Aries. The first is the quadrangle of the first part, as 15 Cancer is to 15 Aries, and it is a left-hand quadrangle. The second is the diameter <note>opposition</note> of the first part. The third is the right-hand quadrangle of the first part. The last is the conjunction of the first part. These possess real forces and powers in which the Moon is full and perfect, because in aspect and configuration it was as if fully and perfectly present. Therefore, the Moon exercises full and integral powers in them. For this reason, since the critical days are more potent and fuller than the rest, they will obtain these powers and virtues through the Moon's passage through these angles.

<margin>Where the powers of critical days lie. For we shall speak copiously in our book on the path of nativities. 1521. Election.</margin>
Therefore, when the Moon reaches the first angle, it will be the critical angle of the first seven-day period, and the seventh day. When it reaches the second angle, it will be the angle of the second seven-day period, and the fourteenth day. When it reaches the third angle, it will be the angle of the third seven-day period, on the twenty-first day. When it reaches the head or the first part in which it was, it will be the angle of the fourth seven-day period, on the twenty-eighth day. These are the causes of critical days; now I shall speak of the indicative days.

<margin>On the decretory powers of indicative days. Which is the annual conversion.</margin>
The half-full angles are placed between the full ones at the midpoints. The first angle was at the designated starting place at seven <note>parts</note>; the half-full one is at fifteen parts and lies between the beginning and the first angle of the whole figure. The first angle was ninety parts from the beginning; therefore, the half-full one will be placed at forty-five parts from both, as in 30 degrees of Taurus; and here the first half-full angle will be placed. It lies where there is a full angle at ninety parts from the first, in the 15th part of Libra; the half-full one, which is in the interval between the sixth part and the first angle, is placed at forty-five, as in the 30th of Leo. The third full angle and the second were separated again by ninety parts, as in the 15th part of Capricorn; the half-full of these thirds, namely in the part mediated between these, stood as in 15 Scorpio. There is a fourth full angle in the designated starting place and a third placed at ninety parts; the interval from the third comprised forty-five parts, which is the fourth half-full angle, namely in the 30th part of Aquarius. Now, a half-full angle is a semi-quadrangle <note>45 degrees</note> from a full one, and a quadrangle <note>90 degrees</note> from its own half-full; therefore, while the Moon exercises full power in the seven-day periods, it exercises half-full powers and halved potencies in the half-full angles, specifically because they are semi-configurations, such as semi-quadrangles. Therefore, the indicative days are precursory—not a full battle but as it were a halved battle—and through the passage of the Moon through these half-full angles, the indicative powers will obtain their strength. Thus, this configuration at the first half-full angle makes the first indicative day; at the second half-full, it makes the eleventh; the placement at the third half-full makes the eighteenth; the configuration at the fourth half-full makes the twenty-fourth.

<margin>On prognostics. Middle <note>way</note> for physicians. Peter of Abano <note>Petrus de Apono</note>.</margin>
This much for the indicative days. I shall begin on the provocative days. There are four, as we said, which are halved half-full angles. For the half-full angle was at the end of the side at forty-five parts; therefore, the halved half-fulls are established at twenty-two and a half parts from the half-full. There are therefore in any quadrangle two halved half-full quadrangles, each of twenty-two parts and thirty minutes. First, therefore, in the quadrangle, the first halved half-full angle is placed at seven and a half parts of Taurus. The second at 22 degrees and 30 minutes of Gemini. The third in the second quadrangle at seven parts and 30 minutes of Leo. The fifth in the third quadrangle, namely at 7 parts and 30 minutes of Scorpio. The sixth in the same quadrangle at 22 parts and 30 minutes of Sagittarius. The seventh in the fourth quadrangle, namely at 7 parts and 30 minutes of Aquarius. The ninth and last in the same quadrangle at 22 parts and 30 minutes of Pisces.

<margin>Whether the powers are provocative. On chronic diseases. The position for offspring. What at the beginning of the disease. The solution.</margin>
In these halved half-full angles, the Moon exercises halved half-full powers; therefore, the provocative or intercedent days take their strength from the passage of the Moon through these. By similar reasoning, in monthly diseases from the passage of the Sun, and in annual ones from the passage of the other planets, the months or years take on decretory, indicative, and provocative powers. Enough on provocative days.

<margin>Against Galen.</margin>
Wherefore Galen is shown to have erred. For either the days take their powers from the number itself, or from the passage of the Moon through the angles. It is not from the number itself, as Galen himself agrees. But if it is from the passage of the Moon through the angles, there ought to be no counting of numbers, but only an inspection of the Moon’s passage. Thus, those days are critical in which the Moon runs through full angles; those indicative in which the Moon passes through half-full ones; those provocative in which it passes through halved half-full ones. Therefore, whether it is the third, fourth, or fifth day established by another number, it is an indicative day because the Moon has arrived at the half-full angles; and the same is gathered for the rest. Therefore, the enumeration of months and days is superfluous.

<margin>To the mind of Galen. Pico della Mirandola. Peter of Abano. Celsus. In the seventh, more powerful, 13.</margin>
As for what Galen adds—that a month must be mixed because the Moon acts with a double motion—it is nothing. For as the light vanishes after the conjunction, it is null. Many things are written by Peter of Abano, Pico, and Galen which are frivolous and are rejected in this book. And as Celsus says, it is clear that the fourteenth day is more powerful than the seventh. Hippocrates, however, thinks the seventh is more serious than the fourteenth. First, it is established that on the fourteenth day the Moon passes through the diameter <note>opposition</note> from the part it held at the beginning; the diameter is the most powerful for harm. Therefore, with respect to the lunar course, the fourteenth is more powerful than the seventh. Conversely, with respect to the bodily virtue, the seventh is more powerful than the fourteenth, since the virtue is then strong and the humor is most heavy for these things. Thus, the fourteenth is more powerful in consideration of the eternal celestial cause; the seventh, conversely, is more powerful in consideration of the corruptible cause. The same is gathered for monthly and annual diseases from the passage of the Sun and the other planets.

<margin>Epilogue.</margin>
And these things are enough regarding the causes of critical days.

### The Third Book of the same Agostino Nifo on Prognostics.

#### The First Enunciation.

<margin>Diseases from an eclipse. Rule. Ptolemy.</margin>
<note>An ornamental woodcut initial M featuring a leafy, scroll-like design.</note>
The mathematicians gather the diseases of the born from the nativity by many and various reasons, as Ptolemy does in the third book of his Tetrabiblos <note>Apotelesmaton</note>, chapter 12. We have now compiled those things which the physician and mathematician observe with more frequent use in the diseases themselves, and we shall follow them in order.

<margin>From a comet. John Eschiud <note>John of Ashenden</note>.</margin>
There are therefore three general causes of diseases: namely, the eclipse itself. We saw in 1511 from the eclipse that occurred so many labors, aggravations, and various types of diseases increased that people died beyond measure.

<margin>From conjunctions.</margin>
That from the movements and crossings of the comets themselves, most atrocious (and especially premature) diseases have increased, not only the wise like Ptolemy but even the common people cry out. And we have written about these in our book on the causes of our calamities.

<margin>Eclipse. But the lord of time <note>Chronocrator</note>.</margin>
So also from the conjunctions of Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars, diseases are engendered and most atrocious exiles made; many famous histories pass this down. Whence (on the authority of John Eschiud) in 1465, when a gathering of the three superior planets preceded in the second decan of Pisces, there were so many pestilential diseases in the whole world as had never been seen before, especially when an eclipse, a comet, and these gatherings occurred in human signs. But Ptolemy explained this nowhere.

In the book of nativities (on the authority of Masha'allah), that planet is the lord of the entire birth, which in Latin signifies the years and months.

<margin>The first part.</margin>
It is that one which is the lord of that sign which the Moon enters in second place after leaving the sign in which it was at the time of a man's birth. The efficient causes of a salutary crisis are the bodily virtues and the Sun; the instrumental causes, however, are the provoking humors and the beneficial constitution of the Sun. For ruinous crises, the opposite is true, as we have said. Likewise, in other diseases measured by years, one must judge by the other planets: the only difference between these and those <note>daily diseases</note> is that there the Moon is observed, while here the Sun or other planets are observed.

### The Seventeenth Enunciation.

<margin>The construction of the sixteen-sided figure. On the causes of the day.</margin>
**The passage of the Moon through the angles of a sixteen-sided figure in daily diseases is the cause of predictable critical and indicative days; likewise the passage of the Sun in monthly diseases, and of the other planets in annual ones.**

<note>An ornate initial capital letter F.</note>
You should construct the sixteen-sided figure, as we have said, so that out of every thirty-two parts and thirty-six minutes <note>of the zodiac</note>, one side is formed. This number, multiplied by four, fills a quarter of the sky, which is ninety degrees; this calculation shows that two degrees and six minutes multiplied sixteen times complete three hundred and sixty degrees, which is the total circuit of the heavens. These sixteen sides, therefore, established from every two signs, degrees, and thirty minutes, make the sixteen-sided figure. Once this is constructed and the angles of the sides are properly considered, one will have the keys to all diseases, not only those called decretory <note>critical</note> but also the indicative and provocative days. For, as we said, the Moon—certainly because of the powers and potencies inherent to it—stirs the humors of our bodies and moderates them at will. Therefore, its location must be diligently inspected at the hour anyone begins to fall ill; likewise, the place opposite to this, and the midpoint of both to the right and left. Since these three places, which the Moon held at the hour of illness, strike with hostility by opposite rays—or as the Greeks say, by diameters and quadrangular rays—whenever the Moon passes through any of those places, it is necessary for that disease to cause greater commotions than on other days, due to the degrees of the opposing places to which the Moon pertains. Thus it happens that the passage of the Moon through these angles is the cause of critical commotion, indicative intensification, and provocation.
<margin>The passage of the Moon and its causes.</margin>

As we have said regarding the passage of the Moon in daily diseases, so it is in monthly ones with the passage of the Sun and in annual ones with the passage of the other planets. For by every powerful passage, this sixteen-sided figure is described; we have stated in the fourteenth enunciation what the strengths of the angles and powers are, and from where and how great they are.

### The Eighteenth Enunciation.

**The causes and powers of critical days arise from the passage of the Moon through the full angles. Those of the indicative days arise from the passage through the half-full angles; and those of the provocative days from the passage through the quarter-full angles. Gather the same for other diseases and the passage of the other planets.**

<column-break/>

<note>An ornate initial capital letter D containing a human figure.</note>
<margin>Full angles. Aristotle. Pythagoras.</margin>
Insofar as a day is a time, and as time is a number, no inherent force or power is in numbers according to Aristotle, whatever Pythagoras might have thought. Therefore, a critical day is not a "warrior" simply because it is held by such a number, as the ancient physicians wrote under the authority of Pythagoras. Rather, its power is inherent to it from the passage of the Moon through the angles. For this day is beneficial because in it the Moon alters the air with beneficial powers; and it is harmful because it spoils the air with harmful and ruinous powers. Therefore, the powers born in the days themselves are inherent from the Moon's passage. Just as in the sixteen-sided figure there are four full angles: the first is established at the first ninety-degree part, such as 15 degrees of Cancer. The second is established at the one-hundred-and-eightieth part, such as 15 degrees of Libra. The third is placed at the two-hundred-and-seventieth part, such as 15 degrees of Capricorn. The fourth and last is in the first part which the Moon held in the disease <margin>Against those who attributed critical powers to numbers. Others <note>attribute it</note> to the powers of the days.</margin>

at the beginning, such as in the 15th part of Aries. The first is the quadrangle of the first part, as 15 Cancer is to 15 Aries, and it is a left-hand quadrangle. The second is the diameter <note>opposition</note> of the first part. The third is the right-hand quadrangle of the first part. The last is the conjunction of the first part. These possess real forces and powers in which the Moon is full and perfect, because in aspect and configuration it was as if fully and perfectly present. Therefore, the Moon exercises full and integral powers in them. For this reason, since the critical days are more potent and fuller than the rest, they will obtain these powers and virtues through the Moon's passage through these angles.

<margin>Where the powers of critical days lie. For we shall speak copiously in our book on the path of nativities. 1521. Election.</margin>
Therefore, when the Moon reaches the first angle, it will be the critical angle of the first seven-day period, and the seventh day. When it reaches the second angle, it will be the angle of the second seven-day period, and the fourteenth day. When it reaches the third angle, it will be the angle of the third seven-day period, on the twenty-first day. When it reaches the head or the first part in which it was, it will be the angle of the fourth seven-day period, on the twenty-eighth day. These are the causes of critical days; now I shall speak of the indicative days.

<margin>On the decretory powers of indicative days. Which is the annual conversion.</margin>
The half-full angles are placed between the full ones at the midpoints. The first angle was at the designated starting place at seven <note>parts</note>; the half-full one is at fifteen parts and lies between the beginning and the first angle of the whole figure. The first angle was ninety parts from the beginning; therefore, the half-full one will be placed at forty-five parts from both, as in 30 degrees of Taurus; and here the first half-full angle will be placed. It lies where there is a full angle at ninety parts from the first, in the 15th part of Libra; the half-full one, which is in the interval between the sixth part and the first angle, is placed at forty-five, as in the 30th of Leo. The third full angle and the second were separated again by ninety parts, as in the 15th part of Capricorn; the half-full of these thirds, namely in the part mediated between these, stood as in 15 Scorpio. There is a fourth full angle in the designated starting place and a third placed at ninety parts; the interval from the third comprised forty-five parts, which is the fourth half-full angle, namely in the 30th part of Aquarius. Now, a half-full angle is a semi-quadrangle <note>45 degrees</note> from a full one, and a quadrangle <note>90 degrees</note> from its own half-full; therefore, while the Moon exercises full power in the seven-day periods, it exercises half-full powers and halved potencies in the half-full angles, specifically because they are semi-configurations, such as semi-quadrangles. Therefore, the indicative days are precursory—not a full battle but as it were a halved battle—and through the passage of the Moon through these half-full angles, the indicative powers will obtain their strength. Thus, this configuration at the first half-full angle makes the first indicative day; at the second half-full, it makes the eleventh; the placement at the third half-full makes the eighteenth; the configuration at the fourth half-full makes the twenty-fourth.

<margin>On prognostics. Middle <note>way</note> for physicians. Peter of Abano <note>Petrus de Apono</note>.</margin>
This much for the indicative days. I shall begin on the provocative days. There are four, as we said, which are halved half-full angles. For the half-full angle was at the end of the side at forty-five parts; therefore, the halved half-fulls are established at twenty-two and a half parts from the half-full. There are therefore in any quadrangle two halved half-full quadrangles, each of twenty-two parts and thirty minutes. First, therefore, in the quadrangle, the first halved half-full angle is placed at seven and a half parts of Taurus. The second at 22 degrees and 30 minutes of Gemini. The third in the second quadrangle at seven parts and 30 minutes of Leo. The fifth in the third quadrangle, namely at 7 parts and 30 minutes of Scorpio. The sixth in the same quadrangle at 22 parts and 30 minutes of Sagittarius. The seventh in the fourth quadrangle, namely at 7 parts and 30 minutes of Aquarius. The ninth and last in the same quadrangle at 22 parts and 30 minutes of Pisces.

<margin>Whether the powers are provocative. On chronic diseases. The position for offspring. What at the beginning of the disease. The solution.</margin>
In these halved half-full angles, the Moon exercises halved half-full powers; therefore, the provocative or intercedent days take their strength from the passage of the Moon through these. By similar reasoning, in monthly diseases from the passage of the Sun, and in annual ones from the passage of the other planets, the months or years take on decretory, indicative, and provocative powers. Enough on provocative days.

<margin>Against Galen.</margin>
Wherefore Galen is shown to have erred. For either the days take their powers from the number itself, or from the passage of the Moon through the angles. It is not from the number itself, as Galen himself agrees. But if it is from the passage of the Moon through the angles, there ought to be no counting of numbers, but only an inspection of the Moon’s passage. Thus, those days are critical in which the Moon runs through full angles; those indicative in which the Moon passes through half-full ones; those provocative in which it passes through halved half-full ones. Therefore, whether it is the third, fourth, or fifth day established by another number, it is an indicative day because the Moon has arrived at the half-full angles; and the same is gathered for the rest. Therefore, the enumeration of months and days is superfluous.

<margin>To the mind of Galen. Pico della Mirandola. Peter of Abano. Celsus. In the seventh, more powerful, 13.</margin>
As for what Galen adds—that a month must be mixed because the Moon acts with a double motion—it is nothing. For as the light vanishes after the conjunction, it is null. Many things are written by Peter of Abano, Pico, and Galen which are frivolous and are rejected in this book. And as Celsus says, it is clear that the fourteenth day is more powerful than the seventh. Hippocrates, however, thinks the seventh is more serious than the fourteenth. First, it is established that on the fourteenth day the Moon passes through the diameter <note>opposition</note> from the part it held at the beginning; the diameter is the most powerful for harm. Therefore, with respect to the lunar course, the fourteenth is more powerful than the seventh. Conversely, with respect to the bodily virtue, the seventh is more powerful than the fourteenth, since the virtue is then strong and the humor is most heavy for these things. Thus, the fourteenth is more powerful in consideration of the eternal celestial cause; the seventh, conversely, is more powerful in consideration of the corruptible cause. The same is gathered for monthly and annual diseases from the passage of the Sun and the other planets.

<margin>Epilogue.</margin>
And these things are enough regarding the causes of critical days.

Let gloomy clouds depart from the starry sky. Let <term>Hippotades</term> <gloss>Aeolus, god of the winds</gloss> restrain them by his command, and keep the winds, shrieking with a raving murmur, shut in their prison. Let all things be occupied with jests, free from grief. Let the flute and flute-players be present, and the <term>Arcas</term> <gloss>Mercury</gloss> who invented the lyre, and the inspired shell <note>the tortoise-shell lyre</note> which grants human minds wisdom, so that we may sing a joyful <term>Paean</term> <gloss>hymn of praise</gloss> to the renowned newlyweds. You also, Phoebus, clothed in gold and a proud garment, whether you inhabit Delos or frequent Parnassus, arrange your beautiful hair with your pressing thumb; touch the sacred lyre with your fingers and ivory quill, so that we may modulate a festive song of joy with skillful throats. You also, <term>Pierides</term> <gloss>the Muses</gloss>, the slender deities of poets; whether you play by the waves of the leaping <term>Aganippean</term> spring, or in the leafy fields of Helicon, or tread the flowery ridges of the <term>Pimplaean</term> mountain, sweep the ground with your garments saturated in Tyrian purple, and crown your golden heads with Parnassian laurel. Let the left hand hold the lyre adorned with gems and Indian ivory <note>original: "dentibus Indis"</note>, let the other hand hold the plectrum; turn your sweet-sounding voices to a sweet song, and strike the resonant strings with a tender thumb, and draw out joyful songs with an eloquent plectrum. A beautiful fortress lies where the <term>Mulda</term> <gloss>Mulde river</gloss> beats with rapid storms and roars around <term>Grima</term> <gloss>Grimma</gloss> with swelling waves; there the festive solemnities of the marriage bed are prepared for the noble spouses. The spacious house echoes with the sound of the lyre, all things shine adorned with glittering tapestries, and poured balsams moisten the covered tables. Even the earth, sprinkled over, holds its own ornament, <pb n="10"/>for it bears various flowers: blueberries, marigolds, threads of saffron, rue, and the ears of green nard. All things are devoted to joy and all things to the newlyweds.

<note>A small horizontal floral ornament or flourish appears here.</note>

And now the renowned groom is present, whom all things expect. Grimma, open your doors! Come, Grimma, open the thresholds and unbar the gates! For no Babylonian mistress comes, nor a cruel prefect of the Iberian kingdom, but a hero rich in the endowments of the Muses seeks entrance—illustrious, born of a noble lineage. I add that a wonderful skill in the <term>Ausonian</term> <gloss>Italian/Latin</gloss> tongue commends the youth, as does his prudence in the law. Enter, excellent hero, with happy fates! Who would forbid entry? Who would not admit into the city a man worthy of praise? Who, unless lacking in mind, will not joyfully receive the sweet foster-son of the Muses? For you (as the Muses preserve in their mindful breast) did not join yourself, in the green flower of youth, to those whose cold blood around the heart hindered their natural talent—those whom the <term>Camoenae</term> <gloss>Muses</gloss>, Pallas, and Phoebus put to flight from the learned fountain, and whom the winged <term>Tegeatic</term> <gloss>Mercury</gloss> looks upon with a grim eye at their unlucky birth. You did not imitate, in the years of your first downy beard, those Centaurs who grow brutal with excessive luxury and compete in setting out unmixed wine—those whose custom it is to wear down their strength by drinking, whom the headlong dice strip bare, whom Venus enervates, and whom all-night drinking casts out from their ancestral hearths. These are the ones whom poverty presses, whom swords and brawls delight, and whom a <term>Lethean</term> <gloss>forgetful/death-like</gloss> laziness, devoted to sleep, keeps busy with no cares. But because God and a better mind called you to better things, being set apart from the dull-blooded common crowd, you thought it a disgrace to have remained among your father's household gods. Wherever Phoebus provides in <term>Teutonic</term> <gloss>German</gloss> lands, you took up full cups of the Pimplaean liquor <note>the waters of poetic inspiration</note>.
</translation>

<pb n="590"/>regarding these words, look at that greatest falsifier of the Talmudic codex, whom Socinus calls to his aid in the passage you cited above. He renders the prophet thus: *They shall look to me, together with him whom they pierced.* What, I ask, is this if not deflecting this piercing elsewhere? For I indeed believed it a sin to add even the slightest bit to the text, or to take even less away from it. Yet it seemed fitting to substitute <term>elayv</term> <gloss>to him</gloss> in the Talmudic text, lest our people should struggle with the prophet’s meaning. What? Note that the change in speech must be observed so as not to leave the reader in ambiguity. And that is ultimately the reason for the changed wording in the Talmud: <term>alav</term> <gloss>over him</gloss> is immediately added. Therefore, lest anyone should imprudently think the persons vary, it was decided to help the text by this very reasoning and to add some light to it: *I will pour out the spirit of mercies upon the house of David and the inhabitants of Jerusalem; these shall look* <term>elayv</term> <gloss>to him</gloss> *whom they pierced, and they shall mourn* <term>alav</term> <gloss>over him</gloss> *with the mourning for an only son, and they shall be in bitterness* <term>alav</term> <gloss>over him</gloss>, *as one is in bitterness for a firstborn who has died.* I do not even understand what could be more aptly connected or what I could have brought forth more correctly. L. Take away the veil placed before your eyes. It is not proper to change the former parts of that scriptural phrase because of the subsequent ones; but on the contrary, the things that precede confirm us regarding those that immediately follow. If you had wished to sacrifice to the truth, and not to mix the lowest things with the highest, I am mistaken if you should not have prepared this exposition: *I will pour out upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem the Spirit of mercies, and they shall look* <term>eli</term> <gloss>to me</gloss>, *whom they pierced, and they shall mourn* <term>alav</term> <gloss>over him</gloss> <note>Note: The speaker argues for the preservation of the first person 'me' while the mourning shifts to the third person 'him'.</note> *with the mourning for an only son, etc.* Now as for your nonsense about the Messiah, son of Joseph, to what does it refer? Do you mean our Jesus? Truly, no one could say how the families of David, Nathan, and Levi mourn him. Men and women every year, every month, every day <pb n="591"/> execrate and detest him. But if you have some other person in mind, consult the memory of former times, whether it has ever brought forth such a Messiah: a descendant of the son of Joseph, whom the Jews treated most unworthily and pierced, and to whom those things can be attributed which are assigned to the Messiah by the divine oracles, and which most aptly fit our Jesus, the son of God and Mary. We assert that the Epistle <term>tēn ek Laodikeias</term> <gloss>the one from Laodicea</gloss> in Colossians 4:16 was not written to the Laodiceans, but was written or sent from Laodicea.

And through this, it seems very probable that the Apostle denotes the first epistle to Timothy.

In Ephesians 4:24, we judge that <term>hosiotēti tēs alētheias</term> <gloss>in holiness of the truth</gloss> is better translated as a holy <pb n="18"/>zeal for truth than as true sanctity.

From John 20:19, regarding "the doors being shut" <note>original: "thurōn kekleismenōn"</note>, it cannot be inferred that Christ passed through closed doors.

In Luke 24:31, the word "vanishing" <note>original: "aphantos"</note> does not denote that he was made invisible, but that he suddenly withdrew himself from their sight.

In Matthew 14:25, "the fourth watch of the night" <note>original: "tetartē phylakē tēs nyktos"</note>, we are persuaded that the hours from three in the morning until six are noted by the Evangelist.

It is probable that the name Cainan in Luke 3:36 was added by Luke himself.

We maintain that the Gospel according to Mark was not composed in Latin, but in Greek.

### IX.

It appears that only the Pentateuch was translated by the Seventy <note>the Septuagint</note>.

### X.

In the New Testament, such Greek language as prevailed among the ancient Greeks was not employed.

### 49.
Next, the Renewal or restoration of the Confraternity belongs to this class: concerning which *Carpzov on the pact of the Saxon-Hessian Confraternity* provides several points, where he prudently warns that it ought to be instituted more rarely. It must be held that both the solemnity of the oath and that of the renewal do not serve to constitute the matter, but rather to confirm the validity and more solemn illustration of what is already constituted. See Lord *Hahn on the Law of Things*, thesis 75.

### 50.
By way of a conclusion <gloss>Greek: koronis</gloss>, the more powerful effects of the Confraternity must be tasted, at least with the tips of the lips. The primary and more noble effect is that it introduces the Right of Civil Agnatic Succession <gloss>legal kinship through the male line</gloss>. For this is established by that agreement, and is so close that the right of brotherhood is united. If you desire to know its qualities, I would have you hold them as follows: it is (1.) <term>noo katalambanomenon</term> <gloss>perceived by the mind</gloss>, as *Theophilus* speaks everywhere, that is, intellectual. (2.) Reciprocal. (3.) Conditional, by the argument of Law 54, On the Signification of Words. (4.) Public (see thesis 40). (5.) Perpetual (see the same thesis). (6.) Solemn (see thesis 48).

### 51.
The secondary effect is that it grants a real right <gloss>jus in re</gloss>, in some way the same as that which the other part of the contracting parties obtains at the time of the contract. Lest this seem an overstatement and offend anyone too sharply, we wish it to be understood with this grain of salt: since we have already established that the right of agnatic succession is conditional, one should think that this real right is assigned to them not in the second act <gloss>actual exercise</gloss>, as the Philosophers say, but in the first act <gloss>potentiality</gloss>; insofar as they have the hope that, through the continuation of ownership after the death of the other family, they may obtain the free administration of the goods. By this reasoning, nothing prevents the Confratres from being considered, in a way, Lords even while the other family still survives, by the argument of those things which Paul teaches in Law 11 of the Digest, On children and posthumous heirs. From this continuation of the real right, which is proposed to the contracting <pb n="24"/> parties, it happens, I believe, that our pact is considered irrevocable.

*As the pen meditates on more things, it is checked by the narrowness of time by which we are circumscribed; and it encourages me to postpone what remains to be said to a more convenient time, if God shall grant it. Therefore, the thread being broken, we submit those things which it was permitted to record at present in an Academic style for the sake of eliciting the truth to public judgment, with that modesty which is fitting, ready both to refute without stubbornness and to be refuted without anger. Wherever there is a straying, or anything said less aptly or correctly, or not perfectly explained, the difficulty of the subject-matter will excuse us, who follow probabilities and cannot progress beyond that which occurs as likely. Just as in a game of ball it is for one to throw conveniently, and for the other, even if a mistake is made, to catch it as handsomely as possible and correct it with skill; so it is thought to be the part of a fair reader to turn certain things toward a more benign interpretation.*

***

Finally, what was left of *Hungary* passed to the reigning family of the *Austrians*, who collect the remains of a most noble kingdom from the flames and ruins: a part held to be greater and more narrow <note>meaning more strategically defensible or constricted</note> than that empire which sticks in the throats of *Germany* and *Italy* and has boasted a renowned name through many ages.

<margin>Hieronymus Ortelius, Hungarian Affairs, parts 2, 3.</margin>
XXXIII. Thus *Hungary*, torn into two parts, is oppressed in the one by *Turkish* rule and in the other adheres to the power of the *Austrians*; a most harmful division, since an empire that could be sustained by one is torn and worn down between two, so that clearly now *Hungary* must be sought within *Hungary* itself. For peace between the *Christians* and *Turks* is always treacherous and prone to raids, since a treaty is hardly considered broken unless the siege engines are brought out. But the *Ottoman* dominion is far larger <pb n="17"/> than the Austrian, since out of the 60 Counties into which all Hungary is now divided, twenty-seven obey the Turks, and twenty-five the Austrians: while the remaining eight, which the Transylvanian has plucked away, have also withdrawn into Turkish clientship. The primary care of the Turks in their governance is to press all families of renown and high blood into that same single servitude to which they have condemned themselves with sordid reverence. Hence arises that great persistence of the remaining Hungarians against the Ottoman empire, since the nation shudders at every footprint of tyranny; nor are they truly faithful even to Christian Lords, if they are forced toward reverence for Princes by sharp fear and by that which crushes all hope of liberty.

<margin>Barclay in Euphormio’s Satyricon chapter 8, part 4.</margin>
XXXIV. Happier and more sacred is the fortune of those who find rest under the mildness of the Austrians. For there is great glory of liberty for the people, even within a kingdom: and also vast wealth for the Leaders, by which they hold a faithful multitude of clients in their debt. The Nobles have an erect mind and a spirit made for magnificence: they have no greater care than to possess their prerogatives and immunities, which they obtained from the Kings, untarnished and safe. And a distinguished Magistrate, whom they call the Palatine, is said to protect the liberty of the people: wherefore, as Barclay affirms, very many revere him as a champion of liberty, set in opposition to the Kings, just as the Tribunate once set a limit on the power of the Roman Consuls.

<margin>The same, in the same place. Hieronymus Ortelius, Chronicle of Hungarian Affairs, part 1.</margin>
XXXV. The more serious affairs of the Kingdom are dispatched in the Diets: here sacred and major civil laws are aired, and here the judgment of war and peace is weighed. In these, the people appear through their Envoys, whom they commonly call the Estates. Among these, the Archbishops and Bishops hold the primary place; their fortune was once ample and powerful in riches, before the Turk had yet gushed forth to the destruction of many, or those devoted to the new religion <note>referring to the Protestant Reformation</note> had plucked away their choice patrimonies. The Magnates constitute the second order of the Estates, who, distinguished by the name of hereditary Counts and Barons, have excelled with great authority since the passing of Andrew III. Then there are the States and Cities, whose power was great a century or two ago: now the strength of most has been worn away by the Turkish war: many, buried in their own ruins, can boast of their antiquity more than their strength.

In this **Chapter** the **Holy Spirit** first applied a most useful and most health-bringing **Office** concerning wretched sinners, and proposed the means of true **repentance**, **saving faith**, or of **salvation** itself, and exercised it in the sinning **subjects**, those truly **repenting** and believing. <pb n="6"/>and Monachus write. Less correctly. For prescription does not claim a place among the modes of constituting, but rather of acquiring a Feud, as Lord Ludwell and Lord Snobelius rightly warn after Vulteius and others.

### VII.

Antonius Monachus of Turin, a legal consultant, in *part 2 of the Treatise on the Right Interpretation of Feuds* <note>original: "Tractatus de Recta Feudorum Interpretatione"</note>, reviews more modes of acquiring a Feud than anyone else we know of, since he writes that Feuds are acquired by Investiture, quasi-Investiture, Privilege, contract, last will, Donation, Prescription, Sentence <note>judicial decree</note>, Purchase, arms or the force of war, succession, and the Right of Accretion <note>the right of a co-heir or joint owner to the share of another which has become vacant</note>. While we have very little doubt that he, along with the rest of the Italians, confuses the modes of constituting and acquiring Feuds; we shall be content with three modes—Investiture, Prescription, and Succession—along with Lord Ludwell and Snobelius. For the rest are either easily reduced to these, or are not modes of acquiring at all.

### VIII.

Petrus de Bella Pertica, Vulteius, and recently Antonius Monachus write that a Feud is acquired by the sentence of a judge. Ludwell’s assertion is more in accord with the law: that by a sentence of this kind nothing new is acquired, but only that which already exists is declared. They testify that Vulteius also finally conceded to this in his *Summaries, book 1, chapter 9, number 24 of the latest edition*.

### IX.

That a Feud is acquired by Prescription, not only for the reason that it is presumed from the lapse of so many years that an Investiture was <pb n="8"/> made; but even in that case where it is established that someone has not been invested: and so we support Lord Suevus, Ludwell, Friedrich Lentz in the *Disputations held at Basel*, and Setserus, that this mode of acquiring is distinct from Investiture, contrary to the Doctors commonly and among them Vulteius, Niellius, and Lord Struvius.

### X.

For the prescription of a Feud in a public or ecclesiastical matter, forty years are required by Alvarottus, Isernia, Zasius, Gothofredus Antonius, Schraderus, Borcholt, Rosenthal, Rittershusius, Molinaeus, Mynsingerus, Duarenus, Hanneton, Schneidewin, Fornerius, and Lord Struvius. But Nicolaus of Naples, Baron Schenck, Vulteius, Bocerus, Hunnius, Lord Snobelius, and Lord Ludwell judge thirty years to be sufficient. The former opinion is more pleasing to us, which Gothofredus Antonius and Lord Ludwell himself testify to be the common one.

Above all, I prefer pills made from washed aloes in a dose of one to one and a half scruples, for they remarkably comfort the stomach. Accustomed evacuations <note>namely the menstrual flow, hemorrhoids, or nosebleeds</note> should be encouraged, and if they do not flow by themselves, they must be aided by art so that Nature may be relieved.

### LIX.

Once this regimen is established, bloodletting is beneficial for those in whom blood is abundant, especially in the Autumn and Spring, in the manner we described above. In weaker patients, scarification and leeches have their place; scarifications can be repeated every three months. In cases of <term>Podagra</term> <gloss>gout of the foot</gloss>, they should not be administered on the feet, lest more humor be attracted there. When blood and melancholic humor are abundant, others highly extol leeches applied to the hemorrhoids in the Autumn. Nor are <term>fonticuli</term> <gloss>small artificial sores or "issues" kept open for drainage</gloss> lacking in praise <note>from experience</note> in the arms or feet, and so on. Likewise, emetics and sudorifics <gloss>sweat-inducing agents</gloss> are beneficial; all the most distinguished practitioners, along with Avicenna, prefer vomiting to every other kind of purging, and it should be provoked every month, especially when an attack is feared. Concerning diaphoretics and diuretics, see above. Purges must be applied especially to those with <term>cacochymia</term> <gloss>bad humors</gloss> in the Spring and Autumn, before the Equinox. Besides those we noted above, the <term>Pilulae Magistrales</term> <gloss>Masterful Pills</gloss> are excellent: Take half an ounce of washed aloes, one and a half drachms of white hermodactyls <note>meadow saffron, a traditional gout remedy</note>, one and a half drachms each of turbith and agaric, six grains each of mastic, Indian salt, and ginger, with laxative syrup of roses and wormwood juice. Let pills be made. The arthritic powder ascribed to Crollius and Paracelsus is praised, differing little from <term>Caryocostinus</term> <gloss>an electuary of costus and cloves</gloss>.

### LX.

Truly, in treatment and preservation, exhibit preparatory medicines before the use of purgatives, such as syrup of rose infusion, betony, myrtle, stoechas, wood sorrel juice, sugar, syrup of citron peel, betony water, borage syrup, lemon balm water, sorrel water, and plantain. The anti-gout hydromel <gloss>honey-water</gloss> of Quercetanus is excellent.

### LXI.

The use of specifics and anti-gout remedies must also not be neglected, of which even the ancients, such as Aetius, Trallianus, and others, and from them <pb n="19"/> Sennert, in his particular treatise on arthritis; likewise Horstius the Elder in part 2, book 3 of his *Observations*, and Crato in various places, make mention. What Paracelsus also promises regarding the <term>Senior Nigra</term> <gloss>Black Elder</gloss> can be read in his treatise on contractions; Helmont also commends it for these uses. Also the spirit of quicklime, first described by Basil Valentine, and indeed revived from there by certain empirics with additions, provides a sufficiently secure and not to be despised prophylactic.

### LXII.

Finally, the affected parts must be strengthened, for which the <term>Diachalciteos</term> plaster is commended, from which a shoe may be made covering the foot, or it may be worn during the day, removed and dried at night, and replaced in the morning. The urine of boys is recommended; hence fullers are more rarely afflicted by gout. Grape-skins may be used, to which an ointment of earthworms and marshmallow root can be added. Let herbs and flowers <note>mentioned above regarding anodynes</note> be boiled in salted chalybeate <gloss>iron-bearing</gloss> water and the vapor be received. Moderate exercise on an empty stomach is beneficial; as is very frequent rubbing with salted oil. Frequent cleansing can be done with a dry sponge, or one lightly sprinkled with a decoction. Fumigation is praised by others made from sandarac, frankincense, cloves, cinnamon, and nutmeg; mix the powders with gum tragacanth. Immature rose oil with salt added to the yellow part of rose powder is approved. It is excellent if the affected part is protected by hare skins. Crato places mugwort and wormwood under the soles of the feet. A dog skin may be anointed with oil of costus. Grembs commends the following wine infusion: Take one ounce of chicory root, half an ounce each of swallow-wort and avens root, two drachms each of devil's bit and peony, half a handful each of betony, maidenhair fern, ground pine, primrose, rosemary flowers, sage, and thyme, one handful of blessed thistle leaves, and six pounds of Rhenish wine. Thermal baths have the best use <note>but applied moderately</note>, whether they be salty, aluminous, sulfurous, vitriolic, or nitrous, or those containing a copper vein; but the mud of this kind is even better. Consult Jacobus Theodorus Tabernaemontanus's *Water Treasure* <note>original: "WasserSchatz"</note>. But it must be noted that strengthening remedies are only to be applied when the pain, swelling, and <term>tophi</term> <gloss>stone-like deposits</gloss> have vanished, nor should the parts be so strengthened that they become over-powerful.

### LXIII.

The imbalance of the principal organs must also be corrected. To strengthen the stomach, the Elixir of Property is beneficial, as is the wine of Paracelsus...
</translation>

What Paracelsus also promises regarding the <term>Senior Nigra</term> <gloss>Black Elder</gloss> can be read in his treatise on contractions; Helmont also commends it for these uses. Also the spirit of quicklime, first described by Basil Valentine, and indeed revived from there by certain empirics with additions, provides a sufficiently secure and not to be despised prophylactic.

### LXII.

Finally, the affected parts must be strengthened, for which the <term>Diachalciteos</term> plaster is commended, from which a shoe may be made covering the foot, or it may be worn during the day, removed and dried at night, and replaced in the morning. The urine of boys is recommended; hence fullers are more rarely afflicted by gout. Grape-skins may be used, to which an ointment of earthworms and marshmallow root can be added. Let herbs and flowers <note>mentioned above regarding anodynes</note> be boiled in salted chalybeate <gloss>iron-bearing</gloss> water and the vapor be received. Moderate exercise on an empty stomach is beneficial; as is very frequent rubbing with salted oil. Frequent cleansing can be done with a dry sponge, or one lightly sprinkled with a decoction. Fumigation is praised by others made from sandarac, frankincense, cloves, cinnamon, and nutmeg; mix the powders with gum tragacanth. Immature rose oil with salt added to the yellow part of rose powder is approved. It is excellent if the affected part is protected by hare skins. Crato places mugwort and wormwood under the soles of the feet. A dog skin may be anointed with oil of costus. Grembs commends the following wine infusion: Take one ounce of chicory root, half an ounce each of swallow-wort and avens root, two drachms each of devil's bit and peony, half a handful each of betony, maidenhair fern, ground pine, primrose, rosemary flowers, sage, and thyme, one handful of blessed thistle leaves, and six pounds of Rhenish wine. Thermal baths have the best use <note>but applied moderately</note>, whether they be salty, aluminous, sulfurous, vitriolic, or nitrous, or those containing a copper vein; but the mud of this kind is even better. Consult Jacobus Theodorus Tabernaemontanus's *Water Treasure* <note>original: "WasserSchatz"</note>. But it must be noted that strengthening remedies are only to be applied when the pain, swelling, and <term>tophi</term> <gloss>stone-like deposits</gloss> have vanished, nor should the parts be so strengthened that they become over-powerful.

### LXIII.

The imbalance of the principal organs must also be corrected. To strengthen the stomach, the Elixir of Property is beneficial, as is the wine of Paracelsus...

<margin>Book 7, chapters 7 and 26.</margin>
Finally, *Celsus* in other places, rendering the <term>ankteras</term> into Latin, spoke of *a sharp little hook, blunted hooks, and being gripped by little hooks*: which formulas of speaking sufficiently indicate that the material of the <term>ankteres</term> was metallic; as *Guido* <note>Guy de Chauliac, 14th-century surgeon</note> clearly teaches, contrary to what *Fallopius* <note>Gabriele Falloppio, 16th-century anatomist</note> thought, because the Latin word **ACIA** <gloss>thread/fiber</gloss> was not understood: for all <term>fibulae</term>, as *Oribasius* <note>4th-century Greek medical compiler</note> relates, were made of bronze, iron, or gold.

<margin>On Machines, chapter 4.</margin>
This, therefore, was the application of <term>fibulae</term> or little hooks according to *Celsus*. Where there was a wound in the flesh, and it stood open; and the edges were not easily drawn together into one, for which a suture would be unsuitable; the <term>fibulae</term> were applied to the wound in this manner. With one hook of the clasp (for it consisted of a pair, one curved inward, the other curved back, in the shape of a longer letter S and hooked on both sides), one lip of the wound was gripped with the flesh and skin from the inside, beginning from the flesh. Then, the <term>fibula</term> having been pulled back, the opposite lip was seized by the other hook from the outside, by biting the skin before the flesh: and thus the edges of the gaping wound, which could not be sewn together because of the distance, were drawn back and held. In almost the same manner *Guido* says: *The lips of the wound are joined together in turn with hooks, which ought to be small in proportion to the limb; from each side*
</translation>

<summary>Chifflet argues that Celsus's fibulae were metallic surgical hooks (ankteres) rather than thread, citing classical poets and medical authorities to prove the "biting" nature of these instruments. He describes the S-shaped design of these hooks used for closing deep wounds where traditional suturing was impossible.</summary>

<keywords>Celsus, surgery, fibula, ankter, medical instruments, suture, Guido de Cauliaco, Fallopius, Oribasius, Roman medicine</keywords>

### §. XV.

We must now consider the images of the ancients, which were fashioned likenesses of men, sketched in colors, and preserved either in the more prominent parts of houses or in some public place.

### §. XVI.

Most people trace their origin back to the statues of the pagan gods. Mortals, considering this honor and worship of images to be more excellent than others, took care to have such things erected for themselves or certainly for their deceased friends. (In much the same way, people today still build such chapel-like structures in cemeteries for themselves and their descendants.) Formerly among the Romans, it was permitted only to those holding a magistracy to set up images, from which the <term>jus imaginis</term> <gloss>the right of images</gloss> was named. But it is nonetheless established that this right was not granted absolutely to everyone performing a public duty in the Senate or magistracy, but only to those who had presided over those honors with distinction. For this reason, even later, with the addition of the Emperors' power, it was not permitted to set up images or statues except by their permission. *Suetonius in the Life of Tiberius, 10.* Nevertheless, *Godescalc Stewechius* in his *Commentary on Vegetius Renatus, On Military Matters, book II, chapter 6*, mentions that images were also set up for philosophers, based on *Petrus Crinitus, On Honest Discipline, book I, chapter 11*. To this he refers an inscription in Rome on the Aventine Hill at Saint Alexius: TI. CLAVIVS. SECVNDVS. COACTOR. CVM. TI. CLAVDIO. TI. QVIR. SECVNDO. VIATORIBVS. III. VIR. ET IV. VIR SCHOLAM. CVM. IMAGINIBVS. ORNAMENTIS QVE OMNIB. SVA. IMPENSA. FECIT. <note>original: "Tiberius Claudius Secundus, a collector, with Tiberius Claudius Secundus of the Quirina tribe, messengers to the board of three and board of four, built this school with images and all its ornaments at his own expense."</note>

### §. XVII.

Therefore, when a funeral was to be conducted for them, the Romans placed the collected images of their ancestors on certain biers and carried them before the funeral procession. Also on feast days, they would open that cabinet in which it was the custom for images to be kept, and they would adorn them in various <pb n="10"/> ways and rituals, scattering flowers, wreaths, and crowns, and adding a garment according to the status of that dignity and public office which he, whose face the image represented, once held. They acted no differently than if a living person were present; they even venerated the likeness with honorary titles and set forth and recited their achievements. For this reason, *Martial, book V, Epigram 21, line 7, calls these images "proud."*

### §. XIIX.

It is certainly most laudable what is said concerning these images of the ancients: that they passed down to posterity, yet not so that the descendants themselves could use them for their own honor and praise, but only for the glory of the family, which had accrued to it through the man portrayed in the image. Therefore, it was permitted that this image of a well-deserving man be carried out at the funeral of some relative from the family, but not equally so that it belonged to all his descendants, unless they had likewise acquired that right of images. See *Höpping*, who treats these matters professionally in *On the Right of Insignia, chapter XIX*; *Gabriele Paleotti's treatise On Images*; *Rosinus's Antiquities*; *Jacob Pontanus's Preparatory Exercises, book IV*; and *Polydore Vergil, On the Discovery of Things, book VI, chapter 13*, who also complains at length about the worship of images being transferred to Christians.

### §. XIX.

The condition of statues was different from the images just mentioned. Namely, a statue was placed either for the dead or the living on account of distinguished services to the Republic in some conspicuous place, as a lasting <term>mnemosynon</term> <gloss>memorial</gloss>; and at first they were made from cypress, cedar, oak, stone, marble, etc.; then they were additionally fashioned from various metals. Their origin is the same as that of images. They used to be distinguished according to the degree of those well-deserving in the republic, or of their dignities, into equal, great, greater, and greatest. These latter were those which exceeded human stature threefold or more, and they were set up for the gods. The "greater" ones...
</translation>

<summary>This text discusses the Roman tradition of ancestral images and public statues, detailing the legal right to display likenesses and their ritual use in funerals. It explores the transition of these honors from political figures to philosophers and the eventual adoption of similar practices within Christian contexts.</summary>

<keywords>jus imaginis, Roman funerals, ancestral images, statues, public honors, magistracy, commemorative art, memorialization</keywords>

For the character of majesty confers trust and public authority upon the coin; namely, by looking upon the face and insignia of their prince, subjects are reminded of the majesty, love, and loyalty of the prince, by argument of laws 1 and 2 of the Code on counterfeit money, and law 3, using the phrase "eternal faces" <note>original: "æternales vultus"</note> in the Code on the power of old coinage.
