Monet."</note> in the section "How, however, the aforementioned" <note>original: "Wie aber vorgestelte etc."</note> That we may understand that all right of coinage depends on the will and governance of Majesty: although sometimes the sign of at least that prince who has the right of minting may suffice and be used, with the authority of Majesty nevertheless understood, Bornitius, book 1 <note>on coinage</note>, chapter 8, at the end. *c* Valuation, from the French <term>Evaluer</term> <gloss>to estimate</gloss>. This estimation ought to be public, fair, certain, and constant, nor shall the Prince value coins for more than the raw mass of gold or silver can be worth, law 3 of the Digest on the oath in court, law 1 of the Digest on contracting a purchase. Molina on Usury, question 80, number 789. Budé, book 1 on the <term>As</term> <gloss>a Roman coin</gloss>. For if the estimation exceeds the material weight and goodness, an unjust valuation is established, Antonius Faber <note>on the payment of various coins</note>, chapter 1, at the beginning. Furthermore, the estimation of gold coins and Thalers is defined in the Monetary Ordinance of the year 1559, in the sections "First" and "Hereupon they ordain." Imperial Recess of the year 1566, in the section "Accordingly we have," and of the year 1576, in the section "And from special reasonable," etc. *d* The size <note>original: "Magnitudo"</note> ought to be such that the use of coins in commerce is easy and manageable, not in the manner that Livy records of the old "heavy bronze" <note>original: "as graue"</note> being carried in wagons among the Romans. Camerarius on ancient coinage, page 275. The figure shall also be round and circular, as if more perfect and less subject to clipping, Bodin, book 6 of the Republic, chapter 3. Monetary Ordinance of the year 1559, in the section "How, however, the aforementioned," there: "in its circle" <note>original: "in ihrem Circkel etc."</note> A number is usually impressed upon the character, as a Ducat is valued at one hundred and four kreuzers, a Rhenish <note>guilder</note> at 75, Imperial Recess of the year 1576, in the section "And from special," etc. Names are changed either from the Efficient Cause, such as the <term>Philipsthaler</term> <gloss>a thaler of King Philip</gloss>; or from the material, such as <term>aurei</term> <gloss>gold coins</gloss>; or from the form, such as <term>coronati</term> <gloss>crowned coins</gloss>; or from the nation, such as <term>Angloti</term> <gloss>Angels</gloss> and <term>Sterlingi</term> <gloss>Sterlings</gloss>, etc., with more distinctions in Jakob Bornitius, book 1 <note>on coinage</note>, chapter 10, at the end.

->## SEVENTH ASSERTION.<-

The primary purpose of coinage consists in the measurement and estimation of commercial things *a*. Coinage is indeed necessary <pb n="13"/> both outside and inside the territory of every well-constituted Republic, the mutual necessity of commerce so decreeing; for no Republic or region exists so rich in the abundance of all things that it does not need the help of another, since divine providence has so wonderfully and variously endowed the parts of this terrestrial globe that men might be drawn to friendship and concord, if not by nature, then at least by mutual need of things *b*. This need is addressed by the exchange of things, which is not easily managed without coinage—the most useful medium and instrument of human society—because the price of merchandise and things is variable and unequal *c*. The secondary purpose of coinage is visible in loans, usury—which are the fruits and returns of money *d*—leasing *e*, exchange, etc. *f*.

*a* By argument of law 1 of the Digest on contracting a purchase, and the text in law 42 of the Digest on sureties. *b* By argument of laws 3, 5, and 6 of the Digest on Justice and Law. Nicole Oresme on the origin and law of currencies, chapter 1. Bodin, Method of History, chapter 6. *c* *Indeed, public utility and safety in civil life, both in time of war and peace, could not sustain itself without the medium of coins, which assists the difficulty of exchanges by its own equivalency*, Antonius Faber in the treatise, chapter 1. Pinellus on the redetermined Code on rescinding a sale, part 1, chapter 1. Negelin, book on the Civil State, part 1, chapter 11. Tiraqueau on the lineage withdrawal, section 1, gloss 20, number 9. By argument of law 1, section 20, of the Digest on Questions; Novel 128, chapter 15; Novel 161. Guazzo on civil conversation, book 2, page 262. Bodin, book 6 of the Republic, chapter 2. *d* Law 2, section 1, of the Digest on credited things; law 34 on usury; law 38 of the Digest on usury; law 88, at the end, of the Digest on the Falcidian Law. Cujas, 9th observation, 15. Heigius, question 2, 1. *e* By argument of law 3, at the end, of the Digest on loans. *f* *For the use of coinage is both proper and improper (as Aristotle writes of the shoe in his Politics, that its proper use is in covering the foot, but its improper use is occupied in the exchange and sale of merchandise). The former estimates all things, while the latter performs the office of merchandise*, by argument of the final law of the Digest on the recovery of things given for a cause, etc.; law "with these," section "if to anyone," of the Digest on transaction. Antonius Faber in the Compendium of the treatise, conclusion 11. Hence Exchange <note>original: "Cambium"</note>, <term>der Wechsel</term> <gloss>the exchange</gloss>; on which Hieronymus Pistor, book 3, question, and Berandutius have more.

### EIGHTH ASSERTION.

It is not yet enough to have well-established coinage in the Republic; the care of increasing and preserving it also belongs to the political magistrate...
</translation>

<summary>These pages discuss the "character" or physical form of coinage as a mark of sovereign majesty and its practical function as a stable medium for trade. The author emphasizes that while coins have a proper use in valuation, they also serve secondary roles in loans, interest, and international exchange.</summary>

<keywords>coinage, majesty, valuation, commerce, usury, exchange, monetary ordinance, imperial eagle, public utility</keywords>

The primary purpose of coinage consists in the measurement and estimation of commercial things *a*. Coinage is indeed necessary
pages.13:
both outside and inside the territory of every well-constituted Republic, the mutual necessity of commerce so decreeing; for no Republic or region exists so rich in the abundance of all things that it does not need the help of another, since divine providence has so wonderfully and variously endowed the parts of this terrestrial globe that men might be drawn to friendship and concord, if not by nature, then at least by mutual need of things *b*. This need is addressed by the exchange of things, which is not easily managed without coinage—the most useful medium and instrument of human society—because the price of merchandise and things is variable and unequal *c*. The secondary purpose of coinage is visible in loans, usury—which are the fruits and returns of money *d*—leasing *e*, exchange, etc. *f*.

Pinellus on the redetermined Code on rescinding a sale, part 1, chapter 1. Negelin, book on the Civil State, part 1, chapter 11. Tiraqueau on the lineage withdrawal, section 1, gloss 20, number 9. By argument of law 1, section 20, of the Digest on Questions; Novel 128, chapter 15; Novel 161. Guazzo on civil conversation, book 2, page 262. Bodin, book 6 of the Republic, chapter 2. *d* Law 2, section 1, of the Digest on credited things; law 34 on usury; law 38 of the Digest on usury; law 88, at the end, of the Digest on the Falcidian Law. Cujas, 9th observation, 15. Heigius, question 2, 1. *e* By argument of law 3, at the end, of the Digest on loans. *f* *For the use of coinage is both proper and improper (as Aristotle writes of the shoe in his Politics, that its proper use is in covering the foot, but its improper use is occupied in the exchange and sale of merchandise). The former estimates all things, while the latter performs the office of merchandise*, by argument of the final law of the Digest on the recovery of things given for a cause, etc.; law "with these," section "if to anyone," of the Digest on transaction. Antonius Faber in the Compendium of the treatise, conclusion 11. Hence Exchange <note>original: "Cambium"</note>, <term>der Wechsel</term> <gloss>the exchange</gloss>; on which Hieronymus Pistor, book 3, question, and Berandutius have more.

It is not yet enough to have well-established coinage in the Republic; the care of increasing and preserving it also belongs to the political magistrate...

<pb n="52"/># Monday at Prime.

In the time of Lent, Antiphon: As I live, says the Lord, I do not wish the death of the sinner, but rather that he be converted and live.

In the time of the Passion, Antiphon: Deliver me, O Lord, and set me beside you, and let any man's hand fight against me.

In the Paschal time, Antiphon: Alleluia, alleluia, allel. allel.

In the weekday Office throughout the Year, Antiphon: Serve the Lord in fear and exult to him with trembling.

Chapter. 1 Timothy 1:17.
To the King of ages, immortal and invisible, the only God, be honor and glory, forever and ever, Amen.

R. Thanks be to God.

This Chapter is said on all Solemnities, and Feasts of Saints, and throughout Octaves <note>the eight-day period following a major feast</note>, and throughout the entire Paschal time.

For Weekdays only.
Chapter. Zechariah 8:19.
Love peace and truth, says the Lord almighty. R. Thanks be to God.

V. Arise, O Christ, help us.
R. And deliver us for the sake of your name.

Lord have mercy. Christ have mercy. Lord have mercy.

Our Father. <note>said</note> silently until V. And lead us not into temptation.
R. But deliver us from evil.

The following Prayers are not said on Double Feasts, nor within Octaves: but then after the Our Father is said, The Lord

<column-break/>

be with you. and the Prayer.
O Lord God almighty, as below.

But when the Prayers at Prime and Compline are said on bended knees, they are stated in the general Rubrics concerning Prayers and genuflection.

P R E Y E R S.
I believe in God, <note>said</note> silently until V. The resurrection of the body.
R. Life everlasting, Amen.

V. Our help is in the name of the Lord.
R. Who made heaven and earth.

Then the Hebdomadary <note>the choir member assigned for the week to lead the office</note> makes the Confession.

I confess to almighty God, to blessed Mary ever Virgin, to blessed Michael the Archangel, to blessed John the Baptist, to the holy Apostles Peter and Paul, to blessed Benedict, and to all the Saints, and to you brothers: that I have sinned exceedingly in thought, word and deed: through my fault, through my fault, through my most grievous fault. Therefore I beseech blessed Mary ever Virgin, blessed Michael the Archangel, blessed John the Baptist, the holy Apostles Peter and Paul, blessed Benedict, all the Saints, and you brothers, to pray for me to the Lord our God.

The Choir responds.
May almighty God have mercy on you, and, having forgiven <pb n="53"/> your sins, lead you to everlasting life. Amen.
Then the Confession is repeated, and where it is said, "to you brothers," and "you brothers," it is said "to you father," and "you father."
The Confession having been made by the Choir, the Hebdomadary says:
May almighty God have mercy on you, and, having forgiven your sins, lead you to everlasting life.
R. Amen.
May the almighty and merciful Lord grant us indulgence, absolution, and remission of our sins.
R. Amen.
And he continues V. Vouchsafe, O Lord, on this day.
R. To keep us without sin. V. O Lord, hear my prayer. R. And let my cry come unto you.
V. The Lord be with you.
R. And with your spirit.
Let us pray. Prayer.
O Lord God almighty, who has brought us to the beginning of this day: save us today by your power; that on this day we may turn aside to no sin; but may our words always proceed, and our thoughts and works be directed, to doing your justice. Through our Lord etc. R. Amen.
V. The Lord be with you.
R. And with your spirit.

<column-break/>

V. Let us bless the Lord.
R. Thanks be to God.
This being said, Prime of the Blessed Mary is said, if it is to be said.
Then in Choir the Martyrology is read immediately.
Afterwards the Hebdomadary says V. Precious in the sight of the Lord.
R. Is the death of his Saints.
And absolutely without "Let us pray."
Prayer.
May holy Mary and all the Saints intercede for us to the Lord, that we may be worthy to be helped and saved by him, who lives and reigns forever and ever.
R. Amen.
V. O God, come to my assistance. R. O Lord, make haste to help me.
And it is said three times: at the last is added Glory be to the Father.
As it was in the beginning.
Lord have mercy. Christ have mercy. Lord have mercy.
Our Father. <note>said</note> silently. V. And lead us not into temptation.
R. But deliver us from evil. V. Look upon your servants, O Lord, and upon your works, and direct their children.
R. And let the brightness of the Lord our God be upon us, and direct the works of our hands upon us, and direct the work of our hands.
Glory be to the Father. As it was in the beginning.
Let us pray.</translation>

<summary>This portion of the Monastic Breviary details the order of Prime for Monday, including seasonal antiphons, the Chapter, and the communal Confiteor. It provides instructions for the Hebdomadary and Choir, concluding with the ritual prayers following the Martyrology.</summary>
<keywords>Prime, Monastic Breviary, Order of Saint Benedict, Confiteor, Hebdomadary, Liturgy of the Hours, Latin Rite, 18th century</keywords>

<pb n="10"/><meta>continues from previous page</meta>He lifts the swellings of the marble sea, and prevents the sails committed to the blind whirlwind from being submerged by fierce <term>Nereus</term> <gloss>a sea god, here representing the sea itself</gloss>. Nor does he allow the sails, driven by swift course, to fall into <term>Charybdis</term> <gloss>a dangerous whirlpool in mythology</gloss> among the jagged rocks of the salt sea. This faithful pilot will break the power of <term>Nereus</term> and will direct the tossed skiff with a steady hand, until a life, blessed and eternal, feels the anchor and the breath of <term>Favonius</term> <gloss>the gentle West Wind</gloss> favors it, joined with the constant labor of the <term>Aeolids</term> <gloss>descendants of Aeolus, ruler of the winds</gloss>. For just as he, an exile in foreign lands, used to fill those eager for the healthy food of the Word with his divine voice and previously proved it with sounds, he declared that he would never be inclined toward Christians who are heavily pressed by the yoke of troublesome anxiety, and that the company of the pious, while laboring, would never be destitute of help. Whenever they raise their arms and right hands, entwined toward him with dark countenances, and call out at the same time with a uniform <pb n="11"/>divine power from his inward breast and mouth. Nor do they cease to offer prayers and vows incessantly, always proceeding from the temple of the heart. O faithful leader through the sea, through the inhospitable way, through the ridges of the terrestrial <term>Caucasus</term> <gloss>a mountain range representing a difficult barrier</gloss>, and on the marine path that must not be approached by anyone without you! O unique end of our entire journey! To be held fast by a threefold-double <note>sixfold</note> hand! O rest from labors! Harbor and breeze away from troubles! Whoever, thirsting for salvation, wishes soon to be brought into the sacred assemblies of the pious, will follow **Christ** as leader with swift chariots for all time. And he will take care to carry out the commands hidden in the whole of his breast and with all the strength of his mind kept safe, and will cherish them from this time on with unremitting zeal. He will decorate his life with a crown and with the flourishing flower of those teaching morals, a life undertaken in quiet peace and easy, without a cloud of disaster.
</translation>

It emphasizes the necessity of following Christ to find spiritual rest and the ultimate reward of a peaceful, virtuous life.</summary>

<keywords>Jesus Christ, navigation metaphor, Nereus, Charybdis, Favonius, Caucasus, salvation, divine protection, piety, spiritual journey</keywords>

<pb n="11"/><meta>continues from previous page: ...our</meta> imagination alone must picture the individual acts of the drama that played out in the souls of the masses as they wavered back and forth between <term>Ormuzd</term> <gloss>Ahura Mazda, the supreme Zoroastrian deity</gloss> and the Trinity. We know only the result of the struggle: Mithraism was defeated, and undoubtedly it had to be. However, its defeat is not to be attributed exclusively to the superiority of evangelical morality or apostolic preaching over the doctrine of the mysteries; it perished not merely because it was weighed down by the inherited burden of an outlived past, but also because its liturgy and its theology had remained too Asiatic for the Roman spirit to accept without resistance. Conversely, that same struggle, which had flared up at the same time in Iran between the two rivals, remained without success for the Christians, if not without honor, and in the states of the <term>Sassanids</term> <gloss>the last pre-Islamic Persian empire</gloss>, Zoroastrianism never allowed itself to be seriously challenged.

But the defeat of <term>Mithras</term> did not mean the end of his power. He had prepared minds for the reception of a new faith which, like himself, came from the banks of the Euphrates and reopened hostilities with altered tactics. <term>Manichaeism</term> <gloss>a major dualistic religion founded by the prophet Mani</gloss> appeared as his heir and continued his work. It was the last assault that Persia undertook against the Occident, and it was bloodier than the others, but it too was ultimately to fail against the resilience of the Christian empire.

This fleeting sketch will, I hope, reveal the importance of the history of Mithraism. A lateral shoot of the old Mazdean stem, it has in many respects preserved the peculiarities of the ancient nature religion of the Iranian tribes and allows us, by comparison, to better understand the much-debated significance of the <term>Avestan</term> <gloss>relating to the Avesta, the primary collection of Zoroastrian sacred texts</gloss> reformation. On the other hand, it helped to define, if not inspire, certain doctrines of the Church, <pb n="12"/>such as the conceptions of hellish powers and the end of the world. Thus, its rise as well as its fall contributes to illuminating the history of the origins of two great religions. In the time of its full strength, it exercised a no less remarkable influence on Roman society and the Roman government. Perhaps Europe was never closer to becoming Asiatic, even in the epoch of the Muhammadan invasions, than in the 3rd century of our era; and there was a time in which <term>Caesarism</term> <gloss>autocratic imperial rule</gloss> apparently stood on the verge of transforming into a Caliphate. Point has often been made of the similarity existing between the court of Diocletian and that of the <term>Chosroes</term> <gloss>the title of Sassanid Persian kings</gloss>. The sun cult and specifically the Mazdean theories popularized the ideas upon which the deified rulers sought to found their monarchical absolutism. The rapid spread of the Persian mysteries among all classes of the population served the political ambitions of the emperors in an admirable way. A tidal wave of Iranian and Semitic thoughts broke in, swallowing almost everything that the Greek or Roman spirit had built up through laborious work; and when the flood finally receded, it left behind a strong sediment of Oriental conceptions in the popular consciousness that never completely disappeared.

I believe I have sufficiently shown to what extent the subject I have attempted to treat deserved a more detailed investigation. Although the study of it has led me much further in every respect than I was initially able to foresee, I do not regret the years of work and travel that I had to devote to it. That the task I had to solve was a difficult one became apparent soon enough. <pb n="226"/>the method for it, which is more difficult than all others. This is what flashes in the <term>Elixir</term> <gloss>the transformative agent</gloss>, because here concerning the <term>tincture</term> <gloss>dye or transformative power</gloss> it begins from potential, that is, from the potential matter most fit for such a form, and it arrives at the act, that is, the form of gold and silver, for which it was in potential. For into such a species of metal is the moisture congealed, of which there is smoke and vapor: because like is not generated except from its like by nature. Then the author rails against the vain workers of this art, who have neither the root nor at least the preparation, saying: Every preparation of that thing is good, except this hidden preparation of the Philosophers. But they themselves have established the prohibition of it in its actual practice, because they are always preparing, and never prospering. Because as <note>the legendary alchemist</note> Morienes says to the king: Know that earth, or stone, or egg, or blood, or vinegar, or all such things as sulfur, quicksilver <note>original: "arg.viuum"</note>, orpiment <note>arsenic trisulfide</note>, are false, useless for this <term>magisterium</term> <gloss>mastery or Great Work</gloss>, and have a bad end; and men often grind and cook all these, and extract from their decoction, and bury the extract, and according to their own opinion believe they are doing well. And so that their error might be more confirmed, and lest they despair of <pb n="227"/>that which they seek, they are unable to find it, but they hope to find it. And concerning the composition of false books, Senior says: For he composed his book, thinking that he understood that hidden mystery, and he himself neither knows nor understands one letter of those things which he composed in the book, being far removed from the books of the Philosophers. And if he is questioned about them, he responds through metaphors, and if they are proven against him, he defends himself through quibbles and vain metaphors. It follows: In the firm thing, that is, in the firm root of the art, their preparation is made unknown, because they do not have the being, and even if they have the root, they do not have its preparation, and because of this they do not know it. Every mind following its own desire, that is, its own vain opinion, flows, that is, fluctuates and wanders through various erroneous ways, so that at last they say: We have prepared it with every preparation, and we have not obtained it, and we have made it with science, and we have operated wisely with its preparations. These things which we have said concerning these causes are not to be taken simply and absolutely, but with respect held for their subjects upon which they act—that is, the bodies—among which two certain requirements are needed (as <term>Galen</term> teaches in *On the Causes of Diseases*, chapter 2), namely: time, magnitude, proximity, and the preparation of the body.

### 88.

Having explained the causes, we proceed to the *differences* <gloss>distinctions/classifications</gloss> of Melancholy, some of which are taken from the subject in which they are generated. Thus, one is *Essential and Primary*, which surely occurs by a fault of the head itself; another is by *Consensus* <gloss>sympathy/agreement</gloss> or *Accidental*, if it is caused from elsewhere. This latter is divided into *Universal and Particular*. It is called *Universal* when it is caused by the whole; *Particular* is that which is specifically called *Hypochondriacal*.

### 89.

By reason of magnitude, one kind is *Strong and Vehement*; another is *Strongest and Most Vehement*, in which all melancholic symptoms appear most powerfully; another is *Mild*, in which the symptoms are not seen with such force; and another is *Most Mild*.

### 90.

On account of the duration of time, one is *Recent*, which namely has not yet afflicted for long, but began quite recently; another is *Inveterate*, which has lasted through a long space of time and has driven deep roots.

### 91.

On account of the continuity of time, one is *Intermittent*, which namely has periods of worsening by turns; another is *Continual*, which lasts continuously.

<pb n="13"/><meta>continues from previous page: is in heaven</meta> personally, while on earth he stands naturally, where neither presence hinders or removes the other.

For a local presence does not destroy a personal one, nor does a personal presence destroy a local one. For the one, namely the natural presence, comes to the human nature from the property of its own essence, which since it is and remains finite, was circumscribed in only one place during the <term>status exinanitionis</term> <gloss>state of humiliation/emptying</gloss>. The other presence, however, comes to the flesh of Christ from the personal union, insofar as the humanity of Christ has been exalted and assumed into the unity of the infinite person of the Son of God, above and beyond all creatures. Since, therefore, both are understood according to different modes, they can easily exist together. For it is necessary to confess that the human flesh of Christ exists in a terrestrial place with Nicodemus by one reasoning, but in another way, and ineffably more closely and nearly, that same humanity is united to the <term>Logos</term> <gloss>Word/Divine Reason</gloss>. He is present to Nicodemus in a terrestrial place and through natural proximity, or physical contact. 

In the person of the <term>Logos</term>, however, it would be both impious and absurd to say that the human nature of Christ subsists in such a physical or local manner. Since the union is not physical, nor local, but personal, it is exempt from all laws of nature and the conditions of this world, so that no creature can intervene that is able to tear apart the natures personally united in Christ.

Nor indeed does the Apostle Paul fight against these things just mentioned, who writes that Christ according to his humanity now after his ascension into the heavens fills all things. For the Article of the personal union confirms for us <pb n="14"/> that the <term>Logos</term>, even in the state of humiliation, was incarnate wherever he was: that is, he had the human nature inseparably united to himself. The Article of the Sitting at the Right Hand <note>original: "sessio ad dextram", referring to Christ's position of power in heaven</note> confirms for us that the <term>Logos</term> not only has his flesh present to himself everywhere, but through that same flesh he now powerfully and presently administers all things in heaven and on earth. And as was said above, Christ has it from the personal union that he is omnipotent, but from the sitting at the right hand he has it that he declares that majesty everywhere and reigns, having been appointed Lord everywhere over all the works of the hands of God; which majesty of governing all things omnipresently, the Apostle calls "to fill all things," implying not a bare presence but showing a full administration.

IV. Having explained the three previous members of our proposition, we now approach the fourth, by which it is affirmed that no one ascends into the heavens except the Son of Man, which indeed might seem no less a paradox to anyone than the earlier points. For Enoch and Elijah ascended into heaven, as did the other patriarchs, and furthermore all who believe in Christ, who are said to have wandered in the world under this name because they seek the future heavenly <margin>Philippians 3</margin> city, whose <term>politeuma</term> <gloss>citizenship/commonwealth</gloss> is in the heavens. How, therefore, is it said that no one except the Son of Man ascends into the heavens? The sense of the words of Christ, therefore, is that no man after the Fall is able to climb to heaven by his own merits or strengths or proper holiness. For heaven is closed by nature to all men because of sins. But to the Son of Man alone, who did not commit sin,

It is therefore sufficiently certain and manifest that the power of signifying this or that exists in words not by nature or from some intrinsic necessity, but from the mere will, convention, sense, judgment, and institution of men. To this is added such a great variety and inconstancy of words. *For otherwise, I ask you, give me a solid reason why different words should denote the same thing in different languages.* The same judgment applies to the marks and shapes of letters. <note>Compare Augustine, On Christian Doctrine, Book 2, Chapter 24.</note> *A single shape of a letter, which is marked crosswise <note>the letter X</note>, has one value among the Greeks and another among the Latins, not by nature, but by the pleasure and agreement of signifying; and therefore, he who knows both languages, if he wishes to signify something to a Greek man by writing, does not place this letter in that signification in which he places it when he writes to a Latin man. BETA is a letter with one and the same sound among the Greeks, but among the Latins it is the name of a vegetable <note>the beet</note>. And when I say 'lege' <gloss>read / gather</gloss>, in these two syllables a Greek understands one thing and a Latin another.* You say: *It is the mark of a wise man to impose names on things.* True, but is there not a twofold kind of names? Some are primitive, for which no reason can be provided; others are derived from them, which ought to be aptly formed and imposed by wise men based on those already established. We also admit that there are not a few words, and many things (though this is difficult to prove for all), which have a certain aptitude from their own nature to designate the character or principal affection of certain things; nevertheless, those very primitives from which they are deflected import the thing from mere institution.

Indeed, it is not my intention to dwell for a long time on general matters; but for the present, we direct our cares toward demonstrating how that which is just and lawful concerning speech <pb n="10"/> <note>Two decorative asterisks flank the page number at the top of the page.</note> ought to be used rightly and well for its purpose in joining human society or public life. The words of <term>Tullius</term> <gloss>Cicero</gloss> are worthy of note in Book 1 of *On Duties*: *The bond of society is reason and speech, which, by teaching, learning, communicating, debating, and judging, conciliates men among themselves and joins them in a certain natural society.*

Although indeed speech, the interpretation of the mind, and also voices and other types of signs, are employed to promote the common utility as was agreed upon and received by use: nevertheless, we are by no means bound by that very fact, always and in all cases, to express most exactly in words to another either our innermost feelings of mind, or concepts, or particular business. It would indeed be most desirable, along with the aforementioned Tullius in Book 3 of *On Duties*: *Would that all simulation and dissimulation were removed from human life;* it is desirable that all men were of such a disposition and such character that no one would envy the goods of others, or lay snares, nor abuse the simplicity of others to intend fraud against them. But in truth, the arts of simulation and dissimulation can hardly, or not at all, be removed from human society until all the malice or folly of men has been changed into probity, virtue, and honesty. It is therefore permitted sometimes to prudently keep the truth silent. Whence also it is expressly read in <term>Ecclesiasticus</term> <gloss>The Book of Sirach</gloss>: *Do not manifest all your heart to every man.* Moreover, we can and ought to do this when no genuine cause is present which bids us answer another according to his mind, and the other has no right to know such things from me. Nay, rather, where the right of another is not violated, while on the contrary my safety or that of another cannot be procured or preserved in any other way. For thus it is permitted to say at the beginning what is true in one sense, although the other perhaps asks about another, and is about to receive an answer. But beware, lest you employ the arts of simulation and dissimulation further than for your own

<pb n="13"/>...only that can be held for a lawful cause of killing a man which God approved in his law as just, either expressly or by evident consequence. However, that the proposed case is excepted anywhere in the command of not killing, it is scarce possible to prove with a suitable argument.

### Thesis XV.

Next, they violated the negative precepts of the Law of Nature: *Harm no one*, and *Evil things are not to be done so that good may come*. And since these precepts, like all negative precepts of the Law of Nature, prohibit what is simply dishonest, it is manifest enough that no necessity can be found which could place Dishonesty in the category of permitted things, or for the sake of which it is ever or anywhere lawful to do Dishonest things.

### Thesis XVI.

Furthermore, this case seems to participate more in the voluntary to the degree that the prior deliberation concerning the means of obtaining food is out in the open, as is the subsequent choice to cast lots, so that from the seven they might set apart one upon whose flesh the remaining might feed.

### Thesis XVII.

Next, the life of a neighbor is not subject to the judgment of anyone except Him who is the author and Lord of life, and to whom He has given an express command for killing. Excepting these, if anyone else takes away the life of another, he sins gravely; for he deprives God of a chief creature, founded by Him in His own image; he deprives the Republic of a citizen; he deprives a family of either its head or a member; and he deprives the one killed of the greatest benefit which he holds from the Divinity—and which he can never restore to him.

### Thesis XVIII.

Furthermore, it is established that they vented their rage against the life of their companion for the purpose of benefiting themselves and their stomachs. If, therefore, no one ought to be made wealthier through the injury of another, how can it be lawful to obtain advantages for ourselves from the disadvantages, injury, and death of others <pb n="14"/>? If the license to use the goods of another is not granted to someone—even though restitution for them can be made—if the possessor himself is held by an equal necessity; what right, then, will a hungry man have over the life and flesh of a starving man? Correcty does Cicero say in *Book 3 of On Duties*: "Would not a wise man," he asks, "if he were being consumed by hunger itself, take away food from another man who is useful for nothing? Not at all. For my own life is not more useful to me than such an affection of the mind: that I should violate no one for the sake of my own advantage."

### Thesis XIX.

Nor does it stand against this that the Most Serene Prince <note>original: "S.P." for Serenissimus Princeps</note>, against Ziegler, denies that the remaining men exercised cruelty against their companion, since he who died received the iron blade in his throat for the safety of all with less pain than if another had inflicted it. Answer: Is it not cruelty if those who are the parents of their own life slaughter their neighbor—whom they are commanded to love not above themselves, nor below themselves, but as themselves—contrary to nature, so that their own life might be preserved?

### Thesis XX.

Nor does it stand against this that the Most Serene Prince denies that danger to the soul was to be feared for the one killed. Answer: It was to be feared for him as a <term>αὐτόχειρ</term> <gloss>self-killer/suicide</gloss>. For the one killed had previously consented to his own death, and afterwards offered it of his own accord, even though he had received his life from the Supreme Lord not for the purpose of destroying it, nor for the purpose of filling the hunger of another, but for the purpose of preserving it.

### Thesis XXI.

Nor does it stand against this that the greatest necessity demanded this. Let him who says this hear the response of Aristotle in the *Ethics, Book 3, Chapter 1*: There are some things of such a kind that perhaps we ought to be driven to do them by no force or necessity, but rather death is to be sought by us, and the most heavy tortures must be endured.

<margin>
QUESTION III.
</margin>

### Thesis XXII.

It is also asked, *whether pardon from the ordinary penalty for homicide was rightly given to the Britons?* which, along with Master Röhrenseen, we deservedly affirm.
</translation>

<summary>The author argues that killing a companion for food, even by lot or consent, violates natural and divine law. He concludes that while the act was a grave sin, the legal pardon granted to the surviving British sailors was justified.</summary>

<keywords>cannibalism, necessity, natural law, Cicero, Aristotle, homicide, shipwreck, ethics, divine law, self-preservation</keywords>

Next is the diet, which often achieves more than all other things; it consists in the legitimate use and application of the six non-natural things <note>the six factors essential to health in Galenic medicine: air, food/drink, sleep/wake, motion/rest, excretion/retention, and passions of the soul</note>, in suitable quantity and quality, and finally at the opportune time and order.

XLVIII. Therefore, let a temperate and bright air be chosen; if such is not available by nature, it must be prepared by art, which is done by sprinkling herbs and flowers of a warming and moistening nature, such as borage, bugloss, violets, and others. LII. From the passions of the mind, all cares and anxieties and sorrows must be removed; instead, their minds should be called back

<pb n="13"/>Rhosny, enough to buy the greatest kingdom <note>original: "quantum regno maximo emendo satis sit"</note> <margin>Warem. on royal subsidies chapter 6, number 19, page 93.</margin>. Someone has deservedly greeted such men as **Practical Empire-Makers** <note>original: "Practiken-Reichmacher"</note>. Therefore, the Prince must be warned not to believe them rashly when they say: he ought to return his subjects thoroughly combed <note>original: "depexos"</note>, so that they may submit their spirits; nor should they, relying on riches, long for revolution. Likewise, that his own business is being handled: nor have they any reason to complain if enough is left to them that they may barely drag along their wretched soul; that willows are pruned every three years so that they may strive upward more strongly. Furthermore, they say a cause should be feigned if another is lacking; that this is permitted. Finally, that all the goods of the subjects belong to the Prince, and they have nothing except by grace and from his pleasure. And that this is the right of the king proven in holy scripture, 1 Samuel 8, verse 11 and following. But who would believe these things to be true, when they are clearly lies? Poverty often does not so much break as uplift spirits: and writers of history teach that the worst crimes are often begun by the very poor. Even Catiline, himself surrounded by every necessity, is said to have joined to himself men <note>original: "quibus maxima necessitudo, & plurimum audaciae, malaque abundè omnia fuerint"</note> who had the greatest need and the most audacity, and all evils in abundance: but neither wealth nor any good hope. <margin>Sallust, Catiline, page 37; more in Clapmarius, book 2, chapter 23, page 112; Scipio Ammirato, discourse 6 on Tacitus, book 17, page 550; Forstner on Tacitus, page 303.</margin> If indeed things are taken from the subjects down to the very dust <note>original: "cum pulvisculo"</note>, who will wonder afterward that there is nothing left for you to take again? A gardener cutting out herbs from the root will expect fruit in vain. Not everything belongs to the subjects of the Prince, although in a sense everything does. They are his by reason of protection, jurisdiction, and administration; they are not his by reason of ownership: these rights are assigned to individual masters. <margin>Arnisaeus on the rights of Majesty, book 3, chapter 1, number 4, page 448; Seneca on Benefits, book 7, chapter 3, page 173.</margin> As for what is found in Samuel regarding the right of the king; to one looking correctly, it is entirely apparent that it is not to be understood as true and genuine right (concerning which see Deuteronomy 17), but as usurped right. <margin>Wilhelm Zepperus in Explanation of Mosaic Law, book 3, chapter 8, page 215; Carpzov in Royal Law, chapter 1, section 5, number 14, page 26; Adam Contzen, book 6, chapter 2, paragraph 9, page 336; Compare Gerhard, volume 6, Theological Commonplaces on Political Magistracy, number 125, page 760 and following.</margin> Nor is it concerning a bare fact, but one which has some legal effect, that is, an obligation of non-resistance. <margin>Hugo Grotius on the Law of War and Peace, book 1, chapter 4, number 3, page 90.</margin> The matter therefore returns to this, that it can be said: I have never seen better advice given: but something else <pb n="14"/>is what drives these men off course, namely the sweet smell of profit, which these eloquent men—or should I say "talkative" men—scent out; they increase their own wealth in the Prince's name, and if you pay closer attention, you will see that those who especially urge these things are those who hope that either the Treasurership or large portions of the spoils will fall to them from it. Therefore, public misfortune feeds these men: and quiet affairs set in motion are a profit to them: just as for fishermen, for whom an eel is not prey unless the water is troubled. <margin>Faust von Aschaffenburg on the Treasury, Consultation 64, Order 657, page 312.</margin>

Such things, however, are especially presumed by foreigners, whom the Prince is accustomed to prefer over natives; but he does so badly. Indeed, their minds cannot help but be alienated toward a foreign Republic in which they always think: *For me here, there is neither sowing nor reaping.* <margin>Lipsius in notes to book 3 of Politics, chapter 6, page 574.</margin> Regarding natives, however, we believe they would not dare such things, out of memory of the land that bore and nourished them: although experience cries out that even this does not always hold true. The Prince should flee these men as if from a reef <margin>Bodin on the Republic, book 6, chapter 2, page 1037.</margin> and keep them away, for they are the true reefs to his safety. For if the subjects feel themselves exposed as prey to these few greedy courtiers, will they not denounce his rule as unjust? Will not the common people, having found a leader, seize these men to be torn apart? Will they not approach him with arms? In the year 1316, the commoners of France were moved to action during the reign of Philip V, because he, prevailing more by physical strength than by virtue of mind, through laziness kept advisors too liberally: for those insolent men were exercising domination. <margin>Serres in Philip V, History of the Kings of France.</margin>

These counsels, since they are uncertain in themselves and not without danger, are the worst for the counselor. <margin>Drexel in Phaethon, letter C, chapter 8, paragraph 1, page 188.</margin> Also in other cases, if you have advised anything well, it is considered done under the Prince’s auspices: but all adverse things, and those which turn out unsuccessfully, are imputed to the counselor. Alva had written to the King of Spain from Belgium that he had found a most fertile vein of gold, meaning the tithes <note>original: "decimas"</note>: because of this, and because he had invaded the province with an army brought in with fire and sword (whence the greatest disturbances arose), he became hateful to the king and never afterward softened his mind. Even the statue which he had placed for himself at Antwerp was pulled down. <margin>Meteren, part 1, book 3, at the year 1571, page 134.</margin> where a little before it is seen engraved in bronze. <margin>Compare Pierre Matthieu, History of France, book 1, narrative 4, number 6.</margin> After that man died, the king went out in public showing no grief of mind. This was different from the greater <note>original: "majocum"</note>...
</translation>

<summary>This page warns Princes against greedy advisors who propose heavy taxation and the seizure of private property under the guise of royal right. It highlights the dangers of such advice, noting that extreme poverty often leads to rebellion rather than submission.</summary>
<keywords>taxation, property rights, 1 Samuel 8, advisors, rebellion, Duke of Alva, Philip V of France, political stability, corruption</keywords>

### LXXX.

For when a promisor simply promises that he will pay what either he himself or another owes, it is manifest that he is obligated without the solemnity of words, nor can he elude judgment through the exception of a faulty stipulation; a simple agreement is sufficient for the plaintiff, which rests upon a preceding obligation and is clothed by this benefit of the Praetor.

### LXXXI.

From which the diversity of this action from that of suretyship clearly shines forth, since a surety is obligated by a formal stipulation and cannot be sued without it, as is the more accepted opinion of the <term>Doctors</term> <gloss>legal scholars</gloss> through the law *blanditus*, <term>Codex</term>, title *de fideiussoribus*, and the law *stipulationum aliae*, paragraph *satis acceptio*, <term>Digest</term>, title *de verborum obligationibus*, along with similar passages.

### LXXXII.

Furthermore, a constitution <note>a formal promise to pay an existing debt</note> is preferable to a novation <note>the replacement of an old contract with a new one</note>, because the former does not abolish the prior obligation, as the latter does; and when one person promises on behalf of another, both are obligated, which does not occur in a novation, since it does not change the person <note>the original debtor is usually released in novation</note>.

### LXXXIII.

Moreover, the bare pact of the Ecclesiastics <note>referring to Canon Law</note> from the first chapter *extra de pactis* does not diminish the utility of this action, because that is not received into the civil forum by the more accepted calculation, and the denunciations of the canons are in many places today disregarded; but where an account of them is still held, there this civil action concurs with the said pact and surpasses its companion in its place and manner of being proposed.

### LXXXIIII.

Just as the prior obligation can be weaker for many reasons than that which arises from a constitution, because the latter adds something of benefit to the former, either by reason of place, time, or some other quality and circumstance. And even if at times nothing more is in the constitution than in the preceding obligation, nevertheless in that case its own utility is established for it: that it may be expedient for the plaintiff to hold the defendant liable to several actions, and to be able to choose which of them he wishes.

### LXXXV.

And although mention is made only of money in the formula, nevertheless that designation now pertains to all things, both movable and immovable—transferred here from the <term>receptitia</term> <gloss>an older, abolished form of promise</gloss> which is now antiquated—not only to those <pb n="18"/> things which receive their function in their own kind, to which antiquity had narrowed it in law 2, <term>Codex</term>, title *de constituta pecunia*.

### LXXXVI.

Following the action concerning promised money in Justinian is the action concerning the <term>peculium</term> <gloss>private property or savings held by a subordinate</gloss>, which the Praetor introduced moved by natural equity, lest those who contract with slaves or sons under their father's power, to whom masters or fathers permit to trade in private matters, be utterly mocked.

### LXXXVII.

Now, the name <term>peculium</term> is indeed derived from *pecunia* <gloss>money</gloss>, as if "tiny money," that is, a tiny patrimony, in the last paragraph of the <term>Digest</term>, in the same title. But sometimes it is also taken for any patrimony of any person, as in the law *cogit*, <term>Digest</term>, title *ad Trebellianum*. Occasionally also for money set aside for the sake of protection, whence it is customary to say: "money without a <term>peculium</term> is fragile," in the law *si chorus*, paragraph 1, <term>Digest</term>, title *de legatis 3*. In this form of action, however, <term>peculium</term> is taken in that meaning which was placed by us in the first instance.

### LXXXVIII.

So that the <term>peculium</term> is that which a son under his father's power or a slave has as his own by permission of the father or master, separated from the accounts of the father or master, after deducting what is owed to the father or master, or to those who are in their power, tutelage, or care: law *peculium*, and the following law at the last paragraph, <term>Digest</term>, title *de peculio*.

### LXXXIX.

Not that we think it necessary for the master or father to always grant a <term>peculium</term> to those whom they have in their power, because in that way the son of a madman, or the slave of a ward or a madman, would not have a <term>peculium</term>; but because we think, with Julian, it is enough that persons of this kind do not take away the <term>peculium</term> from those to whom prior masters or fathers had previously granted it: law *quam Tuberonis*, <term>Digest</term>, title *de peculio*.

### LXXXX.

Although, however, we attribute a <term>peculium</term> to slaves as well as to sons under their father's power, it is not in the same way for both: since the <term>peculium</term> of slaves is uniform, while that of sons is fourfold, according to whether it proceeds from different causes—from the father or on his account from elsewhere, or simply from elsewhere, or from military industry or its equivalent.

### LXXXXI.

Neither, however, is this action accommodated to all these species, but only to that which comes from the father; because in the case of military property, or property like it, the son under his father's power
</translation>

<summary>This section discusses the legal actions "de constituta pecunia" (promised money) and "de peculio" (private property held by subordinates). It explores the advantages of formal promises over other legal obligations and defines how property managed by sons or slaves is treated under Roman civil law.</summary>
<keywords>Roman law, Justinian, Digest, Codex, peculium, constitution, debt, obligation, civil law, father and son, slavery</keywords>

Since therefore we are surrounded by such a great cloud of witnesses, why should we not apply faith to them, especially because these saints of ours clearly could not have risen to eternal life if Christ had not risen, since our resurrection depends uniquely and most closely upon the resurrection of Christ and its efficacy, as the Apostle prolixly teaches in 1 Corinthians 15, as will soon be mentioned.

§ 13. The second corollary concerns the universality of the future resurrection. Resurrection is distinguished: 1. into the singular, which is that of Christ, occurring on the third day, Matthew 16:21; 2. into the particular, of certain pious people, resuscitated by Christ in the individual years of his ministry and by the Apostles, regarding whom the Savior says in Matthew 11:5: The dead rise. Such a particular resurrection was also this one of our saints. 3. into the universal, on the last day, where not only the pious shall rise, but also the impious, according to the Scripture, Daniel 12:2: Many (that is, all, John 5:28) of those sleeping in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to eternal life, others to everlasting reproach. A distinction must nevertheless be made between resurrection and resurrection to glory. Only the latter, not the former, is denied to the impious. For the impious shall not rise, that is, they shall not triumph or stand in the judgment, Psalm 1:5. These things are argued against the Photinians <note>a sect following Photinus of Sirmium, who denied the pre-existence of Christ and certain aspects of the resurrection</note> and the Jews, who deny that the impious will rise.

§ 14. The third corollary is therefore regarding the diversity of the meritorious cause of the resurrection of the pious and the impious. The resurrection of the pious <pb n="10"/>is uniquely owed to the merit of Christ, John 6:39–40. In 1 Corinthians 15:20, Christ is called the firstfruits of those who sleep; having been raised from the dead, he brought this forth for us, so that a full harvest might follow this offering of firstfruits, that is, the universal resurrection of the pious. For the harvest is the consummation of the age, Matthew 13:39. Whence Tertullian calls the resurrection of Christ the example of our hope, the key of our sepulchers, and the pledge of our resurrection. And Augustine piously says:
> What preceded in the head, shall follow in the body.

§ 15. **The resurrection of the impious**, however, even when accepted generally for mere vivification, does not depend on the merit of Christ, but on his just judgment and omnipotence, insofar as he is the divinely constituted Judge of the living and the dead. John 5:27–28; Hebrews 9:27. For that unhappy resuscitation of the impious would have occurred even if Christ had never suffered nor been resuscitated, because divine justice would not be satisfied by the punishment and damnation of the soul alone, but of the body and soul together: Genesis 2:17. Because the whole man had sinned, hence the body also had to be resuscitated.

§ 16. But a passage of the Apostle in 1 Corinthians 15:22 can be raised against this opinion of ours:
> *Just as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive.*

Where some think that in this verse and the whole chapter the concern is with both the resurrection of the pious and the impious together, since this is proved by: 1. the sign of universality, "all"; 2. the Subject; 3. the aim of the Apostle.

§ 17. But it is more correctly established if it is said that this passage, with the entire chapter, deals only with the resurrection of the pious directly and immediately, and not also with the impious. For:
1. The sign "all" is restricted by the Apostle himself to a particularity, in verses 1, 3, 18, 19, and 20: the firstfruits of those who sleep.
</translation>

He asserts that while the pious rise through Christ's merit, the impious rise by His power as Judge to face bodily justice.</summary>

The deed of that Appius <note>Appius Claudius Caecus, the Roman statesman</note> who was blind, I hold in great praise (most excellent Fathers and Colleagues). Upon hearing that a matter of the weightiest concern was to be treated in the Senate <note>original: "Curia"</note>, he wished to be carried there, so that he might assist his endangered fatherland with his counsel. I would also imitate what I praise, did not health, old age, and the weakness of my voice prevent me. For my care for Venice is no less than was Appius's for Rome, nor have I been less engaged in my Republic than he in his. Sixty years have now passed since I sailed on an honored embassy to Asia and Egypt; admitted thereafter to the Senate not a few years ago, I endeavored to distinguish our youth with my diligence and zeal in delivering my opinions. What I have truly achieved, let the judgment rest with others; certainly, I soon sat in the Council of the <term>Pregadi</term> <gloss>the Venetian Senate</gloss>, and then in the Council of the Ten Sages <note>the Savi del Consiglio</note>, nor from that year onwards was it granted to me to be vacant from public business. I have traveled as an ambassador to Constantinople, England, Germany, France, and Spain, and even visited Belgium as a soldier. Nor did I pass by any celebrated man in Europe with whom I did not dispute; I have diligently turned over the ancient and modern writers on the Republic, so that what I could not attain through experience, I might learn further by reading. Since, however, several members of the most excellent College recently visited me and sought my opinion in the name of the Great Council regarding the wars we are now waging, I wished to dictate these few things to my secretary <note>original: "Amanuensi"</note>, so that as I die, I may leave a witness of my judgment to the most Serene Republic, my most beloved fatherland.

In the first place, I establish that the goal of our Republic is that which was once the goal of the Roman: to spare the subjected and to war down the proud; to acquire the empire of all Italy and (if the fates second our thoughts) of the entire world.

Secondly, to achieve this so noble an end, just as many and great protections are available to us, so also great difficulties and impediments are cast in our way, either by ourselves or by others. These must be overcome and removed by force and by art, for that greatness of soul stood at no small price either for the Romans or for any who wished to extend the borders of their empire and impose a yoke on their neighbors. Countless myriads of Roman citizens perished in war, and by their own strength gave birth to even greater wars for their descendants; until, carried to the height of power and the height of dangers, they fell most abruptly and served miserably. The Macedonian himself, whose homeland is neighbor to us, counts more wounds than limbs. What of the Ottomans? Do they not bring security to the empire for one through domestic blood and the deaths of brothers? The empire of human affairs, therefore, costs a great deal: the cause of which is that many wish to command, but few to obey, and because he who attempts to grow and dominate others does so to the detriment and insult of others; therefore, he is rendered suspected and hated by all, and he who is feared by many is forced to fear many. I advise this, therefore, lest in the shadow and savage <pb n="4"/> ferocity of our boats we aspire to the empire of the world.

Thirdly, our advantages must therefore be compared—wealth, arms, men, fleets—with those things that stand in the way: with the forces of the enemies, and not only those which are apparent, but also the arts and counsels by which, if we can be made superior, we may bravely wage the war we began in Styria, which we sparked in Savoy, and which we endure in the gulf and sea betrothed to us. Let us enrich the Republic by the addition of new strengths; if we are inferior, or if we must fight at the greatest risk to the Republic, let us make peace. We shall obtain a fair peace while the war has inclined to neither side; while we fear and are feared in turn, we shall find moderate treaties.

Fourthly, we must think seriously about the subsidies of war, and especially that the die of Mars is uncertain; for often he who has all the momentum for winning is cast down by a weakling; one betrayal, one voice, one stratagem often ruins everything. But nevertheless, let us now see our protections. The things, then, that can give us courage are cities, wealth, arms, men, allies, and confederates. When I consider our city, it is most fortified by nature; in riches and splendor and the frequency of trade, it surpasses all cities of the entire world, so that by a certain right of nature the empire of the earth seems to be owed to it. The Great Council, which is the basis of the Republic, has more than two thousand five hundred of the most noble Senators, mixed with no contagion of plebeian blood. We possess so much money, indeed, that to count the millions would be laborious and difficult. Looking at it, I am accustomed to exclaim:

> ->O how much could have been prepared of earth and sea<-
> ->With this gold, which we hide away anxious behind bars.<-

The ordinary revenue is twenty hundred thousand gold pieces when we act most lightly; if we are more attentive to the matter, we shall collect another such amount without grievance. If we adjudicate the tributes, we shall collect fourfold. I pass over the extraordinary revenues which Turks, Jews, and foreigners are forced to pay, which come from fines and from the trade of the most Serene Republic. If all these should fail, we can exact tithes, and double or triple them according to the ancestral custom. We can increase the tax on merchandise as much as we like. In the Genoese war, we ennobled three hundred of the wealthier citizens for accepted money; for if we lack money, let us select a thousand of the wealthiest and command them to be nobles, and grant them our privileges; believe me, at their own expense they will wage a whole year of war for us. For this is ancient law; if that levy be carried out in the ancient manner and with rustic simplicity, it will be a great help; if some craftiness intervenes, it will be the most excellent of all. For if it be arranged so that wealthy, delicate men who are averse to war are touched by the levy, they will redeem their exemption at any price. we hold armories full in all places; men also cannot be lacking. In Italy, we hold the most noble cities, Padua, Verona,

<pb n="12"/>how this sink of errors rightfully flows from the Stoic <term>ἀδιεξάτῳ</term> <gloss>inextricable</gloss> entanglement, I shall show in what follows.

The God of the Stoics is impotent, both as to his mode of existing and his mode of acting. The former is proved because he depends so much on the matter which he informs that he cannot exist outside of it for even a moment. The latter shines by its own light, since nothing can be accomplished by him which matter refuses.

Chrysippus is my witness <margin>1) in Gellius, book 6, chapter 1.</margin>: *When the author of nature,* he says, *was begetting and bringing forth many great things, most fit and useful, other things also were born at the same time, inconvenient to those very things he was making and cohering with them: and these were made not through nature, but through certain consequences.* I ask, by whose consequences, if not those of matter? Behold a Chrysippean God so weak that he could not even fashion a human being free from diseases, however much he might have wished. Matter has cast a halter upon him. Go now, you miserable Stoic, and lift your hands to heaven so that your Jupiter, by whom you are afflicted, may drive away the disease from you: what response will you bring back except this? "I cannot do otherwise for you than what is being done." What need is there, finally, for a tethered God of this kind, who cannot consult for himself in the workshops of his own matter, much less for another established in dangers?

§. II.

In vain do the Stoics busy themselves by rolling all depravity back onto matter to free their Jupiter: certainly, while they strive to avoid Charybdis, they throw themselves headlong into Scylla. If all evil owes its birth to matter, why does God take punishment for the <term>ἀνόμοις</term> <gloss>lawless</gloss> actions of men? He is therefore second to none of the tyrants in injustice, because he carries off the innocent to the sharpest punishments. Guided by sound reason, we absolve him from fault who cannot act otherwise than as he does. To me, the Jupiter of the Stoics seems like a man driving a dog with clubs or spurs because it does not turn its upright face to the stars, even though nature fashioned it prone and looking at the earth: just as such an insane flagellator would incur the censure, if not of an unjust man, then at least of a fool; so the same sentence will remain for the Stoic Jupiter, who afflicts, presses, and indeed overwhelms a creature as noble as man with thousands of marching <pb n="13"/> torments. O worst of all four-footed beasts, this <term>Deastrum</term> <gloss>petty god</gloss> which you fashion for yourself, **Chrysippus**, by your fate!

### §. III.

Again in another form, and one no less monstrous, the **Jupiter of the Stoics** comes forth: namely, in the habit of a slave <margin>m) book 1.</margin>. For those things which happen, happen so for **Chrysippus** that not even God can effect that they happen less. Hence **Herodotus** m) says: <term>τὴν πεπρωμένην μοῖραν ἀδύνατόν ἐστιν ἀποφυγεῖν καὶ Θεῷ</term> <gloss>it is impossible even for God to escape the destined lot</gloss>. **Seneca** confesses the same things, a son of the Stoa so little degenerate that rather it could be said of him what was once said of **Chrysippus**:

->If Chrysippus were not, the Porch <note>the Stoic school</note> would not be:<-

<margin>n) Natural Questions, near the end.</margin>
*Whether in many things the materials to be handled fail him, and many things are formed wickedly by the great craftsman, not because his art ceases, but because that in which it is exercised is unyielding to art* n). This unyielding matter has cast its shackles so tightly upon God that his power cannot run out even a hair's breadth wider than the bonds of fate allow. Therefore we conclude, the Stoic petty god is a true slave, over whom necessity has its dominion, exactly as **Philemon** says:

> Slaves are of kings, kings are of Gods,
> God is of necessity.

### §. IV.

The **God of the Stoics** himself betrays his own ignorance: for thus he speaks in the great council of the Gods in **Virgil**, who was most addicted to the Stoic sect:

> *Since it is not permitted for the Ausonians to be joined in treaty with the Teucrians, nor does your discord find an end: whatever fortune each has today, whatever hope each carves out, whether he be Trojan or Rutulian, I shall hold them with no distinction: whether the camp is held in siege by the fates of the Italians, or by a wicked error and the sinister warnings of Troy.*

These words, says the Excellent **Fellerus** o) <margin>o) p. 500.</margin> — a truly most keen-scented nose <note>meaning a person of sharp discernment</note> in the book of much reading and varied erudition which he inscribed with the title **Philosophical Flower** — show Jupiter not only impotent but also ignorant,
</translation>

<summary>Loscanus argues that the Stoic conception of God is logically flawed because it subordinates the divine to the constraints of matter and fate. He characterizes the Stoic Jupiter as an impotent, unjust, and enslaved figure who lacks true sovereignty over the physical world and human suffering.</summary>

<keywords>Stoicism, Chrysippus, Jupiter, Fate, Matter, Necessity, Theodicy, Seneca, Virgil, Divine Impotence</keywords>

# Apollo sings a congratulatory song to the Lion exalted among the stars,
### and recorded into the number of the Gods.

<note>An ornate woodcut initial letter M decorated with scrolling foliage and floral motifs.</note>

Though I am unworthy, your Virtue has drawn me to the heavens, your irradiating sight with trembling majesty: the flaming apex of fire, the heat of celestial sharpness; that impulse of yours, force both bestowed and innate; and the hidden vigor, filled with a wondrous magnet, that Genius of yours, yours, O that Spirit of **JEHOVAH** which is yours, and diffused thoroughly through your limbs; that latent and all-powerful four-lettered Virtue <note>Refers to the Tetragrammaton, the four-letter Hebrew name of God</note>, by which you penetrate the clouds, you penetrate the adamantine firmaments of Heaven and the two poles; having cast these aside with your claw, you penetrate that inaccessible chamber of the Gods; seeing wonders, marveling at secrets, searching out the Great Works <note>term: Magnalia</note> which are in the fates, hidden in the heart of the Gods above. I repeat that I am unworthy, and distant from you by as many windings as the Earth is distant by steps from the ether; I, even yet rude iron, a useless weight of the earth: nevertheless, that magnetic ardor of yours <pb n="10"/>along with a heavy mind <note>Nature of the Gods was astounded</note> and a body which is truly not impenetrable to the touch; it seized me like a wind toward the heights of the Celestial Colossus. <pb n="277"/>When Pythagoras had begun to write on nature, he spoke thus in the beginning: "No, by the air I breathe, no, by the water I drink, I shall not allow any censure of this discourse." Pythagoras wrote three volumes: On Education, On Statesmanship, and On Nature. However, the work read under the name of Pythagoras actually belongs to Lysis of Tarentum, a Pythagorean who, having fled to Thebes, became the teacher of Epaminondas. Heraclides, the son of Serapion, reports in his Epitome of Sotion that he also wrote a work in verse, On the Universe. Likewise, a second work titled Sacred Discourse, the beginning of which is:

> *O youths, honor these holy rites with silent quietude.*

A third, On the Soul; a fourth, On Piety; a fifth, Helothales, the father of the comic poet Epicharmus; a sixth, Croton, and others besides. Furthermore, they say the Mystic Discourse was the work of Hippasus, written to spite Pythagoras; likewise, many things written by Aston of Croton were inscribed with the name of Pythagoras. Aristoxenus says Pythagoras received many of his moral doctrines from his sister Themistoclea. Ion of Chios, however, says in his Triaginis that Pythagoras, when he had written a certain poem, attached the name of Orpheus to it. They say the Scopiads also belong to him, the beginning of which work is: "Be a king in need of no one." Sosicrates, in his Successions, says that when he was asked by Leon, the tyrant of the Phliasians, who he might be, he replied: "A Philosopher." He used to say that the present life was very similar to a great public festival. For just as some come to it to compete, others to do business, and the best come as spectators, so in life some are born as slaves to glory and hunters of desire, while others are seekers of truth. And these matters are indeed so. But in those three small works of Pythagoras which we mentioned, the following are generally reported. He does not permit anyone to pray for themselves, because they do not know what is beneficial for them. He calls drunkenness a distinct ruin, and rejects every excess, saying that no one should exceed the proper measure of either labor or food. And concerning sexual matters, he spoke thus: that they should be performed in winter, not in summer; more lightly in autumn and spring. At all times, however, they are burdensome and not at all conducive to health. When asked <pb n="278"/> one should engage in intercourse, he said: "Whenever you wish to become weaker than yourself." He distinguishes human age in this way: a boy completes twenty years, a youth <note>adolescens</note> twenty, a young man <note>iuvenis</note> twenty, and an old man twenty. These ages are also adapted to the seasons of the year: the boy to spring, the youth to summer, the young man to autumn, and the old man to winter. By "youth" he understands the pubescent; by "young man," the adult male. He was the first, according to Timaeus, to say that "friends' things are all common" and that "friendship is equality." His disciples also used to deposit all their possessions into a single fund and made them communal; they likewise remained silent for an entire five-year period, hearing only what was said, and never seeing Pythagoras until they had been proven. From then on, they were admitted to his house and his presence. They abstained from cypress wood for coffins because the scepter of Jupiter was made from it, as Hermippus says in the second book On Pythagoras. Furthermore, it is handed down that he was of such beautiful form that his disciples thought him to be Apollo who had come from the Hyperboreans. There is a report that once, when his thigh was bared, it appeared to be golden; nor were there lacking those who said that when he crossed the river Nessus, he was hailed by it. Timaeus also says in the tenth book of his Histories that he said those women who lived with men were regarded by the name of the gods as <term>koras</term> <gloss>maidens</gloss> and nymphs, and were subsequently called mothers. Anticlides is the authority in the second book On Alexander that he perfected geometry, after Moeris had previously discovered the first principles of its elements; and that Pythagoras especially devoted himself to the arithmetic aspect of it, and discovered the rule of the single string <note>the monochord</note>. Nor did he neglect medicine. Apollodorus the calculator reports that he sacrificed a <term>hecatombe</term> <gloss>a sacrifice of a hundred oxen</gloss> when he discovered that the side subtending the triangle (which they call <term>orthogonion</term> <gloss>right-angled</gloss>) is equal in power to those that contain it. And there is an epigram that goes like this:

> *Pythagoras once made a noble sacrifice to the gods,*
> *Because a famous diagram had been discovered by him.*

He is also said to have been the first to nourish athletes with meat; previously (as Favorinus says in the third book of his Commentaries), they were accustomed to nourish their bodies with dried and soft figs and wheat, as the same author says.

<summary>This passage details the bibliography attributed to Pythagoras, his philosophical views on lifestyle and moderation, and his contributions to mathematics and communal living.</summary>
<keywords>Pythagoras, Lysis of Tarentum, Ethics, Geometry, Pythagorean Theorem, Asceticism, Vegetarianism, Metempsychosis</keywords>

<pb n="11"/>of children, following the example of other public duties.

### LX.
For we maintain that both guardianship <note>original: "Tutela"</note> and curatorship <note>original: "cura"</note> are public duties.

### LXI.
However, what we have said regarding children is not understood in such a way that we say adopted children are of benefit, or those who have died, but only those surviving or those who have fallen in battle for the republic.

### LXII.
Likewise, one who administers the affairs of the treasury <note>original: "res fisci"</note>, one who is absent for the sake of the republic, one who holds some office of power, one who is engaged in a lawsuit with the minor or adult, or one who is already burdened by three non-sought burdens of guardianship, deserves an excuse.

### LXIII.
Furthermore, an excuse is granted on account of poverty, adverse health, and illiteracy.

### LXIIII.
Likewise, if a father has appointed someone as a guardian in a testament on account of enmity, this very fact provides him an excuse.

### LXV.
However, the excuse of one who relies solely on the fact that he was unknown to the father of the minors shall not be admitted.

### LXVI.
Moreover, capital enmities which someone maintained with the father of the minors or adults, if no reconciliation has intervened, are accustomed to excuse him.

### LXVII.
As is also a controversy regarding legal status <note>original: "status controversia"</note> which someone suffered from the father of the minors.

### LXVIII.
On account of age, those older than seventy years are excused, and those younger than twenty-five are prohibited, as are also soldiers.

### LXIX.
Likewise, in Rome, grammarians, rhetoricians, and physicians <pb n="12"/> who practice these arts in their own country, if they are within the prescribed number, have an exemption from guardianship and curatorship.

<margin>LXX.</margin>
Those, however, who wish to excuse themselves do not indeed appeal, but within fifty continuous days from the time they learned they were appointed as guardians or curators, they must excuse themselves.

<margin>LXXI.</margin>
If someone has earned an excuse from guardianship through false allegations, the excuse shall not be valid from the beginning.

<margin>LXXII.</margin>
Finally, this must not be overlooked: all guardians can become suspected <note>original: "suspectos"</note>, and the accusation of a suspect is open to all.

<margin>LXXIII.</margin>
To such an extent that even women are admitted to this, who, not overstepping the modesty of their sex, do not tolerate the injury of minors out of a certain sense of duty <note>original: "pietate"</note>.

<margin>LXXIIII.</margin>
However, those below the age of puberty <note>original: "impuberes"</note> themselves cannot demand their guardians be declared suspect; but those above the age of puberty <note>original: "Puberes"</note> can do so against their curators upon the advice of their relatives.

<margin>LXXV.</margin>
Lest anyone err in this, a suspect is one who does not carry out the guardianship in good faith, even if he is solvent.

<margin>LXXVI.</margin>
But even before someone begins to carry out a guardianship, he can sometimes be removed as if he were a suspect.

<margin>LXXVII.</margin>
A removed suspect, if indeed it was on account of fraud <note>original: "dolum"</note>, is marked with infamy <note>original: "famosus"</note>, unless he was a <term>Patronus</term> <gloss>a former master and legal protector</gloss>; if it was on account of negligence <note>original: "culpam"</note>, he is not equally so marked.

<margin>LXXVIII.</margin>
If someone is demanded as a suspect, his administration is forbidden until the inquiry is finished.

<margin>LXXIX.</margin>
The inquiry into a suspect is extinguished by the death of the guardian or curator.
