<pb n="15"/>But he was a most prudent lawgiver, for he wrote laws for his citizens. And under Philistion, an eminent physician <note>original: "sub Philistio medicus insignis"</note>—moreover, Plato, who warned us not to believe in astrologers, mocked them and commanded that it be so. Indeed, mathematical reasoning demonstrates that Plato should be given more weight than Eudoxus <note>Correcting "Doychilax" or "Doychilae" likely referring to Eudoxus of Cnidus</note> and Archelaus, even though he excelled in astronomy. On this matter of predictions, you should never follow Panaetius <note>original: "Pane ti"</note>, nor Diogenes of Halicarnassus <note>original: "Doychilax halicarnasse"</note>, whom he considered most learned in all mathematics, yet he repudiated this entire genre of divining by the stars. I shall come to the moderns. Nicole Oresme <note>original: "Nicolaus Oresmius"</note>, a most acute philosopher and most skilled mathematician, also pursues astrological superstition with a specific commentary, full of indignation. He judged that nothing is more deceptive, nothing more detestable to all ranks of people, but especially to princes and great men. Giovanni Marliani <note>original: "Joannes Marlian"</note> in our own age was and is considered supreme in mathematics; he not only abstained from these predictions, but had even begun to write about their falsity in his final years, though he did not complete it, being intercepted by a long-delayed death. He used to say as a boastful man <note>original: "homine gloriosus"</note> that he held most certain demonstrations against the astrologers, as his associate Luchino, himself an excellent mathematician, related to me more than once. Paolo of Florence <note>original: "Paul Florentin"</note>, learned in medicine but especially in Greek and Latin mathematics, as often as he was asked about that profession, he always asserted it was uncertain and deceptive, bringing forward among other things an evident experiment on himself. For though he had already completed eighty-five years, he had found no vital constellation in his own birth chart <note>term: "genitura"</note>, which he had examined most diligently. I could bring forward many of those who are still living and are astronomers who feel the same. But I do not know if they wish to stir up envy against themselves from men who are powerful through this heavenly faction. Furthermore, our Marsilio <note>note: Marsilio Ficino</note> wrote openly against them, following the footsteps of Plotinus. In interpreting and explaining him, he greatly joined, increased, and illustrated Platonic thought. ## XVIIII.

It provides not only the necessary qualities, but also, if it be the form of a living thing, it provides a fitting bulk through the passage of time. Since that bulk is a certain accident inhering in prime matter, and prime matter cannot naturally lack a substantial form: it is necessary that together with the addition of bulk, another and another substance is added and generated, and therefore nutrition is given along with growth. It is certain that this nutrition is distinguished from generation only by an accidental difference.

## XX.

Some things are nourished by food digested within, others by food prepared without. It is necessary that those which digest food within have at least a mouth and a certain gullet or belly. Most of the Perfect Animals <note>Complex organisms such as mammals</note> also possess a small stomach, an intestine, a liver, and veins. The stomach, by the service of its oblique fibers, so embraces the food fallen from the mouth that the undigested matter would necessarily rush out of the pylorus <note>the opening from the stomach into the small intestine</note> if provident nature did not prevent it by certain glandular tubercles.

## XXI.

Immediately the cooking faculty, which is identified with the substance of the stomach itself, having applied heat as its chief instrument, industriously applies itself to digestion, while the liver, spleen, diaphragm, and heart press the work from all sides. When the work is finished, the pylorus is opened, and the chyle <note>milky fluid of digested food</note> entering the duodenum <note>the first part of the small intestine</note> tends straight toward the large intestine and even to that extreme part of the large intestine which is called the bowel, and offers itself to be sucked out through the very frequent openings of the mesenteric vessels as it runs through the winding turns of the intestines, so that it retains nothing except the feces.

## XXII.

The mesenteric veins carry the juice and flower of the chyle through the mesentery to the portal <note>the portal vein of the liver</note>, from which, as any part of the liver immediately attracts it, it is dissipated throughout the liver into many narrow branches, and there undergoes the making of the chyme or the four humors; so that from the hotter parts yellow bile is generated, from the colder and more earthy parts black bile, from the more temperate and subtle parts blood, and from the less subtle parts phlegm <note>original: "pituita"</note>.

## XXIII.

Just as the four humors differ in species and nature, so they are not all assigned to the same duty. For the yellow bile is received by the follicle <note>gallbladder</note> suspended in the hollow part of the liver, and from there it is poured into the duodenum for the sake of purging the intestines with its sharpness. <pb n="10"/> The spleen exhausts the black bile and partly converts it into itself, and partly vomits it back into the stomach, as some of the more skilled physicians maintain, though the passage for this is disputed among physicians. The phlegm, like a vehicle, carries the blood down into the Great Cava <note>the vena cava</note>.

### XXIIII.

From there, it is carried into all parts of the body, both heterogeneous and homogeneous, to whichever any access lies open, being conveyed by the phlegm through almost innumerable meanders of the veins in a way that is utterly inexpressible. For whatever is most familiar to any part either floats to it of its own accord or is invited and attracted from a distance by an attracting power.

### XXV.

Meanwhile, the phlegm partly takes on the nature of blood; the remainder enters the emunctory veins, then the kidneys, and finally the bladder, and is turned into urine <note>original: "lotium"</note>. Finally, that digestion which is carried out in all parts of the living thing, and by which the blood, having left its own form, passes into the substance of the animal, is nutrition. If not only growth but also rarefaction <note>the thinning or expansion of matter</note> accompanies this, the animal will spread into a larger bulk; otherwise, not at all.

### XXVI.

But when the parts of a living thing become rarefied, they do not acquire some new quantity, but only a new place while the old is cast off; they exhale an excremental vapor, loosen the pores, and more largely imbibe nourishment. Just as a vacuum cannot be given universally by the forces of nature, so it is not introduced into the rarefying parts of a living thing.

### XXVII.

The growth of a living thing, according to its formal meaning, is the action by which the quantity of food is joined to the quantity of the living thing. It is either an action of the same power as nutrition—which power we distinguish from the substance of the living thing only by reason—or of another power, which we judge to be identified with the unions of prime matter.

### XXVIII.

Both growth and the nutrition of individual parts can occur continuously, and indeed during the whole time of life, unless diseases and other inconveniences of that kind interfere and, as it were, sever the thread of nutrition and growth. Nevertheless, the remaining powers subordinate to nutrition, in the absence of the final boiling <note>original: "lixatione"</note>, act as much as impediments allow, and flee idleness as if it were a plague.

</translation>

<pb n="238"/>and by her providence, as it were, reborn, to restore them once again to the courses of a new Salvation <note>original: "Salutis"</note>. Therefore, I too ought to endure the celestial command, although I had already been named and destined for this happy service by the clear and evident favor of the great deity; and no differently than the other worshippers, I must from now on abstain from profane and forbidden foods, so that I might more rightly penetrate the purest secrets of the religion.

The priest had spoken: and my obedience was not corrupted by impatience; but intent with a mild quiet and a worthy silence, I performed the diligent service of the worship of the sacred rites every day. Nor did the saving kindness of the powerful Goddess deceive me, nor did she torture me with the delay of a long time; but by the not-obscure commands of a dark night, she clearly warned me that the day I had always hoped for had arrived, on which she would grant me my greatest wish. She also determines with what expense I should provide for the supplications, and she appoints Mithras <note>the high priest of Isis</note> himself, that chief priest of hers, joined to me, as he said, by a certain divine fellowship of the stars, as the minister for the rites. Refreshed in my spirit by these and other benevolent commands of the highest Goddess, while it was not yet clear daylight and my rest was shaken off, I immediately hasten to the dwelling of the priest; and meeting him just as he was coming out of his bedchamber, I greet him. I had already determined with more than usual resolution to demand, as if a debt, my obedience to the rites. But he, as soon as he saw me, spoke first: "O my Lucius," he said, "how happy you are, how blessed, whom the august deity so greatly deigns to favor with a propitious will! And why," he said, "do you stand idle now and delay yourself? The day you have longed for with constant prayers is here, on which you shall be initiated into the most holy secrets of the rites by the divine commands of the Goddess of many names <note>original: "Deae multinominis"</note>, through these hands of mine." And, having cast <pb n="239"/>his right hand upon me, the very courteous old man leads me immediately to the very doors of the most spacious temple; and having celebrated the service of the opening with the solemn ritual, and having performed the morning sacrifice, he brings forth from the secret places of the sanctuary <note>original: "adyti"</note> certain books, inscribed with unrecognizable letters: partly with figures of every kind of animal, suggesting the condensed words of a conceived discourse; partly with knotted characters, twisted in the manner of a wheel and crowded together like vine-tendrils, protected from the curious reading of the profane. From these he proclaims to me what things were necessary to be prepared for the use of my protection.

I immediately procure those things diligently, and somewhat more liberally, partly by myself and partly through my companions, to be bought. And now, the time requiring it as the priest said, he leads me, escorted by a religious company, to the nearest baths; and having first been committed to the usual washing, after praying for the pardon of the Gods, he washes me by sprinkling water around most purely; and having led me back again to the temple, when two parts of the day had already passed, he places me before the very feet of the Goddess. Having secretly commanded certain things which are better than voice <note>too sacred to be spoken aloud</note>, he clearly instructs this before all witnesses: that for those ten continuous days I should restrain the pleasure of food, and that I should eat no animal, and that I should be without wine. When these things had been duly observed with venerable continence, the day destined for the divine pledge was now at hand; and the curving Sun drew on the evening. Then behold, crowds flow together from all sides according to the ancient ritual of the rites, each honoring me with various gifts. Then, all the profane being removed far away, and I being covered in a wrap of unrefined linen, the priest, having taken my hand, leads me to the inner recesses of the sanctuary itself. You might perhaps ask quite anxiously, studious reader, what was then said, what was done? I would tell, if it were lawful to tell; you would know, if it were lawful to hear. But equal guilt <note>would bind both me for my speech and you for your curiosity</note>
</translation>

<pb n="14"/># Corrections.

->E<-

**The second Echium** <gloss>Vipers bugloss</gloss> ] I confess that I do not yet perceive any specific difference between the common Vipers bugloss and that which grows everywhere on walls among us: let others examine more strictly.

->G<-

**Geranium malacoides or lesser dove’s-foot** <gloss>Cranesbill</gloss> ] It is not sufficiently clear to me whether the little plant we understand here is entirely of the same species as the lesser dove’s-foot Geranium of Caspar Bauhin.

**Lesser foxtail-like grass with a short rough spike** ] The London botanists call this Crested grass, nor would I deny it.

**Dog’s grass** ] This is the same as what Joannes Bauhinus describes under the title cited: and therefore what I have noted here must be retracted, for I had not observed the panicle myself before I published the Catalogue: but I rashly believed others.

**Greater hairy grass** ] I now suspect that this grass does not differ specifically from the small hairy grass, but only in size and other accidents, by reason of the place in which it grows.

->M<-

**Mountain Madder or Bedstraw** <gloss>Mollugo</gloss> ] These two synonyms, *Another wild Madder* of *Gesner* and *Woodruff 2* of *Tragus*, do not belong here but to the first *Mollugo* of *Dodoens*, which has a round stem and is erect.

It is not yet fully discovered by me where this plant, which grows everywhere in hedges, should be referred; whether to the *Mollugo*, where we have referred it here, or to the wild Madder. I do not doubt but that this is the same as what Joannes Bauhinus described under the title *Rough angular Madder*, indeed even the London botanists name it *Wild Madder*. It seems likely to me that the same plant is described under both titles. <pb n="15"/>Joannes Bauhinus doubts, to be sure, whether the *Mollugo* of Clusius corresponds to his angular Madder or not. Now indeed the *Mollugo* of Clusius is the same as the first *Mollugo* of Dodoens, the mountain *Mollugo* of Gerard, and the more common *Mollugo* of Parkinson. For the figure is everywhere the same; and both the figure and description agree with this plant: but the short descriptions of wild Madder in Gerard and Parkinson do not likewise agree.

Caspar Bauhin incorrectly applies the *Mollugo* of Clusius and the mountain *Mollugo* of Gerard to his first *Mollugo*, or branched broad-leaved mountain [type]; since these synonyms look toward the second no less than the first *Mollugo* of Dodoens.

---

-> O <-

**Common Marjoram** ] *The plant that grows in Bowyers close at Cherry-hinton is not this, but* **Common Wild Basil**. *We mistook it when it was young.*

-> P <-

**The Milkwort of Cortusus** ] In place of this substitute, **German Horseshoe Vetch with pods at the top** of *Caspar Bauhin*, the synonyms for which you may seek in the Additions.

-> R <-

**Ivy-leaved Crowfoot of the brooks, etc.** ] The flowers of this plant are white, not yellow as we conjectured; and it arises everywhere in watery places: therefore the synonyms cited do not correspond to it, unless perhaps it varies in flower color in lands across the sea.

-> S <-

**The Western English Saxifrage** ] In place of **English chickweed-leaved Saxifrage** of the *corrected Gerard* substitute **Squinancy-wort of Lyon, page 1125 of the corrected Gerard** and add the synonyms **Squinancy Madder** of *Joannes Bauhinus volume 6*, or **Squinancy-wort** of *Caspar Bauhin*.

**Tiny grassy Saxifrage** ] *I find upon comparing that this is the same plant described by Johnson upon Gerard under the name of* **English chickweed-leaved Saxifrage** *or* **Pearlwort.**
</translation>

<summary>John Ray provides taxonomic corrections and synonymy updates for various plants including grasses, madders, and saxifrages. He acknowledges several errors in his previous Catalogue, citing recent observations and the works of other botanists like Bauhin and Gerard.</summary>

<keywords>botany, taxonomy, John Ray, Cambridge flora, plant synonyms, Caspar Bauhin, Joannes Bauhinus, 17th century science, Cherry Hinton</keywords>

<pb n="13"/><meta>continues from previous page</meta> signify a promise. If you falter, she will support you; if you are pushed toward a fall, she will lift you up; if you are hemmed in by the enemy, she will open a wide field of hope; if you are summoned into danger by the secret councils of the opposing side, she will open a crack for you into the hidden plots of fraud with a celestial arrow; for as much as these things harm when hidden, they wither once recognized. Finally, she will make it known to all that she is that leader of war who, if Cologne must be defended alongside the Rhine and the forces of the enemy broken by disasters, would rival Deborah in fortitude, show herself as Judith in magnanimity, and exhibit the trophies of Tomyris, the victories of Artemisia, and the palms of Zenobia through her skill in fighting and conquering; and she shall obscure the so-often celebrated wars of the Amazons.

Enjoy, therefore, the auxiliary favors of your most brave Patroness, Rhenish Nation. You, who were once famous for triumphal fortitude, when already the Euphrates and Tigris, the Propontis <note>the Sea of Marmara</note> and the Nile, the Seine and the Rhône, the Volga and the Borysthenes <note>the Dnieper</note>, the Baetis <note>the Guadalquivir</note> and the Thames, along with the Upper and Lower Seas <note>the Adriatic and Tyrrhenian</note>, had served the Tiber <note>Rome</note>; you alone dared to defend the Rhine against the looming power of the Romans. And having already overcome Pyrrhus, defeated Antiochus, routed Hannibal, subjugated Mithridates, scattered Pharnaces, bridled Asia, tamed Africa, and with the vast expanse of Europe reduced almost to the necessity of ignominious obedience, you, by the slaughter inflicted upon the army of Varus <note>referring to the Battle of the Teutoburg Forest</note>, dared to rise up against the people who were the victors of nations. Trust now that you will obtain even more distinguished victories, which, beyond the ancestral fortitude of your spirit, the subsidiary army of the Divine URSULA protects against the enemy. To this, the most August Monarch joins his allied forces, he who, after the power of the defeated Thracians <note>the Ottoman Turks</note> was buried among the banks of the Raab <note>original: "Arrabonis"</note>, is about to illustrate the most famous river of Germany with victories, so that he may protect all Germany against the armed ambition of the enemies; for the defense of the Rhine alone, he directs the mass <pb n="14"/> of his victorious arms. If you honor the former with constant piety, and the latter with faithful obedience, you will certainly bring it about by your piety and fidelity, Rhenish Nation, that with the wonders of Cologne and the Rhine—freed once again from the enemy—renewed, and secure under the twin protection of most flourishing armies amidst the assaults of rushing enemies, you shall spread your victorious Majesty far and wide, inviolate, to the terror of the people prowling for the destruction of the German Empire.

In such a case, Clement VI, in his Bull, wishing to signify his Clemency toward men of this sort, commands the Angels of Paradise to lead the Soul, entirely absolved from Purgatory, into the Glory of Paradise; Nicholas V, Urban VIII, and Innocent X of this century imparted the same Grace to them. Among these, Urban writes thus in his Bull: <note>Pope Urban VIII (1623-1644) continued the tradition of granting indulgences to those who died en route to a Jubilee.</note>

> Since it can happen that of those who have undertaken the journey for this reason, or have traveled to the City, some in the way or even in the City itself, hindered by disease or another legitimate cause or prevented by death, may be unable to execute the premises and visit the Church and Basilicas of this kind, the defined number of days being incomplete, and perhaps not even begun: we, desiring to favor their pious and prompt Will as much as we can in the Lord, will that those truly penitent and confessed become participants in the aforesaid Indulgence and remission, as if they had actually visited the Church and Basilicas aforesaid on the days prescribed by us,

compare Marchantius on the Bull of Urban VIII. <note>Jacobus Marchantius was a 17th-century theologian and canonist.</note>

§. 4. Regarding the absent Celebrants of the Jubilee who do not come to Rome, the Roman Pontiff, out of his benignity, diverts his wells to them also—as Marchantius raves—and sends out streams to various provinces, so that all may be able both to be washed and to drink, provided they visit the local churches analogous to those Roman ones according to the judgment of the Pontiff or his Emissaries. This is believed by them to be a singular Proof of papal beneficence and largess, which the recently mentioned Marchantius praises everywhere; he says <term>this largess is made by the Pontiff to various regions of the World, so that the benignity of the Father toward his scattered sons, and of the Pastor toward the Sheep, who cannot flow together into one place at once, may shine forth more brightly.</term> Hence he says the Pontiff grieves <term>that to certain Provinces and regions these living waters, these streams of Grace, cannot be diverted, because they have cut themselves off from Unity, and like ungrateful sons have left Mother Church, kicking back after they have sucked the breasts, namely rebelling against her faith and Doctrine, and immersing themselves in the foul waters of perverse and heretical Doctrine.</term> Alexander VI granted this great Grace, as they esteem it—namely the Indulgences of the Holy Year—even to the most remote Provinces to enrich his bastards, as Polydore writes; and according to Frostius, Sixtus IV and Gregory XIII granted it to the Catholics of England, both those existing in England and elsewhere, who could not travel to Rome. To these, finally, must be added the dead and those already burning in purgatory: even these can be liberated from the flames of purgatory by the grant of the Roman Pontiff, if the power of applying the Jubilee to them is expressly held in the promulgatory bull, and if by the prayers of heirs or Friends <pb n="21"/> they are helped, to whom *Clemens VI*—when they had set out to Rome for the sake of the Jubilee—granted the power that each might select three or four Souls as they wished; for these would immediately, on account of his Indulgences and their Merit, fly up from purgatory into Heaven. *Santarellus* <note>Antonio Santarelli (1569-1649), a Jesuit theologian known for his controversial views on papal power.</note> is even bolder, saying that the Pontiff through a most plenary Jubilee can in one day liberate all the Souls of purgatory, Chapter 3, Doubt 12. But there is no reason for us to refute with many words that preposterous Boldness which the Roman Pontiff assumes for himself: for he who is not ignorant of the foundation upon which that Pontifical power rests—which he puts forward, and how it is not Apostolic but Anti-Christian—will find it not difficult, we believe, to judge these pompous promises. Let the Papists show what Divine Author wished to enrich his Church with such an abundance of Grace that the Roman Bishop could dispense it; otherwise, what forbids us from saying with the Poet:

->What will this Promiser bring forth worthy of such a great gape?<- <note>A quote from Horace's Ars Poetica, mocking someone who promises more than they can deliver.</note>

§. 5. Therefore the Jubilee of the Papists is nothing but a mere Invention; its Privileges are Market-tricks; its Indulgences are snares. The reasons which they bring forward here for cloaking this Simony <gloss>the selling of spiritual things</gloss> of their Church are of such a sort that if you recount them, you have already refuted them. Indeed, regarding what *Turrecremata* <note>Juan de Torquemada (1388-1468), a Spanish Dominican theologian.</note> dreams here in *Jacobus de Graffiis, Golden Appendix, Book 1, Chapter 8, Section 13*:

> That the Jubilee was instituted as a help for human infirmity, since some men are weighed down by so great a burden of sins that they are insufficient to pay those due penalties in this life, whence commonly the pious Mother Church acts at a certain time in their life, so that the faithful may have the help of this grace, by the mediation of which they can be absolved from the debts of penalties,

all of that, since it overflows with slippery Presumption—as if our Works could merit any grace from GOD—has an easy refutation through the words of the Savior himself:

> When you have done all things that are commanded you, say: we are unprofitable servants, we have done what we ought to do. <note>Luke 17:10</note>

If these things are true of those whom a true Love toward God impels to walk in the commands prescribed by him; they will hold much more regarding those of whose Works, dedicated to the study of <term>ethelothreskeia</term> <gloss>will-worship or self-chosen religion</gloss>, the Prophet says:

> Who has required these things from your hands? Isaiah 1, 12.

Furthermore, if the Papists are solicitous about this elective Worship out of fear of the penalties to be suffered in Purgatory, let them first set fire to that chimerical figment, and then we will have a care for escaping the flames of purgatory. <margin>XXXIII.</margin>
The nutritive power and the augmentative power are distinguished only formally, but in reality they are one and the same power.

<margin>XXXIIII.</margin>
Although the power of generating and of altering is not in the thing that arises or is changed, nevertheless the power of increasing must necessarily be in that which grows.

<margin>XXXV.</margin>
The augmentation of the whole living being is not properly one single motion. For the unity of motion requires unity of the thing moved, of the boundary, and of time, as is written in the 5th book of the *Physics* <note>Aristotle's Physica</note>, text 34; if these are taken in their proper sense, they are found lacking in this increase.

<margin>XXXVI.</margin>
The augmentation of all parts of a living being taken together is not a continuous motion.

<margin>XXXVII.</margin>
The augmentation of no individual small part is continuous by its own proper continuation.

<margin>XXXVIII.</margin>
Augmentation can be called continuous in the same way as alteration: namely, when no instant passes in which it could happen without it actually happening.

<margin>XXXIX.</margin>
The augmentation of a living being is sought by nature for its own sake and primarily for the benefit of the living being itself. However, the augmentation of metals, stones, and similar things pertains more to the benefit of the species than to any specific individual.

<pb n="12"/>Although, on account of the variety of temperaments <note>original: "complexionum"</note>, locations, foods, and other things, a fixed number of years cannot be assigned in which the augmentation of humans is completed, nevertheless, if we speak of a man who is in any way well-constituted and of what happens for the most part, we must establish with the ancient philosophers and physicians that growth according to length lasts until the 24th year, but according to width until more or less the 30th year. After the 30th year until the 35th or 40th, no augmentation or diminution occurs; but from the 40th until the 60th, a certain obscure diminution follows, which is finally succeeded, until death, by an obvious loss of parts. These things, however, in our age, on account of the corrupt and foul life of certain men and the weakness of nature itself now growing old, sometimes tend to happen a little differently.

Truly, so that this may also be handled by reference, a judge in these matters ought to be provident and cautious, and above all attend to the custom of the court, whether other indications concur along with such an accusation—for instance, that the defamed Titius was found in the place of the inflicted wound with a drawn and bloody sword; likewise whether threats and enmities preceded it. Therefore, if these things concur, I think it is not only sufficient for inquiring, but also for torturing, which the Ordinance of the Empire <note>The Constitutio Criminalis Carolina</note> also proves in chapter 27, paragraph *Zum Sechsten* <gloss>sixthly</gloss>, in that place:

> If a harmed person, for several (which should be noted) reasons, accuses someone of the misdeed and dies upon it etc.

But if other indications or supporting evidence are lacking, then although the naming alone may create some presumption and an indication for inquiring, it is nevertheless not sufficient for torture, nor for imposing an oath of purgation, even if the one confessing is of the most proven faith, or the confession was made under oath. <pb n="17"/># XII. JOHANNES CONRADUS FINCKHER, OF CELLE.

## FROM THE BOOK ON PHYSICS. ASSERTION XXXV.

<note>An ornamental woodcut initial 'T' features scrolling foliage and floral motifs.</note>
Time, in its material and real sense, is motion itself. Formally, it is the <term>passio</term> <gloss>attribute or property</gloss> of motion, consisting firstly in a continuous, successive, divisible duration; secondly, in the nature of a measure—primarily the measured and intrinsic measure or the potential number of the numbered—which is the aforementioned duration, insofar as it renders the motion in which it exists formally fit to be numbered and measured by the duration of another motion. Thirdly, it consists in the nature of an extrinsic and measuring measure, or the numbering number; this measure and number is the same duration of motion insofar as it is distinguished by the Intellect into certain parts such as days, weeks, months, and so on. Thus distinguished as something better known to us, it is applied to discern the durations of various actions, motions, and things as they are subject to change.
<margin>Aristotle, Physics, text 131.</margin>
In the first and second ways, the formal nature of Time is a <term>ens praedicamentale</term> <gloss>categorical being</gloss>; in the third way, it is a <term>ens rationis</term> <gloss>a being of the mind</gloss>, such that if the soul were removed, Time would not exist. The Aristotelian definition from text 101 can be accommodated to both of the latter formal senses of Time: the number of motion according to before and after.

---

## XXXVI.

From this it becomes clear that particular times are multiplied according to the multitude of motions, since individual numerical motions claim their own durations, which are also called the intrinsic measures of the same. However, there is only one Universal Time in number, which is the duration of the first motion distinguished by the numbering Intellect into certain parts to measure our actions and the motions of things. Duration in reality is nothing other than existence, though it differs formally.

---

## FROM LOGIC.

### XXXVII.

<pb n="18"/><note>A decorative initial letter D features a small landscape scene with a building and trees.</note> Demonstration most closely contains the demonstration <term>Propter quid</term> <gloss>of the "why" or the cause</gloss> and the demonstration <term>Quia</term> <gloss>of the "fact"</gloss>. <note>Aristotle, Posterior Analytics, Book 1, Chapter 10.</note> For the medium of a demonstration <term>propter quid</term>, and therefore the most powerful one, nothing else is required nor suffices except the causal definition of the property to be demonstrated, which is always simultaneously the proper and proximate cause of that same property.

---

### FROM THE BOOK ON THE HEAVENS. ASSERTION XXXVIII.

<note>A decorative initial letter C depicts a figure in a landscape setting within an ornate circular frame.</note> Celestial bodies differ from one another both in number and in essential species; however, any star differs from its own sphere only in accidental species, like a denser and more luminous part of its sphere continued like a knot in wood. And therefore, a star does not wander in the heavens by its own motion, as fish do in water or birds in the air.

---

## FROM LOGIC.

### XXXIX.

<note>A decorative initial letter F with floral and scrollwork ornamentation.</note> Form, which is the internal and essential principle of a syllogism, can be described as a certain complication or arrangement of matter fit for inferring a conclusion. This arrangement, if it concerns the remote matter—that is, the middle term with the extremes—is called the Figure. If it concerns the proximate matter—namely, the propositions according to a certain essential quantity and quality—it is called the Syllogistic Mood. Conversion, which is the extrinsic formal principle of syllogisms of the second and third Figure, is a formal and therefore necessary consequence, but it is not an argumentation.

# XII. JOHANNES CONRADUS FINCKHER, OF CELLE.

## FROM THE BOOK ON PHYSICS. ASSERTION XXXV.

<note>An ornamental woodcut initial 'T' features scrolling foliage and floral motifs.</note>
Time, in its material and real sense, is motion itself. Formally, it is the <term>passio</term> <gloss>attribute or property</gloss> of motion, consisting firstly in a continuous, successive, divisible duration; secondly, in the nature of a measure—primarily the measured and intrinsic measure or the potential number of the numbered—which is the aforementioned duration, insofar as it renders the motion in which it exists formally fit to be numbered and measured by the duration of another motion. Thirdly, it consists in the nature of an extrinsic and measuring measure, or the numbering number; this measure and number is the same duration of motion insofar as it is distinguished by the Intellect into certain parts such as days, weeks, months, and so on. Thus distinguished as something better known to us, it is applied to discern the durations of various actions, motions, and things as they are subject to change.
<margin>Aristotle, Physics, text 131.</margin>
In the first and second ways, the formal nature of Time is a <term>ens praedicamentale</term> <gloss>categorical being</gloss>; in the third way, it is a <term>ens rationis</term> <gloss>a being of the mind</gloss>, such that if the soul were removed, Time would not exist. The Aristotelian definition from text 101 can be accommodated to both of the latter formal senses of Time: the number of motion according to before and after.

---

## XXXVI.

From this it becomes clear that particular times are multiplied according to the multitude of motions, since individual numerical motions claim their own durations, which are also called the intrinsic measures of the same. However, there is only one Universal Time in number, which is the duration of the first motion distinguished by the numbering Intellect into certain parts to measure our actions and the motions of things. Duration in reality is nothing other than existence, though it differs formally.

---

## FROM LOGIC.

### XXXVII.
pages.18:

->OF WANGEN.<-

### FROM THE BOOK ON THE HEAVENS. ASSERTION XXXVIII.

<note>A decorative initial letter C depicts a figure in a landscape setting within an ornate circular frame.</note> Celestial bodies differ from one another both in number and in essential species; however, any star differs from its own sphere only in accidental species, like a denser and more luminous part of its sphere continued like a knot in wood. And therefore, a star does not wander in the heavens by its own motion, as fish do in water or birds in the air.

---

## FROM LOGIC.

### XXXIX.

<note>A decorative initial letter F with floral and scrollwork ornamentation.</note> Form, which is the internal and essential principle of a syllogism, can be described as a certain complication or arrangement of matter fit for inferring a conclusion. This arrangement, if it concerns the remote matter—that is, the middle term with the extremes—is called the Figure. If it concerns the proximate matter—namely, the propositions according to a certain essential quantity and quality—it is called the Syllogistic Mood. Conversion, which is the extrinsic formal principle of syllogisms of the second and third Figure, is a formal and therefore necessary consequence, but it is not an argumentation.

## Epitaph of Elpis

### Wife of Boethius

I was called Elpis, a daughter of the Sicilian region, whom love for a husband led far from her fatherland. Without him, the day was sorrowful: the night anxious, the hour tearful, and there was not only one spirit for the husband: my light is not closed while such a husband remains, and I shall survive in the greater part of my soul: now a pilgrim I rest in the sacred porches, having <unclear>testified before</unclear> the throne of the eternal Judge. Let no hand violate this tomb, lest by chance this ash should desire to join these limbs to her spouse again.

## A Song of Georgius
## Tiphernus to the Blessed Virgin

Virgin, ornament of heaven, most holy virgin, virgin to be venerated above the angelic choirs. You, beautiful, surpass snowy roses: you surpass white lilies: you surpass even the stars with your countenance. Pure, like a small dove, whom no milky wing knows: nor does any blemish sit upon your whole body. How far you excel the Sibyls, O Virgin; what nymph, finally, can be compared to you: you are called the beloved mother of God: you are called the spouse.

# THE PRECEPTS OF THE MOSAIC LAW
->Reduced into a compendium.<-

## THE FIRST PRECEPT
### YOU SHALL HAVE NO OTHER GODS
This consists of the fear of God rooted in love, true faith, solid hope, in prosperous and adverse circumstances, and finally in the entirety of life.

### GUILTY OF THIS PRECEPT
One who ascribes his life and condition, in every state of fortune, to another rather than to God, or who trusts in himself or his own people instead of God.

## THE SECOND PRECEPT
### YOU SHALL NOT TAKE THE NAME OF YOUR GOD
->In vain.<-
This consists of attributing glory, honor, and blessing to God, worshiping him alone, crediting whatever good you have to this one alone, invoking him, and detesting yourself. Indeed, no one doubts that whatever is good is the name of God.

### GUILTY OF THIS PRECEPT
One who uses the name of God for anything other than his glory. One who flatters himself for some good of his own, or seeks virtue and praise from any source other than God.

## THE THIRD PRECEPT
### YOU SHALL SANCTIFY THE SABBATHS
This consists of focusing on God, and desiring and seeking his grace alone.

### GUILTY
Whosoever does not rest in spirit for God, but insists on work upon the holy day; whoever does not care for divine things, or cares for them coldly; and whoever does not observe a rest and a sabbath from vices.

## THE FOURTH PRECEPT
### HONOR YOUR FATHER AND MOTHER
This consists of obeying God, and for God’s sake obeying every power, even unto tyranny; to help parents not only with greetings and a nod, but with the very diligence of works, and to follow them especially with benefits.

### GUILTY
<pb n="18"/>
One who flees from, despises, and neglects parents; who turns away from and hates magistrates and the law; who does not obey power, or obeys it unwillingly.

### THE FIFTH PRECEPT
## YOU SHALL NOT KILL

This consists of patience, peace, humanity, mercy, and (to say it in a word) the whole of life without the bitterness of malevolence, being ready and beneficent even toward an enemy.

### GUILTY

One who does not help a brother with counsel, aid, and labor, and does not prevent evil from reaching his neighbor.

### THE SIXTH PRECEPT
## YOU SHALL NOT COMMIT ADULTERY

This consists of purity and modesty of souls, speech, and works; parsimony of diet; the untainted love of heavenly things; contempt for pleasures; and the love of God alone.

### GUILTY

Whosoever is dissolved in pleasures, or enjoys laughter and joy too immodestly, or does not restrain and bridle those who are enjoying them. And those who permit the soul to be occupied with the care of things other than God.

### THE SEVENTH PRECEPT
## YOU SHALL NOT STEAL

This consists of the flight from all avarice, joyful poverty, liberality, and humanity.

### GUILTY

Whosoever is unwilling to give a loan to a neighbor freely and without usury; those who attach their souls too immoderately to some goods of the world; those who endure poverty unwillingly, deny alms, or do not bestow them in a timely manner; and those who circumvent a neighbor through guile and deception.

### THE EIGHTH PRECEPT
## YOU SHALL NOT BEAR FALSE WITNESS

This consists of the naked and simple truth of words and deeds; a tongue fostering peace, seeking the advantage of a brother, desiring to settle discord, refuting detraction, and clearing and covering the infamy of a neighbor.

### GUILTY
</translation>

<pb n="11"/><meta>continues from previous page: for otherwise to run together with the sword,</meta> my companions would dare to fight hand to hand with arms, so that perverse men would not kill me by a cruel death. Pilate addresses the crowd again with his voice: "This man is upright in life, and pure from every crime, whom you make out to be a source of guilt, and for whom you desire hanging." The people further insisted with bitter words: "He is powerful in sedition, and an open inventor of crimes, who has taught impious dogmas with a blasphemous tongue, and filled all the Galilean countryside with tumult." But the Lord remained silent; he added not a single word more, which seemed sufficiently wondrous to Pilate. But when Pilate, that cunning fox, perceived that Herod held jurisdiction over Jesus, he sent him away to that harsh and cruel tyrant. Herod conceives new joys in his happy soul; he hopes for a marvelous deed, imitable by none, to be performed by this man. Although Herod moved words on various matters, Jesus answered nothing; he prepared nothing in return with his voice. The mocker <note>Herod</note> turned up his hooked nose at Christ in derision, and sent him back to Pilate adorned in a shining robe. Therefore, having been punished with rods, he shall leave his chains." There was an ancient custom for the Jews that, in any given year, whichever prisoner the people desired should go free. At that time, a sower of discord and an author of shed blood was imprisoned, called by the name Barabbas. Pilate asks the people, according to the ancient custom: "Which of these two shall succumb to death, and who shall go free?" He says this while sitting upon the high urn <note>the judgment seat</note> of the judge.

But the first of the nobles were inflaming the hearts of the changeable commoners, so that they might cry out that Christ must be killed by death. Pilate wished to leave Jesus safe; he addresses the standing commoners and the cloud of men: "This man has committed nothing unjust; he is pure and innocent of crime, he has done nothing to be atoned for by a cruel death." The impious crowd insisted with such shouts: "Take him away! Snatch away his life on a fixed stake! Bring ladders quickly! Give the wood so he may hang parched!" <pb n="11"/>### The Monastery of the Holy Stephen, commonly called Weihenstephan.

A higher path leads you to the house of Stephen;
->Here is the first glory of the first Martyrdom.<-
These very stones, by which Stephen once fell,
->This place shows to you with great honor.<-
Whoever you are that sees a stone here, either you are a stone yourself,
->Or you will become gentler by having seen the stone.<-

---

### On the sacred Chest in which the stones of Saint Stephen are preserved.

Collected long ago from the death of Saint Stephen,
->This sacred casket preserves the sacred stones.<-
You say, I thought that gems were enclosed here;
->Correct; but God gave the stars in exchange for these gems.<-

---

### The stones of Saint Stephen ward off pleurisy <note>original: "pleuritidem"; a sharp pain in the side or chest</note>.

If a cruel piercing of your sides vexes you,
->This will be the certain remedy for your pain:<-
Diligently wash these stones with wine poured over them,
->If you drink from there, the pain in your side soon departs.<-
But unless a holy compunction <note>pricking of the conscience or repentance</note> of the soul touches you then,
->You are worthy that the pain which was there before should return.<-

<pb n="12"/>### *Saints Peter and Paul, Patrons of the Monastery of Neustift <note>original: "Nova-cella"</note>.*

<note>The letter P is decorated with a small ornamental design.</note>
While Peter opens the stars with the Apostolic keys,
Paul terrifies the Horrible Styx <note>the underworld or hell</note> with his Sword.
Therefore, are the stars of heaven safely climbed here?
Since Paul helps from this side, and Peter helps from that.
O how well! Now, as I see, there is little difference *between*
*Both heaven and your cells, O Neustift.*

---

### *Freising, rich in Patrons.*

<note>The letter O is decorated with a small ornamental design.</note>
How Freising rejoices in such munificent Patrons!
One teaches, another fights; this one preserves, that one blesses.
After the help of the Divine Mother, and after Corbinian,
Great also is the assistance of Sigismund.
Those protect from the Mount, George from below,
Outside the City, Stephen along with Michael provides help.
Whatever is sought from these Patrons with a sincere mind,
God grants, with their prayer intervening.
Hence, when Freising refuses help, it seems
God Himself has now refused His own help.

---

### *The Mount of Freising and the Mount of Weihenstephan compared between themselves.*

<note>The letter F is decorated with a small ornamental design.</note>
Happy Mounts by the seat of two Stephens,
That one of its Martyr, this one of its Prelate <note>Saint Stephen the Martyr and Saint Stephen the Bishop</note>.

<pb n="11"/><meta>continues from previous page: saying:</meta> thinks far better and more honorably than he, whose successors the Roman Pontiffs falsely boast themselves to be: the Apostle Peter, saying: We have a more sure prophetic word, to which you do well to pay attention, as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in our hearts. 2 Peter 1:19.

### LII.

But being utterly maddened and suffering from a spirit of vertigo <note>original: "Spiritu vertiginis," a common theological term for spiritual blindness or dizziness leading to error</note>, by this very objection of theirs they openly betray that they are not the true and Catholic Church as they boast, but a false church of the malignant, indeed people blinded by the Devil and plainly unbelieving.

### LIII.

For Paul judges thus of such people: If, he says, our Gospel is hidden, it is hidden **TO THOSE WHO ARE PERISHING**: in whom the God of this world has blinded the minds of **UNBELIEVERS**, so that the light of the Gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God, should not shine. 2 Corinthians 4 verse 3.

### LIV.

<margin>Whether Scripture itself is ambiguous</margin>
The third accusation against the Scriptures labors under no less impiety: by which they say that it is ambiguous and a matter for strife; also that it has a nose of wax <note>a metaphor for something easily twisted or reshaped to suit one's purpose</note>, and for that reason can be twisted in all ways like some Proteus <note>the sea-god of Greek myth capable of changing his shape at will</note>.

### LV.

For by this reasoning they treat with signal insult not so much the Scripture, as its primary author, God, the Best and Greatest.

### LVI.

As if, forsooth, that most kind God, laboring under the crime of envy in the manner of the ethnic oracles, or like a Sphinx, should delight in errors and verbal involvements, and by deliberate effort should be unwilling to instruct us openly concerning eternal salvation.

### LVII.

Or certainly that He is so powerless that, although He gave to man (created by Him in His own image) the power of aptly speaking the secrets of the mind through the ministry of the voice and tongue, He Himself however cannot make Himself known, nor bring forth His own will in suitable speech. <pb n="12"/>

### LVIII.

But the Lord vindicates Himself from this crime, while through Peter He constantly asserts that the prophetic word is FIRM. 2 Peter 1 verse 19.

### LIX.

For as to the fact that heretics abuse the authority of Scripture for the defense of their errors: that certainly cannot and should not be rightly or deservedly attributed to the Scripture as if it were ambiguous.

<margin>7 7</margin>
### LX.

For as the speech of all truth is simple, so especially is the divine speech contained in the Scriptures, which is simple, constant, and not at all perplexed.

### LXI.

But it is the fault of petulant minds that things rightly said in the Scriptures are corrupted and twisted into a malignant sense, since nothing can be said so well that it cannot be corrupted by telling it badly.

### LXIII.

For what is otherwise commonly said, that anyone is the best interpreter of his own words: that has a place especially in Scripture, which cannot be explained any better than by itself.

But by this very accusation of the ambiguity of Scripture, the Papists <note>original: "Pontificii"</note> again openly betray from what parent they are born and of what spirit they are sons: namely, of Satan, who himself in Paradise did not blush to charge the speech of God with ambiguity, and by this trick deceived our first parents. Genesis 3 verses 4 and 5.

<pb n="21"/><meta>continues from previous page: Of adultery</meta> there were various punishments among various nations, which I believe is not unknown to you, and it shall be explained in its own place and time. Regarding this same matter, Zaleucus had also proposed a law: that whoever was convicted of adultery should have both eyes gouged out. When, however, the son of Zaleucus himself had sinned against it and was found guilty of adultery, and was now to be punished according to his father's law, the entire city declared that they would not reluctantly pardon the son's crime out of respect for the father's virtue and merits. But the father, urging the law and contending that it ought to be confirmed even by his own punishment and that of his family, since he could not obtain from the people that the son be deprived of both eyes, finally achieved this by an admirable balance of justice and paternal devotion: that the law remained inviolate and, as far as was possible while keeping the law safe, he showed a father's affection for his son. For he ordered one of his son's eyes to be plucked out, and one of his own. At last, however, as Suidas noted, he met his death fighting most bravely for his fatherland, so that he might teach others by his own example how sweet and fitting it is to die for one's country.

You have, excellent listeners, what I have been able to learn concerning Charondas and Zaleucus. I earnestly ask that you allow this commemoration, such as it is, to be not unpleasing to you, and that you do not regret this time spent.

Concerning myself and the duties of this office entrusted to me, I would not wish you to expect me to say anything. For I prefer to contribute whatever is in me to the utility of the studies of our most flourishing youth and to the adornment of this <term>Sparta</term> <gloss>metaphorical area of responsibility</gloss> by action rather than by promising at length in words. That I may be able to provide this, I suppliantly worship and pray to God, the Greatest and Best, the author of honorable laws and political order, and the fountain of all good.

# TO THE BENEVOLENT READER, GREETINGS.

<note>Decorative drop cap 'C' at the start of the text, featuring an ornate floral background with scrollwork.</note>

Since our lawmakers in their prefaces deter men from evil deeds primarily by the mention and respect of death, because everyone is usually tormented by the conscience and repentance of those deeds when death is near: but they did not add the cause of this matter, which is undoubtedly that a guilty mind presages a future judgment and impending punishments (for what would he fear, who believed that all things were finished by death): so that it may be clear that not even this was unknown to the Gentiles, I am pleased to subjoin here the most distinguished iambic verses of the comic poet **PHILEMON**, which I once translated into Latin from the Greek. The Greek verses are extant partly in Justin Martyr, in his book *On Monarchy* <note>original: "ἐν τῷ περὶ μοναρχίας"</note>, partly in Eusebius in the 13th book of the *Evangelical Preparation* <note>original: "προπαρασκευῆς εὐαγγελικῆς"</note>, and in Clement of Alexandria, though these latter two refer them to **DIPHILUS** as the author. I desire this work to be approved by you, friend reader. V.

> Do you suppose, Nicostratus, that the dead,
> Who wallowed in every luxury while they lived,
> Are so buried in the ground that they lie hidden
> From the Divinity for eternal time,
> And thus exempt themselves from Him by flight?
> There are eyes of Justice that perceive all things.
> For we believe there are two paths to the underworld,
> One of which belongs to the just; the other to the wicked.
> For if the same fortune awaits the pious and the impious,
> Why not carry off, steal, and snatch
> Whatever you can, and mix the lowest with the highest?
> What stands in the way? Do not let error, O good man, fascinate you:
> Their own judgments await each man in the underworld,
> Over which **GOD**, the ruler of all, will preside:
> Whose tremendous name I am hardly able to speak:
> Who often prolongs life for those who sin.
>
> But if any of mortals, while he daily commits
> Evil deeds, thinks he will be hidden from the Gods,
> He thinks falsely, and leads himself into traps,
> Until the vengeance of **GOD** rests for a little while.
>
> Look to yourselves, you for whom the Divinities are fables:
> There is, there is a **GOD**. But if anyone acts wickedly
> Out of a depraved nature, let him gain time for himself.
> For afterwards, once time has elapsed, he shall pay the penalties.
</translation>

The text transitions into a preface to the reader featuring a Latin translation of Greek verses by Philemon or Diphilus concerning divine justice and the afterlife.</summary>

<translation>
<pb n="10"/><meta>continues from previous page</meta> often says things that should be kept silent to a friend, whom he then begs by all things sacred and profane to suppress what he has heard in eternal silence. Do you wish, O <term>Corydon</term> <gloss>a conventional name for a rustic or shepherd</gloss>, for others to be silent? Be silent yourself, and say *Nothing*. <term>Ardelio</term> <gloss>a busybody or meddler</gloss> wanders through the city all day, always asking, what is new? what is good? While he believes everything from everyone with a simple mind, he ensures that *Nothing* is believed of him. The <term>Statesman</term> <gloss>original: Politicus</gloss> prudently despairs of all things, and bravely hopes for all things, and diligently guards against all things, and thus at last fears *Nothing*. If you are wise, do all things cautiously and quickly, but do *Nothing* rashly or timidly, suddenly or too late. Do you ask what you can do without the help of the Best and Greatest **GOD**? *Nothing*. Among Christians, life will condemn some, and doctrine others. There are not a few who would defend their religion even unto the fire **EXCLUSIVELY** <note>Meaning they would see others burn but not sacrifice themselves, or perhaps stopping just short of the stake.</note>. It is a wonder that pure religion may indeed persuade one toward piety, but for the most part obtains *Nothing*. Often you will see men who are joyful, fond of drink, and rowdy throughout their whole lives. But when a more unfortunate hour falls upon them, they hurry to their prayer books, and having first wiped off the dust, they fashion grim faces for devotion, and with much sighing they seek out certain little prayers suitable for their misfortune. Then they count the pages of those prayers, and if they are too long, they either look for shorter versions or close the books again. These people, because they are destitute of harmony between their heart and their mouth, deserve to receive *Nothing* from **GOD**. If eyes were dug out as often as they took offense and sinned, the whole human race would shortly see *Nothing*. On the last day, certain rich men will say that they threw away gold—that cursed metal, that incitement of all evils—at the feet of the harp-player and the flute-player. But to the poor, the friends of Christ, they will cry out that they gave with a religious hand *Nothing*.

<pb n="11"/>Magistrates and other wealthy citizens and peasants are accustomed to send roosters, capons, geese, thrushes, and other things to Great Men. But to the poor they give *Nothing*. O insane people! If you wish to send gifts suitable to each person, send food to the poor, and to your patrons either hunger or *Nothing*. Dung, though it is a vile excrement, is nevertheless not useless. For without it, Physicians and Farmers possess *Nothing*. <term>Lawyers</term> <gloss>original: Juris-Consulti</gloss> love to drag out a litigious matter as if it were never to be finished, and when they have lost the case, and the client indeed has lost his property, they nonetheless demand a fee, at least because they had to blush. If the client is wise, he gives them *Nothing* for the sake of testifying to his gratitude. The Statesmen, who returning from Italy and France depart from the customs of our fathers, and hear every flea cough, and are always noisy about new institutions—not because they are good, but because they are new; these men, I say, sometimes seem to imitate <term>Orbilius</term> <gloss>a famously harsh schoolmaster mentioned by Horace</gloss>, who, intending to reform Grammar, did not want his students to say *Sum, Es, Est* <gloss>I am, you are, he is</gloss>, but *Sum, Sus, Sut*. The merchant, if he has lost his property and his credit, sings as a traveler with empty pockets in front of the thief, because he sees that hereafter *Nothing* remains for him. The ancients trusted coins without a written contract and without wax seals. Now, without both, they trust *Nothing*. To <term>Dindymus</term> I was faithful in both types of fortune; he began to be treacherous to me</translation>

<pb n="13"/>The blood-stained TYRANNY also struck my soul, by which they busily strive to expand the Church of Christ, drunk with the (l) blood of the saints. But what they write in the blood of Christians, every generation will read; no posterity will erase it.

And so, by these causes, as if by repeated cock-crows, I was awakened to go out from Babylon: lest the plagues, destined by the just Divine judgment, should also fall upon me.

*I have gone out!* Now I pass over to *You*, who profess the true faith. I have presented a CONFESSION to the Overseers of your Church, the summary of which will be read aloud, so that it may be known to all. This I solemnly testify before GOD, before the FOSTER-ER <note>likely referring to a royal protector or patron</note> of the Church, and before YOU ALL, that I profess with my (*m*) MOUTH and believe with my HEART.

I promise nothing; I am but a man; but this I hope for with certainty from Divine grace: that NOTHING in the world, whether favorable or adverse, shall change my mind.

With this spirit I GIVE MY WORD to you, and I earnestly entreat your prayers. May you receive me AS ONE NEWBORN, (*n*) whose desire is to overcome the world through faith. Thus, therefore, I am YOURS, and by the grace of God, I shall remain YOURS.

---

(l) Revelation 17:6. (*m*) Romans 10:9. (*n*) 1 John 5:4, 5.

<pb n="14"/>Wherefore, to Your highness, MOST SERENE PRINCE, I lift up my eyes. You have received me, and so that my exile would neither be a cause of shame nor of want, you have sustained me with MAGNIFICENT MUNIFICENCE. May GOD repay this CLEMENCY to YOU AND TO YOUR ROYAL FAMILY. I cast myself at your feet; protect me; if I am worth anything, employ me. I shall be yours while I live, in faith, prayers, obedience, and service. May God give You long life, a lasting Reign, peace to Your Lands, Victory over the enemy, and through You, GLORY for RELIGION, Your NAME, and Your FAMILY.

Indeed, to all of you who are present here, *I commend myself to your counsels, prayers, favor, love, and support*. Finally, to Thee, BEST GOD! I give immortal thanks, because Thou hast led me wonderfully to this LIGHT OF THE GOSPEL, and hast inclined toward me the hearts of those who have aided me in this work, both through *benefits* and through *efforts*. Now confirm me *by Thy grace*. Confirm this COVENANT, which I profess in the death of THY SON through this solemn <term>Synaxis</term> <gloss>liturgical assembly or Holy Communion</gloss>, so that it may be for the certainty of my SALVATION. I HAVE SPOKEN.

->Ambrosius<-

> (Truly I) am not confounded to confess my own sins 
> (and error); let those who persecute me be confounded, let me not be confounded.
</translation>

<keywords>conversion, Babylon, patronage, confession of faith, religious exile, gratitude, Prince, Synaxis, Ambrose</keywords>

<pb n="15"/><meta>continues from previous page</meta> is a witness that <note>Trebeta, the stepson of Semiramis</note> had been cast out for the sake of the kingdom. Here, therefore, since he knew his mother was hostile to him, it is written that he set out from Asia into Europe with a fleet, settled in Gaul along the Rhine and Moselle, and built a most flourishing city, which he called Treves <note>original: "Trevirim"</note> after his own name. They say that in the year 1200 a poem was found carved into stone as follows:

> Semiramis of Ninus, who, happy with such a husband,
> Possessed many things, but added more to those before,
> Not content with her own, nor with the whole borders of the world,
> Expelled her stepson Trebeta from his father's kingdom,
> Who, as a famous fugitive, founded our city.
> Treves stood one thousand two hundred years before Rome.

But these are without doubt the delusions of an idle monk, which we wish to recount but not refute, following Philipp Cluver in *Ancient Germany*, Book 2, chapter 14, concerning Treves, page 383.

Section 15. Go forth now, all you who keep the weaker sex away from every kind of key to power and from the commerce of virtues. We do not hear or approve of everything without exception that Bodin in *The Republic*, Book 6, chapter 5; Arnisæus in *Political Doctrine*, Book 1, chapter 9, and *Political Reflections*, Book 2, chapter 2, section 12; Menochius in *Hierapoliticus*, Book 1, chapter 5; Petilius in *The Exarchate*, Book 2, chapters 29 and 30; and Schönborn in *Politics*, Book 2, chapter 12, page 122, have devised for the subversion of <term>Gynaecocratia</term> <gloss>rule by women</gloss>. Virtue is closed off to no one; she admits all, and chooses neither sex nor wealth; with Seneca, we embrace the opinion of Tholosanus in *The Republic*, Book 7, chapter 11; Adam Conzen in *Civil Doctrine*, Book 1, chapter 26; and Danaeus in *Politics*, Book 6, chapter 4, as far as is fitting, and say: Not always in the 

--- narrow breast of women 
> Does a fragile mind fluctuate with the easy tide of vices:

And Schurman has something to reply, saying: Perhaps such thinking torments them out of rivalry, or certainly out of fear, lest that old saying of Ennius should someday come true:

> For you, young men, carry the spirits of women,
> That Virago <note>A woman acting with the spirit of a man</note> has the spirit of a Man.

More rightly, Alexander the Great admired no one more than Semiramis and Cyrus; Curtius, Book 7, chapter 6. Julius Caesar also prudently appeals to the rule of Semiramis in Suetonius, section 23.

<pb n="16"/>Section 16. Lest, however, the truth of that Maronian line should fail:
->Each of us suffers his own ghosts;<-
Semiramis also performed magnificent deeds toward her disgrace, not only for her praise, as Berosus says on page 48 of the Monk Annius of Viterbo. Nor is any other fault more attributed to her than lust, by which she admitted all the most vigorous soldiers to her intimacy, and having been delighted by the use of her body, she removed them from her midst, lest the rumor of her fornication spread among the common people. Claudian derives the first eunuchs from Semiramis; yet, due to the silence of Diodorus, Claude Barth seems to doubt this in his *Observations on Eutropius*, Book 1, page 1325. Ammianus Marcellinus in Book 14, as cited by Henelius in *Wroclaw Leisure*, chapter 35, page 274, takes the side of Claudian when he says: Wherever anyone travels, seeing the columns of mutilated men, let him detest the memory of Semiramis, that ancient Queen, who was the first of all to castrate tender males. Pliny writes from Juba in *Natural History*, Book 8, chapter 42, that she even had an affair with a horse. Indeed, Paulus Orosius in Book 1, chapter 4, witnesses that she finally commanded that sexual intercourse and marriages between parents and children should be lawful. It is handed down by Justin and others that, intending to give an example of the observance of this law, she sought the bed of her son Ninyas, and was killed by him as he turned away from such a nefarious crime. Yet the history of her death is doubtful, and it is not sufficiently clear whether she perished from wounds in war or by the crime of her son. Wagner, *Historical Institutions*, Book 3, page 201.

Section 17. The remains of Semiramis are said to have been stored in a tomb which she built for herself while alive in a high and conspicuous place in Babylon, with an inscription added: IF ANY KING SHOULD LACK MONEY, LET HIM TAKE AS MUCH AS HE WANTS BY OPENING THIS MONUMENT. When Darius Hystaspis had read this, he ordered the sepulcher to be opened, in which he found no gold, but written: UNLESS YOU HAD BEEN AN EVIL MAN, YOU WOULD NEVER HAVE VIOLATED SEPULCHERS. If you except Herodotus, who attributes this tomb to Nitocris, you will hardly find anyone who calls it into doubt. I marvel at the woman’s wit! Semiramis, imposing upon the living after her funeral, would have been worthy of another epitaph, and perhaps such a one as that Felicianus of Verona has in Camerarius’s *Leisure Hours*, Century 1, chapter 97, page 455: FELICIANUS OF VERONA ESTABLISHED THIS SACRED MARK FOR MYSELF, WHO, RESTLESS WHILE ALIVE, NOW AT LAST BEING DEAD, DO NOT WILLINGLY
->REST.<-

<note>A symmetrical ornamental printer's mark consisting of stylized foliate scrolls.</note>
</translation>

It concludes with an anecdote regarding her deceptive tomb and a defense of women's capacity for political virtue against contemporary critics.</summary>

<keywords>Semiramis, Trebeta, Treves, Gynaecocratia, women in power, Darius Hystaspis, Babylon, ancient history, legendary founders</keywords>

<pb n="8"/>### XVI.

The external form consists in the formalities, <note>original: "solemnitatibus"</note> which are either common to both written and oral <term>nuncupative</term> <gloss>declared aloud</gloss> testaments, or specific to one or the other. The summoning of witnesses is common to both, whose quality must be considered, and they ought to be invited by a formal request; finally, their number is defined by law, so that seven are summoned.

<margin>a. Donellus, book 6, chapter 7, at the beginning. b. Clarus, in the said section "testamentis," question 58. f. Said law "hac consultissima"; final law in the Code on Trusts; Matantius in the "Mirror," section "iudicii tela aggredi," page 2, number 22. Clarus, said section, question 55, number 1, and question 56, number 1. See Matthew chapter 18, verse 17; chapter "licet" 23 on testaments and attestations. Covarruvias in said chapter "cum esses," numbers 7 and 14. It is asked whether a smaller number of witnesses can be accepted under municipal law? We believe it is possible, which practice confirms, and it proceeds to such an extent that an heir may even obtain goods located outside the territory by the strength of a testament so composed; by the argument of the section "sed naturalia" 11, Institutes on natural law and the law of nations; law "si non speciali" 9; law 21, Code on Testaments; law 1 at the end, on the inspection of the womb; law "si fundus" 6, on evictions; law "in hac" 30, Code on Donations, joined with the title in the Institutes on the Fufian law; Gail, book 2, observation 123; Mynsinger, century 5, observation 20. Fachineus dissents in the 5th book, controversy 91.</margin>

### XVII. <note>OCR reads XVIII, but follows XVI</note>

We understand the quality of witnesses such that those who are not prohibited from being witnesses are considered suitable. For, as nature dictates, some are barred from testimony, such as one under the age of puberty, the insane, the spendthrift, the deaf, and the mute, to whom the blind is rightly added. Also, for other reasons, the slave, the woman, the infamous <note>one who has lost their legal reputation</note>, the appointed heir, and the domestic servants of the heir or the testator himself are excluded; not, however, the legatee <note>one receiving a specific gift rather than the whole estate</note>. The condition of all these persons must be inspected at the time they are summoned.

<pb n="6"/>the custom of Saxony has approved, as witnessed by <term>Carpzov</term> <gloss>Benedikt Carpzov the Younger, a German jurist</gloss> in Part 2, Constitution 13, Definition 20. However, a donation conferred by a commoner husband upon a noble wife during the marriage is less rightly upheld, since all the prohibitive reasons for donations between spouses apply in that case, as <term>Treutler</term> <gloss>Hieronymus Treutler</gloss> feels in Volume 2, Disputation 13, Thesis 4, letter b, and there also <term>Bachov</term> <gloss>Reinhard Bachov von Echt</gloss>.

## THESIS VII.

The number of paraphernalia is increased by Wedding Gifts <term>die Braut-Taffel Gelder</term> <gloss>bride-table money</gloss>, of which a half-part belongs to the wife. This is a most equitable opinion received from <term>Panormitanus</term> <gloss>Niccolò de' Tudeschi</gloss> in Chapter 2, Extra <note>the Decretals of Gregory IX</note> on donations between husband and wife, and in the Electorate of Saxony in Part 3, Constitution 22, by way of a special pragmatic sanction. This is so true that even if, according to the custom of the region or by reason of the occasion given, a gift is offered to only one of the spouses, it is nevertheless common to both and is to be divided equally between them, by the argument of Law 10 in the Digests on donations. This is all the more so because it is certain that marriage is held to be a species of partnership <note>Latin: "societas"</note> according to Section 1 of the Institutes on paternal power, Law 1, Paragraph 3 of the Digests on Justice and Law, and Law 1 of the Digests on the Rite of Marriages. The nature of such a partnership is this: that things given to partners for the purpose of better conducting business and handling common affairs must, upon the dissolution of the partnership, be divided equally between them and their heirs, by the argument of Law 29 of the Digests on partnerships and <term>Carpzov</term> in Part 3, Constitution 22, Definition 1. The Academy of Helmstedt <note>a university in Lower Saxony</note> fosters this opinion. It does not approve the opinion of <term>Bartolus</term> <gloss>Bartolus de Saxoferrato</gloss>, who in Law 10, Paragraph 6 of the Digests on vulgar and pupillary substitution, attributes to each spouse what their respective blood relations, kinsmen, and friends have given them, nor the opinion of others who assign everything to the wife, as <term>Hahn</term> <gloss>Heinrich Hahn</gloss> testifies in his observations on the summaries of <term>Wesenbeck</term> <gloss>Matthäus Wesenbeck</gloss> under the title on the law of dowries, number 11, at the end.

<pb n="7"/>
## THESIS VIII.

Let us proceed to the FORM, of which mention was made above in the explanation of the definition under the term "specific difference." It consists in the administration of the goods brought by the wife being granted to the husband, whether that grant rests on express or tacit consent. It is referred to as express if the woman records the things existing in the husband's house into a ledger and takes care that it is signed by the husband when presented to him, as if he had received the things, or if the paraphernal things are found recorded in the dotal instrument <note>the marriage contract</note> according to Law 9, the last paragraph of the Digest on the law of dowry, and the last law of the Code on agreed pacts. By this, it is subsequently fully proven that certain things are paraphernalia. That grant is truly tacit, however, if the husband has administered the goods brought in addition to the dowry for many years with the wife's knowledge and patience. Nevertheless, in that case where a woman has married a husband simply without any certain dowry being established, should all the goods which the woman has be considered dotal <gloss>dowry</gloss> or paraphernal <gloss>extra-dotal</gloss>? We see that the Doctors <note>learned legal scholars</note> disagree. In doubt, they ought to be seen as dotal, since it is more useful to the wife for her goods to be reckoned as dotal than as paraphernal. For although women have obtained a tacit mortgage on the husband's property in place of paraphernalia, they are nonetheless destitute of the remaining privileges of a dowry and lack them, especially the benefit of preference <note>the right to be paid first among creditors</note>. Thus, where it concerns the favor of women, in doubtful cases, one must favor them, as Law "in ambiguous matters" of the Digest on the law of dowry suggests. This is supported by the fact that marriage, as the principal thing, can be induced not only by express agreement according to Law 129 of the Digest on the Rules of Law and the Novels 22, Chapter 3, but also by tacit agreement if the circumstances of the things and persons suggest it; therefore, the same will prevail much more in its accessory, such as the dowry, without which indeed marriage can exist, but the dowry can never exist without the same
</translation>

<summary>This page discusses the legal classification of wedding gifts as shared property between spouses under Saxon law and the Academy of Helmstedt's teachings. It also defines the "form" of paraphernalia based on whether the husband's administration of the wife's extra-dotal goods is granted through express written consent or tacit long-term practice.</summary>

->*On the three lights by which GOD, Most Great and Good, offers*<-
->*Himself to be known.*<-

<note>A large, slightly decorative initial letter P at the start of the section.</note>

The Father of lights (James 1:17) manifests himself under three lights: under the light of nature for those who understand the sun, under the light of grace for those holy in the sun, and under the light of glory for the elect in the sun. Great is the light of nature, greater the light of grace, greatest the light of glory. The former shines in the Macrocosm <gloss>the great world or universe</gloss> and the Microcosm <gloss>the little world or man</gloss>; the second shines in the Church, visible and invisible; the last glows in the seat and assembly of the blessed and the Angels. These three lights are subordinate to one another. For the light of nature was kindled for this purpose: that we might be led to the light of grace and the light of glory.

<pb n="17"/>## SECTION II.
->proposing<-
## THEOREMS.

1. **IN GOD** there is given an antecedent and a consequent Will. However, whether the former is rightly called the Will of Mercy and the latter the Will of justice does not seem to be without doubt, since the consequent Will is also of Mercy and grace.
2. The object of infinite power is said to be everything possible. And this is hinted at by the created Angel in Luke 1, verse 37, and the uncreated one <note>the Lord</note> in Genesis 18:14. It is customary to note in this place a Hebraism, by which a word is put for the thing itself. But what if someone should raise a doubt whether a place can be given in which it is taken in such a way?
3. Creation is rightly attributed to the only and entire Most Holy TRINITY: but whether the SON OF GOD is signified by *the act of* speaking <term>tò legein</term> in the History of Creation is entirely doubted, nor are there lacking reasons for doubting, which we shall reserve for public debate.
4. Not without justice is Jerome condemned of error because he denied God’s Providence regarding irrational animals, since sacred scripture clearly testifies that individual animals and types of animals are subject to divine Providence. Compare Matthew 10:29. Some philosophers and theologians strive to vindicate Jerome from this injury, but with useless effort. Let Jerome himself be seen in his Commentary on Habakkuk, chapter 1, page 187.

***

<note>A large, slightly decorative initial letter P at the start of the section.</note>

The Father of lights (James 1:17) manifests himself under three lights: under the light of nature for those who understand the sun, under the light of grace for those holy in the sun, and under the light of glory for the elect in the sun. Great is the light of nature, greater the light of grace, greatest the light of glory. The former shines in the Macrocosm <gloss>the great world or universe</gloss> and the Microcosm <gloss>the little world or man</gloss>; the second shines in the Church, visible and invisible; the last glows in the seat and assembly of the blessed and the Angels. These three lights are subordinate to one another. For the light of nature was kindled for this purpose: that we might be led to the light of grace and the light of glory.
