## SECTION II.
->proposing<-
## THEOREMS.

1. **IN GOD** there is given an antecedent and a consequent Will. However, whether the former is rightly called the Will of Mercy and the latter the Will of justice does not seem to be without doubt, since the consequent Will is also of Mercy and grace.
2. The object of infinite power is said to be everything possible. And this is hinted at by the created Angel in Luke 1, verse 37, and the uncreated one <note>the Lord</note> in Genesis 18:14. It is customary to note in this place a Hebraism, by which a word is put for the thing itself. But what if someone should raise a doubt whether a place can be given in which it is taken in such a way?
3. Creation is rightly attributed to the only and entire Most Holy TRINITY: but whether the SON OF GOD is signified by *the act of* speaking <term>tò legein</term> in the History of Creation is entirely doubted, nor are there lacking reasons for doubting, which we shall reserve for public debate.
4. Not without justice is Jerome condemned of error because he denied God’s Providence regarding irrational animals, since sacred scripture clearly testifies that individual animals and types of animals are subject to divine Providence. Compare Matthew 10:29. Some philosophers and theologians strive to vindicate Jerome from this injury, but with useless effort. Let Jerome himself be seen in his Commentary on Habakkuk, chapter 1, page 187.

***

## TOPIC IV.
## CONCERNING CHRIST AND HIS TWOFOLD STATE
## SECTION I.
->presenting<-
## CONTEMPLATIONS
## on John 1:14.

1. **THE WORD**, which gave the counsel, brought the aid; THE FLESH, where there was the complaint, there was the remedy; WAS MADE, by remaining what He was, and assuming what He was not.
2. THE WORD above us, THE FLESH like us, WAS MADE for our sake.
3. THE WORD which was, THE FLESH which was not, WAS MADE into one, which is and remains both.
4. THE WORD: behold the Divinity! THE FLESH; behold the humanity! WAS MADE, behold the Unity of the Person!

# BY JACOB LOCHER PHILOMUSUS
## A poem of ten lines.

Anne, the Mother of God rejoices to call you mother,
and the world always exults in your Name.
Anne, Clavus has sung your praises, and he now prays
that you, divine patroness, bring help to the wretched.
The German <note>original: "Teutona"</note> people hope in you, they consecrate altars to you,
and as suppliants offer incense and sacred prayers.
Thus, Anne, assist with your help the poor
and infirm flock, which inhabits your temples.
And extinguish various diseases with sacred remedies,
which your daughter and your grandson, God, bestow upon you.

## BY JOHANNES BOEMUS AUBANUS.

Whoever wishes to know how merciful and how kind
the blessed Anne stands toward her servants,
let him read the sweet song which the venerable Phileremus
gave from the highest diligence of his soul.

## TO JOHANNES CLAVUS PHILEREMUS, HIS MOST LOVING CONFRERE, ALEXANDER BRASSICANUS OF TÜBINGEN.

If blessed Anne were to breathe the air in our regions,
she would wish to be more renowned by no other <term>chelys</term> <gloss>lyre/song</gloss>.
Thus you are able to move the Gods, and even the dark <term>Manes</term> <gloss>spirits of the dead</gloss>.
</translation>

<summary>This section concludes Johannes Clavus's Sapphic odes to Saint Anne with prayers for Europe and scholars, followed by commendatory verses from fellow humanists Jacob Locher, Johannes Boemus, and Alexander Brassicanus. The text emphasizes Anne's role as a protectress of the German people and a patroness of the arts and Latin learning.</summary>

<pb n="10"/>## Chorus.

The true prophets are led to death by the order of Jezebel.

## Scene Four.

Obadiah <note>Latin: Abdias</note> advises Elijah <note>Latin: Elias</note> to avoid by flight the persecution raging against the true prophets of God. Elijah, inflamed by the zeal and spirit of God, not only does not take flight; but he encounters King Ahab <note>Latin: Achabus</note> as he is going to worship Baal, threatens him with heavenly punishments, and suddenly flees. The King, driven into a fury, pronounces a sentence of death against him.

## Scene Five.

Elijah, uncertain where to flee, is warned by God through an Angel to set out toward the East, and to hide in the region of the Jordan near the brook Cherith <note>Latin: Carith</note>. Divine Providence becomes his companion.

## Chorus.

Divine Vengeance puts the water signs <note>astrological or elemental symbols</note> to flight and brings fiery signs over the Kingdom of Ahab; from these a famine arises, which the Household Gods <note>Latin: Dii Penates</note> attack, but in attempting to tame it, they are overcome by it.

<note>A horizontal ornamental divider composed of a repeating row of small floral printer's ornaments.</note>

# ACT TWO.

## Scene One.

As the famine grows stronger in the Kingdom of Ahab, many die, some cursing Ahab as the cause of such great calamity, others cursing Elijah. Some attack the true prophets, some the false, and unless they obtain rain, they threaten them with death.

## Scene Two.

A Raven, summoned by Divine Providence, brings nourishment to Elijah.

<pb n="11"/>### Scene Three.

Ahab, troubled by the great confusion of his people, orders a search for Elijah through all regions so that he may kill him, as Saint Augustine believes.

### Scene Four.

When the brook Cherith has dried up, Elijah is commanded to go to Zarephath <note>Latin: Sareptha</note> of the Sidonians; there he is to be fed by a widow woman, whom he finds gathering wood with her son. Elijah asks for nourishment, with the promise that the flour shall not fail, from which the woman makes for him a bread baked in the ashes <note>Latin: panem subcinericium</note>.

### Scene Five.

The widow of Zarephath cheerfully offers the ash-baked bread to Elijah. She tells of the flour not being diminished at all, she blesses the God of Elijah, and asks the Prophet to deign to stay at her home as a guest.

### Scene Six.

The son of the widow falls ill and then dies; Elijah restores him to life and returns him to his mother.

### Chorus.

Twelve small Sidonian children give a round of applause for the son of the widow of Zarephath who has been restored to life.

<note>A horizontal decorative divider composed of a sequence of seventeen floral circular ornaments, divided in the center by three horizontal bars.</note>

# ACT THREE.

### Scene One.

Ahab, lacking a plan, asks his followers what must be done in this extreme scarcity of resources. At last, he himself and Obadiah set out separately into various regions for the sake of searching for food; Ahab indeed travels in a disguised garment.
</translation>
